docs.title: NGED ML research
docs.text:
This site holds the machine-learning experiments and studies for the NGED substation forecast. The production service, its architecture, and its roadmap are documented in the nged-substation-forecast docs.

The two kinds of research page live in two sections. The Studies section holds open-ended studies, each with a page of its own. The ML experiments section holds the small, focused experiments that test one change to the research default, together with the research defaults themselves.

docs.title: ML experiments
docs.text: Each folder here is one small experiment that tests one hypothesis about improving the production forecast, and the experiments are grouped into themes. A theme has three pages: a Summary (where one has been written) that states the answer so far, an Experiments page that lists every experiment tried, and a Research plan that lists what is planned next. The folders are named <id>-<slug>, where the id is a five-digit integer that orders the experiments by the order in which they were started. A folder holds result.md and its figures.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
• Calibration and uncertainty: Whether the forecast's quantiles and ensemble members are well calibrated, and how to widen or sharpen them.
  • Curtailment cost: Scoring a forecast by the curtailment cost of its errors, and by how well its tails are calibrated.
  • Demand inputs: Which extra inputs lower the error of the substation demand forecast.
  • Differentiable physics: long history and drift: Whether a differentiable-physics model of Primary substation demand can use old years of history and cope with drift in the demand level.
  • Generator forecasting: Forecasting the output of solar and wind farms.
  • Hierarchy and pooling: Forecasts that share information across substations or across levels of the electricity network hierarchy.
  • Lagged power and error correction: Where recent measured power should enter the forecast, and how to correct the forecast's recent errors.
  • Production reference and best guess: How the production forecast compares with the best-guess recipes and with a perfect weather input.
  • Retraining and training history: How often to refit the XGBoost models, and how much training history to give them.
  • Solar disaggregation: Separating embedded solar from substation demand.
  • Switching detectors: Detecting load transfers between substations, called switching events, from power data alone.
  • Switching labels in the forecast: Using switching labels to forecast the demand under the normal running arrangement.
  • Weather products and blending: Which weather data improves the forecast, and whether blending several weather products helps.

docs.title: How an experiment is recorded
docs.text:
The front matter of result.md is the only place that records an experiment's theme, verdict, and status, and the theme pages build their tables from it. The Experiments table of each theme, the planned-experiments table of each Research plan, and the candidates table below are generated from the front matter when the documentation is built, so adding a finished experiment means writing its result.md and editing nothing else. The ml-experiment skill (.claude/skills/ml-experiment/SKILL.md) lists the front matter fields and their allowed values, including the optional kind and promoted_to fields of the research default rule.

uv run python scripts/mkdocs_hooks/experiment_tables.py --check validates every front matter block, and the documentation build runs the same check. uv run python scripts/mkdocs_hooks/experiment_tables.py --theme <theme> prints a theme's Experiments table as markdown.

docs.title: The research default
docs.text: The research default rule fixes one forecast per target family and one test for adding a change to it. The log of versions lists each family's versions, for example "Primary demand research default 1". An experiment with kind: change in its front matter is measured against the current version, and the rule says when a win is adopted.

docs.title: Data processing
docs.text: The data-processing page lists the processing that the experiments showed the data needs. Each entry says whether it applies to experiments, to production, or to both.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The background pages state what earlier experiments established about the data sets and the scoring rules, and a planner reads them before planning an experiment.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: The glossary defines the terms that the experiment pages and the theme Summary pages use without redefining. Each definition links the experiment or code that fixes its meaning.

docs.title: Planned experiments and their order
docs.text:
Each theme's Research plan page holds its own priority table and the detailed proposals for that theme. A planned experiment has a result.md with status planned, committed before any code runs. An idea that has no folder yet is marked "proposed" in the priority table and carries a tentative id, P1, P2, and so on, which the proposal sections use as headings. A proposal receives its numeric id when its plan is committed, and the tentative id then disappears. The design under test is the staged probabilistic forecast, in which stage 1 turns weather into power, stage 2 calibrates the result, uses lagged power, and blends weather products, and a coupling step restores coherent ensemble members.

The sample resolves gains of roughly 0.3 points of capacity or more, and no smaller gains. A point of capacity is 1% of a series' capacity. The sample is 16 Primary substations, 9 generator series, and one validation year with 12 months. The Research plan pages flag the experiments whose planned contrasts the sample cannot resolve.

docs.title: Candidates for the next release
docs.text:
These experiments are flagged candidate and are not yet adopted. The flags are proposals for the maintainer to confirm. The maintainer decides which candidates to port into a new model release. The release log records which experiments each release adopted.

Experiment Theme Verdict Take-home message 00425 best-mdn-architecture-assembly-with-ablations production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Pretraining the pooled mixture density network on ERA5-and-CAMS rows before fine-tuning it on ensemble rows lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.050 points of capacity (-0.078 to -0.021) at the six signed-MW Primaries and by 0.124 (-0.219 to -0.048) at the eight MVA-only Primaries. The gain is clear at the MVA-only eight and probable at the signed-MW six, where the interval just misses the registered bar of -0.03. The assembled network beat the monthly XGBoost recipe and BG2 at both of those groups and trailed BG2 at D15 and D18, so pretraining is a candidate for a numbered release of the production forecast and the Primary embedding is the component to protect. 00424 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-ens-serving-test production-reference-and-best-guess supported With ensemble weather forecasts instead of recorded weather, the neural network with the export gate still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with the gate shut (a gain of 15.7 points of capacity, 95% interval 13.8 to 17.4, against 19.2 with recorded weather), and it harms the forecast by no more than 0.05 points where no solar farm exports. The gate opened at the same two of the eight apparent-power-only substations as before. An unplanned finding is that the network trained on recorded weather and applied unchanged to ensemble weather scored 5.5 points better (95% interval 4.4 to 6.6) than the network retrained on ensemble weather, so how to train on ensemble weather is the open question. 00422 mdn-train-with-varied-origin-hour-and-age-inputs-stale-input-step-2 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Training the pooled neural network with the forecast made at eight different hours of the day removes almost all of its extra error when the newest power reading is 12 hours late (0.18 down to 0.04 points at the six signed substations). The two extra age inputs did not help, so the simplest recipe is enough. Training this way raised the error on fresh inputs by 0.04 to 0.11 points at the eight MVA-only substations, which is within the range that seed-to-seed noise could produce for the lower values, and training with some readings missing cut the missing-readings error from 2.4 to 0.3 points. These are five test months, so every number is interim. 00420 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-final production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A neural network with a gate that decides once per Primary substation whether it exports power forecasts signed power much better than the same network with the gate shut on the half-hours with reverse flow (7.1 against 26.3 points of capacity) and does no harm beyond the registered tolerance (+0.03 points at D5) where no solar farm exports. Most of that gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero at all, because the ungated network scores the same on reverse-flow half-hours, and the gate's job is to stop invented reverse flow where there is none. Adding a PV-proportional variance did not help, so the next step is a serving test with real ensemble forecasts, not a further change to the network. 00418 mdn-pretrain-on-era5-and-cams-then-fine-tune-on-ens retraining-and-training-history supported Teaching the neural network first on six years of past weather and power, then on the forecast archive, lowers its error by about 0.06 points of capacity (2.1%) at the six signed-direction substations and 0.16 points (4.2%) at the eight apparent-power-only substations over 12 test months. Changing how much of the network is retrained, or adding forecast-like noise, changes the score by less than the interval of the estimate. With only 6 months of forecast archive on 4 test months the gain is about 1.3 points, although the ENS-only baseline degrades badly there. 00399 xgboost-short-history-start-cut-d15-d18 retraining-and-training-history partly supported Dropping the noisy first weeks of D15 and D18 from the training rows helps the monthly XGBoost forecast only a little: about 1% lower error at both, mostly in the first scored months, when the history was shortest. Cutting 6 months is not safe, because it made D18 worse. The larger problem at D15 is a level error that no start cut fixes: the median forecast is about 21 points of capacity too low, against 3 for the generalised additive model (GAM) stack, so the next experiment should look at D15's level, not its start. 00396 xgboost-recipe-screen-demand-calendar-winter-hyperparameters-ensemble-summary production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Giving the weekly XGBoost demand model the ensemble's view of the weather, either its mean and spread or a model trained on the ensemble mean, lowered the error by 0.4% to 2.7% in both test months, and no other change we tried did so as clearly. Holiday columns help on Easter bank holidays but raised the error on all days in January and at the signed-MW six at Easter, and winter weather columns do not help, so a full-year test should start with the ensemble-input arms. 00381 simple-weekly-xgboost-demand-against-gam-stack production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A single XGBoost model per Primary, refitted weekly, is as good as the GAM stack at 9 of 14 Primaries and better on average at the eight whose meters hide reverse flow (D8 by 1.6 points; clearly so at D8, D12, and D22), so the stack's extra parts do not pay at those eight. At the six Primaries with signed readings the XGBoost model is level on average (+0.08, not distinguishable from zero) but worse at D11 and D14 and has a narrower upper tail, so the stack still protects against curtailment better there: its avoidable curtailment cost at a limit of 0.9 times the maximum observed export is lower at 4 of 6. The input changes that helped in practice were a daily solar summary (-0.05) and a 1-year half-life (-0.02); an Economy 7 input did nothing, and no input tried fixed the 4.9-point under-forecast of sunny demand at D12. 00357 wind-default-2-monthly-head-longer-retest generator-forecasting partly supported Retraining Wind farms research default 2's head every month improves the forecast slightly, by about 0.04 to 0.05 points over the scored year and about 0.10 points in the latest 2.5 months, and no scope shows harm to the score. The scored-year interval still touches zero, so the change is a candidate and is not adopted. The upper tail stays too heavy (1.7% to 2.0% of observations above the 0.99 quantile), so retraining does not fix it. 00348 wind-plant-mdn-upper-tail generator-forecasting partly supported The frozen physics plant with a mixture head stays about 0.23 points of capacity better than the research default over days 1 to 10, but none of the four tail fixes inside the head brings the top quantile into calibration without losing score at that quantile, and none of their intervals excludes zero. Blending the plant's residual band with the default's XGBoost quantiles gains less (0.15 points) but is the arm of the five whose gain is clear and whose 0.99 quantile is no worse, so that recipe, not a better head, is the next step. 00347 wind-physics-hybrid-plant-then-mdn generator-forecasting partly supported A physics model of each wind farm, run on every ensemble member and corrected by a small neural network, forecasts 0.27 points of capacity (2.4%) better than the research default over leads of 0.5 hours to 15 days, and 0.23 points over true days 1 to 10, but the neural network given only the plant's median and the farm already gets 83% of the gain, and the upper tail is still over-confident. The next step is to fix the upper tail (the neural network caps its quantiles at capacity, and 0.9% of observations exceed it) before any plant-based arm is adopted. 00346 wind-research-default-1-offset-table-refit-cadence generator-forecasting partly supported Refitting the wind forecast's offset table every month on recent runs makes the forecast a little better (a 0.4% to 1.1% lower quantile score), using only data the service already stores. It does not fix the upper quantiles, which still miss in 1.7% of half-hours against 1% intended. So the change between the training years and the scored year is a minor cause, and the upper-tail miss needs another explanation. A monthly job that refits the table on all earlier daily runs passes the adoption conditions and is a candidate. 00345 pooled-solar-wind-mixture-density-network metered-solar-farms partly supported One neural network trained on all six solar farms forecasts each farm as well as a separate network on the physical plant model (within 0.8%), so a production forecast could use one neural network per fuel. Adding wind farms to the same network does not help either fuel and makes solar 0.7% to 2.3% worse, so solar and wind are better trained separately. In this experiment, a wind farm with no history scored 18% worse at day 1 when trained on public wind farms alone than when trained on other metered wind farms. 00339 wind-research-default-1-adapter-plus-mixture-head generator-forecasting partly supported A small neural-network head that re-draws the physics-plus-adapter wind forecast's quantiles gains 0.27 points of capacity (2.4%) on the farms' normal half-hours and keeps that gain on the replicate months, but the same head given no weather summaries does as well, so the gain is a recalibration that a simpler correction partly reproduces. A simple rule that predicts the idle floor at low wind recovers none of the head's loss on the idle-band readings, and training the head on those readings removes the gain. 00337 primary-demand-standard-architecture-168-to-240-hours production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported The standard architecture (a neural network that corrects the forecast of the convex stack, with a learned input adapter and a mixture-density output) forecast Primary demand at 7 to 10 days ahead with a lower error than the current research default over the 12 months scored. Most of the gain comes from the mixture-density output and from two Primaries (D10 and D16). The 12 months of data cannot establish the gain, so the standard architecture is a candidate for demand across NGED's 1-to-10-day range, not yet a replacement. 00336 wind-research-default-1-below-cut-in-zeroing generator-forecasting partly supported Setting the wind forecast, or the training target, to zero below the turbines' cut-in speed does not improve the forecast, because the farms still produce small real output there. Leaving the low-wind rows out of training gains 0.12 points of capacity (about 1% of the default's score) on the kept rows, but mostly by lifting the quantiles upward, which a constant upward shift may reproduce (not yet tested). 00327 lsc-label-free-detect-mask-train-pipeline lsc-detectors partly supported A forecast of the normal running arrangement recovers faster after a load shift when the readings that a label-free detector flags are treated as missing: during and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04 points of capacity. On ordinary days the masked forecast is no worse, and slightly better. Without one site (D11) the gain shrinks to 0.30 points, and retraining the demand model on masked power adds nothing beyond masking the filter. 00326 wind-research-default-1-change-arms generator-forecasting supported Feeding XGBoost the neural adapter's corrected wind speed lowers the wind forecast's score by 0.10 points of capacity, about 0.9% of the default's score, at 1 to 10 day leads (99.75% interval -0.19 to -0.01). The change is negative at every farm and at short and long leads. The three other changes were not separable from zero. Only a port that puts the adapter in the production service can use the gain, so the maintainer decides. 00322 primary-demand-default-2-daylight-only-heuristic-blend-and-sunshine-graft-replication production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported At 7 to 10 days the blend with the manual heuristic gains about 4% at all hours, and about 2.4% when it is used only by day, which is the version with no harm on the coldest winter nights. Counting how many of the 51 ensemble members are cold finds 72% of those nights (the ensemble mean finds 41%), and a hard switch on that count keeps the whole 4% with almost no cold-night harm, but that switch was not pre-registered. The sunshine response of the depth-1 XGBoost refit explains about half of the refit's advantage on the worst April-to-June half-hours in both years, so a flexible sunshine term in the convex fit is worth testing. 00321 metered-farm-lower-tail-recalibration-and-tail-head metered-solar-farms partly supported The solar-farm forecast's lowest quantile was already close to correct: only 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below the 0.01 quantile, because the earlier 3.3% counted the 3.0% of half-hours that read exactly zero. A recalibration table, a zero-inflated head, and a tail head each lower the own-history score by 0.04 points or less (the unshrunk table raises it by 0.03 to 0.05 points), so none is adopted. A shrunk recalibration table does lower the score by about 0.05 points for a farm with no history, and two heads lower the 0.99 pinball loss by 3.7% to 8.5% while covering the 0.99 quantile only 98.3% to 98.9% of the time. 00320 primary-demand-default-2-night-aware-heuristic-blend-and-night-band-width production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported A blend with the manual heuristic still improves the 7 to 10 day Primary demand forecast by about 4%, and the harm it does on the coldest winter nights cannot be removed by switching it off when the weather forecast says the night will be cold, because at 7 to 10 days that forecast spots only between one and two cold nights in three. Narrowing the night prediction bands helps one Primary (D10, by 0.25 points on night half-hours), leaves the other five unchanged or slightly worse, and makes the cold-night tails worse. 00319 primary-demand-default-1-solar-summary-and-heuristic-blend-at-7-to-10-days production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported The demand forecast for 7 to 10 days ahead improves by about 2% when its solar term also uses the spread between the 51 weather-forecast members, and the gain is largest on sunny days (6.6%), where the forecast had been worse than the manual heuristic that National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) staff use. Blending in the manual heuristic improves the forecast by 4.5%, but the blend worsens the coldest winter nights beyond the agreed tolerance, so only the solar change is adopted. 00318 metered-farm-mdn-head-more-features metered-solar-farms partly supported Giving the solar-farm head more inputs does not improve its overall score at any lead from 1 to 10 days, so the head's inputs are not what limits the forecast. The extra clock and cloud-spread inputs do lower the loss at the 0.99 quantile (the tail that matters for curtailment) by about 5% at days 3 to 7, and none of the changes fixes the lower tail, where 3.3% to 3.7% of actual values fall below the 0.01 quantile, where 1% is expected. Training one head for all leads makes the network with no plant nearly as good as the plant-based head at days 8 to 10 (0.4% worse), so the plant adds little there. 00314 primary-demand-gated-or-pinball-band-head calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported Experiment 311's neural band head was stopped by harm on sunny daylight half-hours. Keeping the current bands on those half-hours fixes that harm, and the gated head scores 0.041 points better than the current Primary demand forecast bands (research default 1, lower is better). The gain is still almost entirely one substation, D10: without it the gain is 0.015 points and its interval touches zero, so the gated head is a candidate and not an adoption. Training the head on the quantile score directly gave no improvement. 00313 metered-farm-pure-xgboost-and-mdn-vs-plant metered-solar-farms partly supported A forecast that sees only weather and the calendar, with no physical plant model anywhere, scores almost as well as the plant-based forecast for the six solar farms, up to 10 days ahead, even when the farm has no history. The plant's added value is small, between 0% and 3.4%, and its intervals include zero except for XGBoost. For wind, the same kind of network also matches the best plant-based forecast, so a plant model is not needed to be competitive on these farms. 00311 primary-demand-mixture-density-band-head calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported A neural network that sets the forecast bands from the weather state scores 0.037 points better than the current Primary demand bands over the scored year, and 0.034 better in the year before, but the gain comes almost entirely from one substation (D10) and the new bands are worse on sunny daylight half-hours. The band head is a candidate, not an adoption; the next test should keep the current bands on sunny daylight half-hours or train the head on the quantile score directly. 00310 metered-farm-long-lead-scoring metered-solar-farms partly supported The assembled solar-farm forecast still beats the seasonal-average forecast (climatology) at every lead up to 10 days, by 39% at day 1 and 10% at days 8 to 10, so NGED can use it across its whole horizon of 1 to 10 days ahead. A plant-fed XGBoost model loses its skill by day 8, so a simple first production forecast should be the mixture-density neural network on the plant, which is the best single family at every lead, and the blend of the GAM, MDN, and XGBoost adds more than 1% only at days 1 and 2. 00300 metered-farm-best-guess-assembly metered-solar-farms partly supported The assembled solar-farm forecast (a physical power model, two correction stages, and a blend with XGBoost) scores 3.3% better than plant-fed XGBoost (XGBoost on the plant forecast, its ensemble spread, the unit mean, and the availability ratio, with no weather features of its own) on the quantile score, which averages the pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, when each farm trains on its own history. It is 43% better at the 0.99 quantile, which bounds how much output NGED may need to curtail. With no history for a farm, the gain over XGBoost is smaller (2.0%) and below the 3% we predicted, so the physical model helps less than we expected when a farm's history is missing. 00287 metered-farm-spread-binned-plant-heads metered-solar-farms supported On top of the spread-binned solar-farm power model, an additive model gives a better forecast band than a neural network that adjusts each quantile, so the explainable model is the candidate. A neural network that outputs a three-component Gaussian mixture scores 1.3% better than the additive model in own history, mostly in the upper tail, but not clearly in zero history, so it needs one more test before it is preferred. A blend of the additive model, a neural network, and XGBoost scores 0.8% better than XGBoost alone and fixes XGBoost's weak 0.99 quantile. 00285 wind-effective-wind-adapters generator-forecasting partly supported The physics model of a wind farm matched XGBoost once a small neural network adjusted the wind speed it takes as input, so XGBoost's lead can be reproduced by a smooth correction of wind speed. On the ensemble weather, mapping each member's wind speed to ERA5's helped by 0.31 points but fixed only a small part of the ensemble's low bias, and a lookup table of power offsets by lead day helped more. 00270 metered-farm-xgboost-vs-plant-diagnostic metered-solar-farms partly supported XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model by about 3% in the quantile score even when it sees only the power model's own weather inputs, and the gain is in the width of the forecast band (the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles), not in the median forecast. The same gain comes from giving the power model a forecast band that depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index, and that band also beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile. Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead generator-forecasting partly supported Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. 00260 metered-farm-quantile-combination metered-solar-farms partly supported Blending the three stored forecasters with a separate weight at each quantile level scores 2.1% better than H5 alone, and every one of the six farms improves, because the neural network without the plant is best at the top quantile and H5 is best at the bottom one. About a quarter of the gain comes from averaging the five seeds, not from the weights. The rolling adjustment of the outer quantiles corrects the coverage of both tails but raises the error by 1.2%. 00259 wind-plant-plus-quantile-offset-head generator-forecasting partly supported A correction learned from 15 months of daily ensemble forecasts lowered the wind forecast's quantile score by 4.5% to 5.5% on the three metered wind farms, but the neural network and the ensemble's wind summaries were not what earned it. The 51 ensemble members' median sits too low: the observed power was below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%. A lookup table with one offset per lead day, quantile, and farm recovers 92% of the gain. The open question is where that low bias comes from. 00257 metered-farm-fair-plant-arm metered-solar-farms supported The neural network was not needed. Giving the solar-farm power model the lagged power and the spread of the ensemble members, through a plain linear fit, recovers about 90% of the neural network's gain and scores within half a percent of it. The linear fit is no worse at the 0.99 quantile (the 99% interval of the gap includes zero) and is simpler to serve, so it is the metered-farm candidate. 00256 wind-temperature-density-shear-columns generator-forecasting partly supported Giving the XGBoost wind forecast the air temperature helps a little, about 0.7% of the score, and the evidence just misses the bar we set beforehand. Columns that carry the time of day and the season help more, and their gain sits in daytime and summer rows. That pattern is not explained by the air density we could test (a function of temperature alone) or by shear, and it is consistent with a correction for biases in the ensemble wind at certain hours and seasons. A repeat on other months would show whether the time-of-day and season columns still help. 00251 dp-final-best-guess-assembly-clip-and-coast-against-bg2 production-reference-and-best-guess supported Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess demand forecast (arm D, a small neural network that corrects its median, and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5%; lower is better) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points, and it beats the manual heuristic on every headline metric we scored, including curtailment cost. The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. 00243 metered-farm-architecture-comparison metered-solar-farms partly supported A small neural network sitting on top of a solar-farm power model forecasts a metered solar farm about as well as XGBoost and improves on the power model alone by 4.4% in the quantile score, when the network outputs the whole forecast band. Networks that adjust a single number (the scale, a correction, or the sunlight fed to the power model) gain under 1%. The hybrid is far better than XGBoost at the upper tail (0.99 quantile, 29% lower pinball loss), which matters for curtailment. The neural network without physics does better still at that tail (32% lower pinball loss than XGBoost). 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. 00237 dp-two-number-solar-summary-with-clip differentiable-physics-embedded-generation supported At D5, in one year of data, summarising the ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation keeps at least about 90% of its gain when the solar output is clipped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (110%, interval 91% to 141%). On the sunniest third of daylight rows the point estimate of the remaining gain is about half (interval -12% to 88%). A post hoc arm using the standard deviation alone kept the gain there, which suggests testing that form. 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. 00228 dp-bg-rolling-origin-stack-against-bg2 production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the solar summary) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5% of BG2's 2.715; lower is better), and most of the gain comes from November to March. From April to June 2026 the stack is worse than BG2, and arm D without the neural network head is worse than BG2 in summer. The year-long gain is only just separable from zero, and we cannot test other years until BG2 is re-run for them. 00227 lsc-fewer-false-alarms-and-softer-use-part-2 lsc-detectors partly supported Keeping only the learned score's most confident alarms gives a mask that finds 21 of 35 real load shifts with 5 alarms per match, recovers most of the forecast gain after a load shift, and does no measurable harm on ordinary days. A gentler use of the alarm is not needed at that setting. The result rests on 11 load shifts after which the gain is measured, so the next step is to confirm it on more load shifts before porting it. 00220 dp-bg-stage4-assembly-with-drop-one differentiable-physics-forecast-engine partly supported Adding two parts to the best-guess demand forecast lowers its quantile score by 0.136 points (5%) of substation effective capacity. The parts are a small neural network that corrects the forecast's median, and a two-number summary of the 51 ensemble members' solar response. Each part's gain is almost exactly what it achieves alone, so the two parts remove different errors. The network's own 11 quantiles reached 0.904 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights without the hand-fitted band fixes, and scored 0.048 points better than the corrected forecast overall, mostly at one substation. The coast-and-widen rule for missing readings was not scored with the stack. 00214 dp-pv-clip-ceiling-as-of-and-screen differentiable-physics-embedded-generation partly supported Capping the solar output that the demand forecast subtracts from one Primary substation (D5) at 60% of its solar capacity lowers the forecast error on sunny days by about 0.13 MW. Almost all of that gain (97%) remains when the cap is chosen using only data from before each monthly retraining. The five other Primaries tested show no clear gain, so the cap should be treated as specific to D5 for now. 00211 dp-boosted-tree-calibrator-and-input-ablations differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A gradient-boosted tree model given the same inputs as the neural network, and no recent errors, lowers the error score of our best day-ahead forecast by about as much as the network does (0.098 against 0.100 points). The interval is wide, so a loss of up to 0.03 points against the network is not ruled out. The gain comes mostly from two inputs, the forecast level and the weather-data era. 00205 dp-gamk-gap-robustness-coast-or-frozen-gam differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive When readings stop for 3, 6, 24, or 72 hours, keep running the Kalman filter, which corrects the convex demand model using its recent forecast errors, without feeding it new readings, and widen the quantile bands. At each of those four gap lengths that forecast scored 0.25 to 0.44 points of quantile score better than the convex demand model with no correction (a quantile score is an error measure in percent of the substation's effective capacity, and lower is better; the gain is 8% to 14% of the uncorrected model's score). At 72 hours the 99.4% bootstrap interval for the gain runs from 0.04 to 0.48 points, so the gain may be small. The data cannot show whether dropping only the filter beats coasting after a gap of about 72 hours: at every gap length the difference between the two forecasts is smaller than the variation between months. The forecast with the filter, winter night offset, and recipe R was still 0.025 points worse than its no-gap score 48 hours after a 24-hour gap ended. The filter alone was within 0.02 points of its no-gap score 24 hours after the gap ended. 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. 00195 switching-neural-plus-detector-features lsc-detectors partly supported A learned score on the features that RO-NC and the pair alarm already compute finds 22 to 24 of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, against 18 or 19 for RO-NC, at the same number of unexplained alarms. A plain logistic regression finds 22 even without any look-ahead feature, so most of the gain is in the features, and the extra transfers are small ones (under 1 MW each). The next step is to test whether the extra alarms help the gated mask, which this experiment did not run. 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack differentiable-physics-forecast-engine supported Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. 00180 dp-sunny-daylight-fix-d5-solar-shape differentiable-physics-embedded-generation supported D5's net power flattens like an export limit: capping the solar output the forecast subtracts from demand at 60% of the capacity held for D5 cuts the best GAM's sunny-daylight loss to BG2 from 0.20 MW to 0.07 MW, and moves the two placebo substations, D10 and D16, by under 0.01 MW on sunny half-hours. A different panel tilt or azimuth does nothing measurable. D5 is the only one of the six substations whose site table marks an export clip, so the next question is whether the 60% ceiling is stable from year to year. 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift differentiable-physics-long-history-and-drift supported Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner calibration-and-uncertainty supported The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves differentiable-physics-pooling-across-substations partly supported In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction differentiable-physics-forecast-engine inconclusive Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. 00148 switching-end-rule-lookahead-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported On injected transfers, a live service needs only 6 hours of data after the candidate end to fix the end of a switching interval, with no loss of recall against the offline rule. The call then comes a median 30 hours after the true end, and 24 of those hours are the step statistic's own window, so a longer lookahead of 24 or 48 hours only delays the call to 48 or 72 hours without finding more. The 35 real transfers give the same 18 found at every lookahead from 1 hour up. A lookahead of 0 hours is wrong in six transfers in ten, because the end is called about 8 hours early. 00147 causal-live-end-rule-for-ro-nc lsc-detectors supported The end of a switching interval can be called from data available at the time, with no loss of recall against the offline rule, by waiting until the step statistic falls to 0.8 of its running peak. The call comes a median 29 hours after the true end. Ending the interval at the first sign of a return step is wrong in about six transfers in ten, because it fires about 8 hours early. Merging overlapping alarms on one Primary substation cuts the share of transfers reported as 2 or more intervals from 0.57 to 0.03. 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k differentiable-physics-forecast-engine small gain Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step differentiable-physics-demand-calendar-and-weather inconclusive Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 differentiable-physics-forecast-engine partly supported Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand demand-inputs small gain The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). 00087 bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations production-reference-and-best-guess partly supported BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). 00082 sw2-18-19-combined-refit-offset-and-same-sign-count lsc-detectors supported Using the refit offset and the same-sign neighbour count together found 0.770 of the moved power on injected transfers, against 0.656 for the benchmark detector. The gain of 0.114 is about the sum of the gains of 0.056 and 0.050 from each change alone. On the 35 labelled real transfers of more than 1 day the combined detector found 12 and the benchmark 8, which is a weak signal on a small sample, and transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days gain nothing. 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). 00078 pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages solar-disaggregation small gain Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowered the error of experiment 64's best forecast by only 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold, and by 0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012, an interval that includes zero) at leads under 48 hours. 00071 sw2-18-refit-offset-and-gap-bridging lsc-detectors supported The detector ignored every alarm within 24 hours of the monthly refit of its forecasting model, which lowered recall by about 5% of the moved power. Lifting that rule recovers the loss, and the second residual model added to replace the ignored alarms adds nothing on injected transfers. 00070 sw2-19-same-sign-neighbour-count lsc-detectors supported Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation found 0.048 more of the moved power on injected transfers than the single-series detector, at the same number of unexplained alarms. The 35 labelled real transfers are too few to confirm the gain (7 found, against 8 for the benchmark), and the gain does not extend to transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar solar-disaggregation supported Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand retraining-and-training-history supported B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators retraining-and-training-history supported C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models calibration-and-uncertainty supported Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand retraining-and-training-history inconclusive C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). 00033 best-guess-architecture-vs-production production-reference-and-best-guess supported The best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), each wholly below its threshold. 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand demand-inputs inconclusive C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost hierarchy-and-pooling supported Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. 00020 solar-wind-stack-cams-stage0-spread-margin calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For wind, a starting guess from the turbine power curve lowered the error by 0.055 points of capacity (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), and adding a spread factor made the total 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014); the spread factor's extra -0.016 (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. For solar, no change helped detectably, and the full stack was 0.035 points higher with an interval that includes zero (-0.075 to +0.116). 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic production-reference-and-best-guess supported C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand retraining-and-training-history supported C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). 00016 pooled-mixture-calibration-solar-wind calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported For solar, one spread factor brought the 5% to 95% band from covering 94.3% to 95.3% of cases down to 89.5% to 91.8%, with no detectable change in accuracy. For wind, no planned correction fixed the first two days, and a spread factor on two lead groups, added after seeing the results, brought every lead band to 90.7% to 92.5% coverage and has not been tested on another year. 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand weather-products-and-blending inconclusive C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep demand-inputs partly supported P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. 00002 stage2-calibrator-and-mixture-vs-ens-quantile calibration-and-uncertainty partly supported Pooling the ERA5-trained solar and wind quantiles over the 51 weather-forecast members beat a model trained on archived weather forecasts: wind by 0.62 points of capacity (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and solar by 0.24 (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. A second calibration model on top did not improve on the pooling and made solar worse by 0.40 points (+0.26 to +0.61). The result rests on 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and one validation year. 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained weather-products-and-blending supported P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond.

docs.title: What the experiments taught us so far
docs.text:
• Retrain the Primary demand model weekly, and do not add a 14-day error correction. Weekly retraining without the correction scored 0.20 points of capacity below the best-guess stack, whose frozen model has the correction (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035), and a 7-day correction on the weekly model raised the score by 0.16 (-0.06 to +0.36), unresolved (00048). Experiment 34 found the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained, and hurts at weekly and daily cadence. The 14-day correction (00019, 00021) was measured on a frozen model, and the retraining results supersede it for Primary demand.
  • The 14-day correction on a frozen model is a historical result. It lowered the quantile score of N1, a model frozen at its training end, by 0.99 points (00019). At 4 bulk and grid supply point series it did not lower the score (00021), and at the supply points in experiment 87 adding it raised the score by 0.305 points.
  • A weather product as accurate as ERA5 would lower the Primary demand score by 1.9%. ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score by 0.10 points, nearly all from shortwave radiation and none up to 2 days ahead (00022).
  • Check for calendar memorisation. When the same valid time repeats across many ENS runs, a model with calendar columns can memorise it. Give each experiment a climatology row, and group folds by valid time.
  • Choose a row set that covers every weekday. The 53 Tuesday runs of 00001 and 00002 put every case of the first day on a Tuesday or Wednesday, which does not suit demand.
  • Training on ERA5 weather helps solar and wind, but a longer history does not add to it, and for demand a long history hurt. The solar and wind gain appeared even when the ERA5-trained model saw only the ENS-era months, so the gain comes from the weather it was trained on and not from the years. For demand, training from 2019 was worse than training from 2023, probably because the customer mix and embedded generation drifted.
  • Put recent power in the stage 2 calibrator, and calibrate before judging it. For Primary substations, the calibrator with recent-origin inputs beat a stage 1b correction, and a lag-free calibrator is worth about 1 point of capacity at short leads (00005).
  • The term and return-to-work columns showed no detectable gain on top of the Christmas column for Primary demand. Over the three validation years, the return and term columns moved the Primary error by +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 at Easter (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half terms (-0.68 to +0.07), and Both was not 0.2 points better than a calendar shifted by 17 days (00011). The arm with the full history and the COVID indicator scored 0.26 points higher on the whole year than the base arm.
  • A change that helps the point forecast of solar or wind need not help the pooled mixture's CRPS. CAMS-trained solar lowered the member-average error by 0.14 points (00012) and the mixture's CRPS by 0.009 (00020), and a stage 0 mapping widened the member spread by a quarter. A power-curve base margin lowered the wind CRPS by 0.055 (00020).
  • Attach the forecast solar term to the XGBoost model as a base margin, with a weight fitted on the training window and zero beyond 10 days. The base-margin arm lowered the Primary demand quantile score by 0.152 points (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111) against the best guess d0 and 0.256 against d1l, where the fixed-coefficient shift of 00046 lowered d1l by 0.056, and subtracting the forecast solar from a model trained on gross demand was not shown to match the best guess (00064).
  • Do not expect a zero start to help the production XGBoost models. Experiment 78 found that a zero base margin lowered its reference model d0 by 0.071 points, but on the production recipe the zero start changed the Primary score by -0.017 (-0.072 to +0.054) and the solar score by -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028), and worsened wind models without a power-curve margin by 0.049 (00080).
  • Refresh the capacity table that feeds the base margin once per season-year. A table refreshed that often captured almost all of the gain from a current capacity (00078).

docs.title: Data processing to apply in future experiments and production
docs.text: The experiments so far show that the power readings, the switching log, and the embedded-solar capacity estimates all need processing before an XGBoost model trains or scores on them. This page lists each step as an instruction. Every entry says where the step applies (experiments, production, or both), links the experiments that are the evidence, and states the scope the evidence covers. An entry whose evidence is a first look at the data gives its confidence in words. A plan for an experiment begins by reading this page.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• D code: an anonymised series label, such as D4, used in the experiment write-ups (see experiment 51). The page also names a few substations (Stickney, Kirton, Wrangle T1, Wrangle T2, and Mount Bridge Boston) as the experiment write-ups name them. A D code and a substation name are different labels, and the page does not say which D code matches which name.
  • Primary: a Primary substation, which steps 33 kV down to 11 kV. Sixteen of the 32 trial series are Primaries.
  • Point of capacity: 1% of a series' capacity. Scores in points of capacity are smaller when the forecast is better.
  • Season-year: a 12-month period running from September to August.
  • Best guess: the project's current forecasting recipe, assembled in experiment 33.
  • Skill: the percentage by which the best guess's quantile score is lower than the score of the rule-based forecast manual_heuristic.
  • Dark row: a half-hour in which the irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) is below 1 W/m².
  • Closure: a period in NGED's switching log in which an operator closed a switch that is normally open.
  • Transfer: a switching operation that moves part of one Primary's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The Primary that loses the load is the donor substation, and the receiving load is the usual load of the substations that gain it.
  • Labeller: a language model that reads the power readings and judges whether a transfer is visible, as in experiment 41.
  • Residual panel: the stored table of residuals, each the measured power minus the power an XGBoost model predicted.
  • Error correction: the 14-day correction that adds the forecast's recent errors to the next forecast.
  • Abnormal running arrangement (ARA) and normal running arrangement (NRA): an ARA is a period in which an operator has closed a normally open switch, so that one Primary carries load that belongs to a neighbour. The NRA is the usual layout.
  • Tail coverage at q95: the share of observed values that fall below the forecast's 95th percentile, which is 0.95 for a forecast with correct tails.
  • Curtailment cost: the avoidable cost, in pounds, of a forecast's errors when a node is held to a limit (experiment 84).

docs.title: Series and units
docs.text:
Count 32 time series in version 1 of the trial area. They are 16 Primary substations, 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, 2 grid supply points, 2 bulk supply points, and 3 other generators or storage units, as the home page lists. Applies to experiments and production.

Read each series' unit from the units column of the metadata table, and treat the Primaries metered in MVA as a different kind of series. A series is metered in MW (signed active power) or in MVA (apparent power, which is never negative). Eight of the 16 trial Primaries are metered only in MVA. Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: experiment 79 found no reverse flow at 7 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries from April to September, and experiment 56 could not tell the best guess's skill at the 8 MVA-only Primaries from its skill at the 8 MW Primaries (inconclusive). Experiment 110 fitted a power factor to only 2 of the 8 MVA-only Primaries (and recovered one of them, D12), because the other 6 have almost no reverse flow in their training rows. It held the power factor at 0.97 at those 6, and modelling the meter as apparent power scored 0.13 points of capacity better than reading it as real power. Experiment 204 summed the apparent-power children of two bulk supply points into the bulk supply point's reading: reading the magnitude as signed power or converting it with a fitted sign scored within 0.03 points at one bulk supply point and 0.02 to 0.03 points better with the sign at the other, where Stickney (D12) has reverse flow. Provisional.

Read power through the cleaned table, and read the raw table only when the question is about availability. The cleaned table holds only unflagged rows (nged_data.storage.scan_cleaned_power). Applies to experiments and production. Evidence: the data-cleaning roadmap page and experiment 6, which scores on cleaned power.

Count a series' history from its first unflagged row, which is later than its first row of any kind (high confidence). D9 starts in 2023-04 and its first unflagged row is in 2023-08. Only five Primaries hold long histories: D5, D10, and D11 start in 2019-09, D14 in 2019-10, and D16 in 2020-12. The late starters begin between 2023 and 2025. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

docs.title: Trim the start of each series
docs.text:
Cut the first months of most demand series (high confidence for D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18, medium to low for the rest). The first 1 to 19 months of a series often sit far from the same months in later years. A new meter can read near zero for days to weeks and then step up, and a new site can commission in stages. Cut until the level, the daily shape, and the share of rows present match the same months in later years. Cut more when the match is uncertain, and let a later look move a cut later and never earlier. Applies to experiments, and to production for a series that has just started reporting. The cuts found so far cover 16 of the 20 series examined (experiment 103, figure 4):

Series Cut Confidence Reason D4 19.4 months High Level 1.5 to 2 times too high, a stuck plateau, then too low, until a step on 2021-04-12 D14 8.3 months High Level about half of later years until a step of 2.2 MW on 2020-06-15 D17 5.6 months Medium Reads about 0, then 4 months of ramp and erratic swings D5 4.5 months Medium Night level 15% to 30% low until a step on 2020-01-09 D3 3.5 months High Night level 30% to 50% low and 15% to 60% of half-hours missing D18 2.6 months High Zeros, then a level near 0 to 1.5 MW with negative rows, then erratic D1, D10, D21 2.5 months Medium D1 unusually smooth then volatile; D10 and D21 have 30% to 70% of half-hours missing D22 1.5 months Low Gaps in most days and a night step D9, D16 1.3 months High Near zero, then a staged switch-on D13, D19 0.9 months Low Level steps in the first weeks D15 0.8 months Medium Erratic for 2 weeks while the meter was commissioned D12 7.4 months Low Night level 1.5 to 2 times later years; the start-of-series review recommends no cut, and the 15-point rule cuts it

Figure 1 shows the dropped months sitting far from the kept months at D4, D14, D9, D16, and D18. The figure draws 7 Primaries, and the cut dates come from the start-of-series review that experiment 103 confirmed. The grey dropped months are read from the raw power table, because the cleaned table removes flagged rows and the early months are often flagged. The blue kept months are read from the cleaned table. At D10 and D5 the dropped months look less different from the kept months, which fits their medium confidence.

An uncut start hurts a model without recent power far more than a model with it (high confidence for D18). In experiment 102, D18's training rows began with a late start at zero output. A weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three recent-power inputs forecast 20% of capacity in December 2025 against an actual of 75%, and its score at D18 was 5.7 points of capacity worse than the same model with the inputs. With the start cut (training from a later date), the difference at D18 fell to -0.03 points. The cost of removing the inputs across the 16 Primaries fell from 0.710 to 0.361 points. Applies to experiments, and to any comparison of a model with and without recent power. A comparison that cuts the start for one arm must cut it for every arm.

Train D15 and D18 only on rows from 2025-03-01 on (medium confidence, provisional). On the monthly XGBoost demand model, this cut lowered the days 1 to 10 CRPS by 1.3% at D15 and 1.2% at D18 against training on every row, and was lower in all 4 scored months at D15 and 3 of 6 at D18 (experiment 399, 2026-01 to 2026-06). A longer cut is not safe: dropping 6 months raised D18's CRPS by 7.2%. Removing readings within 0.009 MW of zero does not help, because at D15 most of them are real crossings of zero. Applies to experiments and to production. A cut does not fix D15's level error (median forecast 16 to 21 points of capacity too low).

docs.title: Decide which rows are demand
docs.text:
Use a Primary metered in MVA for demand only on dark rows (high confidence). An MVA reading cannot show reverse flow, so the solar output behind the Primary reads as demand in daylight. A filter that keeps rows with irradiance below 100 W/m² still keeps rows with solar output, because the filter admits irradiance above 1 W/m². After the start cuts, the dark rows leave 2.4 to 3.3 site-years per MVA Primary with the 2020 lockdown kept, 2.3 to 2.7 with the fixed lockdown window removed, and 0.9 to 1.0 in 2023-07 to 2025-06. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Figure 2 shows that the daylight half-hours at an MVA-only Primary carry a solar dip that the dark half-hours lack. The grey daylight half-hours sit in the middle of each day, where embedded solar output reduces the net flow and the apparent power cannot show its sign. The blue dark half-hours form the smooth evening and night curve that holds demand alone. The figure draws one Primary (D2) for two weeks of July 2025.

Do not let a loss on the absolute value of a latent power set the sign of the latent power (medium confidence, provisional). A folded loss cannot tell a latent power from its negative, so the sign follows the start of the fit. At six signed-MW Primaries with no injected solar, a folded XGBoost model still reported negative power at sunny midday on 41% to 97% of half-hours. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 387. The readings at D12, the Primary with known reverse flow, do not reach zero: the 0.1% quantile of its training readings is 4.3 points of effective capacity.

Do not treat grid supply points or bulk supply points as clean demand (high confidence). The grid supply points are dominated by generation: D1 is below 5 points of capacity on 75% of nights. The bulk supply points sum the trial Primaries: D17 reverses flow on 51% of May to August days at midday. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103.

Screen for embedded generation with the share of negative dark half-hours (high confidence). Series with 26% to 82% of their dark half-hours negative carry embedded generation or an exporting grid connection. The screen cannot work on an MVA Primary. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103, figure 9.

Count the half-hours that substation_zero flags before scoring a detector on a transfer. (Provisional.) The rule flags a reading of exactly 0 at a Primary substation, and a transformer that was switched out read exactly 0 in the 5 transfers we checked. At the series P12 and P13, the two transformers of one Primary substation, the rule flagged 426 half-hours inside 5 of the 6 labelled real transfers lasting more than 1 day, and the panel of residuals used to score detectors held no readings there. The cleaned power table keeps flagged rows with their original readings, and restoring those half-hours let the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) find 4 of the 6 transfers. This applies to experiments on switching. For production, the maintainer has to decide whether the rule should keep a zero reading when the other transformer of the same Primary substation carries the load of the switched-out transformer. Evidence: experiment 132. Confidence: medium, from 5 transfers at one Primary substation.

Treat an isolated zero reading between readings of 43 to 59% of effective capacity as missing (provisional; low confidence). The cached power readings hold 6 half-hours of exactly 0.0 MW at two Primary substations, D9 (5 half-hours) and D16 (1 half-hour). The zeros look like telemetry dropping out. A scorer that keeps them adds about 42 points of capacity to the error of each affected forecast row. Experiment 87 stored these actuals as missing, and experiment 379 scored them. The signed-MW six's CRPS then moved by about 0.002 points. Applies to experiments. For production, the maintainer has to decide whether the rule applies. Evidence: experiment 379. Confidence: low, from 6 half-hours at two Primary substations.

docs.title: Unlabelled jumps
docs.text:
Before reading flow on two substations with no interconnection (a placebo pair) as a fault of a method, check whether either substation has unlabelled jumps (low confidence). In experiment 131's replicate year (2024-25), the edge-flow fit with a drift term put 4.27 MW-days a year on D16 and D10. Of those, 1.58 lie inside the two D10 windows described under "Expect D10 to carry unlabelled jumps" below. Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 131.

Do not train a learned load-shift score with every real candidate as a negative and then score it on the months it trained on (medium confidence). Real load shifts that start in the training months are then taught as negatives: the score trained that way found 0 of the 15 logged load shifts that start in training months, against 7 for the same score with logged and labelled spans removed from its negatives. In the 20 load shifts that start in other months both found 13 (post hoc, experiment 302). Applies to experiments; provisional.

docs.title: Fixed windows
docs.text:
Use the fixed lockdown window, 2020-03-23 to 2021-07-19, and do not detect the window from the data. Experiment 6 defines its indicator with these dates, and the indicator lowered the error by 0.26 points of capacity on the selection fold. A window found from the data picks up drift and solar growth as well (experiment 103, figure 12; medium confidence): a drift-removed fit finds April 2020 more than 5 points low only at D11 (-26 points) and D10 (-7 points), and August 2020 to September 2021 sits 5 to 17 points above the fit at D5, D10, D11, and D14. Applies to experiments and production.

A dataset of dated events that ends before 2021-07-20 cannot be compared with the demand-model fit's training rows, because the lockdown window removes every earlier row from training. The feed-in tariff register, a list of small solar installations, ends on 2021-03-24, so none of its dates falls in a month on which the fit trains (experiment 215). Applies to experiments.

Check how many days of training rows a demand-model fit kept after the lockdown window is removed, and flag a fit with fewer than 180 days (provisional; medium confidence). Leaving the lockdown window out of training left Christmas 2020-21 fits with 51 to 143 days of rows. Every substation's Christmas 2021-22 fit had the same 104 summer days and no winter, and D9's 2023-24 fit had 31 days. The fits with under 180 days scored 1.38 to 1.91 times their ordinary-weekday error pooled over substations at Christmas, and D9 alone scored 5.6 times, where fits with at least 180 days scored 0.97 to 1.22 times (experiment 173; the 180-day threshold was chosen after the scores were read, and thresholds of 90 and 270 days gave the same picture for 2022-23 onwards). The Kalman filter and recipe R in that experiment do not repair a fit that saw little or no winter. Applies to experiments and production.

Give the series that changed regime an individual start date or a flag (medium confidence). D8 weekday daytime demand falls from about 9 MW to about 3 MW between 2023-10 and 2025. D12 switches between a high-night and a low-night regime. D18 steps up about 1.1 MW at night around 2026-07-03 (a date after the experiment's window, not rechecked there), and D5 shows a flat midday floor since 2022. Month-mean steps of over three monthly standard deviations occur at D6 (a drop of 218 MW in 2023-07) and D11 (2020-04). Applies to experiments. Evidence: experiment 103 for the step list and D8.

Treat D8's reading as including one gas engine's output until 2023-08-15, and as excluding it afterwards (provisional, medium confidence). The engine connected on 2023-06-13 and its own readings carry output from 2023-07-03. While those readings arrived, D8's residual rose by 0.02 MW per MW of engine output, where a reading without the output would fall by 1 MW per MW.

D8's share of half-hours with a residual below -2.5 MW then stepped from 0.010 to 0.257 in the week of 2023-08-14 and stayed between 0.10 and 0.46 in every month to January 2026. The share fell from 0.292 in January 2026 to 0.070 in March and 0.008 in April, with no matching change in the engine's own readings, so whether the engine is visible in D8 from 2026 is unknown. Applies to experiments; whether it applies to production awaits NGED's answer. Evidence: experiment 194.

Give a forecast the engine state it will have at forecast time, and train the engine term on that same lagged state (provisional, medium confidence). Applies to: experiments. D8's engine detector gives a state for each half-hour that is built from that half-hour's own reading. A coefficient fitted on that contemporaneous state is 3.6 MW per half-hour with one or more units running, but the state of the last settled day is worth 0.15 MW (interval -0.06 to 0.32) out of sample, so applying the contemporaneous coefficient to the lagged state makes the quantile score 10% worse. Trained on the lagged state, the coefficient is 0.9 to 1.0 MW and the score is 3% better than a model without the term (experiment 294).

Do not fit calendar and seasonal terms exactly (by variable projection, which solves the linear coefficients exactly at each step) to a window of three months or shorter. An exact least-squares fit of a per-substation model with holiday, tent, harmonic, and profile terms to 4 weeks or 3 months of data extrapolates those terms badly: the per-site fits scored 70.6 and 48.4 points at the five decision substations, against 15.1 and 5.5 for the gradient fits that stop before convergence. No window between 3 months and 2 years was tested. The pooled model with its interaction network failed the same way on four days of the scored year, where an exact fit with weak penalties forecast up to 280 points too high (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.

Treat a heating threshold above a substation's highest temperature, and any per-site threshold of a pooled model, as unidentified. Above the highest temperature the heating hinge is always on, and the deviation absorbs a shift, so only the prior sets the threshold; at real noise (standard deviation 5 points) a synthetic fleet with a 14 degree threshold was recovered to 2.7 to 5.7 degrees with the interaction network off or on (experiment 112; medium confidence; provisional). Applies to experiments.

docs.title: Drift in demand over the years
docs.text:
Do not assume that one level shift removes drift, because drift differs by series and by hour band. In 12 of 13 series some band moves by at least 1 point of capacity a year. From April to September the pooled slope is -1.30 points a year at midday (95% interval -2.32 to -0.92), -0.88 in the evening, and +0.69 at night. The all-hours slope is +0.04 because series drift in both directions (experiment 92). Subtracting a trailing 365-day level removed 42% of the old training year's penalty only when the largest series was included, and none of the penalty without that series (experiment 93). Applies to experiments and production. Scope: 13 Primary series with at least 24 months of data.

Do not expect an older training year to become usable by matching its weather product. Changing the weather product from 18 km to 9 km grid spacing does not explain why an old training year scores worse than a recent one (experiment 95). Applies to experiments and production.

Allow for a demand drop shared across sites in season-year 2022 (medium confidence). Evening demand fell by 7 to 10 points and night demand by 2 to 7 points of capacity at D10, D11, and D5 against season-year 2021, and recovered partly by 2025 at D5 and D11 but not at D10, probably after the rise in energy prices. Evidence: experiment 103, the season-year means in report.txt. A model trained across years can read the drop as a trend. Applies to experiments.

Expect monthly night demand to move together across the long-history Primaries, and expect the winter heating slope of night power not to drift (medium confidence). Winter heating slopes of night power show no detectable drift between the first and last winter at the long-history sites. Monthly levels move together across sites, with a mean pairwise correlation of 0.56 at night and 0.47 in the evening after the seasonal cycle is removed (experiment 103, figure 8). Applies to experiments, before pooling sites.
