In a further check that was not planned, it found about 9 in 10 of the large, long transfers when the receiving substation has its own power readings (46 of 52), and 6 in 10 when it does not (25 of 42).

Partly supported: Sonnet called no placebo window visible and timed starts and ends well, but found only 0.74 of the large, long fake transfers, under the 0.80 bar. On 120 placebo cards Sonnet called 0 visible (95% interval 0.00 to 0.03). It found 25 of 34 injected transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load lasting 6 hours or more (0.74; 0.57 to 0.85), or 71 of 94 (0.76; 0.66 to 0.83) with 60 further cards from the same band. Where a metered receiver exists the recall is 0.89 (46 of 52; 0.77 to 0.95); where the receiver is unmetered and only the donor steps it is 0.60 (25 of 42; 0.44 to 0.73). The rules-only labeller reaches 0.65 (22 of 34) with 3 of 120 placebo cards called visible. The maintainer waived the bar for naming the receiving substations after seeing the rules-only results, so the waiver is post hoc.

docs.title: The first test set had tells
docs.text: A Sonnet reviewer found that the first 300 test cards were easier to reject than real ones, so all gate figures here come from a rebuilt set. In the first set the injected cards' log times ended in :05 or :35 only, while placebo cards carried real minutes; every injected card showed a metered side B while 39 of 120 placebo cards showed "side B: not metered"; and the injected start times were spread over the whole day while the placebo times kept real clock times. In the rebuilt sets (test2, testbig2) both kinds of card take a real operation's log times, sheet sides, duration, and clock time, shifted by whole weeks into a quiet period. The minute, side-B and night-share distributions now match. The first set gave Sonnet a placebo rate of 1 of 120 (1 of 81 without the side-B tell) and a recall of 0.92 on its 25 large, long cards; those figures are not used. The 100 development cards came from the first generator.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• The hindsight model (a model that sees weather and the following months, so it predicts demand better than any live forecast could) is a leave-one-month-out XGBoost quantile model (q10, q50, q90) on experiment 6's 13 input columns for each of the 16 substations, with every logged closure (padded 24 hours) removed from training. The hindsight model is supporting evidence on a card and is never the deciding evidence.
  • Cards hold the log times, step features F1 to F7 with percentiles against up to 400 quiet-week draws, and hourly values. The 300 test cards are 150 injected, 120 placebo, and 30 injected with the log time 1 to 3 hours off. A further 60 injected cards in the 25%-or-more, 6-hour-or-longer band were added after the first scoring, at the planning session's request, because 34 cards in that band give a wide recall interval.
  • The injected cards follow the real mix of sheets. 60 of 150 injected cards sit on a sheet with no metered side B, so the load goes to an unmetered receiver and only the donor steps. The design assumed 15%; the real log has 30% to 40%.
  • Both labellers saw the same cards. The rules-only labeller applies percentile bars (0.97 at the close, 0.90 at the open, 0.985 for one-sided) that were set before the first development card was scored and not changed. The Sonnet labeller read ten cards per run with a written brief and no plots. The second Sonnet labeller read the 168 test cards the first called visible or low confidence, plus a random quarter of the rest.

docs.title: Hindsight model checks
docs.text: Excluding logged closures removed contamination, and the hindsight model did not absorb the closures. In the 7 days either side of 358 side-windows of closures over 3 days, the mean hindsight z is 0.004 (standard error 0.054), and 19.4% of observations fall outside the q10 to q90 band (nominal 20%). Training with the logged closures removed gave a lower out-of-event mean absolute error than removing the same volume at random positions in 5 of 6 substations tested; the gap is 0.043 MW on substation 3 (interval 0.008 to 0.081) and 0.010 MW on substation 14 (0.001 to 0.020), and the other four intervals include zero.

docs.title: Gate on 300 rebuilt test cards
docs.text:
Check Bar Rules only Sonnet Placebo labelled visible 5% or less 3 of 120 (0.01 to 0.07) 0 of 120 (0.00 to 0.03) Placebo labelled conserved 2% or less 0 of 120 0 of 120 Recall, 25% or more and 6 h or more 0.80 or more 0.65 (22 of 34) 0.74 (25 of 34; 0.57 to 0.85) Same band with 60 further cards 0.80 or more 0.64 (60 of 94; 0.54 to 0.73) 0.76 (71 of 94; 0.66 to 0.83) Onset within 1 h of truth, found injections 90% or more 100% (63 of 63) 99% (77 of 78) End within the larger of 2 h and 10% of duration 80% or more 97% 100% Moved MW, median absolute relative error 25% or less 22% 11% Receivers named, share 30% or more 80% or more, waived 53% 35% Jittered: onset nearer the truth than the log 80% or more 4 of 4 found 14 of 14 found Event F1 (events found against events wrongly called, matched event by event) on all injected cards at least the rules' 0.52 0.68 Kappa (agreement beyond chance) between the two Sonnet labellers 0.7 or more not applicable 0.79 (0.83 visible against not; bootstrap 0.74 to 0.90)

Sonnet's recall of 0.76 is under the 0.80 bar. The upper end of its interval, 0.83, is above the bar, so a recall of 0.80 is not ruled out but is not shown either. The jittered check rests on 14 of 30 cards for Sonnet and 4 of 30 for the rules, because the labeller called the rest not visible. Sonnet found 78 of 150 injected transfers and the rules 63 of 150. Under the pre-registered rule, a placebo rate under 10% and all bars met except recall give partly supported, and the bands where recall is under 0.80 become don't-care bands, whose labels later experiments do not use to score detectors.

Both labellers miss small and short transfers, and Sonnet reaches 0.80 only for transfers of 25% or more lasting over 1 day. The over-1-day band gives Sonnet 0.83 (30 of 36; 0.68 to 0.92) and the rules 0.75. Transfers of 25% or more lasting 6 to 24 hours give 0.71 and 0.57. Recall is 0.14 to 0.38 under 10% of the receiving load and 0.50 to 0.63 for 10% to 25%.

Recall depends on whether a metered receiver exists. For the 52 large, long injections with a metered receiver Sonnet's recall is 0.89 (0.77 to 0.95) and the rules' 0.79 (0.66 to 0.88). For the 42 where only the donor steps, Sonnet's is 0.60 (0.44 to 0.73) and the rules' 0.45 (0.31 to 0.60). This split was made after seeing the results and is not a planned row. A bar of 0.80 on the real sheet mix fails, and on cards with a metered receiver the point estimate passes.

docs.title: Receivers named (waived bar)
docs.text: The maintainer waived the receivers-named bar after the rules-only results, so the change is post hoc, and the figure is reported only. Sonnet names a receiver with a share of 30% or more in 27 of 75 cases (0.36). It names the receiver in 26 of 58 cases it calls conserved (0.45) and in 1 of 17 it calls one-sided. By count of metered receivers in the truth, it names 6 of 27 (one), 14 of 37 (two), and 7 of 11 (three). By series type, it names 20 of 54 on MVA series and 7 of 21 on MW series, and 3 of 6 on cards with an unmetered share. The rules-only labeller names 53%.

docs.title: Token cost
docs.text: Sonnet labelling cost 14.9 million subagent tokens for 1,156 card labellings, about 12,900 each. Labeller 1 used 10.5 million on 820 cards (100 development, 300 test, 60 further, then 300 test and 60 further after the rebuild) and labeller 2 used 4.4 million on 336 cards, as the harness reports each subagent run. The development set and the first, flawed test set cost 8.3 million of the total. No Opus run was needed, because the injected truth settles every disagreement. The full run SW2-0b is about 770 cards (533 operations, 36 edge events, 50 short closures, and about 150 alarms); at the same rate, one labeller costs about 10 million tokens and a second labeller on half of them about 5 million more.

docs.title: What was not done
docs.text:
• The development set confirmed that Sonnet labels in the right schema (100 cards, event F1 0.75); no prompt was tuned, and the rules-only thresholds were not tuned either.
  • No card used a plot. The design allowed one.
  • Bank holidays are not excluded from the same-weekday reference.
  • The hindsight model uses 150 trees at learning rate 0.1, shallower than experiment 17's fits.
  • The absorption check against random exclusion ran on 6 of the 16 substations.
  • The kappa subset is not random: it holds the 168 cards that the first labeller called visible or low confidence plus a random quarter of the rest, so kappa describes agreement on that enriched sample.
  • The real-operation cards of SW2-0b have not been compared with the hidden test cards yet; that check comes before the full run.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• Score detectors only in the band where Sonnet's recall has a point estimate of 0.80 or more: 25% or more of the receiving load, lasting over 1 day.
  • A detector's recall against labelled events overstates its recall against all real switching, because Sonnet misses between a third and a half of transfers of 10% to 25% and 40% of donor-only transfers of 25% or more.
  • The second labeller agrees with the first (kappa 0.79), so a second labeller on a sample of the cards in SW2-0b is plausible, though kappa was measured on an enriched sample and agreement on the other cards is untested.

Code: ml-experiments/00041-sw2-0a-labeller-gate/. Numbers above are printed by e00041_report.py, e00041_kappa.py, e00041_diagnose.py, and e00041_checks.py.

docs.title: Known defect in the labelled set
docs.text: The labelled set's moved_share_of_receiver column is missing for most events. The labeller wrote donor and receiver series ids as text, and the calculation that turns the moved MW into a share of the receiving load compares them with whole numbers, so the share is empty for any event whose receivers are text. Counts of events by share band in the labelled-set page were corrected for events lasting over 1 day; use experiment 44's load_events for every other use.

docs.title: Experiment 43: how well do the two existing LSC detectors find transfers?
docs.text: We asked how well two simple detectors, built in an earlier experiment, find a transfer of load between two substations when we know it happened. A detector compares the weather model's forecast with the power actually drawn at each of the 16 Primary substations; the difference is the residual. It raises an alarm when the average residual over a window of hours steps up or down. The single-series detector (D0) looks at one substation. The neighbour-balance detector (D1) also requires a neighbour to step the opposite way. We added 600 known transfers to the real power readings, in nine groups by size and length. A detector gets credit for a transfer only if it puts the start within 2 hours of the truth and the end within 6 hours (or 10% of the length). Each detector finds under a fifth of all the transfers and at most 0.29 in any group, and the neighbour check helps only with the 4-hour window.

docs.title: Headline
docs.text:
Over a 24-hour window the neighbour check finds fewer large transfers than the single-series detector, so the hypothesis is refuted at that window. On the 160 injected transfers that start at 25% to 40% of the receiving load and last over 1 day, the 24-hour D0 finds 47 (0.29) and D1 finds 34 (0.21). D1 minus D0 is -0.081 (95% interval -0.130 to -0.037, resampling whole calendar months). The decision rule names event F1 (recall combined with the alarms' precision), and the F1 difference is -0.055 to -0.049 across the precision bounds; the interval is on recall. Event F1 is 0.36 for D0 and 0.30 to 0.31 for D1.

At the 4-hour window the order reverses. D1 finds 40 (0.25) and D0 finds 26 (0.16), a difference of +0.087 (+0.044 to +0.136), and the F1 difference is +0.07. The decision rule was written for the 24-hour window, so this reversal changes no verdict.

One part of the prediction held and two failed. D1's 24-hour F1 of 0.30 to 0.31 lies in the predicted 0.30 to 0.60, and D0's 0.36 lies in 0.15 to 0.45. D1 does not beat D0 by 0.10, and most misses are not wrong ends: 50% to 71% of the headline transfers get no interval with the right start, and a wrong end explains 13% to 21%.

docs.title: What the scoreboard measures
docs.text:
• Windows and thresholds: D0 and D1 run with a 4-hour window (8 half-hours) and a 24-hour window (48 half-hours), at the four thresholds fixed in experiment 37 (D0 6.0 and D1 3.75 at 4 hours, D0 4.0 and D1 2.5 at 24 hours). An interval builder from experiment 38 turns each alarm into a start and an end.
  • Found: a detector interval on the donor or a receiver with a start within 2 hours of the truth and an end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration. The end is the interval's final estimate, and a live system learns it only later (see the delay below).
  • Event F1: the harmonic mean of the share of injected transfers found and the alarms' precision. Precision comes from the real alarms, not the injections, so it does not depend on how many events we inject.

Precision lies between two bounds because the logs miss real switching. The lower bound is the alarms that fall within 24 hours of a logged closure on their series, over all alarms. The upper bound adds the unmatched alarms times the share of SW2-0b's labelled alarm sample that was visible. That share is a floor on the true share, because the labeller misses some real transfers, and counts of 0 to 4 in 37 are too thin for a point value: the Wilson upper limit for 0 of 37 is about 9%.

Setting Alarms Matching a logged closure Not matching Of the sample labelled visible Precision D0, 4 h window 432 202 230 4 of 37 0.47 to 0.53 D1, 4 h window 444 187 257 2 of 37 0.42 to 0.45 D0, 24 h window 297 137 160 0 of 37 0.46 or more D1, 24 h window 110 59 51 3 of 37 0.54 to 0.57

docs.title: Recall by band
docs.text:
All four settings find more transfers that are large and long, and none exceeds 0.29 (47 of 160) in any band. The table gives, for 600 injected transfers (55 per band, 160 in the headline band), the share found, then the share whose start alone was found. A transfer's size band is the share of the receiving load at its start, and the share then drifts between half and twice that.

Setting All bands Start only, all bands Headline band Start only, headline Median end error, starts found D0, 4 h window 0.11 (64 of 600) 0.16 0.16 (26 of 160) 0.29 4.5 h D1, 4 h window 0.17 (99 of 600) 0.22 0.25 (40 of 160) 0.39 3.5 h D0, 24 h window 0.11 (65 of 600) 0.18 0.29 (47 of 160) 0.50 5.5 h D1, 24 h window 0.08 (47 of 600) 0.13 0.21 (34 of 160) 0.34 5.5 h

D1 finds almost no transfer that has no metered receiver, which explains much of its 24-hour loss. In the headline band 84 of 160 transfers have no metered receiver, because the sheet has no metered second side and the load goes to a substation without power readings. D1 needs an opposite step on a neighbour, so it can fire on those only by coincidence. The 4-hour D0 finds 0 of 84 and D1 5 of 84; the 24-hour D0 finds 12 of 84 and D1 2 of 84. Where a metered receiver exists (76 transfers), the 4-hour D0 finds 26 and D1 35, and the 24-hour D0 finds 35 and D1 32. On those 76 the 24-hour D1 minus D0 is -0.039 (-0.091 to +0.000), and the 4-hour difference is +0.118 (+0.031 to +0.196). The generator gives the headline band this mix because 28% of the real operations' sheets have no metered second side (experiment 41's check) and the drawn transfers over-sample them.

The end of a found transfer is known about a day late. The median time from the true end to the interval's end being known is 19.2 hours (D0, 4 h), 20.0 hours (D1, 4 h), 22.5 hours (D0, 24 h), and 24.0 hours (D1, 24 h). Experiment 38's post hoc variant of the interval builder finds fewer at the 4-hour window (0.05 and 0.08) and about the same at 24 hours (0.11 and 0.07).

docs.title: Real labelled events
docs.text:
Only 14 labelled real transfers meet the size and length condition, so the real-event result is a count and carries no verdict. The share of the receiving load is recomputed here as the median moved MW over the named metered receivers' usual power in the 28 days before the event, the definition experiment 44 uses, because the stored share is missing for most events. The 14 events (25% or more of the receiving load, over 1 day) are 6 conserved (two substations step in opposite directions) and 8 one-sided (only one substation steps, or a conserved call reclassified because a substation's readings are mostly missing). Found events: the 4-hour D0 finds 0 of 14, the 4-hour D1 2, the 24-hour D0 1, and the 24-hour D1 3 (1 of 6 conserved and 1 of 8 one-sided for the 4-hour D1; 2 of 6 and 1 of 8 for the 24-hour D1). Starts alone are found for 1, 5, 6, and 4 of the 14.

A second set, chosen after seeing that count, is the 35 visible operations lasting over 1 day. Of the 35, the 4-hour D0 finds 1, the 4-hour D1 finds 3, the 24-hour D0 finds 2, and the 24-hour D1 finds 5 (starts alone: 2, 6, 11, and 9). Of the 10 conserved, the 24-hour D1 finds 3 and the 24-hour D0 finds 1. Of the 35, 14 have a share of the receiving load of 25% or more (the one band where the labeller finds 0.83 of injected transfers), 11 have a share under 25%, and 10 have no named metered receiver and so no share. This recall measures a detector against what the labeller could see, not against all real switching.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The injected events sit in calm periods. Each has no logged closure within 7 days and no real alarm within 2 days on its series, so recall is optimistic compared with the real alarm mix that sets precision.
  • The true partners are always in D1's candidate list. Donors and receivers come from the same static interconnection list that D1 searches, which flatters D1.
  • The interval builder reads later data. An interval's pre-level skips stamps inside earlier intervals whose ends are known only afterwards, a mild hindsight effect.
  • Event F1 combines two sources. Recall comes from injections and precision from the real alarms, so the F1 depends on the logs missing nothing that the labeller cannot see.
  • The residual needs ERA5 weather. ERA5 arrives about 5 days after the event, so the detectors run retrospectively.

Code: ml-experiments/00043-sw2-1-detector-scoreboard/, with every number printed by e00043_report.py. The reusable harness is e00043_inject.py and the matching rule is e00043_score.py.

docs.title: Experiment 44: how much do labelled load shifts hurt the best guess?
docs.text:
Experiment 33 produced the best forecast it found of demand at the 16 Primary substations (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), which we call the best guess. We asked how much of the best guess's error, for July 2025 to June 2026, falls on half-hours affected by a switching event, an operation in which engineers moved load from one substation to a neighbouring substation. We split the summed error three ways: half-hours inside an event labelled in experiment 41, half-hours outside every event whose lagged power (the earlier power readings the forecast takes as inputs) falls inside one, and all other half-hours. We kept only the larger transfers that lasted over 24 hours, the events that experiment 41's labeller finds most reliably. The first two groups together are 1.35% of all half-hours scored and carry 3.4% of the summed error. A perfect switching detector would lower the summed error by 0.42%, with a 95% interval from -0.47% to 1.96%.

Refuted: in the trustworthy band, a perfect detector would lower the quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and the tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3% set in the plan. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, as in experiment 33, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a series' capacity). The tail score is the threshold-weighted continuous ranked probability score (twCRPS) at each series' 99th percentile of power, which counts only errors above that level. The trustworthy band is the visible events that moved at least 25% of the receiving substation's load and lasted over 24 hours; experiment 41's labeller recovered 83% of the artificial transfers of that size and length that it was tested on. The perfect-detector bound gives each flagged half-hour its series' mean score outside every flag, so the bound is the largest reduction a detector could deliver. The plan is in [PR

docs.text:
Each cell below is a percentage of all half-hours scored (or of the summed quantile score), with the 95% interval in brackets. The first three rows sum to the fourth only to rounding.

Trustworthy band Share of half-hours Share of quantile score Mean quantile score Target in an event, onset after the forecast was made 0.12% (0.00 to 0.28) 0.78% (0.00 to 2.04) 35.8 (17.7 to 53.3) Target in an event, onset before the forecast was made 0.03% (0.00 to 0.07) 0.15% (0.00 to 0.37) 25.9 (16.1 to 37.6) Target outside events, lagged power inside one 1.20% (0.02 to 2.87) 2.49% (0.02 to 6.26) 11.0 (3.8 to 13.5) Any of the three 1.35% (0.04 to 3.22) 3.43% (0.04 to 8.68) 13.5 (4.4 to 17.3) Outside every flag 98.65% 96.57% 5.21 (4.76 to 5.63)

The prediction held for the two ratios and failed for the size. Flagged half-hours are under 3% of all half-hours (1.35%), and their score share is 2.5 times their half-hour share, above the at-least-1.5 times the plan predicted. The flagged share did not reach the predicted 5% to 15%, and the bound did not reach the predicted 1% to 5%.

The intervals are wide because only 6 trustworthy events fall in the scored year. The events lie on the series with time_series_id 10, 12, and 13, with onsets in July, September, and October 2025 and June 2026. The other 13 Primary series have no trustworthy event in the year, so the result says little about those 13 series. The intervals resample whole months of forecast origin, so they understate that uncertainty.

docs.title: What a detector could and could not help
docs.text:
Only two groups of half-hours are open to a detector. They are the half-hours whose lagged power falls inside an event, and those whose target falls in an event that started before the forecast was made. The metered view scores the forecast against the power actually measured, which includes the effect of the switching, and counts both groups. The normal running arrangement (NRA) view scores against the power the electricity network would have carried without the switching, so it counts only the first group, scored outside every event. The ceiling also counts events that started after the forecast was made, which no detector can anticipate.

For the quantile score, with the series-mean counterfactual, the bounds are:

  • Metered view: 0.42% (-0.47% to 1.96%).
  • NRA view: 0.34% (-0.51% to 1.79%).
  • Ceiling: 0.96% (-0.30% to 3.42%).

The counterfactual that matches each flagged half-hour to unflagged half-hours of the same series, forecast lead time, and hour of day gives the same point estimates to two decimals, and interval ends within 0.02 points. For the tail score every bound is slightly negative (-0.85% for the metered view), because the flagged half-hours have a lower tail score than the unflagged half-hours.

The all-visible sensitivity, which uses every event the labeller found visible whatever its size or duration, gives larger and far less certain figures. In the scored year it holds 22 events on 11 series. Flagged half-hours are 7.4% of the total (3.8% to 11.3%) and carry 11.6% of the quantile score (4.8% to 18.6%). The bounds are 2.35% (-0.22% to 5.73%) for the metered view and 4.11% (0.16% to 8.34%) for the ceiling.

The all-visible tail results rest on a few short events. The flagged half-hours carry 55% of the tail score (2% to 70%), far more than their 11.6% of the quantile score, and the metered tail bound is 32.7% (-6.0% to 61.1%).

Dropping the events that rest on one badly metered substation removes the effect. Of the 22 trustworthy events in all years, 10 have a receiving or donating substation with over half its readings missing during the event. Without them 2 trustworthy events remain in the scored year, and every bound's point estimate lies between -0.3% and -0.1%.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Few events. The decision rule was written in the plan before the scoring, and the verdict follows it. The month-resampling interval understates how little 6 events on 3 series can show.
  • The stored receiver shares are missing for most events. The labelled set's moved_share_of_receiver is NaN (missing) for 62 of the 81 visible events that touch a Primary series (82 in all). The causes are that the labeller wrote some donor or receiver ids as strings and the share code dropped them, and that 20 events name no metered receiver. This experiment recomputes the share as the moved MW over the named receivers' mean absolute power in the 28 days before the onset. The recomputed share agrees with the stored share where both exist (for example 0.33 against 0.34), but it ignores how the load splits between receivers, so it understates the share when a receiver takes only part of the load. The recomputed share exists for 61 events, of which 22 are 0.25 or more with a duration over 24 hours.
  • Slightly favourable detection time. An event counts as known to a detector once the forecast origin (the time the forecast is made) passes its onset, but telemetry arrives 3 hours late, so the score is slightly too favourable for events that start less than 3.5 hours before the origin.
  • Nested lag definitions. The correction's 14-day window (1.20% of half-hours) contains the three lags the forecast reads (0.48%), so the combined lagged-power group equals the window group.
  • Primary series only. The labels cover the 16 Primary series, so the bulk supply point and grid supply point series, solar farms, and wind farms have no figure.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text:
• In this year, the labelled events do not justify a detector for the forecast error alone.
  • Figures 2 and 4 show that the all-visible tail-score share rests on a few short events, which a first detector experiment could look at before it looks at the whole year.

Numbers come from e00044_score.py and e00044_report.py, and figures from e00044_charts.py.

docs.title: Experiment 45 (PVDIS-4): a weekly capacity series that rises easily and falls reluctantly
docs.text:
Weekly changes in embedded solar capacity cannot yet be read from the Primary-substation data at the accuracy a weekly series needs. For SW2-10, use one capacity per season-year as the solar capacity input, and read it as a range. SW2-10 is the planned experiment in the switching work that fits a weather baseline, embedded solar capacity, and each labelled transfer of load in one linear fit. A season-year is one 12-month period, and the season-year constant is one capacity per season-year with no weekly freedom. The next approaches to try are a penalty set separately for each Primary substation, and step detection that fires only above about 25% to 30% of capacity.

The verdict is refuted, because no pair of penalty settings on the grid met the limits fixed in advance for tuning. We asked whether the amount of embedded solar behind each of 8 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV distribution network) can be tracked week by week. Embedded solar is solar connected inside the distribution network, mostly unmetered by NGED, and its capacity here means the 99th percentile of its half-hourly AC output, in MW. A weekly fit has two penalty settings: a sets the penalty on a weekly rise in capacity, and r is the factor by which a fall is penalised more than a rise. The limits were at most 0.5 false steps per Primary-year at the median Primary (a false step is a rise or fall of 10% of capacity found on a series whose true capacity is constant), at most 1.0 at the worst Primary, and at least 0.5 of a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks recovered. The pair with the smallest shortfall (a=4 and r=30) was frozen, which means it was chosen on tuning units before the scoring run. It recovered 0.000 of the fall and gave a median of 0.66 false steps per Primary-year. A looser pair chosen after the scoring run (a=2 and r=10) recovered 0.576 of the fall and gave a median of 1.22 false steps.

The comparison with the season-year constant is not what decides the verdict, and the two baselines used to score it disagree. The path error is the mean absolute gap between the fitted and the true weekly capacity, as a share of the true mean capacity. On the semi-synthetic baseline, which is the worse of the two scorings for the frozen fit and so the one condition (i) uses, the median path error on ramps and steps was 0.027 for the season-year constant, 0.040 for the frozen weekly fit, and 0.159 for a weekly fit with no penalty. No weekly fit beat the constant there, but that baseline favours the constant by construction, because it is built by subtracting the season-year constant fit. On the real series plus injection, every weekly fit beat the constant on ramps and steps (0.012 to 0.017 against 0.020), and the free and symmetric fits also beat it on steps and falls. The comparison also points the same way as the verdict on the plan's main interval, which resamples the 8 Primaries only: the lower limit of C2 (the relative change in path error against the constant) is +0.029, above 0, so the clause "the asymmetric fit is worse than the yearly constant" fires as a second route to refuted. The two-way interval, which also resamples farm-seeds, is [-0.078, +0.773] and contains 0. The experiment's reason for refuted is the tuning-limit route.

The experiment could not tell whether a better-tuned penalty would see a real fall in capacity, such as a feeder reconfigured permanently, or whether a penalty set per Primary would work. The one pair that followed falls (a=2 and r=10) was chosen after the scores were seen, and a penalty set per Primary was not tested.

Four further findings limit what the series can be used for. The smallest step that the frozen pair detected in 80% of injections is above 25% of capacity at all 8 Primaries in both seasons: at 6 Primaries no step of 30% or less reaches 80%, and at the other two 30% does from April to September only. The free weekly fit reaches 80% for 5% steps at 3 of the 8 Primaries from April to September, and for 10% steps at 5, but with a median of 11.6 false steps per Primary-year. The latest week of a real-time estimate had 3.63 times the path error of the same week in the final fit. The 90% intervals covered 0.62 of the weeks without a step and 0.35 of the weeks with a step. The three outside checks (national statistics, the Feed-in Tariff register, and the Embedded Capacity Register) each count only part of the installed solar, so they can neither confirm nor refute the series.

The plan's literal clause order gives inconclusive, and refuted applies instead. The first clause (the smallest detectable step exceeds 25% of capacity at 5 or more Primaries in every season) holds, but it was evaluated on a degenerate pair. With no feasible pair, the frozen configuration fell back to the pair nearest the limits (a=4, r=30), which scores the same as the strictly non-decreasing fit and detects 0.28 of steps from April to September and 0.23 from October to March. refuted applies for two reasons. The plan says that when no pair on the grid meets both tuning limits, the verdict is refuted for the asymmetric design and the limits are not relaxed. And the detection failure belongs to the penalty, not to the data: the free weekly fit detected 0.85 of steps from April to September and 0.75 from October to March, with a median of 11.6 false steps per Primary-year.

docs.title: Terms used on this page
docs.text:
• Unit: one solar farm's recorded output, injected at one Primary substation with one path seed in one case (a ramp, a step, a temporary fall, a transfer, a seasonal load, or a constant path). Tuning units use Solar farms A to C and scoring units use Solar farms D to F.
  • Path error: the mean absolute gap between the fitted and the true weekly capacity, as a share of the true mean capacity. A path error of 0.10 means the fitted capacity is on average 10% of the true mean capacity away from the truth, which is 0.4 MW on a 4 MW series.
  • Primary-year: one Primary substation observed for one year. False steps are counted per Primary-year.
  • Placebo sky: the solar shape shuffled between days of the same month, so the true capacity is constant and any step the fit finds is false.
  • Semi-synthetic baseline: the real power minus the fitted season-year-constant solar component, plus a known solar path, so the true capacity of every week is known.
  • Real series plus injection: the real power with the injected path added, scored by comparing the fitted path with and without the injection.
  • Frozen pair: the pair (a, r) chosen on tuning units and written to a committed file before the scoring run.

docs.title: What was fitted, and the two tuning attempts
docs.text:
Each weekly fit explains daylight power as a demand term minus one capacity per week times a solar shape from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), and the penalised fits penalise each weekly change. The frozen pair is a=4 and r=30: a scales the penalty on a weekly rise in capacity (in units of one weekly standard error), and r is the factor by which a fall is penalised more than a rise. The comparison fits are a weekly capacity with no penalty (free weekly), a symmetric penalty (r=1), a strictly non-decreasing capacity (r=infinity), and the season-year constant. The penalty pair was chosen on tuning units (Solar farms A to C) and scored once on scoring units (Solar farms D to F, 1,320 of the 1,344 planned units, because Solar farm E's record is too short for 24 injections at Mount Bridge Boston).

The first tuning attempt was invalid and was redone, and the redone attempt is the one reported. The first attempt's semi-synthetic baseline subtracted the real series' fitted weekly capacity, which removed the weekly noise that is correlated with the solar shape, so the baseline was too clean. The second attempt subtracts the season-year constant fit, which keeps that noise, and scores the fit of baseline plus injection against the known path. The constant-path unit was also redefined after the first attempt's tuning results were seen. It first injected a constant capacity into a baseline that still held real growth within each year, so real rises counted as false steps. It now uses the placebo sky, so the true path is constant. The change was made on tuning units only, and the scoring units were never fitted before the pair was frozen. Neither attempt found a pair that met the limits, as the table shows.

a r Path error, mixture (second attempt) Constant-path false steps, median (second attempt) 26-week fall recovered (second attempt) Largest excess over a limit (second attempt) Constant-path false steps, median (first attempt) Largest excess over a limit (first attempt) 0.5 10 0.119 4.800 1.132 7.182 4.630 7.239 0.5 30 0.083 1.696 0.903 4.149 1.691 3.806 1 10 0.096 2.500 1.006 5.751 2.677 5.866 1 30 0.054 0.841 0.657 1.975 0.636 1.975 2 10 0.066 1.043 0.787 2.719 0.915 2.662 2 30 0.046 0.511 0.135 1.517 0.499 1.377 4 10 0.045 0.620 0.476 1.117 0.529 1.141 4 30 0.045 0.382 0.000 0.888 0.414 1.141

No pair on the grid meets all three limits: pairs that follow a fall are too noisy, and pairs that stay quiet do not follow a fall. The limits are at most 0.5 false steps at the median Primary, at most 1.0 at the worst Primary, and at least 0.5 of a 26-week fall recovered. The excess column gives the largest amount by which a pair misses any limit, in the units of that limit. Pairs that follow a fall (the r=10 rows with a up to 2) are far too noisy. The a=4, r=30 pair stays quiet and does not follow a fall (0.000). The a=4, r=10 pair comes closest on the fall, recovering 0.476 of the 26-week fall, but its false steps are 0.62 at the median Primary and 2.12 at the worst. The pair a=4, r=30 had the smallest excess in the second attempt, so the configuration was frozen there as a fallback, and it is the pair called "frozen" below. The pair a=2, r=10 was the pair chosen by an earlier tuning run on a baseline without weekly noise (commit 75005575). It was scored afterwards on the same scoring units, so every number for it is post hoc, and it is not part of the verdict.

Figure 6 shows that no cell of the grid is green in both rows of false steps and fall recovery. The frozen pair is marked F and the post hoc pair is marked P.

docs.title: Scores on held-out injections
docs.text:
On the semi-synthetic baseline, no weekly fit beat the season-year constant on ramps and steps, and the free weekly fit was the worst. The table gives each fit's absolute score on the scoring units. Scores are medians over farm-seeds and cases within a Primary, then medians over the 8 Primaries. False steps are of 10% of capacity per Primary-year on the constant path, as median and worst Primary. Drift is the rise of the path over 5 years on a constant path, as a share of capacity. The fall column is the share of a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks that the path shows (0 means the path ignores the fall and 1 means the path follows the fall fully).

Fit Path error, ramps and steps (semi-synthetic) Path error, ramps and steps (real series plus injection) False steps, constant path (median, worst) Drift on constant path 26-week fall recovered Season-year constant 0.027 0.020 0.17, 0.25 -0.037 -0.043 Frozen asymmetric (a=4, r=30) 0.040 0.017 0.66, 1.43 +0.137 0.000 Strictly non-decreasing 0.040 0.016 0.66, 1.43 +0.137 0.000 Symmetric (r=1) 0.102 0.012 3.01, 6.29 -0.026 0.920 Free weekly 0.159 0.014 11.60, 12.27 -0.019 1.250 Post hoc (a=2, r=10) 0.064 0.013 1.22, 3.32 +0.055 0.576

The real series plus injection reverses the ranking on ramps and steps, and the two baselines disagree. Every weekly fit scores 0.012 to 0.017 there, against 0.020 for the season-year constant. The free and symmetric fits also beat the constant on steps (0.009 and 0.010 against 0.014) and on falls (0.007 each against 0.035), while the frozen fit is worse on falls (0.039 against 0.035). The semi-synthetic baseline favours the constant by construction, because it subtracts the season-year constant fit and so removes that fit's own sampling error. The plan scores condition (i) on the worse of the two baselines, which for the frozen fit is the semi-synthetic baseline.

The frozen pair fails five of the six pre-registered conditions. Condition (i), a median path error of at most 0.15 on ramps and steps, passes at 0.040. A flat path that detects nothing scores 0.097 there, so condition (i) is nearly trivial. Condition (ii) needs the upper limit of C2 below -0.20, and C2 is +0.400. On the plan's main interval, which resamples the 8 Primaries only, C2 has 95% interval [+0.029, +0.634]. The two-way interval, which then resamples farm-seeds within each drawn Primary, is [-0.078, +0.773]. The post hoc pair's C2 is +1.193, with a Primaries-only interval of [+0.296, +1.708] and a two-way interval of [+0.272, +1.809]. Condition (iii), false steps, fails at a median of 0.66 and a worst of 1.43 on the constant path (the placebo sky gives 0.07 and 0.54). Condition (iv), the drift, is +0.137 on the constant path and +0.090 on the placebo sky against a limit of 0.05. Condition (v), the fall, recovers 0.000 of a 26-week fall and 0.000 of an 8-week fall. Condition (vi), interval coverage, is 0.620 of non-step weeks and 0.347 of step weeks.

Figure 7 shows the path error by family of injected change. For ramps the season-year constant scores 0.032 (95% interval 0.027 to 0.053), the frozen fit 0.041 (0.034 to 0.053), and the free weekly fit 0.151 (0.104 to 0.239). For steps the scores are 0.024 (0.018 to 0.043), 0.037 (0.026 to 0.052), and 0.164 (0.107 to 0.251). On the real series plus injection every fit scores between 0.009 and 0.026 on ramps and steps, because that scoring compares paths fitted with and without the injection. The verdict uses the worse of the two scorings.

The penalty does most of its work against noise: the frozen fit cut the free weekly fit's path error by 0.12. On steps of 10% or more, the frozen fit's path error minus the free weekly fit's is -0.120 (95% interval -0.212 to -0.069), and on ramps -0.110 (-0.198 to -0.066). The frozen fit and the strictly non-decreasing fit differ by 0.000 (-0.002 to 0.000) on temporary falls. The frozen pair is the strictly non-decreasing fit in practice.

Figure 9 shows that only the symmetric, free weekly, and post hoc fits follow a fall. The post hoc pair recovered 0.576 of a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks and 0.518 of one lasting 8 weeks, so the post hoc pair also follows a short fall, which the plan wanted held back (below 0.5).

The smallest detectable step of the frozen pair is above 25% of capacity. At the frozen pair, 6 of the 8 Primaries have no step size (5%, 10%, 20%, or 30%) detected in 80% of injections in either season, and 2 Primaries (Donington and Wrangle T2) reach 30% from April to September only. A 10% step, which was the step the series was meant to show, is detected in 0.00 to 0.33 of injections at every Primary. The free weekly fit detects far more steps, with many false steps: it reaches 80% for 5% steps at 3 of the 8 Primaries from April to September (and at 2 from October to March), and for 10% steps at 5 (and at 3), with a median of 11.60 false steps per Primary-year. The detection curves are in figure 8.

A real-time estimate is worse than the final fit. On injections, the latest completed week of a real-time vintage has a path error of 0.122, against 0.027 for the same week in the final fit (ratio 3.63, limit 2.0). The ratio falls to 2.43 at 8 weeks of age, 1.95 at 13 weeks, and 1.63 at 26 weeks (figure 12).

The intervals under-cover. The 90% residual block bootstrap refits the whole path. It covered 0.620 of non-step weeks and 0.347 of step weeks for the frozen pair, and 0.708 and 0.470 for the post hoc pair, against the plan's 0.85 to 0.95 and at least 0.60 (figure 13). The coverage is scored on 94 bootstrapped units. The plan said 96, but two Mount Bridge Boston units could not be built. Every interval is clipped to include the point estimate, and the clipping touched 12.0% of observed weeks for the post hoc pair, 3.4% for the frozen pair, 1.4% for the free weekly fit, and 0.0% for the season-year constant.

docs.title: On the real series
docs.text:
On the real series the free weekly fit swings too much to read, and the season-year constant is the series to read. The count of weekly changes of 2% of capacity or more at Kirton is 105 rises and 113 falls for the free weekly fit over 359 weeks, 12 rises and 17 falls for the post hoc pair, 1 rise and 0 falls for the frozen pair, and 3 rises and 3 falls for the season-year constant. The season-year constant rises from 2.294 to 4.400 MW at Donington and from 2.080 to 4.241 MW at Mount Bridge Boston (means of the first and last 4 observed weeks). The recommended series for SW2-10 is the season-year constant, chosen after the held-out scoring results were seen.

Figure 14 shows that the season-year constant and the post hoc path agree on level from about 2021 and differ within each year. At the 2019 and 2020 starts they differ in level (means of the first 4 observed weeks): the season-year constant is 2.758 MW at Horncastle against 1.244 MW for the post hoc path, 1.847 against 1.196 MW at Spilsby, and 2.080 against 1.081 MW at Mount Bridge Boston. Mount Bridge Boston has 198 unobserved weeks of 354 (weeks with fewer than 3 usable days), and its season-year constant falls to about 0 MW from 2023-09-04 to 2025-08-25 (104 weeks, all unobserved). Those weeks must not be read.

The outside checks are partial counts and are descriptive. Of the 14 level comparisons against the national small-scale solar statistics (DESNZ), 3 pass, 9 fail, and 2 are report-only. Of the 27 Primary-years, the season-year constant lies inside experiment 00040's interval in 18, and the post hoc path in 19, both below the plan's 80% bar. The Embedded Capacity Register total is at or below the series' upper bound at 6 of 6 comparisons. Only the DESNZ local-authority series could be tested for growth (1 pass and 5 inconclusive), and the Feed-in Tariff register and the constituency table could not. Every source is a floor or a partial count, so a ratio below 1 is expected and a mismatch does not show the series is wrong (figure 16).

docs.title: Limits that remain
docs.text:
The review of the code left these limits in place. Each affects how far a number can be trusted.

  • The detection metric has no false-alarm control. A fit that rises at every week would count as detecting every step.
  • Condition (i) is nearly trivial. A flat estimator scores 0.097 on ramps and steps, against the limit of 0.15.
  • Path error and false steps are scored on observed weeks only. Mount Bridge Boston has 198 of 354 weeks unobserved.
  • The post hoc intervals are clipped to the point estimate in 12.0% of weeks.
  • The constant-path false-step threshold is reported on two bases. The median at the frozen pair is 0.66 when a step is 10% of the real series' mean capacity and 0.36 when it is 10% of the injected capacity. The post hoc pair gives 1.22 and 0.77. The condition uses the first basis.
  • The season-year constant's own sampling error cancels by construction, because the baseline subtracts the season-year constant fit, which favours that arm on the semi-synthetic baseline.
  • The drift limit has a floor for short series, and Wrangle T1 and T2 have only 76 and 74 weeks.
  • The post hoc pair was chosen and scored after the frozen pair failed. No number for it carries the weight of a pre-registered score.

The four figures above carry the argument. The others are linked here.
