docs.title: Splits for sunshine-dependent demand, and the temperature read
docs.text:
The splits do not show that the knee comes from demand that rises with sunshine, or that it does not. Demand such as cooling or visitor load at coastal resorts rises with sunshine and would mimic a clipping knee. Of the 5 Primaries, 2 are within 10 km of the open coast, so the coastal split compares 2 series with 3. The slope above each series' own knee is 24.1 at the 2 coastal series and 22.7 at the other 3. It is 25.2 on term-time weekdays and 17.3 on school-holiday weeks and weekends; these are point estimates with no intervals. The hinge is lower than the line by 0.161 points (-0.282 to -0.038, 10 weekly blocks) in holiday-and-weekend rows, and by 0.081 points (-0.253 to +0.097) on term-time weekdays. Of the 7 scopes read (all rows, day+2 and day+3, sunny, coastal, inland, term-time weekdays, and holiday-and-weekend), this is the only one whose interval excludes 0. Chance alone would produce about 1 such interval in 7. The holiday period (22 July to 31 August) also covers most of August, so the split confounds holiday demand with the month.

At fixed clear-sky index, the sunniest rows' error rises with 2 m temperature, and demand is only one explanation. The rise is 0.67 points per kelvin (0.21 to 1.15), from the mean of e in three temperature bands within each series and 0.1-wide index bin (-2.27, -0.17, and +2.49 points in the coolest, middle, and warmest band). Demand that rises with heat could cause it. So could panel temperature: output of crystalline-silicon panels falls by roughly 0.4% per kelvin, so a shift that ignores cell temperature over-states the panels' output on hot days. This page did not check whether the CAMS unit output models cell temperature. Hot rows also cluster in few weeks (8 weekly blocks in the warmest sunny band), and d1l already takes temperature as an input.

docs.title: Noisy ENS members add to the loss (cause c)
docs.text:
The member spread adds 0.129 points to the ENS shift's score at day+2 and day+3, which is under half of the 0.324-point loss of the ENS shift against d0. The table gives the quantile score of the first arm minus the second, at day+2 and day+3 pooled (2,340 cases), with its interval. Cause c is met as the rule is written, because the interval of the ENS-shift-minus-ensemble-mean-shift row lies wholly above 0 and 0.129 exceeds half of the ENS-shift-minus-d1l difference (0.057). The rule compares with d1l, and the lead above compares with d0. The test is weak: the interval of the ENS-shift-minus-d1l row spans 0, so almost any positive spread effect would pass it.

Contrast (negative favours the first arm) Difference (95% interval) ENS shift minus d0 (experiment 46's C6) +0.324 (-0.144 to +0.761) ENS shift minus d1l (experiment 46's C3) +0.057 (-0.495 to +0.570) ENS shift minus ensemble-mean shift (cause c) +0.129 (+0.057 to +0.212) Ensemble-mean shift minus d1l -0.072 (-0.625 to +0.441) Fitted-coefficient ENS shift minus ENS shift (post hoc) -0.435 (-0.689 to -0.139) Fitted-coefficient ENS shift minus d0 (post hoc) -0.111 (-0.348 to +0.110)

The loss that prompted the experiment reproduces: experiment 46's C6 is +0.477 (+0.057 to +0.842) at day+2 and +0.172 (-0.580 to +0.807) at day+3. Over the two days pooled, the interval of C6 includes 0 when 13 weeks are resampled, so the loss is small and uncertain here. The fitted-coefficient shift of experiment 46, fitted on its training window, removes the loss: it scores +0.004 (-0.255 to +0.241) against d0 at day+2 (post hoc, with a wide interval). The oracle shift puts too few sunny actuals below the 0.05 quantile as well (0.002 to 0.015, against 0.05; the ENS shift puts 0.010 to 0.027 there), so member noise cannot be the only source of a lower tail that is too wide.

docs.title: What it could not show
docs.text:
• The hinge test has little power. Its half-width is 0.13 points, as set out under cause a.
  • The folds are weeks of the valid time. One forecast run spans up to 3 valid middays and can fall into both folds, which mildly favours every repair. The intervals resample fixed fits and are somewhat narrow. The free intercept of the hinge and the line favours both against the coefficient repair.
  • Hour of day and month are untested as causes. The 2 hour bins differ by at most 0.09 within a month, and the month differences come from one summer.
  • The coastal flag rests on a coarse coastline (7 coastline points and a 10 km threshold), and 2 of 5 Primaries qualify.
  • The experiment cannot say which of the six causes of a slope below 1 is at work. Several can act together.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: A design for PVDIS-5 (the planned retest of the solar term with weekly capacity estimates) could fit the solar coefficient per lead band and season on the ENS shift, test non-inferiority against d0, and report no clipping knee. The margin of 0.10 points of capacity was set in the plan: it is about 2% of d0's mean quantile score of 4.62 points, and close to the 0.104 points by which d0's radiation inputs improved on d1l over April to September. A margin as large as the whole effect of the radiation inputs is generous. On these summer-midday rows the gap between d1l and d0 is about 0.27 points. The PVDIS-5 plan could confirm 0.10 or halve it to 0.05 after a power calculation. Non-inferiority means the upper end of the 95% interval of (solar term minus d0) lies below the margin. The fitted shift's upper end here is +0.110 over 13 weeks at day+2 and day+3 (post hoc), and the half-width of about 0.23 would fall to about 0.16 with 25 weeks, so a pass at 0.10 needs a true difference below about -0.06. Resampling at least 25 weeks of forecast start (April to September) and repeating the test for 0 to 48 hours separately would be sensible. A per-Primary clipping knee would need a different design: rows at or near the inverters' rated output, such as the clearest days at midday, a hinge fitted after the coefficient repair, and more than two coastal series.

docs.title: Experiment 52: do more weather forecasts lower the wind farms' error at 1 to 2 days ahead?
docs.text:
Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts did not resolve any gain at 1 to 2 days ahead. The best guess is the quantile forecast of wind-farm power from experiment 33. It is built from the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast (ENS) and a wind-power model trained on ERA5, the ECMWF estimate of past weather. We fed that wind-power model the 100 m wind forecast of ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional weather model) and of the ECMWF high-resolution forecast (IFS, on a 0.25 degree grid). We then averaged each quantile with the best guess's, using weights chosen only on earlier months. Over the three metered wind farms, the average scored 0.055 points of capacity better (a lower quantile score is better) than the best guess at lead days 1 and 2. The 95% interval, -0.200 to +0.072, includes zero, so the experiment cannot say whether the extra forecasts help.

Inconclusive: at lead days 1 and 2, the primary blend (the best guess averaged with ICON-EU and IFS) scores 0.055 points of capacity better, with a 95% interval of -0.200 to +0.072. A lead day counts calendar days from the date of the ENS run, so lead days 1 and 2 are the two days after the run's date. This decisive contrast (C1) must lie wholly below -0.15 for the verdict supported. The same contrast over all leads (C2) is +0.018 (-0.020 to +0.054) and does not change the verdict. The intervals resample whole months and the three seeds, so they describe these three farms and cannot speak for other farms. The prediction (-0.2 to -0.4 at days 1 and 2) was too large.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
The blend scores 0.055 points better at lead days 1 and 2, 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6 (because of the spread factor), and the same from day 7, where no product exists. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better). Coverage is the share of cases inside the 5% to 95% band, which is nominally 0.90. At lead days 1 and 2 the share of cases above the 0.95 quantile is 0.053 for the best guess and 0.056 for the blend. The cases are three farms, three seeds, and the 53 Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026.

Scope Best guess Primary blend Cases Coverage, best guess Coverage, blend Lead day 0 6.722 6.525 13,695 0.902 0.903 Lead days 1 and 2 6.701 6.646 44,328 0.909 0.901 Lead days 3 to 6 9.702 9.824 88,716 0.909 0.917 Lead days 7 and later 13.154 13.154 174,624 0.916 0.916 All leads 11.037 11.054 321,363 0.912 0.914

Per farm, the two arms differ by at most 0.07 points over all leads. The best guess scores 10.67, 12.38, and 10.06 at W1, W2, and W3, and the primary blend 10.68, 12.36, and 10.13.

docs.title: What else the numbers show
docs.text:
All reads in this section are exploratory.

  • The farms disagree at lead days 1 and 2. The primary blend minus the best guess is -0.087 (-0.330 to +0.156) at W1, -0.233 (-0.447 to -0.035) at W2, and +0.151 (+0.028 to +0.287) at W3.

  • The blend scores worse at lead days 3 to 6 only because of the spread factor. The primary blend minus the best guess is +0.122 (+0.028 to +0.221) at days 3 to 6, and +0.005 (0.000 to +0.016) without the spread factor. From August the chosen weights there are 1, 0, and 0, so the blend equals the best guess, but the spread factor (1.65 in August, 1.35 in September, 1.2 in October) was fitted on earlier months blended under other weights. At day 0 the contrast is -0.197 (-0.460 to +0.051).
  • At day 0, 8 of the 16 blend contrasts exclude zero. They are all four with GFS, the two one-weight arms with ICON-EU alone, and the two one-weight arms with ICON-EU and IFS. The best guess averaged with the US Global Forecast System (GFS), also from the Open-Meteo archive, scores -0.229 (-0.371 to -0.090). These reads are many, correlated, and chosen after the fact.
  • No single extra product resolves a gain at lead days 1 and 2. The best guess averaged with ICON-EU only gives -0.053 (-0.199 to +0.079), with IFS only +0.071 (-0.034 to +0.185), and with GFS only -0.069 (-0.172 to +0.034). The IFS arm with one weight is worse, +0.101 (+0.036 to +0.194).
  • Each product's own forecast is far worse than the best guess at lead days 1 and 2. With a spread factor (a multiplier that widens each quantile band about its median), ICON-EU's own forecast scores 2.469 points worse, IFS's 1.264, and GFS's 1.853. The wind-power model receives raw product winds with no bias correction, so the gap may reflect that mismatch and not only the ensemble's advantage; the experiment does not test which.

Over the first 6 months, the plan's stop rule (drop any product more than 1.0 points worse) fired for all three products. The exploratory arms ran for all three products anyway, and the primary arm was fixed before the run. - At lead days 1 and 2, the chosen weights stayed mostly on the best guess. Averaged over the scored months, days 1 and 2 gave 0.72 to the best guess, 0.24 to ICON-EU, and 0.05 to IFS. Day 0 gave 0.51, 0.34, and 0.15. Days 3 to 6 gave 0.94, 0.03, and 0.03, which is 1, 0, and 0 in every month from August; July, with no history, used equal weights. One weight for all leads (-0.060, -0.200 to +0.065, at days 1 and 2) scored about the same as weights per lead band (-0.055). - Widening the quantile bands with a spread factor did not help. Without it, the primary blend minus the best guess is -0.080 (-0.217 to +0.039) at lead days 1 and 2 and -0.018 (-0.043 to +0.005) over all leads. The factors ranged 1.0 to 1.25 for days 0 to 2 and 1.0 to 1.65 for days 3 and later. - The placebo passes: weight selection rejected the shuffled forecasts, and its positive score comes from two other steps. The placebo shuffles the product forecasts among cases of the same farm, month, lead day, and time of day. In every month after July the chosen weights are 1, 0, and 0, so the placebo equals the best guess apart from July (equal weights, no history) and the spread step. It scores +0.343 (+0.061 to +0.762) at lead days 1 and 2.

docs.title: How the experiment was run, and where it departs from the plan
docs.text:
• Cases and benchmark: the 53 Tuesday runs of experiment 33's wind best guess (bg_full), three farms and three seeds, scored on its stored half-hourly cases. The farms are labelled W1 to W3.
  • Product age: previous_day(d+1) selects runs about half a day older than the ENS run (0 to 24 hours older, depending on the hour of day). The service reads at 09:00 UTC, so the 00 UTC runs of ICON-EU and IFS from the ENS run's own date would be available. The experiment therefore tests deliberately aged products, which rules out lookahead and handicaps the products.
  • July: July 2025 has no earlier months, so it uses equal weights and no spread factor. At lead days 1 and 2 the primary blend minus the best guess is +0.188 in July, against a mean of -0.070 over the other eleven monthly differences, and July's cases shape the factors of August onwards.
  • Product forecast: experiment 33's ERA5-trained wind-power model, refitted per seed on valid times before 2025-06-17, fed each product's wind at the farm's grid point from Open-Meteo's Previous Runs archive. A case at lead day d reads previous_day(d+1), which the archive defines as a run initialised at least that many days before the hour, so the run was initialised no later than 00 UTC on the ENS run's date. The experiment did not check that definition against the archive itself; the matched-lead study checked it on GFS for 2 days. A case beyond a product's horizon (ICON-EU after lead day 3) or with a missing value keeps the best guess.
  • Blend: the average of each quantile level, with weights on a grid of quarters chosen per lead band on earlier months only, then a spread factor fitted on earlier cases. The spread factor is fitted for lead days 0 to 2 pooled and days 3 and later pooled, so that each fit has enough cases; the plan said per lead band. A half-hour valid time takes its speed and direction from the averaged east-west and north-south wind components of the two hours either side.
  • Not run: the solar arm (the matched-lead study found no solar gain at this lead), AIFS (the ECMWF machine-learning forecast, which needs its own rows because its weather-model version changes over time), and the climatology row.
  • ICON-EU's mean 100 m wind speed is highest (8.90 m/s) and IFS's lowest (7.56), against 8.18 for ERA5. GFS is 8.00. Each product's mean covers only the cases it covers, so the comparison flags a bias without measuring it. ICON-EU's 100 m wind is Open-Meteo's rescaling of its 120 m level.
  • The plan and code reviews found no leakage. The Sonnet code review noted that the availability check in e00052_fit.py cannot fire, because the lead rule already guarantees availability. Code: ml-experiments/00052-more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms/.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Whether the products help when read at the service's own time. The next experiment should feed the 00 UTC runs of ICON-EU and IFS from the ENS run's own date, correct each product's wind speed for bias, and fit the spread factor on blends made under the same weights. A day 0 test needs more wind farms than the three metered ones can supply, and the day 0 reads here (GFS in particular) were generated after the fact, so a confirmation must name them in advance.

docs.title: Experiment 53: does the UKV forecast the solar anomaly better than ENS?
docs.text:
We asked whether the Met Office UKV (a 2 km weather model of the United Kingdom that runs to 2 to 5 days ahead) predicts how sunny each half-hour will be better than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble forecast (ENS) that the forecast uses today. We converted each forecast's sunshine into the output of a generic solar fleet, subtracted that forecast's own monthly average for each half-hour of the day (the "anomaly"), and compared the result with the anomaly of satellite-based sunshine estimates from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) at 5 Primary substations, on 72 forecast runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The UKV alone was worse than ENS at every lead time. A mix of ENS and UKV, with weights fitted on the earlier 15 months, had a squared error 4% to 14% lower than ENS within 2 days in a cross-validation on those 15 months. In the validation year its correlation with CAMS was higher than ENS's by only 0.02 to 0.03 within 24 hours, and several of those gains are within the range that chance alone could produce. The mix was no better beyond 54 hours. The one UKV we found with a long matching history is the CEDA archive, which differs from the live UKV and is licensed for non-commercial use, so any gain is an upper bound. This experiment was run post hoc and was not pre-registered, as explained below.

The verdict is small gain for the blend, and no gain for the UKV alone. The blend clears the 1% cross-validation margin of the stage 1 gate in every lead band within 54 hours, and the UKV alone clears it in none (relative mean squared error +12% to +31% against ENS). The gate therefore does not stop the experiment as refuted, and the verdict follows the pre-stated all-months gate. The correlation evidence from the validation year is weaker than the gate: the blend-minus-ENS interval touches zero at 0 to 6 hours (+0.019, -0.000 to +0.038) and includes zero over 0 to 54 hours (+0.011, -0.006 to +0.027), and at 48 to 54 hours the blend's validation mean squared error (0.0382) is worse than ENS's (0.0337), although the cross-validation says the blend is 3.8% better there. As the brief says, the experiment stops at the gate: the demand contrasts were not run, and the manager decides whether to run them (see "The demand step was not run").

What was fixed beforehand and what was chosen after seeing results. The brief for PVDIS-8b and the PVDIS-8 plan fixed the three arms (ENS, UKV alone, a fitted blend), the lead bands, the 1% margin, and the 15-fold month-block cross-validation before any score existed. No prediction was written down. The ukv3w control and the t54_late variant were added after the first scores were seen, so they are post hoc, and neither changes the verdict.

All figures are for 5 Primary substations (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16, anonymised as in experiment 46), daylight half-hours of April to September, valid from July 2025 to June 2026, on 72 forecast runs (one every 5 days). The 1,000 to 4,714 half-hour rows per lead band come from only 6 or 7 calendar months of forecast origin (July to September 2025 and March to June 2026), so every interval below, which resamples those months, understates the true uncertainty.

docs.title: What was compared, and when each forecast would have been available
docs.text:
Lead is counted from the forecast origin that the production service has, which is the 00 UTC ENS run plus 9 hours, 09:00 UTC. Each arm uses the freshest forecast available at that origin.

  • ENS is the daily 00 UTC run, as in experiment 46.
  • UKV, t54 is the 06 UTC run of the same day (leads to 54 hours from the run, so to 51 hours from the origin), assuming a run is available 3 hours after its initialisation.
  • UKV, t120 is the 03 UTC run of the same day, whose T120 files reach 120 hours from the run (114 hours from the origin, since the run starts 6 hours before the origin).
  • UKV, t54_late is the 00 UTC run of the same day, a sensitivity check that assumes the 06 UTC run is not yet available (leads to 45 hours from the origin).
  • CAMS is the reference: experiment 39's half-hour irradiance for the substation, kept where CAMS reliability is at least 0.9.

The five arms are ENS alone, the UKV alone (native steps), the blend, and two controls that separate the time resolution of the UKV from its skill. Control ukv3h subsamples the UKV to ENS's 3-hourly steps and passes the instantaneous values through the production ENS resampler, labelled as if they were ENS's 3-hour window means, as the maintainer asked. Control ukv3w first forms 3-hour window means from the UKV (the trapezoid mean of the instantaneous values inside each window) and then uses the same resampler. The second control was added after the first scores because the first has a half-window timing error built in: in the hour-of-day figure below, the mean fleet output u of ukv3h peaks at 10 UTC, while CAMS, ENS, the UKV, and ukv3w all peak at 12 UTC.

The calibration is a slope through the origin of the CAMS anomaly on a forecast's anomaly, fitted per series and lead band on the training window (valid times to 2025-06-30), leaving out site-band cells with fewer than 50 fitting rows. The blend regresses the CAMS anomaly on the ENS and UKV anomalies, with two coefficients and no intercept, and its weights are fitted rather than equal. Fitted on the whole training window, the ENS weight is 0.57 to 0.83 per series and band and the UKV weight is 0.17 to 0.46, with no negative weight (t54).

Each source's climatology keeps, for every valid time, the run with the shortest lead. The same rule applies to ENS, the UKV, and the controls, so they have the same lead mix. Experiment 46 averages its ENS climatology over all leads instead. The two ENS climatologies correlate at 0.998, and the rebuilt ENS anomaly correlates with experiment 46's calibrated ENS anomaly at 0.986 to 0.989 (t120, t54, t54_late). That difference follows from the lead rule and is not a defect, so the script requires only a correlation above 0.98.

The cross-validation removes the held-out month from the climatology. The fitted climatology therefore uses the neighbouring months only for a held-out month other than April to June, which has two neighbours inside the window, while the validation scores use the full 15-month climatology. This affects every arm alike.

The latency of the 06 UTC run is assumed, not measured. The t54 arm assumes that the 06 UTC run is available 3 hours after its initialisation, so just in time for the 09:00 UTC origin, with no slack. No source for the real delivery time of the live UKV was checked. The t54_late and t120 arms are the cautious readings. The latency at which the blend's gain would disappear was not measured: even when the 06 UTC run is replaced by the 00 UTC run (a delay of more than 3 hours), the blend's cross-validated error is still 3.6% to 7.7% lower in every band.

docs.title: Shortwave conventions and how each was aligned with CAMS
docs.text:
CAMS and ENS are half-hour or window means labelled at the period end, and the UKV and MOGREPS-UK are instantaneous values, so only the UKV and MOGREPS-UK need the interpolation.

Source Shortwave convention Valid-time stamp Alignment with CAMS CAMS (experiment 39) Half-hour mean irradiance End of the half-hour None needed ENS Mean over the native window (3 hours to 144 hours, 6 hours after) End of the window The production resampler _upsample_nwp_to_half_hourly shapes each window by the clear-sky index and conserves its energy, giving half-hour means ending at the stamp CEDA UKV, shortwave_down Instantaneous flux, not a mean The instant, init time plus step; hourly steps to 48 hours, then 3-hourly The clear-sky index (flux over the Haurwitz clear-sky flux at the same instant) at each step is interpolated linearly in time to the midpoint of each half-hour, then multiplied by the clear-sky flux at that midpoint MOGREPS-UK, shortwave_total Instantaneous, as the archive notes (no cell methods or time bounds in the files) The instant; hourly steps The same as the UKV

The same fleet chain then turns each half-hour irradiance into u. A clear-sky index is only formed where the clear-sky flux is at least 20 W/m2, and a midpoint more than 3 hours from a usable step takes the nearest step's index, so nothing is interpolated across a night. Beyond 48 hours the native UKV steps are 3-hourly, so the interpolation there spans 3 hours. The index is capped at 1.5. Each site's UKV value is the cell whose centre is nearest (the largest distance is 1.09 km).

docs.title: Raw data first
docs.text:
The UKV anomaly follows the CAMS anomaly, with a wider scatter than ENS. The panels show the calibrated forecast anomaly against the CAMS anomaly at leads under 24 hours. The ukv3h control is visibly the worst, with a flat top.

All sources peak at 12 UTC, as CAMS does, so no label is shifted, except the ukv3h control, whose mean u peaks at 10 UTC. The UKV's mean u is 0.875 of CAMS's at leads under 24 hours and ENS's mean u is 1.023 of CAMS's. A multiplicative bias of the UKV does not affect its anomaly, which is taken against its own climatology.

The number of blocks with a higher correlation is 5, 6, 5, 5, 3, 3, and 5 of 7 in the same bands.

Time resolution is not what limits the UKV. The ukv3w control, which forms 3-hour window means from the hourly UKV as ENS delivers its flux, scores 0.019 higher in correlation than the native steps over 0 to 54 hours (0.011 to 0.027) and has a lower mean squared error by 4.2% (2.3% to 6.2%). The literal ukv3h control scores 0.122 lower than the native steps over 0 to 54 hours (-0.150 to -0.093), because the instantaneous values stand in for window means, which moves the peak of its mean u from 12 UTC to 10 UTC.

docs.text:
The blend clears the 1% margin in every band within 54 hours and the UKV alone in none. The table gives the cross-validated mean squared error relative to ENS, pooled over the five verdict series (t54). The last column restricts the same cross-validation to the folds of local months April to September, the months the validation year scores. The verdict follows the all-months column, as the decision rule states.

For t120 the blend is 3.4% lower pooled over 0 to 120 hours and 1.1% lower at 54 to 120 hours, just over the 1% margin, while the validation correlation gain at 54 to 120 hours is +0.004 (-0.020 to +0.025). If the 06 UTC run were not available at the origin (t54_late), the UKV alone is worse by 18.2% to 41.5% in the bands to 48 hours, and the blend is still lower by 3.6% to 7.7% in every band.

docs.title: The check on MOGREPS-UK
docs.text:
MOGREPS-UK, the live ensemble of the Met Office, is no better than ENS on 14 days of overlap with CAMS. Its point estimates are above ENS's in some bands, but an equal-weight blend is not distinguishable from ENS. MOGREPS-UK has 3 members and about 7 weeks of archive (27 August to 16 October 2026), so nothing was calibrated or fitted. The blend here averages the two anomalies with equal weight. The check starts after the holdout date of 2026-07-01, so it uses holdout-period data that no calibration touched, outside the validation year. MOGREPS-UK is anomalised against the CAMS climatology of experiment 46, while ENS is anomalised against ENS's own climatology, so MOGREPS-UK's bias is not removed. The mean squared error of MOGREPS-UK is therefore unfavourable, and its correlation is not affected. CAMS ends on 11 September 2026, so the reference covers only 14 forecast origin days (27 August to 10 September). Correlation with the CAMS anomaly, 95% interval from resampling whole origin days:

Lead Rows ENS MOGREPS-UK Equal-weight blend 0-6 h 770 0.761 (0.572-0.866) 0.654 (0.426-0.795) 0.768 (0.551-0.864) 6-12 h 490 0.582 (0.135-0.813) 0.645 (0.384-0.813) 0.656 (0.359-0.837) 12-24 h 291 0.787 (0.562-0.885) 0.795 (0.598-0.882) 0.832 (0.611-0.915) 24-48 h 1,501 0.690 (0.502-0.795) 0.438 (0.204-0.631) 0.637 (0.421-0.764) 48-54 h 720 0.414 (-0.089-0.791) 0.418 (0.139-0.578) 0.481 (0.104-0.723) 54-120 h 3,063 0.393 (0.178-0.593) 0.310 (0.176-0.447) 0.394 (0.217-0.565) 0-24 h 1,551 0.741 (0.584-0.847) 0.627 (0.416-0.771) 0.742 (0.538-0.845)

At 6 to 12 hours, 12 to 24 hours, and 48 to 54 hours, the point estimates of MOGREPS-UK and of the blend are above ENS's, but every interval overlaps ENS's widely, on 12 to 14 days. Over all 49 origin days from 27 August 2026, the MOGREPS-UK anomaly correlates with the ENS anomaly at 0.768 within 24 hours, 0.699 at 24 to 54 hours, and 0.545 at 54 to 120 hours. That correlation between the two anomalies is not a skill score, because neither anomaly is the reference. MOGREPS-UK's mean u is 0.303 against ENS's 0.373 and CAMS's 0.378 on those rows.

docs.title: The demand step was not run
docs.text: Experiment 46's contrasts C3 and C6 (the demand forecast with the solar term, at 0 to 48 hours) were not run with the blend. The blend's gain is a ceiling from a product that is not the live one (the CEDA UKV) and whose licence is non-commercial. The interval of the blend's gain over ENS across 0 to 54 hours includes zero (+0.011, -0.006 to +0.027). The scores here predict a change in the demand contrast of the order of a 0.02 gain in correlation, which experiment 46's intervals (half-widths of 0.13 to 0.32 points of capacity at 0 to 48 hours) could not resolve. A non-live product with a licence that forbids production is a weak case for the spend, so the manager decides whether to run the contrasts.

docs.title: What these data could not show
docs.text:
• The live UKV is not the CEDA UKV. The CEDA archive differs statistically from the live feed, the CEDA licence is non-commercial, and the live product has no history at the Primaries, so the blend's gain is a ceiling.
  • The delivery delay of the 06 UTC run is assumed. See "What was compared" above: it was not measured, and the blend's gain survived the t54_late reading, so no latency at which it disappears was found.
  • The demand-forecast effect is untested. A 0.02 gain in correlation of the anomaly need not carry through experiment 46's solar term, whose coefficient the residual fitted below 1.
  • The 48 to 54 hour band is thin. It holds 1,225 rows from leads of 48 to 51 hours and its intervals are wide.
  • Calibration and the blend use 15 months. Each source's climatology is fitted on the same 15 months, with neighbouring local months pooled as in experiment 46.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The manager decides whether to run experiment 46's C3 and C6 contrasts at 0 to 48 hours with the blend's anomaly. See "The demand step was not run" for why the case is weak.

docs.title: Experiment 54: does UKV, learned from its own history, help the wind-farm forecast?
docs.text:
Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to a wind-farm forecast that already uses the European Centre's ensemble (ENS) lowered the error by about 0.2 points of the farms' capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead, a small but real gain, so the verdict is small gain. The error is the quantile score, a measure of how well a forecast's range of likely power fits what happened, and 1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity. The 95% interval is 0.07 to 0.32 points, so the 0.15-point gain we decided in advance would justify a new weather feed lies inside it. UKV, the Met Office's 2 km weather forecast, adds information and does not replace ENS: UKV alone scores 0.88 points worse than ENS alone. The UKV data come from a research archive (CEDA), not the live feed, so even this is an upper limit on what a service could get. We tested it by training XGBoost models, each on its own forecast history, for three metered wind farms, with the same training window and settings, at 24 to 54 hours after the ENS run's 00 UTC start (UKV's forecasts stop at 54 hours). The next step is to find or build a live UKV history for the farms, or to test UKV at lead day 0, the first 24 hours, where a live history exists.

UKV helps as an addition to ENS, and the gain is not an artefact of extra columns. The placebo (the UKV values shuffled among similar rows) differs from ENS alone by no more than 0.04 points (+0.013, -0.012 to +0.040). At W1 the gain is clear (-0.413), at W2 it probably exists (-0.198, with the end of its interval nearest zero at -0.000), and at W3 there is none (+0.018). The 95% interval excludes a gain larger than 0.32 points at these three farms. The ENS-only model scored 0.218 points better than experiment 33's ERA5-trained best guess at these leads, but the interval (-0.472 to +0.069) includes zero, so that comparison is unresolved.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The primary contrast C1 is the ENS-plus-UKV arm minus the ENS-only arm, for cases 24 to 54 hours after the 00 UTC start of the ENS run's date. UKV's leads stop at 54 hours, so these cases are lead day 1 and the first 6 hours of lead day 2. C1 is -0.198 (95% interval -0.316 to -0.069; 28,230 cases, three farms, three seeds, whole months re-drawn), and the pre-registered threshold was -0.15 for the end of the interval nearest zero (-0.069 here). The CEDA archive is not the live product: its licence is non-commercial (from the archive's catalogue) and the UKV-CEDA blends study found it statistically different from the live feed. The page therefore reports the result as a ceiling: a gain a matched UKV might add, not one a service could now deliver. The prediction was -0.2 to -0.5, and -0.198 is at the weak end of that range.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Arm B scores best at 24 to 54 hours (5.921), and arm C, UKV alone, scores worst (7.000). The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better). Coverage is the share of cases inside the 5% to 95% band (nominally 0.90), and the 0.95 column is the share above the 0.95 quantile. Arm A is the ENS-only XGBoost model, B adds UKV, C is UKV alone, and the placebo is B with the UKV values shuffled. The reference rows are experiment 33's ERA5-trained best guess and its ENS-trained model on the same cases, which are the 52 Tuesday runs that have a complete UKV run.

Arm Lead day 0 (0 to 24 h) 24 to 54 h All cases Coverage, 24 to 54 h Above 0.95, 24 to 54 h A, ENS only 6.337 6.119 6.189 0.924 0.031 B, ENS plus UKV 5.963 5.921 5.935 0.900 0.042 C, UKV only 6.666 7.000 6.892 0.858 0.062 Placebo 6.334 6.133 6.198 0.925 0.030 Reference, ERA5-trained best guess 6.789 6.337 6.483 0.915 0.050 Reference, ENS-trained (experiment 33) 6.312 6.137 6.193 0.947 0.019

At 24 to 54 hours, arm B's band is slightly narrower than arm A's (coverage 0.900 against 0.924, and 0.042 above the 0.95 quantile against 0.031). The experiment did not test why. Per farm at 24 to 54 hours, the scores are A 5.871, 6.382, 6.109 and B 5.458, 6.184, 6.127 at W1, W2, and W3.

docs.title: What else the numbers show
docs.text:
All reads in this section are exploratory.

  • W1 gains clearly, W2 probably gains, and W3 shows no gain. B minus A at 24 to 54 hours is -0.413 (-0.686 to -0.155) at W1, -0.198 (-0.378 to -0.000, the upper end rounds to zero) at W2, and +0.018 (-0.177 to +0.219) at W3.

  • The gain holds across the UKV upgrade and without July. B minus A is -0.189 (-0.342 to -0.025) before UKV's upgrade of 2026-01-21, -0.210 (-0.387 to -0.006) after it, and -0.180 (-0.309 to -0.045) without July 2025.
  • The point estimate is larger at lead day 0. B minus A at 0 to 24 hours is -0.374 (-0.526 to -0.203), and over all cases it is -0.255 (-0.348 to -0.145). The experiment did not test whether lead day 0 differs from 24 to 54 hours, and lead day 0 lies outside the contrast.
  • The placebo differs from arm A by no more than 0.04 points. The placebo minus A is +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040) at 24 to 54 hours, and B minus the placebo is -0.211 (-0.334 to -0.076).
  • At 24 to 54 hours, UKV alone is far worse than ENS alone. C minus A is +0.881 (+0.460 to +1.308) at 24 to 54 hours and +0.329 (-0.113 to +0.795) at lead day 0.
  • ENS plus UKV beats the ERA5-trained best guess. B minus the best guess is -0.416 (-0.693 to -0.136) at 24 to 54 hours and -0.826 (-1.586 to -0.103) at lead day 0.
  • The ENS-only model scores 0.218 better than the best guess, an unresolved difference. The difference is -0.218 (-0.472 to +0.069) at 24 to 54 hours, and the experiment 33 ENS-trained model minus A is +0.018 (-0.026 to +0.064). Experiment 1 had the ERA5-trained model ahead by 1.70 points; this contrast covers only the first 54 hours.
  • UKV's wind speed is lower than ENS's. Over the scored cases, UKV's mean 10 m wind speed is 4.46 m/s against 5.00 m/s for the ENS control member.

docs.title: How the experiment was run
docs.text:
• Arms: every arm is an XGBoost model with nine quantile levels, trained per farm and per seed (0, 1, and 2) with experiment 33's recipe for its ENS-trained model: the ENS control member of the daily 00 UTC runs from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, recency weights with a half-life of 2 years, lead_hours, and three lags of power from the 09:00 UTC origin. The three farms have 40,864, 40,876, and 40,846 training rows (W1, W2, W3), identical for every arm. Arm B runs once per ENS member with the UKV columns fixed, and the 51 member quantile sets are pooled.
  • UKV: the CEDA archive's 00 UTC run of the ENS run's date, at each farm's nearest 2 km cell (0.9 to 1.1 km away). The four columns are 10 m speed, the sine and cosine of the 10 m direction, and the speed at 925 hPa, because the archive holds no 100 m wind. The store lacks hourly steps 49, 50, 52, and 53, which are interpolated linearly, and a valid time at :30 averages the east-west and north-south components of the hours either side. All 455 of the 456 training runs and 52 of the 53 validation Tuesday runs have a complete UKV wind set at each farm; the run of 2026-06-30 is missing and its cases are dropped from every arm.
  • Latency: the experiment assumes the 00 UTC UKV run is available within 8 hours of its start, from the Met Office's published schedule, and did not measure it. The service reads ENS at 09:00 UTC.
  • No matched live history: Open-Meteo's UKV history at the farms holds only previous_day1 (lead day 0), starting on 2024-08-06 and covering 71% of the training window at one farm.
  • Departures from the plan: none.
  • Code: ml-experiments/00054-product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms/. One Sonnet plan review and one Sonnet code review found no leakage; the code review noted that the UKV run coverage is counted per run in the fit script, so a separate check script counts it per farm (455 and 52 at every farm) and finds no placebo group of one row.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Whether a live UKV feed gives the same gain. The Met Office's live UKV forecast is the product a service would receive, and the CEDA archive differs from it statistically. The next experiment could build a matched history of the live UKV for the three farms, which needs a source that holds live UKV at lead days 1 and 2 (Open-Meteo's history stops at lead day 0), and rerun arms A and B on it. A second option is a lead day 0 test on Open-Meteo's live UKV, where the CEDA arm already gains -0.374.

docs.title: Experiment 55: does a neighbour veto help the single-series LSC?
docs.text: A neighbour veto makes the single-series detector slightly more precise, and at the strengths tried it finds only about 1 point more of the injected transfers. We kept every alarm of the single-series detector D0, which raises an alarm when the 24-hour mean of one Primary substation's residual (measured minus predicted power) steps up or down. We then removed the alarms that look like a weather or calendar miss, because at least two neighbouring Primary substations stepped the same way and none stepped the opposite way. With those alarms gone the threshold could fall from 4.00 to 3.70 noise units at the same rate of unexplained alarms, and the detector found 0.363 of 620 injected transfers against 0.355 without the veto (+0.008, 98.75% interval -0.003 to +0.022). The verdict is inconclusive. We tried veto strengths of 1.5, 2.0, and 3.0 noise units, and a stronger veto was not tried. D2 denotes D0 with the veto. The small gain came through the lower threshold, mostly in the transfers with no metered receiver, which are 44% of the headline band. D0 finds 0.17 of those and D2 finds 0.19, against 0.50 for the others. The gap may come from step size, because the injection gives those transfers a smaller donor step (limits).

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
C1, D2 minus D0M in the share of transfers found, is +0.008 (98.75% interval -0.003 to +0.022). D0M is D0 with its threshold chosen by the same search as D2's and no veto, so that neither detector gets a threshold step the other was not offered. The search returned D0's own thresholds (4.00 and 6.00), so D0M and D0 at experiment 43's thresholds are the same detector. The population is the 620 injected transfers that move 25% to 40% of the receiving load for over 1 day and start in even months: 89 of experiment 43's 160 and 531 of the 1,000 new ones. The rule asked for an interval wholly above zero and a point value of at least +0.01. The rule called the hypothesis refuted only if the upper end fell below +0.01. The verdict is therefore inconclusive. Of the 620 transfers, D2 finds 7 that D0M misses and misses 2 that D0M finds.

Contrast Window, transfers D2 D0M D2 minus D0M 98.75% interval C1 24 h, all (620) 0.363 0.355 +0.008 -0.003 to +0.022 C2 4 h, all (620) 0.237 0.231 +0.007 -0.004 to +0.015 C3 24 h, metered receiver (346) 0.500 0.503 -0.003 -0.007 to +0.000 C4 24 h, no metered receiver (274) 0.190 0.168 +0.022 +0.000 to +0.041

The gain sits in the transfers that have no metered receiver. For those, the lower threshold finds 6 more of 274. For transfers with a metered receiver, the veto changes nothing (-0.003). The lower end of C4 and the upper end of C3 sit at exactly zero because every changed transfer moved the same way, so read C4 as "at least 0". C1 rests on 9 changed transfers (7 gained, 2 lost).

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Held: C1 lay in the predicted 0.00 to 0.02 (+0.008, point value just under the +0.01 bar).
  • Held: the veto cost few found transfers. It removed 2 of the 220 transfers D0M finds, under the predicted 10%.
  • Partly held: the veto separates unexplained alarms from logged ones weakly. The prediction gave 18% of the unexplained odd-month alarms and 12% of the logged ones at a veto of 2.0 on the original thresholds. At the matched threshold of the chosen veto (1.5) it removes 37% of the unexplained 24-hour alarms in odd months, 35% of those in all months, and 20% of the alarms a logged closure explains, a ratio of 1.8. At 4 hours the ratio is 1.5 (38% to 25%). The 35 vetoed 24-hour alarms that a logged closure explains are spread over 12 of the 16 series.
  • Held: the confirmed tier is explained by a logged closure more often. At 24 hours 64% of confirmed alarms, 46% of unconfirmed ones, and 30% of vetoed ones lie within 24 hours of a logged closure.
  • Held at veto 2.0, exceeded at the chosen strength: the matched threshold fell by 0.15 at 2.0 (predicted 0.05 to 0.20) and by 0.30 at the chosen 1.5. Odd months chose the strongest veto, 1.5 noise units (odd-month share found 0.304, against 0.287 at 2.0 and 0.274 at 3.0). The threshold fell by 0.15 at 2.0 and 0.00 at 3.0. The strongest veto was the edge of the grid, so a stronger one was not tried.

docs.title: Precision, and what the confirmed tier tells us
docs.text:
The veto raises the precision of the real alarms by about 3 points at 24 hours and 6 to 7 points at 4 hours. In even months, the lower precision bound (alarms within 24 hours of a logged closure over all alarms) of the 24-hour detector rises from 0.441 to 0.474 and event F1 (the harmonic mean of the share found and the precision) from 0.393 to 0.411. At 4 hours the bounds rise from 0.471 and 0.528 to 0.538 and 0.588, and F1 from 0.310 and 0.321 to 0.329 and 0.338. D2 raises 137 24-hour alarms in even months against 143 for D0M, and 72 unexplained ones against 80, so D2 sits at a slightly stricter operating point, which biases the comparison against D2.

The confirmed tier is not more often a visible transfer. Of experiment 41's 148 labelled alarms, 5 of the 79 confirmed, 4 of the 49 unconfirmed, and 0 of the 20 vetoed were labelled visible transfers. The sample is too coarse to separate the tiers, so the 148 labelled alarms do not support using the confirmed tier as a training mask for the normal-running-arrangement forecast.

D2 finds 88% of the transfers with a metered receiver through an alarm that names the donor or a receiver. Of the 360 such transfers that D2 finds at 24 hours, over all months, 316 are found by such an alarm.

docs.title: Near bank holidays
docs.text: The veto loses transfers near bank holidays: of 300 transfers that start within 1 day of one, D0M finds 94 and D2 finds 90. D2 loses 6 and gains 2. The holiday set is drawn with logged closures only, and 206 of its 300 onsets lie within 2 days of an alarm of experiment 43's four settings. Under experiment 43's full quiet mask, only 94 of the 300 would have been kept (a separate count from the 94 that D0M finds). Experiment 43's 160 transfers are found at 47 (D0M) and 53 (D2), and the new 1,000 at 321 and 336.

docs.title: Real transfers
docs.text: D2 finds 2 of the 14 labelled real transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load that last over 1 day, against 1 for D0M, and 3 of the 35 labelled transfers over 1 day against 2. At 4 hours the counts are 0 of 14 and 1 of 35 for both detectors. The real-transfer counts carry no verdict.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The 0.17 against 0.50 gap mostly reflects the injection. A transfer with no metered receiver moves 25% to 40% of half the donor's load, a median step of 16% of the donor's load, while a transfer with a metered receiver has a median step of 55% (interquartile range 26% to 80%). The 44% share of the band is a property of the sampler, and not a measure of the real electricity network.
  • The veto strength sits at the edge of the grid. The strongest value, 1.5 noise units, won on odd months, where its gain over no veto was +0.030 (22 transfers gained, 6 lost) against +0.013 at 2.0 and 0.000 at 3.0. The even-month gain was +0.008, so the interval's upper end of +0.022 is not a ceiling for a stronger veto.
  • The pre-registered veto rate was checked on the alarms, not on the scored run. The prediction of 14 of 80 unexplained odd-month alarms vetoed at 2.0 noise units and threshold 4.00 comes from e00055_prerun.py; the scored run reports the rates at the chosen strength and matched threshold.
  • The 24-hour precision is a point value. The sample of 148 labelled alarms had no visible transfer among its 24-hour alarms, so the upper precision bound equals the lower. The 4-hour bounds reuse D0's sampled visible rate for D2, although the veto changes which alarms survive.
  • The injected transfers sit away from alarms. Experiment 43's quiet mask keeps the original and new sets at least 2 days from an alarm of its four settings on every series, which understates how often a wrong veto happens. The holiday set drops that condition.
  • Transfers injected in one batch could interact. A batch keeps events apart only when they share no series, so simultaneous transfers on adjacent substations could trigger or block a veto, which affects D2 and not D0M. We did not measure this.
  • D0M equals D0. The matching search returned D0's thresholds, so comparing with D0M adds nothing beyond comparing with D0.
  • The residual needs ERA5. ERA5 (the ECMWF Reanalysis, version 5) arrives about 5 days after the event, so the detectors run retrospectively.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The next experiment should show whether the missed transfers are steps too small to detect or detectable steps that the detector misses. It re-cuts recall by the donor's step in noise units, split by metered receiver, and extends the veto grid to 1.0 and 1.25 noise units. Small missed steps would argue against a better step statistic. Detectable missed steps would argue for the shape-aware switching detector planned as SW2-7. SW2-7 models the moved load as a share of the donor's expected daily profile, which is also how the injection builds transfers, so its recall on injected transfers would flatter it. The plan for SW2-7 should therefore score transfers injected with a different shape, and the 14 and 35 labelled real transfers.

Code: ml-experiments/00055-sw2-8-neighbour-veto-single-series-detector/, with every number printed by e00055_report.py.

docs.title: Experiment 56: does Flexpectation v1 need special handling at MVA-only Primaries?
docs.text: At sunny middays the best-guess forecast has 5.6 percentage points less skill at the 8 Primary substations metered only in MVA than at the 8 metered in MW, but the 95% interval (-5.0 to 14.6) includes zero, so 8 time series against 8 cannot say whether MVA metering hurts the forecast. The experiment found no evidence that Flexpectation v1 needs special handling, and could not rule out a loss of up to about 15 percentage points. A Primary substation steps the voltage down to 11 kV or 33 kV. Eight of the 16 trial-area Primaries have a meter that records signed real power in megawatts (MW). The other 8 record only the magnitude of apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA), with no sign. When embedded solar pushes a substation's net flow through zero, an MVA reading no longer shows which way the power went. We took the forecasts that experiment 33 stored for every half-hour from July 2025 to June 2026. They come from its best-guess forecast of Primary-substation demand (an XGBoost model with a 14-day error correction and a 1.15 spread factor) and from a simple rule-based forecast, manual_heuristic. Skill is the percentage by which the best guess's quantile score, the standard error measure for a probabilistic forecast, is lower than manual_heuristic's. At sunny middays (April to September, 10:00 to 13:30 UTC) the skill is 15.9% at the MW substations and 10.3% at the MVA substations. Nothing was fitted.

docs.title: Result
docs.text:
The verdict is inconclusive, by the rule fixed before the run. The rule called MVA clearly worse when the interval's lower end was above zero and the gap was 5 percentage points or more, and called Flexpectation v1 safe to ignore when the upper end was under 5. The gap is 5.6, but the lower end is below zero and the upper end is above 5. Each interval resamples whole months.

Skill is lower at the MVA substations all year, not specifically at sunny middays. Skill is pooled over a group's cases (figure 1). In all hours the MW group's skill is 15.0% and the MVA group's 4.5%, a gap of 10.5 percentage points (2.1 to 17.5). Outside sunny middays the gap is 11.2 (2.7 to 18.3). At sunny middays it is 5.6 (-5.0 to 14.6), and the MVA group's skill is higher (10.3%) than in other hours (3.7%).

Hours Best guess, MW group manual_heuristic, MW group Best guess, MVA group manual_heuristic, MVA group All hours 5.22 6.13 5.41 5.67 Sunny midday 7.23 8.60 7.47 8.34 Other hours 5.03 5.90 5.22 5.42

Pooled mean quantile score in points of capacity, July 2025 to June 2026, 16 Primary substations.

The substations are too few to separate the groups. Resampling the time series within each group, instead of the months, gives a sunny-midday gap of 5.6 percentage points with an interval of -2.8 to 14.0 (figure 2 shows each substation). The all-hours gap's interval then runs from -2.0 to 20.2, and includes zero.

Half-hours near zero flow are few, and the best guess's skill there is lower in the MVA group. Of the 403,712 half-hours scored across the 8 MVA time series, 5,904 (1.5%) have the magnitude of the power within 10% of capacity of zero, and 500 of those are at sunny middays (1.5% of 34,176). For the 8 MW time series the figures are 8,954 of 364,361 (2.5%) and 2,167 of 31,044 (7.0%). On those half-hours the best guess's skill is 18.8% in the MVA group (4.1 to 30.2) and 46.1% in the MW group (25.2 to 58.7), a gap of 27.4 percentage points (-0.3 to 48.2). Away from zero flow the gap is 7.8 (1.0 to 13.8). At sunny middays, leaving out the near-zero half-hours cuts the gap from 5.6 to 2.0 percentage points (-4.6 to 8.0). So the near-zero half-hours account for part of the sunny-midday gap, but every interval on them includes values near zero or is wide, so the data do not settle it. A second measure is the share of a substation's sunny-midday half-hours in which the magnitude of the power is under 10% of its own 99th percentile. It is 0% at 5 of the 8 MVA substations, at most 1.5% at 7 of them, and 9.0% at the highest (series 26), against 26.1% and 23.7% at 2 MW substations, series 10 and 12 (figure 3).

docs.title: Check added after seeing the results: one MW substation
docs.text: One MW substation (series 12, with 31% skill over all hours and 29.9% at sunny middays) accounts for most of the MW group's advantage. Leaving series 12 out of the MW group, and changing nothing else, moves the sunny-midday gap from 5.6 percentage points to -0.3 and the all-hours gap from 10.5 to 3.8. Leaving out any other single substation moves the sunny-midday gap by no more than 1.4. The verdict does not use this check.

docs.title: Failures and caveats
docs.text:
• Eight time series against 8 cannot exclude a skill gap of up to about 15 percentage points at sunny middays, and the groups differ in more than meter unit, such as the substations' size and solar capacity.
  • Skill is measured against manual_heuristic, which also forecasts the magnitude at the MVA substations, so the result measures a relative disadvantage.
  • Experiment 41's labeller (the tool that finds switching events in the telemetry) was to be scored on how often it found events at MVA-side against MW-side substation pairs. That optional comparison was not run.
  • Time series 7, 12, 13, and 18 have shorter histories than the other 12, so the counts of low-magnitude half-hours over each time series' whole history, which sit in the experiment's private folder, cover different periods. The figure counts only the scored year.

docs.title: Lessons for later experiments
docs.text: The experiment found no case for special handling of the MVA-only Primaries in Flexpectation v1, and no strong evidence against one; the half-hours near zero flow are the place to look next. PVDIS-7 is the planned work to recover signed MW at the MVA-only Primaries. The case for it rests on separating solar from demand, which the PVDIS series tests, and not on forecast skill. A later comparison of unit groups should use more than 8 time series or show each series, and should say which series account for the gap.

docs.title: Experiment 57: does UKV, learned from its own history, help the solar-farm forecast?
docs.text: Giving the Met Office's UK Variable-resolution (UKV) weather forecast, which has a 2 km grid, to a solar-farm forecast that already uses the 51-member ensemble forecast of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ENS) lowered the error by only about 0.03 percentage points of the farms' capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead, so the verdict is inconclusive. The error is the quantile score, which measures how well a forecast's range of likely power fits what happened (smaller is better), and 1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity. The 95% interval of the difference is -0.12 to +0.04 points. It includes zero, so the data cannot show any gain. It includes -0.10, the gain we decided in advance would justify a new weather feed, so the data also cannot rule out a gain of that size. It excludes gains above 0.12 points. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms of experiment 54, where it lowered the error by 0.2 points. An XGBoost model given only UKV scores 0.40 points worse than an XGBoost model given only ENS. We trained one XGBoost model per farm on ENS alone and another on ENS plus UKV, each fitted to the archived forecasts of the weather sources it is given, with the same training window and settings. We scored them at 24 to 54 hours after the 00 UTC start of the ENS run's date, because UKV's forecasts stop at 54 hours. If solar is worth more work, the next step is a source of a different kind, since a second numerical forecast of sunshine adds little at these leads.

docs.title: Results
docs.text: The primary contrast C1 is the ENS-plus-UKV arm minus the ENS-only arm, for cases 24 to 54 hours after the 00 UTC start of the ENS run's date. C1 is -0.035 (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037; 16,016 cases scored for each of three seeds, so 48,048 rows, six farms, whole months re-drawn). The pre-registered threshold was a gain of 0.10. The verdict is inconclusive because the interval of C1 includes both zero and -0.10. The prediction was -0.03 to -0.12, and -0.035 is at the weak end of that range. The archive of the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA) is not the live UKV product. Its licence is non-commercial, and the UKV-CEDA blends study found it statistically different from the live feed. Any gain would therefore be a ceiling and not a gain a service could now deliver.

docs.title: Absolute scores
docs.text:
Arm B scores best at 24 to 54 hours (3.105), and arm C, UKV alone, scores worst (3.544). The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over nine quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better), pooled over day and night cases; night cases score near zero for every arm. Coverage is the share of cases inside the 5% to 95% band (nominally 0.90), and the 0.95 column is the share above the 0.95 quantile (nominally 0.05). Arm A is the ENS-only XGBoost model, B adds UKV, C is UKV alone, the placebo is B with the UKV values shuffled, and B3h is B with UKV rebuilt from its 3-hourly steps. The reference rows are experiment 33's ERA5-trained best guess and its ENS-trained model on the same cases. The cases are the 52 Tuesday ENS runs that have a complete UKV run.

Arm Lead day 0 (0 to 24 h) 24 to 54 h All cases Coverage, 24 to 54 h Above 0.95, 24 to 54 h A, ENS only 4.987 3.140 3.757 0.941 0.028 B, ENS plus UKV 4.957 3.105 3.724 0.938 0.028 C, UKV only 5.440 3.544 4.178 0.935 0.026 Placebo 4.992 3.142 3.760 0.941 0.028 B3h, ENS plus 3-hourly UKV 4.963 3.119 3.735 0.936 0.028 Reference, ERA5-trained best guess 5.018 3.247 3.838 0.913 0.038 Reference, ENS-trained (experiment 33) 5.220 3.283 3.931 0.950 0.023

The band is slightly too wide for every arm at 24 to 54 hours (coverage 0.935 to 0.941 against 0.90). Per farm at 24 to 54 hours, the scores are A 3.292, 2.936, 2.780, 3.461, 3.559, and 2.947 and B 3.221, 2.925, 2.738, 3.389, 3.509, and 2.978 at farms A to F.

docs.title: What else the numbers show
docs.text:
All reads in this section are exploratory.

  • The placebo and the 3-hourly control differ little from the plain arms. The placebo minus A is +0.002 (-0.007 to +0.012), so extra columns alone do nothing. B minus the 3-hourly control B3h is -0.014 (-0.049 to +0.008), so UKV's hourly steps are not what separates B from A.
  • Five of the six farms point towards a gain, one resolvably. B minus A at 24 to 54 hours is -0.070 (-0.144 to -0.009) at farm A, -0.011 (-0.119 to +0.083) at B, -0.042 (-0.115 to +0.023) at C, -0.072 (-0.221 to +0.044) at D, -0.050 (-0.137 to +0.033) at E, and +0.031 (-0.065 to +0.152) at F. Only farm A's interval excludes zero. With six farms, at least one interval excluding zero by chance happens about one time in four, and more often because the farms share weather.

  • The point estimate is more negative after UKV's upgrade. B minus A is +0.020 (-0.040 to +0.089) before the Met Office's upgrade of 2026-01-21 and -0.133 (-0.262 to -0.017) after it. The two intervals overlap, and the difference between them was not tested. The split also mixes season with upgrade (before is July to December, after is January to June) and is one of about ten exploratory splits. The XGBoost models trained wholly on pre-upgrade UKV, so the post-upgrade difference is a lead for a later test and not a result.
  • Daylight cases alone give a larger point estimate with a wider interval. B minus A at 24 to 54 hours on cases with the sun above the horizon is -0.074 (-0.259 to +0.079), which includes zero, and without July 2025 it is -0.048 (-0.137 to +0.028).
  • Lead day 0 and all leads agree with the primary read. B minus A is -0.031 (-0.121 to +0.065) at lead day 0 and -0.033 (-0.076 to +0.009) over all cases.
  • UKV alone is worse than ENS alone. C minus A is +0.404 (+0.103 to +0.764) at 24 to 54 hours and +0.453 (+0.214 to +0.710) at lead day 0.
  • The ENS-trained XGBoost model scores close to the ERA5-trained best guess. A minus the best guess is -0.107 (-0.327 to +0.053) at 24 to 54 hours, unresolved. Experiment 33's ENS-trained model scores 0.143 points worse than A (+0.087 to +0.201). Arm A is therefore not a copy of experiment 33's model, and the experiment did not find why.

docs.title: How the experiment was run
docs.text:
• Arms: every arm is an XGBoost model with nine quantile levels, trained per farm and per seed (0, 1, and 2) with experiment 33's recipe for its ENS-trained model: the ENS control member of the daily 00 UTC runs from 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-30, recency weights with a half-life of 2 years, lead_hours, and three lags of power from the 09:00 UTC origin, with no calendar column. The six farms have 37,021 to 38,768 training rows, identical for every arm. Arms A, B, the placebo, and B3h run once per ENS member and pool the 51 member quantile sets. A has 13 columns, B 16, and C 9: the three UKV columns, the solar zenith and azimuth, lead_hours, and the three lags.
  • UKV: the CEDA archive's 00 UTC run of the ENS run's date at each farm's nearest 2 km cell: downward shortwave flux, total cloud cover, and 1.5 m temperature, joined linearly between the hourly steps (3-hourly beyond 48 hours), with a half-hour as the mean of the hours either side. 455 of 456 training runs and 52 of 53 validation runs are complete at every farm; the run of 2026-06-30 is missing and its cases are dropped from every arm.
  • Checks: UKV shortwave is never negative, peaks at 12 UTC like ENS shortwave and farm power, and is at most 3.4 W/m2 with the sun below the horizon up to 48 hours. Beyond 48 hours the linear join between 3-hourly steps gives up to 57 W/m2 before sunrise, which affects the last 6 of the 30 scored hours. UKV's mean shortwave on the scored cases is 105 W/m2 against 114 for the ENS control member. In the shuffled-UKV placebo no group of rows shuffled together has only one row, so no row kept its own UKV values.
  • Latency: the experiment assumes the 00 UTC UKV run is available within 8 hours of its start and did not measure it. The service reads ENS at 09:00 UTC.
  • Departures from the plan: none. The plan review, before any fit finished, had already changed the threshold from 0.15 to 0.10.
  • Code: ml-experiments/00057-product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms/. One Sonnet plan review found no leakage.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: Whether a satellite-based nowcast at lead day 0 helps the solar farms. The two second forecasts tested so far (UKV here, and the Global Ensemble Forecast System, GEFS, in experiment 50) added little at 1 to 2 days ahead, so a test is better spent on a source of a different kind. The post-upgrade lead (-0.133) can be checked cheaply by retraining on the post-upgrade UKV months only, once a year of them exists.

docs.title: Experiment 58: is the recall gap without a metered receiver a step-size effect, and does a stronger veto help?
docs.text: Much of the gap in recall between injected load transfers with and without a metered receiver comes from the injected step being too small for the detector to see, and a stronger neighbour veto adds almost nothing. We tested a detector that raises an alarm when the 24-hour average of one Primary substation's residual (measured minus predicted power) steps up or down. To test it, we injected known load transfers: a donor substation loses load, and receiver substations gain it. A receiver is metered when its own power is measured. The detector found 0.50 of the injected transfers that have a metered receiver and 0.17 of those without one. We re-cut the share found by the size of the injected step, in noise units (multiples of the usual size of the 24-hour step statistic on a quiet day), to see whether the gap belongs to the detector or to how we built the transfers. We also made the neighbour veto stronger: the veto removes an alarm when at least two neighbouring substations stepped the same way, and its strength is the size of step, in noise units, that counts. Step size explains at least half of the gap, and between about half and all of it: 211 of the 274 transfers without a metered receiver step by less than the alarm threshold of 4.0 noise units. The stronger veto raised the share found by +0.013 (98.33% interval 0.000 to +0.029, resampling whole calendar months), against +0.008 in experiment 55.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
Partly supported. C1 (the gap) is supported on the pre-registered match and mixed on the check, and C2 (the veto) is inconclusive. All intervals are 98.33%, from 20,000 resamples of whole calendar months, over the 620 injected transfers that move 25% to 40% of the receiving load for over 1 day and start in even months.

Contrast Result Reading C1, gap in share found, metered minus unmetered receiver, at equal largest step -0.002 (-0.166 to +0.119); raw gap 0.33 Step size explains at least half the gap C1 check, the same on the donor's step alone +0.161 (+0.013 to +0.322) Mixed; reported, not decisive C2, D2 at veto 1.0 minus D0M, share found +0.013 (0.000 to +0.029) Inconclusive: needs an interval wholly above zero C3, the same, transfers with no metered receiver (274) +0.037 (+0.011 to +0.055) Reported only

D0 is the detector without the veto. D0M is D0 at experiment 43's thresholds (4-hour window 6.0, 24-hour window 4.0); experiment 55 showed the threshold search returns them. D2 is D0 with the neighbour veto. C1 to C3 are the three planned contrasts. Odd months chose a veto of 1.0 noise units, but the odd-month shares found were 0.306 at 1.0, 0.302 at 1.25, and 0.304 at 1.5, so the choice is close to arbitrary, and the selection is not reflected in the C2 interval. The matched 24-hour thresholds were 3.55, 3.65, and 3.70, and the even-month unexplained 24-hour alarms were 63 for D2 against 80 for D0M. The veto lost 6 of the transfers D0M finds and gained 14 that D0M misses.

docs.title: Recall by step size
docs.text:
The share found rises steeply with step size, and the two groups differ in step size more than in detection. Among the transfers with a metered receiver, 40 of 346 step by less than 4.0 noise units and the detector finds 2 of those; 172 of the 306 that step by 4.0 or more are found (0.56). Among those with no metered receiver, 211 of 274 step by less than 4.0 and 24 are found; 22 of the 63 that step by 4.0 or more are found (0.35). The median largest step is 8.9 noise units with a metered receiver and 3.3 without one. In the four equal-count bins of the range the two groups share (0.4 to 6.8 noise units, 358 of the 620 transfers), the metered group has only 19, 5, 7, and 53 transfers per bin against 71, 84, 82, and 37 for the unmetered group, so the matched comparison rests mostly on the top bin (26 of 53 against 16 of 37).

The conclusion holds less firmly when the groups are matched on the donor's step alone. A transfer with a metered receiver also has a chance to alarm on the receiver, so the pre-registered match uses the largest step over the donor and the metered receivers. That largest step can exceed the donor's step only for transfers with a metered receiver, which favours the metered group. The donor-only match is therefore the fairer check. Matched on the donor alone, the gap is +0.161, which is just under half of 0.33, and its interval (+0.013 to +0.322) lies on both sides of 0.165. A logistic regression of found on the logarithm of the step and on a metered-receiver flag gives a metered-receiver coefficient of +0.26 when matched on the largest step and +0.81 when matched on the donor's step. A coefficient of +0.81 is 2.2 times higher odds of being found at equal donor step.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Partly held: the gap shrank, but to zero, not to 0.05 to 0.15. The pre-registered gap was -0.002 on the largest step.
  • Not held: odd months picked 1.0, not 1.25. Odd months picked 1.0 by 0.002 over 1.5.
  • Held: the even-month gain was +0.013, inside the predicted +0.01 to +0.03. The matched threshold fell to 3.55, inside the predicted 3.4 to 3.6.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The bins are thin where the groups overlap. Only 12 transfers with a metered receiver fall in the middle two bins, so the matched gap has a wide interval.
  • The bin edges are fixed from the pooled transfers, not redrawn inside each resample. The C1 interval is therefore slightly narrow.
  • We estimated the noise units from odd months, and the 620 even-month transfers were already used in experiment 55, which is where 0.17 and 0.50 came from. Those data informed the C1 design.
  • 19 of the 1,900 injected transfers move no MW, because the donor's power is zero or missing there (2 of the 620 even-month transfers). They stay in every count.
  • A veto of 1.0 or 1.25 noise units falls below the 2.0 noise units at which a neighbouring substation counts as a partner. The loss of 6 transfers and gain of 14 shows no harm at these strengths.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
The next experiment should show why the detector misses about half of the transfers whose step is 4.0 noise units or more. Of the 306 transfers with a metered receiver that step by 4.0 or more, 134 are missed, and the cause is unknown. A shape-aware detector, SW2-7, models the moved load as a share of the donor's expected daily profile, which is how the injection builds a transfer, so its recall on the injected transfers would flatter it. Score SW2-7 on transfers injected with a different shape, such as a flat MW step or a profile reversed in time, on the 14 and 35 labelled real transfers, and by bins of step in noise units. Report each against D0M in the same bins, so that a gain shows up as recall at a step the detector already sees, not as a gain from the injection's own shape.

Code: ml-experiments/00058-sw2-8b-donor-step-recut-and-stronger-veto/, with every number printed by e00058_report.py and e00058_steps.py.

docs.title: Experiment 59: does one detector over several windows find more transfers than the best single window?
docs.text: Neither of two ways of combining four window lengths found more of the moved MW than the 24-hour window alone. Among large transfers with a metered receiver, most misses are an interval end placed outside tolerance, not a missed alarm. We tested a detector, experiment 43's D0, that raises an alarm when the average of one substation's residual (measured minus predicted power) over a window steps up or down against the average over the window before it. We injected known load transfers into the power: a donor substation loses load, and receiver substations gain it. We counted the share of the moved MW whose transfer the detector finds, with windows of 4, 12, 24, and 48 hours, and with two ways of combining all four windows: the maximum of the four windows' scores, and their sum. A transfer counts as found when an alarm places its start within 2 hours and its end within the larger of 6 hours and 10% of its duration. We set every detector to the same count of alarms that no logged closure explains on odd months, and we scored the transfers that start in even months. The 24-hour window found 0.473 of the moved MW. The maximum found 0.423 and the sum found 0.451, so the 24-hour window misses 0.527 of the moved MW. For 541 rows of large transfers with a metered receiver (a receiver whose own power is measured), the 24-hour window misses 223, and 170 of those have a found start and an end placed outside tolerance, against 4 with no alarm at all.

docs.title: How to read the numbers
docs.text:
• Noise unit. A step is measured in multiples of the usual size of that window's statistic on the same substation in odd months (1.4826 times the median absolute deviation). A "large" transfer moves at least 4.0 noise units of load off the donor over its first 24 hours.
  • Unexplained alarm. An alarm with no logged closure within 24 hours on the same substation. Every detector is held to at most 80 of these on odd months, which is the count of experiment 43's 24-hour detector.
  • Rows. Each injected transfer appears once for each of two shapes, a constant MW and a share of the receivers' profile, so a count of 620 transfers is 1,240 rows. A "row" count below says so.
  • Shapes. The donor-profile shape is a drifting share of the donor's own power, as in experiment 58. The constant-MW shape moves the same MW at every half-hour. The receiver-profile shape is a drifting share of the receivers' summed power.
  • Weighted share. Each row is weighted by the MW the donor loses over the transfer's first 24 hours, so a transfer that moves more MW counts for more.

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text:
Refuted. Neither combined detector beat the best single window. The maximum was worse, and the sum was not better. The intervals are 97.5%, so that two contrasts together keep a 5% chance of a false signal (a Bonferroni correction), from 20,000 paired resamples of whole calendar months. The transfers are the 620 that move 25% to 40% of the receiving load for more than 1 day and start in even months, in the constant-MW and receiver-profile shapes (1,240 rows), each weighted by the MW the donor loses over the first 24 hours. The best single window, chosen on odd months, is the 24-hour window.

Contrast Weighted share found, difference Unweighted, difference Reading C1, maximum minus 24 hours -0.050 (-0.094 to -0.022) -0.037 (-0.071 to -0.018) Refuted: upper end below +0.02 C2, sum minus 24 hours -0.022 (-0.062 to +0.001) -0.002 (-0.020 to +0.009) Refuted: upper end below +0.02

The odd-month choice of window was clear: the MW-weighted shares found on odd months were 0.211 (4 hours), 0.317 (12 hours), 0.384 (24 hours), and 0.323 (48 hours). Every detector was calibrated to at most 80 unexplained alarms on odd months, and the achieved counts were 78, 79, 80, and 79 for the four windows, 76 for the maximum, and 80 for the sum. On even months the counts of unexplained alarms on the real residual were 65, 68, 80, and 72 for the four windows, 72 for the maximum, and 91 for the sum. The sum's 91 is 11 above the 24-hour window's 80. The pre-registered rule allows at most 10, so C2 could not have been supported, and the refutation rests on its interval alone.

docs.title: Share found, by detector
docs.text:
The 24-hour and 12-hour windows find about the same share (0.473 and 0.471), and the other windows and both combinations find less. The table gives each detector's share of the moved MW found, with a 95% interval from resampling whole calendar months, on the pooled constant-MW and receiver-profile shapes. The unweighted share counts each row once, whatever its size.

Detector MW-weighted share found Unweighted share found Share of moved MW missed 4 hours 0.367 (0.264 to 0.464) 0.223 0.633 12 hours 0.471 (0.390 to 0.551) 0.327 0.529 24 hours 0.473 (0.410 to 0.511) 0.360 0.527 48 hours 0.376 (0.294 to 0.434) 0.294 0.624 Maximum of the four 0.423 (0.340 to 0.472) 0.323 0.577 Sum of the four 0.451 (0.374 to 0.496) 0.358 0.549

The two shapes agree: the 24-hour window finds 0.487 in the constant-MW shape and 0.459 in the receiver-profile shape. In the donor-profile shape, which experiment 58 used, the differences from the 24-hour window are -0.060 (-0.103 to -0.033) for the maximum and -0.027 (-0.062 to -0.007) for the sum. On the 300 transfers that start within 1 day of a bank holiday, the differences are -0.069 (-0.226 to -0.050) and -0.022 (-0.031 to 0.000).

docs.title: Why large transfers are missed
docs.text:
Most large transfers that the 24-hour window misses have a found start and an end outside tolerance. The figure covers the 541 pooled rows of transfers with a metered receiver and a donor step of 4.0 noise units or more of the 24-hour statistic. The 24-hour window finds 318 of the 541 rows (0.588 by count, 0.595 by MW) and misses 223, each for one reason, tried in this order:

  • End outside tolerance (170 rows). An alarm places the start within 2 hours, and the interval places the end outside tolerance.
  • Absorbed (46 rows). The score exceeds the alarm threshold within 2 hours of the start, but a larger peak within 24 hours took the alarm, or a monthly refit of the expected-power model dropped it.
  • Start outside tolerance (3 rows). An alarm lies within 24 hours of the start but not within 2 hours.
  • No alarm (4 rows). The best score near the start has a median of 0.34 of the alarm threshold.

The maximum and sum detectors give the same pattern, with 165 and 169 rows of missed ends.

The missed ends are 7.0 to 10.5 hours out at the quartiles, against a tolerance of 6 hours. The median of these 170 rows lasts 32 hours, so the tolerance (the larger of 6 hours and 10% of the duration) is 6 hours. The missed ends are off by 7.0, 7.5, and 10.5 hours at the quartiles, and by 23% of the duration at the median. The interval builder follows the transfer's level in whole 24-hour blocks, so it can place an end only to about a day. A post hoc variant that takes the step from the first 24-hour block and ends the transfer after two failing blocks leaves the counts almost unchanged (171 missed ends for the 24-hour window, against 170).

docs.title: Share found by donor step
docs.text: The combined detectors find about as many transfers as the 24-hour window at each donor step, and the maximum never finds more. With a metered receiver the 24-hour window finds 35 of 87 rows at a step of 2 to 4 noise units and 318 of 541 at 4 or more. Without one it finds 41 of 363 at 2 to 4 and 51 of 133 at 4 to 8. The sum finds 120 of 197 at 4 to 8 with a metered receiver, against 111 for the 24-hour window, and 195 of 344 at 8 or more, against 207. No row without a metered receiver steps by 8 or more.

docs.title: Labelled real transfers over 1 day
docs.text: Of the 35 labelled real transfers that last over 1 day, the 4-hour window finds 0, the 12-hour 3, the 24-hour 2, the 48-hour 3, the maximum 4, and the sum 5. The counts are too small to rank the detectors.

docs.title: What held in the prediction and what did not
docs.text:
• Not held: the best single window found more than predicted. The prediction was 0.20 to 0.40 of the moved MW and the 24-hour window found 0.473. Earlier experiments reported unweighted shares, and large transfers are found more often than small ones: in the donor-profile shape the 24-hour window finds 0.355 unweighted and 0.466 by MW.
  • Not held: the combinations lost instead of gaining. The maximum changed the share by -0.050 against a predicted +0.02 to +0.06, and the sum by -0.022 against a predicted -0.01 to +0.04.
  • Held: the 24-hour window was the best single window, chosen on odd months.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The injected transfers set the answer. The 24-hour window's 0.47 is a share of injected transfers, and the 35 real transfers over 1 day are too few to confirm it.
  • The unexplained-alarm count includes real events that no log records. A detector that finds more of those real events is held to a higher threshold than a less sensitive detector.
