• Median minus mean: the median of the forecast sits 5.2 points below the mean on the kept rows for A0r and 5.3 for B1, so all arms share the same skew and the mean-error contrasts agree in direction with the quantile-score contrasts.
  • A0r reproduces A0 on the nine shared levels (11.035 against 11.037, all rows).
  • Leave-one-farm-out: C1 stays positive without any single farm (0.11 to 0.14), and C3 stays negative, though its interval includes zero without W1 or without W3.
  • Row sets: on the rows above the farm's fitted rated speed, C1 is +0.43 (0.30 to 0.57). On all rows it is +0.10.
  • Audit triggers 1 and 4 of the ml-experiment skill fired, and trigger 7 may have. No Opus audit was run, because the manager ruled it out to save quota.

docs.title: Departures from the plan
docs.text:
• ENS control member: A1 and B2 train on the ENS control member, not on the ENS mean.
  • Temperature-only density correction: ERA5 surface pressure is not on disk, so the core uses a fixed 100 kPa.
  • Idle layer: the idle layer shapes the mean, and the spread comes from the residual quantiles.
  • Hub height: the fitted hub heights (32 to 37 m) are not physical, because they absorb the 25 km cell's sub-grid wind.
  • Seeds: the physics arms are deterministic, so their three seeds repeat one fit.
  • Post hoc arms: E0 (ERA5 as the forecast) and A0rT (A0r with air temperature) were added after the plan.
  • Not run: B10 to B13, the no-history tests, and the curtailment-cost metric.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: How much of the 5-point gap between the ensemble wind forecast and ERA5 wind can a better forecast input, such as a blend of weather models, close?

docs.title: Photovoltaic (PV) capacity audit: where does the recovery shortfall go?
docs.text:
Take-home message: the capacity estimator misses about 0.17 of an injected solar farm for two reasons. The demand terms of the fit take part of the solar signal, and the fixed solar shape does not match the farm's flat top. The sunshine input is not the limit.

What was done. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm to a Primary substation's power, at 50% of the Primary's pinned capacity (the unmetered solar capacity that experiment 45's real-time estimate gives the Primary). Then we asked the capacity fit of experiment 129 how much of the farm it finds again. The share found is the recovery: the capacity found with the farm added, minus the capacity found without it, divided by the injected capacity. The full fit finds 0.827 (median over the five decision Primaries, 80% interval 0.814 to 0.842). Five further fits, each simpler or narrower, show where the missing 0.173 goes. Fitting the farm alone against the fixed solar shape finds 0.931, the highest recovery any fit of that shape can reach. Fitting the full model with its demand terms frozen finds 0.928. The verdict is partly supported: demand absorption took the share the plan predicted, and the other three predicted shares were wrong.

Terms used below. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five decision Primaries of experiment 103's data set, and D9 is shown beside them. Farms A to F are metered generators and are never named. A season-year runs from July to June and is labelled by the year of the July; the recovery is read at season-year 2024. The capacity unit is the 99th percentile of alternating-current output over daylight half-hours, in MW. The shortfall is 1 minus the recovery of the full fit. A rung is one fit of the ladder (rungs 1 to 4, and the season refits that are rung 5; rung 6 is the flat-top check). Demand absorption is the full fit attributing part of the solar signal to its demand terms (the daily profile, heating, lighting, and annual harmonics). The flat top is the 99th percentile of the solar output. CAMS is the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite irradiance. The intervals resample whole months of training rows.

Figure 1. Fitting the farm alone finds 0.93 of it; adding the demand terms drops that to 0.83.

Figure 2. Demand absorption and the plant shape account for the whole shortfall.

Figure 3. Winter rows find about half of the farm, and April-to-August rows find more than all rows.

Figure 4. The recovered output's flat top is a fifth to a quarter below the farm's in spring and summer.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• Demand absorption is the largest share, and the irradiance input is none of it. The pre-registered prediction scored as follows (pooled median over the five decision Primaries). Demand absorption was 57.7% of the shortfall (80% interval 54.1% to 62.7%), predicted at least 40%, met at all five Primaries. The irradiance input was -5.8% (-11.8% to -2.4%), predicted at least 25%, met at none. The season share (April-to-August rows only, against all rows) was 19.3% (13.1% to 28.2%), predicted under 15%, met at one Primary. The divisor share was 27.3%, predicted under 15%, met at none.
  • The rungs, pooled, with 80% intervals: farm only 0.931 (0.920 to 0.943); farm only on clear half-hours 0.929 (0.910 to 0.930); demand frozen 0.928 (0.924 to 0.941); full fit 0.827 (0.814 to 0.842); full fit on April to August rows 0.864 (0.847 to 0.880); full fit on November to February rows 0.475 (0.450 to 0.522).
  • The plant shape and flat top are 47.1% (43.0% to 53.5%) of the shortfall. The fleet shape with one fitted scale reaches 0.929 on clear half-hours, so the fleet shape cannot reproduce about 0.07 of the farm's capacity.
  • Demand absorption costs 0.098 (0.089 to 0.110) of the injected capacity. The estimator noise with the demand terms frozen is 0.003 (-0.007 to 0.004).
  • Clear half-hours at the Primary's CAMS point fit the farm no better than all daylight half-hours (0.929 and 0.931). Experiment 218 reported 0.973 and 0.953 for the same comparison. Those figures are the fraction of squared output explained, which measures scatter. This page measures the fitted scale, and scatter does not lower the scale.
  • April-to-August rows alone raise the recovery from 0.827 to 0.864 at all five decision Primaries, and D9 is unchanged. November-to-February rows alone find 0.475 (0.450 to 0.522).
  • Reading the capacity at the 99th percentile makes the shortfall larger, not smaller. The whole-year ratio of the recovered output's 99th percentile to the farm's is 0.75 to 0.82 over the five decision Primaries (range over farms 0.71 to 0.83). That is 0.039 to 0.050 below the recovery of the full fit. The ratio is 0.74 to 0.80 in spring and summer and 0.90 to 0.96 in winter.
  • A heat derating that is too strong is one possible cause of the flat-top gap, and this experiment did not test it. The fitted shape derates for heat loss, and experiments 183 and 218 found no heat or clip term that explains the farms' flat top. A derating that is too strong would make the flat top fall more in the fit than in the farm from spring to summer.
  • The injected fit reproduces experiment 129 exactly. The injected-fit capacity equals experiment 129's matched-farm capacity at every Primary and farm (the printed relative difference is 0.000, and the check tolerance is 1e-6). With experiment 129's base (fitted on all rows) the recovery matches exactly. With this experiment's base (fitted on the rows where the farm has a reading) the recovery differs by 0.007 to 0.019.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Data cut: the fits stop at 2026-07-01, so the maintainer's labelled exception (data to 2026-07-31) is not used. No forecast is scored.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"):
    • Fired: the result contradicts three of four pre-registered shares and seems to contradict experiment 218's 0.973. The explanation was tested by reading experiment 218's definition of "fraction of output fitted" (above).
    • Fired: the designs of later experiments depend on this result and it has not been replicated. Whether a second, Opus review runs is for the maintainer to decide, so the pull request stays open until that is settled.
    • Did not fire: a failed control (none ran), a mean-forecast contrast that disagrees (no forecast), a leave-one-site-out sign flip, a nested arm beating its container (the summer-only fit is the measured contrast), and a headline interval more than twice or under half a sister experiment's width.
  • Review: one Sonnet code review found no finding that changes a result, and one Sonnet review of the page checked every number against the printed report.
  • No Opus audit was run. The ML manager decided that quota did not allow an Opus review of any of this series' experiments, so every audit trigger listed above stays unaudited and a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the page instead.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Matched sunny-minus-cloudy day pairs target demand absorption, the largest cause that can be fixed. Experiment 235 plans this.
  • A shared seasonal efficiency curve targets the flat-top gap and the season share, and should run after the day-pair test.
  • The clear-sky fit and the nearest-metered-farm sunshine reference both target the irradiance input, which explains none of the shortfall here (-6%), so their predicted gains are unlikely to hold. Experiment 236 plans the clear-sky fit.
  • Neural components: a learned smooth response of the solar term to temperature and irradiance could replace the fixed heat derating if the seasonal curve helps. The prediction that could fail is a flat-top ratio of 0.9 or more in every season.

docs.title: Plan: the ladder of fits
docs.text:
Every rung reports the recovery at season-year 2024, as a median over the five farms, with a month-block 80% interval (a stratified bootstrap of the training months, 200 resamples, the same draws for every farm at a Primary). The brief's "injection start months" is read as the training months, because the injection covers the whole history.

  • Rung 1, farm only: the least-squares scale of the farm's output on the temperature-derated fleet unit shape (CAMS irradiance), over all daylight half-hours of season-year 2024. No demand.
  • Rung 2, farm only on clear half-hours: the same scale over the half-hours where the Primary's CAMS global irradiance is at least 0.9 of its clear-sky value and the clear-sky value is at least 200 W/m².
  • Rung 3, demand frozen: the base fit (no injection) is solved first. Then the injected series is fitted with every column except the capacity increments held at the base fit's values.
  • Rung 4, full joint fit: experiment 129's arm 2 (convex, ridge 0.1) fitted to the base and the injected series; the recovery we report.
  • Rung 5, season rows: rung 4 refitted on April to August rows only, and on November to February rows only, read at the same season-year.
  • Rung 6, divisor check: the 99th percentile of the recovered solar output (rung 4 capacity difference times the derated shape) over daylight half-hours, divided by the farm's own 99th percentile over the same half-hours, for the whole season-year and for each season (spring March to May, summer June to August, autumn September to November, winter December to February). Point values per farm; the interval is the range over farms.

The shares of the shortfall 1 - R4 are: plant shape 1 - R2, irradiance input R2 - R1, estimator noise with frozen demand R1 - R3, demand absorption R3 - R4. They sum to the shortfall. The season share is R5_summer - R4 and the divisor share is |R4_p99 - R4|, where R4_p99 is the whole-season-year 99th-percentile ratio of rung 6; both are alternatives to the ladder and not terms of the sum.

docs.title: Plan: checks
docs.text:
• Read-out year (changed before the real run): the first draft of this plan read the recovery at season-year 2025. A one-farm pilot at D10 (10 resamples, not a result) then showed that experiment 129's known-answer table stops at season-year 2024, so the plan reads season-year 2024 to make rung 4 comparable with it. The pilot's numbers played no part in the choice.

  • Reproduction: the injected fit's capacity must equal experiment 129's kat_arm2 matched-farm capacity (50% injection, no cloud load, season-year 2024) to within 1e-6 relative at every Primary and farm. Experiment 129 subtracts one base capacity fitted on all rows from every injected fit, whereas this experiment fits the base on the rows where the farm has a reading, so that the two fits of a recovery share one row set. The page reports rung 4 with both bases, and the two recoveries must agree to within 0.02.

  • Wiring: the monthly Gram matrices must sum to the Gram matrix of accumulate_gram to within 1e-8 relative, and the rung-4 base capacity must equal fit_gam's.

docs.title: Do the correction heads close D5's sunny-daylight gap, and do they stack with the 60% clip?
docs.text:
The correction heads of experiment 201 do not clearly fix D5's sunny-daylight loss, and added to the 60% clip they partly undo the clip's gain at D5, though the estimate is imprecise. The result supports using the clip alone. D5 is an anonymised Primary substation, which feeds homes and businesses. Arm D is the demand forecast of the best convex generalised additive demand model with its Kalman filter, winter night offset, and error recipe. BG2 is the best-guess forecast that serves as the benchmark. A correction head is a small neural network that adds a shift to the demand forecast, using the forecast's own inputs.

Experiment 178 found that arm D has a higher mean absolute error than BG2 on the sunniest third of daylight half-hours, mostly at D5. The "gap" is arm D's mean absolute error minus BG2's, and it is +0.202 MW at D5. Experiment 180 closed most of that gap by capping the solar output that the forecast subtracts at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 ("the clip"). We asked whether the stored heads of experiment 201 close the same gap, and whether a head adds to the clip. We fitted no demand model and no head. We added each head's stored median shift and quantile offsets to arm D and to arm D with the clip, and scored the same half- hours as experiment 178 (each row is one half-hour of one substation's forecast).

The head alone closed 12% of the gap (+0.202 MW to +0.178 MW). The head on top of the clip left a gap of +0.169 MW. The clip alone leaves +0.069 MW.

Verdict not supported. Four criteria were set. The first holds: the head alone closed 12% of the gap, under the predicted 30%. The second fails: the head with the clip left D5 at +0.169 MW, not +0.05 MW or less. The third fails: the clip and head effects overlap by +0.124 MW, not to within 0.02 MW. The fourth fails: head arm 2 moves the placebo D16 by -0.052 MW and the clip and head move the placebo D10 by +0.052 MW, against a limit of 0.02 MW.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms: C is arm D (the control), K is arm D with the 60% clip, H is arm D plus a head, and KH is the clip plus a head. Heads are arms 1, 2, and 3 of experiment 201 (19, 28, and 32 input columns), with three seeds averaged, and the planned head is arm 2. Experiment 200's head stored only monthly scores, so it is not rescored.
  • Rows: experiment 178's rows at D5, D10, and D16 in the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads to 168 hours, outside the load shifts. D5 has 14,045 sunny half-hours.
  • Construction: arm H is arm D's median plus the head's median shift, with the head's own quantile offsets from its median. This reproduces the stored head forecast. Arm KH puts the same shift and offsets on the clip's median. The head was not trained on the clip's forecast.
  • Absolute scores, D5 sunny: the mean absolute error (MW) is 0.655 for C, 0.523 for K, 0.632 for H (arm 2), 0.623 for KH, and 0.453 for BG2. The pinball loss (MW) is, in the same order, 0.185, 0.154, 0.178, 0.173, and 0.130.
  • Head alone, against arm D (98.75% interval): arm 1 -0.017 MW (-0.096 to +0.112), arm 2 -0.024 (-0.082 to +0.064), arm 3 -0.002 (-0.059 to +0.099). The gap to BG2 falls from +0.202 to +0.185, +0.178, and +0.200 MW. Arm 2 closes 12% of the gap.
  • Clip and head against the clip alone (D5 sunny): arm 1 +0.138 MW (+0.033 to +0.260), arm 2 +0.100 (-0.007 to +0.211), arm 3 +0.121 (+0.013 to +0.231). The gap to BG2 is +0.207, +0.169, and +0.190 MW. The clip alone has +0.069 MW.
  • Overlap (clip and head minus clip minus head plus control): arm 2 +0.124 MW (+0.029 to +0.204), arm 1 +0.155, arm 3 +0.123. The clip and the head together do not have the sum of their separate effects. We have not tested why. The clip arm is a separate fit, so K minus C also includes refit differences.
  • Placebos, sunny, change against arm D (MW): the clip moves D10 by +0.004 (-0.025 to +0.037) and D16 by -0.004 (-0.051 to +0.049). Arm H (arm 2) moves D10 by +0.018 (-0.027 to +0.072) and D16 by -0.052 (-0.076 to -0.017). Arm KH (arm 2) moves D10 by +0.052 (-0.006 to +0.122) and D16 by -0.024 (-0.070 to +0.024). Only D16's change with the head alone has an interval excluding zero, so the head's shift on sunny rows is not specific to D5.
  • All half-hours at D5: the head alone changes the error by -0.008 MW (-0.022 to +0.004), the clip and head by -0.003 (-0.019 to +0.013).
  • Shifts on D5's sunny rows: the clip raises the median forecast by 0.031 MW on average and the head by 0.139 MW. The clip's shift and the head's shift have a correlation of 0.43 across half-hours.
  • Tails at D5, sunny. Coverage is the share of actuals at or below the quantile. Each cell is coverage and pinball loss (MW).
Quantile C K H KH q01 0.051, 0.025 0.056, 0.023 0.065, 0.026 0.060, 0.024 q05 0.168, 0.097 0.176, 0.085 0.201, 0.094 0.198, 0.086 q95 0.967, 0.081 0.996, 0.076 0.982, 0.075 0.992, 0.075 q99 0.993, 0.022 0.999, 0.021 0.995, 0.020 0.998, 0.020

The lower tail stays under-covered in every arm, and the head raises q01 coverage from 0.051 to 0.065 and q05 coverage from 0.168 to 0.201 (nominal 0.01 and 0.05). - Clip form for the assembly: the hard 60% clip at D5, in the form experiment 214 selected as-of, with no correction head.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast: arm D's stored mean equals its median (experiment 180). The heads stored no mean, so the head arms have no mean forecast to compare.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile score: the head arms store only quantiles. Mean absolute error and pinball loss point the same way for every contrast above.
  • Triggers fired: the second trigger of the ml-experiment skill's audit list (a result contradicts its own prediction). The clip and head leave D5 far above the predicted +0.05 MW. The partial explanation we tested is the overlap row: the clip's shift and the head's shift both raise the forecast on the sunny rows (correlation 0.43), and the head's shift is larger. We did not test why a head trained on unclipped forecasts hurts after the clip. No audit has run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The head is a three-seed average and was trained once. Experiment 201 trained it on arm D's errors, with 4,320 training rows (0.8%) whose valid times fall inside the scored year, and did not refit it through the year. Arm H averages the seeds, so it matches a stored forecast per seed only.
  • The head helps D16. Head arm 2 lowers D16's sunny error by 0.052 MW (-0.076 to -0.017). The finding is about D5 and the clip, and does not rule out a head elsewhere.
  • The head was trained on the unclipped forecast. Experiment 201 trained it on arm D's errors, so applying its shift to the clip's forecast is a stacking test, not a head trained for the clip.
  • One substation and one year. The intervals come from 12 monthly blocks and are wide. The head-alone gain at D5 is not distinguishable from zero.
  • The prediction is not independent of the scores. The plan was committed after the rescore ran. The prediction and decision rule are the ones written in the maintainer's brief before the rescore.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Retrain the head on the clipped arm D's errors, so the head and the clip share one set of residuals.
  • The next experiment in this series tests a cap learned from the metered series, which tests the clip's form and does not involve the head.

docs.title: Can a fitted wind-turbine physics model show that a wind farm has lost 25% of its capacity within 60 days, without raising false alarms on a slow seasonal drift?
docs.text: The planned monitor found a 25% loss within 120 days at only about half the start dates at W1 and W2, and at none at W3. The verdict is not supported: the pre-registered rule for stopping (a median delay above 60 days at 2 or more farms at a 25% loss) is met. W1, W2, and W3 are three metered wind farms, anonymised.

docs.title: Question and answer
docs.text:
We asked whether the fitted wind-turbine model of experiment 230 (called "the core" below) can show that a farm has lost capacity. The monitor divides observed power by the power the core expects, adds up both over a trailing 60 days of strong-wind half-hours (those where the core expects at least 95% of the farm's fitted maximum output, its "scale"), and divides by the same ratio before July 2024, so that 1.0 means normal. An alarm is raised when that relative ratio falls below the lowest value seen in 2021-09 to 2024-06.

The planned monitor was too slow in a simulation. We cut observed power by 10%, 25%, and 50% from 30 random start dates and counted the days until an alarm. A 25% loss raised an alarm within 120 days at 50% of start dates at W1, 63% at W2, and 0% at W3 (29 start dates at W3, after one that already alarmed was excluded).

A variant added after the results were seen did better but is not trustworthy. It uses every half-hour at 20% of scale or more. It found a 25% loss within 120 days at 100%, 87%, and 100% of start dates (26 at W3 after exclusions). A smooth seasonal swing of 9% in observed power with no loss, the size seen in experiment 183's solar farms, raised extra alarm days at all three farms.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Strong-wind half-hours are rare. They are 2% of half-hours at W1, 4% at W2, and 0.6% at W3 over 2019-09 to 2026-06. The plan predicted 3% to 14%, from counts that its own text gave wrongly; its stated counts imply 1.6% to 9%.
  • The planned monitor has a reading on few days. A 60-day window holds enough strong-wind half-hours (at least 4 half-hours on each of at least 6 days) on 21% of days at W1, 45% at W2, and 5% at W3. The post hoc rows give 97%, 97%, and 93%. W3's planned result is mostly a coverage failure, not a measure of sensitivity.
  • Alarm thresholds (planned rows): 0.956 at W1, 0.832 at W2, and 0.926 at W3. The W1 threshold sits 4% below 1, so a slow drift of 4% or more alarms there.
  • A 25% loss, planned rows: median delay 121.5 days at W1 (bootstrap 95% interval 79 to not reached), 105.5 days at W2 (77.5 to 162), and never at W3. Shares within 120 days: 0.50 (0.22 to 0.76), 0.63 (0.37 to 0.88), and 0.00. The intervals resample 18 calendar months of start dates.
  • A 25% loss, post hoc rows: median delay 27 days at W1 (24.5 to 36), 51.5 at W2 (42 to 75), and 34 at W3 (27 to 43). A 50% loss: 12.5, 27, and 15 days. A 10% loss is found within 120 days at 0.27 (W1), 0.60 (W2), and 0.73 (W3) of start dates.
  • Constant expected power on the planned half-hours gave the same shares and median delays as the core at the 25% and 50% losses at every farm, and within 0.04 in share at the 10% loss. The fitted power curve adds almost nothing on the flat top.
  • 9% seasonal swing, extra alarm days over two years: planned rows 50 at W1 and 42 at W2, and 0 at W3 (where only 5% of days have a reading); post hoc rows 10, 28, and 62. Swings of 15% and 25% raise 152 and 340 extra alarm days at W1 on the post hoc rows.
  • Real series with no loss, alarm days after 2024-07-01: planned rows 0, 102, and 36 (W1, W2, W3); post hoc rows 13, 32, and 202. The monthly observed over expected power on the post hoc rows ranges from 0.71 to 1.20 (W1), 0.74 to 1.31 (W2), and 0.35 to 1.27 (W3). On the planned rows, W2 falls to 0.39 in one month of winter 2025 to 2026, and W3 to 0.51 in one month of 2024 to 2025. No cause is claimed.
  • W1's output shows no step. Its monthly 99th percentile is mostly 18 to 21 MVA and falls to 9 to 15 MVA in some summer months, so it follows the wind.
  • Starts inside and outside the core's fitting data (before and after 2025-06-17), post hoc rows, 25% loss: shares within 120 days of 1.00 and 1.00 at W1, 0.79 and 1.00 at W2, and 1.00 and 1.00 at W3. Starts before 2025-06-17 sit inside the data the core was fitted on, so the after-2025-06-17 figures are the honest ones.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• No forecast is produced, so forecast-error and tail-calibration checks do not apply.
  • Audit triggers (listed in the ml-experiment skill): trigger 1 fired (the 9% control raises extra alarms at W1 and W2) and trigger 2 fired (the predicted detection within 60 days at W1 and W2 failed; the rarity of strong-wind half-hours explains it, shown in Figure 3 and by the post hoc rows). A fresh Sonnet auditor re-derived the shares, thresholds, median delays, and drift alarm days with its own code from the raw inputs and matched every one. It found no error in window indexing, loss timing, or missing-data handling. It noted that the calibration years overlap the core's fitting data, which tightens the thresholds, and that the loss-free run's alarm days are masked, which makes the delays slightly longer than a plain count.
  • Hold-out check of the threshold: calibrating on 2021-09 to 2023-06, 51 of 104 days with a reading in 2023-07 to 2024-06 alarm at W1 and 50 of 50 at W3, so the minimum-over-years threshold is not stable out of sample there; at W2 none of 159 alarm.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• The post hoc rows are not pre-registered, and they fail the 9% drift test at all three farms.
  • Lab conditions: the core is frozen, the loss multiplies observed power, and an export cap would hide a loss at strong wind, so the delays are optimistic. Start dates that already alarmed without a loss are excluded, so the farms are compared on slightly different start sets.
  • Next: a monitor on all half-hours above cut-in with a baseline that depends on the month, which may absorb the 9% swing (untested), then a check of the W2 and W3 low months against NGED's outage records. A learned correction of the ratio by wind speed is a candidate neural component; its prediction that could fail is that the 9% swing then raises no extra alarm at W1.

docs.title: Can demand, metered solar farms, and metered wind farms each be forecast without XGBoost, and where does the XGBoost-free forecast lose?
docs.text:
Take-home. An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead. XGBoost is a gradient-boosted decision-tree model, and production uses it today. The XGBoost-free forecasts for metered solar farms and metered wind farms score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, which is over the 2% tolerance the maintainer set. The next experiment, Part 2, tests small XGBoost components inside the solar and wind forecasts.

We asked whether each of the three series types that National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) needs can be forecast without XGBoost: Primary substation demand (substations that step power down to the local distribution network), metered solar farms, and metered wind farms. We recomputed one comparison per type from forecasts stored by earlier experiments, on identical rows. Each gap is a percentage of the XGBoost forecast's quantile score. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, and lower is better. A lead is the number of hours between the forecast time and the time forecast. Nothing was refitted.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Verdict per type (rule: gap at most 2% at 12 to 36 hours). Demand is within tolerance. Solar is over it: the point estimate, 2.8%, is above 2%, and the interval's lower end, 1.0%, is below 2%. Wind is over at 12 to 36 hours and within at all leads.
  • Demand arms. The XGBoost-free forecast is arm D (a convex demand model with a Kalman filter) plus a neural-network correction of the median and the two-number summary of the 51 ensemble members' solar response (experiment 228, experiment 220). The XGBoost forecast is BG2.
  • Solar arms. The XGBoost-free forecast is a physical model of the solar farm (a plant model) fed the mean and spread of the 51 European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble members. The XGBoost forecast is arm 5 of experiment 224 (PR 1533, open when written).
  • Wind arms. The XGBoost-free forecast is a physics-based wind model, B1. The XGBoost forecast is the best guess refit with 11 levels, A0r. Both come from experiment 230, read from its work folder before that experiment merged, so the wind numbers are provisional.
  • Quantile score, 12 to 36 hours (XGBoost-free / XGBoost; gap, 95% interval from resampling whole months).
    • Demand: 2.258 / 2.440; -7.5% (-13.7% to -1.9%); 82,479 forecast rows at six substations.
    • Solar: 5.598 / 5.446; +2.8% (+1.0% to +5.2%); 41,676 forecast rows at six farms, pooled over rows (experiment 224's farm-weighted 5.64 and 5.49 give the same gap).
    • Wind: 5.112 / 4.870; +5.0% (+3.0% to +6.8%); 22,788 forecast rows at three farms with three XGBoost training seeds.
    • Units are percentage points of effective capacity for demand (the substation's usable capacity) and of installed capacity for solar and wind.
  • All leads. Demand 2.579 / 2.715, -5.0% (-9.8% to -0.5%), 0.5 to 168 hours. Wind 8.636 / 8.556, +0.9% (+0.6% to +1.3%), 0.5 to 351 hours. Solar was scored on the 12 to 36 hour rows only (experiment 224 also has 60 to 84 and 108 to 132 hour rows, not used here).
  • Mean absolute error (MAE) of the median, 12 to 36 hours. Demand 3.945 / 4.254 (-7.2%). Solar 9.918 / 9.810 (+1.1%). Wind 9.383 / 8.872 (+5.8%).
  • Pinball loss at four quantile levels, 12 to 36 hours (XGBoost-free / XGBoost), with the share of actuals at or below the quantile (coverage). The 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles are written q01, q05, q95, and q99.
    • Demand: q01 0.157 / 0.205, q05 0.558 / 0.582, q95 0.608 / 0.673, q99 0.188 / 0.228; coverage 0.013 / 0.008, 0.048 / 0.036, 0.952 / 0.948, 0.984 / 0.985.
    • Solar: q01 0.374 / 0.352, q05 1.433 / 1.365, q95 1.367 / 1.214, q99 0.386 / 0.478; coverage 0.032 / 0.034, 0.055 / 0.068, 0.963 / 0.956, 0.991 / 0.996.
    • Wind: q01 0.239 / 0.224, q05 1.019 / 0.975, q95 1.327 / 1.285, q99 0.368 / 0.360; coverage 0.032 / 0.032, 0.038 / 0.043, 0.951 / 0.953, 0.984 / 0.985.
    • The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts lose at q01, q05, and q95, and wind loses at q99 too. Only solar q99 favours the XGBoost-free forecast. No middle quantile was scored.
  • Curtailment cost was scored for demand only. Experiment 228's node-only curtailment proxy (GBP million over the scored year, scaled limit 0.9, scored at the five decision substations only) is 2.14 for the XGBoost-free forecast and 1.45 for BG2, with overlapping 95% intervals. Threshold-weighted continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) was not scored for any arm compared here.

docs.title: Remaining XGBoost dependencies
docs.text:
• packages/xgboost_forecaster is the only trained forecaster class the audit found. It owns the one-booster-per-series save format (.ubj files and meta.json) and train and predict. An XGBoost-free forecast needs its own BaseForecaster subclass with its own save and load.
  • conf/model/xgboost.yaml names XGBoostForecaster as _target_, and conf/cv/default.yaml uses xgboost_no_power_lags as the reference experiment name. A new forecaster class needs its own config file and its own reference experiment name.
  • PowerForecast is an ensemble of deterministic members. The XGBoost-free forecasts store 11 quantiles. The climatology forecaster already maps quantile ranks to member indices, so the same mapping would carry the quantiles after interpolating the 11 levels to 51 members, and no contract change would be needed.
  • src/.../live_forecast_assets.py and cv_assets.py call forecaster.predict, so they are model-agnostic. Only an error message and some descriptions and comments mention boosters.
  • packages/ml_core mentions boosters in docstrings and the .ubj compression note, with no import in src. The default TabularFeatureEngineer builds the tabular AllFeatures frame, and the convex model would need its own FeatureEngineer, as the BaseForecaster design allows.
  • packages/baseline_forecasters has no XGBoost dependency (one docstring mentions it).
  • The XGBoost-free demand, solar, and wind forecasts live in packages/studies/. Production code may not import studies, so they would first move to a reviewed package. The root pyproject.toml still installs xgboost_forecaster, and packages/studies itself depends on xgboost.

docs.title: Consistency checks on the headline gaps
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site. Not recomputed here. Experiment 228 reports the difference for the demand arms, and experiment 230 reports -4.6 to -5.5 points at all three wind farms for both wind arms.
  • Error of the mean or median forecast beside the quantile score. The MAE of the median moves the same way as the quantile score for demand (-7.2%), solar (+1.1%), and wind (+5.8%).
  • Audit triggers. None applies: no control, nested arm, or leave-one-out check is needed for a collation of stored forecasts.

docs.title: Caveats and what to try next
docs.text:
• The wind numbers come from experiment 230's work folder before that experiment merged. Re-run e00234_score.py after experiment 230 merges.
  • The demand comparison covers one scored year and six substations. Experiment 228 found the XGBoost-free forecast worse than BG2 from April to June 2026.
  • Wind is scored on experiment 33's Tuesday runs and solar on experiment 224's daily runs, so the gaps across types compare different rows.
  • Part 2 (separate PR) is the planned test of an XGBoost residual correction and an XGBoost spread model inside the solar plant forecast and the wind physics model. A sprinkled arm is kept if it closes at least half the gap at no worse than +0.01 on the placebo series (a series the correction should not change).

The code is in ml-experiments/00234-no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1/.

docs.title: Photovoltaic (PV) capacity: does matching sunny and cloudy days remove the demand?
docs.text:
Take-home message: pairing a sunny day with a cloudy day of the same day type and temperature removed none of a synthetic load that follows cloud, so the pair estimator is no better than the convex fit. The convex fit is the least-squares fit of solar capacity per season-year that experiment 129 used. The synthetic load is 10% of the injected capacity, scaled by each day's cloudiness, which is the variable the pairs are chosen on. The synthetic load therefore tests the worst case, not a measured demand response. With the load added, the load adds about 0.3 of the injected capacity to the pair estimator's recovery, against about 0.2 for the convex fit.

What was done. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm to a Primary substation's power, at 50% of the Primary's pinned capacity (the unmetered solar capacity that experiment 45's real-time estimate gives the Primary). The five farms A, B, C, D, and F are metered generators and are never named. Then we measured how much of the farm a matched-pair estimator finds. The recovery is the share of the injected farm found: the capacity found with the farm added, minus the capacity found without it, divided by the injected capacity.

A pair is two days of the same day type and clock offset, with similar temperatures and different cloudiness. The day types are weekday, Saturday, and Sunday. The clock offset is local time minus Coordinated Universal Time, which separates summer-time days from winter-time days. The two days are at most 21 days apart, and their mean daylight temperatures differ by at most 1 kelvin (K). The clear-sky index is the satellite global irradiance divided by its clear-sky value, and the sunny day's index exceeds the cloudy day's by at least 0.4.

The estimator regresses the pair's difference in net power on the pair's difference in solar shape. The net power is the Primary's demand minus its solar output. The solar shape is the unit PV output per MW of capacity, derated for temperature. The regression is a least-squares scale through the origin and has no demand terms.

The recovery is read for the five decision Primaries. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the substations whose capacity is judged, and D9 is shown beside them. The recovery is read from pairs in season-year 2024 (July 2024 to June 2025), and the capacity unit is the 99th percentile of alternating-current output over daylight half-hours, in MW.

Figure 1. Matched pairs find 0.76 of the farm, and a cloud-driven load adds 0.3 to the recovery.

Figure 2. The matched-pair capacity of the real power is 0.75 to 1.01 of the convex fit's.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• The pre-registered prediction failed. The plain recovery was predicted at 0.90 to 1.10 at 4 of the 5 decision Primaries, and it was in that range at 0 of 5 and under 0.88 at 5 of 5. The plan's rule drops the estimator when the recovery is under 0.88 at 3 or more Primaries, as here. The placebo was predicted under 0.15 and was above 0.15 at 5 of 5. With the cloud-driven load, the recovery was predicted to stay within 0.10 of the plain recovery, and the recovery with the load was within 0.10 of the plain recovery (the recovery with no load added) at 0 of 5 Primaries.
  • Pooled, with 80% intervals from resampling whole months (median over five farms, then over the five Primaries):
    • Plain recovery 0.758 (0.742 to 0.783); over the five farms the range is 0.65 to 0.82.
    • With the cloud-driven load 1.058 (1.041 to 1.075), so the load adds 0.295 (0.286 to 0.304).
    • Placebo (pairs whose sunny day is in December or January; the cloudy partner can fall up to 21 days away) 0.328, with 0.24 to 0.34 across Primaries. The placebo has one month per resampling stratum and so no interval.
    • Capacity of the real power 0.905 (0.838 to 0.956) of the convex fit's.
  • The estimator is linear, so the plain injection test cannot show demand absorption. The recovery equals the farm-only scale on the pair differences, which is why the cloud-driven load, the only input among those tested that reaches demand, is the informative test.
  • The placebo is not a clean zero. The injected farm still produces output in winter, and experiment 231's winter-rows fit found 0.475, so 0.33 is a farm-only winter scale and not an invented solar signal. The 0.33 is below the 0.475 of experiment 231 probably because the pair estimator uses only pairs whose sunny day is in December or January, not every winter row. The plan's limit of 0.15 was too low because the placebo still contains winter farm output.
  • Post hoc sensitivity, days with at least 20 daylight half-hours (10 hours). The plan fixed no minimum number of daylight half-hours for a day to be paired. The first choice, 20 half-hours, left no December or January day, so the placebo had no pairs, and the minimum was lowered to 10 half-hours for the main run. The run with 20 is kept as a post hoc sensitivity. The post hoc run's pooled recovery is 0.908 (0.899 to 0.928), in 0.90 to 1.10 at 4 of 5 Primaries (D5's recovery is 0.8997, just under 0.90), with 43 to 90 pairs per Primary against 122 to 181. The load still adds 0.266 (0.263 to 0.272), and the capacity of the real power is 0.969 (0.914 to 1.006) of the convex fit's. Restricting to days with at least 10 hours of daylight finds more of the farm. That agrees with experiment 231's finding that winter rows weaken the fit, though the split also changes which pairs exist.
  • Pair counts: medians over the farms of 122 to 181 pairs per Primary (2,100 to 3,500 half-hours) for the main run, and 84 to 140 for the placebo.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Data cut: the fits stop at 2026-07-01, so the maintainer's labelled exception (data to 2026-07-31) is not used. No forecast is scored.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Toy check: the pair estimator returned a synthetic capacity of 7 MW and a recovery of 0.5 of the injected farm to within 1e-6 before any real fit ran.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"): none fired. The month-block interval covers month-to-month variation only, and the spread over farms is reported separately. The result contradicts the pre-registered prediction, but the plan's own linearity caveat anticipated why the plain test was uninformative, so trigger 2 does not fire.
  • Review: one Sonnet code review and one Sonnet review of the page.
  • No Opus audit was run. The manager of the experiment sessions decided that quota did not allow an Opus review of any of this series' experiments, so the judgement that no trigger fired has no Opus audit, and a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the page instead.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Pairing did not remove the synthetic cloud-driven load, so a different remedy is worth testing. A learned demand-response model, fitted to the Primary's own cloud dependence, is one option.
  • Neural components: a small neural network for the demand's dependence on irradiance could separate the demand's dependence on irradiance from the solar term. The prediction that could fail is a bias under 0.10 on the cloud-driven load test.

docs.title: Plan: design
docs.text:
• Pairs. Within season-year 2024, a day is sunny when its daylight mean of the clear-sky index (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service global irradiance over clear-sky irradiance at the Primary) is at least 0.4 above the other day's. A pair needs the same day type, a mean daylight temperature within 1 K, and the two days within 21 days of each other. Each sunny day takes at most three cloudy partners, the ones with the smallest temperature gap. Holiday periods are excluded.
  • Estimator. The least-squares scale through the origin of the pair difference in net power on the pair difference in the temperature-derated unit shape of the fit in experiment 129, over the daylight half-hours at which both days have a training row. The recovery is the scale found with the farm's output added, minus the scale found without it, divided by the injected capacity.
  • Linearity caveat. The estimator is linear in the power, so the difference of its two scales is the scale fitted to the farm's output alone. A farm injection alone therefore cannot show demand absorption, and the recovery without load is a property of the estimator's shape and weather error (experiment 231's rung 1 reads 0.93). The informative tests are the cloud-driven load of experiment 129 (added to the net power, scaled to 10% of the injected capacity) and the placebo.
  • Placebo. The same pairing and estimator on December and January days only, where the sun is low, reported as the share of the injected capacity found. The injected farm still produces a little output in those months, so the placebo's expected value is small and not zero.
  • Intervals. A month-block bootstrap of the pairs by the month of the sunny day, 200 resamples, stratified as in experiment 231, and the range over the five farms.

docs.title: Plan: checks
docs.text:
• Pair count: report the number of pairs and the usable half-hours per Primary. A Primary with fewer than 30 pairs is reported and left out of the "4 of 5" count.
  • Toy check: the script runs its pairing and scale on a synthetic series with a known capacity and no demand, and must return that capacity to within 1e-6 before any real fit runs.

docs.title: Photovoltaic (PV) capacity: does fitting only on clear, high-sun half-hours help?
docs.text:
Take-home message: fitting the solar capacity only on clear, high-sun half-hours does not find more of an injected solar farm, and the interval gets wider. Consistent with experiment 231, the irradiance input does not appear to be the limit, and restricting the rows seems to move the loss into the demand terms.

What was done. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm to a Primary substation's power, at 50% of the Primary's pinned capacity (the unmetered solar capacity that experiment 45's real-time estimate gives the Primary). Then we asked the capacity fit of experiment 129 how much of the farm it finds again, using only the half-hours where the Primary's satellite irradiance is at least 0.9 of its clear-sky value, the clear-sky irradiance is at least 200 watts per square metre, and the sun is at least 20 degrees above the horizon. The share found is the recovery: the capacity found with the farm added, minus the capacity found without it, divided by the injected capacity. The five farms A, B, C, D, and F are metered generators and are never named. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five decision Primaries of experiment 103's data set, and D9 is shown beside them. The recovery is read at season-year 2024 (July 2024 to June 2025), and the capacity unit is the 99th percentile of alternating-current output over daylight half-hours, in MW.

Figure 1. Clear half-hours leave the recovery at about 0.82 and widen the interval.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• The pre-registered prediction failed. The recovery was to rise by at least 0.05 at 4 of the 5 decision Primaries and the interval was to widen by no more than 50%. The rise was at least 0.05 at 1 of 5 Primaries (D11, +0.082), and the interval was no wider than 1.5 times at 0 of 5.
  • Pooled recovery (median over five farms, then over the five Primaries; 80% interval from resampling whole months): 0.827 (0.814 to 0.842) on all rows and 0.818 (0.799 to 0.851) on clear rows. The change is -0.002 (-0.040 to 0.023). The pooled interval is 1.8 times wider on clear rows.
  • The farm alone fits better on the clear half-hours (0.965; 0.951 to 0.967), but the full fit does not. Demand absorption, the farm-alone scale minus the full-fit recovery, is 0.147 on clear rows and 0.104 on all rows (experiment 231's rung 1, the farm alone on all daylight half-hours, minus its rung 4, the full fit on all rows: 0.931 and 0.827). A possible cause is that the clear-day solar curve is smooth. A smooth curve is closer to the seasonal demand terms, so the demand terms may take more of it. The smooth-curve explanation was not tested directly here.
  • The clear rows are a small share of the training rows. At the five decision Primaries, 5,600 to 5,900 of 78,000 to 89,000 training half-hours remain (3,300 of 45,000 at D9), and 1,300 to 1,600 remain in the read-out season-year.
  • The all-rows fit reproduces experiment 231's full fit (the maximum absolute difference over every Primary and farm prints as 0.000 at three decimals).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Data cut: the fits stop at 2026-07-01, so the maintainer's labelled exception (data to 2026-07-31) is not used. No forecast is scored.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"): none fired. The result contradicts the pre-registered prediction, but experiment 231 had already lowered that prior and the result agrees with its finding that the irradiance input is not the limit. The coverage test of experiment 129 (23 of 30 cells) was not re-run; the interval-width condition stood in for it. The intervals are month-block bootstrap intervals only; the plan's range over the five farms is not reported.
  • No Opus audit was run. The ML manager decided that quota did not allow an Opus review of any of this series' experiments, so the judgement that no trigger fired has no Opus audit, and a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the page instead.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Reduce demand absorption. Matched sunny-minus-cloudy day pairs (experiment 235) target demand absorption directly.
  • Neural components: a learned smooth response of the demand's dependence on irradiance could separate the demand's cloud response from the solar term. The prediction that could fail is a full-fit recovery of 0.90 or more on all rows.

docs.title: Plan: design
docs.text:
• Rows. The row rule is applied through month weights and a row mask on the per-month Gram matrices (the sums of products of the design columns), as in experiment 231, so that the base and injected fits share one row set.
  • Demand terms. The demand columns of the fit are unchanged. On clear days the solar shape is closer to a smooth seasonal curve than on all days, so the demand harmonics may absorb more of it; the experiment reports demand absorption as the contrast between the farm-only scale on clear rows and the full fit on clear rows.
  • Reported rows. The recovery on clear rows, the recovery on all rows (rung 4 of experiment 231), the number of training rows kept, and the share of each season-year kept.
  • Intervals. A month-block bootstrap, 200 resamples, stratified as in experiment 231, and the range over the five farms.

docs.title: Plan: checks
docs.text: • Reproduction: with the row rule switched off the script must reproduce experiment 231's rung 4 at every Primary and farm to within 1e-6.

docs.title: Does the two-number solar summary keep its gain when the solar term is clipped at D5 and D9?
docs.text:
Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation lowers the D5 daylight quantile score about as much with the solar clip as without it, but on the sunniest rows the gain from the mean appears to be largely lost once the clip is in. D5 and D9 are anonymised Primary substations, which feed homes and businesses. Each demand forecast subtracts an estimate of the embedded solar generation, called the solar term. The ensemble weather forecast has 51 members. Experiment 187 passed each member through the solar term. That pass lowered the daylight quantile score of the demand forecast. Experiment 193 found that the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 members' solar responses keep 98% of that gain. We call this the two-number summary. Experiment 180 and experiment 214 capped the solar output that the forecast subtracts at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5, and we call this cap "the clip". Cloud uncertainty and the clip both matter at midday, so we asked whether the clip removes part of the gain from the two-number summary.

We built two conditions at D5 and D9 with experiment 193's method. In the no-clip condition the forecast and the 51 member responses are experiment 184's. In the clip condition each member passes through the clipped fits of experiment 214 (the 60% clip, and the 50% clip at the cuts where experiment 214 chose it as-of), and arm A is experiment 214's forecast. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, in points of effective capacity (percentage points of the substation's rated demand), and a gain is the change from arm A as a percentage. Arm M uses the 51 members and arm Q2 uses the mean and standard deviation. The retained share is Q2's gain with the clip divided by Q2's gain without the clip. A row is one forecast of one half-hour at one lead, so a half-hour appears in several rows.

Verdict supported. At D5 the retained share of the daylight gain is 110% in the scored year (95% interval 91% to 141%) and 102% (70% to 136%) in the replicate months, so the prediction of at least 70% holds. At D9 it is 76% (27% to 163%), and that interval includes 70%. Two checks qualify the result: the sunniest third has a retained share of 48% (-12% to 88%), and on those rows the clip turns the two-number summary's 4.8% reduction in the median's absolute error into a 4.6% increase.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Rows: experiment 178's rows at D5 and D9 in the scored year (2025-07-02 to 2026-06-29), leads to 168 hours, outside the load shifts. Daylight means the sun is at least 5 degrees above the horizon. D5 has 39,874 daylight rows and 14,045 sunny rows (the sunniest third); D9 has 43,551 and 15,415. Offset and spread factors are fitted on the tuning months of D5 and D9 together, separately for each condition.
  • Arms: A is the forecast without member information, M the 51 members, Q2 the mean and standard deviation of the responses, and SG (post hoc) the standard deviation of the responses only, with the mean response set to zero.
  • Quantile score, D5 daylight, scored year: A 5.294, M 5.129, Q2 5.117 without the clip; A 5.028, M 4.848, Q2 4.842 with the clip. The clip alone changes arm A by -5.0% (-10.9% to +0.4%).
  • Gain of Q2 (95% interval): D5 -3.34% (-4.50% to -2.12%) without the clip and -3.68% (-4.66% to -2.71%) with it. D9 -1.58% (-2.46% to -0.71%) and -1.21% (-2.02% to -0.35%). D5 and D9 pooled -2.63% and -2.67%, retained 101% (85% to 129%).
  • Retained share of Q2's gain: D5 110% (91% to 141%), D9 76% (27% to 163%). A ratio is not meaningful where the gain without the clip has an interval that includes zero, as at D9 in the replicate months and on sunny rows. Replicate months: D5 102% (70% to 136%, the lower end only touches the 70% bar), D9 22% (-255% to 273%), pooled 84% (54% to 110%). M's retained share at D5 is 115% (95% to 151%).
  • Q2 against M under the clip: on daylight rows D5 -0.11% (-0.43% to +0.14%) and D9 +0.07% (-0.14% to +0.25%), so the two numbers match the 51 members to within about half a percentage point there. On sunny rows Q2 is worse than M by 0.61% at D5 (-0.06% to +1.08%) and 0.41% at D9 (0.05% to 0.81%).
  • Sunniest third at D5: the Q2 gain is -5.57% (-8.60% to -3.24%) without the clip and -2.67% (-6.85% to +0.45%) with it, a retained share of 48% (-12% to 88%). The clip alone lowers arm A's quantile score on those rows by 15.2% (3.4% to 25.4%).
  • Median error: with the clip, Q2 raises the mean absolute error of the median by 1.4% (0.9% to 2.0%) on D5 daylight rows and 4.6% (0.7% to 7.5%) on sunny rows, where without the clip Q2 lowers the error by 0.7% (-1.6% to +0.3%) and 4.8% (3.6% to 6.1%). At D9 on daylight rows the change is +0.2% (-1.0% to +1.5%) with the clip and -0.1% (-0.8% to +0.6%) without it. On D9's sunny rows it is +1.8% (-1.2% to +4.2%) with the clip and -2.5% (-4.2% to -1.4%) without it.
  • Rescale-only control (post hoc): arm A with only its offset factor refitted, and no member information, changes D5 daylight rows by -0.65% (-1.19% to -0.10%) with the clip and -0.69% (-1.19% to -0.18%) without it, and D5 sunny rows by -0.63% (-1.60% to +0.19%) with the clip. Recalibration alone therefore explains little of the spread-only gain below.
  • Spread only (post hoc): SG's D5 gain is -4.11% (-5.09% to -3.22%) with the clip and -2.86% (-4.05% to -1.79%) without it; on sunny rows -4.18% (-5.75% to -3.04%) with the clip, better than Q2's -2.67%, and -1.89% without it. Its median error with the clip changes by +0.3% (daylight) and +1.5% (sunny, 0.5% to 2.5%).
  • Tails, D5 daylight, scored year (coverage; pinball loss in points):
Quantile A, no clip Q2, no clip A, clip Q2, clip q01 0.023; 0.355 0.012; 0.317 0.025; 0.328 0.010; 0.272 q05 0.075; 1.293 0.047; 1.192 0.089; 1.219 0.053; 1.054 q95 0.902; 1.365 0.927; 1.256 0.918; 1.349 0.942; 1.210 q99 0.974; 0.388 0.981; 0.345 0.982; 0.359 0.989; 0.324
  • Clip form this experiment would suggest for the assembly: the as-of 60% clip of experiment 214, with the standard deviation of the member responses and without their mean on the sunniest half-hours. The mean-free form is a post hoc finding.
  • Post hoc: arm SG, and every sunny-row cut. The pre-registered contrast is the daylight retained share of Q2 at D5.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast: the arms store quantiles only, so no mean forecast exists to compare. Arm A's mean equals its median in experiments 180 and 193.
  • Median error beside the quantile score: the quantile score and the median's absolute error point in different directions in the clip condition. Q2 lowers the quantile score by 3.7% on D5 daylight rows and raises the median's absolute error by 1.4%. Arm SG shows the disagreement comes from the members' mean, because SG keeps the quantile gain and its median error rises by only 0.3%.
  • Triggers fired: the third trigger of the ml-experiment skill's audit list (the quantile- score contrast and the median-error contrast point in different directions). The mean-free arm SG is the explanation we tested. No audit by a second reviewer has run.
  • Control: the no-clip condition reproduces experiment 193's D5 gain (-3.34% against -3.27%), with factors refitted on D5 and D9 only. Experiment 193's arms were not re-run.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Two substations and one year. The D9 intervals are wide. The replicate months hold six months.
  • The mean and standard deviation are taken after each member is passed through the clipped solar term. The clip is nonlinear, so taking them before the clip would give a different answer.
  • The clip ceiling was chosen by experiment 214 as-of and is read from that experiment's stored fits. Arm A in the clip condition is experiment 214's, whose mean forecast differs from experiment 184's through the clip only.

  • The plan was committed after the first run, so the pre-registration holds only for the prediction and decision rule in the maintainer's brief.

  • Fitted factors at the edge of the grid. The clip condition's spread factor is 1.5, the top of the grid, in the shortest lead band for Q2 and the spread-only arm, so the spread may be truncated.

  • The member deltas are not checked against experiment 214's mean. The reproduction gate of experiment 184 compares against an unclipped mean, so it applies only to the no-clip arm, where it passes (4e-6). Experiment 214's stage-2 mean also recomputes the filter on the clipped residuals. We did not test that the deltas sit consistently on that mean.
  • The sunny mask differs slightly from experiment 214's. It is the top third of each period's own unit-shape values and includes rows where no member is available. Experiment 214 used the period before 2024-07, so the cut differs slightly. The tuning and replicate months use the fixed 60% clip, as experiment 214 chose 60% at every cut there.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• A pre-registered test of the spread-only form at D5 on a later scored period is possible once the period from 2026-07-01 onwards, which is held out from all experiments, is released for scoring.
  • The final assembly could include one combined arm with the two numbers and the clip, scored per substation and on the sunniest third.

docs.title: PV capacity: does a nearby metered farm work as the sunshine reference?
docs.text:
Take-home message: a nearby farm's measured output finds more of an injected solar farm than the satellite irradiance does, but the result does not yet show that the irradiance is the limit. The pooled recovery rises from 0.780 to 0.867, and the gain is at least 0.05 at all five decision Primaries. The nearby farm's output also carries plant effects, so part of the gain may come from the plant shape, which experiment 231 found explains much of the shortfall.

What was done. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm (farms A to F are metered generators and are never named) to a Primary substation's power at 50% of the Primary's pinned capacity, as in experiment 231. The convex fit of experiment 129 then reported how much of the farm it found again, under two solar shapes. The first is the satellite-based shape. The second is the recorded output of a different farm, the one nearest to the Primary within 30 km of the injected farm, divided by its 99th percentile with the temperature derating divided out. The Primaries are 3 to 23 km from their reference farms. D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five decision Primaries (the substations whose capacity is judged), and D9 is shown beside them. The recovery is the 99th percentile of the recovered output over daylight half-hours of season-year 2024 (July 2024 to June 2025), divided by the 99th percentile of the injected farm's output over the same half-hours, both in alternating-current MW. Fits stop at 2026-07-01, so the maintainer's labelled exception (data to 2026-07-31) is not used, and no forecast is scored.

Figure 1. A nearby farm's output as the solar shape finds 0.87 of the injected farm, against 0.78 for the satellite shape.

Figure 2. The gain is 0.17 to 0.24 for the one pair of farms 2 km apart and 0.02 to 0.14 for farms 5 to 25 km apart.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• The prediction was half met. The recovery rose by at least 0.05 at 5 of 5 decision Primaries (the prediction asked for 4 of 5). The farm alone, fitted on one scale of the shape, explains 0.953 of the injected farm's squared output, below the predicted 0.97, against 0.895 for the satellite shape.
  • Pooled recovery, with 80% intervals from resampling whole months (median over the injected farms, then over the five Primaries):
    • Satellite shape on all rows 0.780 (0.767 to 0.791), and on the rows where the reference farm has a reading 0.780 (0.765 to 0.790).
    • Nearby farm's output 0.867 (0.863 to 0.878).
    • Gain on the same rows (median over farms of each farm's paired difference, so not the difference of the medians) 0.090 (0.074 to 0.100). Per Primary the gain is 0.058 (D5), 0.138 (D10), 0.115 (D11), 0.066 (D14), and 0.090 (D16), and 0.168 at D9.
  • The gain is smaller in the capacity unit of experiment 231. The plain capacity ratio rises from 0.826 to 0.869, a gain of 0.052 (0.029 to 0.061), and the gain reaches 0.05 at 3 of 5 Primaries (D10, D11, and D16). The two readings differ because the reference farm's 99th percentile over the rows is higher than the injected farm's.
  • The 5 pairs under 5 km are the same 2 farms (A and C) in both directions. They may flatter the result, because two farms 2 km apart probably share nearly all their weather. The median gain is 0.198 for the 5 pairs less than 5 km apart, 0.069 for the 8 pairs 5 to 12 km apart, and 0.073 for the 16 pairs 12 to 30 km apart. Without the pairs under 5 km, the median gain per decision Primary is still 0.058 to 0.116, at least 0.05 at 5 of 5.
  • The gain shrinks with the demand terms frozen, but remains. With the demand terms frozen at the base fit, the recovery rises from 0.897 to 0.959 (gain 0.064, 80% interval 0.057 to 0.080), against 0.090 with the demand terms free.
  • The farm-only gain is small. The share of the injected farm's output that one scale of the shape explains rises by 0.025 (0.018 to 0.047), from 0.929 to 0.954. The share of squared output rises by 0.054, from 0.895 to 0.953. The prediction quoted 0.953 as the satellite shape's value from experiment 218, a different statistic (a fit at the farm's own site), so the 0.97 target is not comparable with the figures here.
  • The decision rule is met on the pre-registered metric. The recovery rises by at least 0.05 at 5 of 5 Primaries by the 99th-percentile ratio and at 3 of 5 by the capacity ratio. The reference is kept only as a test of plant shape, not as a sunshine measure.
  • Row counts. The reference farm's dropouts remove 151 to 3,941 (median over farms) of 45,168 to 89,172 training rows per Primary. The satellite and reference arms use identical rows.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: the satellite shape on all rows reproduces experiment 231's rung 4 (the full joint fit on all rows) at every Primary and injected farm, with a largest difference of 0.000 at three decimal places.
  • Derating: the script checks that the reference shape, derated by the fit, equals the farm's output to within 1e-6 on every half-hour at which both farms have output, and it did at every Primary.
  • Same rows: the satellite and reference arms train on the same number of rows at every Primary, as the script asserts.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"): trigger 2 fires, because the result is in apparent tension with the finding of experiment 231 that the irradiance contributes almost none of the shortfall, and the explanation in the Limits section was not tested here. Trigger 7 fires because the design of experiment 239 (the seasonal efficiency curve) depends on whether the gain is plant shape or sunshine. The maintainer's decision on an audit is pending.
  • Review: one Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code, and one of the page.
  • No Opus audit was run. The ML manager decided that quota did not allow an Opus review of any of this series' experiments, so every audit trigger listed above stays unaudited and a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the page instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The reference farm's output holds more than sunshine. It reflects the farm's tilt, orientation, curtailment, and soiling, so the gain may come from plant shape that the plant model lacks. A null result would have meant that one farm is not a clean sunshine index, and the gain has the matching reading: it does not show that a better irradiance product would help.
  • Distance between the injected farm and the reference farm is up to 25 km, often larger than the distance from a real unmetered farm to its nearest metered farm. Figure 2 shows the gain against that distance.
  • A reference farm metered behind the Primary would sit in both the base and the injected series and cancel in their difference, so it should cancel to first order (the bounded, penalised fit is not linear).
  • The interval covers month-to-month variation only, and the spread over injected farms is shown by the dots of figure 2.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does the gain come from sunshine or from plant shape? Fit the shared seasonal efficiency curve of experiment 239 on the farms' output first. If the curve recovers most of the 0.09, the nearby farm was supplying plant shape. The prediction that could fail is a gain from the curve of at least 0.03 at 4 of 5 Primaries.
  • A neural component that learns the plant shape from the farms' output could be tested against the satellite shape and the reference shape together.

docs.title: Plan: design
docs.text:
• Distances. Each Primary has a metered farm within 30 km (the brief's rule). The nearest farms to the five decision Primaries and D9 are 3 to 23 km away.
  • The reference farm. For an injected farm X, the reference is the nearest farm to the Primary among the other farms with data from 2019-09 (A, B, C, D, F), provided it lies within 30 km of X. A reference at X itself would return the injected output and make the test trivial. The injected farm and the reference farm are different sites, as a real unmetered farm and a metered reference would be, but their distance (up to 25 km) is often larger than the distance from a real unmetered farm to its nearest metered farm. The recovery is therefore also reported against the distance between the injected farm and the reference farm. Farm E is neither injected nor a reference, because its record starts later than 2019-09. A Primary with fewer than three eligible farms is reported as not testable.
  • The shape. The reference farm's output divided by its 99th percentile over daylight half-hours, with the temperature derating divided out, so that the fit does not apply the derating a second time. The fit's derating is u (1 - 0.004 (T + 25 u - 25)) for the shape u and the Primary's temperature T in degrees Celsius, and u is found by fixed-point steps. The script checks that the fit's derated shape equals the farm's normalised output to within 1e-6 on daylight half-hours. The reference farm's own temperature differs from the Primary's, which this approximation ignores. Night half-hours take a shape of zero, as the farm output does. Half-hours at which the reference farm has a dropout or no reading drop out of both the base and the injected fit.
  • Controls. The CAMS shape on the identical rows (so a change in the rows is not mistaken for a change of shape), and the CAMS shape on all rows. The script asserts that the satellite and reference arms train on the same number of rows. The CAMS shape on all rows, fed through the same shape-substitution code, must reproduce experiment 231's rung 4 (the full joint fit on all rows) to within 1e-6.
  • The farm-only fit. The share of the injected farm's squared output explained by one scale of the reference shape and of the CAMS shape, on season-year 2024 daylight half-hours, as in experiment 231's rungs 1 and 2.
  • Intervals. A month-block bootstrap, 200 resamples, stratified as in experiment 231, and the range over the eligible farms.
  • Limits to state. The reference farm's output also reflects its tilt, azimuth, curtailment, and soiling, so a null result can mean that one farm's output is not a clean sunshine index, not that a better reference would not help. A reference farm metered behind the Primary would sit in both the base and the injected series and cancel in their difference.
  • Stop rule. If the reference does not explain more of the injected farm than the CAMS shape on the farm-only fit, the injection fits still run, because they are cheap, and the write-up says the reference carries no new information.

docs.title: Plan: checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction and derating: as above.
  • Review: one Sonnet review of this plan, one of the code, one of the write-up.

docs.title: PV capacity: does a shared seasonal efficiency curve help?
docs.text:
Take-home message: twelve monthly efficiency factors fitted on the metered farms' output do not close the recovery shortfall, and the injection of experiment 231 was itself part of it. The curve raises the farm-only fit from 0.946 to 0.949, below the target of 0.968. The curve raises the pooled recovery by 0.039 with the injection of experiment 231 and by 0.025 when the injected farm keeps its low-sun output. Keeping that output raises the recovery by 0.033 on its own. Every "gain" on this page is the median over farms of each farm's paired difference, so it can differ from the difference of two medians (0.780 to 0.825 is 0.045, against the paired 0.039).

What was done. We added the recorded output of a real solar farm (farms A to F are metered generators and are never named) to a Primary substation's power at 50% of the Primary's pinned capacity, as in experiment 231, and the convex capacity fit of experiment 129 reported how much of the farm it found again. The fit used the satellite-based solar shape, with and without a seasonal efficiency curve. The curve has 12 monthly factors, each the mean over the four other farms of the least-squares scale of a farm's output on its own satellite-based shape, divided by the mean of the 12 values. The injected farm is never one of the four. Figure 1 shows the curve of all five farms.

A deviation from the plan. The plan described only the injection of experiment 231, which sets the farm's output to zero when the sun is under 15 degrees above the horizon (zenith over 75 degrees), so that December has almost no output. The first fit of the curve showed a December factor near zero, so we added a full-sun injection that keeps the output at every sun height, and we fitted the curve at every sun height. The full-sun injection takes its unit from the same 99th percentile, so the two injections differ only in the low-sun half-hours and in a few training rows. The full-sun arm is exploratory. The plan's check that a curve of 12 ones reproduces the arm without the curve was not run.

D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are the five decision Primaries (the substations whose capacity is judged), and D9 is shown beside them. The recovery is the 99th percentile of the recovered output over daylight half-hours of season-year 2024 (July 2024 to June 2025), divided by the 99th percentile of the injected farm's output over the same half-hours, both in alternating-current MW. Fits stop at 2026-07-01, so the maintainer's labelled exception for capacity experiments (data to 2026-07-31) is not used, and no forecast is scored.

Figure 1. The farms fall below the satellite shape in November to January and differ by 3% from April to September.

Figure 2. The curve raises the pooled recovery from 0.780 to 0.825 with the injection of experiment 231 and from 0.822 to 0.843 with a full-sun injection.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• The farm-only fit missed its target, and the planned recovery condition was met. The farm-only fit rose from 0.946 to 0.949 over all years and from 0.955 to 0.962 in season-year 2024 (median over farms), against a target of 0.968. With the injection of experiment 231, the recovery rose by at least 0.03 at 5 of 5 Primaries. The decision rule needs both, so it is not met, and the verdict rests on the farm-only fit. With the full-sun injection, which the plan did not include, the recovery rose by less than 0.03 at every Primary.
  • The factors are lowest in November to January. They are 0.82 in January, 0.88 in November, and 0.71 in December, and 1.01 to 1.10 from February to October. The factors are a description of the fit, not a cause: most of the half-hours fitted in December and part of those in November and January have a sun under 15 degrees above the horizon (the share of the fit weight above that height is 1% in December, 69% in November, and 43% in January). Refitted on half-hours with the sun above 15 degrees only, the factors are 0.89 in January and 0.91 in November, so the dip shrinks but remains. From April to September the largest factor is 1.03 times the smallest, so the 6% to 9% fall of the flat top from spring to summer does not appear as a monthly scale on the satellite shape. The range over farms is 0.62 to 0.80 in December.
  • Pooled recovery, with 80% intervals from resampling whole months (median over the five injected farms, then over the five Primaries):
    • Injection as in experiment 231: 0.780 (0.767 to 0.791) without the curve and 0.825 (0.810 to 0.828) with it. The paired gain is 0.039 (0.034 to 0.042), at least 0.03 at 5 of 5 Primaries.
    • Full-sun injection: 0.822 (0.806 to 0.823) without the curve and 0.843 (0.831 to 0.849) with it. The paired gain is 0.025 (0.023 to 0.028), at least 0.03 at 0 of 5 Primaries. The gains at D10 (0.027) and D14 (0.026) lie within resampling noise of 0.03.
    • With the demand terms frozen at the base fit, the gain is 0.021 (0.017 to 0.024) with the injection of experiment 231 and 0.015 (0.012 to 0.017) with the full-sun injection.
  • Keeping the farm's low-sun output raises the recovery. The pooled paired gain is 0.033 (80% interval 0.027 to 0.035), and 0.029 to 0.036 at each decision Primary. The injection of experiments 129 and 231 therefore understates the recovery of a farm that produces in winter. The two injections also differ in their training rows (the full-sun injection removes 89 to 223 of 45,000 to 89,000 rows per Primary, median over farms, where a dropout falls between 15 and 0 degrees of sun height), and the full-sun output carries its own noise at low sun.
  • The capacity ratio of experiment 231 falls with the curve (0.827 to 0.812, paired change -0.021), while the ratio of 99th percentiles rises. The curve has mean 1 over the year, so it raises the shape from February to October and lowers it from November to January, which changes the scale that the fit finds. The 99th percentile of the derated shape over the read-out year, which summer half-hours dominate, rises from 0.948 to 1.019 of the injected farm's, while the fitted capacity falls by 1.8%. The ratio of 99th percentiles therefore reads summer-peak output only, and part of its gain is the curve lifting that peak; winter output is not measured by it.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: the satellite shape with the injection of experiment 231 reproduces experiment 231's rung 4 (the full joint fit on all rows) at every Primary and injected farm, with a largest difference of 0.00e+00.
  • Derating: the script checks that the curved shape, derated by the fit, equals the satellite shape times the curve to within 1e-6, and it did at every Primary and farm.
  • Same rows: the satellite and curved shapes train on the same number of rows under each injection, as the script asserts. The two injections do not share rows exactly.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because the experiment scores no forecast.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"): trigger 2 fires, because the farm-only fit missed its prediction, and the low-sun refit above is the explanation tested here. Trigger 7 fires, because the finding on the low-sun cut changes how experiments 231, 235, 236, and 238 should be read. The maintainer's decision on an audit is pending.
  • Review: one Sonnet review of the plan, one of the code, and one of the page.
  • No Opus audit was run. The ML manager decided that quota did not allow an Opus review of any of this series' experiments, so every audit trigger listed above stays unaudited and a Sonnet reviewer read the code and the page instead.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The month-block intervals assume independent Primaries. Each Primary draws its own resamples, although the Primaries share the same calendar months, so the pooled intervals are probably too narrow.
  • The farm's temperature is the mean of the six Primaries' temperatures, because the farm frame holds no temperature. The temperature derating at the farm's own site is approximate, and the curve partly absorbs the heat loss, so the curve overlaps with the derating that the fit applies.
  • The curve has no interval for its own uncertainty. Each resample holds the curve fixed, and the range over farms is reported separately. The curve also uses the other farms' rows from the read-out year, so it is not a hold-out in time.
  • The satellite shape at the farm and at the Primary differs, because the farm sits tens of kilometres from the Primary, so the curve fitted at the farms is applied to a different shape.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does the full-sun injection change the winter finding of experiment 231? Experiment 231 found 0.475 from winter rows with the farm's low-sun output zeroed. The recovery in winter rows with the full-sun injection has not been measured.
  • How much demand absorption remains once the injection keeps the low-sun output? With the demand terms frozen at the base fit, the pooled recovery is 0.919 with the full-sun injection and 0.883 with the injection of experiment 231, against 0.822 and 0.780 with the demand terms free.

docs.title: Plan: design
docs.text:
• The curve. For each farm and calendar month, the least-squares scale of the farm's output (divided by its 99th percentile) on the temperature-derated satellite shape at the farm's own site, over half-hours with the sun up before 2026-07-01 (the plan said daylight half-hours with the sun under 75 degrees of zenith; the fit used every sun height, as the deviation above explains).
