docs.text: Experiment 268 found crossing quantiles in 26,344 of its 77,897 generator-forecast rows (34%), but all of them belong to three generators that are not solar farms, so none is on this page. Experiment 273 counted 0 crossing rows in every arm here, because the fit scripts sorted the 11 quantiles before writing them, so sorting does not change the scores on this page.

docs.title: Experiment 249: retraining the learned load-shift score on its own consistent events finds no more real transfers
docs.text:
Retraining the learned load-shift score on real events that pass a consistency check, which needs no NGED label, did not find any extra real transfer. A transfer is a period in which a change to the network arrangement moves load from one Primary substation (a substation that steps transmission voltage down to distribution voltage) to its neighbours. The score is the neural network of experiment 195, which ranks candidate alarms. Before retraining (round 1) it finds 24 of the 35 hand-labelled real transfers lasting over 1 day, at 80 unexplained alarms in odd-numbered months. After retraining (round 2) it finds the same 24: the difference is 0 in every resample of whole pairs of Primary substations. The prediction was at least 3 more of the 35, so the hypothesis is refuted. The likely cause is a shortage of examples: 38 to 47 real events per fold (56 distinct events across the three folds, because folds share events) pass the check, against about 2,000 injected transfers per fold. A fold is one third of the Primary pairs, held out while the score is trained. Giving the real events more weight, using a stricter check, using even-numbered months only, and adding a third round changed the count by between −2 and +1 transfers.

What we asked. Flexpectation version 2 will have no NGED labels, so the score must be trained on injected (synthetic) transfers alone. We asked whether retraining it on its own most consistent real events, as pseudo-labels, lets it find more real transfers. We fixed the consistency check before scoring any transfer. A real event counts as consistent when the forecast error steps by at least 2.5 noise units over 24 hours, a neighbouring Primary substation steps the opposite way, the logistic regression scores it in the top quarter of candidates, and the error returns to its old level at the estimated end. The full design, including the hold-out of each pair's own transfers, is below.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Headline. No round 2 or round 3 arm of the re-ranker (the neural network that re-scores RO-NC's candidate alarms) finds more transfers than round 1, which finds 24 of 35 (MW-weighted recall 0.752, 95% interval 0.585 to 0.865). RO-NC is the refit-offset neighbour-count detector of experiment 82. Round 2 with pseudo-positive weight 0.25 finds 24 (0 gained, 0 lost). Weight 0.5, even-month events only, and the strict tier each find 22 (−2, interval −4.7 to 0). The series-level hold-out finds 23. Round 3 finds 24. The heavy-weight arm finds 24.
  • Heavy weight (post hoc). This arm gives the pseudo-positives together a quarter of the total weight of the injected positives, about 15 to 20 times the per-row weight of the 0.25 arm.
  • Logistic regression. Round 1 finds 22. Every round 2 and round 3 arm finds 22 except the heavy-weight arm, which finds 23 (+1, interval 0 to +3, so indistinguishable from no change). The one transfer gained lasts 48 hours and moves 0.4 MW, and neither the pair alarm nor RO-NC finds it.
  • Reproduction. The retrained round 1 finds 24 (re-ranker) and 22 (logistic regression), the numbers of experiment 195, and its re-runs of RO-NC and the pair alarm find 19 and 5.
  • Confirmation bias. Round 2 gained no transfer, so no sign of it re-finding what the pair alarm finds is visible. Of the 56 distinct pseudo-positives, 12 lie within 2 hours of a labelled transfer's onset (counted after scoring, for this page only). The report does not separate the other 44 into unlabelled real events and false alarms.
  • Pseudo-positive mix. Of the 130 fold-level rows, 99 step under 1 MW and 31 step 1 to 3 MW, and none steps over 3 MW. They sit on 13 of the 16 Primary series, 23 of them on series 24. Each fold holds 16 to 19 events in odd months, where the alarm threshold is chosen.
  • Injected-world recall. Rounds 1 and 2 agree to within 0.01 on both injected sets. On the held-out pairs, recall over 1 day is 0.595 for round 1 and 0.588 for round 2 at weight 0.25, so retraining did not reduce recall on injected transfers.
  • Downstream test not run. The decision rule marks the experiment refuted when the count difference is 0 or below. The headline arm finds exactly the transfers that round 1 finds, but its alarm sets differ elsewhere (277 against 266 alarms over all months), so the gated-mask replay of experiment 203 would not be identical. It was not run.
  • Tail calibration, curtailment cost, and forecast quantiles do not apply: the experiment scores alarms, not a forecast.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site: not applicable; no forecast is produced.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast: not applicable, for the same reason.
  • Triggers: the "Audit before merge" trigger for a result that contradicts its prediction fired. The explanation, too few consistent events, was tested in the same run with the heavy-weight arm, which moved the count by 0 to +1, so no audit was run. The failed-control trigger did not fire: the reproduction of experiment 195 is the positive control. The other five triggers do not apply or did not fire.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Lab shortcuts: the logged closures and labelled transfers define the hold-out, the explained-alarm flag in the threshold, and the negatives, as in experiment 195.
  • Printed numbers: printed_report.txt, printed_stage_a.txt (pseudo-positive counts), and printed_counts.txt (2,980 real candidates, 17 block days, injected training sizes).
  • Schedule: a single fit per arm and fold, three seeds averaged in each network; no weekly refits, because no forecast is trained.
  • Rule changes: the first draft of the strict tier passed 2 candidates per fold, so the thresholds were relaxed and the loose rule added before any transfer was scored.
  • Next step. Neither remedy was tested: a richer injector, or a longer record that holds more consistent events, such as the full history if disaggregation allows it. The choice belongs to the roadmap.

docs.title: Pre-registered design
docs.text:
• Round 1 is experiment 195's re-ranker and logistic regression, retrained here from the same stored injected worlds with the same seeds.
  • Pseudo-positive rule (label-free; evaluated on every real candidate of every source, over all months). Every pseudo-positive is outside the D8 drops and the 17 block days, has a logistic-regression score above the 75th percentile of that fold's scores over all real candidates (the re-ranker scores only RO-NC's candidates, so the logistic regression is the gate), and has a clean return. A clean return means the estimated end lies 48 to 176 half-hours after the step (so that the 12 half-hours after the end lie inside the 4-day window) and the own residual falls across the end by at least 50% of the step (mean of the 12 half-hours before the end minus mean of the 12 after, against the step measured the same way at the onset). The loose rule (headline) needs a 24-hour step of at least 2.5 noise units and an opposite step at any neighbour. The strict tier needs an own 6-hour step of at least 3.0, an opposite 6-hour step of at least 2.0 at a metered neighbour within 4 hours, and an opposite-to-own ratio between 0.3 and 2.0. The first draft of the strict tier (opposite step 3.0, ratio 0.5 to 1.5, return 70%, 90th percentile) passed 2 candidates per fold, so the thresholds were relaxed and the loose rule added before any real transfer was scored. Counts recorded before scoring: strict 14, 15, and 16 candidates in folds 0, 1, and 2; loose 49 in every fold, which falls to 47, 38, and 45 after the event hold-out (below), of which 19, 18, and 16 lie in odd months. The real record holds 2,980 candidates in all.
  • Hold-out. A pseudo-positive that lies within 48 half-hours before the onset to 48 half-hours after the end of a labelled transfer of fold k, on a series of that transfer, is dropped from fold k's round 2 training. The round 1 score that gates fold k's pseudo-positives is fold k's own model, trained without fold k's injector pairs. The series-level hold-out (drop every pseudo-positive on a series of fold k's pairs) is reported as a robustness check.
  • Hard negatives. The label-0 candidates of the injected worlds (as in experiment 195), plus real candidates that fail the rule and are either on an England bank holiday or isolated (no other candidate on any series within 7 days). A candidate is itself an alarm, so "quiet stretch" means an isolated alarm. D8 drops and block days are excluded from positives and negatives.
  • Round 2 retrains the same networks with injected positives at weight 1, pseudo-positives at weight 0.25 (headline) or 0.5, and the negatives at weight 1. A round 3 is run only if round 2 finds events that round 1 missed and the pair alarm did not.
  • Scoring. Operating point at 80 unexplained odd-month alarms, as in experiment 195; the 35 transfers are scored last. The downstream test copies experiment 203's harness with round 2's alarms.

docs.title: Sources
docs.text: Experiments 189 and 195 supply the injector, the scoring that holds out whole pairs, and the learned score. Experiments 171 and 203 supply the downstream harness that this experiment did not run.

docs.title: Does a small monotone neural network between the solar forecast and the demand model beat the hard clip?
docs.text:
On top of the hard clip, the network lowers sunny-daylight error a little, but not by the 50% of the remaining gap that the plan required. The network reads the solar term after the 60% clip, the clear-sky index, the hour, and the cap. At D5 the network lowers the sunny-daylight error by 0.028 MW against the clip alone (figure 1).

Figure 1. Each arm against the 60% clip at D5 and D9. Smaller is better.

At D5, the network without the clip is worse than the clip. The network on the unclipped solar term raises D5's sunny-daylight error by 0.088 MW (0.019 to 0.142) against the clip, and adding the mean and standard deviation of the 51 members' solar responses lowers that excess by 0.008 MW.

Arm D5 gap to BG2 (MW) D5 closure beyond the clip D9 closure beyond the clip 60% clip 0.069 0% 0% Network and 60% clip 0.041 (0.008 to 0.062) 41% (28% to 81%) 38% (-59% to 221%) Network, unclipped 0.157 -127% -56% Network, unclipped, two numbers 0.149 -115% -53%

The gap is the mean absolute error of the median minus BG2's, on the sunniest third of daylight half-hours. The closure at D9 is unstable because the clip's own gap there is 0.042 MW with an interval that includes zero.

The placebos change by less than 0.01 MW. The network and clip arm changes the all-half-hour error at D10 and D16 by -0.002 and -0.003 MW against the clip (figure 2), inside the 0.01 MW limit.

Figure 2. The network arms against the 60% clip at D10 and D16, all half-hours.

The tail check fails for the clip and the network alike. At D5 the 95% quantile covers 99.5% of sunny-daylight half-hours (the clip alone: 99.6%) and 92.3% of all half-hours (the clip alone: 92.3%). Both coverages are more than 2 points from 95%.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The learned-cap arm of experiment 247 scores 0.005 MW worse than the clip on D5's sunny-daylight rows (-0.007 to 0.019), so it does not close the gap either.
  • The band-width factors are fitted on the same rows as the network, of which 85% are in the network's training split. That may narrow the bands and contribute to the 92.3% coverage.
  • Each network fit uses only forecasts whose valid time falls in the 12 months before the monthly cut. The early-stopping rows are the latest 15% of those rows.
  • The network's output at a zero solar term is subtracted, so the network removes nothing at night.
  • The network replaces the solar term in the stored forecast of the unclipped arm (experiment 180) or the 60% arm (experiment 214). The Kalman filter in each stored forecast adapted to its own solar term, not to the network's output.
  • Each network is the mean of 3 seeds.

docs.title: Which clip form the final assembly should use
docs.text: Use the hand-set 60% clip alone. The network removes 0.028 MW at D5 and 0.016 MW at D9 of sunny- daylight error, for a trained component on the serving path.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: A network trained end to end inside the demand model's loss, so the filter adapts to its output, would test whether the stored-forecast replacement in this experiment held the gain down.

docs.title: Does the full best-guess demand stack, with the D5 solar clip and the gap rule added, beat BG2 and the manual heuristic over one scored year, and where does it lose?
docs.text:
The full best-guess demand forecast has a lower error than BG2 and the manual heuristic over 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, but its gain comes from winter, and at substation D5 on sunny half-hours it is still clearly worse than BG2. BG2 is an XGBoost forecast configured like the production service, with the settings that scored best in experiment 87. The manual heuristic is the rule NGED uses today. D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised primary substations, which feed homes and businesses. We took the forecast of experiment 220 (arm 1). Arm D is the convex demand model with a Kalman filter. Arm 1 is arm D plus a small neural network that corrects its median (the neural-network head) and a mean-and-standard-deviation summary of the 51 ensemble weather members' solar response. We called arm 1 "the stack". We then added the 60% solar clip at D5 from experiment 180. The clip caps the modelled solar output that the forecast subtracts from demand at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5. We scored every forecast on the same 561,207 rows from 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30. A row is one forecast of one substation's half-hour from one forecast run, at one lead time. A quantile score (also our CRPS, the continuous ranked probability score) is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles (q01, q05, q10, q25, q40, q50, q60, q75, q90, q95, q99), in points, meaning percentage points of the substation's effective capacity (its rated demand). Lower is better.

The clip arms are an approximation, because we added the clip's per-row shift in the mean forecast to stored forecasts instead of refitting them. That shift includes the clip's effect on the filter state and the fit, so it is non-zero at night as well as at midday, and the solar summary and the network head were built on the unclipped solar term. Arm 2 adds the clip's per-row shift in the mean forecast, measured on arm D alone, to every quantile of arm 1 at D5. Arm 2b adds it to the stack without the head, and arm 2c (post hoc) uses arm 2b at D5 and arm 1 at the other five substations. Experiment 237 scored the solar summary with the clip applied inside the member pass. The coast-and-widen rule of experiment 205 changes only rows after a reading gap, so on the scored year's rows arm 3 equals arm 2 and the rule is reported from experiment 205's injected gaps.

Verdict supported. The gate passed on the five decision substations. Arm A scored 2.7524 against the required 2.7519 ± 0.005, BG2 2.7809 against 2.780 ± 0.005, and arm 1 2.6167 against 2.617 ± 0.005. Arm 1 is the pre-registered winner, because arm 2 was 0.038 points worse than arm 1 on D5 sunny daylight (interval -0.169 to +0.274), not 0.05 points better. It beats BG2 on the six-substation quantile score by 0.136 points (95% interval -0.277 to -0.005). It also beats the manual heuristic on all four headline metrics. The upper bound of the BG2 interval is only 0.005 below zero, so the margin is thin.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Prediction scorecard. P1 held (-0.136, in the predicted 0.10 to 0.17). P2 held: arm 2 equals arm 1 at the other five substations, and at D5 it is worse than arm 1 on sunny daylight (+0.038, -0.169 to +0.274) and on all D5 rows (+0.075, +0.034 to +0.121). P3 held: arm 2b's D5 sunny-daylight median error is 0.103 MW below arm 1's (0.033 to 0.170 MW). P4 held: the heuristic clause on all four metrics, and arm 1 is worse than BG2 in April, May, and June (+0.162, +0.220, +0.054), three of the six months from April to September. P5 held as stated, and see the gap bullet.
  • Absolute scores, six substations (quantile score; mean absolute error of the median; tail-weighted CRPS at the 95th and 99th percentile of earlier power): arm 1 2.579; 4.510; 0.171; 0.044. Arm 2c 2.574; 4.490; 0.171; 0.044. BG2 2.715; 4.767; 0.202; 0.051. Manual heuristic 3.397; 6.034; 0.246; 0.059. Climatology 3.665; 6.558; 0.263; 0.063. Weak XGBoost 5.697; 6.206; 0.360; 0.075. Arm D alone 2.688; 4.623; 0.191; 0.053. Arm D with the head 2.611; 4.510; 0.171; 0.044.
  • Arm 1 minus BG2 (95% intervals, six substations): quantile score -0.136 (-0.277 to -0.005), mean absolute error -0.257 (-0.492 to -0.009), tail-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile -0.032 (-0.073 to -0.004), at the 99th -0.008 (-0.019 to -0.001). It wins 9 of 12 months. All six substations have a negative estimate (D14 -0.266, D16 -0.227, D11 -0.176, D10 -0.108, D5 -0.031, D9 -0.004), but only the D14 and D16 intervals exclude zero (D11's reaches +0.001).
  • Arm 1 minus the manual heuristic: quantile score -0.818 (-1.080 to -0.574), mean absolute error -1.524 (-2.027 to -1.079), tail-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile -0.076 (-0.143 to -0.021), at the 99th -0.016 (-0.031 to -0.004), and 12 of 12 months. Arm 2c differs from arm 1 by under 0.02 on every one of these.
  • Curtailment saving against the manual heuristic (GBP over the scored rows, five substations, limit 0.9 times the largest earlier flow, GBP 2,000 per MWh-equivalent; 95% interval): arm 1 2.14 million (0.21 to 5.29 million), arm 2c 2.14 million (0.21 to 5.30 million), arm D 2.06 million, BG2 1.45 million (0.19 to 3.23 million), climatology -0.01 million, weak XGBoost -1.19 million. At limits of 0.75 and 0.5 the order is the same: arm 1 11.1 and 30.1 million, BG2 7.1 and 21.9 million. The heuristic's implied risk level and the price are the assumptions of experiment 228; the intervals are wide.
  • Where it loses to BG2 (arm 2c minus BG2, quantile score): D5 sunny daylight +0.540 (0.331 to 0.743); arm 1 there is +1.298. Christmas +0.545 (-0.293 to +0.554) on the blocks of two months (December 2025 and January 2026), so the interval is not informative. April to June are positive for arm 1 (+0.054 to +0.220). Winter is -0.425 (-0.586 to -0.259), 12 to 36 hours ahead -0.192, and daylight -0.200.
  • Cold nights below 2 C and bank holidays (arm 2c minus BG2): cold nights -0.711 (-2.825 to +0.828), over 3 months; bank holidays -0.734 (-1.778 to -0.021). On cold nights the q95 coverage is 0.965 for arm 2c, 0.781 for BG2, and 0.538 for the manual heuristic.
  • Tails, six substations (coverage; pinball loss, arm 2c against BG2): q01 0.013; 0.172 against 0.010; 0.211. q05 0.048; 0.621 against 0.041; 0.623. q95 0.950; 0.696 against 0.944; 0.751. q99 0.983; 0.213 against 0.983; 0.253. By UTC hour band the q95 coverage of arm 1 runs from 0.935 (12-18) to 0.960 (18-24), and q99 from 0.980 to 0.986.
  • D5 clip, quantile score change on D5 sunny daylight (95% interval): arm 2 minus arm 1 +0.038 (-0.169 to +0.274); arm 2b minus arm 1 -0.758 (-1.279 to -0.253); arm 2b minus the same arm without the clip -0.933 (-1.473 to -0.367), or 0.124 MW of median error (0.050 to 0.193 MW). Over all D5 rows arm 2b minus arm 1 is -0.034 (-0.126 to +0.057). D5 tail coverage changes by under 0.01 at every quantile for all three clip arms.
  • Gap rule, from experiment 205's stored scores (arm D on injected gaps, quantile score): gaps of 3, 6, 24, and 72 hours score 2.759, 2.788, 2.857, and 2.948 with coasting and widened bands, against 2.747 with no gap and 3.198 for the frozen model alone, so coasting is 0.25 to 0.44 below the frozen model alone. At 72 hours coasting without widening (2.953) and with it (2.948) are not better than the frozen model with its offset and recipe R (2.940). We did not measure the share of scored rows that follow a natural reading gap.
  • Weak production-style XGBoost model (experiment 87's ref_xgboost_baseline): its median error (6.206) sits level with the manual heuristic's (6.034), but its q01 to q99 band is 2.6 points wide against BG2's 36.6, and its q01 and q95 coverages are 0.41 and 0.52. Its quantile score of 5.697 reflects bands that are far too narrow, so only its median error compares fairly.
  • Rows and schedule: experiment 228's rows (561,207 across six substations, 09:00 UTC runs, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside hand-filtered load shifts). Experiments 220, 228, and 87 stored every forecast; nothing was refitted in this experiment. The stack's monthly refits and BG2's weekly refits are those experiments' schedules. Weather at lag times is the ensemble weather available at forecast time. No downloads.
  • Post hoc: arm 2b, arm 2c, and the weak XGBoost comparison; every cut other than the planned D5 sunny-daylight rows.
  • What to try next: the solar term at D5 on sunny hours; a retrained head on clipped residuals, which would replace the shift approximation; and A second scored year would need BG2 to be rerun for earlier months.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, arm 1, per substation (points; the mean is arm D's, before the head's correction): D5 +0.014, D9 -0.746, D10 +0.721, D11 -0.496, D14 -0.200, D16 -0.843. The head moves the median by under 1 point of capacity.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile-score contrasts: the median's absolute error and the quantile score move the same way in every contrast against BG2 and the manual heuristic, so trigger 3 did not fire. For arm 1 the mean's absolute error is 5.31, 4.21, 3.69, 4.48, 6.01, and 4.21 at D10, D11, D14, D16, D5, and D9, against 5.36, 4.20, 3.53, 4.03, 5.83, and 4.25 for the median.
  • Triggers (the seven audit triggers of the experiment guide): the failed control (1), the median-versus-mean disagreement (3), and the interval-width mismatch (6) did not fire; the gate passed and the contrasts agree in sign. Trigger 4 fired in part: leaving one substation out keeps arm 1 minus BG2 negative every time (-0.110 to -0.164), but the 95% interval then spans zero when D11, D14, or D16 is left out, so the gain over BG2 depends on all six substations and its upper bound is only -0.005. A fresh Sonnet agent re-derived the headline contrasts from the stored arrays with its own code and found no difference above 0.005 points. Trigger 5 fired: arm 1, which contains no clip, beats arm 2 at D5 (+0.075, +0.034 to +0.121). Experiment 232 predicted that, and arm 2b tests the explanation. Trigger 2 did not fire, because the plan's P2 predicted that result. Trigger 7 is open: later work depends on the winter gain, which one year of data supports.

docs.title: Does the best-guess demand stack score within 0.05 points of BG2 at the eight Primaries that have no stack forecast yet?
docs.text:
The best-guess demand forecast does not transfer unchanged to the eight primary substations (Primaries) whose meters record apparent power. Those meters read megavolt-amperes (MVA) rather than megawatts (MW). BG2 is the production-style forecast that the best-guess forecast (the stack) must match. A point is 1% of a substation's effective capacity on the quantile score, and lower is better. With no solar term the stack is at most 0.05 points worse than BG2 at only two of the eight (D3 and D4), and the stack is 3.6 points worse than BG2 at D8 alone. D-numbers are anonymised site codes. Fitting a solar capacity at each monthly refit (arm A1, added after the A0 results were seen) puts five Primaries at or below BG2 on the point estimate: D2, D3, D4, D19, and D21. The substation cards are the per-substation pages that show each forecast method's line. Those five cards can show a best-guess line, and the cards of D8, D12, and D22 should show no such line.

We asked whether the stack of earlier experiments, built for six Primaries with an MW meter, scores at most 0.05 points worse than BG2 at eight Primaries that have no stack forecast. The stack is experiment 247's chain: T-all fits (the heating terms split by day type), shared filter noise, ensemble-mean weather, the winter night offset, and recipe R of experiment 155. The ensemble stores and calibrations are those of experiment 152, and BG2 is the production-style forecast of experiment 87. The score is the quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles) in points of effective capacity; lower is better. No real-time capacity vintage was available for these Primaries, so no solar term could be pinned. Arm A0 therefore has no solar term.

Figure 1: the stack with no solar term is level with BG2 at D3 and D4 only.

Figure 2: the gap to BG2 sits in the sunny daylight rows.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. A0 is the pre-registered arm with a zero solar term. A1 is post hoc: the same chain with the solar capacity fitted at each monthly cut (non-negative increments per season-year, as experiment 152's arm N). The neural-network arm (A2) was not run, because it needs a non-zero clipped solar term. Experiment 169's uncertainty-band fixes are not applied. The fits are monthly refits on a 24-month window.
  • Rows. Scored year 2025-07 to 2026-06, leads 0.5 to 168 hours, outside the hand-filtered load-shift events. Each row is one site, forecast run, and valid time; there are 94,444 to 97,046 rows per site.
  • D8. D8 is fitted from 2025-04, has 12 monthly fits and no tuning month, and takes its spread from the tuning residuals of D2, D3, D4, D19, D21, and D22, as experiment 152 does.
  • Gate passed at two sites. The same code, reading experiment 111's stores, reproduces experiment 155's stored arm D at D10 and D11 (maximum difference 0.0 points in the median and the mean, against the 0.001 tolerance). The other four control sites (D5, D9, D14, and D16) were not run, because the code path does not differ between MW sites.
  • Absolute scores (quantile score in points of capacity). BG2 is the best of the five methods at D8, D12, and D22. D12's points are of MVA capacity, and the pooled figures include it.
Site A0 A1 BG2 Climatology Manual heuristic D2 2.419 2.079 2.179 2.932 2.839 D3 1.603 1.417 1.626 2.325 2.052 D4 2.309 2.294 2.393 2.830 2.778 D8 11.212 11.433 7.593 9.757 8.469 D12 7.415 7.414 6.468 8.768 7.836 D19 3.178 2.969 3.047 3.935 3.760 D21 2.348 2.106 2.297 2.907 2.757 D22 4.193 3.937 3.553 5.430 4.628
  • A0 minus BG2 (95% interval over months). Pooled +0.690 (+0.520 to +0.864). By site: D2 +0.241, D3 -0.022, D4 -0.084, D8 +3.619, D12 +0.946, D19 +0.131, D21 +0.051, D22 +0.639.
  • A1 minus BG2. Pooled +0.562 (+0.393 to +0.749). By site: D2 -0.100, D3 -0.209, D4 -0.099, D8 +3.840, D12 +0.946, D19 -0.078, D21 -0.191, D22 +0.384. A1's intervals lie wholly below BG2 at D3 and D21 only.
  • Predictions. Prediction 1 failed: pooled +0.690 against -0.12 to +0.05, and 2 of 8 sites within +0.05. (2) Passed: D8 and D12 are the two worst, and D8 is +3.619 above BG2. (3) Not tested as written, because A1 became a fitted-solar-term arm; A1 minus A0 is -0.34 at D2, -0.19 at D3, -0.02 at D4, +0.22 at D8, 0.00 at D12, -0.21 at D19, -0.24 at D21, and -0.26 at D22 (point estimates). (4) Not run.
  • Groups of rows, pooled A0 / A1 minus BG2. Sunny daylight +1.043 / +0.754; winter +0.441 / +0.292; winter nights +0.286 / +0.280; cold nights -0.143 / -0.143 (intervals include zero). In winter nights A0 is below BG2 at D2 (-0.207), D3 (-0.192), D4 (-0.189), D12 (-0.081), D19 (-0.063), and D21 (-0.244), and above it at D8 (+2.764) and D22 (+0.499).
  • Leaving one site out (pooled A0 / A1 minus BG2). Without D8: +0.272 (+0.117 to +0.424) / +0.093 (-0.032 to +0.213). The verdict does not change for either arm.
  • Tails (the share of readings below the forecast quantile, for A0 and BG2). The q01 target is 0.010: A0 is 0.017 to 0.042 at seven sites and 0.204 at D8; BG2 is 0.002 to 0.011. q95 target 0.950: A0 0.933 to 0.954 at seven sites and 0.736 at D8; BG2 0.935 to 0.985. Cold-night q95 coverage at D8 is 0.640 for A0 and 0.644 for BG2.
  • Caveats. The hypothesised stack had a pinned solar capacity and the 60% clip, which could not be built, so the verdict covers the stack with no solar term (A0) and with a fitted one (A1), not the stack as specified. A1 was chosen after A0 failed, and its five-site reading uses the same 12 scored months with no held-out period. Only A0 was pre-registered, so the card decision on A1 is post hoc. These results do not test the clip. D8's fit rests on fewer than 15 months of data, and its series changed meaning in April 2025 (see the data-processing page).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per site. 0.000 at every site: the spread table is symmetric about the corrected mean, so the median is the mean.
  • Error of the mean forecast beside the quantile-score contrast (pooled, minus BG2's median). A0 +0.487 (+0.198 to +0.754) against +0.690 on the quantile score; A1 +0.212 (-0.063 to +0.487) against +0.562. The signs agree.
  • Triggers. None fired. The control reproduced exactly. The result contradicts the prediction, and the sunny-row analysis and the A1 arm test an explanation. Leaving out D8 does not flip any verdict. A1 does not score worse than A0 except at D8. The six-site stack's pooled interval is 0.27 points wide and this experiment's 0.34, a ratio of 1.3.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Port the fitted solar term. The card lines for five Primaries need a stack forecast with a fitted solar capacity (A1) written in the stored layout; this experiment's predictions are not published to the leaderboard.
  • D8, D12, and D22. D8 needs more history; D12 needs a fold-aware fit (experiment 152's arm F); D22 stays +0.384 above BG2 with unclear cause.
  • Network head. A learned monotone network on a clipped solar term (experiment 250) can be tested only after an as-of solar capacity exists at these Primaries.

docs.title: Experiment 253: does the pair of substations give a better end time for a load shift?
docs.text:
Reading the two substations of a load shift together makes their end times agree and finds the true end more often when an unrelated step follows it, but it finds the true end slightly less often on ordinary transfers, and it leaves the real 14 January 2026 shift between substations D5 and D16 unchanged. A load shift is a temporary move of demand from one Primary substation (the donor) to another (the receiver). The end of the shift is the step that returns the donor's and the receiver's summed demand to its earlier level. Today the forecast card of each substation reports an end time estimated from that substation's demand alone, and the two cards can disagree by days. The load-shift screen (LSC) is the detector that raises an alarm where a substation's demand steps. We took the LSC of experiment 148, whose rule R0 waits 24 hours before it fixes an end, and added three rules (P1, P2, and P3) that estimate the end from a substation together with its metered neighbours. We scored every rule on four sets of transfers. The first is the 1,160 transfers that experiment 148 added to real demand (the clean draw). The second repeats them with an extra demand step, unrelated to the shift, added after the true end of one substation. The third repeats them with the donor's and receivers' steps differing by 10%. The fourth is the labelled real transfers, whose start and end come from NGED's switching log. A side is the donor or a metered receiver of one transfer, and "found" means that the side's alarm starts within 2 hours of the true start and ends within a tolerance of the true end.

On the clean draw the best of the new rules, P2, finds the end for 0.770 of the MW moved, against 0.788 for R0 (-0.017, 98.75% interval -0.034 to +0.007). With the unrelated step added it finds 0.633 against 0.593 (+0.041, +0.007 to +0.074). The decision rule, written before the run, needed the lower end of the clean-draw interval to be above -0.02, and it is -0.034, so the verdict is inconclusive. The next version should keep the balance test (the check that the donor's and receivers' steps sum to about zero), and should let a substation with no return step of its own take the other substation's end.

docs.title: Definitions
docs.text:
• Half-hour stamp: the unit of time of every table here; 48 stamps make a day.
  • Alarm, onset, noise unit: the load-shift screen (LSC) raises an alarm on a substation at the half-hour where its demand steps most, and the alarm opens an interval. The step is measured as the mean demand over the next 24 hours minus the mean over the 24 hours before. A noise unit is the usual size of that step in odd-numbered months, per substation, when nothing is injected.
  • Injected draw: the 1,160 transfers that experiment 148 added to real demand, drawn with seed 8200 and not changed (602 of them start in even months and do not have series 12 as the donor). Each moves a share of the donor substation's demand to one to three receivers, some metered and some not. The shapes S2, S3, and S4 give the transfer a flat, a receiver-shaped, and a mixed daily profile.
  • Detector: arm B of experiment 138, with that experiment's stored scorer and threshold.
  • Share found: the share of sides whose interval starts within 2 hours of the true start and ends within the tolerance of the true end, weighted by the MW moved divided by the number of sides of the transfer; experiment 148 scored a transfer as found if any side was, and R0 reproduces that number as a check.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• R0: experiment 148's rule at a lookahead of 24 hours, each side alone. The end is the stamp of the largest opposite step seen so far, fixed once no larger step follows for 24 hours.
  • P1: R0, but only balanced stamps are candidates. A partner is a neighbouring metered substation (the experiment 138 neighbour table) whose own largest opposite-signed step within 2 hours of the alarm is at least 1.5 noise units. A stamp is balanced when the side's step plus the partners' steps at that stamp is under half the side's step. Unbalanced stamps are skipped. A side with no partner, or with no balanced stamp that meets R0's size test, keeps R0's end.
  • P2: P1 with a joint score. At each balanced stamp the score is the smallest, over the side and its partners, of that substation's opposite step divided by its own onset step. A stamp needs a score of 0.5 or more, and the end is the stamp with the largest score, fixed by the same 24-hour lookahead.
  • P3: P2 with the score replaced by the output of a small neural network (scikit-learn multi-layer perceptron, 8 hidden units, seed 253) over seven features of both sides: own and partner returns, balance, time since onset, return in noise units, and share of the running peak. The target is that the stamp is within the tolerance of the true end. Training uses 600 injected transfers (shapes S2 to S4) that start in odd months, drawn with seed 8400.
  • Causality: every arm uses only the steps up to 24 hours (plus the step window) after the candidate end. The true end is used only to pick populations, to train P3 on its own draw, and to score.

docs.title: Variants of the injected draw
docs.text:
• Clean: experiment 148's draw.
  • Unrelated step (C): on one side of each pair transfer, chosen by seed, an extra step lasting 3 days starts 2 to 20 hours after the true end, in the direction that restores the side's level, at 1.0 to 1.5 times the side's own return step. The other side shows nothing. This is the situation of the 14 January 2026 shift, and the clean draw never contains it.
  • Unequal steps (U10): each transfer's receiver shares are multiplied by 0.9 or 1.1, chosen by seed, so the two sides' steps differ by 10%.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Check: R0 on the full draw, scored as experiment 148 scored a transfer, finds 0.794, as in experiment 148.
  • Ceiling: on transfers with a metered receiver, experiment 148's best-of-sides score is already 0.962 against a ceiling of 0.980 (the share whose start is found), so the brief's predicted gain of 0.03 to 0.10 in that score was out of reach. The plan was revised to score each side before any code ran.
  • Share found, side by side (95% interval), pair transfers, shapes S2 to S4, even months: clean R0 0.788 (0.743 to 0.850), P1 0.760, P2 0.770 (0.718 to 0.848), P3 0.759; unrelated step added R0 0.593 (0.549 to 0.640), P1 0.606, P2 0.633 (0.588 to 0.683), P3 0.628; unequal steps R0 0.781, P1 0.754, P2 0.769, P3 0.754. The offline rule OFF finds 0.785, 0.621, and 0.779.
  • Contrasts (98.75%): clean P2 minus R0 -0.017 (-0.034 to +0.007), P1 minus R0 -0.028 (-0.041 to +0.002), P3 minus P2 -0.011 (-0.023 to +0.016); unrelated step P2 minus R0 +0.041 (+0.007 to +0.074), P1 minus R0 +0.013 (-0.010 to +0.068), P3 minus P2 -0.006 (-0.027 to +0.026); unequal steps P2 minus R0 -0.012 (-0.029 to +0.011), P1 minus R0 -0.027 (-0.042 to +0.002).
  • False-end share: clean 0.047 (R0), 0.052 (P1), 0.053 (P2), 0.052 (P3); unrelated step added 0.041 (R0), 0.104 (P1), 0.093 (P2), 0.112 (P3). P2's false-end share is under the 0.10 limit.
  • Disagreement between the two sides' ends (transfers where both alarmed): clean, the median is 0 hours for R0 and P2, and the share over 6 hours is 0.145 (R0) and 0.153 (P2). With the unrelated step the median falls from 8.5 hours (R0) to 2.5 (P2), and the share over 6 hours from 0.579 to 0.339. P3's median is 5.0 hours.
  • Predictions: the share-found prediction of -0.01 to +0.02 on the clean draw failed for P2 (-0.017) and for P1 (-0.028). The prediction that P1 and P2 keep two thirds of their clean-draw gain under unequal steps cannot be scored, because the clean-draw gain is negative. The predicted gain of +0.05 to +0.20 with the unrelated step was not reached (P2 +0.041, P1 +0.013). The prediction that P3 beats P2 by under 0.02 held, and P3 is not adopted.
  • Real labelled transfers (descriptive): 55 transfers have two or more metered sides (111 sides), and the start is found on 26 sides. The end is within the tolerance of the logged close on 20 sides for R0, 21 for P1 and P2, and 22 for P3, but P3's median end error is 2.8 hours against 0.8 for R0 and P2. For the 6 transfers where both sides alarmed, the median gap between the ends is 6.8 hours for R0 and 0.0 for P2.
  • The 14 January 2026 shift: every rule gives the same ends as the card: D5 ends after 9.2 days and D16 after 2.0 days. D16 has no stamp where the opposite step reaches the 5.0 noise units the rule needs (its largest is 2.1), so its end comes from the level tracker. D5 has 13 qualifying stamps and none is balanced, so P1 and P2 fall back to R0's choice. The pair rule therefore cannot say which card is right.
  • Post hoc, one metered receiver only: P2 minus R0 is -0.009 (-0.038 to +0.012) on the clean draw and +0.055 (-0.002 to +0.105) with the unrelated step; the share of transfers over 6 hours apart falls from 0.604 to 0.321 with the step. The loss on the clean draw is mostly in transfers with two or more metered receivers.
  • Post hoc, group balance (P1G, P2G): summing every neighbour that stepped at the onset, of either sign, gives P2G minus R0 of -0.018 (-0.037 to +0.005) clean and +0.031 (-0.008 to +0.075) with the unrelated step. Group balance does not remove the loss.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Forecast checks: no forecast is scored, so the median-minus-mean and mean-error checks do not apply.
  • Audit triggers: trigger 5 (a nested arm beats the arm that contains it) fires, because R0 beats P1 and P2 on the clean draw, and the unequal-step condition of the decision rule also fails (P2 minus R0 -0.012, -0.029 to +0.011). The explanation tested here is that the balance test rejects the true end when the group is not fully balanced; the single-receiver and group-balance runs above show the loss shrinks to -0.009 for one receiver and does not vanish with group balance. Trigger 2 (a prediction contradicted) fires for the unrelated-step gain, which came out at +0.041 against +0.05 to +0.20. A code and numbers audit by a reviewer agent replaced the Opus audit that the ml-experiment skill asks for; its findings are triaged in the pull request. The seven triggers are listed in that skill's "Audit before merge" section. The other five triggers did not fire. Leaving one series out was not run, and no claim here is per series.
  • Not run on all transfers: the long transfers of experiment 148 and alarm merging were left out.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Series 12 is blanked in the detector's input. Where it is a receiver, its side row can never alarm, so it lowers every rule's share found by the same amount (54 side rows in the clean draw).
  • The unrelated step also changes which alarms exist: the share of sides with a start found falls from 0.836 to 0.784 under variant C for every rule, so absolute shares under C mix the two effects, and the contrasts do not.
  • The fallback to R0's end is reported late. When no balanced stamp exists, P1, P2, and P3 keep R0's end, but the end is reported only when the 14-day search window has ended, because a balanced stamp could still appear.
  • Disagreement counts any transfer with two or more alarmed sides, including transfers with three or four sides; the real-transfer figure rests on 6 transfers.
  • Partner finding is favourable on the injected draw, because the neighbour table that finds partners is the table the injection draws receivers from. The test of 1.5 noise units is the only detection step.
  • The unrelated step is injected by us. Its size (1.0 to 1.5 times the side's own step) and timing (2 to 20 hours after the end) were chosen to resemble the 14 January 2026 shift, so the gain is conditional on such steps being common. The labelled real transfers cannot tell how common.
  • Real pairs are few: the start is found on 26 of 111 sides, and 6 transfers have both sides alarmed.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
The next experiment should make a side with no return step use the other side's balanced end, and should count how often unrelated steps follow real ends. Tying the ends together removes the case the 14 January 2026 shift shows, where one side has nothing to read. Counting unrelated steps in the real telemetry decides whether the gain of +0.04 is worth the loss of 0.017.

Code: ml-experiments/00253-lsc-end-time-pair-rule/; every number above is printed by e00253_contrasts.py (saved at data/ml-experiments/00253-lsc-end-time-pair-rule/printed_report.txt) and e00253_case.py (case_report.txt in the same folder).

docs.title: How many LSC alarms are real load shifts, judged against the full log and a chance base rate?
docs.text:
We estimate that about 45% of the alarms raised by LR_b20 are real load shifts. LR_b20 is the learned alarm score of experiment 227, at the threshold that leaves 20 unexplained odd-month candidates. For each of the 21 logged load shifts that its alarms match, LR_b20 raises 2.7 false alarms (95% interval from resampling whole calendar months, 1.7 to 4.9). A load shift is demand that the electricity network operator (NGED, National Grid Electricity Distribution) moves between neighbouring Primary substations for hours or days. The load shift screen (LSC) raises an alarm when it detects one. A "strict match" is an alarm whose step and end agree with one of 35 labelled load shifts of over 1 day, using experiment 195's rule. We checked, for every alarm that is not a strict match, whether a logged closure on the same or a neighbouring Primary substation starts or ends within 24 hours. We compared that share with the share after moving every alarm by a whole number of weeks (200 shifts of 3 to 100 weeks). For LR_b20, 58.8% of the non-strict alarms have such a closure, against 31.2% after shifting, an excess of 27.7 percentage points. The pre-registered prediction holds on the point estimates, so the verdict is supported. The interval for false alarms per matched load shift includes the bar of 3, so that half of the prediction is not firmly met.

The loose rule overcounts and the strict rule undercounts, so the table states corrected numbers. "Alarms" counts each alarm once per series and stepped time, averaged over the cross-validation folds that held the series out. Shares are shares of the non-strict alarms. "Corrected precision" is the strict-match alarms plus the excess near-closure alarms, divided by all alarms. "False alarms per matched load shift" divides the alarms that are not estimated to be real by the 21 matched load shifts.

Source Alarms Strict-match alarms Matched load shifts Near-closure share of non-strict alarms Shifted share Excess (percentage points) Corrected precision False alarms per matched load shift LR_b20 102.3 25.0 21 58.8% 31.2% 27.7 (18.5 to 36.0) 45.3% (33.3% to 55.5%) 2.66 (1.67 to 4.86) LR_b80 245.3 29.0 24 49.5% 31.0% 18.4 (11.0 to 26.5) 28.1% (19.7% to 37.1%) 7.35 (4.77 to 12.50) RO_b80 296.0 24.0 19 43.8% 25.5% 18.3 (10.5 to 26.3) 24.9% (16.6% to 33.2%) 11.70 (7.34 to 21.18) PG_g70 85.0 3.0 3 52.4% 37.4% 15.1 (0.4 to 29.9) 18.1% (2.8% to 34.0%) 23.22 (9.61 to 80.02)
  • Question and rule. Does LR_b20's near-closure share beat a week-shifted base rate, and what do false alarms per matched load shift become? The pre-registered decision rule is met on the point estimates: share 58.8% against 30%, excess 27.7 against 15 percentage points, 2.66 false alarms against 3. The share lies above the 97.5% point of the shifts (39.7%).
  • Row set and data. Experiment 227's four frozen alarm sources on all 16 series and the whole record (2022-01 to 2026-06), with no tuning. The log is experiment 37's 629 closures of 2 hours to 60 days. Weather is not used. D-numbers are the published labels of Primary substations, and "series N" names an unlabelled Primary substation.
  • Other windows. At 6 hours LR_b20's share is 48.5% against 13.7% after shifting; at 48 hours it is 65.9% against 46.2%. Shifts of 3 to 12 weeks, which keep the season, give 58.8% against 30.5%.
  • Months not used to set the threshold. LR_b20's budget of 20 unexplained odd-month candidates was set on odd months, where "unexplained" means not near a logged closure. That could inflate the share. The even months, which did not set the budget, show a larger share: 72.9% against 33.0% after shifting (39.8 percentage points, 27.4 to 51.2), corrected precision 60.2% (46.1% to 72.0%), and 1.54 false alarms per matched load shift (0.81 to 3.35). Odd months give 48.3% against 29.8% (18.5 percentage points, 4.9 to 31.8) and precision 31.0% (15.6% to 44.7%). This split was chosen after seeing the results. The headline stays on the whole record.
  • Leaving one Primary substation out. The excess stays between 24.5 and 30.4 percentage points. False alarms per matched load shift stay between 2.42 and 3.40, and exceed the bar of 3 without series 9, series 13, D16, or D5 (3.28, 3.14, 3.02, and 3.40). D5 has the highest precision (84.8%, 68.0% to 93.9%).
  • Where the excess is absent. LR_b20's excess at D10 is -3.8 percentage points (-39.0 to 38.6; 5 alarms) and at D8 +20.6 (-12.9 to 62.9; 5 alarms). LR_b80's excess is +1.0 at D10 (-17.6 to 22.4; 20 alarms). RO_b80 gives +4.8 at D9, -1.7 at D10, and +5.8 at D8. The pair alarm gives -10.4 at D10. No source shows an excess at D10, and the D8 and D9 values lie inside the shifted range. The intervals are wide, so the data neither confirm nor rule out real load shifts there.
  • Where the excess is clear. LR_b20's excess is above zero at D5 (+70.5, 49.1 to 83.6), D16 (+36.7), and series 15 (+40.2). The other Primary substations have too few alarms to say.
  • Limits. "Not near a logged closure" is not proof of a false alarm, because the log covers only the trial area and only what NGED logged. Each of the 16 series gets its own independent shift. The shifted alarms keep weekday and hour of day but not season, except in the 3-to-12-week row. The month-resampled intervals hold each alarm's chance probability at its mean over the 200 shifts, so they leave out the shift-sampling noise and are slightly too narrow. The pair alarm is counted as 85 alarm events, whereas experiment 227's interval table has 213 rows that include partner rows, so its false alarms per matched load shift are not comparable with experiment 227's. The balanced- opposite class says nothing about the pair alarm, because the pair alarm is defined by opposite steps; 39 of its 85 alarms land in that class after the strict and near-closure classes have taken theirs. The cleaning flag (substation_zero) is not used as a class, because the cleaned power table is not part of the stored inputs. The false-alarm rate divides by the 21 matched load shifts, not by the 25 strict-match alarms (which would give about 2.2).
  • What to try next. Read the 45 or so LR_b20 alarms that are near a closure but not strict matches (about 21 of them excess over chance) with NGED, and report any harm accounting with those excess alarms counted as real.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median forecast minus mean forecast, per site. Not applicable: the experiment forecasts nothing.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each quantile-score contrast. Not applicable, for the same reason.
  • Triggers. None fired: no control exists, the result agrees with its prediction, leaving one Primary substation out keeps the excess above 24 percentage points, and no nested arm exists.
  • Code review (Sonnet). The review found four defects, all fixed: the threshold might inflate the share (the even-month check shows it does not); per-Primary false-alarm denominators mixed events and alarms, so the per-Primary table shows precision and excess only; the all-false baseline used a different definition of real alarms from the corrected count, so both now count 25 strict-match alarms as real; and the week shift wrapped by 4 days, so it now wraps by 234 whole weeks.

docs.title: Does a better metered solar farm forecast lower the curtailment cost at its bulk supply point?
docs.text: Forecasting each solar farm's output cut the cost of curtailing at Boston and raised it at Skegness, so across the two bulk supply points (132 kV to 33 kV substations) the saving of about a quarter is smaller than the uncertainty in the estimate. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F, beneath these two substations. We asked what it would have cost to cap the generators whenever a forecast said a substation would export more than a limit, using the rule of experiment 84. We swapped in the farm forecasts of experiments 224 and 243, the same substation forecast in every arm, and compared each with a baseline that assumes every generator runs at full capacity. Verdict: inconclusive. At 0.5 times each substation's earlier maximum export, the avoidable cost (the cost above a perfect forecast, GBP 2,000 per MWh) is GBP 1.87 million for H5 (the plant plus a neural network, seed 0), 1.88 million for the plant alone, 1.93 million for XGBoost, and 2.57 million for the baseline. The three forecasts cut the baseline's avoidable cost by 25% to 28%, but every 95% interval includes zero (for example H5 minus the baseline: -0.71 million, interval -2.25 to +0.16 million). The prediction that all three contrasts are significant at the 5% level fails. The neural network's lower pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile cannot show in this rule, which reads only a farm's median. H5 beats XGBoost by 3.2% (99% interval 0.2% to 7.5%), under the 10% that would justify porting a neural network.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Design. The substation forecast is experiment 48's best guess in every arm, and the three generators that are not metered farms keep experiment 48's forecast. Only the six farms change. Farm forecasts are the stored 00 UTC runs at 12 to 36 hours lead, in fractions of capacity, scaled to MW and capped at capacity. Farms get 0 MW when the sun is under 5 degrees above the horizon. Setting those half-hours to zero discards 152.7 MWh of the 15,036.7 MWh metered (1.0%) in the causal rows.
  • Causal rows are the headline. A substation forecast is made at 09 UTC for valid times 12 to 36 hours later, but a farm forecast for a valid time after 12 UTC the next day is the 00 UTC run of that day, which exists only after the substation forecast. The causal rows drop 2,711 of the 11,664 pairs of forecast origin and valid time. Dropping those pairs removes most of the midday and afternoon export peak. The valid-time pairing keeps all 11,664 pairs and gives each farm the forecast stored for its valid time, even when that forecast was made after the substation forecast. The valid-time pairing therefore favours the farm arms.
  • Event half-hours (export beyond the limit, scored rows). Causal: 2 at 0.9 times the maximum, 5 at 0.75, 72 at 0.5. Valid-time pairing: 17, 31, 219. All flows in the window: 17, 36, 259. The stop rule fired (fewer than 20 at 0.75), so 0.5 is the only limit with a pre-registered contrast. Limits are 0.5, 0.75, and 0.9 times the maximum export before 2025-09-01. The published thermal limit was exceeded in 1 half-hour of the window and in none of the causal rows.
  • Avoidable cost at 0.5, causal rows (GBP million, 95% interval): baseline 2.57 (0.59 to 5.18); manual-heuristic floor 2.15 (0.61 to 3.94); climatology floor 2.18 (0.62 to 3.96); plant 1.88 (0.55 to 3.44); XGBoost 1.93 (0.57 to 3.53); H5 1.87 (0.55 to 3.42); H5 zero history 1.87 (0.55 to 3.42). The perfect forecast costs GBP 0.29 million. H5 is GBP 46,300 per MW of forecast generator capacity per year (78.97 MW, 0.51 years of scored half-hours) and the baseline GBP 63,900. The five-seed mean of H5 and its other seeds sit within GBP 6,000 of seed 0 (1.86 to 1.87 million).
  • Contrasts at 0.5, causal rows, with the Bonferroni 99% interval in GBP thousand: C1 plant minus baseline -698 (-2,935 to +258); C2 XGBoost minus baseline -647 (-2,847 to +302); C3 H5 minus baseline -710 (-2,971 to +241); C4 H5 minus XGBoost -62 (-145 to -4), or -3.2% of XGBoost's avoidable cost (-7.5% to -0.2%); C5 H5 minus plant -11 (-41 to +8). C4 is outside the 5% equivalence band (its lower end is -7.5%) and short of the 10% threshold. The 99% half-widths of C1 to C3 are about GBP 1.6 million, so the window cannot resolve a difference under about 60% of the baseline's avoidable cost.
  • The other limits. Causal, 0.75: H5 minus XGBoost -6.1% (99% interval -23% to 0%). Causal, 0.9: -10.5% (99% interval -43% to 0%), on 2 half-hours. Valid-time pairing, 0.5: baseline 10.5, H5 7.25, XGBoost 7.36 (GBP million); H5 minus baseline -3.27 million (95% interval -10.4 to +0.8); H5 minus XGBoost -1.5% (99% interval -3.9% to +0.5%).
  • By substation (causal, 0.5, a sum over the generators beneath each). Boston: baseline 2.06, H5 1.23, XGBoost 1.26 (GBP million). Skegness: baseline 0.51, H5 0.64, XGBoost 0.67. H5 beats XGBoost at both.
  • Tails (daylight farm rows of the scored node rows, fractions of capacity). Coverage at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 levels: H5 0.034, 0.058, 0.935, 0.981; XGBoost 0.039, 0.075, 0.940, 0.993; plant 0.034, 0.053, 0.963, 0.990. Pinball loss at 0.99: H5 0.0039, plant 0.0042, XGBoost 0.0048.
  • Weather and forecast time. The weather input is the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble run issued at 00:00 Coordinated Universal Time (UTC), at the nearest 0.25-degree grid cell. The farm power input is the metered output from one or two days earlier. Both exist at forecast time for the causal rows. One fit on the months before 2025-09 (experiment 243's screening schedule); nothing was refitted here.
  • Departures from the plan. Intervals use 2,000 month-resampled draws (the studies.bootstrap constant). The plan had asked for 20,000. The 0.9 and 0.75 limits are reported for completeness only.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast (points of capacity, mean over farms): H5 +0.38, plant +0.23, XGBoost -0.56.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the contrasts. MAE of the median: H5 9.91, plant 10.07, XGBoost 9.96. MAE of the mean forecast: H5 9.98, plant 10.22, XGBoost 10.19. H5's small gain over XGBoost in cost (3.2%) agrees in direction with both.
  • Triggers fired. Trigger 2 (the result contradicts the prediction): the first part fails on power, which the interval half-widths show; the second part holds in size (3.2%, under 5%) but not in interval, which excludes zero. Trigger 4 (leaving one site out flips a contrast): leaving Boston out reverses the sign of C1 to C3, because H5's avoidable cost at Skegness is 24% higher than the baseline's. Trigger 5 (a more informed arm does worse): the arm that knows every generator's actual output costs GBP 1.96 million against H5's 1.87 million, because a forecast below the actual output sets a lower cap and so cuts more (H5 curtails 491 MWh against 368 MWh, and breaches 29 MWh against 38 MWh), the same pattern as experiment 84.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
Why the baseline beats every farm forecast at Skegness, and whether the same holds at the other bulk supply points when the delivery of about 2,500 series arrives. Two substations and 72 event half-hours cannot rank farm forecasts. A forecast that reads the farm's upper quantiles when it sets a cap is a candidate, since the neural network's gain is in the upper tail that this rule ignores.

Reproduce with uv run --no-sync python ml-experiments/00255-*/e00255_report.py and then e00255_charts.py. The printed report is in data/ml-experiments/00255-metered-farm-node-curtailment-value/report.md.

docs.title: Data-processing note
docs.text: Crossing quantiles affected this experiment's scores, though not the six solar farms' forecasts. Three generators that are not solar farms store a forecast with 9 quantiles (0.05 to 0.95) and no 0.01 or 0.99 quantile. The scorer padded the two missing columns with nulls, and the step that caps every quantile at the generator's capacity (pl.min_horizontal) turned each null into the capacity. The 0.01 quantile therefore sat at capacity, above the 0.05 quantile, in 26,344 of 77,897 generator-forecast rows (34%), in every forecast arm, and the farms' own rows have none. Experiment 268 re-scored with the quantiles sorted first: avoidable cost moves by -3.66% (climatology), -1.90% (manual heuristic), +1.08% (XGBoost), +0.72% (H5), +0.62% (plant), and -0.59% (H5 with zero history), and H5 minus XGBoost moves from GBP -62,407 to -69,766. Sorting only moves the capacity-valued 0.01 quantile to the top of the row, so filling the missing 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles from the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles is the cleaner repair.

docs.title: Do air temperature, air density, or a shear column lower the XGBoost wind forecast's quantile score on the three metered wind farms?
docs.text:
Take-home: air temperature helps the XGBoost wind forecast slightly, but the larger gain comes from columns that carry the time of day and the season, not from air density or atmospheric stability. We scored each XGBoost model with the quantile score, an estimate of the continuous ranked probability score, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of a farm's capacity; smaller is better). Adding 2 m air temperature to the six wind columns lowered the score by 0.083 points, with an interval that touches zero at the strict level we set beforehand. Adding density, shear (the change of wind speed with height), and solar elevation lowered the score by a further 0.069 points. A post hoc arm (added after the plan) that added only the hour and the day of the year to temperature lowered the score by 0.123 points. The verdict is partly supported: temperature helps in direction, and the planned physical columns help, but not for the physical reason predicted.

Experiment 230 found, in an unplanned (post hoc) comparison, that 2 m air temperature improved the XGBoost wind forecast. This experiment repeats that comparison as a planned test. We trained XGBoost quantile models on ERA5 (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' reanalysis, our estimate of past weather) from 2019-09 to 2025-06, and ran them on the 51 members of the ensemble forecast (ENS) from the same centre. We scored the 53 forecast runs that start on Tuesdays between July 2025 and June 2026, for each of three metered wind farms (W1 to W3). The arms differ only in the weather columns they receive. A placebo column and calendar columns show whether a gain is information or only an extra column.

docs.title: Arms and results
docs.text:
Every arm is experiment 230's A0r recipe: an XGBoost quantile model fitted to ERA5 on the power-curve base margin (the binned mean power at each 100 m wind speed, which the trees correct), run on the 51 ENS members, mixed with equal weights, and given the spread factor (a multiplier on the forecast's width, fitted month by month on earlier cases so that the 5% to 95% band covers 90%). colsample_bytree is 1. Each farm and seed has one fit, with no refit during the scored year. T0 uses six wind columns: the 10 m and 100 m wind speeds and the sine and cosine of each direction. Scores are on the kept rows (the rows that experiment 210's mask keeps), over all leads. Intervals resample whole months and the three seeds, at 98.75% for the four planned contrasts (C1 to C4) and 95% for the rest. The farms are not resampled, so the intervals describe these three farms.

Arm Columns Kept rows, all leads Kept rows, lead days 1 and 2 All rows, all leads T0 six wind columns 11.663 7.028 11.035 T1 T0 plus 2 m temperature 11.579 6.931 10.970 T2 T0 plus density at a fixed 100 kPa 11.579 6.931 10.970 T3 T1 plus density (fixed pressure), shear, solar elevation 11.511 6.902 10.918 P1 T1 with temperature permuted by month (placebo) 11.648 7.017 11.024 T2p post hoc: T0 plus density from the ENS pressure 11.628 6.947 11.008 T3p post hoc: T3 with the ENS pressure 11.523 6.904 10.926 T4 post hoc: T1 plus shear 11.596 6.983 10.984 T5 post hoc: T1 plus solar elevation 11.476 6.845 10.895 T6 post hoc: T1 plus hour and day of year 11.456 6.795 10.883 Climatology month, half-hour, and weekend 13.547 13.121 13.124
  • C1, temperature (T1) minus T0: -0.083 (98.75% interval -0.177 to +0.002; 95% interval -0.156 to -0.015). The prediction (-0.04 to -0.12) held, and the planned rule (wholly below zero at 98.75%) missed by 0.002. T1 reproduces experiment 230's post hoc arm A0rT (T0 plus temperature) exactly, at 11.579.
  • C4, the placebo (P1) minus T0, gives no sign of an extra-column effect: -0.014 (-0.055 to +0.016). T1 minus P1 is -0.069 (95% interval -0.152 to +0.011), which also includes zero, so the placebo does not show that the whole of C1 is information in the temperature.
  • C2, T2 minus T1, is 0.000 (-0.002 to +0.002), and the contrast cannot test density. The ENS surface pressure differs from ERA5's by up to 7 hPa in a monthly mean. The plan's pressure rule therefore applied, and T2 used a fixed 100 kPa pressure. Density at a fixed pressure is a function of temperature alone, so T2 carries nothing beyond T1.
  • Density from the ENS pressure (T2p) scored 0.049 points worse than T1 (0.015 to 0.091). The difference may reflect the ENS pressure differing from the ERA5 pressure that the model trained on.
  • C3, T3 minus T1: -0.069 (98.75% interval -0.124 to -0.024), wholly below zero. The gain is not at night, where the prediction expected it (night +0.017, -0.011 to +0.051). It is in daytime (-0.157, -0.226 to -0.083) and summer (-0.103, -0.203 to -0.047), and nil in winter (-0.016, -0.030 to +0.004). The observed gain is also outside the predicted range of -0.05 to +0.02.
  • Post hoc arms split T3's gain. Shear alone made the score slightly worse (T4 minus T1 +0.017, +0.004 to +0.030). Solar elevation alone lowered it by 0.103 (T5 minus T1, -0.156 to -0.057), and hour and day of year lowered it by 0.123 (T6 minus T1, -0.211 to -0.040). T3 minus T6 is +0.054 (-0.005 to +0.116), so T3 is no better than the calendar arm.
  • The 0.99 loss fell slightly more than the 0.01 loss in T1, as predicted. On the kept rows the 0.99 pinball loss is 0.659 (T0), 0.656 (T1), 0.656 (T3), and 0.650 (T6), and the 0.01 loss is 0.285, 0.284, 0.284, and 0.283. Coverage of the 5% to 95% band is 0.915 to 0.918, and of the 1% to 99% band 0.972 to 0.973. Observations exceed the 0.99 quantile on 2.1% of kept rows in every arm.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The arms do not differ in the median-minus-mean skew. In points, for W1, W2, and W3: T0 -5.45, -5.38, and -4.68; T1 -5.43, -5.27, and -4.57; T3 -5.40, -5.31, and -4.38. W3 drifts by 0.3 across arms.
  • The error of the mean forecast agrees with the quantile score in direction. Over all leads on the kept rows, C1 is -0.046 (-0.092 to +0.001), C3 -0.067 (-0.106 to -0.033), and C4 -0.007 (-0.036 to +0.017). At lead days 7 and later, C1's mean-error contrast is +0.008, where the quantile score gives -0.064.
  • C1 rests on W2. Without W2 the contrast is -0.032 (-0.094 to +0.023), against -0.117 without W1 and -0.101 without W3. C3 stays negative when any one farm is dropped (-0.088, -0.041, and -0.077).
  • T0 equals experiment 230's A0r (11.663 against 11.663 on the kept rows).
  • Three audit triggers fired. Trigger 2 is a result that contradicts its prediction: C3's gain is in the day, not the night. The explanation was tested with T4 to T6. Trigger 5 is a control that moves the score by more than its own interval's half-width: the calendar arm T6 moved it by 0.123, against a half-width of 0.085. Trigger 7 is a later experiment whose design depends on this result: the experiment that trains a neural head on daily ensemble hindcasts adds this experiment's best column set to its XGBoost reference if the columns are supported.
  • A fresh audit matched every number and found C1 resting on W2. It re-derived C1, C3, and the calendar arm's contrast from the stored forecasts with its own code. C3 is negative on every farm. The calendar arm's gain is concentrated in W1, W2, and 8 of 12 months. The three seeds agree to about 0.002 points, so the intervals reflect only 12 months of variation. The audit found no leakage route. The report is private.

docs.title: Caveats and departures from the plan
docs.text:
• Solar elevation is a function of the hour and the day of the year at a fixed farm. The plan called it a physical proxy, and the calendar arm T6 shows that it cannot be told apart from a calendar column. The plan did not allow columns that let the XGBoost model memorise calendar effects. That rule is met only in the sense that the scored year was not in training.
  • The ENS 10 m wind is 0.4 to 1.3 m/s below ERA5's, and the 100 m wind 0.5 to 0.9 m/s below. The shear exponent therefore has a different distribution at inference than in training. This difference may be why shear adds nothing.
  • ERA5 temperature comes from the Open-Meteo file that experiment 230 used. The ENS temperature is within 0.22 K of the ERA5 temperature on average.
  • Post hoc arms: T2p, T3p, T4, T5, and T6 were added after the plan. The verdict uses C1 to C4 only.
  • Weather at lag times: the experiment uses none. ERA5 supplies the training columns and is not available at forecast time, and the ENS members supply every column at inference.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Do hour-of-day and day-of-year columns still lower the XGBoost wind forecast's score on months the temperature result did not see?
  • Is the gain a correction for the ENS wind's bias at certain hours and seasons? If so, a bias-corrected wind input would make the columns unnecessary.

docs.title: Is the neural head needed once the solar-farm power model sees the same inputs?
docs.text:
A linear quantile regression on the lagged power and the ensemble spread scores within 0.5% of the neural network of experiment 243, so the network was not needed. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F. Experiment 243 found that H5, which adds a neural network that outputs 11 quantile offsets to the plant (a physical solar-farm power model that turns a weather forecast into a power forecast), scores 4.4% better than the plant alone, but H5 saw the lagged power and the ensemble spread and the plant did not. We gave a linear quantile regression (P2) the same inputs, with no network. With own history (fitted on each farm's own earlier months), P2's quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over the 11 levels, in points of capacity; lower is better) is 5.500 against 5.475 for H5, so P2 is 0.45% worse (95% interval -1.7% to +0.4%; 99% interval -2.2% to +0.6%). P2 is 3.96% better than the plant alone, which is 90% of H5's gain. The prediction fails, so the stop rule set in advance applies: if P2 is within 1% of H5, the gain came from the inputs and not from the neural network. The prediction was that H5 beats P2 by at least 2% in quantile score and by at least 10% in pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile. The quantile-score gap is 0.45%, and at the 0.99 quantile P2 is better, with H5 3.7% worse (99% interval -1.8% to +10.9%). The hypothesis (that the inputs, not the neural network, produced the gain) is supported, because the prediction written to test it (that H5 beats P2) fails.

P2 beats the two-number plant, and the availability ratio adds little. P2 beats the two-number plant (P1) of experiment 224 by 2.5% (99% interval -3.8% to -1.2%). Removing the availability ratio (the farm's power one or two days earlier divided by the plant forecast for that half-hour) worsens the quantile score by 0.33% (99% interval -0.67% to +0.02%). With zero history, P2 is 0.63% worse than H5 (99% interval -0.25% to +1.96%).

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Quantile score (points of capacity, mean over six farms, own history): H5 5.475, XGBoost 5.490, P2 5.500, P2 without the ratio 5.518, P1 5.642, plant 5.726, climatology 8.638, manual heuristic 8.687. Zero history: XGBoost 5.610, H5 5.610, P2 5.645, plant 5.871.
  • Per farm, own history: P2 is within 0.1 of H5 at five farms (A, B, C, D, F) and 0.09 better at farm E (6.26 against 6.35).
  • Median error (mean absolute error, MAE, of the median, points of capacity, own history): H5 9.85, XGBoost 9.89, P2 9.89, plant 9.95.
  • Outer quantiles, own history (pinball loss at 0.01 and 0.99): H5 0.334 and 0.344, XGBoost 0.369 and 0.485, P2 0.349 and 0.331, plant 0.372 and 0.418. Coverage of the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles: H5 0.033 and 0.985, P2 0.035 and 0.985, plant 0.034 and 0.984.
  • Cloudy and clear half-hours (clear-sky index under 0.5 and 0.5 or more): H5 minus P2 is -2.7% when cloudy (99% interval -6.4% to +0.3%) and -0.15% when clear. P2 with the ratio is 0.48% worse than P2 without it when cloudy (99% interval -0.8% to +2.3%) and 0.42% better when clear (99% interval -0.8% to -0.1%).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Fitting fault. P2 beats P1, which the plan named as the test of a fitting fault, so the fit is sound.
  • Member alignment. The mean of the 51 members' responses differs from experiment 224's unit_mean by 0.003 on average (mean absolute gap, 0.0026 to 0.0033 across the six farms), as expected from a non-linear plant, and the correlation is 0.9998.
  • Triggers. The prediction that H5 beats P2 by 2% fails, so the plan's audit trigger for a contradicted prediction fires and no other trigger does. The stored H5, XGBoost, and plant predictions are unchanged from experiment 243, and the rows are experiment 243's, so the contrasts pair on the same half-hours.
  • Departures from the plan. The MAE of the mean forecast is not reported, because P2 outputs quantiles only.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test a small neural network against P2 with extra inputs, such as the neighbouring farms' power. P2 trails H5 by 0.45%, and the 99% interval (-2.2% to +0.6%) is wide enough that a gain of up to about 2% from a neural network cannot be ruled out, so the comparison is made against P2 and not against the plant alone.

docs.title: Data-processing note
docs.text: Experiment 268 found crossing quantiles in 26,344 of its 77,897 generator-forecast rows (34%), but all of them belong to three generators that are not solar farms, so none is on this page. Experiment 273 counted 0 crossing rows in every arm here, because the fit scripts sorted the 11 quantiles before writing them, so sorting does not change the scores on this page.

docs.title: Does the carried LSC mask keep its gain and its no-harm out of sample on every Primary?
docs.text: The result is inconclusive, because the harness failed one of its two known-answer gates. The harness's numbers still say that the carried LSC mask recovers about half of the oracle's gain and scores worse than no mask over every row of 4.5 years. The load shift screen (LSC) detects load shifts. A load shift is demand that the electricity network operator (NGED, National Grid Electricity Distribution) moves between neighbouring Primary substations for hours or days. The mask sets the readings inside a detected load shift aside, so the forecast filter does not learn the temporary level. We scored experiment 227's carried setting, LR_b20, in a new forecast harness on 15 Primary series over about 4.5 years, taking each learned alarm from the fold that held its Primary pair out and scoring ordinary days on odd months only. In the 72 hours after 34 labelled load shifts of over 1 day, LR_b20 recovers 47.1% of the gain of the oracle mask (95% interval 18.4% to 85.0%), which is under the bar of 50%. LR_b20's ordinary-day score difference from no mask is -0.009 points (-0.022 to +0.002), inside the limit of +/-0.05. The harness reproduces experiment 227's gain on real load shifts (gate G1). The harness gains 2.39 points on experiment 141's injected load shifts where experiment 208 found 1.50 (gate G2, limit 30%). The plan makes a failed gate inconclusive. Had both gates passed, the plan's rule would give not supported, because the share is under 50%.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
• Points and score. A point is 1% of a series' effective capacity. The score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, and lower is better. Every arm uses the same quantile offsets, so a score difference is a difference in the forecast's location only.
  • Arms. K0 is the forecast with no mask: the frozen convex GAM forecast of experiment 130, which uses past weather (ERA5 and CAMS), plus the Kalman filter on recent power. A mask arm also sets the readings inside each known alarm span aside. ORACLE masks the 66 labelled load shifts as logged. LR_b20 and LR_b80 are experiment 195's learned alarm score at budgets of 20 and 80 unexplained odd-month candidates, taken from the fold that holds the Primary pair out. RO_b80 is RO-NC at budget 80. HALF averages the K0 and LR_b80 corrections. GAM_ONLY is the GAM forecast with no filter.
  • Row sets. A row is one forecast of one half-hour from one origin (every 6 hours, leads 0 to 7 days). AFTER rows are the 72 hours of target time after a labelled load shift ends, from origins at or after its logged onset. ORDINARY rows lie outside every logged closure that names the series and the 72 hours after each closure. Odd months did not supply the learned score's negative training examples; even months did.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Arm Gain after load shifts (points) Share of ORACLE's gain Ordinary days, odd months Ordinary days, even months Every row LR_b20 +1.69 (0.50 to 3.14) 47.1% (18.4% to 85.0%) -0.009 (-0.022 to +0.002) +0.003 (-0.011 to +0.024) +0.040 LR_b80 +1.80 (0.62 to 3.23) 50.2% (21.6% to 88.1%) +0.039 (-0.007 to +0.108) +0.018 (-0.006 to +0.050) +0.071 RO_b80 +2.52 (0.75 to 4.47) 70.2% (41.0% to 93.7%) +0.082 (+0.003 to +0.194) +0.026 (-0.022 to +0.074) +0.099 HALF +1.19 (0.44 to 2.06) 33.2% (14.8% to 57.9%) 0.000 (-0.014 to +0.017) -0.004 (-0.014 to +0.006) +0.008 GAM_ONLY +3.16 (1.15 to 5.79) 88.0% (66.5% to 96.8%) +0.633 (+0.418 to +0.897) +0.456 (+0.305 to +0.632) +0.582 ORACLE +3.59 (1.60 to 6.23) 100% -0.016 (-0.032 to -0.004) -0.017 (-0.028 to -0.007) +0.000

Gain is the K0 score minus the arm's score on the AFTER rows of the 34 load shifts (146,354 rows, 18 Primary pairs). Ordinary-day columns are the arm's score minus K0's, so negative is better. "Every row" is the arm's score minus K0's over every forecast with a reading, in all 5 calendar years, with no interval.

Gate Result Target Passes G1: K0 minus ORACLE on the 13 load-shift and series pairs that experiment 227 scored (32,148 rows) 5.68 points 5.339 within 30% yes G2: K0 minus PERFECT in the AFTER phase of 141's injected load shifts (717,698 rows) 2.39 points 1.50 within 30% no

  • Question and rule. Does LR_b20's mask keep at least half of the oracle's gain after a load shift, with ordinary-day harm inside +/-0.05 points, on every Primary and on months it did not train on? The harm limit holds. The gain share misses the bar on the point estimate (47.1% against 50%), and its lower bound is above 0%. The failed gate G2 makes the verdict inconclusive.

  • Gate G1 passes. The harness's K0 scores 9.61 points on experiment 227's real load-shift rows against 10.13 in experiment 227, and the gain of the oracle is 5.68 points against 5.34. The gain rises with lead: 2.22 points under 24 hours, 4.49 from 24 to 72 hours, and 8.53 from 72 hours to 7 days.

  • Gate G2 fails. The harness's PERFECT minus K0 gain is 2.39 points, 59% above experiment 208's 1.50. Each lead band is 42% to 69% above experiment 208's gain in the same band (1.98, 2.65, and 2.61 points against 1.25, 1.57, and 1.84). Three post hoc diagnostics, all outside the pre-registered rule, change the gain. Multiplying the quantile offsets by 1.5 lowers the gain to 1.90 points, which is within 30% of 1.50 and would pass the gate. Multiplying by 1.2 gives 2.17. Keeping only injected load shifts in experiment 208's scored year gives 2.15. The gate fails as pre-registered. Whether the gate passes depends on a post hoc setting of the quantile offsets.
  • The gain after load shifts rests on a few events. The largest of the 34 load shifts carries 49.9% of LR_b20's total gain and 20.0% of the oracle's. LR_b20 recovers at least half the oracle's gain after 6 of the 34 load shifts, and between -10% and +10% of the oracle's gain after 22. The median per-shift share (28 load shifts where the oracle gains) is 3.8% for LR_b20 and 98.8% for GAM_ONLY. Leaving out one Primary moves LR_b20's share between 38.8% (without D16) and 63.5% (without D18), so the 50% bar is crossed by dropping D18. The 30 load shifts of 1 day or less give the oracle 0.22 points and LR_b20 0.01.
  • Ordinary days. LR_b20's difference stays inside +/-0.05 in every variant: -0.010 without D8's drops and the 17 block days, -0.011 without D8 and D9, -0.008 when closures of connected neighbours are also excluded, and -0.005 (-0.013 to +0.002) without the 7.5 alarms (of 44 that start on ordinary rows, each alarm weighted 1 over its series' number of folds) that are balanced-opposite candidates. The in-sample even months give +0.003. At 13 of 15 Primaries the absolute difference is under 0.05. At the other two, D18 (-0.195) and D22 (-0.052), the mask improves the score.
