P1 holds on the point estimate: the daylight gap is +0.189 (+0.089 to +0.298) and the night gap +0.087 (+0.016 to +0.145), a ratio of 2.17 whose interval spans 0.94 to 7.29.

Experiment 251 found that the best-guess demand stack beats BG2 over the year, but only through November to March. In April to June the stack is 0.05 to 0.22 points worse, and at D5 on sunny half-hours it is 1.30 points worse. The maintainer suspects that unmetered rooftop solar is modelled badly. This experiment runs six diagnostics on forecasts that earlier experiments already stored, so nothing is refitted.

Terms. Arm 1 (the stack) is the convex demand model with a Kalman filter (arm D), plus a small neural network that corrects the median (the neural-network head), plus a mean-and-standard-deviation summary of the 51 ensemble weather members' solar response (the two-number summary). A+S is arm 1 without the head, A+H is arm 1 without the summary, and arm D has neither. An arm is one configuration of the forecast whose output was stored. The export clip caps the solar output that the forecast subtracts from demand at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (experiment 180). GAM-K is the older generalised additive model with a Kalman filter of experiments 111 and 139, and gam0 is the same model without the filter. Primaries are primary substations, which step power down from the high-voltage network to the local distribution network. The pin is the solar capacity held fixed for each fit, and the clear-sky index is irradiance divided by clear-sky irradiance.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Gate (P0) held. Arm 1 minus BG2 is +0.162, +0.220, and +0.054 in April, May, and June, the numbers of experiment 251. Every arm has the 561,207 row keys, except the as-of and hindsight arms of experiment 139, which have no D9 and so 464,233.
  • Ranked causes. Each cause lists the rows that carry its gap per row, and the causes overlap.
    1. Solar term at D5 and D9. Daylight gap +0.633 (95% interval +0.343 to +0.894) at D5 and +0.499 (+0.055 to +1.083) at D9, against +0.150 over all rows. D5, D9, and D10 together average +0.364 (+0.193 to +0.552) and the other three substations -0.060 (-0.175 to +0.035). At D5 the clip arm (arm 2c) lowers the April to June sunny-half-hour gap from +1.779 (+1.345 to +2.255) to +0.656 (+0.438 to +0.850). Fix experiment needing no refit to start: the 60% export clip of experiment 180 applied to D9.
    2. Solar shape. The mean residual on clear midday half-hours is 1.5 points lower before 12:00 UTC than after it (-1.525, interval -2.390 to -0.779, pooled over six substations), and the asymmetry of P6 is 0.11, 0.61, 0.77, 0.43, 1.81, and 0.64 at D10, D11, D14, D16, D5, and D9, so P6 failed. D9's residuals are positive in both halves of the day, where the other substations' are negative. Fix experiment needing no refit to start: refit arm D with a per-substation morning-and-afternoon split of the solar shape and score April to June.
    3. Night-time error at D10 (post hoc). D10's night gap is +0.776 (+0.381 to +1.116) and its daylight gap +0.269 (+0.022 to +0.526). Fix experiment needing no refit to start: inspect D10's night residuals by month and half-hour.
  • Cleared. The neural-network head lowers the April to June score by 0.125 (arm 1 minus A+S -0.125, -0.191 to -0.050), so P5 failed for the head and the head is not the cause. The two-number summary lowers it by 0.033 (-0.050 to -0.019), so P5 held for the summary. The Kalman filter changes it by -0.157 (GAM-K minus gam0, -0.368 to +0.017), an interval that includes zero but stays below the +0.05 threshold. The ensemble sunshine forecast is cleared by P4: the gap is +0.214 (+0.074 to +0.366) where the ensemble-mean and realised clear-sky indices agree and +0.192 (+0.082 to +0.302) where they disagree; the ratio is 1.12 (0.48 to 2.04). Pooled night half-hours give +0.087 (+0.016 to +0.145), below the +0.15 threshold for the heating and lighting terms.
  • The gap starts in arm D. Arm D minus BG2 in April to June is +0.319 (+0.197 to +0.434), and the head and summary bring arm 1 to +0.150. The plan's literal rule reports a component as masked when single removal clears it while arm D minus BG2 is at least +0.15. Here the head and summary reduce the gap and hide no defect.
  • Not a stack effect. The older GAM-K model with the pinned capacity has the same seasonal pattern against BG2: +0.417 (+0.280 to +0.533) in April to June, +0.151 in July to September, and -0.188 in November to March. The ERA5-driven filter arm scores -0.015 (-0.077 to +0.046) against the ensemble-driven one in April to June (descriptive only).
  • P2 failed. The solar term improves the score more, not less, in April to June: the no-solar-term arm minus the pinned arm is +0.694 (+0.497 to +0.923) in April to June and +0.394 (+0.297 to +0.490) in July to September; the difference July to September minus April to June is -0.301 (-0.557 to -0.070). The as-of capacity (+0.397) and the hindsight capacity (+0.367) score level with the pin (+0.417) against BG2, so the accuracy of the capacity does not explain the gap.
  • P3 failed, with the opposite sign. The capacity correction implied by arm D's residual in April to June is -40.8% at D5 (-48.9% to -33.0%), -14.3% at D9 (-25.1% to -4.0%), -10.2% at D16 (-19.5% to -1.2%), -6.7% at D10, -6.4% at D14, and +0.7% at D11. Negative means the pinned capacity is too high. In July to September the same correction is positive at five of six substations (+3.9% to +14.5%, except D5 at -33.2%). The estimate is measured after the Kalman filter, so it is a pointer and not an independent capacity estimate; experiments 231 and 241 found the capacity estimator recovers 0.83 of an injected farm.
  • P7 held. At D5 on sunny half-hours arm 1 is +1.298 (+0.980 to +1.633) over the year and arm 2c +0.540 (+0.354 to +0.719), the numbers of experiment 251.
  • Where in the day. The April to June daylight gap is +0.398 (+0.241 to +0.552) from 08:00 to 12:00 UTC and +0.316 (+0.143 to +0.492) from 12:00 to 16:00 UTC (figure 3).
  • Rows, schedule, and weather. The diagnostics use the 561,207 rows of experiment 251. The stored forecasts were produced with monthly refits (stack) and weekly refits (BG2). Realised sunshine is CAMS irradiance, which exists only after the fact; the ensemble-mean irradiance is available at forecast time. Nothing was refitted and nothing was downloaded.
  • Post hoc. We chose these cuts after seeing the results: by substation and daylight, the D10 night gap, the pooled morning-minus-afternoon difference, the clip comparison in April to June, and every month of capacity correction.
  • What this cannot tell. One year, and 14 weeks in April to June, so intervals are wide. The stratification by ensemble agreement does not rule out a biased solar response of the ensemble that a refit with realised irradiance as the driver would expose; no such refit was run.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. Arm D's median and mean are identical at all six substations (difference 0.0), because its quantiles are built symmetrically around the mean, so no spread shifts the forecast. The mean forecast of arm 1 is not stored.
  • Error of the median beside the quantile score. The mean absolute error of the median, arm 1 minus BG2, is +0.311 (+0.141 to +0.474) in April to June, -0.084 (-0.151 to -0.015) in July to September, and -0.648 (-0.840 to -0.426) in November to March, the same signs as the quantile score.
  • Triggers (the seven audit triggers of the experiment guide). Trigger 1 (a failed control) did not fire, because the gate passed. Trigger 2 (a result contradicts its prediction) fired: P2, P3, P6, and P5 for the head contradicted their predictions; the explanation tested for P3 is the D5 export clip above. Trigger 3 (median and mean forecasts disagree) did not fire. Trigger 4 (leaving one site out flips a contrast) did not fire: leaving out any one substation keeps the April to June gap positive (+0.087 to +0.201, every interval above zero). Triggers 5 to 7 (nested arms, interval widths against a sister experiment, and later design depending on this result) did not apply. One caveat remains: later experiments will depend on this ranking, and one year of data has not been replicated.
  • Audit. A fresh Sonnet agent re-derived the headline numbers from the stored arrays with its own code and matched them: April to June gap +0.150 (+0.074 to +0.231), daylight +0.189, night +0.087, arm 1 minus A+S -0.125, minus A+H -0.033, minus arm D -0.169, arm D minus BG2 +0.319, agree +0.214 against disagree +0.192, and the no-solar-term arm minus the pinned arm +0.695 and +0.394. It found no row misalignment, duplicate, crossing quantile, or leakage through the normalised solar profile, and could not check whether the stack's settings saw April to June data. Experiments 220 and 251 describe the refit schedule.

docs.title: Plan
docs.text:
• Diagnostic 1, error map. Quantile score of arm 1 minus BG2 by month, by realised clear-sky index band (CAMS irradiance over clear-sky irradiance, from experiment 178's rows), by ensemble-mean clear-sky index band, and by hour of day, at the six substations. Bands apply to daylight half-hours only (clear-sky irradiance above 20 W/m²); night half-hours form their own cut.
  • Diagnostic 2, solar term on and off. The GAM-K arms of experiment 139 (no solar term, pinned capacity, as-of capacity, hindsight capacity) minus BG2 by month. These arms are a proxy for the stack, because the stack with its solar term removed was never stored. The result feeds the solar capacity cause through P2.
  • Diagnostic 3, capacity bias. The capacity held by each monthly GAM-K fit against the capacity that arm D's residual implies: on clear midday half-hours at 12 to 36 hours ahead, regress the signed residual on the normalised solar profile, per substation and month. The implied correction is measured after the Kalman filter and so is not independent of the fit. The independent reference is the recovery factor of the capacity estimator in experiment 231 and experiment 241, which found 0.83 of an injected farm recovered.
  • Diagnostic 4, weather input. Split the daylight gap by whether the ensemble-mean and realised clear-sky indices agree (within 0.1), disagree (by more than 0.2), or lie between, and report experiment 111's ERA5-driven filter arm beside the ensemble-driven one as description only. A refit with realised irradiance as the solar driver is the cheapest fix if the split cannot decide.
  • Diagnostic 5, residual shape. Mean signed residual of arm 1 at clear midday by month, before and after 12:00 UTC, and at D5 against arm 2c.
  • Diagnostic 6, ablations in April to June. Arm 1 against A+S, A+H, and arm D, from experiment 220's stored arms.

docs.title: Unmetered solar capacity at two Primary substations falls below the Feed-in Tariff register in 2021
docs.text:
Take-home message: the 2021 shortfall at D10 and D11 is not a missing correction and not a thin fit window, and a nearby metered farm's output makes the shortfall worse. The card's capacity estimate is already divided by the recovery of the metered farms, so a further division changes it by under 3%. Every Primary has 12 months of data in the 2021 season-year. The nearest-farm shape lowers the 2021 estimate by 7% at D10 and 22% at D11, so the upper end of the 80% range stays below the register floor at both Primaries. The fall is partly a mismatch between the divisors of the two shapes, so it does not show that the nearest-farm shape is worse.

What was asked. Each Primary substation card (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 are anonymised labels) shows the capacity of unmetered solar panels behind the substation, inferred from its power readings, in megawatts of alternating-current (AC) output. A season-year runs from July of the year shown to June of the next. For the 2021 season-year, the estimate is 1.1 MW at D10 and 1.9 MW at D11. The Feed-in Tariff register (the UK subsidy scheme's list of small installations) lists 1.9 MW and 2.6 MW of AC capacity at sites of at most 1 MW in the two Primaries' postcode districts. The register is partial, so we use that capacity as a lower bound, the register floor. A recovery is the share of a metered solar farm's output that the capacity fit finds again after we add that output to a Primary's readings (an injected farm).

The arms. The decision rule reads the 80% range of each estimate, from a bootstrap over resampled months.

  • A0: the card's estimate (experiment 129, fit with an increment penalty of 0.1 and satellite irradiance as the sunshine shape).
  • A1: A0 divided by the median recovery of the other metered farms (experiment 241).
  • A2: the same fit with the recorded output of the nearest metered farm within 25 km as the sunshine shape, divided by the median recovery under that shape (experiment 238).
  • A3: A2 with the number of fitted months per season-year printed and a "thin" mark under 6 months, which no season-year reaches. The fitted months are the same for A0.

All arms are offline checks and score no forecast.

Figure 1. At D10 and D11 the 2021 range of the card's estimate (orange) lies below the register floor (dashed line), and the nearest-farm shape (blue) lowers the estimates.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
• A1, the division by the recovery, equals the card's estimate. The card's capacity estimate is already divided by the Primary's median recovery over the matched farms, which is 0.77 to 0.86 over the Primaries and season-years. Experiment 241's leave-one-farm-out divisor differs from that divisor by at most 0.02. The two estimates differ by at most 3% (D16 2022: 3.25 MW against 3.33 MW). The median absolute error of a held-out farm under the card's fit is 0.063 of the injected capacity.
  • Dividing by the recovery a second time overcorrects. The result is 1.39 MW at D10 and 2.39 MW at D11 in 2021, which are the lifts the plan predicted. The second division corrects the same bias twice and would overstate capacity by about 25%. The upper ends of that range (1.62 MW and 2.62 MW) are still below the AC floor at D10 (1.90 MW) and, at D11, between the AC floor (2.57 MW) and the direct-current (DC) floor (2.78 MW).
  • A3, the thin-window rule, never fires, but the early data have a gap the rule cannot see. Season-year 2021 has 12 calendar months and 16,390 to 16,608 training half-hours (of 17,520) at every Primary (D10's rows start on 19 July, about 11.4 months). Season-years 2022 to 2025 have 15,212 to 17,568 half-hours. D10 has 5,424 half-hours in 2019 (from December) and D11 has 9,002 (from September), and neither has any in season-year 2020. The 2021 capacity is the sum of increments from 2019 onward, so it spans a gap of about 20 months that a count of months within 2021 does not show. The register's last entry (24 March 2021, from experiment 215) falls before season-year 2021 starts, so the estimate is below the capacity the register lists as installed in the district.
  • A2, the nearest-farm shape, lowers every 2021 estimate, partly through a different divisor. The nearest farm to each Primary is 3.1 km (D5), 7.7 km (D10), 23.1 km (D11), 5.3 km (D14), and 5.8 km (D16) away, so a metered farm lies within 25 km of all five. Against A0 in 2021, A2 gives 1.04 MW at D10 (a fall of 7%), 1.46 MW at D11 (22%), 2.74 MW at D14 (17%), 2.08 MW at D16 (20%), and 3.20 MW at D5 (14%). The prediction of a change under 10% at D5, D14, and D16 failed. In 2021 the A2 estimate is the card's times 0.93 (D10), 0.78 (D11), 0.83 (D14), 0.80 (D16), and 0.86 (D5). That ratio is the ratio of the raw fitted capacities (1.00, 0.86, 0.83, 0.93, and 0.99) times the ratio of the divisors (1.08, 1.11, 1.00, 1.17, and 1.14). At D10 the raw capacities agree, so the whole 7% fall at D10 comes from the divisor. A2's divisor is one number per Primary from a fit without the increment penalty, read at season-year 2024, and the card's divisor is per season-year from the penalised fit, so the two are not comparable. D11's reference farm is 23.1 km away, near the 25 km limit.
  • The card's estimate clears the AC floor in 23 of 25 Primary season-years. The check is whether the upper end of the 80% range reaches the floor. A0 misses D10 2021 (1.31 MW against 1.90 MW) and D11 2021 (2.07 MW against 2.57 MW). A2 clears the AC floor in 22 of 25: it misses D10 2021, D11 2021, and D16 2021 (2.18 MW against 2.20 MW), and ties at D10 2022 (1.90 MW). Against the DC floor, A0 misses the same two season-years and A2 misses five.
  • No arm met the decision rule. The rule asks for the upper end to reach the floor at all five Primaries in every season-year with register coverage, and for the estimate to stay within 10% of A0 at the Primaries with no shortfall. A0 and A2 both fail at D10 and D11. A2 also moves D5, D14, and D16 by 14%, 17%, and 20% in 2021. Three of five Primaries (D5, D14, and D16) clear the AC floor in every season-year under A0, as predicted, and two of five (D5 and D14) under A2.
  • The increment penalty does not cause the low 2021 level. Experiment 129's arm 2, which has no increment penalty, gives 0.82 MW at D10 and 1.38 MW at D11 in 2021, no higher than the card.
  • The fitted capacity rises about 75% between 2021 and 2022 at D10 (1.13 to 1.98 MW) and at D11 (1.88 to 3.32 MW). That rise is consistent with a 2021 level that is too low (for example from the data gap above), and equally with real installations during 2021 and 2022.
  • The A2 known-answer check passes at 4 of 5 Primaries. The median absolute error of a held-out injected farm under the nearest-farm shape is 2% of its capacity at D10, 2% at D11, 13% at D14, 4% at D16, and 6% at D5, with 2 to 4 injected farms per Primary. D14 misses the 10% bound.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: refitting the satellite shape with the card's settings reproduces the stored raw capacity of every Primary and season-year to within 1e-6, as the script asserts.
  • A1 covers 2021 to 2024: experiment 241 has no 2025 recoveries, and the A1 divisor pools the injected fractions of 20%, 50%, and 100% without a cloud-driven load.
  • Audit triggers (the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill's "Audit before merge"): trigger 2 fires, because the result contradicts the prediction. The two predicted causes were tested (the division and the fit window). The fall in the estimate under A2 is attributed to the higher recovery under that shape and was not tested further. No Opus audit was run, because the maintainer's rule is Sonnet by default and the conclusion is a null result. One Sonnet reviewer read the code and numbers, and one read the prose.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The register lists installations by postcode district, and the page assigns part of each district's capacity to each Primary. A shortfall at D10 and D11 may mean the register over-states the Primary's share.
  • The A2 range uses 2 to 4 injected farms, so it is narrow and not a calibrated 80% interval (experiment 241). The point estimate divides by the median recovery of the injected farms and the range by every farm's recoveries, so the range is not centred on the point (D14's recoveries span 0.66 to 0.87).
  • The A2 divisors come from experiment 238's injection fits, which use no increment penalty and data to 2026-07-01, and read the recovery at the 2024 season-year. The card's fit uses the penalty and data to 2026-07-31, as experiment 129's real-series fit did.
  • A neighbouring farm's output carries plant effects as well as sunshine (panel tilt, panel orientation, curtailment, and soiling; experiment 238).

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does the register's district share over-state D10 and D11 in 2021? Compare the register's postcode districts with the Primaries' supply areas. The prediction that could fail is a share above 70% of each district's listed capacity at both Primaries.
  • Does the 2019 data drive the 2021 level? Refit the card's estimate on rows from July 2021 only, and compare the 2021 level. The prediction that could fail is a 2021 estimate at D10 and D11 within 10% of the card's.
  • Does a floor constraint hurt the fit? Fit season-year 2021 with the capacity at least the register's AC capacity, and compare the fit's squared error on 2021 half-hours with the free fit. The prediction that could fail is a rise in error of under 1%, which would mean the readings cannot rule the floor out.

docs.title: A node-plus-generators curtailment metric with member-wise ENS inputs
docs.text:
The curtailment metric can now take ensemble members and it reproduces experiment 255, but 34% of the stored solar-farm forecasts it was checked on list their quantiles out of order. The metric prices what it would cost to cap the output of solar farms whenever a forecast says the substation they feed would export more power than a limit. It is step 2 of the load-shift decision program, which asks what knowing about load shifts is worth to the forecast. We asked whether the metric, studies.node_curtailment, can read ensemble members (the 51 runs that make up one ECMWF weather forecast) for a substation's demand and for each solar farm, and whether it then gives the answer that experiment 255 found. We added two functions. We re-scored experiment 255's rows at 0.5 times each substation's earlier maximum export twice: once from the stored quantiles, and once from 101 members drawn from them. We compared both with the avoidable cost (the cost above a perfect forecast) that experiment 255 stored for each forecast, and with its five comparisons between pairs of forecasts.

Verdict: partly supported. The scoring from stored quantiles matches experiment 255 exactly. The scoring from members keeps the sign and the 95% interval verdict of all five comparisons (largest difference 0.58 points of the baseline's avoidable cost, under the 1 point allowed). It misses the 1% allowed on two forecasts' avoidable costs, which differ by 2.0% and 1.1% (the climatology and manual-heuristic forecasts). The cause is in the stored forecasts: 26,344 of 77,897 solar-farm forecast rows (34%) store quantiles that cross, and a set of members cannot reproduce a crossing row. The metric now sorts each row's quantiles by default.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Scoring nodes. The step-1 mapping search found no file linking a farm to a Primary, and the six farms are probably connected at the bulk supply point. The generator-aware nodes are therefore the bulk supply points D13 (farms A, C, E) and D17 (farms B, D, F), with their child Primaries as demand. Primary-level curtailment is a demand-only relative proxy: it ranks forecasts and states no money saved.
  • Member path. net_flow_members pairs the demand's and each generator's members by member number and returns the node's metered flow per member. quantiles_from_members reduces members to the q<percent> columns that node_curtailment reads, interpolating linearly between sorted members. rearrange_quantiles sorts a stored row's quantiles; NodeCurtailmentAssumptions switches it on by default, and the result counts the rows that crossed.
  • Reproduction check. Pre-registered in the plan: tolerance 0.01% for the quantile path and 1% per arm for the member path, contrasts within 1 point, same sign, same 95% interval verdict. The script draws 101 members (probabilities 0, 0.01, ..., 1), because only then does linear interpolation between sorted members return the stored quantile at every whole-percent level. Post hoc: the quantile path with sorting off, and the member path on sorted quantiles.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Quantile path, sorting off. Every arm's avoidable cost equals experiment 255's, with largest difference 0.0000%, and every contrast equals it (e.g. H5 minus XGBoost GBP -62,407).
  • Member path on the stored quantiles. Avoidable cost differs from experiment 255 by -2.00% (climatology floor), -1.09% (manual-heuristic floor), -0.79% (plant), -0.78% (H5 with zero history), -0.76% (H5), and -0.69% (XGBoost). Contrasts differ by at most 0.58 points of the baseline's avoidable cost, keep their signs, and keep their 95% interval verdicts. The 1% arm limit is missed by the two floor arms.
  • Why it misses. 26,344 of 77,897 farm-forecast rows cross in every forecast arm (158,064 rows summed over the six arms). With the quantiles sorted first, the member path and the quantile path agree to 0.0000% on every arm.
  • Sorting moves the costs. With sorting on (the default), avoidable cost differs from experiment 255's by -3.66% (climatology floor), -1.90% (manual-heuristic floor), +1.08% (XGBoost), +0.72% (H5), +0.62% (plant), and -0.59% (H5 with zero history). Contrasts differ by at most 0.81 points; H5 minus XGBoost is GBP -69,766 against -62,407.
  • Rows. Experiment 255's causal rows, 2025-09-01 to 2026-06-30, 12 to 36 hour leads, headline price GBP 2,000 per MWh, Curtailment Limit 0, f = 0.5.
  • Tests. 88 tests in test_node_curtailment.py pass, including hand-worked member cases: members pair by number not by row order, a missing generator member drops only that member, and a 20-member case gives exactly 3.25 MWh planned and GBP 6,500.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast per site, and the mean-forecast error beside each contrast: not applicable, because the experiment trains no forecast.
  • Triggers. Trigger 1 fired (a pre-registered tolerance was missed). The explanation, crossing stored quantiles, was tested directly by sorting first, which removes the whole gap. No audit was run for the member path's miss; the maintainer or manager can ask for one. The other six triggers did not fire.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• We found no member-wise inputs for a real run. In the experiment folders searched, the stored farm outputs of experiments 229 and 246 hold no member column, and the stored 51-member demand forecasts of experiment 125 cover 3 of D13's 7 child Primaries and 3 of D17's 9. A member-wise run at D13 and D17 therefore needs new frames.
  • Step 3 needs no member frames. Its forecasts (climatology, the manual heuristic, XGBoost best guess, and the GAM stack) are quantile forecasts, so step 3 uses the quantile path. Member-wise frames are needed only for step 5's comparison of ensemble-driven forecasts.
  • Sorting changes costs by up to 3.7%, and it swaps H5 and H5 with zero history as the cheapest forecast (GBP 1,878,600 and 1,861,933 sorted; 1,865,144 and 1,872,880 stored).
  • The metric reads each generator's median only, so a better farm tail still does not show in its cost.

docs.title: Data-processing note
docs.text: The crossing rows counted on this page belong to three generators that are not solar farms. Their stored forecasts have no 0.01 or 0.99 quantile, and experiment 255's capacity cap turned the null padding into the generator's capacity, so the 0.01 quantile sat above the 0.05 quantile in all 26,344 of their rows. The six solar farms' own 51,553 rows have none (see experiment 255).

docs.title: PV capacity: where does the nearby-farm gain come from?
docs.text:
Take-home message: the nearby farm's measured sunshine explains almost none of the gain of experiment 238, and the farms' plant shape explains all of it. Experiment 238 added the recorded output of one metered solar farm, scaled to 50% of the substation's pinned capacity, to a substation's demand. It then asked the convex fit of experiment 129 to find that farm's output again. Recovery is the share of the injected farm's output that the fit finds (1 is all of it), read in the ratio of 99th percentiles of alternating-current output over daylight half-hours unless another measure is named. Using a different nearby farm's recorded output as the solar shape raised the recovery from 0.780 to 0.867 (experiment 238). The gain is the difference of two recoveries, and the page quotes the median of per-pair differences, so it can differ a little from the difference of the medians. The recorded output carries the nearby farm's sunshine (the solar irradiance reaching it) and its plant shape (panel tilt, panel orientation, and the flat top of the output curve).

We split the two by replacing the recorded output with a smooth table, learned from the farms' output against the satellite irradiance and the height of the sun (following experiment 218), and read at the substation's own satellite irradiance. The sunshine share is the recovery with the recorded output minus the recovery with the same farm's table. It is -0.014, so the table found as much as the recorded output did. The page calls the five substations whose capacity is judged the decision Primaries (D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16), and shows D9 beside them.

Verdict: partly supported. Every prediction of stage 1 (the injected farms) was met. The prediction of stage 2 (the real substation series) was not met: it said the real capacities would move by under 0.3 MW at 4 of 5 substations, and they did at 3 of 5. The sunny-half-hour score of the forecast was not run (see "What was not run"). Farms A to F are metered generators and stay anonymous. Fits stop at 2026-07-01, and no forecast is scored.

Figure 1. Pooled over the five decision Primaries, the learned plant shape (arms 3 and 4) finds more of the injected farm than the nearby farm's output does, in all four units.

Figure 2. The pooled empirical shape finds 0.90 or more at 5 of 5 Primaries in the capacity ratio and the energy unit, and at 2 of 5 in the ratio of 99th percentiles.

Figure 3. The median sunshine share is above zero only for the pairs of farms under 5 km apart.

Figure 4. The pooled empirical shape lowers each decision Primary's fitted capacity by 0.2 to 0.4 MW, and every value stays inside the 80% range of experiment 129.

docs.title: Arms
docs.text:
• Arm 1, satellite fleet shape (control): the south-facing physical shape of experiment 129.
  • Arm 2, nearby farm's recorded output: the nearest other farm's output, as in experiment 238.
  • Arm 3, nearby farm's plant, satellite sunshine: that farm's learned table (non-negative, smooth, rising with irradiance, as in experiment 218), read at the Primary's satellite irradiance and sun height. Arm 2 minus arm 3 is the sunshine share.
  • Arm 4, pooled empirical shape: the mean of the learned tables of the five farms other than the injected one, read at the Primary's satellite irradiance and sun height.
  • Rows: every arm trains on the half-hours at which the reference farm has a reading (75,107 to 85,231 per Primary, 45,017 at D9).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Pooled recovery, ratio of 99th percentiles (median over farms, then over the five Primaries; 80% interval from resampling whole months): arm 1 0.780 (0.765 to 0.790), arm 2 0.867 (0.863 to 0.878), arm 3 0.886 (0.874 to 0.893), arm 4 0.892 (0.874 to 0.897).
  • Contrasts: total gain 0.090 (0.074 to 0.100); sunshine share -0.014 (-0.023 to -0.002); plant shape of the nearby farm 0.095 (0.083 to 0.103); pooled shape over the satellite fleet shape 0.105 (0.095 to 0.113). The share of the gain not due to sunshine is 1 minus the sunshine share over the total gain: 115% (above 100% because the sunshine share is negative), against the predicted 60%.
  • Other units, pooled recovery for arms 1, 2, 3, and 4: capacity ratio of experiment 231 0.826, 0.869, 0.925, and 0.966 (arm 4: 0.944 to 0.973); ratio of 95th percentiles 0.809, 0.869, 0.890, and 0.905; clear-sky daylight energy 0.917, 0.859, 1.003, and 0.995 (arm 4: 0.978 to 1.004). The sunshine share is -0.060, -0.012, and -0.122 in those three units.
  • Arm 4 at the decision Primaries: at least 0.90 at 5 of 5 in the capacity ratio (0.916 to 0.979) and in the energy unit (0.960 to 1.009), at 3 of 5 at the 95th percentile, and at 2 of 5 in the ratio of 99th percentiles (0.862 to 0.908). Arm 4 is under 0.80 nowhere, so stage 2 ran. D9 reads 0.829 to 0.939.
  • By distance between the injected and reference farms (ratio of 99th percentiles, median over pairs): the 5 pairs under 5 km apart gain 0.198 in total, of which 0.075 is sunshine (range 0.040 to 0.109); the 8 pairs 5 to 12 km apart gain 0.069, sunshine -0.010; the 16 pairs 12 to 30 km apart gain 0.073, sunshine -0.029. One pair at 10 km reaches a sunshine share of 0.054 (figure 3).
  • Without the pairs under 5 km, the pooled recovery for arms 1 to 4 is 0.773, 0.866, 0.884, and 0.879 in the ratio of 99th percentiles, and arm 4 is 0.966 in the capacity ratio and 0.992 in the energy unit.
  • Stage 2, real capacities (season-year 2025, July 2025 to June 2026). Each capacity is divided by the recovery of its own shape (the capacity ratio of this experiment's injections at season-year 2024). The pooled empirical shape moves the capacity by -0.24, -0.29, -0.43, -0.30, and -0.23 MW at D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16 (under 0.3 MW at 3 of 5; the prediction asked for 4), and by -0.21 MW at D9. All five lie inside experiment 129's 80% range (1.2 to 1.6 MW wide). The physical-shape capacities match experiment 129's published estimates to within 0.09 MW at season-year 2024.

docs.title: What was not run
docs.text:
• The sunny-daylight score of arm D with the empirical shape was not run. It needs the empirical shape in the ensemble weather path of studies (a reviewed change, because that path builds the shape from the plant parameters), and monthly refits and ensemble forecasts at six substations for the scored year. That is far above the slot's 4 core-hours. Whether the empirical shape improves the sunny-half-hour forecast therefore stays open.
  • Bootstrap ranges for the stage 2 capacities were not refitted; the table uses experiment 129's ranges as context.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Reproduction: arms 1 and 2 reproduce experiment 238's tables, and the satellite shape on all rows reproduces experiment 231's rung 4, with a largest difference of 0.000 at three decimal places.
  • Median forecast minus mean forecast, and the mean-forecast error: not applicable, because no forecast is scored.
  • Audit triggers: none fired. The result agrees with experiment 231 (the irradiance explains almost none of the shortfall), the injections are those of experiment 238 and give the same interval for the total gain, and no nested arm beats the arm that contains it. This result answers the question behind triggers 2 and 7 of experiment 238. One Sonnet review of the code and one of the page were run; no Opus audit.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• The pooled shape includes plants like the injected one. Farm C sits 2 km from farm A, so the mean over the five other farms holds a close twin of each injected farm in some cases. The sunshine share needs no twin, but the transfer of arm 4 to a farm unlike all six metered farms is untested.
  • Recovery depends on the unit. The same fit reads 0.892 in the ratio of 99th percentiles and 0.995 in clear-sky energy; the decision rule's "some unit" is satisfied by two of four units.

  • The plan left three choices open: the plant-and-unit share is read as 1 minus the sunshine share over the total gain, in the ratio of 99th percentiles; the stage 2 divisors come from this experiment's injections and not from the known-answer grid of experiment 129; and stage 2 fits stop at 2026-07-01.

  • The learned tables read about 0 at low sun. The injected and reference farms' normalised output is set to 0 where the sun is 15 degrees or less above the horizon, and the tables keep those rows, so arms 2 to 4 all carry that zero. The arm comparison stays fair, but the tables understate output at low sun. The farms' unit shapes are also derate-divided at the substation's temperature, not the farm's own.

  • The stage 2 divisor comes from the pooled table of five farms, while the real fit uses all six.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• Does the empirical shape lower the sunny-half-hour error of the forecast? A test would port the pooled table into the ensemble weather path in packages/studies and score arm D at D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16 on the sunny-daylight rows of experiment 178. A candidate prediction that could fail is a change of under 0.02 MW at the five other substations.
  • Is the plant shape of an unseen farm predictable? Leave each farm out of the pool and also leave out its nearest neighbour, then repeat arm 4.

docs.title: Why does XGBoost beat the solar-farm power model on metered farms when a better power model barely helps?
docs.text:
XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model because it draws a better forecast band, not because its median forecast is better, and a plant whose band also depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index gets the same gain. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms in its trial area, labelled A to F on this page. The "plant" is the physical power model of experiment 224: a fixed panel geometry driven by the mean of the 51 members of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast. Its forecast band is the plant's forecast plus residual quantiles taken in four bins of the forecast (the "four-bin plant"). Experiment 243 found XGBoost (Chen and Guestrin, 2016), a gradient-boosted decision-tree library, about 3% better than the plant in the quantile score, with the plant better at the 0.99 quantile. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, in points of capacity, and lower is better. Experiment 218 found that better plant parameters barely help, and experiment 257 found that a linear fit on lagged power and ensemble spread recovers about 90% of a neural network head's gain over the plant. We asked which inputs let XGBoost beat the plant. We gave XGBoost the plant's inputs alone (X1), then added input groups one at a time (rungs L1 to L6: the plant forecast, ensemble spread, lagged power, hour of day and day of year, further ensemble weather, and the remaining weather). We compared those fits with refits of the plant's panel parameters (P), plants whose band is binned by a second input (pq), and an additive model of the plant's residual (G). Each rung has a control, S2 to S6, in which that rung's added columns are shuffled among rows.

The prediction partly holds, and the stated mechanism fails. XGBoost on the plant's inputs alone has a 3.0% lower quantile score than the four-bin plant in own history (98.75% interval from resampling months, -6.1% to -0.9%) and 3.7% lower in zero history (-6.0% to -1.5%). "Own history" means each farm's fits use only that farm's earlier months, and "zero history" means they use only the other five farms. The pre-registered rule asked for an interval wholly below -1.5%. Zero history meets the rule narrowly, and own history does not, so the verdict is partly supported. Lagged power and ensemble spread, the hypothesised causes, carry about 23% of the gain. In own history, 97% of the full ladder's gain appears at the first rung, and 73% in zero history, so prediction B holds. XGBoost on the plant forecast alone gains nothing (+0.2%, -0.5% to +0.6%), so the gain is not a recalibration of the plant's output. The stop rule does not fire, because the gain is above 0.5%.

The gain comes from the band, and a plant with a better offset table matches it. The plant's offsets binned by its forecast and the ensemble spread give a 3.1% lower score than the four-bin plant (-4.4% to -1.3%), which equals XGBoost's gain. The same plant has a 16% lower pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile. We chose the binning after seeing results, from about eight variants the audit tried, so those intervals are not corrected for that search.

docs.title: Where the gain between XGBoost and the plant comes from
docs.text:
Nearly all of the gain comes from the plant's own inputs, and calendar columns subtract from it. We tested five candidate explanations: (a) lagged power, (b) ensemble spread, (c) calendar columns, (d) further ensemble weather, and (e) a better mapping from the ensemble-mean inputs to the band. The shares below are of the plant-to-L6 gain (own history 0.209 points of capacity; zero history 0.320 points). They are rough, because every rung's interval is wide. They do not sum to 100%, because the plant forecast added at L1 carries a further 15% (own history) and 6% (zero history).

  • (e) A better mapping from the ensemble-mean inputs to the band: 82% own history, 67% zero history (X1). Refitting the plant's tilt, azimuth, heat loss, scale, and ceiling on forecast weather scores +0.1% against the four-bin plant, and refitting on observed weather scores +0.5%, so the gain is not a better panel geometry. Binning the offsets by the forecast and a second input scores -3.1% (ensemble spread, 6 by 3 bins; -4.4% to -1.3%), -2.8% (clear-sky index, 8 by 4 bins; -3.7% to -1.9%), and -1.2% (sun height, 4 by 4 bins; -3.5% to +0.3%), with the median error unchanged. The spread is the standard deviation of the 51 members' plant forecasts, so it is not one of the plant's inputs.
  • (a) Lagged power and availability: 19% own history (L3 minus L2: -0.7%, -1.4% to +0.1%), 12% zero history. The audit found that the own-history lag gain is farm A's (-3.7%; the other five farms +0.1% to -0.3%).
  • (b) Ensemble spread: 4% own history (-0.14%, -0.45% to +0.17%), 2% zero history.
  • (d) Further ensemble weather (humidity, longwave, rain, pressure, wind, height, clear-sky index, lead): 20% own history, with neither rung's interval excluding zero, and 25% zero history, where L5 minus L4 is -1.4% (-2.1% to -0.7%) and L6 minus X1 is -1.9% (-2.8% to -1.0%).
  • (c) Calendar columns: -39% own history. Adding hour and day of year makes the quantile score 1.5% worse (+0.3% to +2.9%) than the same rung without them, and the shuffled control S4 shows the cause is the calendar columns. The audit refit shows that day of year alone causes the effect (+1.4%) and hour adds nothing, which suggests that XGBoost memorises dates in the 17 tuning months. The effect is farm A's (+4.7%), and +0.6% to +1.1% at the other five farms. In zero history the effect is +0.7%.

The gain sits in the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles at clear skies and low sun, and not in the median. For L6, the pinball loss is 8% lower at the 0.05 quantile and 14% lower at the 0.95 quantile, and the error of the median forecast changes by -0.05%. The gain is concentrated in the lowest decile of ensemble spread and at clear skies (Figure 5). It appears in the morning and evening and is absent around noon, and at the first daylight hour both X1 and L6 are worse than the plant (Figure 4). The audit found that the quarter of rows with a clear-sky index of 1.0 or more carry nearly all of X1's gain (X1 minus plant is -0.2% without them). On those rows X1 narrows the 5% to 95% band from 44.7 to 26.5 points of capacity, while under-covering the lower tail (coverage 0.070 at the 0.05 quantile). X1's gain is also concentrated in 2025-12 (-22%) and 2026-01 (-12%). At the 0.99 quantile X1 and L6 are 16% and 17% worse than the plant, and G is 15% better (-19% to -10%).

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Rows. Experiment 243's common rows: 41,654 daylight half-hours (sun above 5 degrees) at 12 to 36 h leads, 2025-09 to 2026-08, six farms, equal weight per farm, intervals at 98.75% (a Bonferroni correction across four headline contrasts) from resampling the 12 scored months 5,000 times. XGBoost arms average three seeds.
  • Schedule. One fit on the tuning months (2024-04 to 2025-08), no refit in the scored year (screening schedule), 4 cores, CPU. XGBoost: 11 quantile outputs, 150 rounds, depth 5, learning rate 0.15, subsample 0.8, colsample_bytree 1 in every arm. The differences between arms could depend on a weekly refit, which was not run.
  • Quantile score, own history (points of capacity, 98.75% interval): G 5.44 (4.78 to 6.01); L3 5.48; L6 5.52 (4.77 to 6.12); L1 5.52; X1 5.55 (4.81 to 6.15); pq with spread 5.55; pq with clear-sky index 5.56; pq with sun height 5.66; four-bin plant 5.73 (5.05 to 6.27); X2 (XGBoost on the plant forecast alone) 5.74; P on forecast weather 5.73; P on observed weather 5.75; climatology 8.64; manual heuristic 8.69. Zero history: L6 5.55, L3 5.59, G 5.59, X1 5.66, plant 5.87.
  • Contrasts against the four-bin plant, own history (quantile score): X1 -3.0% (-6.1 to -0.9); L6 -3.7% (-7.0 to -1.2); G -4.9% (-6.4 to -3.5); L3 -4.4% (-7.0 to -2.6). G minus L6: -1.3% (-3.2 to +1.3). Zero history: X1 -3.7% (-6.0 to -1.5), L6 -5.4% (-7.8 to -3.2), G -4.9% (-6.0 to -3.6).
  • Tail calibration, own history (coverage; target in brackets; over the 41,676 rows in the stored files, 22 more than the common rows): plant 0.033 (0.01), 0.064 (0.05), 0.946 (0.95), 0.984 (0.99); L6 0.038, 0.088, 0.938, 0.992; G 0.033, 0.066, 0.945, 0.987. L6's 0.05 quantile sits too high (coverage 0.088 against 0.05). Its 0.99 quantile has coverage near the target (0.992) but a pinball loss 17% worse than the plant's.
  • By slice, L6 minus plant: clear-sky index 0.9 and over -8.9% (-18.0 to -2.5); under 0.3 -8.8% (-18.8 to +0.8); 0.3 to 0.6 -1.7% and 0.6 to 0.9 -0.1% (intervals span zero); lead 12 to 24 h -3.7% and 24 to 36 h -3.5%; December to February -9.2% (-22.5 to +2.0), March to May -3.7%, June to August -2.4%, September to November -3.0%. Leads below 12 h cannot be forecast from a 00 UTC run at forecast time, and leads of 36 to 54 h were not run.
  • Per farm and leave-one-farm-out. L6 minus plant stays between -3.1% and -4.8%, and X1 minus plant between -2.4% and -4.4%, with any one farm left out. X1 is 4.6% worse than the plant at farm A and 1.6% to 5.7% better at the other five.
  • Weather sources at forecast time. Every input is the ECMWF ensemble 00 UTC run at the nearest 0.25 degree cell, which exists at forecast time: mean and spread of shortwave, mean temperature, dew point (relative humidity by the Magnus formula), longwave, rain, surface pressure, mean-sea-level pressure, 10 m and 100 m wind, and 500 hPa height. Lagged power is the farm's own power one day earlier (two days when the lead exceeds 24 h). The plant refit on observed weather uses Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance, a past-weather product that does not exist at forecast time.
  • Departures from the brief. The ensemble store serves no cloud layers or visibility, so those rungs were not run; longwave and humidity stand in. The additive model has no monotonic constraint. The binned gain of Figure 5 replaces partial-dependence plots. Leads 0.5 to 12 h and 36 to 54 h were not run.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast (points of capacity, own history): plant +0.90, X1 -0.49, L1 -0.48, L6 -0.57, G +0.43; per farm the plant is +0.76 to +1.03 and L6 is -1.10 to -0.12.
  • Mean-forecast error beside the quantile contrasts (mean absolute error, MAE, of the mean forecast, pooled over rows): plant 10.12, X1 10.21, L6 10.11, G 9.96. The MAE of the median forecast is 9.88 for the plant, 9.94 for X1, 9.87 for L6, and 9.71 for G. X1's quantile gain (-3.0%) comes with a median MAE 0.6% worse on the equal-farm-weight basis of the contrasts, so the gain is in the band's width, as Figure 3 shows.
  • Quantile crossing. No arm's raw quantiles cross, so sorting changes no score.
  • Triggers fired. Two audit triggers fired: trigger 3 (X1's quantile-score gain and its median error disagree), and trigger 5 (L4, which holds L3's columns, scores 1.5% worse than L3, and 1.4% worse than its shuffled control). A second Sonnet agent re-derived the headline contrasts from the stored predictions and reproduced all six. The audit report is private, under data/ml-experiments/briefs/. Its findings: a binned plant matches XGBoost (now arms of this experiment), the gain sits at clear skies and low sun, day of year alone causes the calendar effect, and farm A carries part of the lag and calendar effects. No Opus audit was run, because the manager's brief asked for Sonnet.
  • Caveat: one fit, 12 months, six farms. Most rung-to-rung intervals include zero. A resample of farms as well as months gives X1 minus plant -7.8% to +2.3% and L6 minus plant -8.4% to +2.1% (98.75%). Only the gain of G (-7.1% to -2.6%) survives that resample, so the X1 and L6 gains are conditional on these six farms.
  • Caveat: unequal clamping and shuffling. The plant and G are capped at the tuning-month ceiling and the XGBoost arms are only floored at zero, which can only help the plant at the upper tail. In zero history the shuffled controls permute rows across the five training farms. The extra weather values of L5 and L6 are the 3-hourly step at or after the half-hour from the same 00 UTC run, so they exist at forecast time.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text: The next experiment should test whether a plant whose band depends on the ensemble spread and the clear-sky index together matches the additive model G at every quantile. In own history the extra weather variables of L5 and L6 add under 1% beyond the plant's inputs, but in zero history L6 is 1.9% better than X1, so a weather-adapter experiment should expect little from more variables for a farm with its own history. A small neural network could replace the additive terms of G, with G and the spread-binned plant as the arms to beat.

docs.title: Do load shifts net out at the bulk supply points in the curtailment metric?
docs.text:
A load shift between two Primary substations under the same bulk supply point (BSP) changes the avoidable curtailment cost at the BSP by 0.2% to 0.7% of its value on the real record, and a shift across the boundary between the two BSPs by 1.4% to 5.5%. A load shift is demand that the network operator moves between neighbouring Primary substations for days. We counted how many real load shifts cross from one of experiment 255's two BSPs to the other. We then simulated 40 years ("worlds") of 8 load shifts each, taking 15% to 45% of a Primary's load for 1 to 8 days, for each kind of shift. We reran the Kalman filter on recent power of experiment 258 on the 15 Primaries' shifted readings, added each Primary's change in forecast to the BSP forecast of experiment 255, and scored the curtailment cost with experiment 255's rule (GBP 2,000 per MWh at a limit of 0.5 times the BSP's earlier maximum export).

Verdict: partly supported. The load-shift decision program's brief set limits of 1% for shifts inside one BSP and 5% for shifts across. Placed at random, the shifts stay under both limits (within 0.24%, across 1.37%). Placed to end 6 to 72 hours before days on which the BSP would be curtailed, the predictions fail: within +0.71% (97.5% interval 0.34% to 1.08%, against 1%), and across +5.50% (3.34% to 7.96%, against 5%).

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Stage 1 count (D-labels). Of the 31 logged load-shift pairs, 22 join Primaries under one BSP, 4 cross (D15-D2, D12-D2, D10-D12, D11-D12), and 5 have an unknown partner. Of the 66 hand-filtered real events, 54 involve two Primaries and 4 of those cross (all D10-D12); of the 28 over 1 day, 1 crosses. Of the 54 interconnected pairs, 33 join Primaries under one BSP, 5 cross, and 16 touch a substation outside the 30 listed.
  • Known-answer gate. The real record reproduces experiment 255's avoidable cost for the plant forecast: GBP 1.876 million against its 1.88 million at 0.5 times the earlier maximum export.
  • Worlds. The run holds 40 worlds of 8 load shifts for each of two kinds (within one BSP, across) and two placements (random, or ending 6 to 72 hours before a day with scored events). Shifts move 15%, 30%, or 45% of the donor's mean load for 1, 2, 4, or 8 days (mean 1.2 to 1.5 MW, at most 5.0 MW), between interconnected or logged pairs. Event days: 21 at D17 and 15 at D13.
  • C1 and C2 (K0, observed power, change in avoidable cost against the real record). Within, targeted +0.71% (0.34% to 1.08%); across, targeted +5.50% (3.34% to 7.96%). Within, random +0.24% (-0.01% to 0.55%); across, random +1.37% (0.47% to 2.35%). The largest single world moves by 3.0% (within) and 28% (across), so a mean under the threshold does not mean every world is.
  • Why within-BSP shifts do not cancel. A 2 MW shift held for 4 days moves the summed forecast of the two Primaries by 0.41 to 1.31 MW, against 1.27 to 2.00 MW for the donor alone, because each Primary's filter has its own hyperparameters.
  • Perfect knowledge (PERFECT minus K0, avoidable cost, targeted). Across: 8% lower before the alarm (-65,000 to +3,000 GBP), 5% lower after (-62,000 to +16,000), 11% higher during (-3,000 to +45,000); within: under 3% in every group. No interval excludes zero for cost. The twCRPS after a shift is lower by 8% across (interval excludes zero) and 2% within.
  • Real record at the two BSPs (descriptive). The oracle mask (the logged shifts, known at once), the carried LR_b20 mask, and no mask have avoidable costs within GBP 600 of 1.876 million. The record holds 639 rows within 48 hours after a labelled load shift, with GBP 13,400 of avoidable cost.
  • Schedule. Filters refit on the real GAM of experiment 130 (past weather: ERA5 and CAMS, so the numbers are a ceiling for a live service); node rows are experiment 48's ensemble-driven forecast at 09 UTC, mapped to the filter's 06 UTC origin.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast. Pooled over both BSPs: +0.11 MW for every arm of the real record; no per-site figure, because the quality sums are pooled.
  • Error beside the quantile score. Across, targeted, G0, PERFECT minus K0: MAE of the median +0.009 MW (0.005 to 0.014), quantile score +0.007 (0.004 to 0.011), cost -0.6% (-3% to +2%). The error is worse because the mask forecasts the normal arrangement and the observed flow does contain the shift; the nra target is not worse (K0 +3.3%, PERFECT +0.8%).
  • Triggers. None fired on this page: the real record reproduces experiment 255, the observed and nra targets agree within one BSP, and a within-BSP effect of 0.7% was traced to differing filter gains. Trigger 7 is a judgement call: steps 4 to 6 of the program may choose their curtailment nodes from this result, whose headline is the real-shift count and the real-record row above, not the injected-world sign.

docs.title: Caveats and next steps
docs.text:
• Arm names. K0 is the filter on recent power with no knowledge of load shifts. GAM_ONLY is the additive model alone. PERFECT masks each shift's readings from the filter, known at once; PERFECT_LAG masks them after the live service's delays. The nra target is the real record without the injected shifts. G1 to G5 are ordinary, before-alarm, during, after (48 hours), and near (7 days) rows, as in the plan. twCRPS is the threshold-weighted continuous ranked probability score on the export tail.
  • Reading of the arms. The base is experiment 48's node forecast, standing for K0. The arms differ by the injected shifts' change in the filter. GAM_ONLY removes K0's real correction, so its cost is 13% higher in every world. LB20_LIKE is PERFECT_LAG on a random half of the shifts, a stand-in because the carried mask has no alarms on injected readings.
  • Not tested. Unmetered substations under the BSP, shifts to another BSP (D17 and D13 have GSPs above), and the generators' forecasts changing with the shifts.
  • Next. A Primary-level curtailment metric (demand-only proxy) for step 4.

docs.title: Does a learned correction to the weather inputs of the solar-farm power model help, and does a neural network beat additive curves?
docs.text:
Extra ensemble weather variables gave no detectable gain in the solar-farm power forecast when they entered as a learned correction to the plant (the physical model that turns a weather forecast into farm power). The National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F. The plant takes the ensemble weather forecast (51 members from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts) and returns the farm's power. We added a learned correction in front of the plant that scales the forecast irradiance and shifts the cell temperature, using eight further variables from the same forecast (downward longwave radiation, relative humidity, precipitation, surface pressure, mean-sea-level pressure, 10 m and 100 m wind speed, and 500 hPa geopotential height). The correction starts at no change, so it can improve the forecast only if the variables carry information. We tried two forms: summed one-variable curves (an additive model, in effect a generalised additive model, GAM) and a small neural network. The design follows the plant of experiment 218 and the folds of experiment 243 and experiment 257, which found that a linear fit on the farm's power one day earlier (the lagged power) and the spread of the ensemble members recovers 90% of the gain of a neural head.

The prediction (a 1% to 2% gain) failed, and the pre-registered stop rule fired: the extra variables did not improve the forecast at the 99.4% familywise level. The score is the quantile score, twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, in points of capacity (smaller is better). In own history (each farm fitted on its own earlier months), the additive curves on all variables (A3) score 5.765 against 5.726 for the plant with the correction at no change (A1'), which is 0.67% higher (95% interval -1.2% to +2.1%). At none of the six farms does A3 score at least 0.5% below the plant, so we stopped before the neural arms. The neural arms ran afterwards, labelled post hoc, because they take little computing time. The neural network on all variables (A5) scores 1.06% higher than the plant. A placebo copy of the extra variables (the values from another day of the same month and cloud band) scores about the same as the real variables for the additive curves (C6 +0.54%, interval -0.34% to +1.40%). For the neural network, the placebo scores 1.4% lower than the real variables (C7 +1.37%, 95% interval +0.23% to +2.44%), and that interval includes zero at the 99.4% level. Curves and network on the three minimal inputs (clear-sky index, relative spread of the ensemble members, and temperature) score 0.33% and 0.19% lower than the plant, and both intervals include zero.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Quantile score (twice the mean pinball loss over 11 levels, points of capacity, mean over six farms; own history, then zero history): H5 5.475 and 5.610, XGBoost 5.490 and 5.610, P2 5.500 and 5.645, blind network (post hoc) 5.570 and 5.658, A2 5.707 and 5.817, A4 (post hoc) 5.715 and 5.862, A1' (the plant) 5.726 and 5.871, A3 5.765 and 5.798, A5 (post hoc) 5.787 and 5.869. Floors: climatology 8.638, manual heuristic 8.687.
  • Contrasts, own history (percent change in quantile score, 95% interval; 99.4% familywise interval in the figure): C1 (A3 minus A1') +0.67% (-1.2 to +2.1); C2 (A3 minus A2) +1.00% (+0.07 to +1.87); C3 (A5 minus A3, post hoc) +0.39% (-0.68 to +1.37); C4 (A5 minus A4, post hoc) +1.25% (+0.05 to +2.30); C6 (A3 minus its placebo) +0.54% (-0.34 to +1.40); C7 (A5 minus its placebo, post hoc) +1.37% (+0.23 to +2.44). C5 (adapter plus head) and the alternating-update check were not run, because the stop rule fired.
  • Decision rule. C3 is not below zero, so the neural network is not preferred. C2 and C4 are above zero, so neither extra variable set is kept. C8: the share of the gap from the plant (fraction of sunny-half-hour output fitted by the median, mean over farms 0.9276) to experiment 218's 0.973 that A3 closes is -6% (A3 0.9247) and A5's is -12% (0.9222). The plant's fraction is 0.9276 on these rows against 0.91 in experiment 218, because the definition of sunny differs, so the shares are indicative only.
  • Post hoc contrasts, own history: A2 minus A1' -0.33% (-1.8 to +0.6); A4 minus A1' -0.19% (-1.7 to +0.8); the blind network (no plant; the raw inputs, lagged power and the extra variables) minus A1' -2.72% (-4.8 to -1.1), with the 0.99-quantile pinball loss 16.0% lower (-19.6 to -12.8) and the 0.01-quantile pinball loss 9.8% higher (-0.3 to +24.1).
  • Zero history. A3 minus A1' is -1.25% (-3.4 to +0.6), because the adapter can correct the borrowed plant scale; A5 and A4 are not better than the plant.
  • Per farm, own history (A3 minus A1', percent): A +1.8, B +0.3, C -0.04, D -0.1, E +2.0, F -0.2.
  • Tails, own history (pinball loss at 0.01 and 0.99, coverage of the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles): A1' 0.372 and 0.418 (0.034, 0.984); A3 0.382 and 0.420 (0.036, 0.984); A5 0.382 and 0.433 (0.038, 0.982); blind 0.409 and 0.351 (0.051, 0.977).
  • Fitted curves (Figure 3). The clear-sky-index curve lowers the irradiance factor from about 1.2 at low index to 0.8 at high index in both forms, so the correction mostly flattens the forecast's irradiance response. Temperature raises the factor and humidity lowers it. The pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height curves are flat. The stronger of the two penalties won in 18 of 18 additive fits and in 24 of 30 neural fits.
  • Monotonicity (share of irradiance steps where power falls as irradiance rises): additive curves 0.6% on average in own history (3.8% at the worst farm), neural network 0.15%; in zero history 1.8% and 1.1%. The 1% pass level is not met at every farm.
  • Quantile crossing. The offset table is built from per-bin residual quantiles, so no adapter's unsorted quantiles cross (crossing rate 0 for every arm run).

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast (mean of the 11 quantiles; points of capacity, mean over farms, own history): A1' 0.87, A2 0.86, A3 0.55, A4 0.84, A5 0.66, blind 0.29. Experiment 243's H5 is 0.78.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast. The mean absolute error of the mean forecast for A3 is 1.6% below A1' (95% interval -3.4% to -0.04%), while its quantile score is 0.67% above and its median error 1.4% above. The two disagree in direction, so audit trigger 3 fires. The extra variables may sharpen the mean forecast and still spoil the quantile score, because the table of quantile offsets is fitted on the plant's own residual spread.
  • Triggers that fired. Trigger 1 (a control moves the wrong way: the placebo of the neural network beats the real variables, C7). Trigger 2 (the result contradicts its prediction). Trigger 3 (above). Trigger 5 (A2 beats A3 although A3 holds A2's inputs). A fresh Sonnet auditor re-derived the scores and checked the method; its findings follow in "Audit".
  • The row set is experiment 257's, and every half-hour of it has all extra variables, so no row was dropped. A1' reproduces experiment 243's plant to the digit (5.7263), which confirms that the torch plant, the table, and the pairing match.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
A fresh Sonnet auditor re-derived the scores from the stored predictions (they match to 0.001), and found no leakage in the join, standardisation, offset-table refit, or placebo permutation. Findings and triage:

  • "Worse" overstated the result (accepted). No contrast excludes zero (C1 95% interval -1.2% to +2.1%), so the page says no detectable gain.
  • Averaging order (accepted, noted). Averaging quantiles over seeds before scoring gives A5 +0.37% and A3 +0.58% against A1'; this page averages per-row losses over seeds (A3 +0.67%, A5 +1.06%). A5's seeds range from 5.756 to 5.837, so part of its 1.06% is seed noise.
  • Per-farm effects are mixed (accepted; already listed): A and E drive the mean, and C, D, and F improve slightly.
  • The adapters learn (accepted). On farm A the training loss falls 5% to 7% and the validation loss about 1%, so the adapters overfit the tuning period, not fail to learn.
  • A5 touches the irradiance bound (accepted): the largest |g| is 0.399 against 0.4 on farm A. The conclusion does not depend on it, because A3 does not touch the bound.
  • Validation set of two summer months (accepted as a caveat): selection of penalty and epoch rests on about 1,650 rows, so differences between arms are within noise.
  • The mean-forecast error improves for A2 (-1.8%, interval -3.3% to -0.6%) and A3 (-1.6%): the adapters may help the central estimate slightly while the quantile score does not improve.

docs.title: Departures and post hoc changes
docs.text:
• Post hoc, before the stop rule was read. The first run fitted the offset table on the two validation months (2025-07 and 2025-08) only, as the amended plan said, and scored A1' 5.857 against 5.726 for experiment 243's plant: a table from two summer months does not describe the year. Every arm now fits the table, by the same code, on all tuning months. The first run also found the stop rule satisfied, so this change did not create the result.
  • Post hoc. A4, A5, the blind network, and both placebo arms ran after the stop rule fired. A3's shuffled and alternating controls, A6, and the heads did not run.
  • From the brief. One fit on the tuning months and no weekly refits; the curves are not convex and are fitted by gradient descent; quantiles are sorted and the crossing rate is zero; the store serves no cloud layers or visibility, so the cloud-layer variables of the brief were not run, and longwave radiation and humidity stand in. The weather source at every input is the ECMWF ensemble 00 UTC run, available at forecast time, at the store's 3-hourly step.

docs.title: What the next experiment should answer
docs.text:
• The blind network beats the plant by 2.7% but does not beat P2, the linear fit of experiment 257, so test the blind network and P2 together. The blind network gains most at the 0.99 quantile (-16%), the tail that matters for curtailment, and it loses at the 0.01 quantile. A blend of the two by quantile could take both gains.
  • The extras may still help through a different route, such as the farm's availability, but the placebo result says the present route does not use them.

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
• Background. Experiment 218 found a better plant barely helps (fraction of output fitted 0.950 to 0.953) while the ensemble irradiance caps the fit at 0.91 on sunny half-hours against 0.973 with observed weather. Experiment 243 found a neural head on the plant 4.4% better than the plant, and experiment 257 found a linear fit on the lagged power and the ensemble spread gets 90% of that gain. Experiment 248 found Met Office UKV columns worth about 1%. This experiment asks whether other ensemble variables, entering through a correction to the plant's inputs, do better than those heads, which correct the plant's output.
  • Rows and fits. Experiment 257's rows and folds. One fit on the tuning months before 2025-09, none in the scored year (screening schedule, 4 CPU cores), the schedule of experiments 243 and 257, so the contrasts against their stored arms pair on the same half-hours. Own-history (fitted on the scored farm's tuning months) and zero-history (leave-one-farm-out, fitted on the other five farms) settings. Weekly refits are not run, which departs from the brief; the contrasts here are between arms sharing one schedule.
  • Weather sources (all exist at forecast time). ECMWF ensemble, 00 UTC run, nearest 0.25 degree cell. Minimal inputs: clear-sky index of ensemble-mean irradiance, relative ensemble spread of irradiance, and ensemble-mean temperature. Full list adds downward longwave flux (a cloud proxy), relative humidity from temperature and dew point, precipitation, surface pressure, mean-sea-level pressure, 10 m and 100 m wind speed, and 500 hPa geopotential height, taken at the store's 3-hourly step holding each half-hour (the extra_<farm>.parquet files of experiment 270). The store serves no cloud layers or visibility, so the brief's cloud-layer variables are not run. No UKV variable is used.
  • The plant and the correction. The plant is experiment 243's fleet-shape plant in torch with the per-farm scale and ceiling (the median of the other five farms' values in zero history), frozen. Effective beam and diffuse irradiance equal the ensemble values times exp(g(x)), and cell temperature is raised by h(x), with g bounded to +-0.4 and h to +-4 K. Both are zero at initialisation, so every adapter starts as the plant. The adapter's quantiles are its power plus a table of 11 offsets per bin of the unadapted plant forecast. The table is trained jointly with the adapter so the training loss is the quantile loss, and then replaced for every arm, by the same code, with the per-bin residual quantiles of the frozen arm on all tuning rows (the plan said the two validation months only; see the departures). Quantiles are sorted, and the crossing rate before sorting is reported per arm.
  • Selection and tuning. Every choice (epoch, penalty strength, which of A3 and A5 goes into A6, which arm gets the alternating and blind controls) is made on the validation months only, with the same budget for every adapter: the same 60 epochs with early stopping on validation, and two penalty strengths (a second-difference penalty of 1e-3 or 1e-2 for the curves, weight decay of 1e-4 or 1e-2 for the network). Input standardisation uses tuning rows only. The final fit includes the validation months for no arm.
  • Arms. A1' plant at identity with the shared table (stored plant of experiment 243 kept as a benchmark). A2 additive curves on the minimal inputs. A3 additive curves on the full list: one piecewise-linear curve with 8 knots per variable for g and another for h, summed, 3 seeds. A4 neural network on the minimal inputs. A5 neural network on the full list, two hidden layers of 32 units, zero-initialised last layer, 5 seeds. A6 the better of A3 and A5 on validation, with experiment 243's H5 head (11 corrections from the lagged power, ensemble spread and the other H5 inputs, with the adapted power in place of the plant forecast) on the frozen adapter, against the same head on the identity adapter. Controls: shuffled (the extra variables, not the minimal ones, permuted across rows within farm and split) and placebo (the extra variables permuted within farm, split, calendar month, and clear-sky-index band, so other days of the same season and cloud class), both with the arms retrained on the permuted columns; blind (the same network with no plant, on the raw inputs plus the full list); an alternating-update check (the plant's scale unfrozen for two rounds) on the better arm.
  • Rows. Every half-hour of experiment 257's rows has all extra variables (checked), so the row set is unchanged. The observed-weather plant is not re-run, so the 0.973 reference in C8 is experiment 218's, from other rows, and the share closed is indicative.
  • Departures from the brief. The additive curves are trained by gradient descent through the non-linear plant, so the fit is not convex and backfitting is not used. Monotonicity in irradiance is measured after the fit, and passes if under 1% of grid steps fall as irradiance rises. Quantiles are sorted after the fact, with the crossing rate reported, and not built from cumulative non-negative offsets. The minimal inputs add temperature to irradiance and spread. Cloud layers and visibility are not served. The interval level is 99.4%, not 98.75%, because eight contrasts are planned. The extras are held from the store's 3-hourly step. One fit is made on the tuning months (no weekly refits).
  • Report. Quantile score and MAE per arm with intervals, share of the 0.91 to 0.973 gap closed (fraction of sunny-half-hour output fitted by the median), tail calibration through studies.tail_calibration, the crossing rate of the unsorted quantiles per arm, the fitted curves of A3 beside the neural network's factor on the same variable, and the Checks bullets of the ml-experiment skill.
  • Reviews. A Sonnet plan review before any fit, a Sonnet audit of the results and the method (which read the code for leakage; there was no separate code review), and a Sonnet prose review before the merge. No Opus was used.

docs.title: Do the metered solar-farm conclusions survive sorting each forecast's quantiles?
docs.text:
The stored forecasts of seven metered-farm experiments have no crossing quantiles, because their fit scripts already sorted the 11 quantiles, so sorting again changes nothing and no verdict moves. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F. Experiments 224, 229, 243, 246, 248, 257, and 260 each forecast a farm's output 12 to 36 hours ahead as 11 quantiles per half-hour. A pair of quantiles crosses when a lower level is above a higher one. Experiment 268 reported 26,344 crossing rows among its 77,897 generator-forecast rows. Sorting the 11 quantiles of a row never raises its pinball loss (the quantile loss the scores are built from), so crossing would make a stored score too high. We therefore asked whether the seven earlier experiments' scores were too high for the same reason. We counted the crossing rows in every stored prediction, then scored each arm (one forecasting method or ablation) as stored and with the quantiles sorted in each row, using each experiment's own scoring method for the five experiments that have a quantile-score table here (224, 243, 248, 257, and 260). For experiments 229 and 246 we only counted crossing rows.

Sorting changes every score by less than 1e-13%, and no headline contrast, interval, or verdict changes. Every arm of every experiment has 0 crossing rows. The fit and combine scripts of all seven experiments already sort or constrain the quantiles before writing them, so the stored scores are scores of monotone forecasts. The crossing rate before that sort cannot be recovered without refitting, and no refit was run.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• Every arm of every experiment has 0 crossing rows, in all 10 adjacent quantile pairs. Arms and stored rows per experiment: 224 has 11 arms and 458,194 rows; 229 has 10 arms and 582,618 rows (finite rows only); 243 has 11 arms and 3,249,012 rows; 246 has 11 arms and 226,735 rows (finite rows only); 248 has 10 arms and 1,024,410 rows; 257 has 8 arms and 916,388 rows; 260 has 13 arms and 1,707,814 rows. A row is one farm, half-hour, and seed on experiment 224's common daylight half-hours, so the reference arms repeat across the tables.
  • Ties are not crossings. The plant's output is clamped at zero and at the farm's ceiling, so equal neighbouring quantiles occur in up to 38% of rows (H5, the plant plus 11 neural-network offsets, with zero history). XGBoost has ties in 4% to 13% of rows. Ties do not change the pinball loss, and sorting leaves them alone.
  • The stored scores reproduce. The scores below are quantile scores (twice the mean pinball loss over the 11 levels, in points of capacity), scored on each farm's own history at 12 to 36 hour leads in 2025-09 to 2026-08, with 95% intervals: H5 5.475 (4.95 to 5.92); XGBoost 5.490 (4.94 to 5.95); the blend C2 of experiment 260 5.358; the linear quantile regression P2 of experiment 257 5.500; the two-number plant of experiment 224 5.642 (5.15 to 6.07).
  • Every headline contrast matches its page, and the sorted score equals the stored score to 13 decimal places. H5 minus XGBoost is -0.27% (-1.17% to +0.83%) in 243. C2 minus H5 is -2.13% (-2.80% to -1.58%) in 260. H5 with UKV (Met Office high-resolution weather model) columns minus H5 is -1.10% (-2.24% to -0.07%) in 248. The share of the members' gain that the two-number plant keeps is 0.95 (0.84 to 1.02) in 224. P2 minus H5 is +0.45% (-0.36% to +1.69%) in 257, where the original page quotes the same contrast as H5 minus P2, with the interval -1.7% to +0.4%.
  • The H5 against XGBoost comparison (5.48 against 5.49) is unchanged. The scores are 5.475 and 5.490 in both columns, and H5's pinball loss at the 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles is 9.5% and 29.1% lower.
  • Experiment 268's crossing rows come from three generators that are not solar farms. Their stored forecasts hold 9 quantiles (0.05 to 0.95). Experiment 255 padded the missing 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles with nulls, and its cap at each generator's capacity (pl.min_horizontal) turned each null into the capacity, so the 0.01 quantile sat above the 0.05 quantile in all 26,344 rows of those generators. The 51,553 solar-farm rows have none. We rebuilt experiment 268's generator frames to trace this.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• The median and mean forecasts per farm were not recomputed, because no forecast changed. The values on the five original pages stand.
  • The error of the mean forecast beside each quantile-score contrast was not recomputed, for the same reason.
  • No audit trigger fired. Every stored score reproduces, which is the control, and sorting is a deterministic operation that needs no placebo.
  • The page covers only the stored 12 to 36 hour rows of farms A to F. The arms are monotone by construction in two ways: most end in np.sort or torch.sort, the pure neural network uses cumulative offsets, and the seed-averaged arms of experiment 260 average monotone rows.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Constrain the quantiles of every new farm head to be monotone with cumulative non-negative offsets from the median, so that no sort is needed. This applies to future briefs for the metered farms.
  • Fill a missing 0.01 or 0.99 quantile from the 0.05 or 0.95 quantile before capping, instead of padding with nulls, in any scorer that reads the three non-farm generators' forecasts.

docs.title: How long can an arrangement last before a no-lag forecast learns it as normal?
docs.text:
A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal. A load transfer is a spell in which an operator moves part of one substation's demand onto a neighbouring substation by changing how the electricity network is connected. The way the network is normally connected is the normal running arrangement (NRA). We took 10 Primary substations (substations that step 33 kV down to 11 kV) and added a transfer of 25% of each substation's own power to its recorded power, for 7 to 90 days or for good. We refitted the forecast at the start of every month. The forecast, called GAM_ONLY, is a generalised additive model fitted by convex least squares, with no lagged power among its inputs. We compared each forecast with the forecast trained on the unaltered series, which stands for the NRA. The difference between the two forecasts is the bias: a positive bias means the transfer was learned as normal.

The prediction was that a 30-day transfer of 25% of load would bias the forecast by under 0.1 points of effective capacity (1 point is 1% of the substation's capacity). The prediction did not hold, so the verdict is not supported: in the 48 hours after the end the bias is 2.49 points (95% interval 2.04 to 3.05), which is 19% of the transfer. Even a 7-day transfer, the shortest we tested, is learned as 8.5% of its size, so any limit on how long an arrangement can last before it counts as normal is shorter than 7 days and is not located. The next experiment should test durations of 1 to 6 days and a training mask. Two conditions limit the result: the weather inputs are the ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather (the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts' reanalysis and the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's irradiance), not ensemble forecasts, and the forecast has no lagged power. The share-of-load injection is the one of experiment 141, and the forecast settings are the GAM-K settings of experiment 252.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Every figure is in points of effective capacity unless it is a percentage, a mean over 10 substations and 4 onset dates, with a 95% interval from resampling substations and onset dates independently. The mean transfer for the 25% size was 13.3 points. e00274_report.py prints every number in printed_report.txt. A receiver is a substation that gains load and a donor is one that loses load. A BEFORE row is a forecast row dated before the transfer began.
