docs.title: Checks and caveats
docs.text:
• Prediction (point estimates): the plain gap matches 11 against the learned score's 10, and 21 against RO-NC's 20. The differences are +1 (-5 to 7) and +1 (-6 to 7) shifts, so the experiment cannot rank the detectors. The learned score's false alarm rate was 1.29 on odd months and 0.55 on even months, while the gap's was 1.17 and 1.21, so on even months the gap raised about twice the learned score's false alarms.
  • Where the plain gap's false alarms fall (at the learned score's rate, 39 episodes in 32.8 Primary-years of ordinary rows): 5 episodes in D9 rows (2.7 per Primary-year, against 1.2 over all series), 0 in D8 rows, 3 on bank holidays or within a day of a clock change, 8 from November to March, and 23 elsewhere. Holidays, clock changes, D8, and D9 do not hold most of the false alarms. The page cannot say how many of the 23 unattributed episodes are weather error, so the prediction's weather-error clause is undetermined.
  • Other shift sets at the learned score's rate: the plain gap matches 1 of D8's 29 multi-day drops and none of the 17 unlabelled single days with block-shaped demand (the 24-hour mean error on those days stays under 2 noise units, and no detector, carried or gap, matches any of them). A noise unit is 1.4826 times the median absolute value of a score on odd-month ordinary rows. The injected shifts add 1,063 events at the six substations, because one transfer moves power at the donor and at each receiver. The plain gap matches 182 of them (17%): 5% of those lasting up to 2 days (380 events) and 39% of those lasting over 5 days (83 events). The median injected step is 0.87 MW.
  • Neighbour check: 22 of the 35 shifts name two Primaries that are both metered, so the check can apply to those and not to the rest. It confirms an alarm origin when a connected metered neighbour has an opposite-signed gap at least 30% the size and the two sum to at most half the node's gap. The check is applied at each origin, so it removes alarm origins more strictly than a rule that kept a whole episode when any origin was confirmed; the episode-level rule is untested. The threshold had to fall from 3.2 to 2.1 to hold the false alarm rate, which explains the extra false alarms. The check cannot apply to injected shifts, whose receivers are unmetered.
  • Match rule changes the ranking: the learned score's mask reaches back to the step stamp after an alarm that opens about 4 days late. When an alarm may open up to 4 days after the shift ends, the learned score matches 27 and the plain gap 16.
  • Deviations from the plan: a noise unit is the robust scale of each score, not of the half-hourly forecast error; and the lag is measured from the forecast origin, which is 4 hours after the last reading the filter used.
  • Data: K0 has no correction before a series' first reading (series 13 and 7 start late), so the gap is not computed there and those rows count for neither alarms nor exposure.
  • Audit rule: none of the seven triggers in the ml-experiment skill fires on this result. Experiment 309 reads the gap, and the maintainer excluded an Opus audit of this work. The median minus mean forecast and quantile-score contrasts do not apply, because no quantile forecast is scored here.
  • Lab conditions: the records, the generalised additive model, and the filter settings come from experiments 130, 141, and 258, with estimates of past weather and not ECMWF ensemble (ENS) forecasts. The thresholds of every detector were fitted on the same real record.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Experiment 309 tests whether the gap, and the 24-hour mean forecast error, can choose between the two forecasts, scored against observed power and against the normal running arrangement.
  • Post hoc: a detector that combines the 24-hour mean forecast error with the gap could be tried.

docs.title: Can the gap between two forecasts tell NGED which one to use, without knowing the truth?
docs.text: This experiment asks whether NGED, which cannot see which switching arrangement is in force, can choose between two forecasts using only the forecasts and recent power. The forecast without lags (GAM_ONLY, from a generalised additive model) predicts the normal running arrangement (NRA). The forecast with lags (K0, a Kalman filter on recent power readings added to GAM_ONLY) predicts what will flow while an abnormal arrangement lasts. A rule that switches to K0 when a signal says "abnormal" and back to GAM_ONLY otherwise recovered none of the gain that choosing correctly would give, in the injected worlds and in the real record. The real record and the injected worlds use different weather inputs. The real record uses the frozen past-weather forecast of experiment 130 (ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather) through experiment 258's harness, scored against observed power only. The injected worlds use the cached ensemble-weather member forecasts (ENS, the ECMWF ensemble) of experiment 297, scored against both observed power and the true normal arrangement. Experiment 308 defined the gap and the carried detectors RO-NC and LR_b20 (the learned score); the row groups G1 to G5 are ordinary rows, before the alarm, during a shift, 48 hours after, and within 7 days.

docs.title: Does the gap carry more than the residual? (maintainer's question)
docs.text:
The residual (measured power minus GAM_ONLY) flagged more real shifts than the gap, clearly at the learned score's false alarm rate only. K0 is GAM_ONLY plus a filter fitted to recent residuals, so the gap is a filtered copy of the same residual. The gap can therefore add no information that the measured power lacks. The residual matched more shifts than the gap by a clear margin only for the 24-hour window at LR_b20's rate (+9, 4 to 14); the other differences include zero, and the page did not test why the filter loses signal. The differences below come from the stored per-shift flags of experiment 308, with whole shifts resampled; no GAM was refitted. In both rows the thresholds were set on odd months to the false alarm rate of the named detector, so each pair shares an operating point to within one threshold step (the odd-month rates sit within 0.2 per Primary-year of each other).

Experiment 308's "supported" verdict rested on point estimates. Its rule asked the gap to match at least as many shifts as the carried detector at equal false alarm rates (11 against 10, and 21 against 20), with intervals reported beside. The intervals on those differences include zero, so "as many as" is the claim and "more than" is not. The operating points in 308 were equal in that sense, so the 11 of 35 and 20 of 35 figures need no correction.

docs.title: Does the position inside GAM_ONLY's bands beat the noise-unit residual? (maintainer's question)
docs.text:
Scaling the residual by GAM_ONLY's own band at each half-hour matched at least as many real shifts as the plain 24-hour residual, and raised more false alarms on the held-out months. The signal pit24 is the 24-hour mean of the normal score of each half-hour's measured power inside GAM_ONLY's band. The band is GAM_ONLY's expected value plus a residual quantile function per series and hour band, fitted on odd-month ordinary half-hours, so the frozen past-weather GAM was not refitted. The signal ext24 is the 24-hour mean of the absolute normal scores, which ignores the direction of the miss. Thresholds were set on odd months to the false alarm rate of each carried detector, as in the table above. Only the real record was scored.

The prediction holds in its point estimates for pit24 and not for ext24. The prediction named the band-position signal in general; pit24 matches 22 and 26 shifts against 20 and 24, and ext24 matches 17 and 25. The gain of pit24 is small, and the interval at RO-NC's rate includes zero. On the even months pit24 raised 2.3 times the false alarms of the residual at the learned score's rate (2.13 against 0.91 per Primary-year), so the equal odd-month operating points do not carry over to the held-out months. The page did not test why; one possible reason is that the odd-month noise differs from the even-month noise.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
In the injected worlds, the rules chosen on odd months scored like the forecast without lags in the rows near a shift. On even months, against observed power, the threshold-weighted CRPS at the 95th percentile (twCRPS95) in the rows within 7 days of a shift is 0.408 for GAM_ONLY, 0.410 for K0, 0.385 for BAND_HEAD (the quantile head of experiment 297), 0.409 for the rule on the 24-hour residual, 0.408 for the rule on the gap, and 0.405 for an oracle that knows the true state. The oracle that picks the better of the two forecasts on each row scores 0.330. It also gains in ordinary rows (2.11 against 2.60 for K0 in quantile score), where no shift exists, so most of its gain comes from selecting on the realised score and not from knowing the arrangement. Both thresholds chosen on odd months were the strictest on offer (4.5), where the rule rarely leaves GAM_ONLY; at the other two thresholds the residual rule scored 0.407 and 0.408. The recovery of the per-row oracle's gain in the rows within 7 days is -0.5% for the residual rule (-4% to 3%) and 0.0% for the gap rule (-3% to 3%), against the pre-registered 60%.

In ordinary rows, the forecast with lags scores better than the forecast without lags, so falling back to GAM_ONLY scores worse than staying on K0. In injected ordinary rows the quantile score is 2.60 for K0 and 2.96 for GAM_ONLY, and the residual rule scores 2.98. The rule is 0.38 points worse than K0 (0.29 to 0.48). Against GAM_ONLY the rule is 0.02 points worse (0 to 0.06), at the pre-registered limit of 0.02, and the gap rule is level with GAM_ONLY. The pre-registered limit was a harm against the better fixed forecast, which is K0 in ordinary rows, so the rule fails it. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over 11 quantiles, which approximates the CRPS.

In the real record, the forecast without lags had the lower score only in the 72 hours after a shift ends. Pinball loss at the 95th percentile (points of capacity, even months, resampling 26 to 29 shifts and 53 months) is, for GAM_ONLY, K0, the rule on the 24-hour residual, the rule on the gap, and the oracle that knows the state: 2.44, 1.81, 2.82, 1.94, and 1.81 during a shift; 0.83, 1.96, 1.84, 1.96, and 0.83 in the 72 hours after; and 0.86, 0.74, 0.85, 0.81, and 0.86 in ordinary rows. K0 minus GAM_ONLY is +1.13 points after a shift (0.03 to 2.84) and -0.12 points in ordinary rows (-0.17 to -0.06). During a shift the interval of the same contrast includes zero (-1.86 to 1.07), so K0's lead there is a point estimate. The true-state oracle equals K0 during a shift, so a perfect state flag helps only after the shift ends. The rules did not recover that gain: the residual rule scored 1.84 and the gap rule 1.96 after a shift. On the real record the residual rule chose the strictest threshold and the gap rule the loosest, so the two rules differ in how often they switch.

For curtailment cost, always using K0 or BAND_HEAD scored better than any rule. In the injected rows within 7 days at 12 to 36 hour leads, against observed power, the cost at the scaled limit 0.5 is 2,488 for K0, 2,478 for BAND_HEAD, 2,698 for GAM_ONLY, and 2,670 for the residual rule (pounds per scored half-hour at a price of 2,000 pounds per megawatt-hour and a 20-times breach penalty). The residual rule costs 7.3% more than K0 (3.6% to 12%). The cost was scored on the injected worlds only.

Against the true normal arrangement, neither rule gained over the better of the two fixed forecasts. The target NGED wants for scenario studies is the true normal-arrangement series. GAM_ONLY is the arm built for it, and in the rows near a shift K0 scored about the same (twCRPS95 0.340 for both). BAND_HEAD scored 0.311 and the per-row oracle 0.271. The page does not recommend an arm for that target.

docs.title: Checks and deviations
docs.text:
• Median against mean forecast error: the absolute error of the median and of the mean forecast differ by at most 0.03 points for GAM_ONLY and K0 at every substation. BAND_HEAD's differ by up to 0.27 points (D16), 0.15 (D9), and 0.14 (D11), because its median and mean come from different heads.
  • Leave one substation out: with any of the six injected substations removed, the residual rule's recovery in the rows near a shift stays between -0.06 and 0.00, so no one substation drives the result.
  • The planned neighbour-check variant was not run. The plan named a rule with the neighbour check on the real record. The plain rules did not beat the better fixed forecast at the thresholds chosen on odd months, the real record printed only those thresholds, and the check cannot apply in the injected worlds.
  • The band-position signal was scored on the real record only. GAM_ONLY's own bands exist on the injected rows only for 131 non-contiguous runs per world, with no trailing 24 hours, so the injected worlds were not scored for it. The real-record bands are a residual quantile function per series and hour band; they carry no lead-time dependence, because the signal reads half-hours that have already happened.
  • Not run: the persistent-regime descriptive item (D8's engine spell and a permanent step), the BSP cost proxy, the real-record cost, the 24 hours to 10 days ensemble range, and the before-alarm group on the real record. The real record has 26 to 29 even-month shifts per group, so its intervals are wide, and the odd-month threshold choice on 35 shifts is noisy. The plan defined the group after the end as 48 hours; the real record uses 72 hours, because that is how experiment 258 scored it.
  • Definitions that differ between the records. In the injected worlds the oracle that knows the state takes its state from experiment 297's phase label, which uses the target time, so a row whose origin is inside a shift and whose target is after its end counts as after the shift. On the real record the state is read at the origin. The oracle that knows the state is defined for observed power only. The better fixed forecast of each group is picked on the same even-month rows that are then scored, and the bootstrap does not re-pick it. The recovery ratio is ill-conditioned where the fixed forecast and the oracle score almost the same (during a shift in the injected worlds), so the page quotes absolute gains there.
  • The ext24 signal is not centred. The mean of absolute normal scores sits near 0.8 in ordinary conditions, so its threshold tests a level, not a departure from a centre, and the contrast with the residual does not test the idea of an extreme position. The pit24 signal is centred.
  • Thresholds sit at the edge of the grid. Both injected signals chose the strictest threshold (4.5) on odd months, so no looser or tuned threshold was tested. The comparison of the gap with the residual windows (e00309_gap_vs_residual.py) is post hoc and was not in the pre-registered decision rule.
  • Both ENS and past-weather scores are upper bounds for a live service, because past weather is more accurate than a forecast and the injected worlds replay one ensemble run per day.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text: A flag for the end of a shift is a possible next test. In the groups scored here, the forecast without lags had the lower point estimate with an interval excluding zero only in the 72 hours after a shift ends. A detector that opens its alarm at the end of a shift, such as one reading the step back to the old level, could be scored directly against those rows. A selector built from the signals here does not do that.

docs.title: Does the metered solar-farm forecast beat climatology at leads of 1 to 10 days, and which single model family is best?
docs.text:
The assembled forecast still beats climatology at day 10, so it can serve forecasts of solar-farm power from 1 to 10 days ahead; plant-fed XGBoost cannot. National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) meters six solar farms, labelled A to F here. Experiment 300 scored a forecast of each farm's power at leads of 12 to 36 hours. The forecast starts from a physics model of the farm's output (the "plant"), corrects the plant's 11 quantiles with a generalised additive model (GAM) and a mixture-density neural network (MDN), and blends those two with XGBoost. We refitted the same forecast at leads of 12 to 252 hours (day 1 to day 10), in six groups of lead times (day 1, day 2, day 3, days 4 to 5, days 6 to 7, and days 8 to 10). We scored it against climatology (the farm's power for the same month and half-hour of day in earlier history), manual_heuristic (quantiles of 13 earlier observed powers), and the GAM, the MDN, and plant-fed XGBoost. "Own history" means the forecast trains on the farm's earlier months, and "zero history" means it trains on the other five farms only. The quantile score is twice the mean pinball loss over the 11 quantiles, in points of capacity (1 point is 1% of the farm's capacity), and lower is better.

The verdict is partly supported. The blend beat XGBoost in every day band, and removing the farm's own power from earlier days changed the score by less than its interval, as predicted. The blend's improvement in quantile score over climatology did not fall under 5% by days 8 to 10, so that part of the prediction failed: the improvement is 10.1% (98.75% interval -13.8% to -5.6%, own history). The stop rule did not fire.

Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity (lower is better). "Blend vs MDN" is the blend's score change against the MDN alone, and the "MDN vs" columns are the MDN's score change against climatology and manual_heuristic. All intervals are 98.75%, resampling the 12 months of the run.
