Median minus mean forecast per farm (true days 1 to 10) is -3.3 to -4.5 points for the default and -3.0 to -4.1 for every arm, so every arm's median stays 3.0 to 4.1 points below its mean, close to the default's. The mean-forecast squared error and the median absolute error move in the same direction as the quantile score for every arm. No audit trigger fired: the head arms' failed predictions (below) are explained in the tails bullet, no control failed, and no sister experiment has an interval to compare with.
  • Pre-registered predictions.
    • z4 brings the share above q99 under 1.5% (holds, 1.11%) and the 0.99 pinball loss within 0.03 of the default's (fails, 0.153 above), so the joint prediction fails.
    • z2 does most at W1 and W2 and less at W3: fails (by share above q99, W2 is worst at 2.57% and W3 best at 0.04%).
    • z1 lowers the 0.99 pinball loss by under 0.03 (holds, 0.013 against y2) and raises the quantile score by under 0.03 (holds, 0.009).
    • The headline stays within 0.05 of y2's for every arm (holds), and the base-only head reproduces at least 70% of the gain (holds for y2, y2p, z1, z3, and z4; fails for z2).
    • z5 lowers the 0.99 pinball loss by 10% (fails, 0.2%), puts the share above q99 under 1.5% (fails, 1.79%), and is within 0.1 of z4 on the headline (holds, 0.098).
  • Adoption (order z4, z5, z3, z2, z1). No head arm passes condition 1 (every 99.8% interval includes zero), and z2 and z4 also fail condition 2 (0.99 pinball loss harm up to 0.212). z5 passes conditions 1 to 4 (gain 0.147, harm to p01 and p99 at most 0.013, replicate -0.209), The replicate of z5 was added after the main scores were read, because the plan said that the default's replicate forecasts did not exist, and they do. Therefore z5 stays a candidate, and nothing is adopted.
  • Serving. z1 to z4 need what y2 needs: the plant run on each member, then the head. z5 needs the plant, a stored table of offsets by bin, and the default's XGBoost quantiles.
  • Curtailment metric. Not scored: studies.node_curtailment needs a node's export and its generators' forecasts together, and this experiment forecasts the three farms alone.
  • Caveats. Scored at true days 1 to 10 only; three farms and 53 runs give wide intervals. z5's blend weights for the first runs of a month use actuals of the earlier month that were not yet observed at those runs' issue times, a small look-ahead. z5 fits on earlier scored months. Each head was fitted once on the hindcast and never refitted. Whether refitting changes the contrast was not tested.
  • What to try next. (1) Fit the point mass's weight with a likelihood or a classification loss on saturated half-hours, then retest z2. (2) Apply the solar recipe to the head's own quantiles (plant plus head, then band, then blend), a tier 1 step. (3) Repeat z5 with a pre-registered replicate before any adoption.

docs.title: Does replacing the pinned solar capacity with the experiment 269 estimate improve Primary demand research default 3 on sunny daylight half-hours?
Take-home message
docs.text:
Replacing the pinned solar capacity with the capacity estimate of experiment 269 did not lower the score on sunny half-hours, and no group improved by more than 0.011 points. The research forecast of demand at six Primary substations (anonymised as D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16) subtracts the output of unmetered rooftop solar from each substation's demand. The size of that solar (its capacity) is pinned to the values of experiment 45. Experiment 269 found that a table learned from six metered solar farms recovers 0.89 to 0.97 of the output of an injected farm, where the physical fleet shape recovers 0.78 to 0.83.

We asked whether a capacity read that way gives a better forecast. We refitted the first stage of the forecast (a convex demand model with a Kalman filter, from experiment 139) with the pinned capacity swapped for the new estimate, which was refitted each month on earlier rows only.

Scores are quantile scores in points of the substation's effective capacity, smaller is better. On the sunniest third of daylight half-hours (the third of each Primary's daylight half-hours with the highest solar output per unit of capacity), the score rose from 4.371 to 4.418, a change of +0.047 points (95% interval from resampling whole months, -0.029 to +0.135). A positive change means a worse score. The interval includes zero, so the data cannot tell. Verdict: inconclusive. The pre-registered rule asks for an interval wholly below zero, which the score did not reach.

The later stages of Primary demand research default 3 (the neural-network head, the solar summary, and the blend with the manual heuristic) and the 168 to 240 hour range were not rerun. The first stage showed no gain to carry into those stages. A gain after the first stage cannot be ruled out.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms and what was refitted. The experiment changes the solar capacity inside the fitted stage and imports the default's code (a tier 2 change), and adds a plant-response table and a capacity fit per month. Arm A is the first stage with the pin (experiment 45's frozen vintage). Arm B replaces the capacity with the experiment 269 estimate, refitted at each of 27 monthly origins (2024-04 to 2026-06) on rows before the origin. Arm C holds arm B's value at the 2025-07-01 origin for the whole scored year. The stack's own unit solar shape is unchanged.
  • How the estimate is scaled. A fit to the real series reads too little of a solar farm's output. Each fit is therefore divided by the median recovery of five farms injected at that origin into the same Primary's demand, each read with the shape of the other five farms.
  • Row set and range. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, six Primaries, rows outside the hand-filtered events, forecast origin 09:00 UTC, lead 0.5 to 168 hours and 24 to 168 hours. The 168 to 240 hour range needs the experiment 317 chain, which was not rerun, so the result covers 7 of the 10 forecast days that NGED (the distribution network operator) cares about.
  • Headline, sunniest third of daylight half-hours (B minus A, scored year). At 0.5 to 168 hours: +0.047 (-0.029 to +0.135). At 24 to 168 hours: +0.044 (-0.037 to +0.133). Error of the mean forecast on the same rows, 0.5 to 168 hours: +0.120 (-0.002 to +0.277).
  • Absolute scores, sunniest third, 0.5 to 168 hours: A 4.371, B 4.418, C 4.448 (24 to 168 hours: 4.511, 4.555, 4.583). All half-hours: A 2.773, B 2.777, C 2.784. C minus A is +0.077 (-0.012 to +0.158) and C minus B is +0.030 (-0.004 to +0.076).
  • Replicate year (2024-07 to 2025-06), sunniest third, B minus A. At 0.5 to 168 hours +0.040 (-0.004 to +0.084). At 24 to 168 hours +0.044 (+0.004 to +0.085), an interval wholly above zero. Error of the mean forecast +0.106 (+0.006 to +0.187) at 0.5 to 168 hours. Both years point the same way, and the replicate year's 24 to 168 hour interval excludes zero. Arms B and C are identical in the replicate year, because both read the 2025-07-01 origin or an earlier one.
  • The other groups, B minus A at 0.5 to 168 hours: no group other than the sunniest third moved by more than 0.011 points, as the table shows.
Group Change in score 95% interval All half-hours +0.004 -0.006 to +0.012 All daylight +0.001 -0.020 to +0.020 Darkest third of daylight -0.011 -0.025 to +0.006 Night +0.006 -0.001 to +0.015 Winter nights (December to February, after dark) -0.007 -0.010 to 0.000
  • By Primary, sunniest third, B minus A (checks.log): D5 -0.023, D10 +0.155, D11 +0.037, D14 -0.046, D9 -0.063, D16 +0.218. Leaving one Primary out gives +0.013 (without D16) to +0.070 (without D9), so the sign holds. On all half-hours, leaving out D16 gives -0.006 (-0.014 to 0.000) against +0.004 with it, so D16 carries the all-half-hours result.
  • Capacities (figure 3; ratios of the estimate to the pin for the latest season-year). At the start of the scored year (2025-07-01) the estimate is 28% below the pin at D16 (30.9 against 43.2 points of effective capacity), 15% below at D9, and 17% above at D14. By 2026-06 the pin has risen above the estimate at D11 (0.79), D14 (0.83), and D16 (0.74), and the estimate is 8 to 10% below at D5 and D9. D10 matches the pin (1.00). D9's first monthly folds keep the pin, because D9 has too little history for an estimate there (1,513 path weeks took the pin in the fit log, about four folds).

Coverage below q01 is 2.20%, 2.17%, and 2.18%; below q05 6.68%, 6.67%, and 6.73%; below q95 94.74%, 94.68%, and 94.67%; below q99 98.35%, 98.30%, and 98.30%. Pinball loss at q01 is 0.215, 0.216, and 0.216; at q05 0.721, 0.725, and 0.727; at q95 0.720, 0.715, and 0.716; at q99 0.220, 0.220, and 0.220. No tail moves by more than 0.006 points.
  • Reference rows. The first stage alone is not Primary demand research default 3, so it is not placed against the manual heuristic or climatology. The research default's own scores (2.727 at 0.5 to 240 hours, against 3.414 for the manual heuristic and 3.664 for climatology) are in the research default log.
  • Model family. The experiment evaluates one model family and no blend.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Wiring gate. Arm A equals experiment 139's stored pin forecasts at all six Primaries (95,939 to 97,046 rows each, largest gap in q01, q50, and q99 0.0; logs/checks.log).
  • Median minus mean forecast, per Primary and arm: 0.0 points for all three arms.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast: it moves in the same direction as the quantile score on the sunniest third (+0.120) and on winter nights (-0.019).
  • Triggers. None fired. B's point estimate on the sunniest third (+0.047) is just outside the pre-registered band (within 0.03 points either way), but its interval covers the band and the predicted direction (no gain) held. Leaving one Primary out does not flip the sunniest-third sign.

docs.title: Caveats and lab shortcuts
docs.text:
• The plant-response table is not as-of. It is fitted once on the six farms' history to 2026-06-30, and the farms' scale (their 99th percentile of output) uses all daylight half-hours. Only the capacity fit, the pin, and the injection recoveries stop at each origin. The capacity is as-of; the shape it is read against is not.
  • The first stage only. The neural-network head, the solar summary, the blend, and the 168 to 240 hour range need the chain of experiments 155, 160, 164, 317, 319, and 322 refitted from the new forecasts.
  • Unit shape unchanged. The estimate is applied to the stack's physical unit shape, not to the empirical shape it was fitted with.
  • No scale factor. Experiment 139's post hoc factor of 1.15 was not repeated.

docs.title: What to try next
docs.text:
• Apply the experiment 269 estimate with the empirical shape it was fitted with, in the first stage and in the ensemble's solar response.
  • Test a scale factor on the estimate.

docs.title: Can a learned curve of irradiance, with no PV capacity estimate, replace the pinned capacity times the unit solar shape in Primary demand research default 3?
docs.text:
Take-home: dropping the PV capacity estimate is not yet safe. A learned curve of irradiance does no better than the pinned capacity over five of the six Primaries (+0.025 points, interval -0.252 to +0.346). Only D5's interval excludes zero (-0.969), where either the pinned capacity or the unit solar shape is probably wrong. D11 is significantly worse with the curve (+0.223 [+0.100, +0.360]). The useful next step is to check the D5 pin and unit shape. A curve is also a low-effort fallback for a Primary with no trustworthy capacity. Verdict: not supported.

Definitions. PV capacity is the peak output of the solar panels behind a Primary, in points (1 point is 1% of the Primary's effective capacity). The pinned capacity is the capacity taken from the weekly vintages of experiment 45. Irradiance is the shortwave radiation reaching the ground, in W/m2. The Primaries are six NGED primary substations (D5, D10, D11, D14, D16, and D9). The gate is the reproduction check that must pass before any contrast is read. CRPS is the continuous ranked probability score. Recipe R is the fitted recipe that turns the Kalman filter's output into quantiles, and the spread table holds the fitted widths of those quantiles.

We asked whether the forecast of Primary demand can do without an estimate of how much solar generation each Primary has behind it. The current forecast subtracts a solar term from demand: the pinned capacity times a fixed unit solar shape. Experiments 110 and 139 had found that fitting the capacity from the Primary's own power did not help. We replaced the solar term with a curve of irradiance that the fit learns, once with one shape shared by all Primaries (arm B) and once with a shape per Primary (arm C), and compared both with the refitted pinned-capacity forecast (arm A). We scored sunny daylight half-hours, the half-hours where the sun is more than 5 degrees above the horizon and the ensemble-mean shortwave is in the top quarter of the Primary's daylight half-hours. Both curves scored better than arm A on average (arm A 4.321 at 24 to 240 hours, smaller is better; 1 point is 1% of a Primary's effective capacity), but not reliably, and only one Primary, D5, has an interval that excludes zero.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. A: experiment 136's convex fit refitted with the pinned capacity times the temperature-derated unit shape. B: the solar term replaced by one monotone curve of irradiance (eight saturating ramps) with a learned scale per Primary, fitted on each cut's training window. C: B with a curve per Primary. The Kalman filter, offset, recipe R, and spread table are refitted for each arm. The neural-network head, the solar summary, and the heuristic blend are not refitted, because they bake in the old solar term. The experiment therefore compares only the convex stage. Monthly refits on a 24-month window. Reference rows: Primary demand research default 3 as stored, the manual heuristic, and climatology.
  • Row set. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, six Primaries, 798,116 half-hours scored 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30 (origin 09:00 UTC), 90,562 of them sunny daylight. Intervals resample calendar months of the forecast's issue time. The decision rule's 1 - 0.05/2 level gives 97.5% bounds in the results below, and the headline row quotes 95% bounds. The conclusion is the same at 95%: the upper bound at 24 to 240 hours is +0.163 for B and +0.092 for C, both above +0.05.
  • Gate. Arm A reproduces the stored convex stage of the chain of experiment 317 to within 0.000 (three decimals; largest quantile difference 0.000), so the gate passes. Arm A scores 0.118 worse than the stored research default 3 on all rows (2.845 against 2.727; interval +0.063 to +0.180) because the head, summary, and blend are not refitted. The stored default is read from experiments 322, 220, and 251.
  • Absolute scores, sunny daylight, 24 to 240 hours. A 4.321 [3.959, 4.707]; B 4.191 [3.918, 4.509]; C 4.122 [3.871, 4.409]; manual heuristic 4.749; climatology 4.834. All rows, 0.5 to 240 hours: A 2.845, B 2.838, C 2.829, stored default 3 2.727, manual heuristic 3.414, climatology 3.664.
  • Stored default 3 beats every arm. On sunny daylight 0.5 to 240 hours the stored default 3 scores 4.021 against A 4.236, B 4.128, and C 4.058. The contrasts below are taken against arm A, the convex stage, because the stored default includes the head, summary, and blend that were not refitted.
  • Headline, sunny daylight, B minus A (then C minus A). At 0.5 to 240 hours -0.108 [-0.407, +0.183] (-0.178 [-0.472, +0.112]); at 24 to 240 hours -0.131 [-0.446, +0.163] (-0.199 [-0.509, +0.092]). The simplicity case (97.5% upper bound under +0.05) fails for both arms at both ranges (upper bounds +0.215, +0.141, +0.190, +0.121), and the gain case (interval wholly below zero) fails too.
  • Leave-one-Primary-out criterion: failed. The decision rule requires that dropping one Primary at a time does not flip the sign of the headline contrast. Dropping D5 flips B minus A from -0.131 to +0.025 at 24 to 240 hours.
  • Predictions. P1 fails: the point estimates are better than the band's lower edge of -0.10 (B -0.108 and -0.131; C -0.178 and -0.199, nearly twice the lower edge), and the upper bounds exceed +0.05. P2 fails: C minus B is -0.070 [-0.111, -0.037] at 0.5 to 240 hours, so a shared shape is slightly too stiff. P3 holds: cold winter nights, q01 and q99 pinball, and the pooled score move by less than 0.03 (pooled B minus A -0.007 and C minus A -0.016 at 0.5 to 240 hours; cold winter nights -0.003 and -0.005). P4 holds. The one no-harm bound that breaks apart from the sunny row is B on all rows at 0.5 to 240 hours (upper bound +0.022 against 0.02).
  • Where the gain is. Only D5's interval excludes zero: B minus A -0.969 [-1.708, -0.176], C minus A -1.106 [-1.958, -0.174], at 24 to 240 hours. Over the other five Primaries together the contrast is +0.025 [-0.252, +0.346] (B) and -0.031 [-0.280, +0.254] (C). D9 has a point-estimate gain (B -0.329 [-0.883, +0.180]). D11 is significantly worse with the curve (B +0.223 [+0.100, +0.360]).
  • Replicate (even months of 2024-07 to 2025-06, sunny daylight): B minus A -0.108 [-0.261, +0.098] and C minus A -0.147 [-0.349, +0.070] at 0.5 to 240 hours; the same sign.
  • Curtailment metric. Not scored: the experiment forecasts six Primaries' demand with no generators beside them.

Tails, sunny daylight and all rows, lead 24 to 240 hours (coverage is the share of observations at or below the quantile; the target is the quantile's level):

Every arm covers the upper quantiles too little on sunny rows: q95 coverage is 0.929 to 0.938 against 0.95, and q99 coverage is 0.973 to 0.977 against 0.99. On sunny rows B and C move the lower tail the wrong way: the share below q01 rises from 0.019 to 0.030 and 0.028, and the share below q05 from 0.063 to 0.083 and 0.081, although the q05 pinball loss falls.
  • Fitted curves (figure 4, last cut 2026-06-01). At 1000 W/m2 arm B subtracts 64.8 points at D5 against a pinned capacity of 70.2, and 29.6 to 43.9 points at the others against pins of 41.5 to 57.2.
  • Check: median against mean. The median forecast minus the mean forecast is 0.0000 at every Primary for every arm.
  • Check: error of the mean forecast. The error of the mean forecast points the same way as the quantile score (sunny daylight, 24 to 240 hours: B minus A -0.284 [-0.860, +0.294], C minus A -0.417 [-1.005, +0.179]), so the mean-forecast-error trigger (trigger 3) did not fire.
  • Check: audit triggers. The leave-one-Primary-out trigger (trigger 4) fired: leaving D5 out flips the sign of B minus A, from -0.131 to +0.025 at 24 to 240 hours. The failed-predictions trigger (trigger 2) fired because P1 and P2 failed; the audit tested the explanation, a gain confined to D5, with the leave-one-out row. The nesting trigger (trigger 5) did not fire, because B is nested in C and loses to it. Triggers 1, 6, and 7 were not assessed from the printed report.
  • Audit. A Sonnet agent ran the audit. The report is private (data/ml-experiments/briefs/e350_audit_report.md). The audit re-derived the numbers from the stored predictions and found no lookahead. Triage of its findings:
    1. The gain is D5's and comes from the median, not the spread. Recentring A's quantiles on B's median takes A's D5 score from 5.678 to 4.825 (B's is 4.710), and giving B A's median raises B's score to 5.771. This page reports the finding.
    2. The gain varies by month. B minus A runs from +0.49 (March; +0.88 in February on 47 rows) to -0.80 (May), and the pooled figure has nine months with sunny rows, so figure 3 shows it.
    3. The headline interval is the most conservative of the block choices: day blocks give [-0.23, -0.04] and ISO-week blocks [-0.33, +0.04]. This page uses the month blocks that the plan specified.
    4. Under other sunny definitions (top decile -0.246, top tercile -0.095, clear-sky index -0.019) the sign stays and the size varies.
    5. B turns A's small positive bias into -0.6 to -0.9 points at D10 and D16, a new bias.
  • Caveats. The head, summary, and heuristic blend were not refitted, so the stack-level effect is unknown. The D5 forecast error does not isolate a cause: A's D5 bias (actual minus median) is -2.5 at 300 to 430 W/m2 (forecast too high) and +5.9 above 550 W/m2 (forecast too low), so a level error alone would not explain it, and either the pinned capacity or the unit shape is wrong. The experiment covers one scored year, nine months with sunny rows (October has 25 rows and February 47), and six Primaries. The cut schedule is monthly refits, which may matter little for a contrast of this size but was not tested.
  • What to try next. (1) Fix or re-estimate the D5 pin and unit shape and rerun arm A against B and C; if D5's gain vanishes the curve has nothing left to offer there. (2) Use arm B's curve as a sanity check on each Primary's pin, and as a fallback where a Primary has no trustworthy capacity. (3) If a capacity-free solar term is wanted for a stack-level port, refit the head, summary, and blend with it first.

docs.title: Does reading the solar capacity out in the stack's own physical unit shape, monthly and as-of each origin, improve Primary demand research default 3 on sunny daylight half-hours?
Take-home message
docs.text:
Estimating the solar capacity with the clear-sky output curve that the forecast already uses made the forecast slightly worse on sunny half-hours, so mixing two curves is not why experiment 349 did not improve the forecast. The experimental forecast of demand at six Primary substations (anonymised as D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16) subtracts the output of unmetered rooftop solar from each substation's demand. The solar capacity is fixed per substation at the values of experiment 45, which we call the pinned capacity. Experiment 349 estimated the capacity from the average daily output curve of six metered solar farms (experiment 269). It then multiplied that capacity by the forecast's own clear-sky output curve (the physical unit shape), which is a different curve. The write-up of experiment 349 lists this as a shortcut that could explain why it did not improve the forecast.

We asked whether estimating the capacity with the physical unit shape, the curve the forecast later multiplies it by, gives a better forecast. We refitted the first stage of the forecast (a demand model fitted by convex optimisation, with a Kalman filter; see experiment 139) at the start of every month (the forecast origin), using only rows before the origin. Each estimate was divided by a recovery ratio: the median fraction of the output of five metered solar farms that the same fit recovered when that output was added to the demand data on purpose (0.74 to 0.86 at the 2025-07-01 origin).

Arm A is the pinned capacity, arm B is experiment 349's estimate, and arm P is the physical-shape estimate. Scores are quantile scores in points of the substation's effective capacity. Smaller scores are better, so a positive change is worse. On the sunniest third of daylight half-hours (the third of each Primary's daylight half-hours with the highest solar output per unit of capacity), arm P scored 4.436 against 4.371 for arm A, a change of +0.065 (95% interval from resampling whole months, +0.017 to +0.126). The pre-registered rule (an interval wholly above zero) gives refuted. A Sonnet audit reproduced the numbers but found that the interval includes zero when D16 or D10 is left out, so the verdict is softened to not supported: no gain, and probably slightly worse, with D16 and D10 carrying the harm. The first stage only was refitted, so the later stages of the forecast and the 168 to 240 hour range are untested.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
• Arms. This is a tier 2 change: the capacity is read inside the fitted stage, with the default's code imported from the experiment folders that hold it. A is the pinned capacity (experiment 45's frozen vintage). B is experiment 349's arm B, refitted here from its stored as-of table. P is the monthly as-of read-out in the physical unit shape, divided by its own injection recovery (a table of 27 monthly origins, 2024-04 to 2026-06, at five Primaries and 24 at D9). R is P without the divisor. Arm P2, a read-out on the stack's own residual solar signal, was skipped because that signal exists only after the later stages are refitted.
  • Code reused. ml-experiments/00351-primary-demand-capacity-physical-shape-readout/ copies the scripts of experiment 349 and drops the empirical shape from the table builder (e00351_asof_table.py); it reads experiment 349's private as-of table for arm B.
  • Row set and range. fold_a_daily_gap_v1, scored year 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, six Primaries, rows outside the hand-filtered events, origin 09:00 UTC, lead 0.5 to 168 hours and 24 to 168 hours. The 168 to 240 hour range was not rerun, so the result covers 7 of the 10 forecast days that NGED (the distribution network operator) cares about.
  • Schedule. Monthly refits of the first stage on a 24-month window, as in experiment 349. The contrast could depend on the schedule only through the capacity path, which changes monthly.

B minus A: +0.047 (-0.029 to +0.135). At 24 to 168 hours C1 is +0.068 (+0.018 to +0.131), C2 is +0.025 (-0.014 to +0.063), and C3 is +0.035 (-0.099 to +0.160). The research default's own scores (2.727 at 0.5 to 240 hours, against 3.414 for the manual heuristic and 3.664 for climatology) are in the research default log.

docs.title: Checks
docs.text:
• Median minus mean forecast, per Primary and arm: 0.0 points for all four arms.
  • Mean-forecast error beside each contrast: P minus A on the sunniest third is +0.142 (+0.070 to +0.249), the same direction as the quantile score. On cold winter nights the mean-forecast error moves the same way as the quantile score (-0.037, -0.050 to -0.015).
