  • Solar-farm outages are too rare to test an availability state. Five of the six farms have at most 34 outage half-hours in the scored year, and the sixth has 165. An outage half-hour is a daylight half-hour with output under 5% of the physical power model's forecast (exp 301; 6 farms, one year; provisional).
  • About 3.0% of the six farms' scored daylight half-hours read exactly zero. Count the zeros before reading coverage at the 0.01 quantile: in own history, 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below it (exp 321; 6 farms, scored year; provisional).
  • A metered solar farm can climb to its rated output in stages over months. One farm took eight months (network page). The metered farms miss 7.6% to 27.6% of their half-hours, so check coverage before comparing farms (exp 179; 6 farms, one year; provisional).
  • A flat top in a farm's output is not proof of clipping. A pre-registered rule found AC clipping at 2 of 6 farms and a post hoc rule at 4 of 6, and an export cap or panel geometry makes the same shape (exp 179; 6 farms; provisional).
  • The farm series behind a disaggregated Primary can be almost absent. For D8, one farm has one raw reading ever, so "missing" is the baseline (exp 182; D8; provisional).
  • A metered farm's effective_capacity_mw may itself be estimated from output. Power over capacity near 1.0 is therefore not an independent level (exp 179, 183; 6 farms; provisional).

docs.title: Capacity
docs.text:
• Scores are in points of capacity, where capacity is the 99th percentile of the absolute power over the series' whole observed history. One point is 1% of that value. See the glossary (code).

Last checked against experiment 321.

docs.title: Problems and the current best forecast
docs.text: The experiments serve three problems: demand at Primary substations, the output of metered generators, and curtailment with its tails. Each bullet ends with an evidence tag (update rule), and the linked page owns the evidence.

docs.title: What NGED asks for
docs.text:
• The project must give NGED new information about forecasting for its assets, and a negative result counts (requirements) (docs).
  • The requirements page sets the forecast's shape, horizon, update cycle, and day-ahead deadline. Users mostly act on 1 to 10 days ahead, so skill in that band matters most (requirements) (docs).
  • The forecast is used for two decisions: buying flexibility ahead of a high-demand risk, and curtailing generators ahead of a high-export risk. The question users ask is how likely net demand is to cross a limit, so the tails of each forecast matter most (requirements) (docs).

docs.title: Problem 1: demand at Primary substations
docs.text:
• Version 1 covers 32 time series, of which 16 are Primary substations (NGED power telemetry counts the rest by type) (docs).
  • manual_heuristic is the baseline NGED recognises, and beating it is the core deliverable. It forecasts each half-hour from 13 analogues of past weeks (manual heuristic; glossary) (docs).
  • climatology is the second baseline. It forecasts from past power in the same calendar cell and uses no weather (glossary) (docs).
  • On 292 daily runs at the 16 Primaries, the quantile score was 6.182 for manual_heuristic and 7.368 for climatology, in points of capacity. The production-style xgboost_baseline scored 10.536, and the stack scored 5.543 (experiment 87) (exp 87; 16 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • At the 4 bulk and grid supply points the same three baselines scored 14.506, 14.883, and 20.859. The stack scored 13.559 (experiment 87) (exp 87; 4 supply points, one year; provisional).

docs.title: Problem 2: generator output
docs.text:
• The generator experiments score 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms (row sets and scoring) (exp 1; fold A; established).
  • On the 292 runs, the two baselines scored 5.718 and 5.708 at solar farms, and 13.906 and 13.461 at wind farms. The production-style xgboost_baseline scored 8.784 and 17.171 (experiment 87) (exp 87; 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, one year; provisional).
  • climatology is level with manual_heuristic at solar farms, so a solar forecast shows skill only by beating both (experiment 87) (exp 87; 6 solar farms, one year; provisional).

docs.title: Problem 3: curtailment and tails
docs.text:
• Curtailment is the capping of generators beneath a substation when its export would pass a limit. The scoring code plans caps from a forecast of the substation's export, and charges the energy lost to the caps plus a penalty for export that stays over the limit (curtailment cost theme) (docs).
  • The two bulk supply points of the pilot hold too few events to rank forecasts at the headline limit, so no forecast has yet been shown to curtail less (experiment 84) (exp 84; 2 bulk supply points; provisional).
  • Tail calibration is reported beside the headline score in every forecasting experiment (row sets and scoring) (docs).
  • The production-style 0.95 quantile was exceeded in 49% of Primary cases, against 7% for the best guess of experiment 33 (experiment 33) (exp 33; 16 Primaries, 73 runs; provisional).

docs.title: The staged design
docs.text:
• The design under test splits the forecast into stages 0, 1a, and 2 (staged probabilistic forecast; glossary) (docs).
  • N1 is a single-stage model that the best guesses below build on (glossary) (docs).

docs.title: The best-guess recipes
docs.text:
• The best guess of experiment 33 beat the production-style forecast by 4.89 points at Primaries, 3.81 at solar farms, and 6.27 at wind farms. The recipe is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 for Primaries, and an ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 members for farms (experiment 33; glossary) (exp 33; 16 Primaries, 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, one year; provisional).
  • BG2 scored 5.260 at the 16 Primaries and 12.925 at the 4 supply points, against 5.543 and 13.559 for the stack. The Primary gain is 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) (experiment 87) (exp 87; 16 Primaries, 4 supply points, one year; provisional).
  • BG2 for Primaries is a blend of five models with a solar offset at 5 of 16 Primaries (glossary lists the models) (exp 87; 16 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Refitting weekly instead of monthly lowers the Primary score by 0.123 points, and the blend by another 0.086. Removing the blend from BG2 raises the score by 0.091 (exp 87; 16 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • The solar offset lowers the Primary score by 0.114 points on the rows it can touch, which are the daylight rows from April to September at 5 of 16 Primaries. Over all rows the gain is 0.010 (exp 87; 5 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Adding the 14-day correction to the supply-point model raises the score by 0.305 points. BG2 serves supply points without it (exp 87; 4 supply points, one year; provisional).
  • For farms, the ensemble-trained model scored 0.050 (solar) and 0.228 (wind) points worse than the ERA5-trained mixture, and neither interval rules out a loss beyond the accepted margin. No farm recipe is ranked (exp 87; 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, one year; provisional).
  • Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost model worsens the Primary score by 0.36 points once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and the supply-point score by 0.28. Farm scores barely change (experiment 102) (exp 102; 16 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • The physics-based demand model could not be told apart from BG2 at 5 Primaries. The convex model with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K; see the animated explainer) scored 2.800 against 2.780 for BG2 (difference +0.020, interval -0.109 to +0.157, not like for like) (experiment 111) (exp 111; 5 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Adding a correction neural network and a two-number solar summary to the physics-based best guess lowered its score from 2.752 to 2.616 (C1 -0.136, 99% interval -0.253 to -0.047). The two gains add (ratio 0.99) (experiment 220) (exp 220; 5 Primaries, one year; provisional).

docs.title: Superseded positions
docs.text:
• A 14-day error correction on a frozen model is no longer the default for Primary demand. The position of experiments 17, 19, and 21 is superseded by weekly refitting without the correction (experiments 34 and 48) (retraining theme) (exp 34, 48; Primary demand; provisional).
  • "Keep ERA5 for stage 1a until a CAMS arm has a bias-corrected ensemble" is superseded. Experiment 14 paired a CAMS-trained stage 1a with a stage 0 correction, and scored 0.067 points better than raw ensemble input (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039); its verdict is inconclusive because the daylight bias check failed in single months (experiment 14) (exp 14; 16 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • "Train demand stage 1a from 2023-09" is superseded. Each Primary now starts at its first usable date (NGED power telemetry), and whether old years help is unsettled (long history and drift theme) (exp 103, 104, 106, 107; 16 Primaries for start dates, 5 for history; provisional).
  • "ERA5-trained" in experiments 1, 3, 9, and 22 assumes ERA5 is the only estimate of past weather. Name the weather source at lag times in every write-up (weather inputs) (docs).

docs.title: What production does today
docs.text:
• No numbered model release exists, so the live service has no adopted experiment winner (model releases) (docs).
  • The production-style forecast loses to manual_heuristic at Primaries. In experiment 13 its mean absolute error of the median was 1.69 points of capacity higher (99% interval +0.98 to +2.59) (experiment 13) (exp 13; 16 Primaries, 73 runs; provisional).
  • The origin of the stored production-style table is unconfirmed, so its scores may not match the deployed forecast (glossary) (exp 87; stored table; provisional).

docs.title: Which results are provisional
docs.text:
• Every score above rests on one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026), and several settings were chosen on that year. The gains are probably optimistic (production reference and best guess) (docs).
  • Scores on different row sets, quantile levels, or series counts are not comparable. The 16 Primary scores near 5 and the 5-Primary scores near 2.7 come from different rows (row sets and scoring) (docs).

Last checked against experiment 225.

docs.title: Row sets and scoring
docs.text: Two scores are comparable only when they cover the same rows, the same series, and the same quantile levels. This page lists the named row sets, the score and its intervals, the tail and curtailment reporting that every forecasting experiment carries, and the retraining defaults. The procedure is in the ml-experiment skill, and terms are in the glossary.

docs.title: Series sets
docs.text:
• The fold-A demand set has 22 demand-side series (D1 to D22): 16 Primaries, 4 BSPs or GSPs, and a battery and a biofuel generator (glossary) (exp 3; fold A; established).
  • The generator experiments score 9 series (6 solar farms and 3 wind farms) (exp 1; fold A; established).
  • The differentiable-physics (DP) series uses five long-history MW Primaries as its decision set (NGED power telemetry) (exp 103; 5 Primaries; established).

docs.title: Row sets
docs.text:
• A row set is a named set of forecast origins, series, and valid times, and experiment_store.read_predictions raises when a prediction set covers a different row set. State the row_set_id in the plan, and read the benchmark from the same row set (code).
  • No experiment scores a valid time on or after 2026-07-01. The ml-experiment skill owns the rule and the reason (code).
row_set_id Rows Defined in fold_a_tuesdays_v1 53 Tuesday ENS runs and the 9 generator series; every case of the first day sits on a Tuesday or Wednesday, so the set does not suit demand Experiments 1 and 2 fold_a_every5d_v1 Every fifth day at 00:00 UTC from 2025-07-01 (73 runs); each lead band has 14% of its cases on each weekday Experiment 3 fold_a_daily_gap_v1 The 292 daily 00:00 UTC runs from 2025-07-01 to 2026-06-30 that fold_a_every5d_v1 does not hold Experiment 48 control_fold_b_daily_v1 274 runs, 2023-07-01 to 2024-03-31, 9 km grid Experiment 81 era5_val_* ERA5-based validation years (for example era5_val_3folds_2023_07_to_2026_06_v1) Experiments 6 and 11 dp_mw_v1 508,341 half-hours at the MW decision series, after the start cuts, the fixed lockdown window, and the switching mask Experiment 103 dp_mva_dark_v1 352,841 dark half-hours at the MVA-only Primaries Experiment 103 dp_christmas_daily_v1, age1_daily_2025_07_to_2026_06_v1 Christmas-period origins; the old-year training check Experiments 173 and 93
  • Read the defining experiment before reusing a row set (code).
  • The DP series uses season-years from July to June. Tuning is 2023-24, the replicate year is 2024-25, and the scored year is 2025-26 (FIRST_SEASON_MONTH in studies.dp_calendar; exp 109; DP series; established).
  • Count eligible long-history sites at each tuning year's first day. Five Primaries qualify at 2024-07-01 (exp 103; 5 Primaries; established).
  • Choose a row set that covers every weekday, and give each experiment a climatology row (exp 3; fold A; provisional).

docs.title: The score and its intervals
docs.text:
• The score, skill, baselines, capacity, and interval level are defined in the glossary. See quantile score, skill, capacity, interval-level convention, and rolling refit. The procedure is in the ml-experiment skill (code).
  • Experiments 33, 34, and 48 use 9 quantile levels (0.05 to 0.95). Experiment 87 and later use 11 levels (those plus 0.01 and 0.99). Scores with different levels cannot be compared (exp 33, 48, 87; all experiments; established).
  • The sample resolves gains of roughly 0.3 points of capacity or more, on 16 Primaries, 9 generator series, and one validation year (experiments README) (exp 3; 16 Primaries, 9 generators, one year; provisional).
  • Half-hours within a day, and members within a run, are strongly correlated, so a row bootstrap understates the interval (code: studies.bootstrap resamples whole months).

docs.title: Tails and curtailment
docs.text:
• Every forecasting experiment reports tail calibration beside the headline score. The tail table gives coverage and pinball loss at 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99, through studies.tail_calibration (code).
  • Write q01 to q99, actual, lead_hours, and time_series_id in the predictions, so the tail and curtailment metrics can score them (code).
  • The curtailment metric is studies.node_curtailment (node plus its generators). The headline limit is a fraction f of the node's maximum observed export before the scored year, with f = 0.9 by default and 0.75 and 0.5 as sweeps. The real published thermal limit appears only as a reference mark and in the event census, because NGED curtails so that one more fault still leaves headroom. Metric details: cost-savings metrics (code).
  • Report the manual-heuristic baseline arm (capacity_forecast) as the maintainer's unconfirmed understanding of NGED's practice. Experiment 84 is the pattern to copy (exp 84; 2 bulk supply points; provisional).
  • Headline f = 0.5, instead of the default 0.9, when f = 0.9 gives fewer than 20 event half-hours. At the Boston and Skegness bulk supply points, experiment 255 found 2 event half-hours at f = 0.9 and 5 at f = 0.75, so it headlined f = 0.5, which gives 72. Experiment 277 also headlines the 0.5 limit (exp 255, 277; 2 bulk supply points, 6 Primaries; provisional).
  • Read the curtailment cost as a ranking, not as money saved. BG2 costs GBP 7.35 million more than the GAM stack on the six Primaries at the 0.5 limit, and the windows around the seven logged load transfers hold too few half-hours to separate the two (exp 277; 6 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Pair a 00 UTC farm forecast with a 09 UTC node forecast only for valid times before 12 UTC the next day. Later valid times need a run made after the node forecast (exp 255; 2 bulk supply points; provisional).
  • The scored lead band for curtailment is 12 to 36 hours, because scoring needs a stored forecast in that window (curtailment theme; exp 84; curtailment; provisional).
  • NGED's horizon is 1 to 10 days, so a result scored only at short leads carries that caveat. The assembled solar-farm forecast beats climatology at every lead up to 10 days, by 39% at day 1 and 10% at days 8 to 10 (exp 310; 6 farms; provisional).

docs.title: Retraining defaults in R&D
docs.text:
• Do not use quarterly refits, three refits a year, or warm-start boosting as a proxy for monthly retraining (exp 34, 85; XGBoost refit cadence, Primary demand; established).
  • Screen a demand-feature contrast with monthly refits on a rolling 12-month window, and judge cadence, absolute scores, and tail scores with weekly refits. The rolling refit glossary entry gives the settings (exp 34, 48, 81; Primary demand; established).
  • Keep the convex demand model's monthly refits (0.4 s per substation), and give the small neural network that corrects the median no retraining schedule. Quarterly refits of the convex model scored 0.010 points worse than monthly refits (not shown to be acceptable), weekly refits gained nothing, and retraining the neural network quarterly or monthly scored no better than training it once before the scored year (exp 278; 6 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Say in each write-up which schedule was used and whether the contrast could depend on it (exp 34, 85; refit schedules; established).

docs.title: How to score and gate an experiment
docs.text:
• Run a known-answer gate before reading any contrast. Inject a known step or shift into real residuals, or use a fake-ensemble gate, so that a null cannot be a wiring fault. Experiments 128, 142, and 172 narrowly missed or failed their gates, so their contrasts are inconclusive, not refuted (exp 111, 128, 142, 172, 175; DP series; established).
  • State the row definition and the lead range before any score. A "sunny" gap was 0.05 MW over six substations, but 63% of it came from D5, and it shrank to 0.015 MW under a different definition of sunny (exp 178; 6 substations; provisional).
  • Use month-block intervals, and report D5 separately where one substation dominates (exp 111, 178, 180; DP Primaries; provisional).
  • Judge calibration where the loss sits: cold nights and daylight bands, not the all-row average. Cold-night q95 coverage was 0.846 under experiment 160's smooth spread table and 0.896 with widening of the upper quantiles only, while ensemble spread added nothing over all rows (exp 160, 164, 169; DP Primaries; provisional).
  • Score a new model component on top of the family's research default, not on a partial stack. The drift term improved the score by 0.40 on the bare GAM-K and worsened arm D by 0.03 once the filter, the winter night offset, and recipe R were in (exp 167, 170; DP Primaries; provisional). The research default rule names the default and says when a win is adopted.
  • Gains do not always remove the same error: the correction network and the two-number solar summary added on arm A. Together they scored 0.136 below arm A, 99% of the sum of their single gains of 0.099 and 0.038 (exp 220; 5 Primaries, one year; provisional).
  • Quote a neural network's score per seed, or say the seeds were averaged. Averaging the quantiles of the three seeds of the correction network scored 0.123 below arm D at six substations, against 0.104 for the mean of the single-seed scores (exp 201, 220; 6 substations, one year; provisional).

Last checked against experiment 321.

docs.title: Substation information fields
docs.text: Four sources describe a substation: the metadata table, NGED's hierarchy files, the effective-capacity table, and the estimates of solar capacity that experiments have built. This page lists what each source holds, where it sits, and which fields have misled an experiment. The power readings themselves are on the NGED power telemetry page, and the paths are on the disk page.

docs.title: The metadata table
docs.text:
• data/NGED/metadata.parquet holds one row per time series, under the TimeSeriesMetadata contract. The field descriptions in packages/contracts/src/contracts/power_schemas.py own the meaning of each column (code).
  • The trial area has 33 rows: 16 Primaries, 2 BSPs, 2 GSPs, and 13 customer connections. Of the 13 connections, 7 are typed PV, 3 Wind, and 1 each BESS, Biofuel, and Other (Generation) (disk).
  • Only the 16 Primaries carry an area polygon (area_wkt), and every customer row has a null polygon (disk).
  • information is a free-text note, filled for 5 of the 33 rows. The notes are a snapshot from July 2026, because the earlier raw files carry no value, so a note cannot say when a fault began (exp 182; 33 rows; provisional).

docs.title: The hierarchy files
docs.text:
• Four NGED files and a README sit in data/NGED/substation_hierarchy_2026-10-15/. They are Substations.csv, Primary Substation Interconnections.csv, Monitor Direction.csv, and Peak Loads.xlsx. They are private (disk).
  • Substations.csv gives each substation's BSP and GSP. The trial area has two GSPs, each with one BSP (disk).
  • Primary Substation Interconnections.csv lists pairs of Primaries that can be connected. Every trial-area Primary has at least one pair, so the topology looks complete (data sources; docs).
  • Monitor Direction.csv gives each series' meter type and flow direction. One solar farm's substation number differs from its metadata row, and the other sources agree with the metadata (docs).
  • Peak Loads.xlsx disagrees with the telemetry at several Primaries, so experiments take the 99th percentile of observed power as the capacity of a series instead (docs).
  • The Primaries beneath a BSP do not sum to the BSP's reading. Primaries that report only apparent power, and the generators and unmetered load beneath the BSP, stop the sum from closing. Adding every child Primary to a bottom-up sum did not improve the BSP forecast (exp 161, 204; 2 BSPs, one scored year; provisional).

docs.title: The effective-capacity table
docs.text:
• data/effective_capacity/ holds one value per series: the 99th percentile of the absolute power over the series' whole observed history, in MW. It is not a nameplate, firm, or connection rating (code).
  • Scores in points of capacity divide by this value. See the glossary (code).
  • The value is built from the series' own output, so a farm's power divided by it near 1.0 is not an independent level (exp 179, 183; 6 farms; provisional).

docs.title: Estimates of solar capacity behind a Primary
docs.text:
• No source tells us the solar capacity behind a Primary, so experiments estimate it from the Primary's power. The estimates are AC capacity in MW, taken as the 99th percentile of the solar output over daylight half-hours (exp 129; 5 Primaries; provisional).
  • Experiment 45 built weekly capacity "vintages", one block per origin Monday, and the frozen variant uses data before the origin only. A cut earlier than a Primary's first vintage receives a later vintage's level, which is hindsight. The rule is in the studies.dp_pinned_capacity docstring (code).
  • The latest week of a real-time vintage has 3.6 times the path error of the same week in the final fit. The pinned-capacity code therefore holds the median of the last 13 weeks (exp 45; 8 Primaries with injected paths; provisional).
  • Experiment 129 gives one capacity per season-year at D5, D10, D11, D14, and D16, with a range. For 2025/26 the estimate is 3.3 to 4.5 MW per Primary at the five tested, and the range is a spread over test scenarios, not a calibrated interval (exp 129; 5 Primaries; provisional).
  • Reading the capacity from the Primary's own power did not improve the forecast. An as-of capacity scored 0.110 points of capacity worse than the pinned vintage on the sunniest third of daylight half-hours (exp 139; 5 Primaries, one scored year; provisional).
  • A curve of irradiance with no capacity estimate matched the pinned capacity at five of six Primaries and beat it at D5. B minus A on sunny daylight half-hours was +0.025 [-0.252, +0.346] over the five and -0.969 [-1.708, -0.176] at D5, so the D5 pin is a suspect (exp 350; 6 Primaries, one scored year; provisional).
  • A monthly capacity path recovered less of an injected farm than a yearly one, 0.67 to 0.78 against 0.75 to 0.87 (exp 157; 6 Primaries, 5 injected farms; provisional).
  • Refreshing the capacity table once per season-year lowered the error by 0.018 points of capacity, and a weekly refresh made no distinguishable difference (exp 78; the fold A row set; small gain; provisional).
  • The one dated list of installations we hold, the Feed-in Tariff register, ends on 2021-03-24. No capacity step after that date can be matched to an installation (exp 215; 6 Primaries; provisional).
  • The published estimates are on the embedded solar capacity study (docs).

Last checked against experiment 218.

docs.title: Weather inputs by product
docs.text: Each weather product reaches the forecast at a different time, and an experiment must name which product feeds each column at forecast time and which feeds it at training time. The two are usually different products. This page is a digest: it holds the table of what exists when, and the traps that cost experiments a re-run. The long accounts are the weather products survey, the data-sources page, the NWP variable conventions, and the ECMWF ENS known issues.

docs.title: Availability at forecast time
docs.text:
Product What it is Delay before use Exists at forecast time? Training rule ECMWF ENS (51 members) Ensemble forecast, stored by delta_store.nwp A run is usable 9 hours after its init_time (NWP_PUBLICATION_DELAY_HOURS) Yes: the production input Train on ENS history, which starts 2024-04-01 on disk ERA5 ECMWF reanalysis, an estimate of past weather About 5 days through the Climate Data Store No: a ceiling at lag times Version-1 plan: the training product for every variable except irradiance CAMS solar radiation Satellite-derived irradiance, point time-series API 1 day: a request that names today is rejected No: nothing about the day being forecast The planned training product for irradiance UKV (Met Office) 2 km deterministic UK weather model Three variants exist; see below Only the live feed Train on the product that will serve; never train on the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA) archive and serve the live feed GEFS, ICON-EU, IFS, AIFS-ENS, WeatherNext 3 Further forecast products Differs by product Studies only Not in production; see the weather theme
  • A weather product that is "as accurate as ERA5" is a ceiling for demand, not a forecast. ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the Primary demand quantile score by 0.10 points (exp 22; Primary demand, one validation year; provisional).
  • Name the weather source used at lag times in every write-up, and say whether it exists at forecast time (data-processing page; exp 33, 37; ERA5 as the lag-time source; established).

docs.title: Training product: the rule
docs.text:
• Train each XGBoost model on the history of the weather product that will serve it. The arms are ENS-trained, ENS plus the other product as columns, and the other product alone. An ERA5-trained XGBoost model is only a reference (weather theme; exp 22; XGBoost models on Primary demand; provisional).
  • Pair a CAMS-trained XGBoost model with a stage 0 quantile mapping of ENS shortwave. The pair scored 0.102 points better than the ERA5-trained arm for Primary demand, against 0.035 without the mapping (exp 14; Primary demand; provisional, and it supersedes the advice of exp 9 to keep ERA5).
  • Calibrate ENS temperature and irradiance before they drive a model trained on past weather. Shifts of up to about 2 K and 20% were needed at five Primaries (exp 111; 5 Primaries; provisional).
  • "Better weather adds little" was measured only for an XGBoost model trained on ENS. Do not read it as a result for an ERA5-trained XGBoost model (weather theme; exp 22; ENS-trained XGBoost; provisional).
  • Training on ERA5 lowered the solar and wind farm error up to day 6, but for demand a long history did not carry over (weather theme; exp 1, 3; 9 generator series, 22 demand series; provisional).

docs.title: ECMWF ENS
docs.text:
• The step grid and the publication delay are owned by the architecture pages. See the step grid and the ECMWF ENS known issues (code).
  • The ENS archive on disk starts at 2024-04-01. Source Cooperative stages about 3 further years as raw GRIB1 (complete dates 2021-03-21 to 2024-03-31), and a pilot decoded them bit-exact. See the training-history page for whether the full fetch has run (disk; docs).
  • Instantaneous and period-ending variables differ. See the NWP variable conventions (code).
  • Drop an ensemble member that has a missing weather value, and refuse a run whose control member is incomplete. studies.dp_ens_weather does both (code; exp 111 dropped one member of one run).
  • Repeated ENS runs repeat each valid time about 15 times. An ENS-trained model with calendar columns can memorise the calendar position, so include a control without them and group inner splits by valid time (exp 1, 3; ENS-trained XGBoost; provisional).

docs.title: ERA5
docs.text:
• ERA5 arrives about 5 days late through the Climate Data Store. A faster public Zarr copy (ARCO-ERA5) carries ERA5T at about a week's lag (data-sources page) (docs).
  • The half-hourly file's :30 values are interpolated. Each is the mean of the two neighbouring hourly values and contains the next hour's reading (exp 104; ERA5 half-hourly file; provisional).
  • ERA5T hours from the last few months are preliminary. See the five traps (docs).
  • ERA5 is one of several estimates of past weather, and it describes past sunshine and wind worse than several current products. CAMS beat ERA5 by 3.7 to 4.1 points of capacity on past sunshine at the solar study's five headline row sets, an exploratory comparison (training-history page; solar study, 5 row sets; provisional).

docs.title: CAMS
docs.text:
• Use the point time-series API, not the gridded product. The gridded product lags years behind (data-sources page) (docs).
  • The latency is 1 day. A forecast job at 09:00 UTC gets nothing about the day it forecasts, so no intraday correction rests on CAMS (docs).
  • Values are accumulated irradiation in Wh/m² and each is stamped at the end of its step. Set time_reference to universal_time (docs).
  • Snapshot each fetch. CAMS recomputes a request against the latest software, so the same timestamp can return a different value later (docs).

docs.title: UKV
docs.text:
• Three UKV variants are different products. The CEDA archive, Open-Meteo's archive, and the live feed differ in lead, irradiance, temperature, and units (data-sources page) (docs).
  • Open-Meteo's UKV archive is the T+0 analysis. It holds no forecast at any lead, so it compares with a reanalysis and does not measure forecast skill (docs).
  • The CEDA archive has no 100 m wind, lacks four hourly steps, and is licensed for non-commercial use. UKV was upgraded on 2026-01-21 (exp 54, 57; CEDA archive; provisional).
  • UKV shortwave is instantaneous, whereas ENS and CAMS are means labelled at the period end. Check the hour-of-day peak of every source (exp 53; UKV, ENS, CAMS; provisional).

docs.title: Findings on the weather inputs of generator forecasts
docs.text:
• A UKV forecast adds 1.1% to 1.8% to the solar-farm score. Experiment 229 found 1.8%, and experiment 248 found 1.1% for the neural head and 1.4% for XGBoost. These gains are upper limits, because they use the research archive and the live UKV feed differs. ICON-D2 adds 1.0% in a blend at 12 to 29 hours only, and experiment 246 advises against adding it (exp 229, 246, 248; 6 farms, 10 months; provisional).
  • The ECMWF ensemble's wind speeds are about 1.1 m/s too slow, which gives the low median. Multiplying every member's wind speed by a factor fitted on the 14 months before the scored year closed about 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle, which is the same physics core fed ERA5 wind as if it were the forecast. A lookup table of power offsets by lead day helped more than mapping the members to ERA5 (exp 261, 285, 307; 3 wind farms; provisional).
  • The 51 ensemble members give better wind tails than their mean. Pooling the AIFS ensemble (ECMWF's machine-learned ensemble) lowers the wind score at days 3 to 6 by about 5% and does not improve the high-power tail (exp 242, 262; 3 wind farms; provisional).
  • Extra ECMWF ensemble variables and the cells around a farm add under 0.4% for solar farms. The variables were longwave radiation, humidity, precipitation, pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height; the neighbouring cells improved the score by 0.36% (exp 272, 292; 6 farms; provisional).

docs.title: Other products
docs.text:
• GEFS did not improve the sunshine anomaly, and its raw anomaly was about 15% too large (exp 50; sunshine anomaly; provisional).
  • ICON-EU and IFS winds scored worse than the best guess when fed alone, as raw winds with no bias correction, to an ERA5-trained wind model: 2.5 and 1.3 points worse at days 1 and 2 (exp 52; 3 wind farms; provisional).
  • CERRA runs about 3 months behind real time. It is deprioritised (data-sources page) (docs).

docs.title: Blending experiments
docs.text:
• Pass a shuffled-product placebo through every step, and give a guard arm the variant it guards (weather theme; exp 52, 54; blending arms; provisional).
  • Feed the run the service would have. Experiment 53 assumed a 3-hour UKV delivery time that no experiment has measured (exp 53; UKV; provisional).

Last checked against experiment 321.

docs.title: What is on disk
docs.text: Everything an experiment reads lives under one data/ folder, which every git worktree shares. This page lists each folder, who writes it, and how to read it. Nothing under data/ is committed. The folder is private: the NGED hierarchy files and the experiments' predictions must not leave the machine.

docs.title: One shared folder
docs.text:
• studies.sources.REPO_DATA_DIR points at the main checkout's data/ from any worktree. Set the DATA_PATH_INTERNAL environment variable to override it. A remote URI is not supported in these scripts (disk).
  • Only one agent may re-run a published study script at a time. All worktrees share the folder, so a second agent's re-run overwrites the first agent's evidence (disk).
  • Name the path through the constants in studies.sources: STUDIES_DATA_DIR, ML_EXPERIMENTS_DATA_DIR, DOWNLOADS_DIR, and the four download folders below (disk).

docs.title: Production outputs
docs.text:
These are written by the Dagster application, not by experiments.

Folder Holds How to read data/NGED/power_time_series.delta Raw power telemetry, appended from NGED's S3 bucket See NGED power telemetry data/NGED/cleaned_power_time_series.delta The raw rows plus a drop_reason column studies.power.scan_power data/NGED/metadata.parquet The TimeSeriesMetadata table pl.read_parquet data/NGED/list_of_downloaded_files.parquet Which NGED files the ingest has downloaded Ingest bookkeeping data/NWP/ The ECMWF ENS Delta table, from 2024-04-01 delta_store.nwp; see weather inputs data/h3_grid_weights.parquet Fractional H3 cell overlap with the Great Britain boundary Spatial NWP aggregation data/effective_capacity/ The effective capacity per series (99th percentile of absolute power) EffectiveCapacity contract data/eligible_time_series/ Which series are eligible per cross-validation fold Delta, partitioned by fold_id data/power_forecasts/, data/forecast_metrics/ Stored cross-validation forecasts and metrics for manual_heuristic, climatology, and xgboost_baseline Delta, partitioned by experiment_name data/production_model/ The promoted production model BaseForecaster.load
  • The hierarchy files sit in data/NGED/substation_hierarchy_2026-10-15/. The folder holds Substations.csv, Primary Substation Interconnections.csv, Monitor Direction.csv, Peak Loads.xlsx, Switching Logs.xlsx, and a README.md. They are private. The folder's README says the switching logs and peak loads were not examined when it was written (disk).

docs.title: Studies
docs.text:
data/studies/ holds the one-off studies' downloads and built frames, in four download folders under data/studies/downloads/.

Folder Holds NWP/ ECMWF AIFS and AIFS-ENS, IFS single runs, GEFS, GFS, UKV from the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA) and from AWS, WeatherNext 3, Open-Meteo previous runs and ensemble means reanalysis/ CAMS, CAMS aerosol, CERRA, ERA5 (and a separate ERA5 wind folder), ICON-DREAM-EU, NORA3 observations/ MIDAS Open weather stations, NGED active network management (ANM) curtailment, SARAH-3 satellite irradiance market/ About 30 folders of Elexon, NESO, Octopus Agile, carbon-intensity, and PV_Live data
  • Check data/studies/downloads/ before fetching a product again. A re-fetch or an egress that costs over £30 needs the maintainer's approval first (disk).
  • Studies write their built frames under data/studies/<study>/, and private tables under data/studies/_private/. Neither goes to git (disk).

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
• Each experiment writes to data/ml-experiments/<id>-<slug>/, created by experiment_store.reserve_experiment. About 320 ids exist (disk).
  • Predictions live at predictions/<name>/ inside that folder, as predictions.parquet and a manifest.json, written by experiment_store.write_predictions and read by experiment_store.read_predictions. The reader raises when the row set differs (disk).
  • Other subfolders vary by experiment (work/, logs/, briefs/, tables). The DP data look of experiment 103 stores rows.parquet, sites.parquet, series_table.parquet, recommended_cut_dates.csv, and decisions.json there (disk).
  • data/ml-experiments/briefs/ holds the manager's private briefs and is not part of any experiment (disk).

docs.title: Disk space
docs.text:
• data/ sits on the second SSD: the main checkout's data/ is a symbolic link to /mnt/data/nged-substation-forecast/data (disk)

Last checked against experiment 321.

docs.title: Evaluation protocol for Primary demand, version 1
docs.text:
This page fixes how every experiment on Primary substation demand is scored, so that results from different experiments can be compared. An experiment records protocol: demand-v1 in its front matter. A change to any metric, fold, series list, slice, interval, or tolerance on this page makes a new version. The superseded text moves to evaluation-protocol-archive/ as demand-v1.md, and the table of versions below gains a row. The protocols for solar and wind have their own version numbers, so a change here does not move theirs. The research default rule defines the research default and the log of its versions. This page defines how a change to it is scored and when the change is adopted.

Version Date Change demand-v1 2026-10-28 First version

docs.title: What is scored
docs.text:
The series are the 16 Primaries, in three groups that are always reported separately. The three groups answer different questions, so no headline pools them.

Group Primaries What the group tests Signed-MW D5, D9, D10, D11, D14, D16 The demand model, because the meter records the sign of the flow MVA-only D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, D22 The demand model plus the effect of hidden reverse flow, because the meter records apparent power with no sign Short-history D15, D18 Report-only: no adoption rests on this group. No experiment we found fitted the GAM stack at D15

D8 is a labelled exception. D8 has no tuning month and borrows the second-stage spread of six donor Primaries (D2, D3, D4, D19, D21, and D22). D8 is scored in two labelled arms: one with donor spread, and one with own-residual bands fitted on earlier folds. The own-residual arm is the D8 row in the per-Primary table, because the donor-spread arm is known to be the weaker one and would make D8 the worst Primary for a reason that is already understood. Donor spread is fitted before D8 is scored, so D8 is fitted last.

Every number for the MVA-only group carries the label "reactive power assumed zero". The rule that picks the fit fails at a power factor of 0.97, and the reactive power of the real MVA-only meters is unknown.

The forecasts compared are the forecast under test, the current research default, and three fixed references. The references are BG2 (the XGBoost-based production-style forecast), manual_heuristic, and climatology. The current research default and each reference are regenerated on the folds and Primaries of this protocol, under new stored-forecast names, because the existing stored forecasts cover six Primaries on another row set and are never overwritten. Each reference is never retuned. Earlier scores of the references, which stop at 168 hours and use other row sets, are not comparable with scores under this protocol.

The lead range is 0.5 to 240 hours, and every experiment scores all of it. NGED's horizon is 1 to 10 days. Days 11 to 14 are reported only for the arms that have forecasts at those leads, and a table lists which arms are covered.

The first run under this protocol produces the forecasts for 168 to 240 hours that the references lack. The stored demand forecasts stop at 168 hours, so BG2 has never been scored past 168 hours, and BG2, the GAM stack, manual_heuristic, and climatology need new runs at those leads. The ML MANAGER schedules this run. Until it has finished, no experiment scores the 168 to 240 hour leads, and the days 8 to 10 and 11 to 14 slices are empty.

docs.title: The three fixed benchmarks
docs.text:
Each family keeps three benchmarks whose recipes never change: manual_heuristic, climatology, and one frozen XGBoost-based reference. The rows grow as months arrive, and the benchmarks are extended with the same recipe and never retuned. Every change page reports the research default's absolute score against the three benchmarks, with intervals, because a chain of small contrasts can hide a drift in absolute skill. Diagnostic pages need not report them.

For Primary demand the frozen reference is BG2. BG2 is the stored arm p_s6_bg2 of experiment 87. BG2 is a quantile blend of five forecasts, with an explicit solar offset at the 5 of 16 Primaries that have a clean solar capacity estimate. The five forecasts are a weekly-refitted XGBoost model, a monthly-refitted XGBoost model, an analogue model (the experiment 87 page does not state its type), an XGBoost model pooled by substation type, and the frozen stack of experiment 48. For the bulk and grid supply points, BG2 is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model alone (b_weekly).

Production does not run BG2. Production serves a much weaker XGBoost model, stored as xgboost_baseline. Experiment 87 scored it at 10.536 points on the Primary quantile score, against 5.260 for BG2. A page that names BG2 as a benchmark says that production does not run BG2.

The GAM stack trails BG2 on sunny April-to-June half-hours. Experiment 251 found the stack worse than BG2 in April, May, and June (+0.162, +0.220, and +0.054 points), and at D5 on sunny half-hours. Every Primary-demand change page reports this finding until a version of the research default closes the gap.

docs.title: Folds
docs.text:
Folds are contiguous months with a training window that ends before the first forecast origin of the scored month. Fold k trains on data up to the end of month M(k), then scores every daily forecast run whose origin date falls in month M(k)+1, at every lead up to 240 hours. The publication lag of the power data counts as part of the training cut. The row set is every daily ensemble run, at the 00:00 UTC origin, in the scored period. It includes the runs that fold_a_every5d_v1 holds, and it gets a new row_set_id when the first experiment under this protocol stores its forecasts. The publication lag of the power data is the lag in production, and studies.eval_protocol states its value.

The experimenter chooses the training regime and states it in the plan. An expanding window and a sliding window (for example, the last 24 months) are both allowed. The regime must be the same for the forecast under test and for its comparison arm, unless the regime is the change under test.

A fold needs at least 12 months of training history before it is scored. The GAM has seasonal terms, and a fold that has never seen a winter measures extrapolation, not the change under test. Each Primary's report says which months were excluded by this rule.

The scored period is 2025-07 to 2026-06, with a replicate period of 2024-07 to 2025-06 for the Primaries that have one. The ENS archive starts on 2024-04-01 at every Primary, so an arm trained on ENS forecasts has a replicate of 2025-04 to 2025-06 only, at 13 Primaries, and none at D8, D15, and D18. Only a Primary with at least 12 months of history before the replicate period has a replicate, and an adoption that needs a replicate cannot rest on the others. Rows inside hand-filtered events are excluded, as in the research default's row set, except that a detected step day at a Primary like D8 is never excluded.

Every Primary in a group is scored over the same months, so that a pooled group score averages the same rows. A Primary whose history is too short for a month is left out of that month for its whole group, or the pooled score is labelled with the months it covers. D15 and D18 are scored from the first month that studies.eval_protocol.fold_plan returns for each of them, with no replicate. The module governs the first scorable month at every Primary, and the scored months are a few. A 95% month bootstrap on four months under-covers, so their numbers are reported only and do not count in the tally of Primaries where the forecast under test wins. D9's history starts on 2023-10-01, so it has no replicate months before 2024-10.

The months that the 12-month rule excludes are reported as their own labelled slice. Cold-start months are where a longer fit history helps most, and a gain there is otherwise invisible.

Stage-2 and filter forecasts for the tuning period are stored for every fold, except at D8. The GAM stack's second stage and the Kalman filter need forecasts from before each scored month, and a missing store blocks a rescore. Every experiment stores its per-run forecasts and its stage columns.

No experiment scores a valid time on or after 2026-07-01. This is an honour-system rule. A replicate that scores later valid times is labelled "tuning-adjacent" and is not read as held-out evidence. The rule truncates the last June origins, whose leads run past 2026-07-01. A physical lock on the held-out data is a separate, later piece of work.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
The three scored metrics are the mean absolute error of the median, the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), and the tail-weighted CRPS (twCRPS). CRPS is estimated as the quantile score over 11 levels, which is the headline metric of every family. The ensemble CRPS of studies.ensemble_scores is a different estimator and is not used here. Pass or fail is judged in points of effective capacity, where a point is 1% of a Primary's capacity, and every table shows megawatts beside it, as the substation cards do. The headline metric is CRPS.

Four tail measures and the curtailment cost are reported and have no pass or fail. The tail measures are pinball loss and coverage at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles, per group and per Primary. The curtailment cost is the avoidable-curtailment-cost measure of studies.eval_protocol. It is read only for the signed-MW group. The MVA-only meters record unsigned apparent power, which hides reverse flow, so the cost is not defined there and carries the label "reactive power assumed zero".

The implementing code is the package studies.eval_protocol. The package lives in src/studies/eval_protocol/, with the modules metrics.py and slices.py, and a separate pull request adds it. Slice masks and the twCRPS threshold are defined there. The definitions are those of the substation cards (sunny by clear-sky index, sunny by unit shape, cold nights at 3 °C or below, and bank holidays). The twCRPS threshold is fixed per Primary and named in studies.eval_protocol. The docstrings of the package are the definition, and a change to a mask or a threshold makes a new version of this protocol. The package defines the slices with the ERA5 2 m temperature at each series' location, and the ENS forecasts are scored over those slices. The slice of a half-hour is therefore the same for every forecast, because it depends on an estimate of the weather that happened and not on any forecast. ERA5 is an estimate of past weather, so a half-hour near a threshold can sit in the wrong slice, equally for every arm.

Experiment code must import the metric definitions from studies.eval_protocol. A hard-coded copy of a metric is a defect, because copies are how a changed definition stops applying to some experiments.

docs.title: Slices
docs.text:
Each metric is reported over the slices below, and every slice row shows its half-hour count. A slice with few half-hours is labelled "thin", as the substation cards do.

Kind Slices Lead time Day 1 (0 to 24 hours), day 2, days 3 to 4, days 5 to 7, days 8 to 10, days 11 to 14. Days 1 to 10 is the headline band Time of day Night, morning, midday, and evening, in local time, with the hour boundaries stated in studies.eval_protocol Condition All days; sunny by clear-sky index; sunny by unit shape; sunny April to June; the months excluded by the 12-month rule; winter (December to February); winter nights; cold nights (3 °C or below); Economy 7 step hours; Christmas (24 December to 1 January); bank holidays Load-shift events During each hand-labelled load-shift event; in the 7 days after each event ends Group Signed-MW, MVA-only, and short-history, each separately Series Every Primary on its own row, and every Primary in each lead band (at least the day 1 band beside days 1 to 10)

The two load-shift slices have no pass or fail. The row set of the main score excludes the rows inside hand-filtered events, so the scores during the events and in the 7 days after each event ends are reported separately. Seven logged transfers are too few for an interval, per experiment 277. The length of 7 days is a choice of demand-v1, which the maintainer may change in a later version. The event list is the hand-filtered list and never the output of a detector.

The tolerance for "sunny daylight half-hours" applies to the sunny-by-clear-sky-index slice. The first run passes the realised clear-sky index (global horizontal irradiance over the Haurwitz clear-sky irradiance). The other sunny slices are reported.

The verdict names the lead band it rests on. A verdict that rests on days 1 to 2 says so, because NGED's horizon is 1 to 10 days.

docs.title: Reporting in every write-up
docs.text:
The twCRPS threshold and the curtailment limit need at least 12 months of readings before the scored period. A series with fewer readings gets a null value and a status, not a threshold from a short history.

An arm that is missing at a Primary is reported as "not fitted", never dropped. The tally of Primaries where the forecast under test wins states its denominator, which is the number of Primaries scored for both arms, and the number of Primaries not fitted.

For each pre-registered contrast, the write-up states the 99% interval of the adoption condition and the 95% interval of the reported contrast, with the direction, the lead band, and the pooling decided before scoring. The 99% interval undercovers on short periods (96.5% at 12 months), and the write-up says so beside it. The first run states, for each Primary, whether it has a replicate and which Primaries have hand-labelled events, since an empty event list gives an empty slice.

Each write-up reports the load-shift slices beside the main score. The write-up shows the score during the events and the score in the 7 days after each event ends, for the forecast under test and for the current research default, with the half-hour count of each slice. The write-up draws no pass or fail from them.

Each write-up carries a per-Primary table, the worst Primary, and a leave-one-out contrast. The table lists every Primary's paired difference and its 95% interval, sorted by gap. Beside the pooled score the write-up shows the worst Primary and the number of Primaries where the forecast under test wins. For each pooled group contrast, it also shows two leave-one-out contrasts: without the Primary with the largest absolute paired difference, and without the Primary with the worst score. The sign of a pooled contrast can change when one Primary is left out.

Intervals are 95% intervals from the paired bootstrap that resamples whole calendar months. Any statistic across Primaries states the number of Primaries, because a correlation across 14 or 16 sites is weak evidence.

The write-up names the research default's version and the protocol version. For example, "default plus x versus Primary demand research default 3, scored under demand-v1". The result.md take-home stays at one or two paragraphs with figures, and the full metric table sits in a collapsed section.

A change aimed at one series or slice names at least two placebo Primaries in its plan. A placebo fails when it moves in the same direction as the target, beyond its own 95% interval. A change with a failed placebo cannot be adopted as a general change.

docs.title: When a change is adopted
docs.text:
These conditions apply only when an experiment asks to adopt a change. Most experiments do not ask. A change is adopted only when all six conditions hold. A change aimed at named Primaries follows the targeted path below, and the other conditions still apply to it.

  1. Gain. The 99% month-block interval of the contrast (default plus x, minus default) on the CRPS of days 1 to 10 lies wholly on the better side of zero, and the point estimate is at least the minimum gain for the change's tier. The contrast is read for the signed-MW group and for the MVA-only group separately, and each group's verdict is stated on its own. With k pre-registered arms, the interval is read at the level 1 − 0.01/k. The short-history group takes no part.
  2. No harm to a group. The signed-MW group passes the gain condition. The MVA-only group stays within the tolerance of its headline, with D8 and without D8, and is not required to show a gain. Each protected slice stays within its tolerance in each group, judged by a one-sided 95% non-inferiority bound. A breach at a group makes the verdict rejected.
  3. No harm to a Primary. A Primary whose point estimate is worse than 0.05 points makes the verdict needs-human, with the Primary named. The interval is not tested at each Primary, because 16 one-sided tests would breach by chance more often than not.
  4. Replication. An arm trained on ENS forecasts can be replicated only over 2025-04 to 2025-06 at 13 Primaries. An adoption that rests on that weak replicate has the outcome needs-human and is never adopted automatically. The gain has the same sign in the replicate period at the Primaries that have one, and the replicate estimate is at least half of the smaller of the main estimate and the minimum gain. Where the minimum gain is zero, the condition reduces to the same sign. Leaving out one series at a time is a check for changes tuned on one series and does not stand in for a second period: a change with no second period stays a candidate. A change that fails replication is not retried on the same replicate period with a changed x, unless the change is pre-registered as a new experiment and the failed attempt is counted. A change that meets this condition satisfies audit trigger 7, and a candidate that fails it never becomes a base for later work.
  5. Controls. The experiment's own controls passed, the placebos did not fail, and no audit trigger in the ml-experiment skill is unresolved. The audit's findings are triaged in the pull request before the adoption.
  6. Serving. The change uses only inputs available at forecast time. If the change would need a serving-path change to port, the page says so.

A change aimed at named Primaries has a targeted path. The gain is judged on the named Primaries instead of the group, because a gain at one Primary is diluted by 8 or 16 in a pooled score. The placebos must stay non-inferior, and the change is adopted only as an automatic per-substation choice. The choice follows a rule fixed at training time from earlier out-of-sample scores alone, and the experiment scores the rule's output, never the better arm at each Primary in hindsight.

The tolerances and minimum gains are fixed here and tweaked only by a new version. A tolerance is the harm a protected group may suffer before an adoption fails.

Protected group Tolerance, in points Headline of each group (CRPS, days 1 to 10), including the MVA-only group with and without D8 0.02 The 0.01 and 0.99 pinball tails, the worse end scored 0.05 Cold winter nights 0.05 Sunny daylight half-hours 0.05 twCRPS 2% relative Each lead band 0.05 Each Primary, on the point estimate 0.05 Per-Primary coverage at the 0.01, 0.05, 0.95, and 0.99 quantiles Flagged when the 95% month-resampled interval of the coverage excludes the nominal level; a flag does not fail the change Tier of the change Minimum gain, in points A changed setting, an added column, or a changed loss 0 A new fitted step, a new input, or a new data source 0.02 A new head 0.03

The adoption outcome is adopted, rejected, or needs-human. adopted sets promoted_to in the front matter, and the outcomes rejected and needs-human appear in the first line of result.md beside the existing verdict, with production_status: candidate.

A neutral change passes a group's harm test with probability Φ(τ/SE − 1.645), where τ is the tolerance and SE is the standard error. A tolerance of 2 standard errors passes a neutral change 64% of the time, and a change that truly harms the group by exactly the tolerance passes 5% of the time. The per-Primary rule is a flag because 16 such tests would breach by chance far more often than not.

When the metrics disagree, the verdict is decided in this order. A breach of condition 2 makes the verdict rejected, unless the change targets a different slice and the maintainer overrules. A Primary breach of condition 3 makes the verdict needs-human. A CRPS gain with the median error moving the other way beyond tolerance gives needs-human. needs-human is also the fallback for any case this list does not cover.

The first experiment under this protocol rescoring the references. Experiments 374 and 376 used one fixed fit and a tuning month, not monthly folds, so their scores are not comparable with scores under this protocol.

A screening arm is allowed. Monthly retraining of 16 Primaries over 12 scored months costs about 384 stack fits per change for two arms. An experiment's plan may screen with fewer folds or Primaries, and says so. Only a full run under this protocol supports an adoption.

The cumulative harm budget is 2 times the group's tolerance, measured against the family's first version. The no-harm condition compares each adoption only with the previous version, so n adoptions that each cost up to the tolerance could cost n times the tolerance in total. At each adoption, the current research default must also stay within the budget against the first version, using the first version's stored forecasts. The retest rules of the research default rule still apply.

A change that wins on the gain condition but fails another condition is recorded as a candidate, not adopted. Candidates are retested when the missing evidence arrives, or when a rebase run is available, as the research default rule describes.

A targeted adoption on a subgroup uses a short list of admissible subgroups, set in advance. The list is cold nights, the Economy 7 step, and sunny daylight. A targeted adoption on a subgroup also needs no harm on the family headline.

An experiment may hold several default-plus-x arms, and at most one of them is adopted. Each arm is read at the level 1 − 0.01/k, and the others become candidates that rebase on the new version. A bundle of two components is adopted as one change only when it was pre-registered as one change and its leave-one-out arms show neither component harmful.

Only a pre-registered arm can be adopted. A post hoc arm becomes a candidate that needs a fresh experiment. When an experiment tests k variants of one change (tilt 20 and tilt 27, for example), the best variant needs replication on its own after the Bonferroni read.

An experiment that evaluates a blend reports each constituent model family alone beside the blend. The single-family table comes first, and the page states the blend's added value over the best single family, with an interval. A blend is adopted into the research default only with that table present. The first production update is a relatively simple model implemented as one model family, for example XGBoost only, while blends stay of interest.

The default plus x is produced on the research default's full row set. Its stored forecasts then serve as the next version without a separate regeneration job.

The ablation that follows every fifth adoption drops a component only on evidence. A component is dropped only when the interval of its removal lies wholly on the better side, or when its removal is non-inferior within the tolerance and the component sits in a higher complexity tier.

The nominal 99% interval covers less than 99% on short periods. A percentile bootstrap that resampled independent normal months with a nominal 99% interval covered 96.5% of the time at 12 months, 92.0% at 6 months, and 83.7% at 4 months (1,500 trials of 2,000 resamples each). The real procedure also resamples seeds and has autocorrelated months, so the figures are indicative. For periods under 12 months, add a t test on the monthly paired differences or use a studentised bootstrap. Adoption contrasts use 99% whatever the number of arms, as a stated exception to the interval-level convention, and a change page says "the 99% interval lies wholly on the better side of zero" in place of the study skill's "statistically significant at the 5% level".

The recorded gain of each version is an upper bound. Winners are selected on the scored year, so the recorded estimate overstates the true gain. In a simulation, a true gain of 2 standard errors was recorded on average as 2.7. The log therefore also reports the cumulative gain on the replicate period, which carries no selection bias, beside the scored-year sum.

docs.title: The holdout
docs.text:
The frozen period is the existing holdout: valid times on or after 2026-07-01. No experiment scores those valid times, which are kept for a finalist. The release-model skill scores the holdout once per release, on the sign of the effect only, and a month may confirm one release only.

The holdout holds under four months and no winter on 2026-10-23. It covers July to October 2026, and the months from November to February arrive by about March 2027. Until then, a change that acts in winter (the heating curve, cold nights, the Economy 7 step) is adopted on the replicate year alone, and its log entry reads "winter-unconfirmed". The holdout confirms its sign in March 2027 or later.

The same-months shrinkage check pauses a family's adoptions only on evidence of shrinkage. The check compares the holdout months with the same calendar months of the scored year (July to October 2025 for the current holdout). Adoptions in the family pause when the one-sided 90% upper bound of the holdout months' cumulative gain lies below half of the cumulative gain on those same scored-year months. A month read for a decision, or for a pause investigation, joins the scored months, and the holdout rolls forward as new months arrive. In a simulation of a 12-month scored year and a 4-month holdout, the check paused the family after 29% of false adoptions, 7% of adoptions with a true gain of 2 standard errors, and 3% of adoptions with a true gain of 3 standard errors. The check understates the chance of a pause for a change whose effect is seasonal.

docs.title: Retraining
docs.text: Retraining is monthly for the GAM stack, and weekly only for BG2 and the production forecast. There is no separate screening tier, because monthly retraining is already the R&D practice.

docs.title: Known-answer tests
docs.text: The protocol requires tests on synthetic series whose correct scores are known. The pull request that adds studies.eval_protocol adds them, and they run in continuous integration. They cover each metric, the month bootstrap, the folds (including the 12-month rule and the training cut), and the slice masks. A change to the evaluation code that breaks a known answer fails the build.

docs.title: What this page does not cover
docs.text:
• A physical lock that stops research sessions reading the held-out actuals.
  • Logging scores to MLflow, which a follow-on pull request adds.
  • Wind and solar, whose own protocols are linked at the top of this page.
  • The bulk and grid supply points. Their row set is fold_a_daily_gap_v1, their lead range is to be named with their first research default, and no adoption happens until then.
  • Scores before demand-v1. Those scores used fold_a_daily_gap_v1 on six Primaries, a scored year of 2025-07-02 to 2026-06-30, a replicate year of 2024-25, and a lead range of 0.5 to 168 hours.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: background
docs.text: This page explains, for a reader who has never fitted a generalised additive model, how the model of Part 2 works and how the planned full model would extend it. The six-part differentiable-physics series builds models of Primary substation demand from physical terms: a daily profile, holidays, heating, and solar output. The techniques page explains the method in general. Experiment 103 looked at the data, and experiment 104 fitted the Part 2 model. Only what those two experiments built counts as built. Everything under "The full model" is a plan, and the plan may change with each result. The six parts are listed at the end of this page.

docs.title: How the Part 2 model works
docs.text:
A generalised additive model (GAM) says that demand is a sum of simple pieces. Each piece describes one effect on its own: the time of day, the day of the week, a holiday, the temperature, or the sun. The GAM adds the pieces to get the forecast. Any single piece can be pulled out and plotted, so each effect stays separate and easy to read. That readability is why people who forecast demand like GAMs.

In a textbook GAM, each piece is a smooth curve whose shape the GAM learns from the data. The usual tool is a spline. Picture a flexible ruler pinned at regular points, called knots. The GAM chooses how high the ruler sits at each knot, and the curve bends smoothly between knots. A penalty on wiggliness stops the curve chasing noise. Lower error pulls the curve towards the data, and the penalty pulls the curve towards a straight line. The balance between the two sets how bendy each curve ends up.

The Part 2 model is a stricter cousin of the textbook GAM. The Part 2 model fixes the shape of most pieces in advance, using physics and common sense, and learns only how big each piece is. The whole fit is then one penalised least-squares problem with exactly one best answer. The Part 2 model forecasts demand minus solar output, in points of effective capacity (1% of a series' effective capacity). It has five pieces, plus two optional pieces that only some arms of experiment 104 used. The pieces use four blocks of hours in the day: night (00:00 to 05:59), morning (06:00 to 10:59), midday (11:00 to 15:59), and evening (16:00 to 23:59).

  • Daily profile. One level for every half-hour of the day, with separate profiles for weekdays, Saturdays, Sundays, and bank holidays.
  • Holidays. Each named holiday period, such as Easter or the school summer break, gets its own adjustment for each block of hours. A small tent-shaped term, rising and falling around Christmas Day, is added on top.
  • Heating. The Part 2 model takes how far the temperature sits below 15.5 °C. At or above 15.5 °C, the heating term is zero. Below 15.5 °C, demand rises in a straight line as the temperature falls. That bent line is called a hinge. Buildings warm up and cool down slowly, so the Part 2 model uses the temperature averaged over 6 hours, 1 day, 3 days, and 1 week, and learns a slope for each average in each block of hours. Every slope is constrained to be zero or positive, because a colder day cannot reduce heating demand. The temperature is an estimate of past weather (ERA5, see the glossary).
  • Lighting. Four small terms measure how dark it is, so the Part 2 model can add demand on winter evenings, when lights come on earlier.
  • Solar. For each half-hour, the Part 2 model calculates how much a panel of unit capacity would produce, from the estimated sunlight (CAMS irradiance, also an estimate of past weather) and the position of the sun, and reduces that output by 0.4% per kelvin of panel heating. The Part 2 model then learns the capacity of solar panels hidden behind the substation, one capacity per season-year (a year from July to June), and subtracts the panels' output. The capacity may grow from one season-year to the next, but never shrinks.
  • Drift (optional; used only in the arms of experiment 104 that include drift). Each block of hours gets a level that can move slowly. The level is set at monthly knots, with a penalty on sharp bends. Drift is the one piece that is a true spline. Drift absorbs slow change, such as a new housing estate or a factory closing, and a forecast holds the last value.
  • Steps (optional; used only in one arm of experiment 104). Occasional sudden level changes, kept rare by a penalty on their total size (an L1 penalty, which keeps most steps at exactly zero).

The yearly cycle comes from several pieces together, not from one piece. Heating carries the winter rise, and is driven by the real temperature rather than by the date. Lighting adds the dark evenings. Solar takes away the summer middays. Underneath sit two smooth waves across the year, one a year long and one half a year long, which pick up any seasonal pattern that weather and daylight do not explain. Because the season comes mostly from weather and daylight, an unusually cold March gets a cold-weather forecast and not an average-March forecast.

Fitting is one large linear regression, because every piece is a number multiplied by a column of inputs. Build a table with one row per half-hour and one column per input: the profile slots, holiday flags, temperature hinges, darkness ramps, solar shape, and drift knots. Then find the coefficients that minimise squared error plus the penalties. The penalties act like priors: each penalty pulls a coefficient towards zero, or towards a smooth path, unless the data argues otherwise. Some coefficients must stay positive (the heating slopes and the solar capacity increments), so the fit cannot be a one-line matrix solution. Instead, a small solver for least-squares problems with sign limits on some coefficients runs on the graphics card. In the experiment 104 benchmark, one fit on six substations took 1.6 seconds on the graphics card and 3.3 seconds on the processor.

The uncertainty bands come from a separate step. Fit the same model 12 months before the end of the training data, measure how wrong that fit was over the following 12 months, and take quantiles of those errors for each block of hours and each quarter of the year. Those quantiles become the bands around the forecast.

The Part 2 model is the starting point for the full model. The full model described next keeps this additive structure and replaces some fixed shapes with learned ones. Experiment 104's verdict was inconclusive: its scores with all usable years, with and without drift, could not be told apart from its score with the last 12 months only.

docs.title: The full model
docs.text:
The full model is a plan with four changes, and each change can be switched on alone, so a later experiment can tell which change helps. The framework module built for experiment 104 (src/studies/dp_pooled.py) contains switches for several of these changes. At the time of writing, no merged experiment has scored them. The 6.6-times GPU speed-up reported in experiment 104 came from a proxy for the pooled model and not from a scored forecast.

  1. Learn shapes that Part 2 fixes. The heating threshold becomes a parameter with a prior (15.5 ± 2 °C), so each substation can move its threshold, and the model learns how to blend the four temperature averages. The fit then loses its single guaranteed best answer and runs by gradient descent on the graphics card.
  2. Pool across substations, which is the heart of the series. All substations would share a small library of daily shapes, perhaps four: one residential with a big evening peak, one commercial and flat through the working day, and so on. Each substation learns its own mix of the daily shapes, plus a small correction of its own that a prior pulls towards zero. The substations would also share one holiday module and one heating-curve shape, which each substation scales. A new substation with a few weeks of history would borrow almost everything, and would learn only its own mix and scale.
  3. Add a small interaction neural network, the first truly neural part. A cold Sunday is not a cold day plus a Sunday, because people at home heat differently from offices. The neural network would take calendar and weather inputs together and add a penalised correction. The neural network would never see sunlight or the trend in time, so it could not quietly absorb the solar or drift pieces and break interpretability.
  4. Wrap two layers around the demand model. A Kalman filter (a method that updates an estimate of a hidden quantity each time a new reading arrives) would track, for each block of hours, a persistent level and a short-lived anomaly. A persistent level is a change that stays, such as a new load or a permanent transfer. An anomaly is a deviation that fades, such as a misjudged cold snap or a football match. The Kalman filter plays the role that lag features play in XGBoost. A meter layer would predict real and reactive power and calculate what an MVA meter would read. An MVA meter reads apparent power, which is never negative, so the reading "bounces" back up after the real power falls through zero, as it does when a substation exports solar power at midday. The framework module contains the meter layer, but only a placeholder for the Kalman filter's state.

Two smaller additions are planned. One is an optional flat unmetered generator, included only if the data argues strongly for one. The other is a soft ceiling on solar output: when many inverters (the devices that convert panel output to alternating current) each cap their output at their own rating, the total flattens gradually and not abruptly. The framework module has switches for both additions and for drift in the pooled model, and turning any of them on currently raises an error (DpConfig.check_supported rejects them).

docs.title: Is the full model still a GAM?
docs.text:
Mostly, but the full model would go beyond a GAM in three places. The demand core stays additive: each piece can still be pulled out and plotted. Priors do not change that, because the wiggliness penalty of a GAM is mathematically a Gaussian prior. A GAM with priors on its pieces, shared across substations, is a Bayesian hierarchical GAM. An interaction term learned by a small neural network is close to a neural additive model, Agarwal et al. (2021), which builds an additive model from one small neural network per input. The full model would extend that design with a network that takes calendar and weather inputs together.

The three places beyond a GAM are the shared shapes, the Kalman filter, and the meter layer. Shared shapes multiplied by each substation's mix form a low-rank model, meaning that many substations are described by a few shared curves. Because the coefficients differ by substation, it is also a varying-coefficient model. The Kalman filter makes the full model a state-space model, in which the GAM gives the expected demand and the filter tracks the hidden persistent level and anomaly. The meter layer applies a square root to the GAM's output (apparent power is the square root of the sum of the squares of real and reactive power), so the GAM sits inside an equation for what the meter reads. A fair short description is "a hierarchical additive model with a small neural network for interactions, wrapped in a Kalman filter and a meter equation". Each piece keeps a physical meaning and can be plotted, and that interpretability is what the series aims to keep, whatever else it adds.

docs.title: The six parts
docs.text:
The series is planned as six parts, and each part is planned from the result of the part before. The list below is the current intention and not a commitment. Each theme's research plan page holds the plan for its own parts.

  1. Data look, with no model. Which substations, rows, and dates are trustworthy. Experiment 103 (merged) decided each substation's start date, a fixed lockdown window (23 March 2020 to 19 July 2021) that training leaves out, and which rows of the substations metered in MVA count as dark rows (rows where CAMS irradiance is below 1 W/m², so solar output is zero and the rows show demand alone).
  2. A GAM for each substation. Does the model gain from older years, with and without drift? (Experiment 104, merged, verdict inconclusive.)
  3. Pooling. Does one shared model match separate models when there is plenty of history, and beat them when there are only 4 weeks or 3 months of history?
  4. Long history. Does the pooled model, trained back to 2019 with drift, beat its best shorter window? This part would bring in the Kalman filter. The comparison is a 2×2 table: with and without drift, crossed with with and without the Kalman filter. A baseline that tracks a running average of recent demand is added for reference.
  5. Embedded generation. A soft solar clip, a flat unmetered generator without inventing one, and the MVA meter layer.
  6. A real-world test on the ECMWF ensemble forecast (ENS), against the second best-guess recipe (BG2). Four arms: the differentiable-physics model alone, the differentiable-physics model supplying XGBoost's base margin (the starting prediction for each row), the GAM with the Kalman filter, and the GAM supplying XGBoost's base margin.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: Economy 7 and modern equivalents
docs.text: This page holds bullet-point notes on what we have found about Economy 7 and its modern equivalents, written on 2026-10-20. The notes are a working record, not a reviewed survey. Findings from our own data are exploratory and come from experiments that were still being reviewed when this page was written. Claims about tariffs and meters come from the documents linked below, and the ones we could not confirm in a document we read in full are marked as unverified.

docs.title: Why it matters
docs.text:
• Economy 7 is a time-of-use electricity tariff with a cheap seven-hour overnight window, used mostly with night storage heaters and immersion water heaters.
  • NGED is expected to see the forecast model for each Primary substation for the first time in winter. A visible night step in demand that the forecast does not reproduce is the kind of miss an operator notices.
