  • The average gain from modelling the step is small, so it is judged on cold winter nights as well as on the overall score. ## What we see in Primary substation demand
  • The step is real and visible at 13 of the 14 Primaries tested. In experiment 123, the 14 Primaries are the six main test Primaries and eight more with long histories, added as a check. The pooled estimate over the six main Primaries at a daily mean temperature of 3 °C is 9.9 points of effective capacity, with an interval of 6.2 to 13.5. The fitted step at single Primaries runs from 0.5 to 33.5 points (median about 13), or 0.05 to 2.67 MW. The one exception, D8, has a step of 0.5 points (interval -0.7 to 1.7).
  • Units. A point is 1% of a series' own 99th percentile of cleaned demand. It is not an electrical rating. At the three Primaries where the step first showed (D5, D10, D16), the raw step on cold nights is 4.8, 8.2, and 9.5 points (0.27, 0.44, and 0.87 MW). The fitted step at 3 °C is larger, at 10.8, 15.4, and 13.4 points.
  • The step starts in the half-hour from 00:30 UTC and ramps over about one half-hour. It reaches 7% to 56% of its plateau in the half-hour starting 00:00 and 81% to 119% by 00:30.
  • The step is fixed to UTC, not to the local clock. On cold British Summer Time nights the largest rise sits at the UTC step on 24% to 100% of nights per series, and at the local-clock step on at most 11% of nights. This is a post hoc finding. No local-clock mixture is shown, though one is not ruled out.
  • No Primary tested shows a second window, meaning a second rise of at least 30% of the main one. The end of the window is not visible, because the morning rise overlaps it.
  • The step grows only modestly with cold. The slope is positive at all 14 series, but the cold-dependent part is only 1.1 to 4.7 points at the six main Primaries. Most of the step is a flat winter-versus-summer difference.
  • The step changes between winters. From winter 2021-22 to 2024-25 it falls at five series, rises at one, and cannot be told at eight. Some series have fewer winters (D9 has two). Winter 2025-26 is held back until the base model's pull request merges.
  • The baseline GAM with a Kalman filter leaves most of the step unmodelled. The baseline leaves 0.53 to 0.78 of the step at D5, D10, and D16. On cold nights it forecasts below actual from 01:00 at D5 and D16.
  • The step was easy to miss. A first test of night-step arms in experiment 121 was not powered, because a step in one night half-hour is diluted in a score over the whole night. Scoring the 01:00 to 03:00 rows on their own detects it.

docs.title: What the documents say about the tariff
docs.text:
• The standard Economy 7 window is 00:30 to 07:30 GMT, seven hours. Elexon's profiling appendix allows regimes up to one hour either side: 00:00 to 07:00, 01:00 to 08:00, 01:30 to 08:30, and 23:30 to 06:30 (Elexon CP1058a). A 01:00 GMT start is therefore an allowed regime.
  • Radio teleswitch times are always UTC. The settlement system converts them to clock time in summer only where a per-regime flag, the GMT Indicator, is set (Elexon, Radio Teleswitch SSC Mapping, v3.0).
  • Which regimes follow GMT all year and which follow BST is unresolved. Two Elexon documents describe the flag in opposite senses (Elexon, MDD made easy v4.0). The meter timeswitch table that settles it is behind the Elexon portal login.
  • Smart meters are unverified. The documents we read in full say only that a smart meter's switching calendar can be set to match the old radio-teleswitch group. They do not say whether a smart meter's window follows BST.
  • A smart meter can hide an Economy 7 window. Meter timeswitch codes were defined before smart meters, so a smart meter cannot be identified from its code (Elexon BSCP40 Issue 67).
  • Of the NGED areas, only the East Midlands appears in the radio-teleswitch mapping. Its seven-hour Economy 7 regimes are all dynamic, with no switching times given. West Midlands, South West, and South Wales were not found.
  • A regional window table in an LLM-written summary is unverified, so we do not use it. It claimed split windows in the South West and meters locked to GMT. We found no source for the regional rows.

docs.title: How many meters, and how the stock is changing
docs.text:
• NGED's four areas hold 1,141,937 of the 3,249,338 Economy 7 and white-meter points in Great Britain (35%), as of November 2022. The East Midlands has 671,198, the second largest of the 14 areas. The Midlands has 242,512, the South West 183,654, and South Wales 44,573 (Ofgem, call for input, 2023).
  • Economy 7 households use more electricity. Ofgem gives 4,748 kWh a year for Economy 7 against 3,245 kWh for the standard class, and about a 60/40 split between peak and off-peak.
  • The radio teleswitch service is being closed. Meters fell from over 600,000 in January 2025 to under 154,000 in January 2026. Withdrawal went by regional group code from 30 June 2025, paused over winter, and restarted on 2 March 2026 (Ofgem, RTS decision, 5 March 2026).
  • The closure may change the step within our history. Ofgem says a smart meter or a preset meter replaces each radio-teleswitch meter. Whether the new window follows GMT or the local clock is not stated. The regional order of withdrawal was not found.

docs.title: Modern equivalents, ranked for modelling
docs.text:
• Intelligent Octopus Go (23:30 to 05:30) is growing fast. The window comes from Octopus notices quoted on third-party pages, so it is unverified. Electric vehicles on the tariff rose from 156,000 to 278,000 between April 2024 and April 2025 (Octopus Energy Ltd annual report FY25). Extra smart-charge slots shift from day to day, so only the fixed window is a daily shape.
  • Octopus Go (00:30 to 05:30) is a fixed window (Octopus Go). The window comes from a web-page summary we did not read in full, so it is unverified. We found no customer count.
  • Cosy Octopus for heat pumps has three cheap windows (04:00 to 07:00, 13:00 to 16:00, and 22:00 to 24:00) and a peak from 16:00 to 19:00 (Cosy Octopus). These times are also from a web-page summary and are unverified. These show as midday and 22:00 changes, not a night step. Heat pumps are still few.
  • Clock type for the Octopus tariffs is unverified. Some forum posts say smart-meter windows follow the local clock, but they are anecdotal.
  • Out of scope: Agile, Tracker, Saving Sessions, and the national Demand Flexibility Service. They respond to prices or events, not to a fixed daily window.
  • Radio-teleswitched dynamic tariffs (Total Heat Total Control and Weathercall) are signal-driven and ending, so they are not modelled. ## What this means for the model
  • The night step is a daily shape fixed in UTC, so the model indexes night shapes by UTC hour. Night shapes are also indexed by local hour, so a local-clock tariff can show up next to the UTC-fixed step.
  • The step size is allowed to change over time, per substation. A slowly changing term, with a non-negativity bound, replaces a single fixed coefficient. The UTC share can change slowly too.
  • The learned shape library (experiment 120) is designed to learn a 01:00 shape from the data. Whether it finds the step unaided is a planned test, with an injected step and a placebo first. A hand-built night-step arm sets the benchmark.
  • Substation cards show the fitted step. Each card shows the step in points and MW, its start time, its size by winter, and the share that follows UTC against the local clock.
  • Calendar and visible-feature checks. A forecast-against-actual figure for cold winter nights goes on each card. A visible miss on a cold winter night counts against release.
  • The Octopus and Cosy tariffs are not visible at Primary level, so they are not modelled. A check in experiment 123 looked for a rise at the window edges on British Summer Time nights (Octopus) and on winter weekdays (Cosy), by year from 2021. The placebo control failed: at half-hours with no tariff edge the interval excluded zero in 76% to 79% of series-years, because the daily load shape is not flat. The year-on-year change cancels the shape, but the placebo false-positive rate was still 21% to 43%.
  • The detection limit is 1.19 points (about 0.06 to 0.22 MW). Beyond it, with the expected sign, only one Primary (D8) shows the Intelligent Octopus Go edges at 23:30 and 05:30, and that Primary has no Economy 7 step and a large fall at 16:00, so it is a load change. No Primary shows the Octopus Go opening at 00:30. Cosy is not distinguished from other load changes.

docs.title: Gaps
docs.text:
• The meter timeswitch table of which regimes follow GMT or BST.
  • The smart-meter specification for the clock basis of tariff switching.
  • Year-by-year Economy 7 meter counts, and NGED-area counts for Octopus tariffs, electric vehicles, and heat pumps.
  • Winter 2025-26 data, which shows whether the radio-teleswitch closure changed the step.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: literature scan
docs.text:
This page holds bare-bones notes from a small literature scan, made on 2026-10-20 to inform the design of the differentiable-physics experiments. A Sonnet agent read the papers listed in the last section in full. Every number below comes from the full text of the paper named, and all the papers are held in the project's private library folder literature/papers/. The notes are a working record, not a reviewed survey. The project's main review is The current state of the art in energy forecasting. The papers report a normalised root mean square error (nRMSE) and a normalised ranked probability score (nRPS), each in its own normalisation.

Scope caveat for all GAM results: they are regional or national load (GB GSP Groups, France, US cities), day-ahead, not Primary substations.

docs.title: 1. Tricks we're missing (ranked)
docs.text:
1. Put the Kalman state on the coefficients of the frozen GAM effects, with learned diagonal noise, not only on a level plus anomaly.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Sec. II-B, Table I. Freeze the fitted effects, standardise them, and let the weight vector theta_t of (effects, intercept) follow a random walk. Q is diagonal, found by greedy likelihood (R package viking).
    • Gain (14 GB GSP Groups, 2021, nRMSE): Kalman-dynamic 0.332 vs offline GAM 0.635, GAM refitted yearly 0.387, GAM refitted daily 0.377, Kalman with Q=0 (static) 0.380. So: Q=0 only matches daily refits; the learned Q is what wins (about 12% better than daily refitting).
    • Second source: de Vilmarest and Goude (2022), Table III (MAE in MW, competition month): linear model offline 22.8, dynamic 14.9, dynamic with Q set big and proportional to I 11.2, VIKING 11.5. Q proportional to I was best there but not in the pre-competition data, so the Q choice depends on how much the data drifts.
    • Slot-in: after the convex fit, freeze the fitted columns (daily profile, heating, solar, holiday). Run a Kalman filter whose state is one multiplier per block of hours on each column. Experiment 106 filtered only level and anomaly; this lets heating sensitivity and PV scale adapt.
    • Cost: CPU seconds per site per year for the filter; minutes to fit Q on a training year.
  2. Let the Kalman state learn capacities, so the explicit capacity input matters less.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Sec. IV-D. Remove the embedded solar and wind capacity inputs: offline nRMSE rises by more than 10%; Kalman-adapted nRMSE falls by 0.4%. Scope: 2019, GB GSP Groups.
    • Slot-in: our convex PV capacity is already non-decreasing; a PV-scale multiplier in trick 1 gives a cheap second estimate, and the gap between the two flags capacity steps.
    • Cost: free once trick 1 exists.
  3. Fit the quantile regression on the Kalman residuals (not the offline residuals), with the GAM prediction, its square, and hour-of-day as covariates; optionally adapt it online.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest et al. (2024), Table II (nRPS, 2019 / 2020 / 2021): offline GAM + offline quantile regression 0.231 / 0.338 / 0.454; Kalman Gaussian quantiles 0.212 / 0.217 / 0.222; Kalman + offline quantile regression 0.206 / 0.214 / 0.217; Kalman + online gradient descent with step size chosen by Bernstein online aggregation (BOA) 0.202 / 0.201 / 0.209.
    • Reading: nearly all the gain comes from filtering the mean (0.231 to 0.206 in 2019). The extra from the online quantile step is 2 to 6%.
    • Slot-in: replace our residual-quantile spread by the covariate quantile regression. Online gradient descent on the pinball loss is five lines. Cost: CPU seconds.
  4. Covariate-dependent Generalised Pareto tails for the extreme quantiles.
    • Paper: Browell and Fasiolo (2021), Sec. V-B and Table IV. Quantile regression on GAM residuals for the body; GPD beyond the 1st and 99th percentile with a scale that depends on covariates. Plain quantile regression is not calibrated beyond 1% and 99%. The conditional GPD cut upward reserve by up to 24.6% and downward by up to 10.8% against a static GPD (probability levels 0.01% to 0.25%).
    • Fit in mgcv (R); in Python it needs a small custom maximum-likelihood fit. Fits our curtailment-tail goal. Cost: CPU minutes per site.
  5. Learn the observation variance online (VIKING) rather than a fixed sigma.
    • Paper: de Vilmarest (2022); used in de Vilmarest and Goude (2022) Table III (VIKING 11.5 vs dynamic 14.9 on the linear model; no better than hand-set big Q). Gain is modest and mainly saves tuning. Cost: CPU seconds.
  6. Exponentially smoothed temperatures with two time constants, plus smoothed daily min and max.
    • Obst et al. (2021), Sec. 3: GAM terms f(Temp95), f(Temp99), f(TempMin99, TempMax99), f(t, Temp), factors per step on half-hourly data. Also the GEFCom2014 winner's smoothed temperature, alpha = 0.95 (Fasiolo et al. (2021), Sec. 7). No paper isolates the gain.
    • Slot-in: add two decayed columns (our 6 h to 1 week means are the same idea) plus smoothed daily extremes. Cost: minutes.
  7. Detrend the target before the tree model.
    • Rubattu et al. (2023), Sec. 3: fit a linear trend in the training fold, subtract it, fit LightGBM, add it back. Shown in Fig. 3 as zero-mean residuals; no number. Same paper: temporal-hierarchy combination improved CRPS about 5% and interval score about 10% (BigDEAL 2022 data, not public). For the XGBoost side of the blend only.
  8. Intraday autoregressive correction of the residuals, one model per horizon.
    • de Vilmarest and Goude (2022), Sec. III-B and Table II: offline GAM MAE 20.7 to 19.3 MW in a stable period; MLP 57% lower in the unstable year. Likely already covered by our anomaly state; check before building.

docs.title: 2. Our current choices against the literature
docs.text:
• Fixed 15.5 C hinge: no paper found uses a hinge. All the GAM papers above fit a free smooth of temperature (cubic spline) and let the data find the threshold (Fasiolo et al. (2021) f(T) with rank 15; Obst et al. (2021)). So the literature neither supports nor contradicts a fixed threshold; a spline would be the check, and a learned threshold is the nearer middle road.
  • Smoothed temperatures (6 h, 1 d, 3 d, 1 week): supported. Every EDF-line paper uses exponential smoothing at two time constants (0.95 and 0.99 per step); see trick 6. With half-hourly steps those are roughly 10 h and 50 h (the scan's own conversion, not stated in the paper).
  • Monthly drift knots: weakly supported. The literature's answer to level shifts is the Kalman coefficient state, which beat yearly and daily refits (trick 1). The finding of experiment 106 (drift adds nothing once the filter runs) agrees. No paper tested monthly spline knots.
  • Kalman level and anomaly states: supported, but narrower than the literature's state (trick 1). Adapting only the level discards the slow-changing heating and PV sensitivities that de Vilmarest et al. found drifted.
  • Residual-quantile spread (per block of hours and quarter): supported as a first step (Table II: offline quantile regression on filtered residuals already gives most of the gain), but poorly calibrated in the tails (Browell and Fasiolo: beyond 1% and 99%).
  • Convex, non-negative, non-decreasing PV capacity: no paper found tests monotonic capacity. de Vilmarest et al. let the capacity coefficient move freely and it learned embedded capacity (trick 2). Tang et al. (2024) estimate capacity with a neural network from 24 h net-load curves, so a convex physical fit is a different route.

docs.title: 3. Hierarchy
docs.text:
• Reconciliation barely helps the bottom level. Nespoli et al. (Swiss low-voltage grid, 24 bottom series): minT with graphical-lasso covariance cut aggregate RMSE by up to 10% but bottom-level RMSE by under 1%; minT with Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage made the bottom level worse. Nespoli et al.'s suggested fix: reconcile conditionally on the previous steps' forecast errors.
  • Projection helps little when every node uses the same model. Brégère and Huard (2022) (GB household populations, 3-month test, errors summed over all nodes): projection alone cut error about 1% for GAM, 5% for random forest; adding an online expert-aggregation step cut it a further 10 to 15%. Read: the gain came from mixing in other nodes' forecasts as experts, not from the constraint.
  • Probabilistic reconciliation: Jeon et al. (2019), temporal hierarchy, two Crete wind farms: reconciling ranked (not stacked) samples improved CRPS; best method cut 24 h CRPS by 26.6% and 21.1% at the two farms. Temporal, not across sites, so only indirect support for our sums.
  • No paper found that tested ensemble copula coupling, the Schaake shuffle, or the variogram score on substation demand; none found for soft hierarchical losses or hierarchical Bayesian load models with measured bottom-level gains. Searches: arXiv API titles and our library. Not exhaustive.
  • Practical reading: for Primaries (bottom), expect under 1 to 5% from reconciliation. The finding of experiment 36 (child forecast error is the limit) agrees. The larger payoff the literature shows is for BSP and GSP aggregates, and from online expert mixing.

docs.title: 4. Solar disaggregation
docs.text:
• Identification by regression on an irradiance proxy plus a load proxy. Kara et al. (2018): net active power regressed on measured reactive power (load proxy) and a nearby irradiance reading, daytime only, with a correction for capacitor-bank switches (threshold 90 kvar per phase). Recovered a 7.5 MWp site with RMSE about 450 kW (about 6%); validated against the site's own meter. Our analogue: MVAr, where NGED telemetry has it.
  • Unsupervised, validated on metered PV. Sossan et al. (2019): PV modelled as capacity-weighted sum over 21 tilt/azimuth planes from transposed GHI; four estimators; best (frequency-band method) nRMSE 4.6 to 5.6% for 4 Swiss houses (35.3 kWp) with ground-truth PV meters. Also tested at 50% and 25% of capacity.
  • Neighbour controls: Cheung et al. (2023) use neighbouring customers without PV as the load model; MAE 28.37% below a prior disaggregation model (Ausgrid, 300 customers). Needs known no-PV customers; at Primary level the equivalent is nearby Primaries with little PV.
  • Capacity from net-load shape. Tang et al. (2024): a model trained on summer data only had 18.1% lower RMSE than an all-year model with a third of the training data; Monday to Thursday only gave 26.9% lower RMSE; error about 10% once more than 20% of households have PV. Supports fitting PV capacity on the summer or shoulder windows only, and averaging curves (doubling averaged curves cut RMSE 25.1%, 17.5 to 13.1 kW).
  • Validation pattern across the papers: a metered subset gives ground truth; sensitivity to sampling time and penetration; none validates at Primary scale against known capacity. A synthetic known-answer injection (as in the gate of experiment 109) is stricter than what they did.
  • Not read in full (so no claims): Kanchana et al. (2026) GAN data curation (paywalled page only).

docs.title: 5. Papers saved (all in literature/papers/)
docs.text:
Newly downloaded:

  • fasiolo-2021-fast-calibrated-additive-quantile-regression.pdf: smoothed pinball loss and calibrated learning rate; beats boosting and the GEFCom2014 winner on EDF data.
  • de-vilmarest-2022-viking-variational-bayesian-variance-tracking.pdf: online noise-variance learning for the Kalman filter.
  • bregere-2022-online-hierarchical-forecasting-power-consumption.pdf: aggregation plus projection on a hierarchy of GB households.
  • jeon-2019-reconciliation-probabilistic-forecasts-wind-power-arxiv.pdf: probabilistic temporal reconciliation.

Already held and read in full for this scan:

  • de-vilmarest-2024-adaptive-probabilistic-net-load.pdf: the main source (tricks 1 to 3).
  • de-vilmarest-2021-state-space-models-win-dataport-competition.pdf: Q choices and intraday correction.
  • obst-2020-adaptive-methods-covid-lockdown-france.pdf: GAM temperature terms; Kalman variants.
  • browell-fasiolo-2021-regional-net-load.pdf: GAM against linear benchmark (pinball skill over 10% better for GAM-Point than a Vanilla linear benchmark, all 14 GSP Groups); conditional GPD tails.
  • nespoli-2022-hierarchical-demand-forecasting-benchmark.pdf, rubattu-2023-probabilistic-lightgbm-temporal-hierarchies.pdf: reconciliation and temporal hierarchies.
  • kara-2018-disaggregating-solar-feeder-level.pdf, sossan-2018-unsupervised-pv-disaggregation-composite-power-flow.pdf, cheung-2023-btm-solar-disaggregation-varying-aggregation-levels.pdf, sensitivity-2024-distributed-pv-capacity-estimation-ann.pdf: solar disaggregation.
  • hertel-2026-load-forecasting-across-grid-levels-v2.pdf: monthly retraining helps; no hierarchy content.

Not found open (searched arXiv titles only): Wickramasuriya et al. minT paper, Ben Taieb et al. smart meter hierarchy, Rangapuram et al. coherent probabilistic forecasts.

docs.title: Calibration and uncertainty
docs.text:
On the 16 Primary substations, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms tested, correcting the spread of the forecast has gained little, and combining forecasts has gained more. A spread factor brought the solar 5% to 95% range from over-covering to about 90% coverage with no detectable change in accuracy, and no recalibration of the stored Primary substation quantiles passed its pre-registered tests. The gains that cleared their thresholds came from pooling ENS members for solar and wind farms, starting wind farms from the turbine power curve, and blending three stored forecasts for Primary substations. Every result rests on one validation year.

Figure 1: the uncorrected 5% to 95% range over-covers for solar in every lead band (a group of forecast lead times) and for wind in the first two days, and a spread factor corrects solar. Source: experiment 16.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Pooling the ERA5-trained quantiles over the ENS members beat an XGBoost model trained on ENS weather for solar and wind farms, and a stage 2 calibrator did not help. In experiment 2, the pooled mixture scored lower in CRPS by 0.62 points of capacity for wind (95% interval -0.99 to -0.26) and 0.24 for solar (-0.36 to -0.06), with the gain in the first six days. The stage 2 calibrator scored 0.40 worse than the mixture for solar (+0.26 to +0.61).

One spread factor brought solar's range to about 90% coverage with no detectable CRPS change. In experiment 16, solar coverage was 94.3% to 95.3% in every lead band before the factor and 89.5% to 91.8% after it (CRPS +0.006, 99.4% interval -0.004 to +0.024). Wind over-covered in the first two days only (95.3% and 94.4%), and no planned correction fixed that. A factor on two lead groups, chosen after seeing the results, reached 90.7% to 92.5% and changed the CRPS by -0.021 (-0.042 to -0.002), a small gain.

For wind, the base margin carries the CRPS gain, and the spread factor is a coverage fix. In experiment 20, the margin lowered the wind CRPS by 0.055 (99.58% interval -0.110 to -0.007), the spread factor alone by 0.021 (-0.043 to -0.002), and both by 0.071 (-0.133 to -0.014). The factor's extra -0.016 over the margin (-0.036 to +0.004) is not detectable. No change helped solar detectably, and the full combination for solar was 0.035 higher (-0.075 to +0.116), an interval that includes zero.

No recalibration of the stored Primary substation quantiles passed the pre-registered tests. In experiment 97, the weekly-refitted forecast of BG2 covered its q05 (the quantile at level 0.05) at 0.035 and its q95 at 0.938 at 12 to 36 hours lead, where 0.05 and 0.95 are nominal, and covered the median at 0.45. The tail test needed q01, q05, q95, and q99 within 0.01 of nominal at both the 16 Primary substations and 4 bulk and grid supply points. For example, the arm that scaled per level, lead band, and class gave Primary q95 coverage of 0.9397 and supply-point q95 coverage of 0.9248. The verdict is refuted, but 9 scored months are too few to separate a real improvement from noise. An arm that replaced the stored tails with fitted Pareto tails lowered the quantile score for Primary substations at 12 to 36 hours by 0.00009 (95% interval -0.00015 to -0.00001, against a stored 0.01882 on the scale that experiment prints) and failed the tail test.

Averaging the quantiles of three stored forecasts lowered the Primary substation quantile score by about 0.1 points, and the solar and wind gains were unresolved. In experiment 35, the lead-band blend of the monthly-refitted N1, a7_cs (an XGBoost model with seven weekly-analogue columns), and the stack scored 5.025 against 5.122 for the best of the three (quantile score -0.097, 98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026). One fixed weight vector, the simpler arm, scored 5.020, and the two differ by +0.005 (-0.008 to +0.023). The blend was not scored against BG2. The solar (-0.039) and wind (-0.074) intervals include zero.

Figure 2: blending lowers the Primary substation quantile score, and the solar and wind gains are unresolved. Negative values are better. Source: experiment 35.

A loss based on the CRPS of the pooled members recovered about half of the harm that extra members do to the pinball loss at 16 Primary substations. In Experiment 99, 6 members per run cost the pinball loss 0.075 points (5.622 against 5.547 for the control member alone), and the CRPS loss beat the pinball loss on the same rows by 0.039 (95% interval -0.057 to -0.018), a small gain. Against the control-member recipe the CRPS arm was +0.036 (-0.022 to +0.111), so the pilot cannot say which is better.

A zero starting value gave no detectable gain for Primary substations or solar farms. In experiment 80, the differences were -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054) for Primary substations and -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028) for solar farms, and the verdict is inconclusive. The wind models that serve already receive a base margin, so a zero start changes nothing there. Wind models without a margin were worse by +0.049 (95% interval +0.032 to +0.065).

Training with lags hidden at random did not widen the 5% to 95% band where a lag is missing. In experiment 100, on 37,394 real half-hours with a missing lag (an earlier power reading) at 16 Primary substations, the band covered 0.799 for the plain XGBoost model and 0.802 for the model trained with lags hidden in 10% of rows, against a nominal 0.90. The verdict is inconclusive.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: These are the best of the recipes tested in this theme, and the experiments did not score them against each other. For Primary substations, the best tested is the one-fixed-weight blend of the monthly-refitted N1, a7_cs, and the stack, which experiment 35 scored against its own members and not against BG2. For solar and wind farms, the best tested is the pooled mixture with a spread factor for solar and a base margin for wind. Experiments 16 and 20 found no detectable solar CRPS gain over the pooled mixture.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Four experiments have production_status: candidate, none is adopted, and a model release plan decides whether any is ported.

  • experiment 2, pooled mixture: pool the ERA5-trained quantiles over the ENS members for solar and wind.
  • experiment 16, solar spread factor: scale the solar mixture's quantiles by one fitted factor.
  • experiment 20, wind base margin: add the power-curve base margin to the wind stage 1a model, which lowered the CRPS by 0.055.
  • experiment 35, Primary substation blend: serve a fixed-weight average of the quantiles of three forecasts, one of them refitted monthly. It was -0.102 against the best member (interval -0.201 to -0.025) and was not scored against BG2.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
Report the pooled mixture beside any calibrator. Without it, a calibrator that is worse than pooling can look like a gain over an ENS-trained model (experiment 2). Re-check if the calibrator gets new inputs, such as lagged power, which experiment 5 found helpful for 16 Primary substations.

Fit each correction only on data from valid times (the times a forecast is for) before the first run it corrects, and expect early months to stay uncorrected. A fit that sees later outcomes flatters the correction. Experiments 16 and 97 fitted each correction only on valid times before the first run it corrected, and the arm of experiment 16 with a spread factor per lead band needed 5,000 earlier non-trivial cases (cases whose uncorrected 95% quantile exceeds 1% of capacity), so the wind 0 to 24 hour band was fitted in only 3 months and the 1 to 2 day band in 8. Re-check if the validation period or series count grows.

Compute solar coverage on non-trivial cases only. Night-time zeros sit inside every range and inflate coverage, so experiment 16 left them out. Re-check for a series that is not zero at night.

Refit each arm's own spread factor on that arm's own earlier cases. A factor fitted for other quantiles does not fit (experiment 20). Re-check if the quantiles come from an XGBoost model that experiment did not stack.

Score tail coverage and pinball loss at q01, q05, q95, and q99, count exceedances (measured values beyond a tail quantile), and keep the stored quantiles at all 11 levels. Nine scored months gave intervals of plus or minus 0.02 on q95 coverage, wider than the 0.01 bar, and cells with fewer than 30 days holding an exceedance were untestable (experiment 97). Re-check once 2 years of scored runs exist.

Test a starting value only on XGBoost models without a base margin. A base margin makes XGBoost ignore its base score, so a zero start changed nothing on the wind model with the margin (experiment 80). Re-check if the XGBoost version or objective changes.

Run a repeat fit to measure the noise floor of GPU XGBoost. Fits are not bit-reproducible: repeat fits of one 500-round model scored +0.004 apart at Primary substations and -0.007 at grid supply points, above the 0.001 tolerance and well below the intervals (experiment 80). Re-check on a different GPU or XGBoost version.

Hold the refit schedule fixed within a contrast. The CRPS-loss arms refit monthly with 150 rounds and scored 0.19 to 0.23 points above BG2's weekly stage, which probably reflects the schedule, so their absolute scores cannot be set beside it (experiment 99). Re-check if either schedule changes.

Pool pinball-trained quantiles with equal weights, not the CRPS atom masses. The CRPS gives each of the 11 quantiles a probability mass (0.02 at q01 and q99, 0.26 at q25 and q75), and pooling with those masses scored 0.025 points worse (experiment 99). Re-check if the pinball arm is replaced by a CRPS-trained one.

Apply the 14-day correction to each member before blending, and leave the monthly-refitted N1 uncorrected. Correcting the blend afterwards scored 0.048 points worse (95% interval +0.008 to +0.101), but that contrast favours the corrected-first arm, whose weights were chosen on its own scores, and correcting N1 too scored 0.135 worse than the headline blend (experiment 35). Re-check if the members change.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text: Whether a calibrator that sees recent power helps solar and wind farms is untested, although experiment 5 found it helped Primary substations. The wind two-group spread factor has not been tested on another year. experiment 99 suggests a tail-specific spread factor, or pooled-member spread statistics as input columns, for the Primary tails. Experiment 100 names an input column that flags a missing lag as an untested way to widen the band where a lag is missing. The blend gains for solar and wind may exist on more than 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. Tracking the month-to-month swing in Primary tail coverage needs at least 2 years of scored runs. The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment tried.

docs.title: Calibration and uncertainty: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00434 demand-ensemble-copula-coupling-and-schaake-reordering-of-stored-forecasts The stored forecast of experiment 425's arm A holds 11 quantiles per Primary and half-hour. Drawing 51 values from those quantiles and assigning them to the 51 ensemble members by the rank of each member's 2-metre temperature (ensemble copula coupling, ECC) gives sample paths that match the observed dependence across Primaries and leads better than independent draws do, by more than the 5% coherence margin on the variogram score, without changing the marginal CRPS. A Schaake shuffle from past observed paths does at least as well as ECC. not supported not-for-production Re-ordering the stored demand forecast's 51 values by member temperature or by past observed paths does not give clearly better sample paths overall. Ordering by temperature made the paths about 7% less coherent across the 16 Primaries and 1.7% more coherent across leads at days 1 to 10 (13% at 12 to 36 hours, an interim band), and the effects cancel in the combined score. A Schaake shuffle from past paths was no worse than independent draws across Primaries and 3.5% better across leads at days 1 to 10 (interval -6.3% to -0.9%, below the 5% margin), so it is the stronger reference candidate if a step 2 runs the 51 members through the neural network. also relevant 00432 wind-cleaned-zero-rescore The maintainer wants a wind forecast to say zero where the farm should output zero, and an evaluation that never asks the forecast to predict the idle noise. If the half-hours that the experiment 210 mask flags as idle are scored against a target of 0 (the cleaned-zero row set), then a forecast that puts its lower quantiles at zero below the turbines' cut-in speed is no longer penalised for the farms' idle floor, so experiment 336's zeroing arm x1, which lost on the raw readings, wins or ties on the cleaned-zero row set. partly supported not-for-production Scoring idle half-hours as zero output does not change which wind forecast is best, and forcing the forecast to zero below cut-in gains nothing: that arm ties the default (-0.002 points, interval -0.008 to +0.004), because the default already forecasts near zero there. The mixture-head arms keep at most a 0.02-point lead on cleaned zeros (none if every ERA5-flagged half-hour is zeroed), against 0.04 on raw rows and 0.23 on masked rows, because those heads rarely forecast zero when the farm is idle. Cleaned zeros can be a headline row set for experiment 429 beside the raw set, but not in place of it. also relevant 00429 unified-forecaster-wind-ablations A single pooled neural network can forecast the three metered wind farms as well as Wind farms research default 2 (experiment 347's y2: a frozen ERA5-trained power curve run on each of the 51 ensemble members, followed by a mixture-density head). Each difference between that design and the Primary-demand design (experiment 425's arm A: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, an unbounded head) is kept only if an ablation shows it is needed. partly supported not-for-production Neural wind forecasts do not need the extra machinery. A plain pooled network fed the ensemble members ties Wind farms research default 2 (10.533 against 10.518 points), and neither passing members through the network (-0.008 against the one-pass design), a power-curve layer (+0.000), nor a censored head (+0.018, worse) changes the score by the 0.10-point margin. The weakness all arms share is the upper tail: 2.2% to 2.8% of observations exceed q99, because the forecasts under-predict windy half-hours, and censoring did not fix it. The plain network is the design that matches the default; the upper tail is the open problem, and the architecture comparison does not explain it. also relevant 00428 day-window-convolution-attention-encoder-replacing-lagged-power-inputs A pooled mixture density network that has no hand-made lagged power input and instead reads the raw half-hourly power of whole recent days through a one-dimensional convolutional network and an attention layer (whose query is the half-hour being forecast) forecasts as well as the pooled plain network with the three origin lags on rows outside load-shift events, forecasts better on harm rows (rows whose target is outside every event but whose recent days are inside one), and follows a step added to the recent days by a much smaller share of the step, with wider bands. not supported not-for-production A neural network that reads whole days of raw power (E3) did not stop the forecast following load-shift events and scored worse than the lagged network (+0.050 on clean rows). Adding the surprise at the three lags (S1) lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.083 percentage points of effective capacity on clean rows, only just above the 0.077 minimum detectable effect, and by 0.060 on injected harm rows, below its 0.071 minimum. No arm followed a smaller share of a step in the recent power or widened its bands. All numbers are interim, from four test months. also relevant 00427 neural-mva-trajectory-labeller-and-two-channel-inputs A small labeller that reads a whole day of folded readings and outputs a probability that each half-hour is reverse flow, trained on the visible signed Primaries with solar farms injected, gives the export-gated neural network of experiment 420 (arm A) a better sign signal than the gate alone. Feeding the neural network separate MW and MVA input channels with a measured flag, and training it with MW masked on pseudo-Primaries that contain injected reverse flow, lets the network treat the hidden Primaries and the visible Primaries as the same kind of input. Together (arm TDL) the two ideas lower the signed CRPS on reverse-flow half-hours below arm A's. not supported not-for-production A small neural network that reads a whole day of meter readings and marks each half-hour as reverse flow or not ranks the half-hours about as well as the gated forecast network of experiment 420, but no better, and it wrongly marks about three in five of D5's sunny middays as reverse flow when no solar farm was added. The labeller was trained on four higher-demand Primaries, so the next step is to train a sign labeller on a mix that includes low-demand Primaries, or to accept arm A as the candidate and test it on ensemble weather. also relevant 00425 best-mdn-architecture-assembly-with-ablations The pooled mixture density network that adds ERA5-and-CAMS pretraining (experiment 418) to the pooled plain network with the Primary embedding, the ensemble-summary inputs, the hand-made calendar columns, and the 1.15 widening (experiments 397, 403, 406, 407, 423) scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network without pretraining, and removing the Primary embedding or the widening makes it worse. partly supported candidate Pretraining the pooled mixture density network on ERA5-and-CAMS rows before fine-tuning it on ensemble rows lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.050 points of capacity (-0.078 to -0.021) at the six signed-MW Primaries and by 0.124 (-0.219 to -0.048) at the eight MVA-only Primaries. The gain is clear at the MVA-only eight and probable at the signed-MW six, where the interval just misses the registered bar of -0.03. The assembled network beat the monthly XGBoost recipe and BG2 at both of those groups and trailed BG2 at D15 and D18, so pretraining is a candidate for a numbered release of the production forecast and the Primary embedding is the component to protect. also relevant 00422 mdn-train-with-varied-origin-hour-and-age-inputs-stale-input-step-2 The pooled plain mixture density network loses CRPS when the newest power reading falls at a time of day, or lies further back, than it saw in training, and when the weather forecast is older than in training. Training with the forecast origin at many hours of the day, the newest reading delayed by a random amount, and the previous weather run sometimes shown, with the age of the weather forecast and the age of the newest reading as inputs, removes that loss without raising the score on fresh inputs. partly supported candidate Training the pooled neural network with the forecast made at eight different hours of the day removes almost all of its extra error when the newest power reading is 12 hours late (0.18 down to 0.04 points at the six signed substations). The two extra age inputs did not help, so the simplest recipe is enough. Training this way raised the error on fresh inputs by 0.04 to 0.11 points at the eight MVA-only substations, which is within the range that seed-to-seed noise could produce for the lower values, and training with some readings missing cut the missing-readings error from 2.4 to 0.3 points. These are five test months, so every number is interim. also relevant 00420 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-final Experiment 417's arm A (a Primary-level export gate in front of the folded likelihood) gives a large gain in signed CRPS on reverse-flow rows over the plain network read as signed, and keeps the no-injection CRPS unchanged. Adding one shared variance term that grows with the fitted PV term improves on A, because the false calls sit next to zero crossings and the q01 coverage on reverse rows is about 0.05 against a nominal 0.01, so the signed distribution is too narrow where PV is large. partly supported candidate A neural network with a gate that decides once per Primary substation whether it exports power forecasts signed power much better than the same network with the gate shut on the half-hours with reverse flow (7.1 against 26.3 points of capacity) and does no harm beyond the registered tolerance (+0.03 points at D5) where no solar farm exports. Most of that gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero at all, because the ungated network scores the same on reverse-flow half-hours, and the gate's job is to stop invented reverse flow where there is none. Adding a PV-proportional variance did not help, so the next step is a serving test with real ensemble forecasts, not a further change to the network. also relevant 00417 hidden-sign-mva-export-gate-zero-crossing-labels The false reverse flow that the signed network of experiment 412 produced at MVA-only Primaries came from a capacity fitted on the rows it labels, so a constraint that fixes the sign with information the capacity cannot fit from the same rows removes the false calls and keeps the skill. Two constraints are tested: a once-per-Primary export gate in front of the folded likelihood (design A, with a hard high-irradiance row gate H layered on it) and training labels taken from the two daily zero crossings of an export day (design C). not supported not-for-production Neither of the two constraints stopped the signed mixture density network from inventing reverse flow at MVA-only Primaries. A Primary-level export gate left a placebo with no injected farm clean, but the injected pair kept 12.0% false reverse flow, and training labels taken from the zero crossings of the daily reading reached the same balanced accuracy (0.82) as the unconstrained reference, with 85% false reverse flow at the no-injection D5. This is the eighth treatment of the MVA problem that did not work, so the stop rule applies. also relevant 00415 pooled-mixture-density-network-at-bulk-and-grid-supply-points A pooled plain mixture density network fitted across the 16 Primaries and the 4 nodes (D13 and D17 are bulk supply points; D1 and D6 are grid supply points) with a node-type input scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 at the nodes than the same network fitted at the 16 Primaries only and applied to the nodes, and is not worse than the stored monthly XGBoost control of experiment 386 by more than 0.30 points of effective capacity at either group. supported not-for-production A pooled neural network trained on the readings of two bulk supply points and two grid supply points together with the 16 Primaries forecasts the bulk supply points a little better than the weekly XGBoost forecast (0.47 points of capacity lower, in all four months) and the grid supply points about as well, with very wide bands. A copy fitted at the Primaries alone fails at these points, partly because of how its inputs were scaled. Giving the network the readings of the Primaries beneath a node did not help. also relevant 00412 mdn-signed-mw-from-mva-meters-known-answer A pooled mixture density network that writes signed power as X = D - C_p u, with D the plain 3-component mixture, u the CAMS unit PV shape, and C_p a learned capacity per Primary, trained with a folded likelihood where u is large, recovers the sign of reverse flow at signed-MW Primaries whose sign is hidden from it, when the sky is real and not when the sky is shuffled. not supported not-for-production A mixture density network that writes signed power as demand minus a learned solar capacity times the CAMS solar shape could not recover the sign of reverse flow without inventing it. With the sign hidden at two Primaries, it found most injected reverse flow in June but also called reverse flow on 17% of the half-hours that had none, and with no farm injected it called it on 18% to 47% of sunny half-hours at D5. Fixing the capacity, or holding it near a prior, removed the false calls and the skill together, so this is the seventh fold treatment of the MVA problem that did not work. also relevant 00410 mdn-stale-weather-and-delayed-power-rescore The stored pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 397 loses little CRPS and little tail coverage when its weather forecast is one run (24 hours) older or its power readings are up to 24 hours later than in training, because it receives the age of each power lag as an input and has a missing-lag path, but loses more than the XGBoost model with the same inputs because it has no stale-input training. partly supported not-for-production A day-old weather forecast raises the forecast error (continuous ranked probability score, days 1 to 10) of the neural network and of the XGBoost model by under 0.05 points at both groups of substations (the signed six and the MVA-only eight), and power readings 6 or 24 hours late raise the error by under 0.05 points too. Readings 12 hours late raise it by 0.10 to 0.31 points in both models, and forecasts made with no recent readings are much worse (4 to 10 points), so the results suggest training should show the models readings at other times of day and a missing-reading case. Tail coverage stayed as it was for fresh inputs everywhere except the missing-reading case, where the neural network's 95% quantile covers 0.56 to 0.67 of outcomes instead of 0.89 to 0.94. These are five test months, so every number is interim. also relevant 00408 xgboost-signed-label-and-cams-columns-at-mva-only-primaries At the eight MVA-only Primaries, the monthly XGBoost demand model gives a signed real-power forecast, without losing skill on the MVA reading, when (a) two CAMS columns (the unit solar shape and the clear-sky index of the half-hour itself) are added to its inputs and (b) reverse flow is labelled before training: a reading is flipped to negative only on very sunny half-hours, where a physics rule says the substation exports power in the shape of solar output. partly supported not-for-production Satellite solar columns lower the forecast error at almost every Primary, but only when the model knows the realised sunshine, which production does not until about a day later. The attempt to read a signed MW forecast from an unsigned MVA meter failed its known-answer test again, so there is still no trusted signed forecast at the eight MVA-only Primaries. also relevant 00407 pooled-mixture-density-network-tail-arms-and-recency-weights The pooled plain network's tails at the six signed-MW Primaries are too narrow (q95 coverage 0.855 and q99 coverage 0.941 in experiment 397), and at least one of five changes lowers the tail loss below a globally widened pooled plain network without raising the CRPS: 5 mixture components, split-normal (skewed) components, a widening fitted per lead band inside each refit, a quantile head trained with the pinball loss, or a different half-life for the row weights. not supported not-for-production Making the shared neural network's outer quantiles 15% wider about the median is the best of the fixes tested for its too-narrow outer bands at the six substations where power can flow both ways (the signed-MW six). None of 5 mixture components, skewed components, a band width fitted per lead time, or a neural network trained directly on quantiles did better on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the loss at the 99% quantile together. The quantile-head neural network cut the loss at the 99% quantile by about a sixth, but raised the CRPS by 0.066 points of capacity. No change brought the coverage of the 95% quantile up to the 0.92 we asked for. Two changes are worth testing next: the quantile-head neural network as a separate tail model, and a widening fitted on weeks closer to the test period. All five test months are interim. primary 00402 lag-gate-learned-weight-injected-load-shifts-part-1 A gate that sets the weight of a mixture of two XGBoost demand forecasts (one with the three power lags, one without) from the surprise of the lagged readings, trained only on injected load-shift events with known truth, beats the fitted constant mixture around real load shifts and costs no more than it outside them. partly supported not-for-production A gate trained only on injected load shifts, with no labels from National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), learns to lower the weight on the forecast with power lags from 0.51 to 0.42 when a lagged reading falls inside a load shift, and so removes most of the harm that the lags do in that case. The gain on real load shifts is small (0.10 points at most against the 50/50 mixture, and 0.04 or less against the constant mixture fitted on injected events), and the gate scores worse than the 50/50 mixture when the target itself is inside a real labelled event at the six Primaries. The fitted constant mixture per group is a simpler forecast than the gate and comes within about 1.4% of its exact CRPS on injected rows. Training the gate on real and injected events together is untested. also relevant 00401 real-and-synthetic-load-shift-median-share-and-fixed-forecast-mixture Job 1. When a synthetic step of the corrected labelled depth is injected into clean periods at the same Primary and the same lag status as each real labelled event, the plain monthly control's median still follows the step by much less than it follows the real event, so the gap between 36.8% (experiment 395 Part E) and 0.94 (Part F) is not an artefact of the depth or the rows. Job 2. A fixed-weight mixture of the weekly forecast with power lags and the forecast without them scores within 0.1 points of effective capacity of experiment 400's learned blend B2 on rows with lags in an event, at the six Primaries with signed readings. partly supported not-for-production The median share of a load-shift step that experiment 395 called "followed" (0.94 with 3 lags in the event) is mostly not a response to the lags: a forecast with no power lags at all reaches 0.95, and the forecast with lags moves its median by at most about 0.03 more than the forecast without lags on the same rows, which is at the noise floor of two different fitted forecasts. Real events are far less visible to the lags than synthetic steps are, so the synthetic lag-encroachment sweep overstates what a real event does to the forecast. A fixed 50/50 mixture of the two forecasts does about as well as the learned blend at the six Primaries with signed readings, and not at the eight, where the interval allows it to score 0.12 points worse. At the six, one event at D16 carries most of the gain over the forecast with lags. also relevant 00400 lagged-lagless-forecast-blend-around-load-shifts-stored A mixture of the weekly XGBoost forecast with power lags and the XGBoost forecast without power lags, weighted by a smooth function of the lags' surprise scores and of lead time, scores better than the forecast with lags on the rows whose lags touch a load-shift event, and costs no more than 0.02 points of effective capacity on rows outside events. not supported not-for-production The lag surprise scores from experiment 391 did not tell a blend when to trust the power lags: the fitted weight hardly moved around events, so every learned blend behaved like a mix of about 60% forecast with lags and 40% forecast without lags. A fixed 50/50 mix helps on event-lag rows at the six Primaries with signed readings and costs a little elsewhere, so a smooth blend driven by these scores is not worth porting. The next step is a learned blender trained on injected events, which supplies the event examples that the real rows are too few to give. also relevant 00397 plain-and-attention-mixture-density-network-for-primary-demand A mixture density network given the simple XGBoost model's inputs, rows, and refit schedule scores within 0.1 points of that model at the six Primaries with signed readings and has tails that cover closer to nominal, and a gate that weights five input groups by lead time, calendar, and Primary lowers the network's score further and shows the weights a reader would expect. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network given the same inputs as the simple XGBoost forecast scores about as well as it, or slightly better, on five test months: 3.49 against 3.54 points of capacity at the six signed-direction substations with one network per substation, and 3.26 with one network across all 16. Adding attention over the input groups did not help, because the gate gave every group nearly the same weight at every lead time.
