Ranking farm forecasts by curtailment cost needs many more substations. also relevant 00251 dp-final-best-guess-assembly-clip-and-coast-against-bg2 The full best-guess stack of experiment 220 (arm D, the neural-network head, and the two-number solar summary) beats BG2, the manual heuristic, climatology, and a weak production-style XGBoost model over the scored year of 2025-07 to 2026-06. Adding the hand-set 60% clip at D5 lowers the D5 error on sunny half-hours when the neural-network head is absent, and adds nothing measurable when the head is present, because experiment 232 found the head cancels most of the clip's gain. supported candidate Over the one year we can score, the full best-guess demand forecast (arm D, a small neural network that corrects its median, and a two-number summary of the ensemble's solar response) beats BG2 by 0.136 points of quantile score (5%; lower is better) and the manual heuristic by 0.818 points, and it beats the manual heuristic on every headline metric we scored, including curtailment cost. The gain over BG2 is a winter gain: the stack is level with BG2 in summer and worse in April to June, and at D5 on sunny hours it is clearly worse than BG2. Adding the 60% solar clip at D5 helps only when the neural-network head is left out at D5, so the next work is the solar term at D5, not another stacked part. also relevant 00213 calibration-online-band-adaptation-from-coverage-misses Moving a scale on each quantile offset of experiment 169's arm A up after a reading falls outside that quantile, and down after a reading falls inside it, in the style of adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candes, 2021), lifts the cold-night q95 coverage to 0.90 or more without a second fitted spread model, because a run of misses on a cold spell widens the band before the spell ends. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the forecast widen or narrow its bands after each recent miss does not fix the under-coverage on cold nights: it lifts the 95% quantile's coverage from 0.896 to 0.906 in the scored year and lowers it in the other months, and it worsens the all-row, bank-holiday, and Christmas scores. A fixed widening of the upper quantiles does as well, so the cold-night gap is a shortfall that a signal arriving after the misses cannot learn in time, and the next step is to correct the mean forecast on the coldest days before any further work on the bands. also relevant 00169 calibration-combined-fixes-and-ensemble-spread The spread across the 51 ensemble members of the temperature and of the downward shortwave radiation at a substation predicts how wide the forecast's residuals are, beyond the hour band, calendar quarter, lead, and the cold-day widening of experiment 164. A convex quantile model that scales the quantile offsets by a non-decreasing function of those two spreads lifts the cold-night q95 coverage of the combined forecast to 0.90 or more. partly supported not-for-production Combining the smooth spread table with the cold-day widening reproduces its 0.896 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights, and adding the spread of the ensemble weather forecast (how much its 51 members disagree) lifts that to 0.907. The lift comes from widening the 95% and 99% quantiles by 4% and 10%, which the same model gives with its spread terms removed, so the ensemble spread is not what lifts cold-night coverage. A later experiment could test a bias correction of the mean forecast on the coldest days, and judge cold nights over more than one winter. also relevant 00164 calibration-cold-night-tail-under-coverage The q95 coverage of experiment 160's smooth-table forecast on cold nights (day mean temperature below 2 °C) stays near 85% because the spread table is too narrow when it is cold, not because the mean forecast is biased. Widening the quantiles on days the ensemble forecasts as cold, by a factor fitted on the tuning months, lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 90% or more without worsening the all-row score. refuted not-for-production On cold nights the 95% quantile of the best forecast is exceeded on about 15% of readings, and mostly because its prediction interval is too narrow, not because its mean forecast is biased. Widening only the upper quantiles on days the weather forecast calls cold reduces that share to about 10% without changing the all-hours score, but no fix reached the pre-registered 90% coverage in the scored year, and only 10 cold days back that year's figure. The coldest forecasts (0 °C or below) are also biased low, so correcting the mean forecast on those days is the next experiment to run. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00084 substation-limit-curtailment-cost-worked-example The substation-limit curtailment metric (studies.node_curtailment) can run end to end on the pilot's two bulk supply points, Boston and Skegness, and the pilot holds enough half-hours beyond a scaled limit to rank forecasts. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Two bulk supply points have 19 half-hours beyond a limit of 0.9 times their earlier maximum export in the scored year, so the pilot proves the arithmetic and cannot rank forecasts at the headline limit. primary 00083 curtailment-cost-and-tail-calibration-worked-example A tail-calibration table, built in packages/studies, can rank the stored quantile forecasts of experiment 48 by how well they cover the tails of the forecast distribution. This is a worked example of new code, not a test of a forecasting idea. inconclusive not-for-production Every forecast is too narrow in both tails: coverage of the 0.05 quantile is 0.066 to 0.085 and of the 0.95 quantile is 0.891 to 0.927. primary

docs.title: Curtailment cost: research plan
docs.text: No proposal in this theme is waiting.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Demand inputs
docs.text:
At Primary substations, a calendar-and-solar set of inputs lowered the demand forecast error by 0.1 points of capacity or more with an interval clear of zero: the hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, a Christmas column limited to the 14 days either side of 25 December, and an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output. A heating term gave 0.14 points in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead on one winter, which is under its 0.3 target. The electricity price, school terms, statistics of installed solar capacity, substation fingerprints, and the PV_Live estimate of solar generation gave no gain of 0.1 points that held up.

The experiments added one kind of information at a time to an XGBoost demand forecast and scored the change against the same XGBoost model without it. They scored 13 to 16 Primary substations (experiment 74: 5), over one or two validation years, and experiments 27 and 28 scored two grid supply points. Errors are in points of capacity, a negative change is an improvement, and each number names its metric: the error of the median (the mean absolute error of the middle forecast) or the quantile score. Several gains in the selection year (the year used to choose inputs) vanished in the confirmation year (the later year used to check them) or against a control.

For Primary substations on the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), adding the hour and weekday to the weather lowered the error of the median by 0.46 points (99.4% interval -0.61 to -0.30), the largest single input. The panels show the same contrasts for the 2 bulk and 2 grid supply points, which have too few series to settle. Source: experiment 6, an ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model on 14 Primaries.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The hour and weekday, the COVID indicator, and a windowed Christmas column help; school terms do not. In experiment 6 the hour and weekday lowered the error of the median by 0.55 points on the selection year, a third of the 1.5 predicted, and the pre-registered COVID indicator by 0.26 (-0.40 to -0.10). The Christmas column is weaker evidence. The 15 December to 7 January window was chosen after the run, and the column lowered the Primary error there by 1.78 points (95% interval -2.30 to -1.26) and changed it by 0.00 elsewhere. The gain is concentrated: the median-error series barely moved (3.96 to 3.95 in the confirmation year) and a series picked after the fact fell from 22.23 to 4.13. Dropping the column from the chosen set changed the selection-year Primary error by +0.14 (-0.06 to +0.35), and the whole-year effect was -0.10. Experiment 11 found no gain from return-to-work or school-term columns on Lincolnshire Primaries: +0.20 at Easter (99.2% interval -0.19 to +0.59) and -0.29 in half-terms (-0.68 to +0.07). The experiment's own rule gives refuted, and its write-up reads Easter and half-terms as inconclusive.

The Christmas columns cut the Christmas error and leave other days unchanged. Source: experiment 6, post hoc windows (chosen after seeing the results), three folds.

An explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output lowers the daylight error; same-time analogues may too, and the data could not rank the two. In experiment 74, five Primaries refitted monthly and scored on daylight April-to-September rows, the explicit offset lowered the quantile score by 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007), against a monthly refit with neither. An offset built from another date's sunshine scored 0.246 worse than the real offset. Statistics of installed capacity did not help 16 Primaries (+0.006, -0.022 to +0.033; experiment 31).

Both ways of telling the XGBoost model about sunshine lowered the daylight error, and the intervals overlap. Source: experiment 74, 5 Primaries, one validation year.

Satellite sunshine as a training input gave no resolved gain, and a correction of the forecast sunshine a further small one. Training on CAMS irradiance changed the Primary quantile score by -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), refuted against 0.2 planned (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS lowered it by a further 0.067 (-0.094 to -0.039), which makes the pair 0.102 better than the ERA5-trained arm, but the monthly ratio to CAMS still ran from 0.81 to 1.13, so the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 14). PV_Live, Sheffield Solar's estimate of solar generation, gave no resolved gain at the two grid supply points Walpole and Bicker Fen (experiment 27, -0.03; experiment 28, -0.14 with interval -0.34 to +0.04).

The electricity price gave no gain that held against a control. The price at the target half-hour lowered the pooled error of the median by 0.52 in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) and 0.18 in the confirmation year (-0.50 to +0.08), and a price from another week matched about 0.45 of the 0.52 (experiment 15). Price changes (experiment 25) and lagged prices (experiment 10) did no better.

Substation fingerprints and a heating term gave little. Fingerprints changed the quantile score by +0.02 (-0.05 to +0.10; experiment 32). A heating term lowered it by 0.143 in cold hours up to 48 hours ahead (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034) and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000), on 16 Primaries over one winter in which three ISO weeks hold 66% of the cold rows. The q95 forecast was still exceeded in 16.2% of those hours (experiment 94). Experiments 24 and 30 are in the candidates below.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: Among the experiments of this theme, no single one assembled the parts; the parts that beat their controls are below. Experiment 87 (the production-reference theme) assembled several of them in BG2. Give the weather-to-power XGBoost model the hour and weekday and the days to Christmas inside a 14-day window (experiment 6). Where a clean solar capacity estimate exists, add the forecast unmetered solar output as a base margin (experiment 74, using the offset of experiment 64; experiment 74 is not-for-production). In BG2 the offset lowered the score by 0.114 on its daylight April-to-September rows at the 5 Primaries that carry one, and by 0.010 over the whole year at all 16 Primaries (experiment 87). The stage 0 mapping (experiment 14) and the heating term (experiment 94) are candidates, not yet part of the design.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Five experiments here are marked candidate, and each rests on one validation year or an unconfirmed input.

  • Stage 1a inputs (experiment 6): the clock, the COVID indicator (-0.26), recency weights (-0.32, half-life 2 years), and the windowed Christmas column for the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model. A training start of 2023-09 stays unconfirmed (0.86 better on the confirmation year, 0.05 on the selection year).
  • Stage 0 (experiment 14): a quantile mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for a CAMS-trained stage 1a, 0.067 points better.
  • Pooling (experiment 24): one XGBoost model per substation type or size band (3 or 4 models instead of 20), 0.15 points worse (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), with the series identifier.
  • Weekly mean and median (experiment 30): two extra columns in N1 with the 14-day correction, 0.05 points better than N1 with it (-0.08 to -0.02). The arm is post hoc, and against the experiment 19 stack the 0.03 gain touches zero (-0.06 to +0.00).
  • Heating term (experiment 94): a per-series base margin. The experiment advises a second winter before porting.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Add a placebo twin of every added input, a copy with the same level but the wrong timing. A price from another week matched 0.45 of the 0.52-point price gain (experiment 15), the shuffled price matched most of the gain at the battery site (experiment 10), an offset from another date scored 0.246 worse (experiment 74), and a shuffled capacity control matched the register products (experiment 31). Without the twin, a column that only carries a level is credited. Re-check with a different data source.
  • Check a calendar column against a half-year flag and score it inside the special days. The unwindowed days-to-Christmas column flips sign every late June, so it acts as a half-year flag, and a time-of-year harmonic matched the Christmas gain but worsened summer (experiment 6). A column can also help a few days a year and barely move the yearly mean. Add a placebo calendar shifted by a fixed number of days (experiment 11). Re-check with more years than 3.
  • Fix colsample_bytree at 1.0 in every arm of a column ablation. Experiments 6, 30, 31, and 32 did so because column subsampling hands the wider arm a free win. None measured the size of that effect. Re-check if the arms are ever given equal column counts.
  • Give every arm the same starting level. A start at zero lowered the error by 0.071 (-0.099 to -0.047) against XGBoost's estimated base score in experiment 78, and experiment 74 quotes 0.07 to 0.10 points, so it started every arm at the median of the training labels (experiment 74). Experiment 76 did not test the effect. Re-check with a different pipeline.
  • Judge a lag set against N1 with the 14-day correction. The weekly lags gained 0.30 without the correction and lost 0.09 with it (experiment 30). Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Read a selection-year gain only after a confirmation year. The price gain at the battery site fell from -0.92 to -0.06 (experiment 10), and a 2023-09 training start gained 0.05 and then 0.86 (experiment 6). Re-check with a third year.
  • Test an input on the weather it will be served with. A CAMS-trained XGBoost model lowered the daylight error by 0.88 reading CAMS and by 0.04 reading ENS (experiment 9), and an ERA5-trained solar forecast ran 1.8 to 3.0 points too high on ENS members (experiment 28). Re-check with a different weather product.
  • Report a pooled share with and without the largest-residual substation. One substation set the pooled share in experiment 7. Re-check on new series.
  • Give every pooled XGBoost model the series identifier, and no fixed-window statistics for a held-out series. Dropping the identifier raised the score by 0.82 for by-type pools (experiment 24), and training-window statistics worsened a held-out substation by 1.39, probably because 7 series learn them as identifiers (experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Score cold-hour and special-day contrasts on more than one winter. Three ISO weeks held 66% of the cold rows at leads up to 48 hours (experiment 94), and the Christmas windows rest on three Christmases (experiment 6). Re-check when a second winter exists.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• A second validation year. The analogues on top of the offset (-0.066, -0.149 to +0.015) and the heating term need one.
  • Battery response to price. Only the largest battery site was testable, and national demand and wind scored at least as well as the price, so the price may be a proxy for them.
  • Stage 0 on more than 14 months of ENS and all members, and half-term effects with more than 9 half-terms.

The theme's research plan lists the proposals still waiting.

docs.title: Demand inputs: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00437 neural-demand-thermal-lag-solar-gain-and-tariff-feature-bundles The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 425 sees one valid time per row, so it cannot see the hours before or after that time. Adding columns that summarise those hours (bundle T, thermal lag; bundle S, solar gain; bundle F, look-ahead) or that carry the calendar, tariff, and national signals (bundle C) lowers its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10, because the network trains across all 16 Primaries (and, in the pretrained form, across 6 years of ERA5 and CAMS history) and may find signal that the per-Primary XGBoost model and the GAM stack missed. not supported not-for-production Adding thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, calendar, tariff, or national-signal columns to the pooled plain mixture density network did not lower its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by the registered 0.03 points of capacity, in either the ensemble-only or the pretrained form. Seven of the eight arms were worse than their control at the six signed-MW Primaries, by 0.016 to 0.059 points. The thermal-lag bundle lowered the CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries (by 0.022 and 0.029) in only 2 of 4 folds, which is too weak a result to act on. The screen could not detect effects below 0.045 to 0.064 points, so the bundles are left out, not ruled out. primary 00423 pooled-mdn-shared-date-time-encoder A small encoder that turns the half-hour of day, day of week, day of month, day of year, and the bank-holiday name into one learned vector, shared across the 16 Primaries, lets the pooled plain mixture density network share what it learns about holidays across Primaries and across holidays of one kind, so it forecasts bank-holiday weeks better than the hand-made calendar columns and is no worse elsewhere. not supported not-for-production A small calendar encoder shared by the 16 Primary substations did not forecast demand better than the 18 hand-made calendar columns. With holiday names and dates it scored 0.27 points of capacity worse (8% worse, in a range of 0.10 to 0.43) on the continuous ranked probability score at the six substations that report signed power, and with dates only it scored 0.37 worse. One possible reason, not tested, is that each day of the year appears only once or twice in the 24-month training window. The planned test on bank-holiday weeks could not detect any difference smaller than 0.34 points, and all five test months are interim. primary 00408 xgboost-signed-label-and-cams-columns-at-mva-only-primaries At the eight MVA-only Primaries, the monthly XGBoost demand model gives a signed real-power forecast, without losing skill on the MVA reading, when (a) two CAMS columns (the unit solar shape and the clear-sky index of the half-hour itself) are added to its inputs and (b) reverse flow is labelled before training: a reading is flipped to negative only on very sunny half-hours, where a physics rule says the substation exports power in the shape of solar output. partly supported not-for-production Satellite solar columns lower the forecast error at almost every Primary, but only when the model knows the realised sunshine, which production does not until about a day later. The attempt to read a signed MW forecast from an unsigned MVA meter failed its known-answer test again, so there is still no trusted signed forecast at the eight MVA-only Primaries. also relevant 00399 xgboost-short-history-start-cut-d15-d18 Dropping the first months of the two short-history Primaries, D15 and D18, from the monthly XGBoost demand model's training rows lowers its error at those Primaries, because the readings taken while the meters were being commissioned teach the model a wrong level. partly supported candidate Dropping the noisy first weeks of D15 and D18 from the training rows helps the monthly XGBoost forecast only a little: about 1% lower error at both, mostly in the first scored months, when the history was shortest. Cutting 6 months is not safe, because it made D18 worse. The larger problem at D15 is a level error that no start cut fixes: the median forecast is about 21 points of capacity too low, against 3 for the generalised additive model (GAM) stack, so the next experiment should look at D15's level, not its start. also relevant 00396 xgboost-recipe-screen-demand-calendar-winter-hyperparameters-ensemble-summary At least one change in each of five families (calendar columns, winter weather columns, hyperparameters, ensemble-summary inputs, a split of the model by lead band) lowers the days 1 to 10 CRPS of the weekly member of experiment 87, refitted monthly, by more than the refit noise floor at the signed-MW six or the MVA-only eight Primaries, and the families that act on a specific slice (holiday days, winter and the top demand quartile, high ensemble spread) gain more on that slice than on all rows. partly supported candidate Giving the weekly XGBoost demand model the ensemble's view of the weather, either its mean and spread or a model trained on the ensemble mean, lowered the error by 0.4% to 2.7% in both test months, and no other change we tried did so as clearly. Holiday columns help on Easter bank holidays but raised the error on all days in January and at the signed-MW six at Easter, and winter weather columns do not help, so a full-year test should start with the ensemble-input arms. also relevant 00394 xgboost-ensemble-mean-and-std-columns-separately Experiment 389's gain from four ensemble columns (the mean and standard deviation across the 51 members of temperature and of shortwave) comes mostly from the two mean columns, because the gain was largest at 0 to 24 hours and at the middle quantiles and absent at q01 and q99. supported not-for-production Giving the XGBoost demand forecast, as an extra input, the mean across 51 ensemble weather members of the temperature and of the shortwave radiation lowers its error (CRPS) by 0.052 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.029 points at the other 8. That is the whole improvement of four extra columns at the 6 and 82% of it at the 8 (0.035 points). The members' spread adds almost nothing, and it does not help more on days when the members disagree most. The tails do not materially improve with either input: on cold nights the forecast's 95% quantile lies above only 0.77 to 0.78 of outcomes at the 6. primary 00387 xgboost-folded-latent-loss-at-mva-only-primaries A single XGBoost model per Primary, refitted weekly with experiment 87's recipe but with a loss that scores the absolute value of a signed latent power against the metered apparent power (a folded loss), recovers the reverse-flow V-shape at the MVA-only Primaries that the plain model misses, and recovers a signed power forecast that agrees with known signed truth. not supported not-for-production Training the XGBoost model on a folded signed power did not improve the forecast at the eight Primaries whose meters report unsigned apparent power, and it did not fix the under-forecast of sunny half-hours at D12. The signed power it reports follows the start we gave it, not the readings, so it cannot yet be shown to NGED as a forecast. A signed forecast needs a structural way to fix the sign, such as demand minus a non-negative generation term. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00094 explicit-heating-offset-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, adding a per-series heating term to the XGBoost model's base margin lowers the forecast error in cold hours (ENS 2 m temperature below 3 C), because the term extrapolates linearly beyond the coldest training hour and cannot be damped at long leads, whereas trees predict a flat response there. The term is the heating degree-hours (15.5 C minus the temperature, floored at zero) times a per-series, per-hour-of-day coefficient fitted by least squares on the training window only. small gain candidate The heating term lowered the quantile score by 0.143 points of capacity in cold hours at leads up to 48 hours (98.75% interval -0.203 to -0.034), under the 0.3 threshold, and by 0.022 over all rows (-0.042 to +0.000). primary 00074 an1-same-time-analogues-vs-explicit-solar-forecast-demand At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, when the XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data (P-roll), an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output, given to the model as a starting offset (experiment 64's arm am), lowers the daylight April-to-September quantile score by more than same-time-of-day analogues do. An analogue is a recent day, at the same half-hour of the day and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday), whose satellite-based sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target. The model receives the observed power on the K nearest such days (K is 1, 3, or 5) as input columns. Once the explicit offset is in the model, the analogue columns add less than 0.05 points of capacity. inconclusive not-for-production Both ways of telling the monthly-refitted model about sunshine lowered the daylight error: the explicit forecast of the panels' output by 0.149 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and the 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007) against the reference. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). also relevant 00031 embedded-pv-features-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 trailing estimates of each substation's embedded (unmetered) solar capacity, built from the Embedded Capacity Register (ECR) as a prior for Primaries and a floor for BSP and GSP series, plus an amount learned from recent power and irradiance, lowers the quantile score on sunny days, and a linear PV offset or a sunshine-shaped correction does so more reliably than extra tree columns. inconclusive not-for-production C3, A3 (PV products with the register) minus B0, quantile score over all leads: +0.006 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.022 to +0.033). primary 00030 lagged-power-feature-sets-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 the 13 power lags that manual_heuristic uses (the same weekday and time of day 1 to 6 weeks back, and 49 to 55 weeks back), as separate columns beside N1's three lags measured from the forecast origin, lowers the quantile score. inconclusive candidate C3, all 13 lags minus N1 (seed 0 only): -0.01 points of capacity on the quantile score (99.375% interval -0.45 to +0.43). primary 00028 pvlive-forecast-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator a forecast of the GSP's solar generation at the target time, from a simple XGBoost model of Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate applied to ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather, lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without a solar forecast. inconclusive not-for-production C1, solar forecast minus no solar forecast, over all leads: -0.14 points of capacity (95% interval -0.34 to +0.04). primary 00027 pvlive-lags-in-stage2-gsp-demand For the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, giving the stage 2 calibrator Sheffield Solar's PV_Live estimate of the GSP's solar generation at the lag times, next to the lagged delta (metered demand minus the stage 1a expectation), lowers the quantile score below that of the same calibrator without PV_Live. refuted not-for-production C3, delta plus PV_Live minus no PV_Live, over all leads: -0.03 points of capacity (98.33% interval -0.13 to +0.09). primary 00025 price-change-features-stage1-demand Giving the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model the change in the intra-day price over the last half-hour, 1 hour, 2 hours, and 6 hours, in addition to the price at the target half-hour, lowers its error at observed power for Primary substations, and by more than the same columns built from a price taken from another week. Batteries and other dispatchable generation respond to how the price moves, not only to its level. small gain not-for-production On Primary substations, adding price changes to the price level lowered the error by 0.037 points of capacity in the selection year (97.5% interval -0.056 to -0.018) and 0.050 in the confirmation year (-0.083 to -0.018). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. also relevant 00015 same-time-price-stage1-demand Adding the intra-day price at the same half-hour as the target (Elexon Market Index Data, observed at time t, not forecast and not lagged) to the ERA5-trained stage 1 demand model, which already sees the weather at time t, lowers its error at observed power across all fitted series pooled, and by more than a price taken from another week does. inconclusive not-for-production C1, price against no price, pooled: -0.52 points (97.5% interval -0.88 to -0.11) in the selection year and -0.18 (-0.50 to +0.08) in the confirmation year. primary 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. also relevant 00011 school-term-and-return-to-work-columns-stage1a-demand For the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model at Primary substations in Lincolnshire, columns for the return to work after New Year and for Lincolnshire's school terms lower the mean absolute error of the median in the weeks after Christmas, at Easter, and in the half-term holidays, against the same XGBoost model with a Christmas column that is set only within 14 days of 25 December. refuted not-for-production Return and term columns against the base arm, Primary substations: +0.06 points from 2 to 20 January (99.2% interval -0.17 to +0.30), +0.20 over the Easter window (-0.19 to +0.59), and -0.29 over the half-term holidays (-0.68 to +0.07). primary 00010 elexon-price-lags-stage1a-demand Adding the Elexon Market Index Data price from exactly 7 days earlier to the ERA5-trained stage 1a demand model lowers its error at the substations that host price-responsive batteries, and does so by more than adding the same-lag national demand and wind output, which price follows. inconclusive not-for-production C1 at B2, price against base: -0.92 points (98.3% interval -2.10 to +0.07) in the selection year and -0.06 (-0.38 to +0.23) in the confirmation year. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. also relevant 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. also relevant 00006 stage1a-demand-input-feature-sweep For a weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 for substation demand, the local clock (hour of day and day of week) is the input that lowers the held-out error most, and the other non-lag inputs tested here (holiday encodings, time of year, trailing temperature means, sun position beyond zenith and azimuth, UTC offset, windchill, and a COVID indicator) each lower it by less. partly supported candidate P1, hour and weekday against the weather block alone, Primary substations: -0.55 (99.4% interval -0.71 to -0.41) on the selection year and -0.46 (-0.61 to -0.30) on the confirmation year, the largest single input but about a third of the predicted size. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather)
docs.text:
This theme covers the demand model of a six-part series on forecasting with physical terms.

Background: Differentiable physics: background explains the models in plain terms.

The series builds models of Primary substation demand from a daily profile, holiday and heating terms, and a solar term, fitted by gradient-based optimisation. This theme holds the part that builds the model and asks whether more years of history help it. The series' finding so far is in experiment 104: the convex model trained on 12 months beat lagless XGBoost with its default start by 0.25 points (post hoc), and all years with drift are level with 12 months, so more years are not yet shown to help. Experiment 63 is an earlier, smaller linear test of the same decomposition into a weather baseline, a solar term, and transfer terms. The Experiments page lists every experiment, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00413 differentiable-physics-demand-network-part-1 A pooled network that forecasts Primary demand as a Primary-specific mix of shared learned daily shapes plus a Primary-specific mix of shared learned temperature and solar responses, with a plain mixture density head on the residual, scores within 0.03 points of the pooled plain mixture density network on the 2026-01 fold, and its learned curves can be read. not supported not-for-production A neural network built from shared, readable parts (learned daily shapes and temperature responses) forecast substation demand less accurately than the plain neural network on five test months: by 0.17 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.23 points at the other 8. Its error in the middle of the distribution was larger at both groups. At the six it covered the highest outcomes better, but at the eight it was worse in both tails. Under the default rule the design does not advance, and whether to pursue it is the maintainer's call. primary 00281 economy7-night-step-smooth-in-temperature A forecast of primary substation demand whose night level is a set of free levels for each UTC night half-hour (experiment 121's NS-U), and then a step whose size is a monotone function of the cold, scores better in the Economy 7 step hours and on cold winter nights than the same forecast with only the winter night offset (experiment 155), when the weather input is the ensemble-mean forecast and not past weather. Economy 7 is the tariff that switches storage heaters on shortly after 00:30 UTC. Experiment 121 found a gain of 0.233 points on winter nights on past weather and asked for a test on weather forecasts. inconclusive not-for-production Fitting the Economy 7 night levels inside the demand model, and not adding a winter night offset afterwards, lowered the day-ahead error by about 0.02 to 0.03 points of rated demand over all rows in both years and by about 0.04 points on winter nights, but the gain in the two hours after the step starts could not be shown: it changes sign between the two years and depends on two or three substations. Letting the step grow with the cold added almost nothing over free night levels. The Economy 7 term does not explain the night-time gap at D10 in April to June. primary 00279 dp-heating-curve-monotone-lagged-temperature-and-wind The heating response of the convex demand model T-all-K (a hinge at 15.5 C on four trailing-mean temperatures, split by day type) is too rigid. A smooth, monotone, non-negative curve on the same temperatures (A1), the same curve also on exponentially weighted and previous-day mean temperatures that carry the building's thermal lag (A2), or a small monotone neural network on three daily mean temperatures and the wind speed (A3), lowers the day-ahead quantile score on cold nights and winter days at the five decision Primaries, and the fitted curve is not a straight line. not supported not-for-production A smooth heating curve, a thermal lag, and wind each leave the day-ahead forecast within about 0.02 points of the straight-line heating response, so the evidence does not justify adding any of them. A small neural network learns a plausible curved heating response and lowers the error on cold nights by 0.13 points, but that gain comes from one cold spell in January 2026, did not appear in the previous year, and the network failed a test on synthetic data, so the substation card keeps the straight line for now. primary 00198 d8-summer-spikes-cooling-load-and-residual-test The summer spikes a colleague saw in D8's power (time series 26, Marsh Lane) are air-conditioning load: they rise smoothly with temperature, peak in the afternoon of the hottest days, and repeat every year. The best-guess forecast has a heating hinge but no cooling term, so its summer residual (metered minus forecast) rises with temperature, and a cooling hinge on the ensemble mean temperature fitted on past residuals lowers its summer score. inconclusive not-for-production D8's afternoon power does not rise with temperature, and its large summer departures from expected power are mostly downward shortfalls of 1.5 MW or more, which grow from 18% of summer half-hours in 2022 to 52% in 2025, so the spikes are not air-conditioning load. A cooling term added to the best-guess forecast changed the summer score at the five decision Primaries by 0.0002 points (interval -0.010 to +0.015), but the 4 fit months held too few hot days and the known-answer control failed, so the experiment cannot rule a cooling term out. On afternoons of 25 degrees Celsius or more, metered power exceeds the forecast by 0.6 to 5.1 points on average at each of six Primaries, so a term fitted on the full multi-year history of past weather, pooled across Primaries, is the next test. primary 00173 dp-christmas-more-years-and-sites The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors and recipe R (the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, held to 0.75 of its size), which scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday over 24 December to 2 January at five substations in two Christmases (experiment 170), keeps a Christmas-to-weekday error ratio under 1.3 in every Christmas back to 2019-20 and at 14 or more of 16 Primary substations, and does not over- or under-forecast 25 and 26 December by more than 5% of that day's demand. inconclusive not-for-production Where the demand model had a winter of training data, the error over 24 December to 2 January was 0.97 to 1.22 times an ordinary weekday in all four Christmases from 2022-23 to 2025-26, so no special-day term is justified. The pre-registered run failed because the training rows of Christmas 2020-21 and 2021-22 (and of one substation in 2023-24) held little or no winter, since the lockdown window is left out of training. A forecast for a substation with under 180 days of usable history should be flagged, not trusted. also relevant 00145 differentiable-physics-analog-day-error-correction-on-gam-k Averaging GAM-K's past day-ahead errors over the days most similar to the target day (same day type, with holiday identity for holidays, similar forecast daily mean temperature, and a season window of a few weeks either side of the date) gives a better correction than averaging the last 14 days alike (recipe R of experiment 115) or the same-day-type days of the last few weeks (experiment 134). The reasoning is that demand errors repeat on days that resemble each other. The errors that repeat most, on holidays and on cold days, are the ones that a 14-day average dilutes. small gain candidate Averaging the errors of the 20 most similar past days (same day type, within 13 weeks of the same date, last year's days included) beat recipe R (the 0.75-weighted mean error of the last 14 days) by 0.041 points at day D+1, the calendar day after the forecast origin (about 1.7% of R's score of 2.436). That gain is larger than the 0.011 points that the weekday term of experiment 134 gained. Matching on forecast temperature helped by only 0.005 points, and copying the error of the same holiday last year made holidays worse, so the next step is a day-type profile with a season window and no correction copied from an earlier holiday. also relevant 00143 differentiable-physics-holiday-aware-updating-of-the-gam-k-filter The Kalman filter of GAM-K lets a holiday's reading error teach it a wrong level, which carries into the days after the holiday; leaving holiday readings out of the filter's update (and nothing else) lowers the day-ahead score on those following days, and does not hurt the holiday targets or the rest of the year. not supported not-for-production Leaving holiday readings out of the day-ahead filter's update does not reliably help the days after a holiday: the effect had the opposite sign after Christmas 2024 and Christmas 2025, and its 99% interval in the scored year (-0.309 to +0.036 points) includes zero. In 10 of 12 holidays, the holiday readings' error had the same sign as the error on the following days, so these readings are not usually contamination. Setting the correction to zero on holiday days, as experiment 118 did, is the action that hurts (+0.62 points on holiday days). Two Christmases give no basis for changing the filter this Christmas. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. primary 00126 differentiable-physics-s1-cheap-screens-added-to-gam-k Each of six families of cheap additions to the day-ahead convex model GAM-K lowers its score after the Kalman filter, winter first: a free or monotone temperature curve (A-free, A-mono), exponentially smoothed temperatures (S-ewma) or smoothed daily extremes (S-mm), wind chill (C-wind) or apparent temperature (C-hw) inside the heating hinge, a school-term term (D-sch), lighting from solar elevation (E-sol), and a filter whose noise differs by regime (F-mix). A second family of four exploratory screens: a switching Kalman filter with three hidden regimes (G-skf), a learned periodic basis for the year cycle (W-basis), a soft cold/mild mixture of heating slopes (W-mix), and a cross-substation anomaly from weather-station residuals (W-stn). One hypothesis per arm, in "Arms" and "Four exploratory screens". inconclusive not-for-production None of the thirteen cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lowered the winter score by a margin we can trust. E-sol (lighting from solar elevation) came closest, at -0.036 points on dark winter evenings, but its interval (-0.122 to +0.024) is too wide to call, because six of the thirteen screens had a half-width above their 0.03 to 0.05-point margin. Only W-basis (learned year cycle) was clearly worse, in every month, site, and year. F-mix and W-stn looked worse too, but each rests on 2 to 3 calendar months. G-skf found injected load transfers 4 to 7 times as often at 25% and 40% transfers as the plain filter, but failed its own power gate and recovered no faster. primary 00123 differentiable-physics-e7-storage-heating-night-step-estimation At Primary substations, demand steps up in the half-hours from 00:30 to 02:30 on winter nights, the step grows with cold, and the pooled step over the six decision series is positive at a daily mean of 3 C. At D5, D10, and D16, which were chosen because winter 2025-26 showed the step, it is 5 to 10 points (1% of each series' 99th percentile of demand); at the other decision series it is smaller. inconclusive not-for-production The night step at Primary substations is about 10 points on a 3 C day, where one point is 1% of a substation's near-peak demand, and it starts around 01:00 and looks fixed to UTC rather than the local clock (a check chosen after seeing the data). The rise on cold winter nights is the feature an operator would see: the day-ahead forecast runs 6 to 10 points below actual demand from about 01:00 at D5 and D16 on the two pre-registered winters, and at D10 in winter 2024-25 alone (7.6 points at 01:00); at D10 in winter 2023-24 the baseline is instead 9 to 17 points too high all night. The step appears at 13 of the 14 substations, and its full size rests on summer nights having no step, which the gate cannot test. The verdict is inconclusive because the gate is weaker than it looks: it holds one real test of the interval, and that test under-covers. primary 00122 differentiable-physics-three-winter-backtest-gam-k On past weather, the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K) forecasts Primary demand one day ahead better than both the plain convex model (GAM) and lagless XGBoost, in each of the three winters 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26, by at least 1 point of mean absolute error. supported not-for-production In all three winters, the convex demand model with the recent-error filter (GAM-K) forecast Primary demand one day ahead 1.8 to 3.1 points of capacity better than the same convex model without the filter, and 2.0 to 3.1 points better than lagless XGBoost. The gain is consistent with the filter removing a level error that a fit frozen for a year carries, and lagless XGBoost has no recent power to correct the same error. GAM-K's filter settings were fitted on the 2023-24 winter, and the convex model's ridge penalty was tuned on a year that contains the 2024-25 winter, so those two gains are partly in-sample. 2025-26 has the least tuning leakage, but it was read in an earlier analysis before this plan, and no winter is clean on both counts. A post hoc check at the audit subtracted each plain model's own winter-mean error at each substation, which no forecaster could know in advance: GAM-K stayed ahead of the plain GAM by 0.63, 0.71, and 0.35 points and ahead of lagless XGBoost by 0.95 to 1.05 points, so 5 of the 6 contrasts would miss the 1-point bar. Most of the gain is therefore level tracking, and this result does not show that GAM-K beats a model that sees recent power. The scoring uses past weather, so the gain under live weather forecasts is unknown. primary 00121 differentiable-physics-mh-multi-hinge-heating-curve-and-night-step In the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K), on past weather, replacing the single fixed 15.5 C heating hinge by five hinges (10, 12, 14, 16, and 18 C) with non-negative slopes, so the heating curve never falls as it gets colder and stays convex, lowers the day-ahead quantile score after the recent-error filter. Second question (NS): GAM-K leaves a 4 to 7 point step at 01:00 on winter nights at three substations (a pattern like storage heating switching on), and a night-step term lowers the score on winter nights without worsening the other rows by more than 0.02 points. Indexed in UTC against local time, the winning indexing is reported. inconclusive candidate Adding night-time levels indexed on the UTC clock lowers the day-ahead error on winter nights by about 0.23 points after the recent-error filter, at all 5 substations in both winters, and the forecast then shows the 01:00 jump in demand that the current forecast misses on cold winter nights. Five heating bends instead of one gain only 0.016 points, within noise. The synthetic tests could not show that a step this small can be detected, so the night result needs a test on weather forecasts and an audit before it enters the model. primary 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00114 differentiable-physics-n3-n4-interactions-and-heating-threshold Two labelled claims about the convex model of Primary demand in the form Part 6 made the DP's candidate (GAM-K: 24 months, no drift, pinned capacity, Kalman filter), on past weather. N3: interaction terms (heating by day-type group, heating on eight sub-band blocks, lighting by day-type group), each shrunk towards the base by a difference penalty, lower the day-ahead quantile score after the filter. N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. primary 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. also relevant 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics (demand, calendar, and weather): research plan
docs.text:
The cheap screens of inputs to the convex model are bundled into one experiment. Experiment 104 found that all years of history without drift scored worse than 12 months, and that a drift held constant recovered that. The recent-level drift and the day-type filter are covered by the KFE experiment, so this page lists the input screens only.

Experiment Question Priority Waits for State N3 and N4, interaction terms and heating threshold Do interaction terms in the convex model, and a heating threshold chosen per substation, lower its error? Done, partly supported None Interaction terms (N3) gained, mostly at one substation, and the per-site heating threshold (N4) tied (experiment 114) S1, cheap screens added to GAM-K (experiment 126) Do cheap additions to the day-ahead GAM-K lower the score, winter first? Done, inconclusive None None of 13 screens showed a trusted gain; E-sol (-0.036 on dark winter evenings) is the lead for a retest on ENS weather; W-basis worse in every month, site and year; F-mix, W-stn undecided on 2 to 3 months E7F, Economy 7 night-step term in the forecast (experiment 137) Does an additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors, lower the day-ahead score on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC? Running None Planned; plan committed before any code Weather encoder retest Does a small learned encoder over a patch of weather cells lower the error on hard cases (convective and frontal days, wind and solar sites) once the base forecast is recalibrated? 3 A plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, which experiment 119 found accounts for most of the encoder's gain Queued, after the recalibration

Later parts are listed in their own themes.

docs.title: Bundled cheap screens
docs.text:
The six screens share one experiment and run on 6 CPU cores in about 2 hours. Each has one hypothesis:

  • Free temperature spline. A free spline of temperature fits better than the fixed 15.5 °C hinge.
  • Smoothed temperatures. Temperature smoothed at two decay rates, plus smoothed daily minimum and maximum, adds skill to the convex model's means of 6 hours to 1 week. The GAM papers on regional load use these terms: Obst et al. (2021) for French load, and Fasiolo et al. (2021) for the winning GEFCom2014 entry. No paper isolates the gain from the smoothing alone.
  • Humidity and wind chill. Feeding humidity and wind chill into the heating hinge lowers the winter error.
  • School-term calendar. A school-term term lowers the error in term-time weeks, once data availability is checked.
  • Lighting from solar elevation. Lighting modelled from solar elevation beats a fixed clock curve on dark winter evenings.
  • Filter-noise mixture. A filter noise that depends on the regime (cold snap, mild, holiday) beats one fixed noise.

docs.title: Weather encoder retest
docs.text: The retest repeats the weather-encoder comparison on the hard cases, with a recalibrated base forecast. The encoder replaces single-cell inputs with a learned view of a patch of cells, and the aim is a lower error on convective and frontal days, when a single cell misses the neighbouring weather. Experiment 119, the first encoder experiment, ended inconclusive, and about two-thirds of its gain survived when the network read the wrong date's weather. The retest therefore waits for a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles, and runs on the GPU. The encoders technique page is the first thing to read.
