docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series models Primary substation demand from physical terms. This theme covers what the connections between Primary substations add: power flowing along the interconnections between neighbouring Primary substations when the network operator switches load from one to another, and a forecast of demand under the normal running arrangement (NRA), with those transfers removed. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. also relevant 00204 dp-bsp-full-bottom-up-with-signed-mva-children A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down when the sum covers every child Primary. Experiment 161 summed only the three children per BSP that report real power (MW) and have a long history, which reached 42% of D13's effective capacity and 56% of D17's, and the bottom-up forecast scored 0.5% to 0.6% worse than the top-down forecast. This experiment adds the children that report apparent power (MVA). A child's apparent-power reading is the magnitude of its flow, so a child with reverse flow at midday needs a signed flow before it can enter a sum. The fold-aware model of experiment 152 supplies that signed flow as a latent variable. inconclusive not-for-production Adding every child Primary to the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point: the bottom-up score matched the top-down score (+0.1% at D13, -0.15% at D17), and the intervals include zero. Converting the children that report apparent power to signed flow changed the score by at most 0.03 points, at the one bulk supply point where a child has reverse flow. Even with every child's reading known exactly the BSP's score gains only 12% to 24%, and the children's forecasts gave no detectable gain over the BSP's own chain, so the next gain may lie in forecasting the generators and the unmetered load beneath each BSP. also relevant 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. primary 00131 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-drift-term Adding a slowly varying offset to each substation, fitted jointly with the flows on the interconnection edges, lets the flow fit find injected transfers that last hours to days without putting flow on pairs of substations that are not connected, which experiment 116's fit could not do. inconclusive not-for-production Letting each substation drift slowly did reduce the load that the fit wrongly moves between substations that are not connected, by half to three quarters at an equal or higher detection rate. It did not remove that false load, and the settings that keep it near zero find only about half of the transfers we added artificially and report them too small. In the replicate year part of the false load sits in two jumps in one substation's data that nobody had labelled. We therefore cannot yet read these flows as switching events. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: the network: research plan
docs.text: The proposed next steps are a topology check on candidate flows, or a smaller level penalty combined with a check for unlabelled jumps; neither option is planned. Experiment 116 ended inconclusive because the known-answer gate failed: every setting that found injected transfers also found flow between substations with no interconnection. Experiment 131 added a per-substation drift term. At equal or higher recall the drift term cuts the flow on unconnected pairs by half to three quarters, but no setting meets the recall targets and the placebo limit together, and the level penalty shrinks the flows the fit finds.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. The differentiable-physics series builds models from physical terms (demand, heating, solar) whose parameters are fitted by gradient descent. This theme covers whether one such model fitted across many Primary substations can match a model per substation, and beat it for a new substation or one with a short history. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, with its verdict and a take-home message, and the Research plan lists what is planned next. Experiment 112 found that fitting the pooled model exactly did not remove its gap to per-substation models: with the interaction network on, the exact fit forecast far too high on four days.

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00200 dp-pooled-correction-head-on-kalman-state Experiment 142's small network failed its known-answer gate with about 1,100 samples from one year at five substations. The same kind of network, trained on rows pooled across many Primary substations and years, learns to correct arm D's forecast from the recent errors, the calendar, the lead, and the ensemble-mean weather, and so beats recipe R (subtract 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days) at day D+1. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network trained on arm D's own past errors lowers the day-ahead score by 0.07 to 0.12 points at five substations, but a copy that sees no recent error gets most of that gain. The gain comes from correcting how arm D's error depends on its forecast level and the calendar, and a pinball-loss table comes within 0.01 to 0.02 points of the network on one year of data. also relevant 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) fitted jointly across six Primary substations, so that each substation's heating curve, lighting curve, daily profile, holiday effects, and Christmas shape are a fleet mean plus a penalised deviation of its own, forecasts better than the same model fitted to each substation alone, now that the solar capacity is pinned and the filter handles recent switching. The mechanism is that a substation sees only two winters and two Christmases in a 24-month window, so its own curves are noisy, and five other substations carry information about the shapes that physically are shared. Capacity, level, and the band means stay per substation. The gain is largest for a substation with 3 months of history and on Christmas rows, and no pooled arm is worse than the per-site fit by more than 0.02 points on ordinary rows. partly supported candidate In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. primary 00154 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-2-heating-error-against-truth When the partly pooled convex regression model of experiment 109 is fitted to only 4 winter weeks of one substation, its fitted heating curve is closer to the injected truth than the curves of the no-pooling and complete-pooling fits. The curve is as close to the truth as a fair oracle's curve (within 10%). The model recovers the sign of the substation's own heating offset relative to the fleet's curve. The fleet's shared curve is recovered as well as an average of per-site fits recovers it. partly supported not-for-production On synthetic substations with a known answer, a partly pooled demand model fitted to 4 winter weeks of one substation estimated that substation's heating response with a smaller error than fitting the substation alone (2.8 to 3.6 against 4.1 to 11.5 points of capacity) and than copying the fleet's curve (3.4 to 4.6), on every seed. It recovered the fleet's shared curve about as well as separate fits did. Neither the pooled fit nor the fair oracle recovered the sign of the substation's own heating offset reliably (the pooled fit got the sign right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds), so on these synthetic fleets and one January, a partly pooled model can share the heating curve but cannot learn a substation's own offset from 4 weeks. primary 00150 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-rerun-fair-oracle-five-seeds When the reference estimator estimates every coefficient from the same 4 weeks of rows (so that no coefficient is fixed at its true value), the partially pooled convex model of experiment 109 recovers the injected truth about as well as that reference on most of 5 random seeds, and its tuning rule picks a deviation penalty within one grid step of the best one on most of the 5 seeds. inconclusive not-for-production The rerun of the synthetic known-answer test could not say whether the pooled model shrinks substation deviations correctly, because a control that keeps no deviation at all passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when 4 June weeks were held. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 synthetic substations on every seed, the tuning rule picked a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error was below a fair reference estimator's on 5 of 5 seeds. The full-history line passed on only 2 of 5 seeds. A post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks separated the controls, so a test that scores heating error against the injected truth in winter should settle the question. primary 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. primary 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. primary 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. primary 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00112 differentiable-physics-vp-variable-projection-fit-of-pooled-model Part 3's pooled DP lost to the per-site DP because gradient descent did not reach the optimum, not because pooling hurts: solving every linear coefficient exactly at each step, with gradient steps only on the non-linear parameters, makes the pooled DP at least as good as the per-site DP on substations with 2 years of history. inconclusive not-for-production Solving the pooled model's linear coefficients exactly did not make its forecasts better. With the interaction neural network on, the exact fit drove the network's last layer and the seasonal and holiday terms to very large, weakly penalised values: it forecast up to 280 points too high on four days of spring 2026 (the weekend of the clock change, Good Friday, and Easter Monday), and it was 0.7 points worse on the other days. With the network off, the exact fit is stable and within 0.03 points of the gradient fit, so the optimiser was not what held the pooled model back; the known-answer test failed, and with the network on the model cannot recover heating even from noise-free data. primary 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. primary 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). primary

docs.title: Differentiable physics: pooling across substations: research plan
docs.text:
The rows below are the planned and proposed experiments of this theme, in priority order (1 is first). Experiment 105, the first of the theme, is finished: pooling helped a new or short-history substation and was worse at full history.

Experiment Question Priority Waits for State Onboarding design (proposed) Does a pooled model for onboarding and a per-site model for mature substations beat either alone? 2 Experiment 105: pooled onboarding scored 4.04 against 14.38 for a per-site model on 4 weeks, and was worse at full history Proposed Part 4 (proposed) Does a drift term (a slowly changing demand level), trained from 2019-09, beat the same model on its best window? 3 Experiment 112 (finished: an exact variable-projection fit did not improve the pooled model, and its known-answer test failed at realistic noise) Proposed Part 5 (proposed) Does the MVA observation layer (a model of how a meter that reads apparent power relates to real power) help the MW sites and recover MW at MVA sites? 4 Experiment 105 and a better capacity fit Proposed N9, scale-up Does the pooled model on every v1 series it can take, including MVA substations, improve full-history skill and capacity identification? 5 Nothing; 3 to 5 GPU hours Queued BSP as a Kalman observation Does treating the BSP reading as an extra observation in the Kalman filter improve the Primaries' forecasts? 6 Experiment 124 (finished: a BSP term in the joint fit raised clean-forecast error) Proposed Top-down against bottom-up Does a direct forecast at a BSP or grid supply point (GSP) beat the sum of the Primary forecasts, and does reconciling the levels help either? 7 The closure audit Proposed Metered generators in the graph Do metered generators, entered as export-positive nodes at the BSP, make the BSP relation close better? 8 The closure audit Proposed Unmetered wind at higher levels Can unmetered wind at the BSP and GSP be estimated as the part of the residual that follows the wind forecast? 9 The closure audit Proposed

Experiment 109 gives the pooled convex model N for the next experiments to start from, and experiment 150 reran its known-answer gate. The rerun was inconclusive: capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% at 8 of 8 substations on 5 of 5 seeds, the tuning rule was within one grid step of the best penalty on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error beat a fair oracle's, but the shrinkage line could not tell a good fit from a bad one on 4 June weeks. Experiment 154 then scored the heating error against the injected truth on 4 winter weeks: the pooled fit beat no pooling and complete pooling on 5 of 5 seeds and recovered the fleet's shared curve as well as separate fits, but the sign of a substation's own offset was found on only 2 of 5 seeds, by the fair oracle no more reliably.

Experiment 158 fitted GAM-K's shared curves jointly across six substations. A substation with 3 months of history scored 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (-0.629, 99% interval -1.639 to -0.091), and a substation with 24 months scored the same as without pooling (+0.004, -0.006 to +0.014).

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: N9: scale-up
docs.text: The proposal fits the pooled model on every v1 series it can take, including MVA substations through the Part 5 meter layer. More substations, and the sunlit rows of MVA substations teaching the solar term, should improve full-history skill and make capacity better identified. The experiment runs no onboarding arms. It starts from experiment 109's convex pooling if the gate rerun supports it, and otherwise from per-site fits with the shared meter layer. It needs 3 to 5 GPU hours.

docs.title: Hierarchy: Primaries, BSPs, and GSPs
docs.text:
Experiment 124 found that adding the BSP reading to the Primaries' fit raised clean-forecast error at every weight tried. The raise was 0.4 to 4.6 points of capacity, although the reading cut the damage from injected metering errors by about 41%. The closure audit found that the Primaries and generators close one of the two BSPs up to factors of 0.85 to 1.16, and an exactly specified synthetic system lost clean accuracy the same way, so the cause is untested. Experiment 36 had found that the sum of Primary forecasts added nothing at the two BSPs.

Three facts shape the design:

  • The remainder is large. In the data checked, the BSP residual has a daily-mean standard deviation larger than the typical switched load, so the audit has to say what the remainder contains before any constraint uses it.
  • The GSP relation cannot be closed. Most of the power at each GSP is unmetered.
  • Reconciliation helps the aggregates most. Nespoli et al. (2022) found that reconciling cut the aggregate error by up to 10% and the bottom-level error by under 1%, and Brégère and Huard (2022) found that most of the gain came from mixing in other nodes' forecasts, not from the constraint. The expected gain at the Primaries is therefore small, and the proposals below aim at the BSP and GSP levels.

The BSP as a Kalman observation tests whether the closure relation, with its unmetered remainder as state noise, helps the Primaries' filters. It runs on the CPU in about 2 hours.

Top-down against bottom-up at the BSP and GSP levels asks which direction gives the better forecast at each level. The arms are a direct forecast of the BSP, the sum of the Primary forecasts plus the generators, and a minimum-trace reconciliation of the two, each scored at both levels. The topology is soft, not a hard sum: the hierarchy enters as a hint that the levels should roughly agree, because the unmetered remainder makes an exact balance wrong.

Metered generators enter the graph as export-positive nodes at the BSP. The Primary series are the disaggregated demand, which already has the metered generators taken out, and the generators connect at the BSP busbar. Adding them as nodes should make the BSP relation close better. Their series are generator data, so any published figure shows them only as an anonymised, capacity-normalised series, never beside a name.

Unmetered wind at the BSP and GSP levels is invisible at the Primaries and may show up higher. The audit's residual, regressed on the weather forecast's wind speed at the BSP, would give a first estimate of how much unmetered wind sits there. The estimate only counts if the wind-driven part of the residual is separate from the solar part, so it waits for the audit.

docs.title: Generator forecasting
docs.text:
For 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms over one validation year, the largest gain was from the Met Office's UKV weather forecast at wind farms, about 0.2 points of capacity at 24 to 54 hours ahead (a small gain: its interval excludes zero but not the pre-registered 0.15), measured on a research archive and not the live feed, so it is an upper limit. No input met its pre-registered gain threshold. Seven of the eight experiments scored forecasts for Tuesday runs from July 2025 to June 2026. The eighth tested a monitor for a lost inverter at the solar farms, and it reliably found only large, long losses. No experiment in this theme is a candidate for production.

UKV is the Met Office's 2 km weather forecast for the UK. Most experiments start from the ENS weather forecast and ask what one added input does. A negative difference in a score means a better forecast, and a point of capacity is 1% of a farm's effective capacity.

At 24 to 54 hours ahead, adding UKV lowers the wind farms' quantile score by 0.198 points (95% interval -0.316 to -0.069), whereas a shuffled copy of UKV changes it by +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040). Source: experiment 54. The bars for lead day 0 are exploratory.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A second weather forecast helps wind farms a little and solar farms by an amount the data cannot resolve. For wind farms, experiment 54 gave UKV's wind to an XGBoost model trained on ENS. The quantile score fell by 0.198 points, a small gain because the interval's near end (-0.069) did not reach the pre-registered 0.15. The gain was -0.413 at one farm and +0.018 at another (exploratory). For solar farms, experiment 57 found -0.035 (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037). That interval excludes gains above 0.12 points and includes the 0.10 that would justify a new weather feed, so the verdict is inconclusive. Both experiments read UKV from the CEDA research archive, whose licence is non-commercial and which differs statistically from the live feed, so each result is a ceiling on what a service could get.

Averaging in two more weather forecasts did not resolve a wind gain. In experiment 52, averaging the quantiles of the best guess with those of the same model fed ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast scored -0.055 (95% interval -0.200 to +0.072) at lead days 1 and 2. The experiment fed runs about half a day older than the ENS run, with uncorrected winds, so it tested a handicapped version of the idea. At days 3 to 6 the blend scored +0.122 (+0.028 to +0.221, worse), because of the spread factor.

Recent power added nothing detectable. In experiment 23, giving the second-stage calibrator (see stages 0, 1a, and 2) the farm's lagged power changed the CRPS by -0.012 for solar (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088) and +0.012 for wind (-0.090 to +0.146). The 14-day correction raised the CRPS of the pooled mixture by +0.437 for solar (+0.215 to +0.664) and +0.413 for wind (-0.003 to +0.924), and cut the 5% to 95% band's coverage to 53% to 77%.

A recent-capacity feature and fitted physics gave no gain, and new training inputs gave small ones. These experiments score the CRPS, except experiment 12, which scores the mean absolute error of the 51-member average.

  • Recent-capacity feature (experiment 26): solar -0.018 (98.75% interval -0.162 to +0.096), wind +0.013 (-0.054 to +0.101). One solar farm gained 0.235 points and another lost 0.085.
  • Fitted physics model in place of the XGBoost stage 1 (experiment 29, 6 solar farms): +0.079 (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135), worse. Adding the physics output to the XGBoost columns changed nothing (-0.000, -0.015 to +0.018).
  • Satellite sunlight (CAMS) as the training input (experiment 12): -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044) for solar (6 farms), just short of the pre-registered -0.15. A power-curve base margin for wind gave -0.030 (-0.061 to -0.007), and a training start in 2023 or 2024 moved the error by under 0.3 points.

On 5 solar farms with artificial losses added, only a 25% loss was found reliably (0.84 to 0.86 for the best monitor at 90 days, and 0.86 for the hysteresis rule at 30 days), and a 10% loss mostly was not. Source: experiment 72. The change-point monitor found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, which breached the pre-registered stop rule of 0.80, so the verdict is refuted. A hysteresis rule (alarm after 7 valid days at least 10% below normal) found 0.86 of the 25% losses lasting 30 days but 0.13 or less of 10% losses. The monitor beat neither baseline by an interval that excludes zero: against the rolling median its difference in detection rate was +0.045 (97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). A farm gives about 3 usable days a week from April to September, and the only real losses held were one farm's three low months.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
No recipe tested here beat the best guess by a pre-registered, resolved margin, so the best guess remains the reference for solar and wind farms. The best guess for farms is a pooled mixture over the 51 ENS members of XGBoost quantile models trained on ERA5, with a spread factor and, for wind, a power-curve base margin. Experiments 23, 26, and 29 used the same mixture without the spread factor as their benchmark.

  • Wind, 24 to 54 hours: an XGBoost model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind scored 5.921, against 6.119 for the same model without UKV and 6.337 for the best guess (experiment 54). The contrast with the best guess is exploratory, -0.416 (-0.693 to -0.136), and UKV comes from the research archive.
  • Solar, 24 to 54 hours: the ENS-trained model scored 3.140 and the best guess 3.247, a difference of -0.107 (-0.327 to +0.053) that cannot be resolved (experiment 57). Adding UKV scored 3.105.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: None of the eight experiments is a candidate: all are marked not-for-production. The wind result of experiment 54 would need a matched history of the live UKV feed, and the Open-Meteo history the experiment found reaches lead day 0 only.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Add a shuffled-input arm beside every arm that adds input columns. The shuffled UKV changed the wind score by +0.013 and the solar score by +0.002, so the gain was not extra columns (experiment 54, experiment 57). In experiment 26 the shuffled solar feature scored 0.023 worse than no feature, so a contrast against the shuffle and one against no feature differ (experiment 26). Re-check: a different model or a larger set of columns.
  • Call a UKV result from the CEDA archive a ceiling. The archive is not the live product, so the gain may not reach a service (experiment 54, experiment 57). Re-check: a matched live UKV history.
  • Say whether night rows are in a solar score. Experiment 57's pooled score includes night rows, which score near zero, and its daylight-only contrast was -0.074 (-0.259 to +0.079), so check the size on daylight rows as well (experiment 57). Re-check: a pre-registered daylight-only threshold.
  • Do not add the mean-error 14-day correction to a farm forecast. Observed power minus the median is positive on average for a right-skewed target even when the quantiles are calibrated, so the correction adds a bias, and coverage fell to 53% to 77%. The post hoc median version scored +0.010 (solar) and -0.064 (wind), with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). Re-check: a daily history, which experiment 23 lacked, because its weekly runs left at most two runs in a window.
  • Test recent power in a calibrator trained on pooled members. The calibrator trained on the ENS control member alone scored 0.27 (solar) and 0.31 (wind) points worse than the pooled mixture in the absolute scores (the contrast interval for wind includes zero), so the lag test used a weaker baseline (experiment 23). Re-check: a calibrator trained on pooled members.
  • Fit a spread factor under the weights the blend will use. A factor fitted on earlier months blended under other weights made the blend +0.122 worse at days 3 to 6, against +0.005 without it (experiment 52). Re-check: a factor refitted after each weight change.
  • Feed other weather products the runs the service would read. Experiment 52 used runs about half a day older than ENS and uncorrected winds, so its null result may understate the products (experiment 52). Re-check: 00 UTC runs of the ENS run's date, with bias-corrected winds.
  • Read per-farm contrasts, and treat intervals as covering these farms only. The intervals resample months and not farms. The UKV gain was -0.413 at one wind farm and +0.018 at another, and one solar farm drove the point estimate of experiment 26 (experiment 54, experiment 26). Re-check: more than 6 solar and 3 wind farms.
  • Test fitted orientation against a different irradiance-transposition model. A test with the fitted model's own physics showed a tilt bias of +0.11 degrees, and a different sky model showed +6.2 (experiment 29). Re-check: a different fitted physics model.
  • Score a monitor on the unmodified record as well as on a placebo. The change-point monitor's false-alarm rate was 0.29 per farm-year on the week-shuffled placebo and 0.54 on the real record, where one farm's winter dip raised 6 of 18 alarms (experiment 72). Re-check: another year of record.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the live UKV feed gives wind farms the gain the research archive did, which needs a matched live history at lead days 1 and 2.
  • Whether solar farms gain from a source of a different kind, such as a satellite-based nowcast, since UKV here added little, and a second global ensemble added under 1% to the sunshine forecast at five Primary substations (experiment 50, as experiment 57 reports it).
  • Whether a wind feature of 75th-percentile power over wind speed cubed helps. It scored -0.061 (-0.107 to -0.025) in experiment 26's contrast C5, one of its 12 contrasts and outside the 4 that decide the verdict.
  • Whether CAMS-trained solar models hold their -0.140 on more than 6 farms or a second year.
  • Whether a loss of 10% or less at a solar farm can be found from outage notices or trip logs, which need labelled events.
  • Whether ENS-trained wind models beat the ERA5-trained best guess at 24 to 54 hours: -0.218 (-0.472 to +0.069) in experiment 54.

The Experiments page lists every experiment in this theme, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Generator forecasting: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00433 solar-idle-noise-data-look H0: the six metered solar farms read exact zeros, or smooth small values, when they are not generating, so the wind farms' idle-noise texture (exact zeros and repeats, quantised values, and a floor above zero that does not follow the season) is absent and no detector or cleaned-zero score is needed for solar. supported not-for-production The metered solar farms read exact zeros at night, unlike the wind farms' noisy floor, so solar forecasts need no idle-noise detector and no cleaned-zero scoring. One farm (Solar B) shows small negative night readings on 8% of night half-hours, and two farms (Solar D and Solar E) have idle runs of 17 to 24 days on clear days, which is an outage question, not a noise question. also relevant 00432 wind-cleaned-zero-rescore The maintainer wants a wind forecast to say zero where the farm should output zero, and an evaluation that never asks the forecast to predict the idle noise. If the half-hours that the experiment 210 mask flags as idle are scored against a target of 0 (the cleaned-zero row set), then a forecast that puts its lower quantiles at zero below the turbines' cut-in speed is no longer penalised for the farms' idle floor, so experiment 336's zeroing arm x1, which lost on the raw readings, wins or ties on the cleaned-zero row set. partly supported not-for-production Scoring idle half-hours as zero output does not change which wind forecast is best, and forcing the forecast to zero below cut-in gains nothing: that arm ties the default (-0.002 points, interval -0.008 to +0.004), because the default already forecasts near zero there. The mixture-head arms keep at most a 0.02-point lead on cleaned zeros (none if every ERA5-flagged half-hour is zeroed), against 0.04 on raw rows and 0.23 on masked rows, because those heads rarely forecast zero when the farm is idle. Cleaned zeros can be a headline row set for experiment 429 beside the raw set, but not in place of it. primary 00431 wind-idle-data-look H1: the idle floor of each metered wind farm has a texture (exact zeros, repeats, a quantised step, small first differences) that genuine low output at the same power level does not have. H2: idle half-hours at high wind (a whole-farm outage or maintenance) follow a weekly cycle, because maintenance is done on weekday daytimes and weather-driven idling has no weekly cycle. partly supported not-for-production A cheap rule that looks at how jumpy a wind farm's recent readings are can tell idle readings from genuine low output at the same power level at two of the three farms, so the texture detector stays in the design. Idle readings at high wind do not follow a weekday-daytime cycle, and the stored series show no idle run of 7 days or more; Farm C has runs of several days that low wind cannot explain, so the whole-farm outage class stays for Farm C at the 1.5-times-cut-in speed (not at the empirical cut-in) and is weak at Farm A and Farm B. Farm A cannot be tested for texture from its power alone. primary 00430 unified-forecaster-solar-and-pretraining-ablations A pooled mixture-density network for the six metered solar farms needs, beyond experiment 345's solar-only pooled network (the demand-style default: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, no pretraining, a clipped Gaussian mixture), only those of four switches that an ablation shows to help: the 51 ensemble members passed through a shared encoder one by one (A2), a PyTorch fleet plant that adds a power channel (A5), ERA5 and CAMS pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the ensemble (A6), and point masses at zero and at capacity in the output (A7). refuted not-for-production One pass of a neural network on the ensemble mean and spread is enough for the six solar farms: none of the four richer designs we tested beats it by the 1% margin. For the 51 coherent member paths that NGED's power-flow modelling needs, reorder the one-pass network's 51 quantiles with a Schaake shuffle, which scores 13% better than ensemble copula coupling on the variogram score of the paths and the same on the energy score. Passing each member through the network alone gives paths that score 11% worse on the energy score and a marginal quantile score 1.5% worse. also relevant 00429 unified-forecaster-wind-ablations A single pooled neural network can forecast the three metered wind farms as well as Wind farms research default 2 (experiment 347's y2: a frozen ERA5-trained power curve run on each of the 51 ensemble members, followed by a mixture-density head). Each difference between that design and the Primary-demand design (experiment 425's arm A: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, an unbounded head) is kept only if an ablation shows it is needed. partly supported not-for-production Neural wind forecasts do not need the extra machinery. A plain pooled network fed the ensemble members ties Wind farms research default 2 (10.533 against 10.518 points), and neither passing members through the network (-0.008 against the one-pass design), a power-curve layer (+0.000), nor a censored head (+0.018, worse) changes the score by the 0.10-point margin. The weakness all arms share is the upper tail: 2.2% to 2.8% of observations exceed q99, because the forecasts under-predict windy half-hours, and censoring did not fix it. The plain network is the design that matches the default; the upper tail is the open problem, and the architecture comparison does not explain it. primary 00357 wind-default-2-monthly-head-longer-retest Retraining Wind farms research default 2's mixture head on the first day of every month (experiment 356's arm u3) gains over default 2 at true days 1 to 10, because a recent head tracks the farms' drift. Experiment 356 measured -0.038 points on 53 Tuesday runs (interval -0.104 to +0.024) and -0.120 on about 16 Tuesday runs of 2026-07 onwards. partly supported candidate Retraining Wind farms research default 2's head every month improves the forecast slightly, by about 0.04 to 0.05 points over the scored year and about 0.10 points in the latest 2.5 months, and no scope shows harm to the score. The scored-year interval still touches zero, so the change is a candidate and is not adopted. The upper tail stays too heavy (1.7% to 2.0% of observations above the 0.99 quantile), so retraining does not fix it. primary 00356 wind-default-2-blend-and-monthly-refit-retest Wind farms research default 2 (experiment 347's arm y2) gains 0.234 points over Wind farms research default 1 at true days 1 to 10 but puts 2.28% of observations above q99 over every lead (2.15% at true days 1 to 10). Either a per-quantile, per-lead-band blend of the two defaults (u2), experiment 348's arm z5 (u1), a monthly offset layer on default 2 (u4), or a monthly retrained head (u3) lowers the 0.99 pinball loss and the share above q99 without losing the gain. not supported not-for-production Blending Wind farms research default 2 with research default 1, or refitting it every month, does not fix its upper tail: the share of observations above the 0.99 quantile only falls from 2.15% to between 1.77% and 2.04%, against 1% intended, and no arm clearly beats default 2 over days 1 to 10. The blend's small gain (0.05 points) is the same with shuffled weights, so it is averaging, not learning. The top quantile needs new information, not a blend or a refit; the monthly retrained head is the one arm worth a longer retest. primary 00348 wind-plant-mdn-upper-tail Experiment 347's best arm (y2: Stage 3 frozen physics plant, 51 ensemble members through it, a three-component Gaussian mixture head on the summary of the resulting power values) beats Wind farms research default 1 by 0.234 points over true days 1 to 10 but is over-confident in the upper tail (2.3% of observations above q99 over every lead, and a 0.99 pinball loss up to 0.084 worse in experiment 347's report). One of five tail fixes (z1 tail-weighted loss, z2 capped quantiles with a point mass at the plant's scale, z3 monotone increments above q90, z4 z1 plus z2, z5 the solar recipe of a plant residual band blended with the default's XGBoost quantiles) brings the share above q99 under 1.5% and the 0.99 pinball loss to within the tolerance, while keeping the headline gain. partly supported candidate The frozen physics plant with a mixture head stays about 0.23 points of capacity better than the research default over days 1 to 10, but none of the four tail fixes inside the head brings the top quantile into calibration without losing score at that quantile, and none of their intervals excludes zero. Blending the plant's residual band with the default's XGBoost quantiles gains less (0.15 points) but is the arm of the five whose gain is clear and whose 0.99 quantile is no worse, so that recipe, not a better head, is the next step. primary 00347 wind-physics-hybrid-plant-then-mdn A physics plant model of each metered wind farm (a smooth cubic speed-to-power curve with cut-in, rated, and cut-out speeds, a direction-dependent loss, and priors that make the untrained model already sensible), fitted on ERA5 before 2024-04-01 and frozen, turns each of the 51 ensemble members into a power value. A three-component Gaussian mixture-density network (MDN) fed the summary of those 51 values, the lead, and the farm then scores within 0.15 points of Wind farms research default 1 on the kept rows at 1 to 10 days, without a neural adapter. A second plant fitted after masking the blocks where the farm fell short of the first plant (a healthy-farm plant) lets the head learn the shortfall. partly supported candidate A physics model of each wind farm, run on every ensemble member and corrected by a small neural network, forecasts 0.27 points of capacity (2.4%) better than the research default over leads of 0.5 hours to 15 days, and 0.23 points over true days 1 to 10, but the neural network given only the plant's median and the farm already gets 83% of the gain, and the upper tail is still over-confident. The next step is to fix the upper tail (the neural network caps its quantiles at capacity, and 0.9% of observations exceed it) before any plant-based arm is adopted. primary 00346 wind-research-default-1-offset-table-refit-cadence Experiment 342 found that the default's offset table, fitted once on the 442 daily runs of 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-16, leaves the upper tail too low in the scored year (observed power above q99 in 1.8% of half-hours against 1% intended) although it fits the hindcast, and blamed drift between the hindcast years and the scored year. The ensemble table holds daily runs up to 2026-10-24, so the table can be refitted each month on runs that had already finished. A table refitted monthly on a trailing 6-month window (x2) scores lower than the table fitted once. partly supported candidate Refitting the wind forecast's offset table every month on recent runs makes the forecast a little better (a 0.4% to 1.1% lower quantile score), using only data the service already stores. It does not fix the upper quantiles, which still miss in 1.7% of half-hours against 1% intended. So the change between the training years and the scored year is a minor cause, and the upper-tail miss needs another explanation. A monthly job that refits the table on all earlier daily runs passes the adoption conditions and is a candidate. primary 00345 pooled-solar-wind-mixture-density-network One mixture-density network (MDN) trained once for all leads on the six metered solar farms and the wind farms together, with a fuel-type indicator and weather inputs common to both fuels, scores as well on each fuel as that fuel's best single-family model, and scores better for a farm with no history. partly supported candidate One neural network trained on all six solar farms forecasts each farm as well as a separate network on the physical plant model (within 0.8%), so a production forecast could use one neural network per fuel. Adding wind farms to the same network does not help either fuel and makes solar 0.7% to 2.3% worse, so solar and wind are better trained separately. In this experiment, a wind farm with no history scored 18% worse at day 1 when trained on public wind farms alone than when trained on other metered wind farms. also relevant 00344 wind-research-default-1-speed-dependent-offsets Experiment 340 found that a constant upward shift of the wind quantiles gains 0.09 to 0.12 points on the kept rows but worsens the rows below cut-in by 0.51 to 0.78, and that the default's median is too low at 8 to 15 m/s and too high below 5 m/s. An offset that depends on the ensemble-mean 100 m wind speed at forecast time lifts the quantiles where the power curve is steep and leaves them alone where the forecast is near zero, so it keeps the gain without the low-wind harm. The starting point is Wind farms research default 1, the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored, and the lead range is 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production Letting the wind forecast's quantile offsets depend on the forecast wind speed gains only about 0.02 points of capacity when fitted on the same retrospective forecasts (hindcast runs) that fit the quantile offset table, and the gain cannot be told from zero. Fitted on the six months just before the scored year (July 2025 to June 2026), the same speed-dependent correction gains 0.146 points and does not worsen the half-hours where the forecast wind speed is below the turbines' cut-in speed. The speed-dependent bias is therefore real, and it changes from year to year. Refitting the correction on recent months is the untested option that could capture it. primary 00343 wind-research-default-1-train-on-ensemble-mean Wind farms research default 1 trains XGBoost on ERA5 and runs it on each of the 51 ensemble members, then corrects with the offset table. The ensemble's 100 m wind speed at the grid cell is lower than at the turbines (a factor of 1.13 closed 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle in experiment 307). An XGBoost model trained on the 51-member mean of the ensemble's own history (arm M, 2024-04 to 2025-06, no calendar columns) would learn that bias and need less offset-table correction. Arm MS adds the member standard deviation of the 100 m and 10 m speeds. The three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored at 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production A wind model trained on the ensemble mean needs almost no offset table (the table changes its score by 0.017 points, against 0.345 for the default), but its forecast is no better than the default's: 0.08 points worse on the headline rows, an amount the data cannot distinguish from zero, and worse at low winds and in the 0.99 quantile. The default's recipe (ERA5 training plus the table) stays; mean training is a simpler recipe that scores about the same. primary 00342 wind-research-default-1-upper-tail-offsets-and-head The upper quantiles of Wind farms research default 1 are too low: in experiment 324 the observed power exceeded q99 in 1.8% of half-hours (1% nominal) and q95 in 6.7% (5% nominal). Three corrections fitted on the hindcast can fix that without harming the headline score. x1 is a table of offsets for q90 to q99 that also depends on the ensemble-mean wind speed. x2 is a small boosted-tree head, fed the default's quantiles and summaries of the ensemble members' wind speed, that adds offsets to q90, q95, and q99. x3 lets the share of ensemble members above the farm's saturation speed set a probability mass at the farm's scale. not supported not-for-production The wind forecast's upper quantiles miss too often (observed power exceeds q99 in 1.8% of half-hours against 1% intended), and corrections fitted on past forecasts do not fix that: the offsets keyed by wind speed, the tail head, and the mass at the farm's cap all leave the share at 1.8% to 1.9% and change the upper-tail loss by about 1% or less. A head that sees the ensemble members does no better than one that sees only the default's quantiles, so in these 3 farms the members add no information about the upper tail. The remaining miss is consistent with the scored year differing from the hindcast years, which the next experiment could attack by refitting more often or by training on the most recent months. primary 00341 wind-capacity-steps-from-strong-wind For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), a change-point search on the upper quantiles (99.9th percentile and maximum) of observed power in the half-hours when ERA5 wind is well above the speed at which the fitted power curve saturates finds a loss of 25% of capacity within 60 days at W1 and W2, with fewer false alarms than experiment 233's ratio monitor under a 9% seasonal swing. Steps come in whole turbines. Weighting lower-wind half-hours by the inverse of their speed-error variance speeds detection up. A neighbouring farm in the same ERA5 cell cancels the shared speed error. not supported not-for-production A change in a wind farm's usable capacity shows up in time only when it is large: a loss of half the capacity is found within 60 days at 91% to 93% of start dates at all three farms, and a loss of a quarter at 26% to 77%. Looking only at the strongest winds, as proposed, does not help, because strong wind fills 0.18% to 1.1% of half-hours and most 28-day blocks hold too few of them. The real records show repaired episodes (a 2-week outage at W1, a loss of 17% and of 31% at W2, a loss of about one of two turbines at W3 from October 2024 to January 2025) and no permanent step. primary 00340 wind-research-default-1-constant-shift-then-low-wind-drop Experiment 336 found that dropping the ERA5 training rows below the turbines' cut-in speed (x2) gains 0.117 points on the kept rows, and its audit traced about 85% of the gain to a constant upward shift of the quantiles. If that is right, a constant shift fitted on the 442-run hindcast (arm S) reproduces most of the gain without changing the training rows. Arm S+X2, which also drops the low-wind rows, then adds little beyond the shift. Wind farms research default 1 is the starting point, the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored, and the lead range is 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production A single upward shift of the wind quantiles, fitted on past forecasts, does nothing, because the forecast's offset table already fits those runs. Moving the quantiles up by 0.8 to 1.2 points of capacity does reproduce most of the gain of dropping low-wind training rows, but it also worsens the forecast at low winds by 0.5 to 0.8 points, the same harm that stops X2 being adopted. An untested option that could lift the forecast at 8 to 15 m/s and leave it alone below 5 m/s is a correction that depends on wind speed. primary 00339 wind-research-default-1-adapter-plus-mixture-head A three-component Gaussian mixture head on the hindcast, fed the quantiles of the physics core plus adapter and the ensemble members' summaries of speed, direction, and temperature (experiment 324's W4), lowers the quantile score of Wind farms research default 1 on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads. The head loses on the idle half-hours because it is trained on kept rows only, and the maintainer's view is that a forecast-time rule (predict the idle floor where the ensemble-mean wind speed is below cut-in) needs no idle detector. Three arms are tested: x1 the head as in experiment 324, x2 x1 plus the rule, x3 the head trained on all hindcast half-hours. partly supported candidate A small neural-network head that re-draws the physics-plus-adapter wind forecast's quantiles gains 0.27 points of capacity (2.4%) on the farms' normal half-hours and keeps that gain on the replicate months, but the same head given no weather summaries does as well, so the gain is a recalibration that a simpler correction partly reproduces. A simple rule that predicts the idle floor at low wind recovers none of the head's loss on the idle-band readings, and training the head on those readings removes the gain. primary 00338 wind-adapter-column-without-neural-network The gain of experiment 326's arm (c), the neural adapter's effective wind speed as an extra XGBoost column, can be kept without a neural network: a lookup table of speed scale by direction sector, speed ratio bin, and temperature bin (x1) keeps at least half of the gain, and a small monotone gradient-boosted tree (x2) keeps at least 80%. not supported not-for-production A lookup table of wind-speed corrections keeps almost none (5%) of the gain that the neural adapter gave the wind forecast, and boosted trees keep about half (0.051 of 0.099 points of capacity, scored at 1 to 10 day leads). Neither passes the adoption rule, so the neural adapter of experiment 326 is the only arm tested that does, and the maintainer decides whether it belongs in the production service. A non-neural column would need to reduce the physics-based wind-power model's error on ERA5 as much as the neural network does. Boosted trees with more inputs might approach that. primary 00336 wind-research-default-1-below-cut-in-zeroing The maintainer proposes that, for wind, rows where the wind speed is below the turbines' cut-in speed carry only noise, so zeroing them lowers the quantile score of Wind farms research default 1 on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads. Three readings are tested, each added alone: x1 sets the forecast to zero power whenever the ensemble-mean 100 m speed is below the farm's cut-in speed, x2 drops the ERA5 training rows below cut-in from the XGBoost model and the offset table, and x3 sets the training target to zero on those rows. At most one is adopted, in the order x1, x2, x3. partly supported candidate Setting the wind forecast, or the training target, to zero below the turbines' cut-in speed does not improve the forecast, because the farms still produce small real output there. Leaving the low-wind rows out of training gains 0.12 points of capacity (about 1% of the default's score) on the kept rows, but mostly by lifting the quantiles upward, which a constant upward shift may reproduce (not yet tested). primary 00326 wind-research-default-1-change-arms Each of four changes, added alone to Wind farms research default 1, lowers the quantile score on the kept rows of the three metered wind farms W1 to W3 at 1 to 10 day leads: (a) 2 m temperature and an air-density column as XGBoost inputs, (b) hour of day and day of year as XGBoost inputs, (c) the ERA5-trained neural adapter's effective wind speed as an extra XGBoost column, and (d) one wind-speed scale factor, fitted on the hindcast to the implied wind, applied to every member's 100 m speed before the XGBoost model. At most one is adopted, in the order c, b, a, d. supported candidate Feeding XGBoost the neural adapter's corrected wind speed lowers the wind forecast's score by 0.10 points of capacity, about 0.9% of the default's score, at 1 to 10 day leads (99.75% interval -0.19 to -0.01). The change is negative at every farm and at short and long leads. The three other changes were not separable from zero. Only a port that puts the adapter in the production service can use the gain, so the maintainer decides. primary 00324 wind-farm-solar-cross-breeds-long-run The solar-farm findings (a mixture-density network (MDN) fed by a physical plant forecast beats the plant alone, lead features help it, and one pooled head across leads matches separate heads per lead band) carry over to the three metered wind farms W1 to W3, when the plant is the physics core with the experiment 285 wind-speed adapter and the weather is the 51-member ensemble. partly supported not-for-production A small neural network that corrects the quantiles of the wind farms' physics-based forecast lowers the quantile score by 0.27 points of capacity against XGBoost plus a lookup table of offsets, on the half-hours when the farm is not idle, at days 1 to 2 and at days 3 to 10. The gain disappears when the idle half-hours are included. The upper tail gets no better. The network needs the farm's own forecast history to learn from. primary 00313 metered-farm-pure-xgboost-and-mdn-vs-plant A predictor built only from weather and calendar inputs, with no plant model anywhere in the pipeline (not even as an input column), scores close to the plant-based forecast in own history and falls behind it where the plant carries what missing history or a long lead cannot. partly supported candidate A forecast that sees only weather and the calendar, with no physical plant model anywhere, scores almost as well as the plant-based forecast for the six solar farms, up to 10 days ahead, even when the farm has no history. The plant's added value is small, between 0% and 3.4%, and its intervals include zero except for XGBoost. For wind, the same kind of network also matches the best plant-based forecast, so a plant model is not needed to be competitive on these farms. also relevant 00307 wind-farm-power-as-wind-sensor The wind that the three metered wind farms' own power implies (the fitted physics core's power curve run backwards) is closer to a high-resolution analysis than to ERA5 at 9 to 14 m/s, and at least half of the ensemble's shortfall (observed power below the forecast's median on 34.1% of rows instead of 50%) is in the spread and timing of the members, not in their mean speed. not supported not-for-production The ensemble's low wind-power forecast comes mostly from wind speeds that are too slow, by about 1.1 m/s on average and more at longer leads. Multiplying every member's wind speed by a factor fitted on the 14 months before the scored year closed about 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle, while widening the members or shifting them in time closed almost none. The median is slightly better calibrated when the factor is fitted to the wind that the farms' power implies than when it is fitted to ERA5 on the same rows (1.7 percentage points), but the quantile score is not better. primary 00303 wind-adapter-in-production-setting Experiment 285 found that, with ERA5 as the weather, a small neural adapter in front of the physics core of a wind farm scored better than XGBoost. On the 51 ensemble members in the scored year, an adapter fine-tuned on the ensemble hindcast beats XGBoost plus experiment 259's offset table (the benchmark that matters), because the adapter corrects the wind speed itself and the table corrects only the power. partly supported not-for-production A small neural correction of the wind speed, fitted to ERA5 and run on the 51 ensemble members, does about as well as XGBoost with a lookup table of offsets (0.09 points better, too little to justify porting). Fitting the correction on the one year of ensemble hindcasts made the forecast worse, probably because that year differs from the scored year; we did not test the cause. primary 00288 pooled-head-on-public-wind-farms A neural head that adds 11 quantile offsets to the XGBoost wind forecast (R0) and was trained on dozens of public onshore wind farms (metered output from Elexon's Balancing Mechanism Reporting Service) lowers the quantile score of the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3) against R0 alone, and a head trained on the pool beats the same head trained on W1 to W3 only, because experiment 259's head had too few farm-years to learn a correction that transfers. A second hypothesis: XGBoost keeps improving as the training history grows from 12 to 48 months while the physics core is flat after 24 months, and a pool of public farms replaces the missing history. not supported not-for-production Training the correction on 40 public wind farms did not help the forecasts for the three NGED wind farms. Applied directly, it made them worse, because the public farms' capacity, turbine rating, and hub height let the head memorise each farm. Without those inputs it did no harm, and after a short fine-tune on the three farms' own data it gained about as much as a simple offset table fitted on those farms, so the public farms added nothing measurable. primary 00285 wind-effective-wind-adapters A small bounded correction of the wind speed that the physics core of a wind farm reads, learned from the wind direction, the 10 m to 100 m speed ratio, the 2 m temperature, and the hour of day, closes at least half of XGBoost's lead over the core on the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3) when ERA5 is the weather. A correction of each ensemble member's wind speed towards ERA5's removes the ensemble's low bias. partly supported candidate The physics model of a wind farm matched XGBoost once a small neural network adjusted the wind speed it takes as input, so XGBoost's lead can be reproduced by a smooth correction of wind speed. On the ensemble weather, mapping each member's wind speed to ERA5's helped by 0.31 points but fixed only a small part of the ensemble's low bias, and a lookup table of power offsets by lead day helped more. primary 00276 wind-xgboost-vs-physics-gap-diagnostics The XGBoost model beats the physics core on the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3) because it learns the metering noise (the reactive-power floor of the apparent-power series, the deadband, and the dip near cut-in) that the physics core ignores. refuted not-for-production XGBoost beats the physics model of the wind farms because it corrects the wind speed using the wind direction, the 10 m wind, and the hour of day. It does not learn the metering noise: the lead is as large on rows without idle readings as on all rows. No change to the physics model's power curve, spread, or scale closed more than about a sixth of the gap, so the next step is a flexible correction to the physics model's wind speed. primary 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a lead-dependent mixture of the ECMWF ensemble's member forecasts, the AIFS ensemble's member forecasts (both run through experiment 230's ERA5-trained XGBoost wind model A0r), and climatology lowers the quantile score and the 0.99 pinball loss against the ECMWF members alone, after both are corrected by a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm; and a small neural gate that reads the two ensembles' spread and disagreement chooses better weights than weights by lead alone. partly supported candidate Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. primary 00261 wind-low-bias-decomposition The low bias in the three metered wind farms' forecast (observed power below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%) comes mostly from the ensemble's weather input, not from the core, the farms, or the mixing of the 51 members. partly supported not-for-production The wind forecast's low median comes mostly from the ensemble's weather: its 10 m and 100 m wind speeds are slower than ERA5's, and the same physics core fed ERA5 wind has 52.8% of rows below its median. Mixing the 51 members adds about a tenth of the shift, and training the physics core and the XGBoost model on 9 months of ensemble forecasts removes between a fifth and a third of the gap. The fix to test next is a correction of the ensemble's wind speeds before the model reads them. primary 00259 wind-plant-plus-quantile-offset-head For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a small neural network that reads the 51-member mixture of a wind model and the ensemble's wind summaries, and adds an offset to each of 11 quantiles, lowers the quantile score against the wind model alone (R1, the physics core), matches the XGBoost best guess (R0), and lowers the pinball loss at the 0.99 quantile, once it can learn from daily runs of the ensemble forecast over 15 months (about 440 runs) instead of the 13 to 40 Tuesday runs that experiment 221's head saw. partly supported candidate A correction learned from 15 months of daily ensemble forecasts lowered the wind forecast's quantile score by 4.5% to 5.5% on the three metered wind farms, but the neural network and the ensemble's wind summaries were not what earned it. The 51 ensemble members' median sits too low: the observed power was below the physics core's median on 34% of rows, not 50%. A lookup table with one offset per lead day, quantile, and farm recovers 92% of the gain. The open question is where that low bias comes from. primary 00256 wind-temperature-density-shear-columns Adding 2 m air temperature (arm T1) to the six wind columns of the XGBoost wind model lowers the quantile score on the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), because air density and stability change the power a turbine produces at a given forecast wind speed. A density column (T2) carries the same information as temperature, and a shear and solar-elevation column set (T3) adds a further gain at night. partly supported candidate Giving the XGBoost wind forecast the air temperature helps a little, about 0.7% of the score, and the evidence just misses the bar we set beforehand. Columns that carry the time of day and the season help more, and their gain sits in daytime and summer rows. That pattern is not explained by the air density we could test (a function of temperature alone) or by shear, and it is consistent with a correction for biases in the ensemble wind at certain hours and seasons. A repeat on other months would show whether the time-of-day and season columns still help. primary 00242 wind-physics-core-part-3-member-tails For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), running each of the 51 ensemble members through an ERA5-trained wind model and mixing the 51 forecasts gives better 0.01 and 0.99 quantiles than running the model once on the ensemble mean of the weather inputs and applying the same spread factor, because the model is non-linear near cut-in and rated wind, so a model of the mean weather is not the mean of the model. supported not-for-production Keep running all 51 ensemble members through the wind model. Running the ensemble mean once raises the error at the 99% quantile by a factor of 2.1 for the physics model and 3.3 for XGBoost, probably because averaging the members removes the high winds that produce full output, and the single spread factor tried here does not repair that. The physics model and XGBoost differ by under 0.01 points on the tails, so the choice between them does not matter here. primary 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 A small XGBoost residual model on the plant forecast's median error, an XGBoost spread model for the quantile offsets around it, or both, close at least half of the gap in quantile score between the XGBoost-free metered solar forecast (the plant fed the mean and spread of 51 ensemble members, experiment 224's arm 3) and the full XGBoost forecast (experiment 224's arm 5) at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. also relevant 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 For Primary substation demand, a metered solar farm, and a metered wind farm, the best forecast that uses no XGBoost anywhere scores within 2% of the quantile score of the best forecast that uses XGBoost, at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. also relevant 00233 wind-physics-core-part-2-capacity-availability For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), the ratio of observed power to the power that the fitted physics core of experiment 230 expects, taken over the half-hours when the core expects rated power and averaged over a trailing 60 days, shows an injected capacity loss of 25% within 60 days of the loss starting, at every farm, and raises no alarm on a slow drift of the observed power of the size seen in the flat top of metered solar farms (experiment 183). not supported not-for-production A monitor that compares observed power with the wind-turbine model only in strong wind, where the power curve is flat, cannot show a 25% loss of capacity in time at any of the three wind farms, because strong-wind half-hours are rare: a trailing 60-day window holds enough of them to give a reading on only 21% of days at W1, 45% at W2, and 5% at W3. A variant added after the results were seen, which uses every half-hour at 20% of maximum output or more, finds a 25% loss with a median delay of 27 days at W1, 52 at W2, and 34 at W3, but a smooth 9% seasonal swing then raises false alarms, and a 10% loss is found at only 27% to 73% of start dates.
