The next step to test is a monitor on the whole power curve with a seasonal baseline; the real series also shows single months with low output (W2 in winter 2025 to 2026, W3 in 2024 to 2025) that nothing here explains. primary 00230 wind-physics-core-part-1 For the three metered wind farms (W1, W2, W3), a physics core fitted by gradient descent (hub-height wind from the ERA5 100 m and 10 m speeds, an air-density correction, a smooth monotone power curve with a cut-out, and an idle layer for the reactive-power floor of the MVA series) run through the 51 ENS members scores within 0.1 points of capacity of the XGBoost best guess (experiment 33) on the quantile score, and the measured gap between the ERA5-input ceiling and a simple power curve is under 0.02 points, which would mean the 25 km weather cell, and not the turbine physics, limits the forecast. not supported not-for-production A physics model of a wind farm, fitted to the three metered farms, forecasts them slightly worse than the XGBoost best guess, so it should not replace it. Most of the forecast error comes from the error in the ensemble wind forecast, not from the power curve: with ERA5 wind as the forecast, the same physics core cuts the score by 43%. The idle layer and the small neural adapter add nothing, and training the physics core on ERA5 instead of the ensemble control member improves it by 0.4 points. primary 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. also relevant 00221 wind-correction-head-on-stored-predictions A small neural-network head, fed the nine quantiles of the wind best guess (experiment 33's ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve base margin and the spread factor) plus the ensemble mean and spread of the 100 m wind speed and the direction sector, lowers the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 against the best guess by at least 0.1 points of capacity. The head is pooled over the three farms and trained on earlier months only. inconclusive not-for-production Training a small neural network to correct our wind-farm forecast did not help at 1 to 2 days ahead: the best version scored 0.05 points better and the version that also sees the weather forecast scored 0.18 points worse, with intervals that include zero. With only three farms and 9 scored months, the network may learn the months it trains on and narrow the forecast band too far on the next month. The stored forecast's band was already near the best width. A different kind of correction, or many more farms, is the next thing to try. primary 00210 wind-idle-noise-mva-artefact H0: the noise in the three metered wind series (W1 and W3 in MVA, W2 in MW) occurs only at low wind speed, because the meters have a deadband, the reactive power drifts, and reactive power control runs only while the turbines turn. If H0 holds, a rule on ERA5 100 m wind speed alone, with no observed power, finds the rows to drop from training and evaluation. not supported not-for-production The noisy near-zero rows in the three metered wind series do not occur only at low wind. A rule on ERA5 wind speed alone drops about 9% to 15% of half-hours but still misses about 60% of the idle-band half-hours, probably because ERA5's 25 km cell is a poor guide to the wind at each farm (untested). The rows this experiment flags are stored for the main wind experiment to use, and W3's first 2 years are a candidate to drop. primary 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00072 p35-step-loss-monitor-for-solar-farms For the 5 metered solar farms with a long record (labelled A, B, C, D, and F), a monitor can find a loss of generating capacity, such as a lost inverter, from the farm's own power telemetry. The monitor divides each day's power by the power a physics model expects on clear, unclipped hours, divides that ratio again by the same day's ratio at the other farms, and fits a piecewise-constant level to the result with an L0 penalty (an optimal-partitioning change-point fit). It finds a 25% loss that lasts 30 days, starting from April to September, within 28 days of its onset in at least 80% of injections, at no more than 0.5 false alarms per farm-year. It finds more injected losses of 10% than two simpler monitors that are tuned to the same false-alarm rate: a rolling median of the same signal, and the hysteresis rule of the capacity studies (called HYST here) run on the same signal. refuted not-for-production A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, below the 0.80 the plan needed, so the verdict is refuted. On 10% losses it did not beat a rolling median by an interval that excludes zero (+0.045, 97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). primary 00057 product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms For the six metered solar farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's shortwave radiation, total cloud, and temperature as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead hours 24 to 54 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. inconclusive not-for-production Giving UKV forecasts to an ENS-trained solar-farm model changed the quantile score by -0.035 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), which is too small to resolve. The data cannot show a gain and cannot rule out the 0.10-point gain that would justify a new weather feed. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms. primary 00054 product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. small gain not-for-production Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to an ENS-trained wind-farm model lowered the quantile score by about 0.2 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval 0.07 to 0.32), and a shuffled-UKV placebo shows the gain is information and not extra columns. The UKV data come from a research archive and not the live feed, so the gain is an upper limit on what a service could get. primary 00052 more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, averaging the quantiles of the experiment 33 wind best guess (the ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve margin and the spread factor) with the quantiles of the same ERA5-trained model fed ICON-EU's and IFS 0.25 degree's forecast wind lowers the quantile score at 1 to 2 days ahead, with weights chosen only on earlier months. inconclusive not-for-production Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts, ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast, scored 0.055 points of capacity better at lead days 1 and 2, but the 95% interval (-0.200 to +0.072) includes zero. Three wind farms cannot show whether the extra forecasts help, and the blend scored 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6. primary 00029 physics-stage1-solar-pytorch For the 6 metered solar farms, replacing the XGBoost stage 1 with a differentiable PyTorch physics model (priors on tilt, azimuth, DC capacity, and the AC-to-DC ratio, fitted to metered power with CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature), applied to each ENS member and followed by a per-farm quantile XGBoost stage 2, gives a lower continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) than the pooled XGBoost mixture of experiment 00020. refuted not-for-production C1, PyTorch physics stage 1 minus the XGBoost stage 1: +0.079 (98.75% interval +0.029 to +0.135), worse. primary 00026 capacity-features-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving each farm's stage 1a quantile model a feature that states the farm's recent effective capacity (the 99th percentile of its power at the steps with the most irradiance for solar, or the most wind for wind, over the trailing 28 days) lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) of the pooled mixture below that of the same model without the feature. inconclusive not-for-production C1, the single 28-day feature minus no feature: solar -0.018 (98.75% interval -0.162 to +0.096), wind +0.013 (-0.054 to +0.101). primary 00023 lagged-power-and-error-correction-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving the stage 2 calibrator the farm's recent observed power (lagged power, or summaries of the latest day), or shifting the forecast by its own recent error (the 14-day correction of experiments 00017 and 00019), lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) below that of the same calibrator without recent power. inconclusive not-for-production C1, lagged power added to the calibrator: solar -0.012 (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146). primary 00012 solar-wind-stage1a-inputs-cams-and-training-start For the ERA5-trained stage 1a XGBoost model of the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, applied to the 51 ENS members and averaged, at least one change to the inputs (CAMS irradiance in place of ERA5 shortwave as the training input, a stage 0 model that calibrates ENS irradiance to CAMS, a clear-sky-ratio target for solar, or a power-curve base margin for wind) lowers the mean absolute error of the member average. inconclusive not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, solar: -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044), short of the -0.15 that counts as a gain. primary

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling
docs.text:
One XGBoost model shared by a group of Primary substations forecasts almost as well as one model per substation (0.15 points of capacity worse, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), but the one test of a substation outside the pool (8 Primaries, one seed) found fingerprints made it worse, and forecasts of the series beneath 2 bulk supply points added nothing.

Pooling means training one XGBoost model on the rows of several series, with the series identifier as a column, so that 20 models become 3 or 4. The pooling results are from one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026) on 16 Primary substations and 4 supply points, with ENS weather. The hierarchy results cover 2 bulk supply points and 2 grid supply points, and 4 series cannot separate the designs.

Every pooled arm scores worse than one model per series (positive is worse), by 0.15 to 0.29 points with the series identifier and 0.8 to 1.0 without it. Source: experiment 24; C1 to C3 and C5 to C7 use 16 Primary series, and C4, C8, and C9 use all 20 series.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Three or four pooled models score 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models on the 16 Primaries, inside the pre-registered margin of 0.30. The scores are the quantile score over all leads after the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 (the stack of experiment 19, with a half-life of 0.5 years). Per-series models score 5.32, one model per substation type 5.47 (C1, +0.15, 99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), and one model per capacity band 5.47 (C3, +0.15, +0.05 to +0.26). The type pools beat manual_heuristic (5.89) by 0.42 (exploratory, -0.68 to -0.19). The verdict is supported (experiment 24).

One model for all 20 series falls outside the margin. It scores 5.61 on the 16 Primaries (C2, +0.29, +0.19 to +0.42). On the 2 bulk supply points alone it loses 0.80 (0.64 to 1.00, exploratory, 95%), and the 4 supply points are too few to separate the type pools from per-series models (+0.03, -0.15 to +0.15, exploratory, 95%; experiment 24).

For Primaries, the number of models matters more than which series share one. Random groups of 5 score 5.47 on the 16 Primaries, the same as the type pools. On all 20 series the type pools beat random groups by 0.06 (C9, -0.13 to -0.01), and on the 4 supply points by 0.29 (exploratory, interval not given; experiment 24).

The series identifier is essential. Dropping it raises the score of the type pools by 0.82 (C7, +0.46 to +1.23) and of the all-series pool by 0.85 (C8, +0.72 to +1.00) (experiment 24).

Describing each substation with numbers added nothing to the identifier for series seen in training. Adding a substation's location, its mean level and shape over the training window, or its level over the previous 14 days to the identifier moved the score by at most 0.02 points (C1 to C4; C4, +0.02, 99.375% interval -0.05 to +0.10). The verdict is inconclusive by the pre-registered rule, though the data exclude a gain above 0.05. Training-window statistics alone, without the identifier, scored 0.01 points worse than the identifier (C5, 99.375% interval +0.00 to +0.02, inside the 0.15 margin; experiment 32).

A substation held out of the pool was forecast worse with training-window statistics than with no fingerprint (C7, +1.39, +0.99 to +1.91), and better with recent power statistics alone (post hoc, -0.23, -0.29 to -0.16, 95%). The test used 8 held-out Primaries, one seed, and a pool of 7 other series. The write-up suggests, without testing it, that 7 distinct fingerprints act as 7 identifiers (experiment 32).

Forecasts of the series beneath a bulk supply point did not lower its score. Adding the summed median forecasts of the Primaries and generators beneath a bulk supply point changed its score by +0.04 (99.17% interval -0.18 to +0.25) at Boston and +0.19 (-0.10 to +0.73) at Skegness. At the 2 grid supply points, generic wind and solar columns changed it by -0.02 (-0.06 to +0.03) and -0.04 (-0.13 to +0.07). The pre-registered rule marks the bulk-supply-point family and the wind-and-solar family refuted and the ERA5-trained family inconclusive, so the experiment is inconclusive (experiment 36).

The six planned contrasts all include zero; the two exploratory rows are the ERA5-trained N1 at the bulk supply points, and Boston's excludes it.

An N1 trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40, but its intervals span -1.8 to +1.0. N1 is the single-stage XGBoost quantile model. Only Boston, a bulk supply point, resolved a gain, of 0.41 (0.15 to 0.66, exploratory, 95%) (experiment 36).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the pooled designs tested, one model per capacity band or per substation type scored best, and with the 14-day correction none beat one model per series on the 16 Primaries.

  1. Train an XGBoost quantile model (experiment 24's recipe, N1 fitted per group instead of per series: 9 quantile levels, ENS control member, lead hour, calendar columns, three power lags, power scaled by each series' effective capacity) on 3 capacity bands (the series split into thirds by effective capacity) or 4 substation types. Each pool holds all 20 series, including the 4 supply points.
  2. Give every XGBoost model the series identifier as a categorical column.
  3. Apply the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15 to each series' quantiles.

The capacity-band and type pools score the same to two decimals (experiment 24). The pre-registered rule chose capacity bands because they have fewer models.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiment 24 is candidate; experiments 32 and 36 are not-for-production.

  • Pooled XGBoost models for Primary demand (experiment 24). The XGBoost forecaster would train 3 or 4 models instead of 20 and store them at 73 to 94 MB instead of 435 MB, for a loss of 0.15 points of quantile score on the 16 Primaries, with the 14-day correction. Each model would need the series identifier, and a new series would need a retrain. The test covered 20 series, so it says nothing about 2,500 substations.
  • Nothing from experiments 32 or 36 is ready. No fingerprint helped a series seen in training, and no forecast column lowered a bulk or grid supply point's score.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Keep the series identifier in every pooled model. Without it, the type pools lost 0.82 and the all-series pool 0.85 (experiment 24). Re-check with a different model type or a different pool of substations.
  • Score pooled arms with and without the 14-day correction. The correction lowers per-series models by 1.0 and type pools by 0.6, so type pools beat per-series models by 0.30 uncorrected (exploratory, 95%, -0.56 to -0.03) and lose 0.15 corrected (experiment 24). A ranking measured on one stack may not carry to another. Re-check if the correction changes.
  • Scale boosting rounds (the number of trees) with the pool size, or say they were not scaled. Experiment 24 fixed 500 rounds and depth 6, so the all-series loss may be partly lower capacity per series. Re-check with rounds scaled to rows.
  • Do not compare fit seconds across arms. Other sessions loaded the machine during the capacity-band and random-group fits of experiment 24, so only model counts and saved sizes are reliable. Re-check with timings on an idle machine.
  • Match a held-out substation's fingerprint window to the pool's. The held-out substation's 28-day statistics differed from the pool's 15-month ones, and using the whole window removed about two thirds of the C7 damage (post hoc; experiment 32). Re-check with a pool of hundreds of series.
  • Do not read the oracle's gain as headroom for forecasts. The oracle is the same XGBoost model given the observed values of the series beneath a bulk supply point. It lowered the score by 5.6 and 3.4, while forecasts of those series lowered it by none (experiment 36). Re-check if the child forecasts come from a different weather source.
  • Note how the columns of forecasts of the series beneath a supply point were built. Experiment 36 fitted them by time block, so a block's forecasting model saw months on both sides, and training used the ENS control member while validation used each member. Look for a gain that changes when the columns are fitted strictly out of time, or when training uses every member.
  • Do not compare supply-point scores across experiments 24 and 36. Experiment 24 applies the 14-day correction to all 20 series, including the 4 supply points. Experiment 36 left it off at supply points because experiment 21 found it unproven there, so its scores are uncorrected. Re-check when a supply-point experiment states which stack it used.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether pooling holds at hundreds of series, and for substations the pool never saw.
  • Whether supply points pool at all; 4 series cannot say.
  • Whether an N1 trained on ERA5 helps at supply points beyond Boston.
  • Whether one model shared across substations, with drift and long history, beats separate models. That is the subject of the differentiable-physics background and the sub-themes long history and drift and demand calendar and weather.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and Experiments lists every experiment. Experiment 103 appears there as also relevant: its data look fixes the rows and dates the pooled differentiable-physics model uses, and it has no pooling result.

docs.title: Hierarchy and pooling: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00434 demand-ensemble-copula-coupling-and-schaake-reordering-of-stored-forecasts The stored forecast of experiment 425's arm A holds 11 quantiles per Primary and half-hour. Drawing 51 values from those quantiles and assigning them to the 51 ensemble members by the rank of each member's 2-metre temperature (ensemble copula coupling, ECC) gives sample paths that match the observed dependence across Primaries and leads better than independent draws do, by more than the 5% coherence margin on the variogram score, without changing the marginal CRPS. A Schaake shuffle from past observed paths does at least as well as ECC. not supported not-for-production Re-ordering the stored demand forecast's 51 values by member temperature or by past observed paths does not give clearly better sample paths overall. Ordering by temperature made the paths about 7% less coherent across the 16 Primaries and 1.7% more coherent across leads at days 1 to 10 (13% at 12 to 36 hours, an interim band), and the effects cancel in the combined score. A Schaake shuffle from past paths was no worse than independent draws across Primaries and 3.5% better across leads at days 1 to 10 (interval -6.3% to -0.9%, below the 5% margin), so it is the stronger reference candidate if a step 2 runs the 51 members through the neural network. also relevant 00426 mdn-neighbouring-primaries-graph-and-bottom-up-design Information from the Primaries connected to a Primary improves the pooled plain mixture density network's forecast at days 1 to 2, the only leads at which recent power helps the signed-MW six, by more than simple neighbour statistics do. Residuals of the stored forecast of interconnected Primaries correlate more strongly than residuals of Primaries joined at random or by distance alone, and a network that passes messages along the interconnection graph beats both its own rewired-graph control and the simple-statistics control. not supported not-for-production In these tests, the recent forecast errors of a Primary's interconnected neighbours predicted none of its day-ahead forecast error, and adding them to a simple regression made it slightly worse on ordinary half-hours. A graph network over the Primaries therefore has no lagged-error signal to pass along, and none was fitted. A scaled sum of the forecasts of the Primaries beneath a bulk supply point scored 34% to 60% higher error than the network that sees the node's own readings, at two bulk supply points. Whether neighbours help inside load-shift events was not measured here, and experiment 404 tests it. primary 00425 best-mdn-architecture-assembly-with-ablations The pooled mixture density network that adds ERA5-and-CAMS pretraining (experiment 418) to the pooled plain network with the Primary embedding, the ensemble-summary inputs, the hand-made calendar columns, and the 1.15 widening (experiments 397, 403, 406, 407, 423) scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network without pretraining, and removing the Primary embedding or the widening makes it worse. partly supported candidate Pretraining the pooled mixture density network on ERA5-and-CAMS rows before fine-tuning it on ensemble rows lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.050 points of capacity (-0.078 to -0.021) at the six signed-MW Primaries and by 0.124 (-0.219 to -0.048) at the eight MVA-only Primaries. The gain is clear at the MVA-only eight and probable at the signed-MW six, where the interval just misses the registered bar of -0.03. The assembled network beat the monthly XGBoost recipe and BG2 at both of those groups and trailed BG2 at D15 and D18, so pretraining is a candidate for a numbered release of the production forecast and the Primary embedding is the component to protect. also relevant 00423 pooled-mdn-shared-date-time-encoder A small encoder that turns the half-hour of day, day of week, day of month, day of year, and the bank-holiday name into one learned vector, shared across the 16 Primaries, lets the pooled plain mixture density network share what it learns about holidays across Primaries and across holidays of one kind, so it forecasts bank-holiday weeks better than the hand-made calendar columns and is no worse elsewhere. not supported not-for-production A small calendar encoder shared by the 16 Primary substations did not forecast demand better than the 18 hand-made calendar columns. With holiday names and dates it scored 0.27 points of capacity worse (8% worse, in a range of 0.10 to 0.43) on the continuous ranked probability score at the six substations that report signed power, and with dates only it scored 0.37 worse. One possible reason, not tested, is that each day of the year appears only once or twice in the 24-month training window. The planned test on bank-holiday weeks could not detect any difference smaller than 0.34 points, and all five test months are interim. also relevant 00421 mdn-history-fingerprint-for-pooled-primary-demand A 1D convolutional encoder over the last 7 days of a Primary's own demand gives the pooled plain mixture density network enough information to infer which Primary it forecasts, so that the network without a learned Primary embedding recovers most of the embedding's gain, and a Primary held out of training is forecast better than by a network given a placeholder embedding. not supported not-for-production The last 7 days of a substation's power do tell a pooled neural network which substation it is forecasting, but the network still forecasts worse with that history than with a learned substation label: 3.64 against 3.32 points of capacity at the six signed-direction substations. The raw history identifies the substation as well as the learned encoder does, so the encoder adds nothing, and giving it to the network that has the label made the forecast slightly worse. For a substation the network never trained on, the simplest network (no label, no encoder, three recent readings) forecast best, and a placeholder label made the forecast much worse. All five test months are interim. primary 00418 mdn-pretrain-on-era5-and-cams-then-fine-tune-on-ens The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 397, pretrained on the Primaries' own power and ERA5 and CAMS weather from 2019-09 and then fine-tuned on the ENS rows, scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network trained on the ENS rows alone, because the ENS archive starts on 2024-04-01 and the pooled network sees at most 18 to 24 months of it. supported candidate Teaching the neural network first on six years of past weather and power, then on the forecast archive, lowers its error by about 0.06 points of capacity (2.1%) at the six signed-direction substations and 0.16 points (4.2%) at the eight apparent-power-only substations over 12 test months. Changing how much of the network is retrained, or adding forecast-like noise, changes the score by less than the interval of the estimate. With only 6 months of forecast archive on 4 test months the gain is about 1.3 points, although the ENS-only baseline degrades badly there. also relevant 00416 mdn-explicit-solar-term-better-powered-follow-up The pooled plain mixture density network can keep its flexible irradiance input and gain an interpretable explicit solar term without losing skill: on sunny-midday half-hours at the six signed-direction Primaries, the network with the explicit solar term (C3), and the hybrid that also keeps the free irradiance input (H1), score within a stated margin of the network with the free irradiance input alone (A0), and they lower the 99th-percentile pinball loss. inconclusive not-for-production Adding an explicit solar-power term to the neural network did not beat letting the network read the sunshine forecast directly: over 12 test months the two score within 0.03 CRPS points overall, and on sunny middays the explicit term is nominally 0.23 points worse, with an interval too wide to call (the design cannot resolve differences under about 0.3 points). The explicit term's upper-tail (99th percentile) loss is slightly lower, but not reliably. Stronger capacity priors made no difference, so the learned capacities cannot yet be read as physical solar capacity. also relevant 00415 pooled-mixture-density-network-at-bulk-and-grid-supply-points A pooled plain mixture density network fitted across the 16 Primaries and the 4 nodes (D13 and D17 are bulk supply points; D1 and D6 are grid supply points) with a node-type input scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 at the nodes than the same network fitted at the 16 Primaries only and applied to the nodes, and is not worse than the stored monthly XGBoost control of experiment 386 by more than 0.30 points of effective capacity at either group. supported not-for-production A pooled neural network trained on the readings of two bulk supply points and two grid supply points together with the 16 Primaries forecasts the bulk supply points a little better than the weekly XGBoost forecast (0.47 points of capacity lower, in all four months) and the grid supply points about as well, with very wide bands. A copy fitted at the Primaries alone fails at these points, partly because of how its inputs were scaled. Giving the network the readings of the Primaries beneath a node did not help. primary 00413 differentiable-physics-demand-network-part-1 A pooled network that forecasts Primary demand as a Primary-specific mix of shared learned daily shapes plus a Primary-specific mix of shared learned temperature and solar responses, with a plain mixture density head on the residual, scores within 0.03 points of the pooled plain mixture density network on the 2026-01 fold, and its learned curves can be read. not supported not-for-production A neural network built from shared, readable parts (learned daily shapes and temperature responses) forecast substation demand less accurately than the plain neural network on five test months: by 0.17 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.23 points at the other 8. Its error in the middle of the distribution was larger at both groups. At the six it covered the highest outcomes better, but at the eight it was worse in both tails. Under the default rule the design does not advance, and whether to pursue it is the maintainer's call. also relevant 00409 mdn-solar-term-day-of-year-and-anomaly-known-answer A pooled mixture density network that has a day-of-year by hour term in its demand module can attribute the monthly daylight profile of a farm to the demand module, so the explicit solar term learns capacity only from the day-to-day sky. Under that repair the known-answer test can be passed, and the solar term then lowers the net-demand CRPS at the six signed-direction Primaries against the same network given no solar term. not supported not-for-production Adding an explicit solar-power term to the neural network did not reliably lower the net-demand error at the six signed-direction substations: the change was about -0.06 points of capacity (about 2%), with an interval that includes zero. C3's pinball loss at q99 was 7% lower than A0-noirr-doy's (0.427 against 0.461; no interval was computed), and the test could not show that the network reads the sky, because an injected solar signal was too small to see above seed noise. The free irradiance input remains about as good as the explicit term. also relevant 00406 pooled-mixture-density-network-without-embedding-and-with-short-history Most of the gain that one pooled mixture density network shows over one network per Primary (experiment 403) comes from sharing parameters, not from the learned Primary embedding, and the gain does not grow when each Primary's training history is cut to 3, 6, or 12 months. not supported not-for-production One neural network shared across all 16 substations only beats separate networks if it knows which substation it is forecasting: without a substation input it is 0.57 points of capacity worse than separate networks at the six signed-direction substations, and with a learned substation embedding it is 0.22 better. The advantage of sharing grows when one substation has little history: with 3 months of its history the shared network is 1.15 points better, because the separate network loses 1.77 points and the shared one only 0.83. All five test months are interim. primary 00405 mdn-explicit-pv-term-learned-capacity-known-answer A pooled mixture density network that forecasts net demand as a demand mixture minus a physical solar-power term, with the term's capacity learned per Primary and season-year under a prior, scores a lower net-demand CRPS at the six signed-direction Primaries than the same network given the irradiance as an ordinary input. A small adapter that modulates the physical solar forecast by weather scenario lowers the score further. inconclusive not-for-production We could not test whether a solar term with a learned capacity improves the forecast, because the known-answer test that gates it could not be passed. On the 2026-06 fold, with 3 seeds and 6 Primaries, adding a real solar farm's output made the network's capacity rise by about the right share, and it rose by 60 to 91% as much when the farm's days were shuffled. A fresh audit found that the shuffled series keeps most of the real series' daylight profile, so the test as built cannot separate a read of the sky from a read of the profile. The next experiment needs a test calibrated to the network. also relevant 00403 pooled-versus-per-primary-mixture-density-network One network trained across all 16 Primaries scores lower CRPS than one network per Primary, with the same inputs, rows, folds, and seeds, and the gain is largest at the Primaries with the shortest history. supported not-for-production One neural network trained across all 16 Primaries forecasts demand better than 16 separate networks: at the six signed-direction substations the error score falls by 0.185 points of capacity (about 5%), at the eight apparent-power-only substations by 0.161 points (about 4%), and 11 of 14 long-history substations gain. The gain does not grow where the history is shorter, and at the two short-history substations the result is mixed. These are five test months, so every interval is interim. primary 00393 gam-mva-fold-data-analysis The GAM stack trails BG2 at the eight MVA-only Primaries (D2, D3, D4, D8, D12, D19, D21, D22) because apparent power (MVA) is a folded, non-linear function of the additive effects that a GAM learns for signed active power (MW), so the stack loses relative skill whenever demand is near zero. Stop-rule count for the idea "the MVA fold explains the GAM's gap": 3 of 3 already, because experiments 152, 372, and 374 each tested a fold treatment and none closed the gap. This experiment is a data analysis on stored forecasts, not a fourth fold treatment. not supported not-for-production The MVA fold does not explain why the GAM trails BG2 at the MVA-only Primaries. Folding the signed series at the six Primaries that report signed megawatts moves the gap by only -0.015 points pooled, because four of the six almost never come near zero; D5 and D10 do (4.6% of half-hours each), yet only D5 moves (-0.092). The gap is larger when demand is low at D12 and D22, but D8, the biggest gap, comes from mid-to-high demand, so a next test could target low-demand half-hours at D12 and D22 and look separately at D8. also relevant 00386 bsp-gsp-demand-v1-top-down-bg2-gam-simple-xgboost At the four bulk and grid supply points that NGED forecasts, fitted and scored top-down on the aggregate series, the best Primary-demand GAM stack is not worse than BG2 (the weekly-refitted XGBoost model alone, b_weekly) by more than 0.20 points of effective capacity at days 1 to 10, separately for the two bulk supply points (BSPs: D13, D17) and the two grid supply points (GSPs: D1, D6). refuted not-for-production At the two bulk supply points and two grid supply points, the GAM stack fitted on each aggregate reading does much worse than BG2 (the weekly XGBoost model), by 1.0 points at the bulk supply points and 2.0 at the grid supply points, and scores about level with the manual heuristic and climatology. The gap is largest on day 1 and shrinks with lead, which is consistent with the stack lacking the recent-power input that BG2 has; this explanation is untested. Both forecasts have tail errors: BG2's 5% quantile covers 2.8% to 4.4% of readings (too wide), and the stack's covers 5.5% to 10.4% (too narrow, most clearly at D1). primary 00223 dp-bsp-generators-as-children-and-double-count-test The metered generators that NGED lists under a bulk supply point (BSP) are children of that BSP as much as the Primaries are: the BSP's reading is the Primaries' demand plus the unmetered load minus the generators' output. If the Primaries' readings already include a generator's output, adding that generator to the sum double-counts it. This experiment first tests, from the readings alone, which generators the BSP's remainder carries and which a Primary already carries, and then asks how much the BSP's forecast improves when the generators the BSP carries are summed as children. inconclusive not-for-production The two bulk supply points' readings move with the metered generators that NGED lists under them, and the Primaries' readings show only small coefficients on the same generators. The size of the movement is not the clean one-for-one that adding the generator to the sum needs, so the experiment did not test whether adding the generators improves the bulk supply point forecast. A better test is to separate the unmetered solar and the battery's price-driven dispatch first. primary 00204 dp-bsp-full-bottom-up-with-signed-mva-children A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down when the sum covers every child Primary. Experiment 161 summed only the three children per BSP that report real power (MW) and have a long history, which reached 42% of D13's effective capacity and 56% of D17's, and the bottom-up forecast scored 0.5% to 0.6% worse than the top-down forecast. This experiment adds the children that report apparent power (MVA). A child's apparent-power reading is the magnitude of its flow, so a child with reverse flow at midday needs a signed flow before it can enter a sum. The fold-aware model of experiment 152 supplies that signed flow as a latent variable. inconclusive not-for-production Adding every child Primary to the sum did not improve the forecast of either bulk supply point: the bottom-up score matched the top-down score (+0.1% at D13, -0.15% at D17), and the intervals include zero. Converting the children that report apparent power to signed flow changed the score by at most 0.03 points, at the one bulk supply point where a child has reverse flow. Even with every child's reading known exactly the BSP's score gains only 12% to 24%, and the children's forecasts gave no detectable gain over the BSP's own chain, so the next gain may lie in forecasting the generators and the unmetered load beneath each BSP. primary 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00158 dp-partly-pooled-gam-shapes-heating-and-calendar-curves A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) fitted jointly across six Primary substations, so that each substation's heating curve, lighting curve, daily profile, holiday effects, and Christmas shape are a fleet mean plus a penalised deviation of its own, forecasts better than the same model fitted to each substation alone, now that the solar capacity is pinned and the filter handles recent switching. The mechanism is that a substation sees only two winters and two Christmases in a 24-month window, so its own curves are noisy, and five other substations carry information about the shapes that physically are shared. Capacity, level, and the band means stay per substation. The gain is largest for a substation with 3 months of history and on Christmas rows, and no pooled arm is worse than the per-site fit by more than 0.02 points on ordinary rows. partly supported candidate In this test on six Primary substations, fitting the demand model's shared curves (heating, lighting, daily profile, holidays) across all six let a substation with only 3 months of history score 3.01 points instead of 3.64 (lower is better), within 0.17 points of the same substation with 24 months of its own history. The gain was largest in winter and on Christmas rows. For a substation with 24 months of history, pooling changed the score by less than 0.02 points, which is too small to justify making each forecast depend on five other substations' data. The test cannot say whether pooling the heating curve alone would help a 3-month substation. also relevant 00154 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-2-heating-error-against-truth When the partly pooled convex regression model of experiment 109 is fitted to only 4 winter weeks of one substation, its fitted heating curve is closer to the injected truth than the curves of the no-pooling and complete-pooling fits. The curve is as close to the truth as a fair oracle's curve (within 10%). The model recovers the sign of the substation's own heating offset relative to the fleet's curve. The fleet's shared curve is recovered as well as an average of per-site fits recovers it. partly supported not-for-production On synthetic substations with a known answer, a partly pooled demand model fitted to 4 winter weeks of one substation estimated that substation's heating response with a smaller error than fitting the substation alone (2.8 to 3.6 against 4.1 to 11.5 points of capacity) and than copying the fleet's curve (3.4 to 4.6), on every seed. It recovered the fleet's shared curve about as well as separate fits did. Neither the pooled fit nor the fair oracle recovered the sign of the substation's own heating offset reliably (the pooled fit got the sign right at 6 or more of 8 substations on only 2 of 5 seeds), so on these synthetic fleets and one January, a partly pooled model can share the heating curve but cannot learn a substation's own offset from 4 weeks. also relevant 00150 differentiable-physics-n0-gate-rerun-fair-oracle-five-seeds When the reference estimator estimates every coefficient from the same 4 weeks of rows (so that no coefficient is fixed at its true value), the partially pooled convex model of experiment 109 recovers the injected truth about as well as that reference on most of 5 random seeds, and its tuning rule picks a deviation penalty within one grid step of the best one on most of the 5 seeds. inconclusive not-for-production The rerun of the synthetic known-answer test could not say whether the pooled model shrinks substation deviations correctly, because a control that keeps no deviation at all passed the shrinkage line on 2 of 5 seeds when 4 June weeks were held. Capacity from 4 weeks was within 25% of the truth at 8 of 8 synthetic substations on every seed, the tuning rule picked a penalty within one grid step of the best on 5 of 5 seeds, and the pooled fit's heating error was below a fair reference estimator's on 5 of 5 seeds. The full-history line passed on only 2 of 5 seeds. A post hoc rerun on 4 January weeks separated the controls, so a test that scores heating error against the injected truth in winter should settle the question. also relevant 00124 differentiable-physics-h-bsp-closure-audit-and-bsp-hint A bulk supply point (BSP) reading, fitted jointly with the Primaries beneath it as the sum of their demand terms plus the metered generators plus a penalised remainder, with a tuned weight, limits the damage that a metering error at one Primary does to that Primary's forecast, without raising the Primaries' forecast error when no error is present. not supported not-for-production The bulk supply point reading halved the damage from injected scale errors, but it made forecasts on clean data worse at every weight above zero: by at least 0.385 points of capacity in the corrected re-run, about 17 times the 0.023-point limit (2.355 points or more in the first run). A synthetic system that closes exactly loses clean accuracy the same way, so the loss does not come mainly from a wrong multiplier. The cause is untested. As a detector of metering errors the reading is weak: a 25% scale error lasting 30 days is found in 0% of cases by a fit that includes it and in 50% by a fit trained only on earlier rows, which then false-alarms on 61% of later windows. also relevant 00120 differentiable-physics-sh-convex-daily-shape-library A convex model in which each Primary's daily profile is a non-negative mix of K = 3 or 4 shared daily shapes per day type, plus a penalised deviation, forecasts Primary demand with 2 years of history at least 0.05 points better than experiment 109's shrinkage towards one fleet-mean profile. That needs the library to beat the per-site profile by about 0.02 points, because the fleet-mean model is 0.031 worse than it; the plan predicts a tie or a small gain, so supported is a long shot. The stability of the shapes and the shape mix of each substation are descriptive. inconclusive not-for-production In a test with synthetic substations, 5 Primaries were too few for a library of 3 shared daily shapes to recover the shapes we planted, so the check failed on 7 of 10 lines and the verdict is inconclusive. In the scored year the library scored the same as the fleet-mean model and 0.030 points worse than a profile per substation (0.068 worse in winter), and its forecast reproduced a tenth to a half of the Economy 7 night step on cold winter nights. also relevant 00117 differentiable-physics-h2-graph-prior-on-pooled-convex-parameters A penalty on the differences between interconnected Primaries' parameters (heating slopes, PV capacity as a share of effective capacity, the profile's scale, and the holiday coefficients) narrows those parameters' month-block bootstrap intervals without breaking their coverage when neighbouring Primaries are alike, and worsens the full-history quantile score by at most 0.03 points. refuted not-for-production At the weight tested, tying the parameters of interconnected substations together did not improve the forecast: in the scored year it worsened the quantile score by 0.020 points on all days (the interval spans zero) and by 0.173 points in winter evening peaks (the replicate year gave -0.021). On synthetic substations with a known truth it narrowed only heating-slope intervals, and the 80% intervals of PV capacity held the truth 17% of the time against 78% without the tie. A tie on heating slopes alone worsened the real score by 0.006 and 0.001 points, an exploratory lead and not a result. also relevant 00109 differentiable-physics-n0-partially-pooled-convex-model A convex model whose per-substation coefficients are a fleet mean plus a ridge-penalised per-substation deviation forecasts Primary demand as well as the per-substation convex model when both have 2 years of history, and clearly better when the substation has 4 weeks or 3 months. inconclusive not-for-production The known-answer test of this method failed under its pre-registered definition, and only one of five runs (each on a new seed, runs 2 to 5 being post hoc redefinitions) passes every line, so the verdict is inconclusive. Taking the numbers alone, for the five MW Primaries tested, one convex model shared across substations forecast a new substation with only 4 weeks of history 3.3 points better than a convex model fitted to that substation alone (and 0.8 points better with 3 months), far more than the 0.5 to 2.0 predicted, and scored 0.03 points worse on substations with 2 years of history. On the six held-out Primaries it came within 0.2 points of experiment 105's neural pooled model with 4 weeks (the neural model 0.13 better) and 0.12 better with 3 months, without that model's loss on long histories, which suggests that the loss in experiment 105 came largely from the neural fit. Complete pooling scored 0.07 points worse than partial pooling at 4 weeks in the scored year (interval touching zero) and no differently in the replicate year. The gains should be relied on only after a rerun of the gate. also relevant 00105 differentiable-physics-3-pooled-and-per-site-demand-model One differentiable-physics model fitted across all the Primary substations forecasts a substation as well as the same model fitted to that substation alone when both have two years of history, and forecasts clearly better when the substation is new (4 weeks of history) or short of history (3 months). inconclusive not-for-production One neural-network demand model fitted across 15 Primary substations forecasts a substation with only 4 weeks of history far better than a per-site copy of the same model (score 4.04 against 14.38 on the six scored substations), but forecasts a substation with 2 full years of history worse than a per-site copy (3.42 against 3.04 on the five decision substations, worse at all 5). By the pre-registered rule pooling is not yet a success, because that full-history result (C1) is refuted, and a failed known-answer check (gate test 2, injected-farm recovery) caps the verdict at inconclusive. Post hoc, for a new substation the pooled model also beat a per-site convex model fitted to the same 4 weeks (mean absolute error 6.88 against 12.79). also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00036 hierarchy-aware-bsp-gsp-forecasts For the two bulk supply points (BSPs) Boston and Skegness and the two grid supply points (GSPs) Walpole and Bicker Fen, forecasts of the series beneath each point, and an N1 model trained on ERA5 and applied to ENS members, lower the quantile score below that of N1 trained on ENS. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasts of the series beneath two bulk supply points added nothing (+0.04 and +0.19 points of capacity), nor did wind and solar columns at two grid supply points; an N1 trained on ERA5 lowered the grid supply point scores by 0.36 and 0.40 with intervals spanning -1.8 to +1.0. primary 00032 substation-fingerprints-pooled-demand For demand series of Primary substations, adding a numeric fingerprint of each substation (its location, its mean level and daily and weekly shape over the training window, and its level over the 14 days before the forecast origin) to a by-type pooled XGBoost quantile model closes part of the 0.15-point gap between the pooled model with the series identifier and per-series models, and lets a substation held out of the pool be forecast better than a pooled model with no fingerprint. inconclusive not-for-production Adding numeric substation fingerprints to the pooled model changed the Primary score by at most 0.02 points of capacity, and training-window statistics made a held-out substation worse by 1.39 (inconclusive overall; recent power statistics alone helped it by 0.23, post hoc). primary 00024 pooling-groupings-demand-xgboost For demand series of Primary substations, one XGBoost quantile model trained across a group of series (all series, one model per substation type, or one model per size band), given the series identifier as a categorical column, scores no more than 0.3 points of capacity worse than one model per series, so that the number of models can fall from one per series to one per group. supported candidate Pooling the 16 Primary substations into 3 or 4 XGBoost models (with the series identifier) scored 0.15 points of capacity worse than 20 per-series models (99.44% interval +0.03 to +0.26), inside the 0.30 margin; one model for all 20 series was 0.29 worse, and dropping the identifier cost 0.8 to 1.0. primary

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction
docs.text:
On 16 Primary substations over one validation year, both recent power fed to a second-stage calibrator and a correction by the mean error of the last 14 days lower the forecast error, by similar amounts against different reference forecasts; on solar farms, wind farms, and supply points neither has been shown to help.

Recent measured power can enter the forecast as input, or shift the forecast by its recent errors. The experiments put lagged power into stage 1b (a second model that corrects the weather-only forecast) or into the stage 2 calibrator, and tested variants of the 14-day correction. All scores are the quantile score in points of capacity, and lower is better. The five experiments of this theme scored 73 forecast runs, one every 5 days from July 2025 to June 2026. Other experiments cited use other run sets, stated where cited. Stage 1a is the weather-only forecast, trained on ERA5 and CAMS estimates of past weather.

Lagged power in the calibrator scored better than lagged power in stage 1b in every lead band (C1, stage 1b with a lag-free calibrator minus the calibrator with lags, where positive means stage 1b is worse; 99% intervals; 16 Primary substations). Source: experiment 5.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Recent power lowers the error, and it lowers it more in the calibrator than in stage 1b. For 16 Primary substations up to 48 hours ahead, the calibrator with lagged power scored 5.31, stage 1b with a calibrator that sees no lags scored 6.14, and a calibrator with no lags scored 7.11. The contrast is +0.84 (+0.28 to +1.50 at 99%), so the pre-registered idea that stage 1b is the better place was refuted. Using both placements lowered the score by at most 0.12 more. Stage 1b scored better at 8 of the 16 series, so the average hides a mixed result (experiment 5).

Summaries of recent power added no resolvable gain to the raw lags. Adding the minimum, mean, and maximum of the last 24 hours and of the same weekday changed the score by -0.02 (-0.14 to +0.13 at 98.75%; inconclusive). Replacing the raw lags with the summaries worsened it by 0.29 (+0.11 to +0.51). Summaries alone still beat no recent power (-1.18, -1.83 to -0.58) (experiment 8). Experiment 30 tested more lag columns in N1 and is on the demand inputs page.

With only the data a live service has, the two-stage chain is not distinguishable from N1. The lagged inputs of experiments 5 and 8 use estimates of past weather that a live service lacks, so they are ceilings. Experiment 18 rebuilt them from weather available at the forecast origin and from NGED's real telemetry delay (the wait before a power reading arrives; 7 hours). Over all leads the chain minus N1 was +0.08 (-0.11 to +0.25 at 99.17%; inconclusive). Up to 48 hours it was -0.27 (-0.62 to +0.03), and beyond 3 days +0.15 (-0.07 to +0.36). The chain scored 0.52 above the manual_heuristic baseline (-0.25 to +1.25; interval includes zero). Lag anomalies lowered the score by only 0.04 against raw lagged power (-0.12 to +0.07).

The chain is level with N1, and above manual_heuristic beyond 3 days (point estimate; the interval includes zero). Source: experiment 18.

The 14-day correction lowered the Primary score by about 1 point, a gain of similar size to lagged power in the calibrator against a different reference. Experiments 19 and 21 scored the correction on the same 73 runs and 16 Primary substations as experiments 5 and 18. N1 plus the correction scored 5.34 over all leads, against 6.33 for N1. The chain of experiment 18 scored 6.41, and lagged power in that chain gained -1.05 (-1.64 to -0.58) against a calibrator without lags (experiment 18, C2). The references differ and no paired interval compares them. Experiment 19 (power 3.5 hours old) gave -0.99 (-1.84 to -0.15 at 99.44%). Experiment 21 gave -0.99 (-1.82 to -0.18 at 99.375%) with power 2 days old. Experiment 19 is on the production reference and best guess page.

The correction lowered the Primary score, no variant beat the plain 14-day additive form, and the correction did not lower the score of the 4 bulk and grid supply point series. Source: experiment 21.

No variant of the correction beat the plain 14-day additive form on Primary substations. A 7-day window was worse (+0.19, +0.11 to +0.28), a 28-day window was level or slightly better (-0.07, -0.15 to +0.01), a multiplicative form was far worse (+2.28, +0.50 to +5.46), and a per-half-hour shift (+0.02) and recency weights (+0.04) changed nothing (experiment 21).

The correction is unproven for supply points, solar farms, and wind farms. On 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98 at 99.375%; inconclusive; experiment 21) and by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594) in the BG2 ablation on 292 daily runs (experiment 87). On 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms (53 Tuesday runs), lagged power left the calibrator's CRPS unchanged to about 0.1 points, and the correction raised it for solar (+0.437, +0.215 to +0.664) and did not clearly change it for wind (+0.413, -0.003 to +0.924) (experiment 23).

Lags near switching were tested in two other themes. Training with lags hidden at random did not widen the 5% to 95% band where a lag is missing. On 292 daily runs, the band covered 0.799 of real masked half-hours (37,394) for the plain model and 0.802 with lags hidden in 10% of rows, against 0.90 nominal (+0.003, -0.093 to +0.101 at 98.75%; inconclusive; experiment 100). Telling a monthly-refitted XGBoost model how unusual each lag is raised the score outside switching by 0.355 (+0.209 to +0.513 at 97.5%; refuted; experiment 90).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
Of the designs tested in this theme, the stage 2 calibrator with raw lagged power is the best use of lagged power, and the additive 14-day correction is the best correction.

  1. Give the stage 2 calibrator (arm L3, the calibrator with lagged power, of experiment 5) the power 24, 48, 168, and 336 hours before the target, the four stage 1a residuals at those times, and five residuals at the newest observation. Keep the raw lags (experiment 8).
  2. For a live service, build the lag residuals from weather available at the origin (experiment 18), and apply a spread factor of 1.15 (-0.04, -0.08 to -0.00). This design did not beat N1.
  3. For Primary substations, add the mean error of the last 14 days of the forecast median to every quantile, using a window of 14 days or longer and an additive shift (experiment 21). No experiment combined the chain with the correction.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: No experiment in this theme is marked candidate; all five are not-for-production. The correction for Primary demand is a candidate in experiments 19, 33, and 87, described on the production reference and best guess page, and experiment 30 is a candidate on the demand inputs page. Experiment 21 supports the correction with power 2 days old, which gave the same all-lead gain as power 3.5 hours old, so the service need not wait for fresher telemetry. It supports no use at supply points.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Compare a lagged arm with a calibrated arm that has no lags. A calibrator without lags lowered the stage 1a score by 1.02 up to 48 hours (exploratory contrast E4, whose interval includes zero at some leads), and stage 1a alone scored 8.12 against 8.14 for day-type climatology. Against stage 1a alone, lags look about 1 point better than they are (experiment 5). Look for a lagged arm whose comparison has no calibrator.
  • Label an arm a ceiling when its lag residuals use estimates of past weather. The arms of experiments 5 and 8 used ERA5 at lag times, and rebuilding them from serving sources worsened the score by 0.13 (+0.02 to +0.25; experiment 18). Re-check with a different weather source for the lag times.
  • State the telemetry delay of every lagged arm. Experiment 5 used 0.5 hours (the newest half-hour before the origin), experiment 13 3.5 hours, and experiment 18 7 hours. Three and a half hours more delay worsened the chain by 0.13 over all leads and 0.16 up to 48 hours, so scores with different delays do not compare (experiment 18). Re-check on a different delay.
  • Report how many series agree with the mean. C1 of experiment 5 (above) was +0.84 on average while stage 1b was better at 8 of the 16 Primary substations (experiment 5). Look for a mean over series with mixed signs.
  • Do not correct a skewed target by the mean of observed minus median. That shift raised the solar CRPS by 0.437 and the wind CRPS by 0.413 (interval includes zero) and cut the 5% to 95% coverage to 53% to 77%. A median shift was tried once, post hoc, and moved the CRPS by +0.010 for solar and -0.064 for wind, with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). Re-check with a pre-registered median shift.
  • Check the base forecast's bias before applying the correction. N1's two bulk supply point series had a bias of +0.01, so the correction only added noise (experiment 21), and in experiment 87 a frozen model with the correction scored 13.559 against 13.369 without it (experiment 87). Look for a base forecast with little bias.
  • Build the correction's error history from the runs a live service would have. Experiments 19 and 21 measured each past half-hour's error from a run 0 to 5 days earlier, with runs 5 days apart, and applied it up to 15 days ahead. A daily service sees smaller errors at shorter leads, and experiment 87 scored the correction on 292 daily runs (experiment 19, experiment 21). Look for a run schedule other than every 5 days.
  • Keep a control that keeps the event rows when testing masked lags. Dropping event and closure rows from training (the mask arm, which also sets lags inside labelled events to missing) narrowed the band on unmasked rows by 4% and lowered its coverage from 0.906 to 0.894, so the masked arms differ from the plain model in more than the dropout (experiment 100). The masked rows came from an estimated 15 to 20 events, mostly at three substations. Look for a masked arm without a control that keeps the rows.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether lagged power helps once the correction is in place: no experiment here combined them.
  • Whether the staged chain beats N1 at leads up to 2 days. Its point estimate was lower there, but the interval includes zero.
  • Whether the correction helps supply points when more than 4 series are scored, or helps solar and wind farms when it uses a median shift.
  • Whether an input that flags a missing lag, or a separate model of the band width, widens the band where a lag is missing. Experiment 100 tested only random dropout.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Lagged power and error correction: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00428 day-window-convolution-attention-encoder-replacing-lagged-power-inputs A pooled mixture density network that has no hand-made lagged power input and instead reads the raw half-hourly power of whole recent days through a one-dimensional convolutional network and an attention layer (whose query is the half-hour being forecast) forecasts as well as the pooled plain network with the three origin lags on rows outside load-shift events, forecasts better on harm rows (rows whose target is outside every event but whose recent days are inside one), and follows a step added to the recent days by a much smaller share of the step, with wider bands. not supported not-for-production A neural network that reads whole days of raw power (E3) did not stop the forecast following load-shift events and scored worse than the lagged network (+0.050 on clean rows). Adding the surprise at the three lags (S1) lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.083 percentage points of effective capacity on clean rows, only just above the 0.077 minimum detectable effect, and by 0.060 on injected harm rows, below its 0.071 minimum. No arm followed a smaller share of a step in the recent power or widened its bands. All numbers are interim, from four test months. primary 00426 mdn-neighbouring-primaries-graph-and-bottom-up-design Information from the Primaries connected to a Primary improves the pooled plain mixture density network's forecast at days 1 to 2, the only leads at which recent power helps the signed-MW six, by more than simple neighbour statistics do. Residuals of the stored forecast of interconnected Primaries correlate more strongly than residuals of Primaries joined at random or by distance alone, and a network that passes messages along the interconnection graph beats both its own rewired-graph control and the simple-statistics control. not supported not-for-production In these tests, the recent forecast errors of a Primary's interconnected neighbours predicted none of its day-ahead forecast error, and adding them to a simple regression made it slightly worse on ordinary half-hours. A graph network over the Primaries therefore has no lagged-error signal to pass along, and none was fitted. A scaled sum of the forecasts of the Primaries beneath a bulk supply point scored 34% to 60% higher error than the network that sees the node's own readings, at two bulk supply points. Whether neighbours help inside load-shift events was not measured here, and experiment 404 tests it. also relevant 00421 mdn-history-fingerprint-for-pooled-primary-demand A 1D convolutional encoder over the last 7 days of a Primary's own demand gives the pooled plain mixture density network enough information to infer which Primary it forecasts, so that the network without a learned Primary embedding recovers most of the embedding's gain, and a Primary held out of training is forecast better than by a network given a placeholder embedding. not supported not-for-production The last 7 days of a substation's power do tell a pooled neural network which substation it is forecasting, but the network still forecasts worse with that history than with a learned substation label: 3.64 against 3.32 points of capacity at the six signed-direction substations. The raw history identifies the substation as well as the learned encoder does, so the encoder adds nothing, and giving it to the network that has the label made the forecast slightly worse. For a substation the network never trained on, the simplest network (no label, no encoder, three recent readings) forecast best, and a placeholder label made the forecast much worse. All five test months are interim. also relevant 00414 post-hoc-gap-filled-counterfactual-lag-rescore Post hoc, because it changes the design of experiment 411 after that experiment's result was read. When the gaps in experiment 391's stage-1 median are filled with the mean reading at the same half-hour of the 4 weeks before, so that more of the 184 corrected load-shift events are scored, replacing the readings inside each event with clean values lowers the CRPS of experiment 392's R1 lagged boosters on harm rows by at least 0.1 points of effective capacity at the six signed-MW Primaries. inconclusive not-for-production The gap-filled re-score changed nothing. Filling the gaps in the stage-1 median added no scored event, and the 15 events of experiment 411 reproduced exactly (the row scores are identical), so the six signed-MW gain stays at -0.836 CRPS points (interval -2.5 to +1.3) and still rests on 9 events. The sample is limited by the 4 test months, not by the gaps. The maintainer still has to decide whether experiment 404 skips batches 1 and 2 on this evidence. primary 00411 counterfactual-lag-rescore-harm-rows-r1-boosters Replacing the readings inside each real load-shift event with clean values, in the lags that experiment 392's R1 lagged XGBoost boosters read, lowers the CRPS of those boosters' forecasts on harm rows (rows whose target lies outside every event but whose lags lie inside one) by at least 0.1 points of effective capacity at the six signed-MW Primaries. inconclusive not-for-production We could not measure the most that a lag-trust method can gain, because the harness scores only 15 of 184 load-shift events. On those events, replacing the lags inside each event with clean values made the forecast worse at the six signed-MW Primaries (a loss of 0.84 CRPS points, interval -2.58 to +1.23), and the result flips to a gain of 0.46 points when one event at one Primary is dropped. The rule in the experiment 404 plan reads the point estimate and would skip batches 1 and 2, but the interval includes both 0.1 and zero, so the maintainer should decide. A wider sample needs boosters and rows for more months, or looser event filters (experiment 414 found that filling the gaps in the stage-1 median adds no event). primary 00402 lag-gate-learned-weight-injected-load-shifts-part-1 A gate that sets the weight of a mixture of two XGBoost demand forecasts (one with the three power lags, one without) from the surprise of the lagged readings, trained only on injected load-shift events with known truth, beats the fitted constant mixture around real load shifts and costs no more than it outside them. partly supported not-for-production A gate trained only on injected load shifts, with no labels from National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED), learns to lower the weight on the forecast with power lags from 0.51 to 0.42 when a lagged reading falls inside a load shift, and so removes most of the harm that the lags do in that case. The gain on real load shifts is small (0.10 points at most against the 50/50 mixture, and 0.04 or less against the constant mixture fitted on injected events), and the gate scores worse than the 50/50 mixture when the target itself is inside a real labelled event at the six Primaries. The fitted constant mixture per group is a simpler forecast than the gate and comes within about 1.4% of its exact CRPS on injected rows. Training the gate on real and injected events together is untested. primary 00401 real-and-synthetic-load-shift-median-share-and-fixed-forecast-mixture Job 1. When a synthetic step of the corrected labelled depth is injected into clean periods at the same Primary and the same lag status as each real labelled event, the plain monthly control's median still follows the step by much less than it follows the real event, so the gap between 36.8% (experiment 395 Part E) and 0.94 (Part F) is not an artefact of the depth or the rows. Job 2. A fixed-weight mixture of the weekly forecast with power lags and the forecast without them scores within 0.1 points of effective capacity of experiment 400's learned blend B2 on rows with lags in an event, at the six Primaries with signed readings. partly supported not-for-production The median share of a load-shift step that experiment 395 called "followed" (0.94 with 3 lags in the event) is mostly not a response to the lags: a forecast with no power lags at all reaches 0.95, and the forecast with lags moves its median by at most about 0.03 more than the forecast without lags on the same rows, which is at the noise floor of two different fitted forecasts. Real events are far less visible to the lags than synthetic steps are, so the synthetic lag-encroachment sweep overstates what a real event does to the forecast. A fixed 50/50 mixture of the two forecasts does about as well as the learned blend at the six Primaries with signed readings, and not at the eight, where the interval allows it to score 0.12 points worse. At the six, one event at D16 carries most of the gain over the forecast with lags. primary 00400 lagged-lagless-forecast-blend-around-load-shifts-stored A mixture of the weekly XGBoost forecast with power lags and the XGBoost forecast without power lags, weighted by a smooth function of the lags' surprise scores and of lead time, scores better than the forecast with lags on the rows whose lags touch a load-shift event, and costs no more than 0.02 points of effective capacity on rows outside events. not supported not-for-production The lag surprise scores from experiment 391 did not tell a blend when to trust the power lags: the fitted weight hardly moved around events, so every learned blend behaved like a mix of about 60% forecast with lags and 40% forecast without lags. A fixed 50/50 mix helps on event-lag rows at the six Primaries with signed readings and costs a little elsewhere, so a smooth blend driven by these scores is not worth porting.
