N4: a per-site heating threshold, chosen by profiling the training loss, is recoverable on synthetic substations at real noise, is identified away from 15.5 C at one or more real substations under the per-site printing rule, and lowers the score after the filter. partly supported not-for-production Splitting the convex model's heating terms between the first and second half of each part of the day lowered its day-ahead error after the recent-error filter by about 0.04 points (97.5% interval 0.014 to 0.070), at all 5 substations in both years, but the gain label rests on one substation (D5), and the gain is a temperature-dependent shape of the day more than a heating effect. Letting heating or lighting differ between weekdays and weekends adds nothing, and choosing a heating threshold separately for each substation did not clearly help (0.01 points, within noise). Every number uses past temperature, not forecasts, so the gain needs a test on weather forecasts before GAM-K's convex model changes; the PV panel-orientation mix (N13) was dropped because earlier experiments found it unidentified. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00108 differentiable-physics-shared-anomaly-factor-across-substations The residuals of the frozen convex demand model carry a component shared across Primaries, and a shared state estimated from the other substations' residuals, available at the forecast origin, lowers the day-ahead quantile score by more than the per-site Kalman filter of Part 4 already does. inconclusive not-for-production The experiment stopped at its known-answer gate, where three of seven tests failed, so it cannot say whether a shared factor improves the forecast. On injected anomalies the shared filter, tuned on 2023-24, carried under 5% of the injected points (the plan asked for 40% or more), and it corrected no better than the per-site filter (2.402 against 2.397 points of mean absolute error over days 2 and 3 of the episodes). Part of the test was mis-specified, so a corrected test would be needed before any real score. primary 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00100 drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals An XGBoost quantile model for Primary substation demand that is trained with labelled switching half-hours removed from its targets and with its lagged power inputs set to missing at random intervals, and that has those lags set to missing when they lie inside a labelled switching event, widens its 5% to 95% band on the half-hours whose lags are missing, so that the band's coverage moves from 0.784 towards the nominal 0.90, without widening the band elsewhere. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand forecast with lags hidden at random did not make its band wider on half-hours where a lag is missing: on real rows the band covered 0.80 (hidden in 10% of training rows) to 0.84 (30%) of actuals, against a nominal 0.90. Hiding lags in 30% of rows did remove the accuracy loss that masking alone causes on injected transfers (-0.02 points, 95% interval -0.35 to +0.38 against the plain model). Hiding lags in 10% of rows left +0.26 (98.75% interval -0.15 to +0.85), not separable from zero or from the loss. An input that tells the XGBoost model a lag is missing, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, are untested routes to a wider band. also relevant 00021 error-correction-variants-bsp-gsp-demand A recent-error correction of N1's quantiles, measured with power that is 2 days old, lowers the quantile score of the 4 bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) demand series as it does for the 16 Primary substations, and some variant of the correction (a 7-day or 28-day window, multiplicative, per-half-hour-of-day, or weighting recent days more) beats the plain 14-day additive correction. inconclusive not-for-production The 14-day additive correction lowered the Primary quantile score by 0.99 points of capacity (99.375% interval -1.82 to -0.18) when the newest power was 2 days old, as it did with 3.5-hour-old power in experiment 19. On the 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98), so it is unproven there. No variant beat the plain additive 14-day form: a 7-day window was worse (+0.19) and a multiplicative form far worse (+2.28). primary 00018 staged-chain-vs-n1-serving-latency-lag-anomalies-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, the staged chain (an ERA5-trained stage 1 and the stage 2 calibrator, with lag anomalies built only from weather that serving has at the forecast origin, and NGED's real telemetry delay) beats the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 and manual_heuristic on the quantile score. inconclusive not-for-production With lagged inputs built only from data a live service has, including NGED's real telemetry delay, the two-stage chain was not distinguishable from the single-stage N1 over all leads: 6.41 against 6.33, a difference of +0.08 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.11 to +0.25; positive means the chain is worse). Up to 48 hours the chain was 0.27 lower (-0.62 to +0.03). It scored 0.52 above the stored manual_heuristic baseline (-0.25 to +1.25), so the staged design is not supported for demand on this evidence. primary 00008 lag-summaries-in-stage2-calibrator-demand For Primary substation demand series, giving the stage 2 calibrator the minimum, mean, and maximum of the most recent 24 hours of power, and of the most recent day on the same weekday as the target, lowers the probabilistic forecast's error below that of the calibrator with only the raw power lags (experiment 00005's L3). inconclusive not-for-production Adding the minimum, mean, and maximum of the last 24 hours of power, and of the same weekday, to a calibrator that already had raw power lags changed the quantile score by -0.02 points of capacity up to 48 hours ahead (98.75% interval -0.14 to +0.13), which cannot be told from no change. Replacing the raw lags with the summaries worsened the score by 0.29 (+0.11 to +0.51), so keep the raw lags. Summaries alone, with no estimate-of-past-weather residual, beat no recent power by 1.18 (-1.83 to -0.58). primary 00005 lag-placement-stage1b-vs-stage2-demand For substation demand series, recent observed power improves a two-stage probabilistic forecast more when it enters stage 1 through a residual-persistence XGBoost model (stage 1b) than when it enters only the stage 2 calibrator, when both placements are given identical inputs and both outputs are calibrated. refuted not-for-production For Primary substations, recent power lowered the forecast error more when it went into the second-stage calibrator than when it went into a stage 1b correction model. Up to 48 hours ahead the calibrator scored 5.31 against 6.14, so stage 1b was worse by 0.84 points of capacity (99% interval +0.28 to +1.50); using both added at most 0.12 points. These are ceilings, because the lagged inputs used estimates of past weather that a live service lacks, and stage 1b was better at 8 of the 16 series. primary

docs.title: LSC detectors
docs.text:
A short report on whether a better detector is worth building is on the decision report page.

The best switching detector, RO-NC, finds most of the moved power (the megawatts a transfer moves) of injected load transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, but only about a third of that of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, and no experiment yet shows that using a detector improves a forecast.

A load transfer is a switching operation that moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. Detectors find these transfers from power readings alone. We score them on injected transfers, whose start, end, and size are known, and on 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day that a language model and a hand filter judged visible. The real transfers include 21 under 25% of the receiving load, so the two scores are not like for like. All results are from the lab, on 16 Primary series, and use hindsight to place the end of each transfer.

RO-NC and the refit-offset detector (X) find the most moved power on the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day (RO-NC 0.357), and the 35 are too few to rank them. Source: experiment 101.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
On injected transfers, RO-NC finds 0.770 of the moved power, against 0.656 for the benchmark PF14. The difference is +0.114 (+0.074 to +0.182; experiment 82). Neither part helps transfers lasting 15.6 to 60 days. Recall here is MW-weighted.

  • Not ignoring alarms near the monthly refit of the demand model removes PF14's blind spot: a second model refitted half a month later gave +0.050 (+0.012 to +0.107), and lifting the suppression alone gave +0.056 (+0.016 to +0.113), so the second model adds nothing on injected transfers (experiment 71).
  • Counting the neighbours that step the same way as the alarming substation: +0.048 (+0.021 to +0.096; experiment 70).

On real transfers, RO-NC finds fewer than injected transfers of the same step size and metering predict: 12 of the 35 lasting over 1 day (0.357 of their moved power; 0.169 to 0.553), against 18.8 expected, and none of the 31 shorter ones. On the 14 real transfers of 25% or more of the receiving load, it finds 0.559 (0.203 to 0.816), an interval that includes 0.770, so that band alone shows no gap, but it finds 6 of those 14 where 10.5 are expected. Of the 35, 6 sit where the detector's residual panel holds no readings and 12 have a step under 4 noise units, and even the 17 with readings and a larger step are found less often than injected ones; the verdict is partly supported (experiment 101).

RO-NC finds none of the real transfers shorter than 1 day, and more of those moving 25% or more of the receiving load than of those without a metered receiver (all 66 real transfers).

RO-NC misses small steps, mostly where the receiver is unmetered. Of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, it finds 6 of 14 of 25% or more of the receiving load and 2 of 10 with no metered receiver. Among injected transfers that step by 4 noise units or more, the single-series detector D0 found 0.56 with a metered receiver and 0.35 without (experiment 58). Before the PF14 end rule, a wrong interval end was most of D0's misses among large transfers with a metered receiver, and about a third of its misses among transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more (experiment 59, experiment 60).

The early detectors D0 and D1 each found under a fifth of 600 injected transfers (experiment 43). Moving D0's interval end to the strongest opposite step found +0.191 more (+0.148 to +0.237; experiment 61), and the post hoc rule PF14 did better (0.688 against 0.646, no paired interval; experiment 66).

The changes listed here found no clear gain. Each was tested against a detector without it, at the same number of unexplained alarms. Refuted: several averaging windows (experiment 59), profile-weighted steps (experiment 60), whitening the residual (experiment 62), scoring onset and return steps as a pair (experiment 61), and one joint fit across substations (experiment 67). Inconclusive or partly supported: a bank-holiday column (experiment 47), a neighbour veto (experiments 55 and 58), refitting without detected transfers (experiment 68), solar and heating corrections (experiment 98), a joint linear fit of solar and transfer terms (experiment 63, of the differentiable-physics demand sub-theme), and accepting weaker onset alarms (experiment 69), and adding neighbours' opposite-sign steps to a substation's own step (+0.019, -0.011 to +0.062; experiment 65).

Using a detector has not yet improved a forecast, in one validation year (experiments 44 and 86) or four (experiment 38) on 16 Primary series. In each result below, a positive change means a worse forecast.

  • Masking: leaving the half-hours that D1 flags out of the 7-day error correction of the stack (experiment 17's H0.5 proxy, with a half-life of 0.5 years) raised the tail error outside logged switching by 57% (0.4% to 134%), because one interval ran for 60 days. A mask from NGED's logs lowered it on the 14-day correction by 8.9% (-21.8% to 0.0%), 95% of that in one closure (experiment 38).
  • Ceiling: in the band of events the labeller finds most reliably (3 of the 16 Primaries), a perfect detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (-0.47% to 1.96%) (experiment 44).
  • Corrected lags: lags corrected with RO-NC's labels raised the score by 0.056 points of capacity outside switching (0.016 to 0.126) and did not lower it inside logged events (experiment 86, of the switching-labels-in-the-forecast theme).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
RO-NC is PF14 with two changes (experiment 82).

  1. Subtract an XGBoost demand model's forecast, which uses no past power, from each Primary's power, and refit the model monthly.
  2. Take the 24-hour step of that residual from whichever of two such models, refitted half a month apart, did not refit within 24 hours of the stamp. Lifting the suppression alone does as well on injected transfers (experiment 71), but RO-NC was tested only with two models.
  3. Score each candidate alarm with a logistic regression on its own step, the largest opposite neighbour step, the number of neighbours, and the number that step the same way.
  4. Set the threshold to allow 80 unexplained alarms over all 16 Primary series on odd months, and end each interval at the first opposite step of at least half the onset step.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Nothing is ready for the serving path. Experiments 70, 71, and 82 are marked candidate, but each is training-time only: the residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days after the event, and the end rule uses hindsight.

  • Experiment 71: +0.050 on injected transfers. Experiment 70: +0.048, unconfirmed on real transfers (7 found against 8 for PF14). Experiment 82: +0.114, and 12 against 8 on the 35 real transfers, a weak signal.
  • An untested option is to run RO-NC retrospectively to build a table of switching events for NGED. Experiment 44 found that a perfect detector would improve the best guess's quantile score by little, so the table would serve NGED's own use of the events (roadmap page: switching events).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Count events, not half-hours, and show every event. In experiment 37, 99.9% of the stack's confirmed tail score lay on two series, almost all in one 370-hour closure, and in experiment 38 one closure in January 2026 held 95% to 105% of every masking gain (experiment 37, experiment 38). A pooled half-hour total then reads as many closures when it is one. Re-check on a longer period or other series.
  • Match the unexplained-alarm count on every month a rule reads. A threshold matched on odd months left even months 15% under the first round's alarm count (experiment 68), and a shared threshold grid left D0 at 0.14 alarms per series-month and D1 at 0.38 (experiment 37). Otherwise a detector looks better by raising more alarms. Re-check if the demand model or period changes.
  • Spread injected transfers across series and time before training on them. Experiment 58's 620 even-month transfers shrank to 103 once no two on one series lay within 1 day (experiment 68). Otherwise a few overlapping events count many times. Re-check if the injection sampler changes.
  • Compare like with like when quoting injected and real recall. 0.770 is MW-weighted recall on large injected transfers, and 0.34 is a count over all 35 real transfers, 21 of them under 25% of the receiving load (experiment 101). Otherwise a gap the sample cannot show is reported as a finding. Re-check if the labelled real set grows.
  • Score on several injection shapes and by donor step. Recall depends on the donor step in noise units (experiment 58), and experiment 60 tested one step statistic on five shapes. Otherwise a mix of small and large steps hides which transfers are missed. Re-check if the injection builds transfers a new way.
  • Interval ends need hindsight. The strongest-opposite-step end rule needs up to 14 days of later data (experiment 65), and an interval that started at a return step ran for 60 days (experiment 38). Otherwise a detector scored with hindsight is mistaken for one that could run live. Re-check when a detector is run on live data, or an end rule without hindsight is tried.
  • Recompute moved_share_of_receiver before scoring against the experiment 41 labels. 62 of 81 stored values are NaN, partly because series ids were written as strings (experiment 44). Otherwise a filter on that column silently drops most events. Re-check if the labelled set is rebuilt.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether any detector finds real transfers with a step under 4 noise units, or shorter than 1 day.
  • How RO-NC does on real transfers once the readings missing for two Primary substations are restored.
  • Whether the detector's labels improve a forecast of the normal running arrangement; the logged events in experiment 86 are too few to show it.

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Is a better load shift detector worth building?
docs.text:
The evidence does not show that a better detector would change the decision, because the case for a detector in the forecast is not yet made on curtailment cost. The current label-free detector (it uses no NGED switching log) finds 25 of the 35 real load shifts lasting over 1 day. Masking the readings it flags (treating them as missing in the Kalman filter) lowers the forecast error during and after injected shifts from 1.79 to 1.04, in points of effective capacity on the 95% pinball loss, where lower is better. Against the power the electricity network actually carries, the mask shows no clear change in curtailment cost.

A load shift is a switching operation that moves part of one substation's demand onto neighbouring substations for hours or days. The normal running arrangement (NRA) is the network as normally configured. Injected load shifts are shifts we add to real power series, so their size and timing are known; the real record has 35 logged shifts over 1 day. Gains during a shift come mostly from injected shifts, and one Primary substation (anonymised as D11) carries part of the main result. Each question below has one answer, one figure, and the experiments behind them.

docs.title: 1. Does perfect knowledge of load shifts help?
docs.text:
For the NRA forecast, perfect knowledge lowers the error during and after a shift, but by far less than predicted and by almost nothing over a year. The error falls by 1.50 points (95% interval 1.08 to 1.96) in the 48 hours after a transfer ends and by 1.46 points (0.69 to 2.29) during it, against a predicted 3 points or more. Averaged over a year it falls by about 0.005 points, because shifts are rare (experiment 208, verdict not supported).

For curtailment cost, the answer depends on the series the forecast is judged against. Against the true NRA series, masking the shifts a label-free detector finds lowers cost by 32.8% (95% interval 17% to 53%). Against observed power, which a curtailment instruction responds to, the change is -3.0% (-24% to +30%) and ordinary half-hours cost 1.3% more (experiment 332). Perfect knowledge beats the best forecast with no detector on observed power only when the true moved megawatts are also added back, by 6.5% (3.9 to 9.2; experiment 297). The real record at the D13 bulk supply point is too small to resolve a cost difference (experiment 332).

docs.title: 2. Do we need an explicit detector?
docs.text:
This is not settled. The label-free pipeline has not been run against the best forecast with no detector, and the existing evidence points both ways.

A forecast that recalibrates its bands with no detector matches or beats masks on the upper-tail score near a shift. Within 7 days of a shift, a quantile head (a small model that predicts forecast quantiles from the Kalman filter's recent correction) beats the RO-NC mask on the upper-tail score. RO-NC is the earlier switching detector built on neighbouring-substation counts. The head also beats the perfect mask, but that margin disappears when one Primary (D16) is left out (experiment 297).

A label-free detector plus a mask beats a Kalman filter with no mask. During and after injected shifts the 95% pinball loss falls from 1.79 to 1.04, against 0.81 when the true spans are masked. Without D11 the loss falls by 0.30 points instead of 0.75. The change on ordinary real days is -0.016 points (98.75% interval -0.060 to +0.010), so the harm-side end is within the ±0.05 bar (experiment 327, verdict partly supported, scored on past weather and not on ensemble weather).

The disagreement between the two forecasts cannot choose which forecast to use. One forecast uses recent power and the other does not. A rule on their disagreement recovered none of the gain from choosing with the true answer, and the disagreement adds no information beyond the residual of measured power (experiment 309). As a detector, the 24-hour mean residual is the better signal: it matches 20 of the 35 real shifts, against 11 for the disagreement (experiment 308).

docs.title: 3. How good must a detector be, and is ours good enough?
docs.text:
On curtailment cost against the no-detector head, a mask needs to find about half the shifts. With the true megawatts added back, the mask still beats the head when it finds half the shifts or when it raises false alarms at 1 in 2. It also wins with a 3-day delay (gain 1.4%, 0.3 to 2.5), and with the megawatts wrong by 50%. It loses at 25% found. On the upper-tail score, a 2-day delay or a 50% megawatt error removes the margin (experiment 312).

The label-free detector finds more than half of the real shifts, but the bar was measured on injected worlds with the true megawatts. The label-free detector finds 25 of the 35 real shifts at 8.8 alarms per found shift (experiment 327), and 15 of the 19 long-and-deep ones. The label-free mask adds no megawatts, and adding them did not help in experiment 332. On the injected worlds RO-NC found 33% of the shifts, and a signal based on how far power sits in the forecast's bands found 37%, with about 90% of its alarms false (experiment 312).

Checking neighbouring substations removes a third of the false alarms. The check removes 30% to 37% of the 24-hour residual detector's false alarms and loses none of the real shifts it found (experiment 315).

Detectors based on the daily mean residual do no better on long, deep shifts. They match 8 to 12 of the 19 long-and-deep real shifts and are clearly worse on the other 16 (experiment 298, verdict not supported). A forecast refitted monthly absorbs long shifts: for a 30-day transfer of 25% of demand it absorbs 19% of the shift. It absorbs 10% to 13% if the flagged days are left out of the refit, and 2.8% if the true shift days are left out.

docs.title: What is still open
docs.text:
• The pipeline against the no-detector head. This comparison decides question 2, and no experiment has run it.
  • A curtailment-cost saving against observed power. None is shown for the label-free mask. Whether NGED's cost is judged against the NRA or against observed power decides whether masking pays.
  • Injected shifts carry most of the evidence. Injected shifts may be easier to detect than real ones, and the real record cannot score the gain during a shift.
  • Message for NGED. A forecast refitted monthly partly learns shifts of 14 days or more as normal.

docs.title: LSC detectors: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00428 day-window-convolution-attention-encoder-replacing-lagged-power-inputs A pooled mixture density network that has no hand-made lagged power input and instead reads the raw half-hourly power of whole recent days through a one-dimensional convolutional network and an attention layer (whose query is the half-hour being forecast) forecasts as well as the pooled plain network with the three origin lags on rows outside load-shift events, forecasts better on harm rows (rows whose target is outside every event but whose recent days are inside one), and follows a step added to the recent days by a much smaller share of the step, with wider bands. not supported not-for-production A neural network that reads whole days of raw power (E3) did not stop the forecast following load-shift events and scored worse than the lagged network (+0.050 on clean rows). Adding the surprise at the three lags (S1) lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.083 percentage points of effective capacity on clean rows, only just above the 0.077 minimum detectable effect, and by 0.060 on injected harm rows, below its 0.071 minimum. No arm followed a smaller share of a step in the recent power or widened its bands. All numbers are interim, from four test months. also relevant 00426 mdn-neighbouring-primaries-graph-and-bottom-up-design Information from the Primaries connected to a Primary improves the pooled plain mixture density network's forecast at days 1 to 2, the only leads at which recent power helps the signed-MW six, by more than simple neighbour statistics do. Residuals of the stored forecast of interconnected Primaries correlate more strongly than residuals of Primaries joined at random or by distance alone, and a network that passes messages along the interconnection graph beats both its own rewired-graph control and the simple-statistics control. not supported not-for-production In these tests, the recent forecast errors of a Primary's interconnected neighbours predicted none of its day-ahead forecast error, and adding them to a simple regression made it slightly worse on ordinary half-hours. A graph network over the Primaries therefore has no lagged-error signal to pass along, and none was fitted. A scaled sum of the forecasts of the Primaries beneath a bulk supply point scored 34% to 60% higher error than the network that sees the node's own readings, at two bulk supply points. The result is inconclusive, and a stronger veto was not tried. primary 00047 sw2-4-better-residual-switching-detector Adding one column, the signed days to the nearest bank holiday in England, to experiment 17's lagless ERA5-trained XGBoost demand model H0.5 (refitted monthly, with H0.5's absolute-error loss unchanged) gives a residual in which the single-series detector D0 at the 24-hour window finds more injected load transfers at the same rate of unexplained alarms. inconclusive not-for-production Adding a bank-holiday column to the demand model raised the share of 89 simulated transfers that the detector found by 0.011 (98.75% interval -0.010 to +0.044), which the experiment is too small to tell from zero. The column lowered the demand error on bank holidays by about 1.15 points of capacity, but the detector's matched threshold rose instead of falling. primary 00044 sw2-2-switching-share-of-best-guess-score Half-hours in labelled switching events, and half-hours whose lagged power falls inside one, carry a larger share of the best guess's quantile score and tail score than their share of half-hours, and a perfect switching detector could lower the Primary quantile score or tail score by 3% or more. refuted not-for-production In the band of events the labeller finds most reliably, a perfect switching detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and its tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3%. Switching in that band touches 3 of the 16 Primary series and few half-hours, in one validation year. also relevant 00043 sw2-1-detector-scoreboard Experiment 37's neighbour-balance detector D1 finds injected load transfers between Primary substations more often than its single-series detector D0, when a transfer counts as found only if both its start and its end are placed correctly. refuted not-for-production Two simple switching detectors each found under a fifth of 600 simulated transfers, and no more than 0.29 in any size group. Over a 24-hour window the neighbour check found fewer large transfers than the single-series detector (0.21 against 0.29), and it helped only over the 4-hour window. primary 00041 sw2-0a-labeller-gate A labeller that reads features computed from raw power and the switching logs, and that uses no forecasting model as its deciding evidence, can find injected load transfers and reject placebo windows well enough to label the real logged closures of the 16 Primary substation demand series. partly supported not-for-production The AI model Sonnet called none of 120 placebo windows a switching event and timed starts and ends well, but it found 0.74 of the large, long fake transfers, under the 0.80 bar. It found 0.89 of them where the receiving substation has its own power readings and 0.60 where it does not. primary 00038 switching-mask-value For the 16 Primary substation demand series, excluding the half-hours of detected switching events from the history of the stack's error correction lowers the stack's threshold-weighted error at each series' historical 99th percentile on half-hours outside logged switching, by enough to justify adding a detector to the serving path. refuted not-for-production Leaving the half-hours that an early switching detector (D1) flags out of the 7-day error correction made the forecast worse on half-hours outside logged switching: the error rose 57% (95% interval 0.4% to 134%), where a 5% fall was needed. The rise came from an interval builder that ran one interval for 60 days, so masking with this detector is refuted as built. primary 00037 switching-first-look For the 16 Primary substation demand series, logged network switching (normal open points closed for hours or days) moves load that appears in the telemetry as a pair of opposite steps whose sum is conserved across the donor and its receiving neighbours, and a detector that tests that balance against the static interconnection list finds those transfers at a lower false-alarm rate than a detector that looks at each series alone. inconclusive not-for-production A detector that compares each substation with its neighbours found 0.33 of the switched power in the 18 visible validation transfers, and beat a single-series detector by about 0.14 in a rough post hoc comparison at equal alarm rates, which has no interval. The 18 transfers are too few to show whether the detector meets the 0.35 bar, so the result is inconclusive. primary

docs.title: SW2: switching-event detection
docs.text:
The SW2 line improves the switching-event detector first, scored by event-level F1 against a labelled set of visible events, and leaves the use of the detector until the detector works. The detector serves two purposes later. The first is a lower forecast error, if switching periods act as unexplained noise for the XGBoost model and corrupt its lagged power inputs. The second, and the more important to NGED, is a forecast under the normal running arrangement (NRA), into which NGED can add its own switching. The switching events roadmap page proposes building that forecast by excluding switching periods from the training target. An event table for NGED is a third purpose, at lower priority. The production detector has to run on power alone, because the switching logs exist only for the trial area, so the logs are used here for evaluation only.

The line reopens a question that experiment 00038 closed, because experiment 00038 tested a different use of the detector. Experiment 00038 masked detected switching from the history of the error correction that runs after the XGBoost model, and the mask made the forecast worse. No experiment has yet masked switching from an XGBoost training target or from a lagged input. Experiment 00037 confirmed 37 of 612 logged closures of 2 hours to 60 days as visible in its own residual, and scored its detectors on the 18 of them in the validation months. That reference set is small, about 6 of the 37 are expected by chance, and the label was built from the residual the detectors use, so a detector that shares the residual's blind spots is flattered by the label. The line therefore starts by building a reference set independent of the detectors.

The full labeller design is in the private file data/ml-experiments/briefs/sw2_labeller_design.md.

docs.title: SW2-4 to SW2-9: detector iterations
docs.text:
Each iteration tests one change to the detector against the experiment 43 scoreboard, tuned on injections and odd months, scored on even months, with recall weighted by the MW moved as the headline from SW2-7 onwards. The order below is a proposal, by expected gain per hour of work, for the plan of each iteration to confirm:

  • SW2-5 (done, experiment 68): three rounds of refitting the lagless XGBoost model without the detected intervals changed the share of the moved MW found by +0.011 and the forecast error by -0.175%, and a random mask did as well.
  • SW2-6 (done, experiment 61): pairing the onset and return steps into one alarm score finds less than D0M at the same alarm rate, but taking the end of D0M's interval from the strongest opposite step in the next 14 days finds 0.19 more of the moved MW.
  • SW2-7 (done, experiment 60): a step statistic that weights each half-hour by the expected power found the same transfers as the constant step on five injection shapes, so the step's shape does not limit the 24-hour detector. About a third of the transfers with a donor step of 6 noise units or more have the right onset and the wrong end, which SW2-6 (paired-step intervals) addresses.
  • SW2-8 (done, experiment 55): a single-series detector first, with neighbour balance as a sense check, not a gate. Every single-series alarm stands. A metered neighbour's opposite step raises the alarm's confidence and names the receiver, a same-sign step on the neighbours vetoes the alarm as a common-mode weather or calendar miss, and an alarm with no metered neighbour keeps its single-series confidence. Experiment 00043 found the neighbour-balance detector D1, which uses the neighbour test as a gate, finding almost none of the injected transfers without a metered receiver. The sum of the neighbourhood's residuals and a subset-sum over neighbours for a split feed the confidence score.
  • SW2-9 (done, experiment 62): whitening, experiment 00037's proposed F4, an autoregressive model of order 1 per series and hour of day fitted to the residual. The filtered detector found less of the moved MW (-0.097 at 24 hours), because the filter shrinks a day-long step faster than the noise of the 24-hour step.

docs.title: Metered solar farms
docs.text: The summary of this theme is in progress. This theme covers the six solar farms whose output NGED meters in the trial area (labelled A to F). The experiments ask what shape each farm's output has, what physical plant (panel tilt, azimuth, ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, heat loss, and inverter clip) reproduces it, and what that implies for the unmetered solar behind Primary substations. The Experiments page lists every experiment tried, and the Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Metered solar farms: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00433 solar-idle-noise-data-look H0: the six metered solar farms read exact zeros, or smooth small values, when they are not generating, so the wind farms' idle-noise texture (exact zeros and repeats, quantised values, and a floor above zero that does not follow the season) is absent and no detector or cleaned-zero score is needed for solar. supported not-for-production The metered solar farms read exact zeros at night, unlike the wind farms' noisy floor, so solar forecasts need no idle-noise detector and no cleaned-zero scoring. One farm (Solar B) shows small negative night readings on 8% of night half-hours, and two farms (Solar D and Solar E) have idle runs of 17 to 24 days on clear days, which is an outage question, not a noise question. primary 00430 unified-forecaster-solar-and-pretraining-ablations A pooled mixture-density network for the six metered solar farms needs, beyond experiment 345's solar-only pooled network (the demand-style default: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, no pretraining, a clipped Gaussian mixture), only those of four switches that an ablation shows to help: the 51 ensemble members passed through a shared encoder one by one (A2), a PyTorch fleet plant that adds a power channel (A5), ERA5 and CAMS pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the ensemble (A6), and point masses at zero and at capacity in the output (A7). refuted not-for-production One pass of a neural network on the ensemble mean and spread is enough for the six solar farms: none of the four richer designs we tested beats it by the 1% margin. For the 51 coherent member paths that NGED's power-flow modelling needs, reorder the one-pass network's 51 quantiles with a Schaake shuffle, which scores 13% better than ensemble copula coupling on the variogram score of the paths and the same on the energy score. Passing each member through the network alone gives paths that score 11% worse on the energy score and a marginal quantile score 1.5% worse. primary 00345 pooled-solar-wind-mixture-density-network One mixture-density network (MDN) trained once for all leads on the six metered solar farms and the wind farms together, with a fuel-type indicator and weather inputs common to both fuels, scores as well on each fuel as that fuel's best single-family model, and scores better for a farm with no history. partly supported candidate One neural network trained on all six solar farms forecasts each farm as well as a separate network on the physical plant model (within 0.8%), so a production forecast could use one neural network per fuel. Adding wind farms to the same network does not help either fuel and makes solar 0.7% to 2.3% worse, so solar and wind are better trained separately. In this experiment, a wind farm with no history scored 18% worse at day 1 when trained on public wind farms alone than when trained on other metered wind farms. primary 00321 metered-farm-lower-tail-recalibration-and-tail-head Metered solar farms research default 1 (the blend assembled by experiment 300, scored to 10 days by experiment 310) lets the actual output fall below its 0.01 quantile 3.3% to 3.7% of the time, and no mixture-density head tried in experiment 318 changes that. Default plus a recalibration table, a zero-inflated lower tail, or a tail-targeted head brings the share of actual values strictly below the 0.01 quantile close to 1% at leads of 1 to 10 days, without raising the quantile score and without losing experiment 318's 0.99 gain. partly supported candidate The solar-farm forecast's lowest quantile was already close to correct: only 1.2% to 1.4% of actual values fall strictly below the 0.01 quantile, because the earlier 3.3% counted the 3.0% of half-hours that read exactly zero. A recalibration table, a zero-inflated head, and a tail head each lower the own-history score by 0.04 points or less (the unshrunk table raises it by 0.03 to 0.05 points), so none is adopted. A shrunk recalibration table does lower the score by about 0.05 points for a farm with no history, and two heads lower the 0.99 pinball loss by 3.7% to 8.5% while covering the 0.99 quantile only 98.3% to 98.9% of the time. primary 00318 metered-farm-mdn-head-more-features Giving the mixture-density head of Metered solar farms research default 1 the forecast lead (lead in whole days), the hour of day and day of year as sine and cosine pairs, and the ensemble spread of the shortwave irradiance lowers its quantile score, mostly beyond 36 hours and in the lower tail, and one head trained on all lead bands beats one head per band. partly supported candidate Giving the solar-farm head more inputs does not improve its overall score at any lead from 1 to 10 days, so the head's inputs are not what limits the forecast. The extra clock and cloud-spread inputs do lower the loss at the 0.99 quantile (the tail that matters for curtailment) by about 5% at days 3 to 7, and none of the changes fixes the lower tail, where 3.3% to 3.7% of actual values fall below the 0.01 quantile, where 1% is expected. Training one head for all leads makes the network with no plant nearly as good as the plant-based head at days 8 to 10 (0.4% worse), so the plant adds little there. primary 00313 metered-farm-pure-xgboost-and-mdn-vs-plant A predictor built only from weather and calendar inputs, with no plant model anywhere in the pipeline (not even as an input column), scores close to the plant-based forecast in own history and falls behind it where the plant carries what missing history or a long lead cannot. partly supported candidate A forecast that sees only weather and the calendar, with no physical plant model anywhere, scores almost as well as the plant-based forecast for the six solar farms, up to 10 days ahead, even when the farm has no history. The plant's added value is small, between 0% and 3.4%, and its intervals include zero except for XGBoost. For wind, the same kind of network also matches the best plant-based forecast, so a plant model is not needed to be competitive on these farms. primary 00310 metered-farm-long-lead-scoring Experiment 300's candidate (spread-binned plant, additive band, mixture head, blend with XGBoost) still beats XGBoost at every day band from 1 to 10 days ahead, and its margin over climatology shrinks as the lead grows. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast still beats the seasonal-average forecast (climatology) at every lead up to 10 days, by 39% at day 1 and 10% at days 8 to 10, so NGED can use it across its whole horizon of 1 to 10 days ahead. A plant-fed XGBoost model loses its skill by day 8, so a simple first production forecast should be the mixture-density neural network on the plant, which is the best single family at every lead, and the blend of the GAM, MDN, and XGBoost adds more than 1% only at days 1 and 2. primary 00304 metered-farm-node-sum-tail For the solar farms that share a bulk supply point, adding each farm's quantiles overstates the upper tail of the farms' summed output, adding independent bands understates it, and summing the 51 ensemble members' farm forecasts member by member gives calibrated 0.95 and 0.99 quantiles, because the ensemble carries the farms' shared dependence on cloud. not supported not-for-production The band for the combined output of the three farms beneath one substation comes out too wide if the weather forecast's 51 members are summed member by member, because the members' forecasts for the three farms move together almost perfectly while the farms' actual forecast errors are less closely linked. That band is almost the same as the band from adding each farm's quantiles. A band that assumes the farms' errors are unrelated is too narrow. A band from a Gaussian copula with a correlation fitted on the errors of the other 11 months comes closest to the stated probability. Only 5 half-hours in the scored year exceed 0.75 times a substation's maximum export, so this experiment cannot say what the band widths mean for curtailment cost. primary 00301 metered-farm-outage-state-band A small availability state (online, partly down, offline) estimated from the last 6 to 48 hours of a solar farm's power against its plant forecast improves the forecast band's lower tail during and after an outage. inconclusive not-for-production Solar-farm outages are too rare in the scored year to test an availability state: five of the six farms have at most 34 outage half-hours, and the sixth has 165. Too few half-hours remain to separate a 10% gain from chance, so the experiment stopped before fitting anything. If outages matter, the next test needs a longer period, such as the full history of farms A, B, and F. primary 00300 metered-farm-best-guess-assembly The assembled candidate (spread-binned plant P2, a generalised additive model (GAM) band on the plant's residuals, a mixture-density head (MDN), blended per quantile with XGBoost) scores better than plant-fed XGBoost on the quantile score and at the 0.99 quantile, and its advantage is larger for a farm with no history because the plant carries what the missing history cannot. partly supported candidate The assembled solar-farm forecast (a physical power model, two correction stages, and a blend with XGBoost) scores 3.3% better than plant-fed XGBoost (XGBoost on the plant forecast, its ensemble spread, the unit mean, and the availability ratio, with no weather features of its own) on the quantile score, which averages the pinball loss over 11 quantile levels, when each farm trains on its own history. It is 43% better at the 0.99 quantile, which bounds how much output NGED may need to curtail. With no history for a farm, the gain over XGBoost is smaller (2.0%) and below the 3% we predicted, so the physical model helps less than we expected when a farm's history is missing. primary 00293 metered-farm-plant-tilt-and-clip The six metered farms fit best at a 15 to 20 degree tilt (experiment 282), while the spread-binned plant (P2 of experiment 270) assumes 35 degrees and caps its forecast at the 0.995 quantile of the tuning months' output. Replacing the fleet tilt with 20 degrees and the hard cap with a higher, soft cap lowers P2's April to July under-prediction and its 0.99 pinball loss. not supported not-for-production Changing the solar power model's panel tilt from 35 to 20 degrees fixes most of its winter over-prediction on clear days and improves the lowest 1% quantile of the forecast by 4%, but it leaves the overall forecast band and the 99% quantile unchanged and slightly worsens summer. A higher or softer cap on the power does nothing, so the shape of the power model is not what limits the upper tail of the forecast band. A tilt between 20 and 35 degrees, or a tilt that varies with the season, is the next tilt to test. primary 00292 metered-farm-ens-neighbourhood A day-ahead cloud field is often right in shape and wrong in position by tens of kilometres, so summaries of the ensemble's irradiance over the hexagonal cells around a metered solar farm carry information that the farm's own cell lacks. Giving H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) those summaries lowers its quantile score at 12 to 36 hour leads. not supported not-for-production At the six metered solar farms tested, the ensemble's irradiance on the cells around a farm adds almost nothing to the day-ahead forecast: the quantile score improves by 0.36%, against the 2% the plan needed, and the gain is not robust to dropping one farm. Adjacent cells, 15 km apart, differ from the farm's own cell by only about 3% of the irradiance, so the ensemble mean is too smooth between them to show where a cloud edge will fall. A weather source of a different kind is the next experiment to run, rather than more processing of the same ensemble. primary 00287 metered-farm-spread-binned-plant-heads On top of the spread-binned plant (experiment 270's P2), an additive model of the residuals gives a band as good as a neural head with monotone quantile output, so the additive model is the explainable candidate and the neural head adds nothing worth porting. supported candidate On top of the spread-binned solar-farm power model, an additive model gives a better forecast band than a neural network that adjusts each quantile, so the explainable model is the candidate. A neural network that outputs a three-component Gaussian mixture scores 1.3% better than the additive model in own history, mostly in the upper tail, but not clearly in zero history, so it needs one more test before it is preferred. A blend of the additive model, a neural network, and XGBoost scores 0.8% better than XGBoost alone and fixes XGBoost's weak 0.99 quantile. primary 00286 metered-farm-drift-soiling-injection A yield index that divides each farm's output by the output of the other farms, on half-hours when the other farms are near clear-sky output, reads a yearly trend more precisely than the monthly yield index of experiment 179, and it can recover a soiling loss that the monthly index cannot. partly supported not-for-production Comparing each metered solar farm with the other farms does not make the yearly trend of its output more precise overall, but of the two indices only the comparison can read soiling, because the plain index shows a false loss slope from weather alone. A loss of 1 %/yr or more is visible at 4 to 5 of the 6 farms, and a loss under about 0.4 %/yr is visible at only 2 farms (C and F). Whether these limits are the best that output alone can give is open: a panel-level or inverter- level record would test it. primary 00284 metered-farm-tail-head-past-weather Experiment 275 found that adding years of past-weather rows lowered the 0.99 pinball loss of the neural head H5 by 4.6% while its overall score moved by 0.47%. A small neural network trained with a loss restricted to the tail quantiles (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.95, 0.98, 0.99), on the same past-weather plus ensemble rows with an era flag, lowers the 0.01 and 0.99 pinball loss of a metered solar farm's forecast below that of XGBoost trained on the same rows. partly supported not-for-production A neural network trained only to forecast the extreme edges of a solar farm's output band does beat XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile (the upper edge that matters for curtailment) by 30%, but the existing H5 network does slightly better still, and most of the gain comes from building the band around the physical power model and not from tail-only training. The years of past-weather rows add under 1% at the 0.99 quantile, and at the 0.01 quantile the share of half-hours below it is outside 0.5% to 1.5% at three farms (marginally at A, because of exact zeros at D, and clearly only at E). primary 00282 pv-plant-curve-audit The curve that turns sunshine into power in our solar models departs from the metered farms' measured curve by more than 5% of capacity somewhere in the clear-sky range, and the departure is the flat-top level (the inverter limit), not the panel tilt or the temperature loss. not supported not-for-production The curve that turns sunshine into solar power stays within 5 percentage points of capacity at 3 of the 6 metered solar farms and departs from their measured output at the other 3 in different directions, so no single fix to the inverter limit repairs it. The best-guess demand stack assumes panels tilted 35 degrees and the farms fit best at about 20 degrees, which makes the stack over-predict output on clear half-hours in December (measured is 0.66 of the stack, median over farms) and under-predict it from April to July by 5 to 8%. Swapping in the pooled shape of the other farms does not help, so the next experiment should try the 20 degree tilt inside the stack. primary 00275 metered-farm-long-history-neural-head Experiment 243 fitted H5 (the solar-farm power model plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) on about 17 months of ensemble forecasts. Adding each farm's rows built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature, back to 2019-09) as extra training rows, with a flag that marks them, lowers H5's quantile score on the ensemble-driven scored year, and the neural head gains more from the extra rows than XGBoost does. not supported not-for-production Training the neural network that corrects a metered solar farm's power forecast on nearly six years of past-weather rows, as well as on 17 months of ensemble forecasts, lowers the quantile score by only 0.5%, far under the 2% we predicted. The same rows improve XGBoost by 1.7%, so the neural network is not the better way to use extra history. The extra rows do lower the loss at the 99% quantile (the upper edge of the forecast band, which matters for curtailment) by 4.6%. primary 00273 metered-farm-sorted-quantile-rescore Some stored forecasts of experiments 224, 243, 248, 257, and 260 have quantiles that cross (a lower quantile above a higher one). Sorting the 11 quantiles in each row can only lower the pinball loss, so the stored scores are pessimistic for the arms that cross, and the arms that cross most gain most. not supported not-for-production The stored forecasts of seven metered-farm experiments have no crossing quantiles, because every fit script already sorted the 11 quantiles before writing them. Sorting the quantiles again therefore changes no score and no verdict. The 26,344 crossing rows found in experiment 268 are not farm forecasts: they belong to three generators that are not solar farms. Future heads should still be monotone by construction. primary 00272 metered-farm-weather-adapter-gam-vs-neural Extra weather variables that the solar-farm power model (the plant) ignores, fed through a learned correction to the plant's irradiance and temperature, close part of the gap between the plant driven by the ensemble weather forecast (about 0.91 of output fitted on sunny half-hours) and the plant driven by observed weather (0.973), and a small neural network does this better than additive curves. not supported not-for-production The extra ensemble weather variables (longwave radiation, humidity, precipitation, pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height) showed no usable information for the solar-farm power model at these six farms, whether they enter through additive curves or a small neural network, and the real variables do no better than placebo copies. A neural network with no plant, given the lagged power and the ensemble spread, scores 2.7% better than the plant but not better than the linear fit of experiment 257, so a correction to the plant's weather is not the route to a better forecast. primary 00270 metered-farm-xgboost-vs-plant-diagnostic XGBoost beats the plant (the solar-farm power model of experiments 218 and 224) on the six metered farms because of inputs the plant never sees, namely the farm's own lagged power and the ensemble spread, and not because of a better map from the ensemble-mean weather to power. Calendar columns and extra weather variables add little once those two are present. partly supported candidate XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model by about 3% in the quantile score even when it sees only the power model's own weather inputs, and the gain is in the width of the forecast band (the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles), not in the median forecast. The same gain comes from giving the power model a forecast band that depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index, and that band also beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile. Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. primary 00260 metered-farm-quantile-combination The three best solar-farm forecasters of experiment 243 win at different quantile levels (the neural network without physics at 0.99, H5 at 0.01), so convex per-level weights fitted on earlier months beat H5 alone, and a rolling adjustment of the outer levels brings their coverage to the nominal level without hurting the quantile score. partly supported candidate Blending the three stored forecasters with a separate weight at each quantile level scores 2.1% better than H5 alone, and every one of the six farms improves, because the neural network without the plant is best at the top quantile and H5 is best at the bottom one. About a quarter of the gain comes from averaging the five seeds, not from the weights. The rolling adjustment of the outer quantiles corrects the coverage of both tails but raises the error by 1.2%. primary 00257 metered-farm-fair-plant-arm The 4.4% gain of H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) over the plant alone in experiment 243 came from the inputs that H5 saw and the plant did not (the lagged power and the ensemble spread), so a convex linear quantile regression of the 11 offsets on those same inputs (arm P2) recovers most of it, and the neural network is not needed. supported candidate The neural network was not needed. Giving the solar-farm power model the lagged power and the spread of the ensemble members, through a plain linear fit, recovers about 90% of the neural network's gain and scores within half a percent of it. The linear fit is no worse at the 0.99 quantile (the 99% interval of the gap includes zero) and is simpler to serve, so it is the metered-farm candidate. primary 00255 metered-farm-node-curtailment-value When six metered solar farms beneath two bulk supply points are curtailed by the node-plus-generators rule of studies.node_curtailment, a forecast of each farm's output (the plant, XGBoost, or the plant with a neural head) avoids more curtailment cost than the NGED baseline, which assumes every generator runs at full capacity, and the neural head's lower 0.99 pinball loss does not show in the metric, because the rule uses only a farm's median. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting each solar farm's output instead of assuming every farm runs at full capacity cut the cost of curtailing at one of two substations (Boston, 40% lower) and raised it at the other (Skegness, 24% higher), so across both the saving is about a quarter, smaller than the uncertainty in the estimate. The neural network's better upper tail does not show in this cost, because the rule reads only each farm's median, and it lowers the cost by 3% against XGBoost, far under the 10% that would justify serving a neural network. Ranking farm forecasts by curtailment cost needs many more substations. primary 00248 metered-farm-architecture-ukv-inputs UKV irradiance and cloud, given as extra inputs to the two best neural heads of experiment 243 (H5, the plant plus 11 quantile offsets, and H2, the plant plus a correction), lower a metered solar farm's quantile score at 12 to 36 hours by more than the 1.8% that experiment 229 found for a blend of ensemble and UKV irradiance, because a neural head can use UKV cloud layers that a blend cannot. small gain not-for-production Giving the neural head on the solar-farm power model the Met Office's UKV irradiance and cloud forecasts lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, the same small gain that XGBoost gets from the same columns. At these six farms, a neural head gained no more from UKV than XGBoost did, so UKV is not worth a second weather source on this evidence. The UKV archive used is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so the 1% gain is an upper limit. primary 00246 metered-farm-ens-ukv-icond2-blend The DWD ICON-D2 regional weather forecast (2 km grid, run every 3 hours, 48 hours ahead) carries information about cloud over a metered solar farm that neither the ECMWF ensemble nor the Met Office UKV carries, so adding it to the ensemble plus UKV lowers the farm's day-ahead error. The evidence against is that at day 1 every single product lost to the ensemble mean for solar in the matched-lead study, and ICON-D2's errors are likely to be correlated with UKV's. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used is the CEDA research archive. small gain not-for-production Adding the German ICON-D2 weather forecast to the ECMWF ensemble and the Met Office UKV lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, which is under the 1.5% we set as worth a fourth weather source. ICON-D2 is available for only 12 to 29 hours of the day ahead at an 08 UTC forecast time, and the UKV archive used is a research archive, so this is an upper limit for production. primary 00243 metered-farm-architecture-comparison A solar-farm power model (the plant) as the base prediction, with a small neural network that adapts its inputs, its output, or both, forecasts a metered solar farm 12 to 36 hours ahead better than the plant alone and better than XGBoost, and keeps the plant's advantage on a farm it has never seen, while a neural network with no physics does not beat XGBoost on six farms. partly supported candidate A small neural network sitting on top of a solar-farm power model forecasts a metered solar farm about as well as XGBoost and improves on the power model alone by 4.4% in the quantile score, when the network outputs the whole forecast band. Networks that adjust a single number (the scale, a correction, or the sunlight fed to the power model) gain under 1%. The hybrid is far better than XGBoost at the upper tail (0.99 quantile, 29% lower pinball loss), which matters for curtailment. The neural network without physics does better still at that tail (32% lower pinball loss than XGBoost). primary 00240 no-xgboost-forecast-sprinkle-part-2 A small XGBoost residual model on the plant forecast's median error, an XGBoost spread model for the quantile offsets around it, or both, close at least half of the gap in quantile score between the XGBoost-free metered solar forecast (the plant fed the mean and spread of 51 ensemble members, experiment 224's arm 3) and the full XGBoost forecast (experiment 224's arm 5) at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate For solar farms, the best way to add XGBoost to the physical plant forecast is to let XGBoost predict the spread around the plant's mean, not to correct the mean: that forecast scores 4.3% better than the plant alone and 1.6% better than full XGBoost, and wins at the upper tail that matters for curtailment. Correcting the mean with XGBoost made the quantile score 0.18 points worse, about as much as a model trained on shuffled residuals. For wind, experiment 230's XGBoost stage on the physics core closes 71% of the gap to full XGBoost at 12 to 36 hours, and 44% over all leads. also relevant 00234 no-xgboost-forecast-audit-part-1 For Primary substation demand, a metered solar farm, and a metered wind farm, the best forecast that uses no XGBoost anywhere scores within 2% of the quantile score of the best forecast that uses XGBoost, at 12 to 36 hour leads. partly supported candidate An XGBoost-free forecast of Primary substation demand scores 7.5% better than BG2, the XGBoost best guess, at 12 to 36 hours ahead, on one year and six substations. The XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts score 2.8% and 5.0% worse, and lose at the 0.01, 0.05, and 0.95 quantiles. Only the solar plant model's 0.99 quantile beats XGBoost, and that is the tail that matters for curtailment. The next experiment tests small XGBoost components inside the XGBoost-free solar and wind forecasts. also relevant 00229 metered-farm-ens-ukv-blend The Met Office UKV weather model (2 km grid, 54 hours) carries information about cloud over a solar farm that the 51-member ECMWF ensemble lacks, so giving a metered solar farm's forecast both products lowers its day-ahead error against the ensemble alone, and closes part of the gap between the ensemble-driven fit (0.91 of output on sunny half-hours) and the fit with observed weather (0.973) of experiment 218. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used here is the research archive on CEDA, which differs statistically from the live UKV. small gain not-for-production Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ECMWF ensemble lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1% to 2%. The gain is under the 3% we set as worth a second weather source, and the farms' fit on sunny half-hours moves only about 6% of the way to the fit with observed weather. The UKV archive used here is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so this result is an upper limit for production; a weather product of a different kind is the option we see for a larger gain. primary 00224 metered-farm-dayahead-two-number Passing each of the 51 ensemble members through a solar farm's plant model gives the farm's day- ahead output a spread that the ensemble-mean forecast does not have, and the mean and standard deviation of the 51 plant responses keep most of that information, as they did for Primary substations in experiment 193. A two-number plant forecast therefore forecasts a metered solar farm 12 to 36 hours ahead about as well as XGBoost, and gives calibrated tails. partly supported not-for-production The 51 members of the weather ensemble help a single solar farm's day-ahead forecast only a little: passing each member through a solar-farm power model lowers the quantile score by 1.8% against feeding the model their mean, and two numbers (their mean and spread) carry 95% of that. An XGBoost model on the same weather scores 2.8% better overall, and the solar-farm model beats it only at the 0.99 quantile, the upper tail of the forecast, which matters for curtailment (switching a generator off when the electricity network is overloaded). primary 00218 metered-solar-farm-plant-fit The six metered solar farms differ in panel tilt, panel azimuth, ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, heat loss, and inverter clipping, so a plant model with those parameters fitted per farm reproduces each farm's output better than the one fleet shape (tilt 35 degrees, facing south, DC:AC ratio 1.15, 0.4% loss per kelvin, cell temperature equal to air temperature plus 25 K times the shape), and explains why the flat top of farms C, D, E, and F falls 6% to 9% from spring to summer (experiment 183). not supported not-for-production Giving each metered solar farm its own panel tilt, azimuth, heat loss, and inverter limit fits its output only 0.003 better than one fleet shape (a fraction of output fitted of 0.953 against 0.950), so the plant is probably not what limits the fit. About 5% of the squared metered output stays unexplained, and the sunshine data is the likelier source. Per-farm plant parameters look unpromising for forecasting; a better sunshine forecast looks more promising, because the same plants fit only 0.91 with the ensemble forecast. primary
