docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Better irradiance for the metered farms
docs.text: Experiment 218 found that the plant's shape is not what limits the fit: giving each farm its own plant parameters raised the fraction of output explained by only 0.003 over one shape shared by all farms. The next question is whether a solar-irradiance product other than the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), or a blend of products, raises the fraction of the six farms' output explained by the plant model. The experiment fails if the best blend raises that fraction by less than 0.02 over CAMS alone.

docs.title: XGBoost with the plant's mean and the members' spread
docs.text: Experiment 224 found that an XGBoost model scores lower pinball loss at the 0.01 to 0.95 quantiles and the plant at the 0.99 quantile. The proposal is to give an XGBoost model two extra input columns, the plant's mean response and the standard deviation of the 51 plant responses, and to refit it weekly. The experiment fails if the quantile score improves by less than 2% over plain XGBoost, or if the 0.99 pinball loss stays above the plant's.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess
docs.text:
On one validation year, the best recipe tested so far beats the stored production-style forecast at Primary substations, supply points, 6 solar farms, and 3 wind farms. Most of the gain at Primary substations comes from correcting each forecast by its mean error over the previous 14 days, and refitting weekly adds a little more. The experiments scored one validation year (July 2025 to June 2026), and several settings were chosen on that year, so the gains are probably optimistic. Nothing from this theme is adopted in production, and the best training source for solar and wind farms is unsettled.

Over all lead times, BG2 has a lower mean absolute error of the median than manual_heuristic for all four target classes, for example 7.43 against 8.70 at Primary substations (experiment 87).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
The stored production-style forecast loses to a simple rule. In experiment 13, the xgboost_baseline forecast had an error of the median 1.69 points of capacity above manual_heuristic's (99% interval +0.98 to +2.59; 16 Primaries). N1 was level with manual_heuristic (+0.22, -0.54 to +0.97), so that verdict was inconclusive.

The 14-day correction supplies nearly all of the early gain. In experiment 19, the correction lowered N1's quantile score by 0.99 points, and the stack of experiment 19 (N1 with the correction, a half-life, and a spread factor) beat manual_heuristic by 0.56 (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). The half-life added nothing to a frozen model. In experiment 87, the correction on a frozen XGBoost model lowers the Primary score by 1.38 of the 1.67 points that BG2 gains, and weekly refitting lowers it by a further 0.12 (95% interval 0.05 to 0.20).

The best guess of experiment 33 beats the production-style forecast by 3.8 to 6.3 points. The experiment 33 contrasts are 4.89 for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar farms (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind farms (-7.65 to -5.28), all at the 98.33% level. The farm contrasts use 53 Tuesday runs and the Primary contrast 73 runs. The correction applied to production explains 1.38 of the 4.89 Primary points. No arm widened production's band, so the share due to calibration is untested. The production-style 0.95 quantile was exceeded in 49% of Primary cases, against 7% for the best guess.

BG2 beats the previous best forecast at Primaries and supply points. BG2 lowered the score by 0.283 at the 16 Primaries (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and by 0.634 at the 4 supply points (-1.111 to -0.279). Adding the five-model blend lowered the Primary score by 0.086 (0.038 to 0.135). The solar offset lowered it by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on the rows it can touch, which are the daylight rows from April to September at the 5 of 16 Primaries that carry an offset. Over all scored rows the gain dilutes to 0.010.

The correction is the largest step, and weekly refitting, the blend, and the solar offset add small steps (experiment 87).

The solar and wind farm models cannot yet be ranked. The ensemble-trained model scored 0.050 points worse than the ERA5-trained mixture at 6 solar farms (98.75% interval -0.125 to +0.168) and 0.228 worse at 3 wind farms (-0.178 to +0.653). Neither interval rules out a loss above the margin we would accept (0.10 and 0.30), which is why the verdict of experiment 87 is partly supported.

Better weather would add little for Primary demand. In experiment 22, ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the score by 0.10 points (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), and not at all within 2 days. A demand model retrained on ERA5 lowered the score by 0.27 against an ENS-trained N1 with the correction (experiment 33). Both are ceilings, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late.

Whether the metering unit causes the MVA-only skill gap is unsettled. In experiment 56, skill was 10.5 percentage points lower at the 8 MVA series than at the 8 MW series over all hours (95% interval 2.1 to 17.5, resampling months), and the gap was smaller at sunny middays (April to September, 10:00 to 13:30 UTC: 5.6, -5.0 to 14.6). Resampling series instead of months gives -2.0 to 20.2 over all hours, so the data cannot separate the metering from which series were chosen. The experiment found no evidence of a need for special handling and cannot rule out a loss of about 15 points at sunny middays.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
BG2 is the best of the recipes tested here for Primaries and supply points, and no recipe is ranked for farms.

  • Primaries: a five-member quantile blend with a solar offset at 5 of 16 Primaries, scoring 5.260 against 5.543 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Supply points: the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no correction, scoring 12.925 against 13.559 for the frozen stack (experiment 87).
  • Solar and wind farms: the ERA5-trained mixture of experiment 33 and the ensemble-trained model of experiment 87 are within each other's intervals.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 19, 33, and 87 are marked candidate; none is adopted.

  • Primary demand: add the 14-day correction and the spread factor of 1.15 to N1 (experiment 19, experiment 33). Applied to the production forecast, the correction raised the threshold-weighted CRPS above the 99th percentile of history from 0.067 to 0.107 (higher is worse), and on N1 from 0.058 to 0.064, so check the tail when porting it.
  • Primaries and supply points: refit weekly, and blend five models at Primaries (experiment 87). Serve supply points without the correction.
  • Solar and wind farms: either the ERA5-trained mixture or the ensemble-trained model beats the production-style forecast, and which to serve is unresolved. Adding the power-curve base margin lowered the wind score by 0.057 (95% interval 0.024 to 0.098), and the solar bands need recalibration (experiment 87).

Experiments 13, 22, and 56 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Score every arm on the same cases. Without it, arms with missing forecasts are compared on different rows. The stored production forecast lacked 124 of 282,916 solar and wind cases and manual_heuristic lacked 195 (experiment 33). Look for arms with different run sets or ensemble members.
  • Compare with manual_heuristic as well as production. The quantile score at the 16 Primaries over 73 runs was 9.52 for production and 5.89 for manual_heuristic, so a gain over production alone overstates a new XGBoost model (experiment 13, experiment 33). Look for a changed production recipe.
  • Do not add the correction to supply points without a new test. It raised the supply-point score by 0.305 (0.060 to 0.594) in experiment 87, and experiment 33 found no gain there (+0.38, -0.12 to +0.92). The farms were not tested. Look for a second validation year or more than 4 supply points.
  • Build the correction history from daily forecasts. Experiment 19 used runs 5 days apart, so past errors were probably larger than a daily service would see, whereas experiment 87 scored 292 daily runs and its assembly script builds each correction from earlier runs. Look for a forecast service that runs less often than daily, which would make the history sparser.
  • Treat settings tuned on the scored year as optimistic. The spread factor, the blend scheme, the choice of which Primaries get the solar offset, and the half-life were chosen on the validation year (experiment 87). Look for results on a later year.
  • Read a staircase and a drop-one ablation separately. Adding the blend lowers the staircase score by 0.086, whereas removing it from BG2 raises the score by 0.091, because each starts from a different forecast (experiment 87). Look for a new member of the blend.
  • Report tail coverage and pinball loss as well as the quantile score. The quantile score hid that BG2's solar bands are too wide (experiment 87) and that production covers only 10% to 20% of cases (experiment 33). Look for a new weather source or target class.
  • Do not rely on the production-style row until its origin is confirmed. It was read from a stored table of unconfirmed origin, so its 10.54 may not match the deployed forecast (experiment 87). Look for a comparison with the current production forecasts.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the correction and the weekly refit hold their gains on a second validation year.
  • Which training source suits solar and wind farms, which needs more than 6 solar and 3 wind farms.
  • Whether the solar offset helps on daylight rows from April to September.
  • Whether the 10.5-point all-hours skill gap of MVA-only Primaries (2.1 to 17.5 over months, -2.0 to 20.2 over series) is caused by the metering, which needs more than 8 MVA series.
  • Whether monthly retraining without the correction beats the best guess of experiment 33: it scored 5.12 on one seed against 5.32, and needs a test on three seeds and more than one validation year.

The Research plan lists what is planned next.

docs.title: Production reference and best guess: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00437 neural-demand-thermal-lag-solar-gain-and-tariff-feature-bundles The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 425 sees one valid time per row, so it cannot see the hours before or after that time. Adding columns that summarise those hours (bundle T, thermal lag; bundle S, solar gain; bundle F, look-ahead) or that carry the calendar, tariff, and national signals (bundle C) lowers its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10, because the network trains across all 16 Primaries (and, in the pretrained form, across 6 years of ERA5 and CAMS history) and may find signal that the per-Primary XGBoost model and the GAM stack missed. not supported not-for-production Adding thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, calendar, tariff, or national-signal columns to the pooled plain mixture density network did not lower its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by the registered 0.03 points of capacity, in either the ensemble-only or the pretrained form. Seven of the eight arms were worse than their control at the six signed-MW Primaries, by 0.016 to 0.059 points. The thermal-lag bundle lowered the CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries (by 0.022 and 0.029) in only 2 of 4 folds, which is too weak a result to act on. The screen could not detect effects below 0.045 to 0.064 points, so the bundles are left out, not ruled out. also relevant 00434 demand-ensemble-copula-coupling-and-schaake-reordering-of-stored-forecasts The stored forecast of experiment 425's arm A holds 11 quantiles per Primary and half-hour. Drawing 51 values from those quantiles and assigning them to the 51 ensemble members by the rank of each member's 2-metre temperature (ensemble copula coupling, ECC) gives sample paths that match the observed dependence across Primaries and leads better than independent draws do, by more than the 5% coherence margin on the variogram score, without changing the marginal CRPS. A Schaake shuffle from past observed paths does at least as well as ECC. not supported not-for-production Re-ordering the stored demand forecast's 51 values by member temperature or by past observed paths does not give clearly better sample paths overall. Ordering by temperature made the paths about 7% less coherent across the 16 Primaries and 1.7% more coherent across leads at days 1 to 10 (13% at 12 to 36 hours, an interim band), and the effects cancel in the combined score. A Schaake shuffle from past paths was no worse than independent draws across Primaries and 3.5% better across leads at days 1 to 10 (interval -6.3% to -0.9%, below the 5% margin), so it is the stronger reference candidate if a step 2 runs the 51 members through the neural network. primary 00430 unified-forecaster-solar-and-pretraining-ablations A pooled mixture-density network for the six metered solar farms needs, beyond experiment 345's solar-only pooled network (the demand-style default: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, no pretraining, a clipped Gaussian mixture), only those of four switches that an ablation shows to help: the 51 ensemble members passed through a shared encoder one by one (A2), a PyTorch fleet plant that adds a power channel (A5), ERA5 and CAMS pretraining followed by fine-tuning on the ensemble (A6), and point masses at zero and at capacity in the output (A7). refuted not-for-production One pass of a neural network on the ensemble mean and spread is enough for the six solar farms: none of the four richer designs we tested beats it by the 1% margin. For the 51 coherent member paths that NGED's power-flow modelling needs, reorder the one-pass network's 51 quantiles with a Schaake shuffle, which scores 13% better than ensemble copula coupling on the variogram score of the paths and the same on the energy score. Passing each member through the network alone gives paths that score 11% worse on the energy score and a marginal quantile score 1.5% worse. also relevant 00428 day-window-convolution-attention-encoder-replacing-lagged-power-inputs A pooled mixture density network that has no hand-made lagged power input and instead reads the raw half-hourly power of whole recent days through a one-dimensional convolutional network and an attention layer (whose query is the half-hour being forecast) forecasts as well as the pooled plain network with the three origin lags on rows outside load-shift events, forecasts better on harm rows (rows whose target is outside every event but whose recent days are inside one), and follows a step added to the recent days by a much smaller share of the step, with wider bands. not supported not-for-production A neural network that reads whole days of raw power (E3) did not stop the forecast following load-shift events and scored worse than the lagged network (+0.050 on clean rows). Adding the surprise at the three lags (S1) lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.083 percentage points of effective capacity on clean rows, only just above the 0.077 minimum detectable effect, and by 0.060 on injected harm rows, below its 0.071 minimum. No arm followed a smaller share of a step in the recent power or widened its bands. All numbers are interim, from four test months. also relevant 00427 neural-mva-trajectory-labeller-and-two-channel-inputs A small labeller that reads a whole day of folded readings and outputs a probability that each half-hour is reverse flow, trained on the visible signed Primaries with solar farms injected, gives the export-gated neural network of experiment 420 (arm A) a better sign signal than the gate alone. Feeding the neural network separate MW and MVA input channels with a measured flag, and training it with MW masked on pseudo-Primaries that contain injected reverse flow, lets the network treat the hidden Primaries and the visible Primaries as the same kind of input. Together (arm TDL) the two ideas lower the signed CRPS on reverse-flow half-hours below arm A's. not supported not-for-production A small neural network that reads a whole day of meter readings and marks each half-hour as reverse flow or not ranks the half-hours about as well as the gated forecast network of experiment 420, but no better, and it wrongly marks about three in five of D5's sunny middays as reverse flow when no solar farm was added. The labeller was trained on four higher-demand Primaries, so the next step is to train a sign labeller on a mix that includes low-demand Primaries, or to accept arm A as the candidate and test it on ensemble weather. primary 00425 best-mdn-architecture-assembly-with-ablations The pooled mixture density network that adds ERA5-and-CAMS pretraining (experiment 418) to the pooled plain network with the Primary embedding, the ensemble-summary inputs, the hand-made calendar columns, and the 1.15 widening (experiments 397, 403, 406, 407, 423) scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network without pretraining, and removing the Primary embedding or the widening makes it worse. partly supported candidate Pretraining the pooled mixture density network on ERA5-and-CAMS rows before fine-tuning it on ensemble rows lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by 0.050 points of capacity (-0.078 to -0.021) at the six signed-MW Primaries and by 0.124 (-0.219 to -0.048) at the eight MVA-only Primaries. The gain is clear at the MVA-only eight and probable at the signed-MW six, where the interval just misses the registered bar of -0.03. The assembled network beat the monthly XGBoost recipe and BG2 at both of those groups and trailed BG2 at D15 and D18, so pretraining is a candidate for a numbered release of the production forecast and the Primary embedding is the component to protect. primary 00424 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-ens-serving-test Experiment 420's export-gated network (arm A) still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with its gate shut (P0) when both are trained and scored on ECMWF ensemble (ENS) mean and spread weather, which is the weather a live service would hold, instead of the recorded CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature of the laboratory test. The gain shrinks, because the ENS forecast of cloud is less accurate than recorded cloud, but most of the laboratory gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero, which does not depend on weather accuracy. supported candidate With ensemble weather forecasts instead of recorded weather, the neural network with the export gate still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with the gate shut (a gain of 15.7 points of capacity, 95% interval 13.8 to 17.4, against 19.2 with recorded weather), and it harms the forecast by no more than 0.05 points where no solar farm exports. The gate opened at the same two of the eight apparent-power-only substations as before. An unplanned finding is that the network trained on recorded weather and applied unchanged to ensemble weather scored 5.5 points better (95% interval 4.4 to 6.6) than the network retrained on ensemble weather, so how to train on ensemble weather is the open question. primary 00422 mdn-train-with-varied-origin-hour-and-age-inputs-stale-input-step-2 The pooled plain mixture density network loses CRPS when the newest power reading falls at a time of day, or lies further back, than it saw in training, and when the weather forecast is older than in training. Training with the forecast origin at many hours of the day, the newest reading delayed by a random amount, and the previous weather run sometimes shown, with the age of the weather forecast and the age of the newest reading as inputs, removes that loss without raising the score on fresh inputs. partly supported candidate Training the pooled neural network with the forecast made at eight different hours of the day removes almost all of its extra error when the newest power reading is 12 hours late (0.18 down to 0.04 points at the six signed substations). The two extra age inputs did not help, so the simplest recipe is enough. Training this way raised the error on fresh inputs by 0.04 to 0.11 points at the eight MVA-only substations, which is within the range that seed-to-seed noise could produce for the lower values, and training with some readings missing cut the missing-readings error from 2.4 to 0.3 points. These are five test months, so every number is interim. primary 00420 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-final Experiment 417's arm A (a Primary-level export gate in front of the folded likelihood) gives a large gain in signed CRPS on reverse-flow rows over the plain network read as signed, and keeps the no-injection CRPS unchanged. Adding one shared variance term that grows with the fitted PV term improves on A, because the false calls sit next to zero crossings and the q01 coverage on reverse rows is about 0.05 against a nominal 0.01, so the signed distribution is too narrow where PV is large. partly supported candidate A neural network with a gate that decides once per Primary substation whether it exports power forecasts signed power much better than the same network with the gate shut on the half-hours with reverse flow (7.1 against 26.3 points of capacity) and does no harm beyond the registered tolerance (+0.03 points at D5) where no solar farm exports. Most of that gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero at all, because the ungated network scores the same on reverse-flow half-hours, and the gate's job is to stop invented reverse flow where there is none. Switching events are the largest group, on days that carry 29% of the excess loss, so a forecast that improves only ordinary days leaves most of the loss in place. Cold snaps carry 5% of the excess in this mild scored winter, so this year cannot show whether a cold-night term pays. The formal verdict is inconclusive because one control narrowly failed. also relevant 00170 dp-bg-stage3-drift-and-holiday-scoring The convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, ensemble-mean weather, the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, and the pinned solar capacity (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when it gets a drift term (experiment 167's D1) on top of the two post-forecast corrections of experiment 155's arm D (a winter night offset and recipe R's 14-day mean error profile). The mechanism is that the drift term removes a slow demand-level error that the monthly refit on 24 months of history leaves in, and neither the offset (winter nights only) nor recipe R (a 14-day profile held to 0.75 of its size) removes that error. Training on every year of history adds a further gain, because the drift term and the pinned capacity let the old years teach the heating and calendar terms. refuted not-for-production A slowly varying demand level (a drift term) improved the forecast by 0.40 points in experiment 167 but worsened it by 0.03 points once the forecast has the Kalman filter on recent errors (lower scores are better), and training on all years of history did not change that. The filter already appears to remove the slow level error that the drift term fixes, because without the filter the drift term improves the score by about 0.2 points. The drift term should not be added to experiment 155's arm D. Christmas (24 December to 2 January) scored 1.13 times an ordinary weekday at the same half-hours, below the 1.5 times predicted, and recipe R improved the Christmas score by 0.04 points. also relevant 00169 calibration-combined-fixes-and-ensemble-spread The spread across the 51 ensemble members of the temperature and of the downward shortwave radiation at a substation predicts how wide the forecast's residuals are, beyond the hour band, calendar quarter, lead, and the cold-day widening of experiment 164. A convex quantile model that scales the quantile offsets by a non-decreasing function of those two spreads lifts the cold-night q95 coverage of the combined forecast to 0.90 or more. partly supported not-for-production Combining the smooth spread table with the cold-day widening reproduces its 0.896 coverage of the 95% quantile on cold nights, and adding the spread of the ensemble weather forecast (how much its 51 members disagree) lifts that to 0.907. The lift comes from widening the 95% and 99% quantiles by 4% and 10%, which the same model gives with its spread terms removed, so the ensemble spread is not what lifts cold-night coverage. A later experiment could test a bias correction of the mean forecast on the coldest days, and judge cold nights over more than one winter. also relevant 00168 dp-gamk-production-cadence-and-3-5-hour-delay The GAM-K forecast of experiment 155's arm D (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, the winter night offset, and recipe R) keeps its score when it is issued the way production would issue it. Production refreshes the forecast every 6 hours from the newest ECMWF run, so the weather forecast is 12 to 30 hours old, and the filter reads only power readings that are at least 3.5 hours old. Experiments 136 and 155 issued one forecast a day, 9 hours after the run. The mechanism is that a fresher filter state makes up for an older weather forecast, so the score at a given lead changes little. inconclusive not-for-production Issued every 6 hours from the newest weather forecast with power readings 3.5 hours old, the stage 2 forecast scores about the same as the once-a-day forecast over the next 24 hours (-0.007 points, 99% interval -0.076 to +0.037). The largest loss, 0.073 points, falls between 09:00 and 12:00 UTC, when the new weather run has arrived and the 6-hourly schedule has not yet used it. The pre-registered same-lead contrast read +0.076 but is confounded with the hour of the day, so the formal verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00166 switching-gated-mask-and-soft-mask-while-alarmed Experiment 165 found that setting recent power missing while a switching alarm is active lowers the error in the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends (13.69 to 6.31 points of effective capacity) but raises it by 0.102 points on rows outside logged transfers, because many alarms are not transfers. Two ways of using the alarm less bluntly keep the gain and remove the harm. (1) A gated mask: mask only when the alarm is a pair alarm of experiment 156 whose opposite steps balance at a metered neighbour with a balance score of at least 0.7, and never for a single-series refit-offset neighbour-count (RO-NC) alarm. (2) A soft mask: keep the readings in the Kalman filter but inflate their observation-noise variance by a factor that rises with the pair alarm's balance score, until the end rule fires. not supported not-for-production Setting recent power aside only when a switching alarm has a balanced opposite step at a metered neighbour (balance score 0.7 or more) keeps 99.6% of the gain after a logged transfer ends (error score 13.69 down to 6.34 points of effective capacity, 7 transfers) and adds only 0.009 points on other rows, against 0.102 for the earlier mask from either alarm. One year of data leaves the interval for the extra error too wide (-0.068 to +0.081) to meet the pre-registered limit of 0.03, so the verdict is not supported. Down-weighting recent power instead of dropping it does not help: the gain and the extra error rise together. also relevant 00165 switching-drop-recent-power-while-alarmed-all-rows A forecast built from a frozen generalised additive model (GAM) and a Kalman filter on its recent errors, with the filter's readings set missing from the moment EITHER the pair alarm of experiment 156 OR the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) is known until the end rule of experiments 147 and 148 fires, forecasts better than the same forecast with no mask while an event is running and in the 72 hours after it ends, and does not make the forecast worse on the real rows outside events, because the filter then restarts and the mask only removes readings that contain moved load. not supported not-for-production Setting recent power aside (a mask) while a switching alarm is active, where an alarm flags load moved between substations, helps only after a logged transfer ends: the mask lowers the forecast error score from 13.69 to 6.31 points of the substation's effective capacity in the 72 hours after (7 transfers). On the other rows the mask raises the score by 0.10 points, about 4% more error, which fails the pre-registered limit of +0.01 points on the upper end of the 95% interval. The next step is a mask gated on how reliable the alarm is, or used in winter only, that keeps reading recent power on rows outside transfers. also relevant 00164 calibration-cold-night-tail-under-coverage The q95 coverage of experiment 160's smooth-table forecast on cold nights (day mean temperature below 2 °C) stays near 85% because the spread table is too narrow when it is cold, not because the mean forecast is biased. Widening the quantiles on days the ensemble forecasts as cold, by a factor fitted on the tuning months, lifts cold-night q95 coverage to 90% or more without worsening the all-row score. refuted not-for-production On cold nights the 95% quantile of the best forecast is exceeded on about 15% of readings, and mostly because its prediction interval is too narrow, not because its mean forecast is biased. Widening only the upper quantiles on days the weather forecast calls cold reduces that share to about 10% without changing the all-hours score, but no fix reached the pre-registered 90% coverage in the scored year, and only 10 cold days back that year's figure. The coldest forecasts (0 °C or below) are also biased low, so correcting the mean forecast on those days is the next experiment to run. also relevant 00163 switching-real-event-comparison-gam-stack-against-bg2 On the logged real load transfers at the six decision Primaries, a forecast built from a frozen generalised additive model (GAM), a Kalman filter on its recent errors, and a mask that sets the readings missing from the moment an alarm is known (the pair alarm of experiment 156, with the end rule of experiments 147 and 148) forecasts the days after a transfer ends better than best guess 2 (BG2), because BG2 takes lagged power as an input and so carries the transfer into its forecast, and the mask does not. The stack costs little on the real rows outside transfers. partly supported not-for-production After a real load transfer ends, a forecast that masks the power readings of the transfer period or ignores recent power has an error score about 40% lower than best guess 2 (an XGBoost forecast that uses recent power) and about 54% lower than the same forecast with no mask (6.32 against 10.09 and 13.69 points of effective capacity). This rests on 7 logged transfers, and two long winter transfers carry most of the gain. On ordinary days the mask scores 0.03 points worse than no mask, and best guess 2 and the stack are indistinguishable over the year, with the stack better in winter and worse in other months. The next step is more logged transfers, or a forecast that drops recent power while the pair alarm or the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) is active. also relevant 00161 dp-bsp-top-down-against-bottom-up A bulk supply point (BSP) is forecast better bottom-up than top-down. The top-down forecast is the best-guess GAM-K chain (experiment 155's arm D) applied to the BSP's reading as a stand-alone series. The bottom-up forecast adds the arm D forecasts of the BSP's child Primary substations that report real power, each times a weight learned from earlier readings, to arm D's forecast of the remainder (the BSP's reading minus those children's weighted readings). The mechanism is that the child Primaries' own forecasts are better than the BSP's chain can infer from the BSP's sum, because each child has its own heating, solar, and calendar response and its own recent errors, and the sum is not exact (losses, unmetered load, children that report apparent power), so the remainder and the weights absorb the difference. inconclusive not-for-production Forecasting a BSP from its children's forecasts plus a remainder did not beat forecasting the BSP as a stand-alone series at either BSP: the bottom-up score was 0.6% worse at D13 and 0.5% worse at D17. The likely reason is that the children this test could use (three real-power Primaries per BSP) cover 42% and 56% of the BSP's capacity, and the BSP's error lives in the rest. The oracle control also missed its pre-registered threshold, which was set too high. The verdict is inconclusive because both intervals include zero. also relevant 00160 calibration-band-width-fix-on-stage-2-winner The q05 to q95 band of the stage 2 winning arm (experiment 155's arm D with arm A's spread table) widens in steps along the lead, because the spread table has only four lead bands (up to 24 hours, 48, 144, and 168), fitted separately per hour band and calendar quarter. Interpolating each hour band by quarter cell between the lead-band centres, forcing the width to be non-decreasing in lead, or both, removes the steps without worsening the quantile score. supported candidate The 90% prediction interval (from the 5% to the 95% quantile) of experiment 155's best forecast was equally wide on lead days 2 to 5, because its stored spread table has only four lead bands. Interpolating the table between the band centres removes the equal days and raises the quantile score by 0.002 points, below the pre-registered ceiling of 0.01, but it narrows the interval at 24 to 72 hours and widens it from 72 hours on, so one substation loses 0.009. It does not fix the cold-night upper tail: the forecast exceeds the 95% quantile on about 15% of cold-night rows, against 5% for a calibrated forecast. also relevant 00155 dp-bg-stage2-assembly-night-offset-and-error-correction A GAM-K forecast (the convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors, experiment 111) that already has the heating split by day type, one shared filter noise setting, the pinned solar capacity, and the ensemble mean as its weather input (experiment 136's arm A2) improves further when two post-forecast corrections are added: a winter night offset (experiment 137) and the 14-day mean error profile of recipe R (experiment 115). The mechanism is that the two corrections remove different errors, a level error that repeats on winter nights and a half-hour-of-day shape error that repeats day to day, so their gains add. The assembled arm then scores below experiment 111's GAM-K and BG2 (experiment 87) over leads 0.5 to 168 hours, and its tails on cold nights and on holidays are no worse than the uncorrected arm's. inconclusive candidate Adding recipe R, which subtracts 0.75 times the mean error of the last 14 days by half-hour, lowers the stage 1 assembly's score by about 0.04 points (1.3%), and the winter night offset adds nothing once R is in. The assembly with R scores 2.754 against BG2's 2.780, which is better by 0.026 points with an interval too wide to rank the two. The pre-registered placebo control failed, so the formal verdict is inconclusive, but the choice of winning arm (R alone) does not depend on it. also relevant 00137 differentiable-physics-e7-economy-7-night-step-term-in-the-forecast An additive night term, fitted on the base forecast's own past errors as a function of the ENS-mean daily temperature and the UTC clock time, lowers the day-ahead quantile score on the half-hours from 01:00 to 03:00 UTC on cold winter nights, without raising the score elsewhere. The mechanism is that the base GAM-K forecast (experiment 133's shared-noise arm) runs below actual demand from about 01:00 on cold nights (experiment 123), so a correction learned from earlier winters removes a bias the forecast repeats. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast runs about 2.5 points too low on cold winter nights from 01:00 UTC, and a correction learned from its own past errors removes that bias and lifts the 0.95 quantile's coverage there from 80% to 93%. An audit showed that a plain winter night offset does as well, so the experiment found a winter night bias, not a step that grows with cold. The verdict is inconclusive: one winter, 365 headline rows, and a failed placebo. also relevant 00136 dp-bg-stage1-assembly-on-the-ensemble-mean A convex demand model with a Kalman filter on recent errors (GAM-K, experiment 111), given experiment 114's heating split by day type (T-all) and experiment 133's single shared filter noise setting (POOL), and driven by the ensemble mean of the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) instead of its 51 members, forecasts Primary demand 0.5 to 168 hours ahead at least as well as BG2 (experiment 87) and better than experiment 111's GAM-K. The mechanism is that the three gains came from different parts of the model (the hinge, the filter noise, the weather input) and so add, and that experiment 125 found that the members' own spread adds no tail skill, so one forecast on the mean loses nothing. inconclusive not-for-production Putting everything that has helped so far into the convex demand model and driving it from the ensemble mean gives a forecast that scores the same as the production recipe (BG2) and as experiment 111's GAM-K, and the experiment cannot tell any of the three apart. Using the ensemble mean makes the score about 0.04 points worse than using all 51 members, and the heating split and the shared filter noise improve it by about 0.05, so the assembly did not add up to the hoped-for gain. also relevant 00128 differentiable-physics-kfd-shared-day-anomaly-and-sparse-q-in-gam-k Adding to experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (GAM-K) one day-level error state shared by all four hour bands, and estimating the level noise sparsely from zero, makes the filter's midday correction track an injected solar-panel-shaped change in real residuals better than GAM-K, and lowers the day-ahead score on ENS. Real residuals carry a day-level error shared across the four hour bands: the daily means of GAM-K's one-step innovations in different hour bands correlate at 0.18 to 0.23 (control P-premise). An earlier diagnosis of experiment 118's residuals gave 0.58 on a different quantity, the daily means of the residuals, which cannot separate a day-level error from a slow drift shared by all bands. inconclusive not-for-production The day-ahead forecast was not scored, because the filter with one shared day-level error state failed its test on injected changes in real recorded errors, and the experiment stopped there. The errors at different times of day do move together (a correlation of about 0.2 between their daily innovations), but a single shared state probably also soaks up errors that belong to one time of day, so it cannot follow a slow, solar-panel-shaped change. Options for a next experiment are a day-level state for each time of day with a shared part, an explicit solar-panel term, and a test with an injected change large enough to detect; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00118 differentiable-physics-kfe-kalman-filter-on-the-gam-effects-on-ens Freezing the convex model's fitted effects and letting a weight on each follow a random walk, with a diagonal noise matrix fitted by likelihood on the tuning months, forecasts day-ahead demand on ENS better than experiment 111's filter of one level and one anomaly per hour band (GAM-K), because heating slopes, PV capacity, profile scale, and holiday effects drift faster than a 24-month fit follows. The fitted noise matrix beats one step variance shared by every weight, so the gain comes from how each effect drifts and not from the weights' freedom alone. inconclusive not-for-production Letting the convex model's PV, heating, profile, and holiday weights drift did not improve the day-ahead forecast over experiment 111's level-and-anomaly filter (0.015 points worse at D+1, interval -0.013 to +0.048), and did no better in winter or on cold days. Switching the correction off on holidays is much worse (+1.24 points) and halving it is not better, so the filter still helps on holidays. The weights cannot be read as measurements, because the known-answer gate failed on real residuals, although two of its bars were mis-set. Keep experiment 111's filter, and the next step is a filter that fixes the PV weight and moves the others; the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00115 differentiable-physics-w1-diurnal-shape-state-on-ens GAM-K's remaining day-ahead error on ENS is mostly in the shape of the day inside each hour band, and that shape drifts faster than the convex model's monthly knots follow. A 48-half-hour shape state with zero mean in each hour band, added to the Kalman filter and updated from every reading the telemetry delay allows, lowers GAM-K's day-ahead quantile score at most decision substations, in months that played no part in choosing the idea's form and in the scored year. inconclusive not-for-production Teaching the physics-based forecast the shape of the day from recent readings lowers its day-ahead error by 0.075 points at five Primary substations (about 3%), in two separate periods and more in winter (0.11, a post hoc breakdown), but averaging the last 14 days' errors by half-hour gains as much, so the learned shape state is not needed on this evidence. The shape state's own check failed: it learns an injected change too slowly (0.35 against a floor of 0.4), so the verdict is capped at inconclusive. A faster shape state, tried afterwards and labelled post hoc, passed that check and beat both K0 and the recipe, which a rerun with the check fixed in advance would need to confirm. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. primary 00087 bg2-best-guess-assembled-with-drop-one-ablations Assembling the best ideas of the last experiments into one forecast beats the previous best forecast of each target class on the 292 daily forecast runs of the validation year (July 2025 to June 2026). For the 16 Primary substations the assembly is a five-member quantile blend of weekly-refitted and monthly-refitted XGBoost models, an analogue model, a pooled-by-type model, and the frozen stack, with an explicit solar offset at the 5 substations that have a clean solar capacity. For the 4 bulk and grid supply points it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model with no error correction. For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms it is the weekly-refitted XGBoost model trained on the ensemble forecast's own history. partly supported candidate BG2 beat the previous best forecast at the 16 Primary substations by 0.283 points (98.75% interval -0.425 to -0.146) and at the 4 bulk and grid supply points by 0.634 (-1.111 to -0.279). primary 00056 mva-only-primaries-skill-against-mw-primaries The best guess (experiment 33's N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor) forecasts the 8 trial Primary substations metered in MVA clearly worse, relative to manual_heuristic, than the 8 metered in MW, and the gap is largest at sunny middays, when embedded solar can push net flow through zero and an MVA meter reads the magnitude of that flow with no direction. inconclusive not-for-production At sunny middays the best guess has 5.6 percentage points less skill at the 8 Primary substations metered only in MVA than at the 8 metered in MW, but the 95% interval (-5.0 to 14.6) includes zero. The experiment found no evidence of a need for special handling of MVA-only Primaries and cannot rule out a loss of up to about 15 percentage points. primary 00033 best-guess-architecture-vs-production The best-guess architecture that the first 32 experiments point to lowers the quantile score below the deployed production recipe by more than the threshold set for each technology (1.0 point of capacity for Primary substation demand, 0.5 for solar farms, 1.0 for wind farms), each scored on its own rows. supported candidate The best guess lowered the quantile score below production's by 4.89 points of capacity for Primary demand (98.33% interval -5.66 to -4.06), 3.81 for solar (-5.07 to -2.64), and 6.27 for wind (-7.65 to -5.28), each wholly below its threshold. primary 00022 era5-weather-ceiling-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the winning recipe of experiment 00019 (the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 with a recency half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day error correction, and the 1.15 spread factor) ERA5 weather in place of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather at serving time lowers the quantile score by at least 0.3 points of capacity over all leads. refuted not-for-production ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score over all leads by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the rule asked for is ruled out. primary 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic For the 16 Primary substation demand series, stacking three changes on the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 (a 14-day correction from the model's own recent errors, a recency half-life of 0.5 years, and a spread factor of 1.15) beats manual_heuristic on ENS weather, which N1 alone does not. supported candidate C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). primary 00013 primary-demand-against-stored-baselines For the 16 Primary substation demand series, a single-stage XGBoost quantile model trained on the ENS control member (N1: the 00006 columns, recency weights, and power lags measured from the forecast origin) beats manual_heuristic, the best stored baseline, and the production recipe loses to manual_heuristic because it has no usable power persistence at short leads. inconclusive not-for-production C1, N1 minus manual_heuristic, Primary substations, mean absolute error of the median: +0.22 points of capacity over all leads (99% interval -0.54 to +0.97) and -0.57 up to 48 hours (-1.33 to +0.27). primary
