docs.title: Retraining and training history
docs.text:
On 16 Primary substations, refitting the XGBoost demand model every week with no error correction scored 0.20 to 0.24 points of capacity below a model fitted once with the correction, on two separate sets of forecast runs (292 runs at 16 Primaries, and 274 control-member-only runs at 13). The gain is fragile: three substations carry much of it, and refitting weekly instead of monthly adds only 0.04 to 0.13 points. Models trained on one old year scored worse than ones trained on a recent year, but one substation drives most of that gap.

This theme asks how often to refit the demand forecast of Primary substations, and how much history to train on. The comparison throughout is the stack: an N1 model fitted once, with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity, and a negative contrast is an improvement. Refitting solar and wind models gained little, and the cause of the penalty on older training years is not yet found.

Monthly and weekly refitting scored below the stack, though monthly minus the stack has a 99.375% interval of -0.44 to +0.08, and the 14-day correction did not help a refitted model (16 Primaries, 73 runs; experiment 34).

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A 12-month window, a half-life of 1 year or less, or the 14-day correction beat training on all history, and a model never retrained lost most (experiment 17). Against an all-history model retrained monthly, the mean absolute error of the median changed by -0.84 for a 12-month window (99.44% interval -1.19 to -0.53), -0.92 for a half-life of 0.5 years (-1.22 to -0.64), +0.52 for yearly retraining (+0.30 to +0.81), and +3.80 for never retraining (+3.12 to +4.47). The test used ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late, so these are ceilings.

Refitting monthly scored 0.20 below the stack in experiment 34, and the pre-registered interval included zero. The contrast was -0.20 (95% interval -0.38 to -0.01; 99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08), so the verdict is inconclusive. Weekly minus monthly was -0.07 (99.375% interval -0.18 to -0.00).

Weekly refitting beat the stack again on two further sets of runs. In experiment 48, on the 292 daily runs that experiment 34 left out, the contrast was -0.20 (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035) and weekly minus monthly was -0.13 (-0.24 to -0.03). In experiment 81, on 274 runs from July 2023 to March 2024 at 13 Primaries, scored with the control member only, the contrast was -0.240 (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145) and weekly minus monthly was -0.039 (-0.064 to -0.012). On an earlier set, July 2022 to March 2023, it was -0.080 (99.17% interval -0.187 to +0.051 in the text; the figure draws 95% intervals, -0.165 to +0.017): the same sign, with an interval that includes zero.

Weekly refitting beat the stack in July 2023 to March 2024 and had the same sign, with intervals that include zero, in July 2022 to March 2023 (13 Primaries, experiment 81).

Three substations carry much of the gain, so it is not established across all 16. In experiment 48 the contrast without D8 was -0.14 (99.44% interval -0.34 to +0.04), and without D8, D12, and D5 -0.08 (-0.24 to +0.10). A t-interval over the 12 months gave -0.43 to +0.04. In experiment 81, D8 alone gained 2.05 (95% interval -2.60 to -1.44), and without D8, D12, and D5 the contrast was -0.093 (95% interval -0.189 to -0.014). Experiment 81 found no sign that the weekly gain grows as 9 km weather data accumulates: it fell from -0.552 in December to -0.137 in March.

The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once in experiments 17, 19, and 48, and stops helping a refitted one. It lowered the frozen model's score by 1.45 (95% interval -1.87 to -0.98; experiment 48), though it did not help the frozen model on experiment 81's runs (+0.091, -0.005 to +0.187). On a weekly model it raised the score by 0.23 (99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44; experiment 34) and by 0.08 to 0.16 with intervals that include zero (experiment 48). It supplied nearly all of the stack's gain over N1: -0.99 of -1.00, and the stack scored 0.56 below manual_heuristic (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26; experiment 19).

Averaging the quantiles of several models gained 0.04 to 0.10 points. Three models gave -0.097 against the best member (98.33% interval -0.187 to -0.026; experiment 35). Five models gave -0.076 against weekly refitting (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023; experiment 49), and four gave -0.038 (99.17% interval -0.070 to -0.007), short of the 0.05 threshold (experiment 81). The three-model and five-model averages include the frozen stack as a member.

Refitting solar and wind models gained little. Monthly refitting minus a frozen model was -0.044 at 6 solar farms (99.44% interval -0.158 to -0.003) and +0.007 at 3 wind farms (-0.001 to +0.014), for ERA5-trained models (experiment 48). Six and three farms cannot say more.

Older training years hurt in models trained once on a single year, mostly through one substation, and neither the average level nor the weather product explains it. A model trained on 2021-07 to 2022-06 scored 1.57 worse than one trained on 2024-07 to 2025-06 on 13 Primaries with control-member weather (98.3% interval 1.14 to 2.00), but 0.61 (95% interval 0.41 to 0.81) without one substation, and removing each substation's trailing 365-day level took off 42% of that, under the half predicted (experiment 93). The gap was 1.71 with ERA5 weather in both years (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29), as large as with forecast weather, so the 18 km to 9 km change of weather product is not the main cause (experiment 95). The long-history sub-theme tests a physics-based model that may use old years. Experiment 95 also gave 0.61 without D8 on the control member and 0.78 on ERA5. Half-life contrasts under refitting were unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

The old-year penalty was as large on ERA5 as on forecast weather, so the weather product is not the main cause (13 Primaries, experiment 95).

These changes did not help a refitted model. Re-tuning the spread factor moved the score by -0.0001 (99.17% interval -0.012 to +0.018), and substation fingerprints in a pooled model by +0.009 (-0.037 to +0.050; experiment 49). A zero starting value moved it by -0.017 (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054; experiment 80). Dropping the Christmas column and changing the half-life from 0.5 to 2 years were unresolved (experiments 49 and 81).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text: The best of the recipes tested here for Primary demand is an N1 per substation, refitted weekly with no correction, with an average of quantiles over other models that includes the frozen stack. Weekly refitting scored 5.44 against 5.64 for the stack on 292 daily runs (experiment 48), and the five-model average scored 4.968 against 5.044 for weekly refitting on 73 runs (experiment 49). The half-life, the Christmas column, and the correction were not shown to help a refitted model (experiments 34, 49, and 81). BG2 builds on this recipe.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 17, 19, 34, 35, 48, 49, and 81 are marked candidate; none is adopted. The other experiments of the theme are not-for-production.

  • Refit the Primary demand model weekly and drop the 14-day correction (experiments 34, 48, and 81). This adds a scheduled job that refits 16 series at about 10 seconds each on a graphics card (experiment 34). Monthly refitting gets most of the gain over the stack (-0.20 in experiments 34 and 81; -0.08 with an interval that includes zero in experiment 48), so the case for weekly over monthly is 0.04 to 0.13 points.
  • Refit the bulk and grid supply point models weekly (experiment 48: -0.66 against the stack, 99.44% interval -1.23 to -0.27, on 4 series).
  • Serve an average of quantiles at Primaries (experiments 35 and 49). It needs several models, and experiment 81 found a four-model version short of its threshold.
  • The 14-day correction helps a model fitted once (experiments 17 and 19). A 12-month window or a 0.5-year half-life beat all history under monthly refitting in experiment 17, on ERA5 weather; their value under weekly refitting is unresolved (experiments 34, 49, and 81).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Use a monthly 12-month-window refit for contrasts of 0.05 or more, and quote absolute and tail scores from weekly refits. The window (150 rounds, learning rate 0.15) reproduced the monthly-minus-weekly gap to within 0.01 at 0.03 to 0.10 of the fit time, but scored 0.16 above full weekly refitting (experiment 85, experiment 34). For contrasts about cadence, retraining rules, or the correction, window, or half-life, use the weekly refit on all history with 150 rounds instead, because conclusions about them change with the schedule (experiment 85). Re-check for another model family or a contrast under 0.05.
  • Do not use quarterly refits to compare arms. Quarterly minus weekly was +0.381 (95% interval +0.207 to +0.565) on the 12-month window, three times the monthly gap (experiment 85). Re-check on other row sets.
  • Compare a refit arm only with a same-code repeat of its control. In experiment 75 only 9% of per-case scores matched the stored weekly run to 0.001, with a largest gap of 4.39 points, although the mean matched to 0.0001. Repeats moved the mean by 0.004 to 0.007 in experiment 80 and by 0.001 in experiment 85. Otherwise a per-case or per-event contrast reads fit noise. Re-check on CPU fits.
  • Retest the 14-day correction after any change of refit cadence or target class. It helps a frozen model, hurts a weekly one in experiment 34 (+0.23, 99.375% interval +0.03 to +0.44), and stopped helping in experiment 48 (intervals include zero). Experiment 81's frozen model gained nothing from it. At supply points adding it raised the score by 0.305 (95% interval 0.060 to 0.594; experiment 87). For farms, a correction by the mean error raised the continuous ranked probability score by 0.437 (solar, 99.58% interval +0.215 to +0.664) and 0.413 (wind, -0.003 to +0.924), and a median of the window's errors moved it by +0.010 and -0.064, post hoc with intervals that include zero (experiment 23). A 7-day window and a multiplicative form were worse than the 14-day additive form, and the correction did not help 4 supply-point series (experiment 21). Re-check with another correction window or model.
  • Report every contrast with and without the series that carries it. D8 alone gained 2.05 (experiment 81) and has a 13.1-point old-year gap while the other 12 substations range from 0.0 to 2.6 (experiment 95). Otherwise a pooled interval reads as a gain across all series. Re-check on other substations.
  • Do not screen features on a frozen model. The weekly-analogue columns gained 0.05 on a frozen model and 0.01 under monthly refitting (experiment 34). Re-check with other recent-demand features.
  • Do not stand in warm-start boosting for refitting. Warm starts got worse with more updates (7.76 against 6.21 for the weekly chain over the daily months; +1.55, +0.33 to +3.21), and a proxy that sees later data is a screening device, not a forecast score (experiment 34).
  • Quote absolute scores only within one experiment's runs. The stack scored 5.32 on experiment 34's 73 runs and 5.64 on experiment 48's 292, and experiment 81's control-only scores match neither. The stack of experiment 19 has a half-life of 0.5 years, and the stacks of experiments 33, 34, 48, and 87 use the 2-year weighting. Re-check which stack a new experiment uses.
  • Check that a 12-month window can test an input. The COVID indicator is constant inside the window, so it cannot be tested (experiment 49). Look for the input's variation within the window.
  • A single month cannot show a weather-product change. The frozen model's lead over manual_heuristic swings from 11.6% in April to 1.2% in June to 8.8% in August (experiment 81). Re-check with a model trained on one product.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether weekly refitting beats the stack at all 16 Primaries on a year the project has not scored, and with the full ensemble; the Research plan lists the longer ENS history.
  • Whether any of the gain is adaptation to the 9 km weather product (experiment 81 could not separate them).
  • What makes older training years worse. Drift differs by series (experiment 92, inconclusive), and experiment 95 suggests changes in solar, heating, or the electricity network without testing any.
  • Whether the Christmas column and the half-life matter under weekly refitting.

The Experiments page lists every experiment of the theme.

docs.title: Retraining and training history: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00419 pooled-mixture-density-network-solar-summary-sunny-flag-and-half-life-input-ports The XGBoost model's gain from a two-column solar summary (experiment 381: -0.051 points at the signed-MW six on the scored year) carries over to the pooled plain neural network, which has the solar geometry but no cloud-aware summary, and the 0.25-year half-life that lowered the score at D15 and D18 and on cold nights in experiment 407 does so again with new random seeds. not supported not-for-production The XGBoost model's solar-summary input did not carry over to the pooled plain neural network: it lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at the six signed-MW Primaries by only 0.012 points of capacity (-0.043 to +0.013), one sixth of the 0.0738 minimum detectable effect. Refitting the same neural network with new random seeds changed the MVA-only eight by -0.047, about six times as far as the solar summary did there (-0.008), and changed the signed-MW six by the same amount as the solar summary did (+0.011 against -0.012). Adding the sunny flag and a 1-year half-life was worse than the solar summary alone, and the 0.25-year half-life raised the signed-MW six CRPS (+0.044) while lowering it at D15 and D18. None of the input changes is adopted, and the reference stays. All five test months are interim. also relevant 00418 mdn-pretrain-on-era5-and-cams-then-fine-tune-on-ens The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 397, pretrained on the Primaries' own power and ERA5 and CAMS weather from 2019-09 and then fine-tuned on the ENS rows, scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network trained on the ENS rows alone, because the ENS archive starts on 2024-04-01 and the pooled network sees at most 18 to 24 months of it. supported candidate Teaching the neural network first on six years of past weather and power, then on the forecast archive, lowers its error by about 0.06 points of capacity (2.1%) at the six signed-direction substations and 0.16 points (4.2%) at the eight apparent-power-only substations over 12 test months. Changing how much of the network is retrained, or adding forecast-like noise, changes the score by less than the interval of the estimate. With only 6 months of forecast archive on 4 test months the gain is about 1.3 points, although the ENS-only baseline degrades badly there. primary 00407 pooled-mixture-density-network-tail-arms-and-recency-weights The pooled plain network's tails at the six signed-MW Primaries are too narrow (q95 coverage 0.855 and q99 coverage 0.941 in experiment 397), and at least one of five changes lowers the tail loss below a globally widened pooled plain network without raising the CRPS: 5 mixture components, split-normal (skewed) components, a widening fitted per lead band inside each refit, a quantile head trained with the pinball loss, or a different half-life for the row weights. not supported not-for-production Making the shared neural network's outer quantiles 15% wider about the median is the best of the fixes tested for its too-narrow outer bands at the six substations where power can flow both ways (the signed-MW six). None of 5 mixture components, skewed components, a band width fitted per lead time, or a neural network trained directly on quantiles did better on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) and the loss at the 99% quantile together. The quantile-head neural network cut the loss at the 99% quantile by about a sixth, but raised the CRPS by 0.066 points of capacity. No change brought the coverage of the 95% quantile up to the 0.92 we asked for. Two changes are worth testing next: the quantile-head neural network as a separate tail model, and a widening fitted on weeks closer to the test period. All five test months are interim. also relevant 00406 pooled-mixture-density-network-without-embedding-and-with-short-history Most of the gain that one pooled mixture density network shows over one network per Primary (experiment 403) comes from sharing parameters, not from the learned Primary embedding, and the gain does not grow when each Primary's training history is cut to 3, 6, or 12 months. not supported not-for-production One neural network shared across all 16 substations only beats separate networks if it knows which substation it is forecasting: without a substation input it is 0.57 points of capacity worse than separate networks at the six signed-direction substations, and with a learned substation embedding it is 0.22 better. The advantage of sharing grows when one substation has little history: with 3 months of its history the shared network is 1.15 points better, because the separate network loses 1.77 points and the shared one only 0.83. All five test months are interim. also relevant 00399 xgboost-short-history-start-cut-d15-d18 Dropping the first months of the two short-history Primaries, D15 and D18, from the monthly XGBoost demand model's training rows lowers its error at those Primaries, because the readings taken while the meters were being commissioned teach the model a wrong level. partly supported candidate Dropping the noisy first weeks of D15 and D18 from the training rows helps the monthly XGBoost forecast only a little: about 1% lower error at both, mostly in the first scored months, when the history was shortest. Cutting 6 months is not safe, because it made D18 worse. The larger problem at D15 is a level error that no start cut fixes: the median forecast is about 21 points of capacity too low, against 3 for the generalised additive model (GAM) stack, so the next experiment should look at D15's level, not its start. primary 00395 xgboost-level-state-winter-spread-anchor-stored-forecasts A level state in the style of the GAM stack's Kalman filter, run on the weekly XGBoost bundle's own residuals, closes the bundle's gap to the GAM stack at D11 and D14, and a one-state filter with three numbers per Primary does so almost as well as the stack's two-state filter. partly supported not-for-production A Kalman-filter-style level state helps the weekly XGBoost model at D14 and hurts it at D11, so the filter is not the whole explanation of the gap to the GAM stack. A cheap one-state version (three numbers per Primary) recovers about half of the two-state filter's gain at D14 only, so the first production update should not carry it. Adding the winter ensemble-spread columns lowers cold-night scores but not cold-night coverage, and does not widen the band where weather is most uncertain. A short-history level anchor cuts D15's median bias but worsens the other 14 Primaries by about 0.1 points. When recent power readings lie inside a labelled load-shift event, every forecast loses q95 coverage on the signed-MW six, and only the GAM stack does on the MVA-only eight. The GAM stack's score worsens most, though its interval overlaps the others'. also relevant 00360 bg2-member-drop-one-at-d8 BG2's lead over the GAM stack at D8 is spread across its five-member blend, so no single member explains it. supported not-for-production BG2's lower score than the GAM stack at substation D8 does not come from blending five forecasts. Four of its members (weekly XGBoost, monthly XGBoost, analogue, pooled by substation type) each score 7.47 to 7.69 alone, against 8.338 for the GAM stack, and dropping any one member changes the blend's score by less than 0.1 points. The XGBoost stack member alone scores 8.562, so the lower score more likely comes from what the other four members learn. This is one substation and one scored year. also relevant 00357 wind-default-2-monthly-head-longer-retest Retraining Wind farms research default 2's mixture head on the first day of every month (experiment 356's arm u3) gains over default 2 at true days 1 to 10, because a recent head tracks the farms' drift. Experiment 356 measured -0.038 points on 53 Tuesday runs (interval -0.104 to +0.024) and -0.120 on about 16 Tuesday runs of 2026-07 onwards. partly supported candidate Retraining Wind farms research default 2's head every month improves the forecast slightly, by about 0.04 to 0.05 points over the scored year and about 0.10 points in the latest 2.5 months, and no scope shows harm to the score. The scored-year interval still touches zero, so the change is a candidate and is not adopted. The upper tail stays too heavy (1.7% to 2.0% of observations above the 0.99 quantile), so retraining does not fix it. also relevant 00356 wind-default-2-blend-and-monthly-refit-retest Wind farms research default 2 (experiment 347's arm y2) gains 0.234 points over Wind farms research default 1 at true days 1 to 10 but puts 2.28% of observations above q99 over every lead (2.15% at true days 1 to 10). Either a per-quantile, per-lead-band blend of the two defaults (u2), experiment 348's arm z5 (u1), a monthly offset layer on default 2 (u4), or a monthly retrained head (u3) lowers the 0.99 pinball loss and the share above q99 without losing the gain. not supported not-for-production Blending Wind farms research default 2 with research default 1, or refitting it every month, does not fix its upper tail: the share of observations above the 0.99 quantile only falls from 2.15% to between 1.77% and 2.04%, against 1% intended, and no arm clearly beats default 2 over days 1 to 10. The blend's small gain (0.05 points) is the same with shuffled weights, so it is averaging, not learning. The top quantile needs new information, not a blend or a refit; the monthly retrained head is the one arm worth a longer retest. also relevant 00355 d8-weekly-refit-and-median-band-swap (H1) Refitting D8's stack weekly instead of monthly is not the main reason BG2 beats the stack at D8. (H2) Most of the stack's remaining gap to BG2 sits in the band, not the median. partly supported not-for-production Refitting D8's forecast every week instead of every month lowers its score by only 0.045 points of capacity, so BG2's weekly refit is not why it beats the stack at D8. The remaining 0.79-point gap is not mostly the band or mostly the median: BG2's band on the stack's median closes 14% of it and BG2's median under the stack's band closes 27%. The next step is to look at how BG2's median and spread are fitted together rather than at either part alone. primary 00354 d8-own-residual-bands-and-longer-fit-history (Fix 1) At D8 (Marsh Lane), a forecast band built from the quantiles of D8's own past residuals scores much better than the band the stack borrows from six other Primaries, and costs little at Primaries with no gas engine. (Fix 3) A GAM fitted on D8's history since 2023-09, with a free level step per hour band at 2025-04-01, scores better than the GAM fitted from 2025-04 only, and the step is needed. partly supported not-for-production A forecast band built from D8's own recent errors lowers D8's score by 2.3 points of capacity and closes about 60% of the gap to BG2, with no change to the median forecast. The same rule raises the score by 1% to 6% at three Primaries that have no engine, so it should apply to D8 only until a version that widens with lead time exists. A longer fit history helps only in the first three scored months, when the stored fits had 3 to 5 months of data, and a level step for the April 2025 change adds nothing measurable. also relevant 00346 wind-research-default-1-offset-table-refit-cadence Experiment 342 found that the default's offset table, fitted once on the 442 daily runs of 2024-04-01 to 2025-06-16, leaves the upper tail too low in the scored year (observed power above q99 in 1.8% of half-hours against 1% intended) although it fits the hindcast, and blamed drift between the hindcast years and the scored year. The ensemble table holds daily runs up to 2026-10-24, so the table can be refitted each month on runs that had already finished. A table refitted monthly on a trailing 6-month window (x2) scores lower than the table fitted once. partly supported candidate Refitting the wind forecast's offset table every month on recent runs makes the forecast a little better (a 0.4% to 1.1% lower quantile score), using only data the service already stores. It does not fix the upper quantiles, which still miss in 1.7% of half-hours against 1% intended. So the change between the training years and the scored year is a minor cause, and the upper-tail miss needs another explanation. A monthly job that refits the table on all earlier daily runs passes the adoption conditions and is a candidate. also relevant 00331 primary-demand-recency-weights-on-gam-and-kalman When the additive (GAM) model with a Kalman filter on its daily residual is refitted monthly, giving older training rows exponentially less weight forecasts the next month better than equal weights on the full history, and no worse than training on the last 24 months only. not supported not-for-production Training the monthly refit mostly on recent data improves the next month's forecast by about 0.025 points of capacity, but a plain 24-month window gets the same gain, so smooth recency weights add nothing and no weights should go into the research default. Half of the gain comes from one Primary substation whose demand shifted in 2023. Giving extra weight to rows from the same time of year in earlier years gave a further 0.012 points and is worth its own test. This is a lab result on past weather with a Kalman filter that already adapts to level changes. primary 00328 lsc-regime-changes-detect-then-model-part-1 A permanent change in the configuration of an electricity network (a large new generator, a new factory) can be found offline from a Primary's own history, and a forecast that keeps the effects of the old behaviour fitted on the full history and adds new effects that exist only from the change onward scores better after the change than the same forecast refitted on a recent window only. not supported not-for-production Adding effects for a detected permanent change does not forecast better than refitting the additive model on the last 24 months, in a lab setting where the model is given past weather. The detectors find a 10% step of a Primary's load within 60 days only 26% of the time at an acceptable false-alarm rate, so there is little time after the alarm for the extra effects to help. On this base, handling a regime change comes down to how often the model is refitted. The rolling-GAM detector might still help when building substation cards, which this experiment did not test. also relevant 00298 lsc-long-deep-detector-and-refit-cleaning A trivial detector on the daily mean residual of the lagless convex additive model (GAM_ONLY) finds load shifts that last days to weeks and cover at least 10% of a Primary substation's load, which the existing hour-scale detectors miss, and excluding the days it flags from the monthly refit stops the forecast learning those shifts as the normal pattern. not supported not-for-production A simple detector on the daily mean error of the forecast that uses no recent power finds about as many of the long, deep real load shifts as the learned score LR_b20 (10 to 12 of 19 for four of the six variants). The cumulative-sum variant B also finds 27 of the 29 multi-day drops at D8, which are probably a gas engine and not load shifts; variant C finds 11. Leaving the days a detector flags out of the monthly refit cuts the share of a 30-day transfer that the forecast learns as normal from about 19% to about 10% to 13%. Excluding the true shift days instead cuts the share to 2.8%. The detectors recover less because each needs 1 to 3 days to fire and misses about 40% of long injected transfers and over half of the real ones. Tell NGED that transfers of 14 days or more are partly learned as normal, and try a detector that fires on the first day next. also relevant 00295 regime-segmentation-part-b-persistent-regimes-without-labels A segmentation of a Primary's whole history with hindsight, using only changes in the distribution of the residual of a lagless convex additive model (GAM), finds regime changes without labels. A regime is the whole period, without gaps, during which one configuration holds. For D8's gas engine, the regime is the whole period in which the engine is installed and included in the meter, including the spells when the engine is off. Whether the engine is running, and whether a load shift is in force, are states inside a regime. A boundary is a regime change when the distribution does not return to its earlier form and no neighbouring Primary shows the opposite change, and a state change otherwise. not supported not-for-production Looking only at the residual of a forecast that uses no recent power, a segmentation finds a lasting change of 25% of a Primary's load and dates it with a median error of 0 days, but it misses about half of 10% changes and cannot reliably tell a 14 to 60 day load shift from a lasting change. At D8 it finds the 2023-08-15 break exactly, but only at penalties that also find 2.5 or more regime changes per Primary-year at the other Primaries. An offset for the latest regime lowers the forecast error after a step by 2.2 points of capacity, but a plain 60-day mean residual does as well, so the segmentation is not worth adding for that purpose. also relevant 00290 lsc-long-shift-cut-date-robustness The 19% of a 30-day transfer that experiment 274 found learned as normal is stable across fit-cut dates, so that the share learned lies within 15% to 25% at every cut date. not supported not-for-production The forecast with no recent power learns about a fifth of a 30-day load transfer as normal, but the share depends on the date: it ranges from 9% to 29% across 12 end dates, so experiment 274's 2.49-point bias is a typical value, not a fixed one. Quote the share as a range of about 9% to 29%. The cause of the spread is not located. also relevant 00278 stack-retraining-cadence The best-guess stack (arm D, the neural network head, and the two-number solar summary) needs its neural network head retrained at least quarterly, but its convex model (a generalised additive model with a Kalman filter on its coefficients) tolerates quarterly instead of monthly refits, because the filter absorbs the drift between refits. not supported not-for-production Retraining the small neural network that corrects the demand forecast's median, every quarter or every month, scored no better than training it once before the scored year, so it needs no retraining schedule over a year. The convex demand model should keep its monthly refits, which take 0.4 s per substation: refitting quarterly instead scored 0.010 points worse overall (not shown to be acceptable) and weekly refits gained nothing. Refitting the two solar factors quarterly instead of monthly changed nothing. also relevant 00275 metered-farm-long-history-neural-head Experiment 243 fitted H5 (the solar-farm power model plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) on about 17 months of ensemble forecasts. Adding each farm's rows built from past weather (Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service irradiance and ERA5 temperature, back to 2019-09) as extra training rows, with a flag that marks them, lowers H5's quantile score on the ensemble-driven scored year, and the neural head gains more from the extra rows than XGBoost does. not supported not-for-production Training the neural network that corrects a metered solar farm's power forecast on nearly six years of past-weather rows, as well as on 17 months of ensemble forecasts, lowers the quantile score by only 0.5%, far under the 2% we predicted. The same rows improve XGBoost by 1.7%, so the neural network is not the better way to use extra history. The extra rows do lower the loss at the 99% quantile (the upper edge of the forecast band, which matters for curtailment) by 4.6%. also relevant 00274 lsc-long-arrangement-audit-gam-refit A forecast with no lagged power learns a long-lasting change of running arrangement as the normal pattern, because the monthly refit trains on whatever the meter recorded. The learned share grows with the duration of the arrangement, and the duration beyond which the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) is wrong by more than a stated tolerance sets the limit that can be told to NGED. not supported not-for-production A forecast that uses no recent power still learns a load transfer as normal, and the forecast learns the transfer quickly: a transfer lasting only 7 days leaves the forecast 1.2 points of effective capacity too high for the next 2 days, and a transfer lasting 30 days leaves it 2.5 points too high (about a fifth of the transfer). No tested duration, down to 7 days, was short enough to avoid this. Masking known transfers out of training is the obvious remedy, but this experiment did not test it, and the next experiment should test it together with transfers of 1 to 6 days. also relevant 00167 dp-full-history-gam-24-months-or-all-years-with-drift With the PV capacity pinned to the as-of table (explicit PV) and the heating split by day type (T-all), the convex demand model (the GAM) trained on every year of history back to late 2019 with a drift term scores better than the same model trained on the last 24 months, when both are refitted at 12 quarterly origins on past weather (ERA5 and CAMS). The mechanism is that explicit PV removes the changing solar capacity from the target, so the old years teach the heating and calendar terms without the capacity growth that made the all-years fits of experiments 104 and 107 unstable, and the drift term absorbs the remaining slow change in the demand level. supported candidate Adding a drift term (a slow adjustment to the demand level) improved the forecast at 11 of 12 quarterly refits. The quantile score, where lower is better, fell by 0.40 points when training on the last 24 months and by 0.55 points when training on all years back to late 2019. Training on all years instead of 24 months adds only 0.10 points on top of a drift term, and gives no gain without one, so extra years of history help little. also relevant 00149 differentiable-physics-full-history-gam-era5-cams When the convex model's solar term is explicit (a pinned capacity times a unit solar shape in both arms), training on every year of a substation's history back to 2019 gives a lower quantile score than training on the last 24 months, once a drift term lets the model follow the slow level change. The mechanism is that more years pin down the temperature, calendar, and weekday terms better, and the drift term absorbs the level change that made all-years training unstable in experiments 104, 106, and 107. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand model on every year back to 2019, instead of the last 24 months, lowered its forecast error by only about 3% (0.08 points of substation capacity), and the difference could be chance. The drift term helped much more, lowering the error by 0.38 points on 24 months and 0.50 points on all history, but a post hoc audit found that a plain correction by the mean error of the last 28 training days recovers 86% to 94% of that gain, so the gain is a recent-level correction and the drift form is not shown to beat the simpler fix. We did not test whether explicit heating, switching, or pooled terms would make the longer history help. also relevant 00107 differentiable-physics-rolling-origin-history-and-tails Refitted quarterly from 2023-07 to 2026-04 and scored on the next 3 months, the convex model's two history contrasts (all years against 12 months, drift against none) keep one sign at almost every origin. A second claim, labelled separately as C5 and not part of the verdict: a level-dependent spread brings its 95% and 99% quantiles within 1 point of nominal coverage without worsening the quantile score. partly supported not-for-production Giving the convex demand model a drift term lowered its score at 10 of 12 quarterly refits, by 0.45 points when trained on all years (interval 0.23 to 0.68). In a post hoc split, about three-fifths of that size is one substation (D10) at the 2023-24 refits, and the 2025-26 refits give 0.30, as in experiment 104. All years without drift scored worse than 12 months at 8 of 12 refits, and all years with drift against 12 months has no stable answer: winter-quarter refits favour more years, summer ones are level. The spread that depends on the forecast level made the 95% and 99% quantiles worse, so the tail coverage still needs a different method. The verdict is partly supported, because only the drift contrast is stable; a second spread (the conformal spread) is not interpreted, because it was built with a flaw. also relevant 00106 differentiable-physics-4-all-years-drift-and-recent-level The differentiable-physics model trained on every usable year from 2019-09 with a drift term forecasts Primary demand better than the same model on its best window, and assimilating recent residuals through a Kalman filter makes it better again, by more than a simple moving-average correction does. partly supported not-for-production Correcting each day-ahead demand forecast with the errors the model made up to 3.5 hours earlier lowered the quantile score by 0.61 points (from 2.90 to 2.29) in the scored year and by 1.02 points in the year before, at all five long-history substations. The gain relies on estimates of past weather that a live service would not have, and against lagged XGBoost at the same lead the filtered model scored 2.349 against 2.487, a difference that is not significant. Whether old years of history help is not settled, because the contrast changed sign between the two years, so the verdict is partly supported. also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00095 age2-old-year-penalty-with-the-same-weather-product-demand The extra forecast error of an old training year (experiment 93) comes mostly from the change of weather product between the old years (18 km grid spacing) and the recent year (9 km), not from the age of the training data, so an old year and a recent year that use the same weather product score about the same. refuted not-for-production The old-year penalty does not shrink when both years use ERA5: the 2021-07 year is 1.71 points worse than the 2024-07 year on ERA5 (99% interval 1.15 to 2.29) and 1.57 worse on the control member (1.12 to 2.03), so the weather product is not the main explanation and the penalty goes with how old the training year is. primary 00093 age1-old-training-year-after-level-normalisation-demand A year of training data hurts a Primary substation demand forecast with its age only because the substation's average demand level differed in that year, so subtracting a trailing 365-day level from the targets and the power lags removes most of the penalty for an old training year. refuted not-for-production Subtracting a trailing 365-day level removes 42% of the old year's penalty (C1 1.57, C2 0.91 points), under the half the prediction required, and without the one series that carries most of the penalty it removes none (0.61 to 0.68). primary 00092 lv0-drift-diagnostics-on-stored-predictions-demand Most of the drift in Primary substation demand since 2022 is a per-series level or smooth trend, not a change of daily shape, so a slow per-series level term, not a new weather response, is what a long-history or pooled XGBoost model is missing. inconclusive not-for-production Drift is large and differs by series, but a level shift alone does not explain the loss from extra history or the pooling gap. primary 00085 cheaper-retraining-schedules-rank-arms-like-weekly-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, a cheaper retraining schedule ranks two pairs of arms the way full weekly retraining ranks them: the cadence pair (monthly minus weekly retraining) and the starting-value pair (a zero starting value minus XGBoost's estimated starting value, the contrast of experiment 80). The cheaper schedules are (a) a monthly refit on a rolling 12-month window with 150 rounds and eta 0.15 (P-roll), (b) the same refit every quarter, (c) a monthly refit at the full setting (whole history, 500 rounds, eta 0.05), and (d) a weekly refit on the whole history with 150 rounds and eta 0.15. A schedule that passes can replace weekly retraining in research experiments. partly supported not-for-production Monthly minus weekly retraining is +0.125 (95% interval +0.036 to +0.229) at the full setting, +0.118 (+0.033 to +0.216) with a 12-month window, and +0.125 (+0.038 to +0.227) with 150 rounds. primary 00081 r11-control-member-second-validation-year-demand The Primary substation demand findings of experiments 48 and 49 keep their sign on forecast runs the project has not scored: the daily 00:00 UTC ECMWF ensemble (ENS) control-member runs of 2023-07-01 to 2024-03-31 (July to March, with no April to June). For the 13 Primary substations that have power data throughout, weekly refitting of the XGBoost demand model N1 without error correction scores below the stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and the spread factor 1.15), and weekly refitting scores below monthly refitting. supported candidate C1, weekly minus the stack: -0.240 points (99.17% interval -0.360 to -0.145). primary 00080 bm0-zero-base-margin-xgboost-quantile-models XGBoost starts a quantile model from a base score that it estimates from the training labels, one value for each of the nine quantile levels (experiment 78 found 0.403 at the 5% level to 0.899 at the 95% level for one series, with 500 boosting rounds and no early stopping). Replacing that start with zero (a base margin of zero in every row, which is the same as a base score of zero) lowers the quantile score of the production-style models for Primary substation demand (retrained weekly), bulk supply point and grid supply point demand (retrained weekly), solar farms, and wind farms. The gap is not a symptom of too few boosting rounds, so four times as many rounds, or early stopping, does not remove it. inconclusive not-for-production Starting XGBoost from zero did not lower the quantile score of any production-style XGBoost model: Primary substations -0.017 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054), bulk and grid supply points +0.006 (-0.091 to +0.092), the frozen Primary stack -0.033 (-0.084 to +0.031), solar farms -0.010 (-0.036 to +0.028). also relevant 00049 vp1-screening-reference-under-p-roll-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, once the XGBoost quantile model N1 is refitted every month without the 14-day error correction, (a) a spread factor chosen on earlier months only lowers the quantile score below the fixed factor 1.15, (b) an average of the quantiles of retrained and stored XGBoost models, with one weight vector chosen per month on earlier months, still lowers it below the best single member, and (c) each adopted input (the Christmas column, the COVID indicator, a half-life of 0.5 years) changes the score when dropped, and the substation fingerprints of experiment 32 change it when added to a pooled XGBoost model, all under the cheap rolling-window refit P-roll. supported candidate B1, the blend minus its best member: -0.076 points (99.17% interval -0.135 to -0.023). primary 00048 weekly-retraining-confirmation-and-extension-demand-generators On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of the validation year that experiment 34's 73 runs leave out, weekly retraining of the Primary substation demand model N1, with no error correction, lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than zero points of capacity; monthly retraining of the ERA5-trained solar and wind stage 1a models changes the score by less than 0.05 points; and, once the model retrains weekly, neither a 7-day nor a 14-day error correction helps. supported candidate C1, weekly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.44% interval -0.40 to -0.035). primary 00035 lead-weighted-quantile-blend-of-stored-models For Primary substation demand, solar farms, and wind farms, averaging the quantiles of two or three forecast models that experiments 19, 20, 30, and 33 already scored (N1 is the ENS-trained single-stage XGBoost model, and the stack is N1 with the 14-day correction and a spread factor of 1.15), with one weight per lead band chosen only on earlier months, lowers the quantile score below the best single member by more than the threshold set for each technology (0.05 points of capacity for Primary demand and solar, 0.10 for wind). supported candidate Averaging the quantiles of three stored demand models lowered the Primary demand error by 0.10 points of capacity against the best single model (98.33% interval -0.19 to -0.03), so the estimate clears the 0.05 threshold for moving it into production. For solar and wind the gains were too small to resolve on 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms. also relevant 00034 retraining-cadence-and-cheap-proxies-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, retraining the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 monthly (half-life 0.5 years, no 14-day error correction) lowers the quantile score below the best-guess stack (frozen N1 with the 14-day correction and spread factor 1.15) by more than 0.10 points of capacity; the gain from retraining more often flattens between monthly and weekly retraining; and the 14-day correction stops helping once the model is retrained. A second, separately reported claim is that at least one cheap proxy for monthly retraining ranks arms the way full monthly retraining ranks them. inconclusive candidate C1, monthly retraining minus the stack: -0.20 points (99.375% interval -0.44 to +0.08, 95% interval -0.38 to -0.01). primary 00023 lagged-power-and-error-correction-solar-wind For the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms, giving the stage 2 calibrator the farm's recent observed power (lagged power, or summaries of the latest day), or shifting the forecast by its own recent error (the 14-day correction of experiments 00017 and 00019), lowers the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) below that of the same calibrator without recent power. inconclusive not-for-production C1, lagged power added to the calibrator: solar -0.012 (99.58% interval -0.122 to +0.088), wind +0.012 (-0.090 to +0.146). also relevant 00021 error-correction-variants-bsp-gsp-demand A recent-error correction of N1's quantiles, measured with power that is 2 days old, lowers the quantile score of the 4 bulk supply point (BSP) and grid supply point (GSP) demand series as it does for the 16 Primary substations, and some variant of the correction (a 7-day or 28-day window, multiplicative, per-half-hour-of-day, or weighting recent days more) beats the plain 14-day additive correction. inconclusive not-for-production The 14-day additive correction lowered the Primary quantile score by 0.99 points of capacity (99.375% interval -1.82 to -0.18) when the newest power was 2 days old, as it did with 3.5-hour-old power in experiment 19. On the 4 bulk and grid supply point series it raised the score by 0.36 (-0.19 to +0.98), so it is unproven there. No variant beat the plain additive 14-day form: a 7-day window was worse (+0.19) and a multiplicative form far worse (+2.28). also relevant 00019 primary-demand-stack-vs-manual-heuristic For the 16 Primary substation demand series, stacking three changes on the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 (a 14-day correction from the model's own recent errors, a recency half-life of 0.5 years, and a spread factor of 1.15) beats manual_heuristic on ENS weather, which N1 alone does not. supported candidate C1, the full stack minus manual_heuristic, quantile score over all leads: -0.56 points of capacity (99.44% interval -0.93 to -0.26). also relevant 00017 training-window-and-retraining-rule-drift-demand For the stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained on ERA5 weather, Primary substation demand drifts (experiment 13 saw every arm under-forecast its validation year by 1.3 to 3.1 points of capacity), so a model trained on a recent window, weighted towards recent rows, retrained monthly, or corrected by the error of the last 14 days, has a lower error than the same model trained on the whole history and never retrained. supported candidate C9, the 14-day correction against A: -1.52 points (99.44% interval -1.95 to -1.13). primary

docs.title: P16: a longer ENS history
docs.text: The ENS backfill from Source Cooperative (2021-03 to 2024-03) could give an earlier validation fold, and the full fetch cannot run autonomously. Issue #959 (Extend ECMWF ENS training history) describes the fetch. The archive is in us-west-2. Fetching the control member alone is about 530 GB and 4 to 5 hours, and fetching all 51 members is about 30 TB, which needs a cloud machine in that region and the maintainer's approval of the cost. The issue also ties autonomous use of the fetch to the scorer-protection work in issue 958. Every experiment since 00003 scores the same year on the same 16 series, so choices tuned there overfit it, and an earlier fold is the remedy. For demand, a longer training history has hurt so far, so the backfill is valuable first as validation data.

docs.title: Solar disaggregation
docs.text:
At the 5 Primary substations with a clean solar-capacity estimate, giving the XGBoost demand forecast a forecast of the output of the solar panels behind the substation lowered its daylight April-to-September error by 0.15 points of capacity in one validation year; against a reference that also starts from zero the gain is 0.08 (post hoc, 95% interval -0.11 to -0.05).

A Primary substation's meter reads demand minus the output of the solar panels connected below it, and NGED does not meter those panels. A least-squares fit of calendar-and-temperature demand minus a solar capacity times a satellite-based sunshine shape recovers most of the solar capacity of solar-farm output that we added to real series. The forecast gain depends on the sunshine forecast: a term built from the true sunshine lowers the error by about a fifth, and a term built from the ECMWF ensemble forecast gains little beyond 2 days ahead.

Arm am (the forecast solar output, given to XGBoost as a base margin) scores 4.467 against 4.620 for d0, the best guess of experiment 33, and every arm scores better than its own placebo twin (the same arm given the sunshine of another date). Source: experiment 64. Scores are quantile scores in points of capacity; lower is better. The rows are daylight half-hours of April to September at the 5 Primaries (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), from July to September 2025 and April to June 2026.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
A simple fit finds most of the solar capacity that we inject, and the capacity is close to unbiased on pure solar output. On the 8 Primaries metered in both directions, the daily fit recovers 0.854 (95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand, and the half-hourly fit 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818). Six of the 8 pass four checks on their real series: placebo sky, season, cloud term, and day type (experiment 39). A misfit test gives a median capacity of 0.992 of the truth on pure solar output (0.951 to 1.032), but detects a load that follows the day's mean cloud in only 0.35 of trials (experiment 40).

An explicit solar term lowers the error of the XGBoost forecast, and the sunshine forecast limits the gain. Built from the true sunshine, the term lowers the score of d1l (d0 without its radiation inputs) by 0.966 (97.5% interval -1.431 to -0.595). Built from ENS sunshine with a coefficient fixed at 1, it lowers it by 0.056 (-0.191 to +0.064), short of the 0.35-point gain the plan required (experiment 46, refuted). With a weight fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and the term given as a base margin, the score of d0 falls by 0.152 (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111), and by 0.272 (-0.420 to -0.145) under 48 hours. With monthly refits the explicit term gains 0.149 (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and three same-time sunshine analogues gain 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007); the two are not separated, and the verdict is inconclusive (experiment 74).

Beyond 10 days all of the gain, and over all leads about half of it, is XGBoost starting from zero. Beyond 10 days the fitted weight is zero, yet a refit with a base margin of zero and no solar term scores 0.102 below d1l and am 0.098 below d1l (both uncorrected, 95% intervals; experiment 76). Over all leads am is 0.152 below d0 and 0.082 below a d0 that starts from zero (-0.113 to -0.052; post hoc, 95%; experiment 78). Whether a zero start matters in production-style forecasts is not settled: see the gotcha below.

The starting-point read in this figure is for am_sy (am with a capacity re-estimated each season-year), which is 0.100 below d0 started from zero, not the 0.082 of am. Source: experiment 78.

Neither the panel shape nor a fresher capacity is where the next gain lies. A fitted blend of east-, south-, and west-facing shapes changed the score of am by -0.001 (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014) (experiment 77, refuted). A capacity re-estimated before every forecast run lowered it by 0.018 (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold (experiment 78, small gain).

A weekly capacity series, the panel mix, and a loss monitor were not shown to work. A weekly capacity fit that penalises falls more than rises recovered none of a 30% fall and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year, against a limit of 0.5 (experiment 45, refuted). The east-south-west shares were not identified: the median share error with noise was 0.200 against a limit of 0.15, although the blend predicted held-out blocks 1.3% better than all-south panels (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%; experiment 73, partly supported). A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days (experiment 72, refuted).

At the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA, the real readings showed almost no reverse flow, so the fit could not be tested on them. In the injection test at the 8 MW-metered Primaries, with the sign of the readings hidden, the unfolding fit's median capacity error was 0.092 against 0.290 for a naive fit, and its balanced accuracy for the direction of flow 0.78 to 0.81, below the 0.80 the rule needed. On the real MVA-only Primaries the fit found no reverse flow at 7 of 8; at the eighth the flow is negative on 75% to 87% of daylight half-hours from 2021, and signed power is needed to check it (experiment 79, partly supported).

The data could not tell us whether the gain holds in a second year, at Primaries without a clean capacity estimate, or on rows outside April to September. The weights of experiment 64 rest on one July-to-September period.

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best of the recipes tested in this theme gives XGBoost a solar offset built from a solar capacity per season-year and a calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly. The steps are:

  1. Fit one solar capacity per Primary per season-year, by least squares, and refresh it once per season-year (experiment 39, experiment 45, experiment 78).
  2. Multiply the capacity by the calibrated ENS sunshine anomaly: how much sunnier or cloudier the day is than average for that month and half-hour, rescaled by a slope fitted on the training window. The weight is fitted per series, forecast-horizon band, and season, and is zero from 10 days (experiment 64).
  3. Give the product to XGBoost as a base margin, not as an input column or a shift after the fit: am beats the input-column arm by 0.093 (95% interval 0.057 to 0.129, exploratory; experiment 64).
  4. Use an all-south panel shape (experiment 77).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Experiments 64 and 78 are candidate.

  • The solar offset (experiment 64). Production would need a capacity table, a table of weights, the ENS calibration slopes at predict time, and a base margin set on each prediction matrix; the write-up says the live service cannot supply these as built.
  • Refresh the capacity table once per season-year (experiment 78). A weekly vintage differs from the season-year vintage by -0.005 (95% interval -0.013 to +0.003, exploratory).
  • A zero start is untested in production-style forecasts, so it is not yet a candidate. Experiment 78 advised testing it; experiment 80 could not tell the two starts apart.
  • The offset's gain inside the full forecast is 0.114 on the rows it can touch. In BG2 (a blend of XGBoost forecasts, with the offset at 5 of 16 Primaries) the offset lowers the score by 0.114 (0.075 to 0.164) on April-to-September daylight rows of the 5 offset Primaries, and by 0.010 (0.000 to 0.019) over all rows of the 16 Primaries, because only 8.5% of those rows can carry an offset. The gate was chosen on the same validation year (experiment 87).

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
Score a zero-start twin before crediting an input. XGBoost's estimated starting prediction (its base score) raised the score of d0 by 0.071 over all leads (zero start minus estimated start -0.071, -0.099 to -0.047), and the gain of am where its weight is zero is reproduced by a refit with a zero margin and no solar term (experiment 76, experiment 78). Experiment 80 (inconclusive) could not tell a zero start from the default at the 16 Primaries refitted weekly (-0.017, 98.75% interval -0.072 to +0.054, which does not exclude -0.07). Re-check: the zero-start twin of whichever recipe, correction, and number of boosting rounds you use (experiment 80).

Give every solar-term arm a placebo twin. The twin of am scores 0.300 worse (0.198 to 0.407), so the gain comes from the timing of the sunshine. Shift the twin cyclically and do not permute it at random: a random permutation paired runs that forecast the same valid time, so the permuted anomaly stayed correlated with the real one (experiment 64, experiment 77). Re-check: a different sunshine source. These experiments ran no shuffled-capacity control.

Report each contrast with and without the 14-day correction. The correction carried the base margin's effect from shorter leads into leads beyond 10 days: am minus am0 was -0.035 corrected (98.33% interval -0.074 to +0.003) and +0.004 uncorrected (95% interval -0.012 to +0.021) (experiment 76). Re-check: a forecast with a different correction window.

Score a solar term on daylight April-to-September rows that have both a CAMS shape and an observed power, and name the row set. Experiments 46, 64, 74, 77, and 78 share 68,903 rows per seed. Experiment 87's headline scored all rows of all 16 Primaries, so its 0.010 cannot be compared with 0.15; on the matching gated rows it found 0.114 (experiment 46, experiment 87). Re-check: a study that scores winter or night rows. CAMS is the Copernicus satellite sunshine estimate (glossary).

Check a contrast's sign in each valid month before reading the pooled interval. The ENS solar term lowered the score of d1l in April, May, and September (-0.204, -0.232, -0.262) and raised it in June, July, and August (+0.117, +0.183, +0.024) under a pooled interval of -0.191 to +0.064 (experiment 46). Re-check: a validation period longer than 6 valid months.

Use one capacity per season-year, which runs from September to August in these experiments. The differentiable-physics code runs it from July to June. The latest week of a real-time weekly estimate had 3.63 times the path error of the same week in the final fit, and no penalty pair met the limits (experiment 45). Re-check: a penalty set per Primary, which experiment 45 did not test.

Do not treat a fitted capacity as a measurement. The fit can absorb cloud-driven demand, and the misfit test misses a load that follows the day's mean cloud. Run the placebo-sky, season, cloud-term, and day-type checks on the real series, and inject more than one farm: the ratios of Solar farm E left the capacity at 0.825 of the truth (experiment 39, experiment 40). Re-check: an independent register of installed solar.

Do not publish the fitted orientation shares. They changed by a median 0.24 between consecutive season-years, and the 1.3% fit gain did not reach the forecast (-0.001; experiment 73, experiment 77). Re-check: shares fitted on a longer record, or a known answer with the real noise that they recover to within 0.15.

Do not fit a signed model to an MVA-only series. The magnitude folds reverse flow into positive power, and in the injection test at the 8 MW Primaries the naive fit's capacity error was 0.29 to 1.00 (experiment 79). Re-check: a few weeks of signed power at the Primary in question.

Read coverage as well as the score. The ENS solar term moved the share of sunny-row actuals below the 0.05 quantile from 0.151 to 0.045, though the score barely changed (experiment 46). Re-check: coverage on sunny and cloudy rows for any new solar term.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the gain holds in a second validation year and beyond the 5 Primaries with a clean capacity estimate.
  • Whether a better sunshine forecast closes the gap to the true-sunshine oracle. The NOAA GEFS ensemble was refuted as a replacement for ENS. The Met Office UKV blended with ENS gave a small gain in squared error of the sunshine-anomaly forecast (not of demand), and the UKV archive used has a non-commercial licence (experiment 50, experiment 53).
  • Why the true-sunshine term loses at sunny summer middays: the coefficient of 1 is too large, and the cause is not identified (experiment 51).
  • Whether a solar term helps a joint demand fit (experiment 63, experiment 104).

The Research plan lists the proposed next experiments.

docs.title: Solar disaggregation: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00427 neural-mva-trajectory-labeller-and-two-channel-inputs A small labeller that reads a whole day of folded readings and outputs a probability that each half-hour is reverse flow, trained on the visible signed Primaries with solar farms injected, gives the export-gated neural network of experiment 420 (arm A) a better sign signal than the gate alone. Feeding the neural network separate MW and MVA input channels with a measured flag, and training it with MW masked on pseudo-Primaries that contain injected reverse flow, lets the network treat the hidden Primaries and the visible Primaries as the same kind of input. Together (arm TDL) the two ideas lower the signed CRPS on reverse-flow half-hours below arm A's. not supported not-for-production A small neural network that reads a whole day of meter readings and marks each half-hour as reverse flow or not ranks the half-hours about as well as the gated forecast network of experiment 420, but no better, and it wrongly marks about three in five of D5's sunny middays as reverse flow when no solar farm was added. The labeller was trained on four higher-demand Primaries, so the next step is to train a sign labeller on a mix that includes low-demand Primaries, or to accept arm A as the candidate and test it on ensemble weather. also relevant 00424 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-ens-serving-test Experiment 420's export-gated network (arm A) still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with its gate shut (P0) when both are trained and scored on ECMWF ensemble (ENS) mean and spread weather, which is the weather a live service would hold, instead of the recorded CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature of the laboratory test. The gain shrinks, because the ENS forecast of cloud is less accurate than recorded cloud, but most of the laboratory gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero, which does not depend on weather accuracy. supported candidate With ensemble weather forecasts instead of recorded weather, the neural network with the export gate still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with the gate shut (a gain of 15.7 points of capacity, 95% interval 13.8 to 17.4, against 19.2 with recorded weather), and it harms the forecast by no more than 0.05 points where no solar farm exports.
