Meter failures at farms A and C therefore do not explain capacity steps at D10, and the other decision Primaries could not be tested. The farms may connect to substations we could not test, so the connection list from NGED would settle it. also relevant 00183 metered-farm-flat-top-cause The flat top at farms C, D, E, and F is a fixed export cap, so its level does not change with season or with the sun's azimuth. not supported not-for-production The flat top of solar farms C, D, E, and F is lower in summer than in spring (by 6% to 9% of its mean level at the 90th percentile, in even and odd years alike), so the flat top does not behave like a fixed export cap. The per-farm plant fit should therefore fit panel tilt, panel azimuth, and a loss that grows with heat or a gradual flattening near the inverter limit, not only one clip level. More cloud in summer half-hours could lower the 90th percentile, because the clear-sky filter is modelled and not observed; the 99th percentile falls by less (1% to 6%). primary 00182 switching-d8-disaggregated-farms-and-drops D8 (Marsh Lane) is a disaggregated Primary: the metadata says the output of two solar farms was added back to its reading, and that both farms' analogues are not working. When an analogue fails, D8's reading loses that farm's output, so D8's multi-day drops (experiment 159) coincide with a stuck, zero, or missing reading at the farms, and the drop depth matches the farms' lost output. inconclusive not-for-production We cannot tell from the farms' own readings whether D8's multi-day drops are the two disaggregated farms dropping out, because the readings for the farms are almost entirely absent from the power table and so look the same inside and outside the drops. D8's shortfall is larger in daylight than at night in 24 of 29 drops, which is consistent with lost solar output, but it is also large in the evening, so the daylight pattern does not settle it. The next step is to ask NGED for the farms' output and capacity, or to model the farms from weather and compare the modelled output with the drop depth. also relevant 00179 metered-solar-farm-exploration At least 4 of the 6 metered solar farms show AC clipping, meaning output that flattens below the level that clear-sky irradiance alone would give, so that the AC limit can be separated from the DC capacity. not supported not-for-production Four of the six metered solar farms have output that flattens at about 1.05 times their effective capacity once clear-sky irradiance passes about 650 W/m² (read off Figure 1), but the pre-registered test was too strict to say so, and the flat top could be an export cap (a limit on grid export set by the network operator), a panel-angle effect, or a summer-heat effect rather than a limit in the inverters. Before any DC-versus-AC follow-up, check each farm's export-cap record and get an independent DC capacity. primary 00157 differentiable-physics-joint-pv-capacity-known-answer Letting the convex demand model (studies.dp_gam) fit the solar capacity as a smooth non-negative path across months, with a penalty on growth, finds more of a known solar farm's injected output than the two-stage capacity of experiment 129, which steps once per season-year and was recovered at 0.78 to 0.88. not supported not-for-production In this test, letting the solar capacity change month by month did not find more of an injected solar farm than a capacity that changes once a year. For the five farms tested, one scale of the fixed fleet solar shape fits a median of 93% of a farm's output, so the target of 0.95 to 1.05 was out of reach for most farms before the fit ran. No forecast was run, and the monthly capacity is not worth taking to the forecast stage. also relevant 00152 dp-mva-fold-aware-gam-k-at-mva-only-primaries At the MVA-only Primaries, the GAM-K forecast driven by the ensemble mean (experiment 136's arm A2) forecasts the MVA reading better when it models the fold: it fits the demand model through the meter (experiment 110's L0), corrects the forecast with a Kalman filter whose state is the signed flow, and builds its quantiles by folding a signed predictive distribution. The gain is concentrated at Stickney (D12), the one trial Primary where reverse flow is the usual state on sunny middays, and the change is harmless at the Primaries without reverse flow. inconclusive not-for-production At Stickney (D12), the one Primary with clear reverse flow, drawing the quantiles around a signed flow and folding them at zero lowered the score by about 0.4 points on sunny middays against the same fit with symmetric quantiles, and it did no harm at the other seven Primaries. The whole-year gain against reading the apparent power as signed power is of similar size, but its interval in the scored year includes zero. The known-answer test on five Primaries with hidden farms passed on the sign at the larger injection and failed at the smaller injection and on the upper tail's coverage, so the experiment does not support a port yet. also relevant 00139 differentiable-physics-pv-as-of-capacity-in-gam-k Feeding the convex model with the Kalman filter (GAM-K, experiment 111) the as-of solar capacity of experiment 129 in place of experiment 45's pinned capacity lowers the quantile score on the sunniest third of half-hours, and does not raise it on the darkest third. The mechanism is that the pinned capacity is a hindsight growth prior, and the as-of capacity is read from each Primary's own power before the forecast origin. refuted not-for-production Replacing the pinned solar capacity with a capacity read from each substation's own power did not improve the forecast, and made sunny half-hours worse by 0.11 points of capacity. A more accurate capacity (the hindsight arm) only matched the pin, so the accuracy of the capacity number is not what limits the solar part of the forecast. This experiment does not locate the remaining sunny-day error; it did not test the ensemble's cloud forecast, the solar shape, the Kalman filter, or the non-solar load. also relevant 00129 differentiable-physics-pv-capacity-known-answer-test The AC capacity of the unmetered solar behind each of the five decision Primaries can be inferred offline, one value per September-to-August season-year, from CAMS irradiance, ERA5 temperature, and the Primary's net power, with an 80% range that holds its coverage when the real panels differ from the assumed south-facing shape and when a day-long cloud-driven demand is present. partly supported not-for-production The capacity of the small solar panels behind five Primary substations can be read from the substations' power. For 2025/26 the arm 2 estimate is 3.3 to 4.5 MW of AC capacity per Primary, and it grew by 0.4 to 2.8 MW since 2021/22. The range around each estimate is 1.2 to 1.6 MW wide, but it is a spread over test scenarios and not a calibrated 80% interval. The method has not been shown to work on real panels that face other ways or on overcast-day demand, so a card should show the range with those caveats. also relevant 00113 differentiable-physics-n5-convex-identification-at-realistic-noise On synthetic substations built from the real calendar and weather, with noise as large and as autocorrelated as the convex model's real residuals, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals cover the truth 70 to 90% of the time, separately for each hour band's heating slope and for the latest season-year's PV capacity. Labelled separately, not in the verdict: the day-of-year harmonics and the drift term make those intervals wide, by absorbing the seasonal cycles of temperature and clear-sky PV. refuted not-for-production At real noise levels, the convex model's 80% month-block bootstrap intervals contain the true heating slope and the true rooftop PV capacity 84% of the time each, but a heating slope is weak (the interval is about 38% of the slope wide). The pre-registered verdict is refuted, because with independent noise the capacity interval covers the truth only 52% of the time, and the cause is mainly a bias of about 0.24 points from the drift penalty at its tuned step of 3,000 (at Part 4's step of 30 the bias is 0.02 points and coverage 78%, a post hoc check). The truth here has the model's own form, so the test cannot show the bias that a wrong PV shape causes. also relevant 00110 differentiable-physics-5-embedded-generation-and-capacity The convex differentiable-physics model can represent the generation side of a Primary substation without making its demand forecast worse: an MVA meter through an observation layer, a flat unmetered generator found where one exists and not invented where none does, and an export-limited PV clip; and its PV capacity stays the same when the routes by which demand terms can imitate solar are closed. inconclusive not-for-production The demand forecast could not yet account for generators connected behind a substation. Rooftop solar capacity fitted from the data was not precise or consistent enough to trust, so the capacity from outside estimates stays in use. A generator-finding component reported a generator at every substation tested, so it stays switched off. A limit on exported solar helped only at the one substation known to export-limit. Treating the meter as apparent power improved the forecast at the 8 substations that report only apparent power by 0.13 points of capacity, but the test of the meter's flow direction failed, so that gain is provisional. also relevant 00104 differentiable-physics-2-simple-structural-model A convex demand-minus-solar model, trained on every usable year with a slowly drifting level per hour band, forecasts Primary demand better than the same model trained on the last 12 months. inconclusive not-for-production A simple model of demand minus solar, trained on 12 months, scored 0.25 points better than lagless XGBoost with its default start (post hoc; a lower score is better). Most of that lead is in the forecast spread, because the error of the mean forecast differs by only 0.08 points, and four of the five pre-registered positive controls failed, so the verdict is inconclusive. More years of history did not clearly help: the scored year and the tuning year gave opposite signs for two history-window contrasts, and a first version of this page had the wrong sign for both because its spread carried the previous year's mean bias. also relevant 00103 differentiable-physics-1-data-look The trial area's power records hold enough clean, demand-only history for the series to go ahead as designed: 6 MW Primaries with at least 12 months before July 2025, and 8 MVA Primaries with over 3 site-years each of rows with no sunlight. supported not-for-production The data lets the series go ahead, with three changes: start 13 of the 16 Primaries later than their first record (19.4 months later at D4), fix the lockdown window in advance because the data does not isolate it from drift, and count eligible long-history MW sites at each tuning year's first day (5 at 2024-07-01, so 4 of 5 must improve in Part 2's tuning contrast). The power timestamps show no 30-minute error on either side of the 2026-03-26 fix: at the 6 metered photovoltaic series the median offsets are +0.9 minutes before it and +4.7 after, and the correction is right to within 3 minutes, but offsets at the Primaries are not resolved beyond 0 to +8 minutes. also relevant 00102 simp1-simplifying-the-bg2-best-guess-before-production A single weekly-refitted XGBoost model without the three power lags, the solar offset, the 14-day correction, or the blend scores within 0.15 points of capacity of BG2 at the 16 Primary substations, within 0.30 at the 4 bulk and grid supply points, within 0.10 at the 6 solar farms, and within 0.30 at the 3 wind farms. We expect the Primary claim to fail and the other three to be close calls (see the prediction). Separately, the solar offset helps most where it should, at midday in summer at the 5 Primary substations that have one. partly supported candidate Removing the three recent-power inputs from the best-guess XGBoost forecast makes it worse at Primary substations (by 0.36 points of capacity once one substation's commissioning months are cut, and most of that comes from one substation whose demand level fell in March 2026) and at supply points (by 0.28). The wind farm forecasts lost nothing measurable and the solar farm forecasts little. The blend of 5 models can shrink to 3, and the solar offset lowers the score by 0.18 points at midday in summer at the 5 substations that use it. also relevant 00079 pvdis-7-mw-at-mva-only-primaries At a Primary substation (a substation that steps 33 kV down to 11 kV) whose meter records only the magnitude of apparent power in megavolt-amperes (MVA), a least-squares fit of the magnitude of "calendar-and-temperature demand minus capacity times a solar shape" recovers the solar capacity and the direction of flow, as long as the power factor is near 1. The fit alternates between choosing a sign for each half-hour and fitting the signed model to the signed series. It is tested first on the 8 Primaries that are metered in MW, by hiding the sign of their readings (taking the absolute value) and recovering it. partly supported not-for-production Hiding the sign of the MW series and recovering it works for the solar capacity (median error 0.09 to 0.11 of the signed fit's, against 0.29 to 1.00 for the naive fit) but not to the pre- registered level for the direction of flow (balanced accuracy 0.78 to 0.81, rule 0.80), so the verdict is partly supported. At 7 of the 8 Primaries metered only in MVA, the fit found no reverse flow. primary 00078 pvdis-5-current-capacity-vintages Experiment 00064's arm am (the XGBoost model given a forecast solar output as a base margin) used one embedded-solar capacity per Primary substation, fitted on data up to 2025-06-30 and held for the whole validation period. That capacity is 5% to 19% below experiment 00045's 2025/26 constants at the five series. Giving am a capacity that is re-estimated before each forecast run, using only data from before the run (a real-time vintage of the season-year constant), lowers its quantile score further, and the fitted solar term still carries solar information, because the same arm with the forecast sunshine taken from another date scores worse. small gain candidate Re-estimating the solar capacity before each forecast run lowered the error of experiment 64's best forecast by only 0.018 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.036 to -0.004), under the 0.05 threshold, and by 0.033 (-0.086 to +0.012, an interval that includes zero) at leads under 48 hours. primary 00077 pvdis-6b-fitted-solar-shape-in-arm-am At the 5 Primary substations (33/11 kV or 66/11 kV substations in the distribution network) of experiment 00064, replacing the all-south solar shape of arm am with a fitted solar shape (a blend of east-, south-, and west-facing output, one set of shares per Primary, fitted on the training window only and held fixed across training years) lowers the quantile score of the forecast, and the gain comes from the timing of the forecast sunshine and not from the shape alone. refuted not-for-production Replacing the all-south solar shape with a fitted east-south-west shape changed the score of experiment 64's arm am by -0.001 points of capacity (98.33% interval -0.018 to +0.014), so a gain of 0.5% (0.022 points) is excluded. primary 00076 pvdis-5-leak-check-beyond-10-days Experiment 00064's arm am (the XGBoost model given the forecast solar output as a base margin) scored 0.082 points of capacity below d0 at leads of 10 days and beyond, where its margin is zero. That gain does not come from information that was unavailable at forecast time. If it is real, it comes from the offset in the training rows at shorter leads, which removes the solar swings from the training target so that the trees fit demand better at every lead (the cleaner-target effect), or from the fit starting at zero instead of at XGBoost's estimated base score. supported not-for-production No route for a leak was found, and a refit with no solar term at all reproduces the gain of experiment 64's arm am at 10 days and beyond (0.102 below d1l without the 14-day correction, against 0.098 for am). The gain matches XGBoost starting from zero when a base margin is supplied, and not the solar offset, with the caveat that the reference d1l came from another pipeline. primary 00074 an1-same-time-analogues-vs-explicit-solar-forecast-demand At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, when the XGBoost model is refitted every month on the latest 12 months of data (P-roll), an explicit forecast of the unmetered solar output, given to the model as a starting offset (experiment 64's arm am), lowers the daylight April-to-September quantile score by more than same-time-of-day analogues do. An analogue is a recent day, at the same half-hour of the day and of the same day type (working day, weekend, or bank holiday), whose satellite-based sunshine was closest to the sunshine forecast for the target. The model receives the observed power on the K nearest such days (K is 1, 3, or 5) as input columns. Once the explicit offset is in the model, the analogue columns add less than 0.05 points of capacity. inconclusive not-for-production Both ways of telling the monthly-refitted model about sunshine lowered the daylight error: the explicit forecast of the panels' output by 0.149 points of capacity (99.17% interval -0.201 to -0.104) and the 3 analogues by 0.095 (-0.185 to -0.007) against the reference. also relevant 00073 pvdis-6-orientation-mix-and-dc-ac-ratio On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, (a) the share of east-, south-, and west-facing solar behind each Primary can be recovered from its half-hourly power, and (b) the ratio of DC to AC capacity of that solar can be recovered from a clipping level fitted on clear days. Both are tested first on known answers: synthetic east-south-west mixes of solar output, and the output of the six metered solar farms, added to the real demand. partly supported not-for-production A blend of east, south, and west shapes lowers held-out error by 1.3% against all-south panels (98.75% interval -2.4% to -0.5%, better at all 8 Primaries), although the shares themselves are not identified: with noise added to the known answer the median share error is 0.200 (limit 0.15), and the shares of the free fit change by a median 0.24 between consecutive season-years. primary 00072 p35-step-loss-monitor-for-solar-farms For the 5 metered solar farms with a long record (labelled A, B, C, D, and F), a monitor can find a loss of generating capacity, such as a lost inverter, from the farm's own power telemetry. The monitor divides each day's power by the power a physics model expects on clear, unclipped hours, divides that ratio again by the same day's ratio at the other farms, and fits a piecewise-constant level to the result with an L0 penalty (an optimal-partitioning change-point fit). It finds a 25% loss that lasts 30 days, starting from April to September, within 28 days of its onset in at least 80% of injections, at no more than 0.5 false alarms per farm-year. It finds more injected losses of 10% than two simpler monitors that are tuned to the same false-alarm rate: a rolling median of the same signal, and the hysteresis rule of the capacity studies (called HYST here) run on the same signal. refuted not-for-production A change-point monitor of a solar farm's daily output found 0.84 of 25% losses lasting 90 days and 0.45 of those lasting 30 days, below the 0.80 the plan needed, so the verdict is refuted. On 10% losses it did not beat a rolling median by an interval that excludes zero (+0.045, 97.5% interval -0.015 to +0.090). also relevant 00064 pvdis-5-net-demand-as-demand-minus-forecast-solar At the 5 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) with a clean solar-capacity estimate, a demand forecast that carries an explicit solar term (the substation's embedded solar capacity times a calibrated forecast of the solar output) scores no worse than experiment 00033's best-guess recipe d0 by more than 0.10 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows, and the solar term carries real solar information, because the same arm with the forecast sunshine taken from another date scores worse. The solar term is built in four ways: added to the forecast after the fit with a coefficient fitted on the training window (sf), given to the XGBoost model as an input column (a), given to it as a starting offset so that the trees fit only the remainder (am), or removed from the training target and added back after the fit (b, "demand minus solar"). supported candidate Giving the XGBoost model the forecast solar output as a starting offset, with a weight fitted on the training window, beat the best guess d0 by 0.152 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.199 to -0.111; leads under 48 hours -0.272, -0.420 to -0.145), and each of the four arms beat its own placebo twin. primary 00063 sw2-10-linear-joint-fit-v2-in-miniature On the 8 Primary substations metered in MW, one linear fit per Primary that holds a weather baseline without radiation inputs, the embedded-solar capacity of experiment 00045 times the CAMS unit PV shape, and one share-of-the-donor's-net-power term per labelled transfer, (C1) lowers the error of the median forecast outside switching on held-out months, in hindsight, below that of the same baseline with radiation inputs by at least 0.35 points of capacity, (S1) recovers an injected solar capacity to within 0.15 of its size, and (S2) recovers an injected transfer share to within 0.05. inconclusive not-for-production C1 is -0.322 points of capacity (-0.437 to -0.207), close to the 0.35-point threshold, but the S1 and S2 gates failed for reasons of test design, so the verdict is inconclusive. also relevant 00051 pvdis-3b-midday-loss-of-the-solar-term At June-to-August midday on day+2 and day+3, the solar term of experiment 00046 scores worse than the best guess d0 (C6 +0.477 and +0.172 points of capacity) mainly because the fixed coefficient of 1 is too large for the sunniest rows, which a PV inverter clips, and not because the ENS members add noise. partly supported not-for-production At June-to-August midday the oracle shift's coefficient of 1 is too large in effect: the residual of the d1l median has a slope of -0.42 to -0.69 on it in every month and hour bin, and a fitted coefficient lowers the median's error by 0.991 points (-1.473 to -0.495). primary 00046 embedded-solar-share-of-primary-forecast-error At the five Primary substations metered in MW that have a clean 2023/24 capacity estimate, an explicit solar term lowers the error of the demand forecast that experiment 00033's best-guess recipe produces without its shortwave and longwave radiation inputs (arm d1l) by at least 0.35 points of capacity on daylight April-to-September rows. The solar term shifts every forecast by minus the capacity of experiment 00040 times the calibrated ENS forecast of the solar anomaly (a fitted slope on the ensemble mean, plus each member's own deviation from the mean), with the coefficient fixed at 1. The contrast is against d1l and not against the best guess. refuted not-for-production The ENS solar term lowers the quantile score of d1l by 0.056 points (97.5% interval -0.191 to +0.064), against a threshold of 0.35, so the verdict is refuted. primary 00045 pvdis-4-weekly-capacity-asymmetric-l1 On the 8 Primary substations (substations that feed 11 kV circuits from the 33 kV network) metered in MW, a least-squares fit of the daylight power to a calendar-and-temperature demand term minus a weekly capacity times one PV shape from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), with weekly capacity increments under an asymmetric L1 penalty (a penalty on the sum of absolute increments, light on rises and heavy on falls), meets six conditions. It recovers a known injected capacity path (ramps, steps, and temporary falls, injected into a semi-synthetic baseline) with a median error of at most 0.15 of the path's mean capacity. It beats a capacity that is constant within each season-year by at least 20% on ramps and steps. It produces at most 0.5 false steps of 10% of capacity per Primary-year at the median Primary, and at most 1.0 at the worst Primary, on the placebo sky and on a constant injected path. Its path drifts upward on noise by at most 0.05 of capacity over 5 years. It recovers a 30% fall lasting 26 weeks at 0.5 or more of its depth, and an 8-week fall at under 0.5. Its 90% bootstrap interval covers 0.85 to 0.95 of non-step weeks and at least 0.60 of step weeks. Capacity is the 99th percentile of the half-hourly AC output, in MW, of the embedded solar (solar connected inside the distribution network, mostly unmetered by NGED) behind a Primary. refuted not-for-production No weekly capacity fit met the limits fixed in advance for tuning: the best penalty pair recovered none of a 26-week fall of 30% and gave 0.66 false steps per Primary-year at the median Primary, against a limit of 0.5. Weekly changes in embedded solar capacity cannot yet be read from Primary-substation data at the accuracy a weekly series needs, so the next experiment should use one capacity per season-year and read it as a range. primary 00040 pv-capacity-error-bars On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, comparing the PV capacity that six least-squares arms fit to the same series (they differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows) detects a cloud-driven demand load that pushes the half-hourly fit's capacity at least 25% off, with at least 80% power and a false-positive rate of at most 10% on pure injected PV, so that a bounded error bar can be attached to the capacity at every Primary where no such load is detected. partly supported not-for-production The misfit test is calibrated (median capacity over truth 0.992, 95% interval 0.951 to 1.032; false-positive rate 0.055) and detects four of the five confound shapes that no fit contains at 25% of capacity, but it detects a day-long cloud load in only 0.35 of draws, so the pre-registered power rule fails and the verdict is underpowered. primary 00039 pv-disaggregation-cams-injection On the 8 directional (MW) Primary substations, a calendar-plus-temperature demand term minus one PV shape driven by Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) irradiance recovers the P99 capacity of real solar-farm output injected into the real demand series to within 25%, and the same fits on the un-injected series pass four checks that a weather-correlated demand confound would fail. partly supported not-for-production A fit of calendar-plus-temperature demand minus one satellite-driven solar shape recovers 0.854 (daily fit, 95% interval 0.815 to 0.866) of the capacity of real solar-farm output added to the demand of the 8 directional Primaries. On the real series 6 of the 8 pass four checks that a demand confound would fail, and one fails the placebo-sky check, so the verdict is partly supported. primary

docs.title: P2: embedded-solar capacity from lagged residuals
docs.text:
The embedded-solar proposal rests on one follow-up check of experiment 00006's residuals, which motivated two different questions. Experiment 00007 then ran a first test and was inconclusive. The check was run by the 00006 session on CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location, and its figures and script are in the write-up of PR #1202 (Experiment 6: which input features work best for the ERA5-trained demand model). It was not pre-registered. At Primary substation 12, the median-error Primary substation, the residual of the chosen-feature stage 1a XGBoost model averaged -5.3 points of capacity from 08:00 to 16:59 in the June, July, and August of the confirmation year (July 2025 to June 2026), against -1.0 at night. In July 2025, a linear fit on 431 daylight hours explained 25.5% of the hourly residual's variance with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), 3.8% with ERA5 shortwave, and 43.3% with both. Across the 14 Primary series that have CAMS values, CAMS alone explained more than ERA5 alone in all 14: a median of 23.7% against 2.9%, and 39.8% with both. In one series the error is a level shift that irradiance does not explain, and in another the residual correlates positively with CAMS irradiance.

The check cannot yet say whether the cause is embedded solar capacity or an error in ERA5's irradiance. At Primary substation 12 the joint fit gives coefficients of opposite sign and similar size for ERA5 and CAMS, and CAMS minus ERA5 alone explains 33.9%, so much of the residual tracks the difference between the two irradiance products. Stage 1a has already learned an irradiance response from ERA5, so a fixed error in ERA5's cloud field would produce the same pattern without any change in solar capacity. Daytime lighting load and behaviour on sunny days could also contribute. At Primary substation 12, CAMS explains 25% of the variance on weekdays and 10% on weekends, so the weekday mix matters too. The check has no time dimension, because it covers one month, one seed, and one fold, and with hourly autocorrelation the effective sample is far below 431 hours. Because stage 1a already uses ERA5 shortwave, the comparison of 25.5% with 3.8% is not like for like, and the partial R² of CAMS given ERA5 would be a fairer figure.

Experiment 00007 was the cheap first test of an irradiance error against a capacity change. It added CAMS irradiance to ERA5 shortwave and fitted a static correction on one year of residuals. The correction removed 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual against the 50% planned, and one substation sets the pooled figure, so the verdict is inconclusive. A further test could compute the three candidate statistics on residuals from walk-forward (out-of-fold) stage 1a fits, because residuals from a model fitted on the same period are shrunk and would look different in operation.

The three candidate statistics each compare what stage 1a predicted with what the substation metered. Each uses the residual, the metered power over capacity minus stage 1a's prediction at the observed weather.

  • The solar slope: regress the residual on irradiance over the trailing 14 to 28 days, in daylight hours only. A more negative slope means more embedded solar than stage 1a learned. The slope mixes capacity change, irradiance error, and other demand that varies with irradiance, so the regression could use the clear-sky index with day-of-week and temperature controls. Noise in the estimation irradiance biases the slope towards zero.
  • The sunny-minus-cloudy daytime residual: the mean residual on sunny days minus the mean on cloudy days at matched hours, with a named clear-sky-index threshold. A day-minus-night residual is not a substitute. Commercial load is daytime-heavy, electric-vehicle charging and storage are night-heavy, and heat pumps are daytime and seasonal, so their trends would appear as false solar change.
  • The change from the same calendar window a year earlier: this year's 28-day slope minus the slope in the same 28 days of the previous year. A ratio of the 28-day to the 365-day slope is unstable, because the slope is seasonal and the denominator can be near zero or change sign.

The correction could be given to stage 2 as a linear offset, not as a tree feature. Gradient-boosted trees cannot extrapolate beyond their training range, and embedded solar capacity grows steadily, so a product of the slope and the forecast shortwave would still be held flat by a tree. A linear term, in stage 1b or in stage 2, would extrapolate correctly, and the tree feature would be the comparison arm. The slope is estimated against observed irradiance and applied to forecast irradiance, which differ in bias and scale, so the conversion has to be stated. The past-weather source used at lag times has to be available at forecast time, because ERA5 arrives about 5 days late, and training has to use that same source. CAMS is observed after the fact and has no forecast, so the CAMS satellite-derived irradiance can feed the statistics only at lag times. The CAMS irradiance at each demand series' own location comes from PR #1201 (Download and validate CAMS irradiance at the demand series' locations), which covers the 22 series of experiment 00003 (16 Primary demand series, 4 bulk-supply and grid-supply point flows, and 2 non-demand series, a battery and a biofuel generator). The experiment could compute each statistic from ERA5 alone and from CAMS and ERA5 together.

A decision rule could be fixed before any fit. One candidate: the trend in the monthly change from a year earlier is negative at 70% or more of the substations in the top quartile of registered embedded solar capacity per unit of substation capacity, with a block-bootstrap 95% interval that excludes zero, and it is absent in the night-time residuals. A second candidate: the linear-offset arm lowers the confirmation-year daylight quantile score at Primary substations by at least 0.2 points of capacity, with a month-block bootstrap interval that excludes zero. Otherwise the hypothesis is refuted. The thresholds are proposals for the planning step to confirm.

Resolution limit. The top quartile of 16 Primary substations by embedded solar capacity is 4 substations, so a rule of "70% of them" means 3 of 4, which no interval can support. The slope statistics need more substations or a continuous measure of capacity.

docs.title: PVDIS: separating embedded solar from Primary demand
docs.text:
The PVDIS line estimates how much unmetered solar capacity sits behind each Primary substation, how that capacity changes over time, and whether an explicit solar term improves or explains the net demand forecast. The line serves three purposes, and the second matters about as much as the first:

  • Skill: a lower error in the net demand forecast at each substation.
  • Explanation: a forecast that NGED can read as demand minus solar. A solar term that leaves the error level but splits the forecast into parts an engineer recognises is still worth keeping, so experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) tested non-inferiority as well as gain.
  • Capacity: a time series of unmetered solar capacity per Primary. NGED holds almost no information on unmetered solar today, so an estimate with honest error bars is useful even when the estimate is far from perfect.

The capacity estimate runs offline, weekly or monthly, and the production forecast only reads the latest capacity table. Nothing in this line adds a fitting step to the serving path. Experiment 73 (PVDIS-6) found that the mix of panel orientations behind each Primary, the quantity the UniversalSolarFleetNode sketched in differentiable physics would fit, is not stable across season-years, so the explicit solar forecast keeps one south-facing shape.

Experiments 00039 and 00040 are parts 1 and 2 of the series, and the parts below follow the exploratory protocol in the ml-experiment skill. Opus plans each part after reading the result of the part before, so the designs below are proposals that each part's plan may change. Experiment 00039 fitted one capacity per Primary per season-year, from a calendar and temperature demand term minus one CAMS-driven solar shape. On real solar-farm output injected into the real demand, the half-hourly fit recovered a median 0.773 (0.740 to 0.818) of the injected capacity, and a fit on daily sums recovered 0.854 (0.815 to 0.866). Experiment 00040 compared six fits, which differ in how much cloud-driven demand each allows, and took the six-arm capacity C as its estimate. C recovered a median 0.992 (0.951 to 1.032) of the injected capacity. Experiment 00040 also attached a bound on the error that an undetected demand load would cause, of 0.18 to 0.23 at five Primaries. A demand load that rises with sunshine cannot be told apart from solar.

The Opus review of experiment 00040 recommended stopping the series, publishing a season-year capacity table, and not using capacity as a forecast feature; the parts below continue because the goals changed. That review judged the series against the questions it had then: whether a further experiment could narrow the capacity bound, and whether capacity improves the forecast score. Four experiments (00007, 00009, 00022, and 00031) found small or no gains from solar inputs. The maintainer has since added two goals: a forecast that explains itself, and a capacity series that changes week by week for NGED. Experiment 64 (PVDIS-5) rested on the explanation goal and on what differs from those four experiments, not on a claim that the review missed the forecast question. The same review found that the daily fit is about 2.6 times more exposed than C to an undetected day-long load, so every part reports C as the capacity and keeps the daily fit as a cross-check.

Rules shared by every part:

  • Substations. Only the 8 Primaries metered in MW, each carrying its status from the earlier review into every result: Kirton is reported only as a range (1.2 to 4.4 MW), because its daylight cloud load was flagged in 6 of 7 season-years; Wrangle T1 is excluded from any claim that a Primary is free of a confound; Trusthorpe is marked low-power. The 8 Primaries metered only in MVA fold solar into the magnitude of the flow, and experiment 00039 fitted a negative capacity at Stickney in every year. Experiment 00079 (PVDIS-7) treats them separately.
  • Service areas. TimeSeriesMetadata.area_wkt holds one polygon per Primary. Wrangle T1 and Wrangle T2 are two transformers at one substation, feeding different circuits, and share one polygon. Each transformer keeps its own capacity fit, and any comparison against an outside count of solar uses the sum of the two against the shared polygon. Before any outside comparison, a check reports overlaps and gaps between neighbouring polygons, whether each Primary's location falls inside its own polygon, and how the union of the polygons compares with the two BSPs' area.
  • Irradiance. CAMS for past weather, because the past-weather solar study found the CAMS solar estimate the most accurate of the products it compared. ENS for forecasts. Where a capacity fitted on CAMS is applied to ENS, the ENS irradiance is first calibrated against CAMS, by lead, on data from the fold's training window only.
  • Capacity used in a forecast is a real-time vintage. A forecast experiment reads the capacity that a fit truncated at the fold's training end would give, never a path smoothed over the whole record. A path fitted once over all data passes information from later weeks back to earlier weeks through the penalty and the constraint.
  • Switching is masked. The logged closures, padded by 24 hours, are removed from every capacity fit until SW2-0b's labels exist. A transfer moves a share of the donor's net load, including the donor's solar, so an unmasked transfer looks like a step in capacity. The logs miss some real switching, so unlogged transfers remain a source of false steps.
  • Known answers first. Every capacity method is scored on experiment 00039's injection harness before its result on the real series is trusted.
  • Loads that track sunshine are a named confound. Seaside visitor load at the coastal Primaries (Skegness, Ingoldmells, Chapel St Leonards, and Trusthorpe), irrigation pumping, cooling of crop stores, and air conditioning all rise on sunny days and bias the fitted capacity low. Daytime domestic load falls on sunny days, as people go outside, and biases the fitted capacity high. Each write-up reports the coastal Primaries separately and compares school-holiday weeks with term-time weeks.

docs.title: PVDIS-T: the capacity table, a study
docs.text: Publish a season-year capacity table now, built from experiment 00040's outputs with no refit, and replace it with PVDIS-4's weekly series once that part has run. NGED's need is to improve on almost no information, so the season-year table is useful before the weekly series exists. The study reports C as the capacity, keeps sampling uncertainty separate from the named systematic scenarios, and carries each Primary's status from the earlier review. The joint fit of experiment 00063 read the same capacities.

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast
docs.text:
Giving the Primary demand forecast switching labels has not yet improved it on real data. On injected transfers it recovers the lost accuracy only when the megawatts (MW) moved are known: it closes 83% of the extra error with the true MW, against 16% (interval -17% to +67%, so not distinguishable from zero) with the MW from the RO-NC detector.

A load transfer moves part of one Primary substation's demand onto its neighbours for hours or days. The question is whether telling the XGBoost forecast about transfers lets it forecast the demand the normal running arrangement would have carried. The labels come from NGED's logs or from the RO-NC detector, whose own results are on the switching detectors page. All results are from the lab: 16 Primary series, one validation year (292 daily forecast runs, July 2025 to June 2026), and labels that use hindsight.

The share of the extra error recovered depends on where the MW comes from: 50% to 83% with the true MW, 16% to 36% with RO-NC's MW as built (intervals include zero), and 43% with the largest overlapping step (chosen after seeing the results). The extra error (the "gap") is the error of the plain forecast minus the error of the same forecast on unmodified lags (the "ceiling"). Source: experiment 88.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
On real data, no label-based change lowered the score by an amount the data can show. A label source is "oracle" when it is NGED's logs and "detector" when it is RO-NC. The score is the quantile score in points of capacity; a positive change is a worse forecast.

  • Dropping labelled switching from the training targets, or adding the moved MW, changed the score outside switching by under 0.06. Masked minus plain was +0.004 (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025); only 22 of the 82 labelled events fall in the scored year (experiment 75).
  • On the 37,394 half-hours whose lag (an earlier power reading used as an input) lies inside a logged event, no correction was shown to help. Oracle labels changed the score by -0.29 (98.33% interval -2.06 to +0.68) and detector labels by +0.48 (-0.06 to +1.72). Outside switching, the detector labels raised the score by 0.056 (+0.016 to +0.126). The detector marks 8.1 times as many half-hours as the logs, and 15% of the logged ones (experiment 86).
  • A perfect detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) on events moving 25% or more of the receiver's load for over a day, against a 3% threshold. Those events touch 3 of the 16 series, and if events on badly metered substations are dropped, 2 remain and every bound's point estimate lies between -0.3% and -0.1%. For all 22 visible events the bound is 2.35% (-0.22% to 5.73%), resting on a few short events (experiment 44).

A perfect detector would lower the quantile score by little in the band of events the labeller finds most reliably. Source: experiment 44.

Two ways of marking suspect lags without a hand label did not help. A probability that a lag lies inside a transfer, built from the causal RO-NC detector, lowered the Brier score (the mean squared error of a probability) by 3.3% against the yes-or-no flag (97.5% interval -7.6% to +1.6%) where the plan needed 20%, and its area under the curve against NGED's logs was 0.53 (experiment 91; the 11.2% gain reported there is a post hoc subset). Giving the forecast the unusualness of each lag against a climatology raised the score by 0.355 (97.5% interval +0.209 to +0.513) and narrowed the band on rows with a lag in a logged event (experiment 90; verdict refuted).

On injected transfers, the true MW recovers most of the error and the detector's MW does not. The cases are forecast origins inside a transfer (2,452 cases from four onset months), scored against the unmodified power. The XGBoost model trained on NGED's logged transfers and given the true MW scored -0.790 points against plain (98.75% interval -1.397 to -0.412), closing 83% (70% to 91%) of the gap. With RO-NC's MW, the model trained on RO-NC's transfers scored -0.149 (-1.174 to +0.148, negative in 2 of 4 months). Counting overlapping detector intervals once, chosen after seeing the results, gave -0.406 (-1.223 to -0.083). After a transfer ended, the as-built MW raised the error by 0.35 to 0.46 for up to 7 days (experiment 88).

Adding about three times as many synthetic transfers to the training data did not help. The synthetic-trained model scored +0.079 (98.75% interval -0.031 to +0.153) against the real-trained model with the true MW, and +0.032 (-0.019 to +0.067) with RO-NC's MW. The MW source set the share of the gap closed (83% with the true MW, 32% to 53% with the detector's). Source: experiment 96.

Hiding lags that lie inside a transfer made the forecast worse. Setting them to missing raised the score by 0.409 (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517) on rows with such a lag, and training on all history since March 2021 instead of 12 months changed it by +0.009 (-0.052 to +0.069) (experiment 89). Hiding lags at random during training did not widen the 5% to 95% band on rows with a missing lag: its coverage was 0.799 for the plain forecast and 0.802 with 10% of training rows hidden, against 0.90 nominal (experiment 100; inconclusive).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best of the recipes tested here, on injected transfers only, corrects each lag by the MW moved, using the largest overlapping detector step as the MW. In experiment 88 this (post hoc) closed 43% (17% to 71%) of the gap with the RO-NC-trained model, and correcting the lags alone closed 48% (18% to 71%). The recipe:

  1. Subtract the signed MW at each lag from the lag, and give the three MW values as columns (experiments 75, 88).
  2. Take one MW per half-hour from the largest overlapping step, not the sum (experiment 88).
  3. Do not also drop the transfer's half-hours from the training targets: it added +0.070 (-0.015 to +0.171) over lag correction alone (experiment 88).

No recipe has beaten the plain forecast on real logged events.

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text: Nothing is ready for the serving path. All 9 experiments of this theme are not-for-production: each uses hindsight labels, and the detector's residual uses ERA5 weather, which arrives about 5 days late. The evidence does not support a detector or a label table in the forecast.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Do not set lags inside a labelled switching event to missing. The forecast got worse on rows with such a lag and on rows outside switching (experiment 89, +0.054 outside switching; the mask arm of experiment 100 lost 1.36 points on injected transfers). Random dropout in 30% of training rows removed that loss. Re-check with a model trained to read missing lags.
  • Count the half-hours a label source marks before using it to mask or correct. The union of RO-NC and the logs marks 9% to 16% of half-hours per year from 2022, RO-NC alone marks 8.1 times the logged half-hours, and masking on the union raised the error (experiment 89, experiment 86). Re-check with a detector that marks about as many half-hours as the logs.
  • Take one MW per half-hour from the largest overlapping detector step, not the sum. The as-built MW, which adds overlapping intervals, did not beat the plain forecast (-0.149, -1.174 to +0.148), and the largest step did (-0.406, -1.223 to -0.083), though that choice was post hoc. A lingering return step kept the correction on after a transfer ended (experiment 88; the loss comes from the 21% of marked cases with overlapping intervals, not from a scale error in the MW). The 16% result rests on February 2026, and the oracle contrast C2 keeps its sign and stays between -0.62 and -0.92 when any of the four months is left out.
  • A detected transfer is known late. At the newest usable lag the detector had marked 32% of the moved MW in the first 24 hours after onset, against 73% in days 1 to 3 (experiment 88), and its probability separated poorly in that first day (area under the curve 0.61 for the calibrated probability and 0.60 for the flag; experiment 91). A gain scored with hindsight ends is therefore an upper bound (experiment 75). Re-check on live data or with an end rule that needs no hindsight.
  • Score a forecast of the normal running arrangement against real data only outside events. Real rows inside an event have no valid normal-arrangement truth, so experiments 75, 86, and 100 score real rows outside events and use injected transfers for the rest (experiment 100). Re-check if a source of the true normal-arrangement power appears.
  • Count events, not half-hours, and expect wide intervals. The 37,394 rows with a lag in a logged event come from an estimated 15 to 20 events, 81% of them from 3 substations (experiment 100). Six trustworthy events fall in the scored year, and without those where a donor or receiver has over half its readings missing, 2 remain and every bound lies between -0.3% and -0.1% (experiment 44). Injected scores rest on 4 onset months (experiments 88 and 96), so read the sign in each month. Re-check on a longer period.
  • Run a same-code repeat of the control arm before reading a change under about 0.05. Only 9% of per-case scores from a graphics-card refit matched experiment 48's to 0.001, the largest gap was 4.39 points, and the +0.004 of masked minus plain is at the level of that noise (experiment 75). Re-check if the fit is made deterministic.
  • Give any "drop the event rows" arm a control that keeps them. The mask arm, which also dropped 9% of training rows, narrowed the band on unmasked rows by 4% and lowered its coverage from 0.906 to 0.894 (experiment 100). Without the control, the effect of dropping rows is credited to masking lags. Re-check with the control run.
  • Report the pre-registered rows first, and name a post hoc subset. Experiment 91's 11.2% gain is on rows chosen after seeing the results; the planned rows gave 3.3% with an interval including zero (experiment 91). Re-check against the plan's decision rule.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text:
• Whether the detector's MW, with each transfer counted once and ended promptly, recovers more than the 43% of the gap that the post hoc rule did in experiment 88.
  • Whether any label improves the forecast on real transfers: the logged events in a year are too few (experiment 86).
  • Whether a missing-lag indicator column, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, widens the band where a lag is missing (experiment 100).
  • Whether synthetic transfers trained with the detector's errors, not the exact MW, help (experiment 96).

The Research plan lists what is planned next, and the Experiments page lists every experiment.

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00283 lsc-perfect-knowledge-value-to-forecast-and-curtailment Knowing every load shift exactly (its true start and end) lowers the error of the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA) in the 48 hours after a shift, and lowers the curtailment cost of the forecast of observed power in the days around a shift, while leaving ordinary rows unchanged. This is question 1 of the LSC decision program. partly supported not-for-production Perfect knowledge of load shifts lowers the forecast's error most in the 48 hours after a shift ends (23% lower upper-tail score, 95% interval 9% to 39%) and by under 1% over a whole year, because shifts are rare. Curtailment cost against observed power falls by 8% (6% to 10%) near a shift only when the known shift's megawatts are added back to the forecast, and does not fall when recent readings are merely set aside. The next step is to ask how good a detector must be to keep that gain, using the megawatts-added-back arm as the target. also relevant 00258 lsc-mask-out-of-sample-all-primaries-whole-history Experiment 227 found that LR_b20 (the learned alarm score of experiment 195, at the threshold that leaves 20 unexplained odd-month candidates) with a mask recovers 83.5% of the logged-oracle gain in the 72 hours after a logged load shift and raises the ordinary-day score by -0.007 points (-0.039 to +0.014). That rests on 11 load shifts at 6 Primary substations, 27 months of cached ensemble forecasts, a threshold chosen on the scored rows, and months that were the re-ranker's training negatives. On all 15 Primary series with a residual from the frozen convex model of experiment 130 (arm B), over the whole residual history of about 4.5 years, and scored only on rows the learned score was not trained on, the LR_b20 mask keeps at least half of that gain and keeps its ordinary-day harm inside +/-0.05 points. inconclusive not-for-production On rows it was never trained on, the carried load shift mask recovers about half of the best-case gain after a load shift (47%, with a wide range of 18% to 85%) and changes ordinary days by less than 0.05 points. Over every row of 4.5 years it scores slightly worse than no mask, because a few long alarms over logged closures add more excess score than the mask removes elsewhere. The check against simulated load shifts failed, so the result is inconclusive, and this page gives no support for porting the mask. also relevant 00249 lsc-self-training-on-consistent-events The learned load-shift score of experiment 195 is trained only on injected transfers. If it is retrained on injected transfers plus the real events that pass a label-free consistency rule (balanced opposite steps at a metered neighbour, a high round 1 score, and a clean return step), it finds more of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day than the round 1 score, at the same 80 unexplained odd-month alarms, because the pseudo-positives show it what real events look like. refuted not-for-production Retraining the learned load-shift score on its own consistent real events found no extra real transfers: the score still finds 24 of 35. Only 38 to 47 real events per fold pass the consistency rule, against about 2,000 injected transfers per fold, so the extra rows probably could not move the score. Self-training may need many more consistent events than 4.5 years of 16 Primary substations provide. also relevant 00227 lsc-fewer-false-alarms-and-softer-use-part-2 Experiment 208 found that no real alarm source stays inside the ordinary-day harm limit of 0.05 points, because each raises 104 to 242 alarms for 15 to 20 matched logged load shifts. (a) A source at a higher threshold, or a union of the pair alarm and the learned score that keeps the learned score only where the pair alarm also fires or its score is high, matches enough load shifts with few alarms per match. (b) A use of the alarm that keeps some recent power (soft down-weighting, a pair-sum correction, or a hedge between masked and unmasked forecasts) costs less per false alarm than a mask and keeps most of the gain after a load shift. partly supported candidate Keeping only the learned score's most confident alarms gives a mask that finds 21 of 35 real load shifts with 5 alarms per match, recovers most of the forecast gain after a load shift, and does no measurable harm on ordinary days. A gentler use of the alarm is not needed at that setting. The result rests on 11 load shifts after which the gain is measured, so the next step is to confirm it on more load shifts before porting it. also relevant 00226 lsc-why-learned-score-mask-lost-part-1 Experiment 203's learned-score mask (7.31 points of effective capacity on the 72 hours after the 7 logged load shifts, against 6.32 for the pair-alarm mask) loses because the learned alarm is known 2 to 4 days after the step, so its mask starts late on long load shifts. If that is the cause, a mask that takes the pair alarm's onset where the pair alarm fires, and the learned score's coverage elsewhere, keeps the learned score's extra matches without the loss. not supported not-for-production The learned load-shift score finds more real load shifts than the pair alarm, but the extra ones it finds do not improve the forecast and do the harm, so merging the two alarms does not give a mask that is both as good after load shifts and harmless on ordinary days. The alarms that both sources raise are harmless but too few to help. The next step is fewer false alarms per matched load shift, not more matches. also relevant 00212 switching-detector-masks-in-gam-training A convex additive model of substation demand (GAM) is trained on readings that include switching transfers, which move load between substations for hours or days. Every earlier GAM in this project trained with the logged and hand-labelled transfers set missing, so nobody has measured what the masking is worth. If masking the detector's own alarms during training does about as well as masking the hand labels, a live service with no labels can train as well as the project does now. inconclusive not-for-production Masking switching transfers when the forecast model is trained barely matters: with no mask the score is only 0.002 points worse on clean rows and 0.003 worse after a logged transfer, and 476 simulated transfers added to the training readings worsen it by just 0.009 points. Training with the detector's alarms masked scores 0.007 points worse than with hand labels masked on clean rows (interval -0.007 to +0.025) and 0.027 worse in winter, so the detector's effect in training is small on average but not resolved from zero. On this record the unmasked fit is already almost as good as the masked fits, so a detector mask has little to improve in training. also relevant 00208 switching-value-of-a-detector-by-phase-and-quality Knowing about a switching transfer lowers the forecast error mainly in the 48 hours after the transfer ends and in the days before an alarm would normally arrive, and the benefit shrinks roughly in proportion to the share of transfers missed and to the delay of the alarm. A detector of the quality of the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) recovers well under half of the perfect-knowledge benefit, so the quality it must reach to be worth building is higher than RO-NC's. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast about a switching transfer lowers its error by about 1.5 points of capacity during the transfer and in the 48 hours after it ends, but by only about 0.005 points averaged over a year, because transfers are rare. A detector that finds about 4 transfers in 10, as RO-NC does, recovers about half of that gain, and none of the real alarm sources tested keeps its ordinary-day error inside the limit. Options for a next step are an alarm source with far fewer false alarms per matched transfer, or a use of the alarm that does not set recent power aside. also relevant 00203 switching-replay-learned-score-in-masked-forecast Experiment 195's learned score finds 22 to 24 of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, against 19 for the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC). If its alarms drive the gated mask of experiments 163 and 171 (readings set missing from the detector's step stamp until the transfer ends), the forecast scores better after real transfers than the pair-alarm mask does, and the mask still does no harm on ordinary days. The mask ignores recent power inside an alarm, so extra true alarms should help and extra false alarms should harm. partly supported not-for-production Masking the forecast with the alarms of experiment 195's learned score did not lower the error after real switching transfers by a reliable margin, and it did not meet the limit for no harm on ordinary days. The learned alarms arrive 2 to 4 days after a step, so they miss the start of the long transfers that the pair alarm catches. A candidate next step is a mask that takes the pair alarm where it fires and the learned alarm elsewhere. also relevant 00195 switching-neural-plus-detector-features A learned score that reads the features the rule-based switching detectors already compute (the 24-hour step statistic of RO-NC, the opposite step at the metered neighbour of the pair alarm, and related quantities), trained only on injected transfers, finds more of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day than RO-NC alone at the same number of unexplained alarms, and more than a rule-based union of RO-NC and the pair alarm. partly supported candidate A learned score on the features that RO-NC and the pair alarm already compute finds 22 to 24 of the 35 real transfers over 1 day, against 18 or 19 for RO-NC, at the same number of unexplained alarms. A plain logistic regression finds 22 even without any look-ahead feature, so most of the gain is in the features, and the extra transfers are small ones (under 1 MW each). The next step is to test whether the extra alarms help the gated mask, which this experiment did not run. also relevant 00191 dp-price-sensitive-assets-in-the-history Some of D8's multi-day drops (experiment 159) and the matching shortfalls at its neighbour D14 are output of price-following gas generation (experiment 186), which no weather input explains and no forecast of the price can reach at a lead of days. Letting the convex demand model (GAM-K) see the half-hourly price in its training history, gated by the registered connection date of the 6 MW gas engine, lets it learn a cleaner baseline for the rest of the demand. The forecast then improves even when the price is unknown at forecast time. not supported not-for-production Modelling a price-following asset in the history does not make the forecast better at D8 or D14. A demand model that is given the true price at forecast time, which no live service has here, gains only 0.6% at D8, and the models that use a price available at forecast time lose 0.9% to 4.4%. The gas engine's response is real enough to fit (1.2 to 1.9 MW at D8 within the training rows), so the remaining D8 error comes from causes that these price indicators do not explain, and NGED's half-hourly output for the engine is the data to ask for next. also relevant 00189 switching-neural-onset-end-block-detector A small neural network (under 50,000 weights) that reads a 7-day window of the convex-model residual of a Primary substation and its connected neighbours, and is trained only on injected transfers and on real stretches without a logged event, finds more of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day than the pair alarm of experiment 156 does, and finds as many as RO-NC (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector), at the same number of unexplained alarms, and places the onset to within 3 hours. It can do so only if the injected transfers resemble the real ones, so the injector is fitted to the real events and checked for realism before training. refuted not-for-production A small neural network trained only on injected transfers finds 7 of the 35 real transfers lasting over 1 day, against 18 for the existing rule-based detector, when both the start and the end must be right. It locates the start of 12 transfers (17 after longer training) to within 2 hours, so the learned start alarm is competitive and the end alarm is what fails. The next step is a learned start alarm paired with the rule-based end rule, or a longer input window that holds the end of multi-day transfers. also relevant 00188 switching-d10-audit-and-onset-location-in-look-back Part 1. Experiment 171 found that ignoring recent power while a gated pair alarm is active scores 0.030 points of effective capacity worse than no mask on rows outside logged transfers (95% interval -0.011 to +0.074), and that leaving out one substation, D10, moves the estimate to +0.002. If D10's gated alarms are real switching that NGED did not log, those rows are not ordinary days, and treating them as events leaves a no-harm interval inside +/-0.03. Part 2. The alarm for a transfer is known hours to days after the step, but the forecast runs every 6 hours, so at each run the readings since the step are in the look-back. A step-fitting search over those readings finds the onset more precisely than the alarm time, and masking from the found onset gives a smaller forecast error in the first 24 hours after the alarm than masking from the alarm time. partly supported not-for-production Once a switching alarm fires, masking recent power back to the alarm's own step stamp removes almost all the extra error of masking only from the alarm time, and searching the look-back for a more precise onset adds nothing. D10's extra error under the gated mask is not shown to be unlogged switching, since an independent step test confirms only 3 of its 13 unlogged alarm intervals (its recall was not measured), so showing that the gated mask does no harm on ordinary days still needs more months of forecasts. also relevant 00181 switching-block-detector-and-like-for-like-table The 17 unlabelled worst days that experiment 175 classed as sharp-edged blocks were missed by the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) and by the opposite-step pair alarm because most of the blocks are shorter than the 24-hour windows those detectors average over and their steps are small in noise units, not because the blocks are invisible. A detector that fits a rectangular block (a step up, a flat level, a step down) at lengths of 6 hours to 5 days finds most of them at the same number of unexplained alarms as RO-NC. refuted not-for-production A detector fitted to rectangular blocks finds none of the 17 unlabelled worst days. It was allowed the same 80 unexplained alarms in odd-numbered months as RO-NC, the existing detector. The days are mostly blocks lasting 12 hours or less and standing 1 to 4 noise units above the residual (one noise unit is the usual spread of the forecast residual), too close to its ordinary variation for an alarm that reads only the residual. The next step is to send NGED the candidate label table, so that NGED can say which of the 17 days were real switching. On the 35 labelled real transfers lasting over 1 day, RO-NC finds 18 on the convex-model residual and 12 on the XGBoost residual. Four of the 6 extra transfers sit at Primaries where the XGBoost panel has no readings, and on the 29 transfers that both residuals cover the counts are 14 and 12. also relevant 00177 dp-worst-days-other-data-sources At least a quarter of the 37 unlabelled worst substation-days of experiments 172, 174, and 175 coincide with an event recorded in data the project already holds: a logged switching operation near the substation, a step in a metered generator on the same or an interconnected Primary, a reading-quality fault in the substation's own series, or a repeat of the substation's own bad weekday or date. refuted not-for-production The 37 worst days of the best-guess forecast that carry no label are not explained by any of the six sources we tested: logged switching, reading faults, repeat bad weekdays, Demand Flexibility Service events, and national price spikes each cover them no more often than they cover ordinary days. The three raw NGED files we read hold only time and power. Sources we have not tested include local outage notices, local events, and a location join to the metered generators. also relevant 00175 dp-unlabelled-day-shapes At least half of the 37 unlabelled worst substation-days of experiment 174 are sharp-edged blocks in the forecast's error (a switching-like change in the power a substation draws), and in at least a third of those a substation interconnected with the first shows a step of opposite sign within 2 hours (a load transfer between the two). refuted not-for-production The forecast's worst unlabelled days are roughly half sharp-edged blocks (a switching-like change in the power a substation draws) and 40% smooth offsets (a change in level or behaviour that lasts the day). Interconnected neighbours do not show the opposite step more often than chance would give, and the existing switching detectors fired on none of the block days. The counts point to two separate problems, level changes and blocks that the interconnection table does not explain. The shape rules miss about 40% of injected blocks, so the block share is uncertain. also relevant 00174 dp-unlabelled-worst-days-weather-shared-or-single-site Most of the excess loss on the unlabelled worst days of experiment 172 is weather error, and the unlabelled worst days are mostly shared with other Primaries. Replacing the ensemble-mean weather with the estimate of past weather (ERA5 temperature and CAMS irradiance) in arm D's forecast removes at least 50% of the unlabelled days' excess loss, and at least a third of the unlabelled days are also in the worst 5% of days of at least one other Primary. partly supported not-for-production Most of the forecast's error on its worst unlabelled days is not weather error: with past weather in place of the forecast weather, about 69% of the excess loss stays. Other Primaries share these days about as often as random shifting gives, so the data show at most a weak shared cause. The remaining loss could therefore come from events at one substation, such as undetected switching, a change in behaviour, or a metering fault. The next place to look is the substation's own recent readings and the switching records on those days. also relevant 00172 dp-error-budget-worst-days The error of the stage 2 assembly (experiment 155's arm D) is concentrated on a small number of days that the project already knows how to label. The worst 5% of days, ranked by their pinball loss above the site's median day, carry at least 30% of the total excess loss, and at least half of those days carry one of six labels: a switching event, a metering error or flagged reading, a cold snap, an Economy 7 step, a holiday, or a combination. inconclusive not-for-production A small number of bad days carries a large share of the forecast's error: the worst 5% of days carry about 42% of the excess loss, and about half of those days coincide with a switching event, a holiday, or a cold snap. Switching events are the largest group, on days that carry 29% of the excess loss, so a forecast that improves only ordinary days leaves most of the loss in place. Cold snaps carry 5% of the excess in this mild scored winter, so this year cannot show whether a cold-night term pays. The formal verdict is inconclusive because one control narrowly failed. also relevant 00171 switching-gated-mask-no-harm-pooled-months Experiment 166 found that ignoring recent power (a "mask") only while a pair alarm with a balance score of at least 0.7 is active (the "gated mask") scores 0.009 points of effective capacity worse than no mask on the real rows outside logged transfers, with a 95% interval of -0.068 to +0.081 from one year of rows. That interval was too wide to show no harm. Pooling every cached forecast run, 27 months instead of 12, shows whether the gated mask does no harm on ordinary days. inconclusive not-for-production Ignoring recent power while a gated switching alarm is active scores 0.030 points of effective capacity worse over 27 months of rows outside logged transfers (95% interval -0.011 to +0.074), against +0.009 in experiment 166's 12 months. That interval is too wide to show the harm is below 0.03, and the difference comes mostly from one substation, D10. Showing no harm needs more months of forecasts, or an explanation of why D10's gated alarms raise the error. also relevant 00166 switching-gated-mask-and-soft-mask-while-alarmed Experiment 165 found that setting recent power missing while a switching alarm is active lowers the error in the 72 hours after a logged transfer ends (13.69 to 6.31 points of effective capacity) but raises it by 0.102 points on rows outside logged transfers, because many alarms are not transfers. Two ways of using the alarm less bluntly keep the gain and remove the harm. (1) A gated mask: mask only when the alarm is a pair alarm of experiment 156 whose opposite steps balance at a metered neighbour with a balance score of at least 0.7, and never for a single-series refit-offset neighbour-count (RO-NC) alarm. (2) A soft mask: keep the readings in the Kalman filter but inflate their observation-noise variance by a factor that rises with the pair alarm's balance score, until the end rule fires. not supported not-for-production Setting recent power aside only when a switching alarm has a balanced opposite step at a metered neighbour (balance score 0.7 or more) keeps 99.6% of the gain after a logged transfer ends (error score 13.69 down to 6.34 points of effective capacity, 7 transfers) and adds only 0.009 points on other rows, against 0.102 for the earlier mask from either alarm. One year of data leaves the interval for the extra error too wide (-0.068 to +0.081) to meet the pre-registered limit of 0.03, so the verdict is not supported. Down-weighting recent power instead of dropping it does not help: the gain and the extra error rise together. also relevant 00165 switching-drop-recent-power-while-alarmed-all-rows A forecast built from a frozen generalised additive model (GAM) and a Kalman filter on its recent errors, with the filter's readings set missing from the moment EITHER the pair alarm of experiment 156 OR the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) is known until the end rule of experiments 147 and 148 fires, forecasts better than the same forecast with no mask while an event is running and in the 72 hours after it ends, and does not make the forecast worse on the real rows outside events, because the filter then restarts and the mask only removes readings that contain moved load. not supported not-for-production Setting recent power aside (a mask) while a switching alarm is active, where an alarm flags load moved between substations, helps only after a logged transfer ends: the mask lowers the forecast error score from 13.69 to 6.31 points of the substation's effective capacity in the 72 hours after (7 transfers). On the other rows the mask raises the score by 0.10 points, about 4% more error, which fails the pre-registered limit of +0.01 points on the upper end of the 95% interval. The next step is a mask gated on how reliable the alarm is, or used in winter only, that keeps reading recent power on rows outside transfers. also relevant 00163 switching-real-event-comparison-gam-stack-against-bg2 On the logged real load transfers at the six decision Primaries, a forecast built from a frozen generalised additive model (GAM), a Kalman filter on its recent errors, and a mask that sets the readings missing from the moment an alarm is known (the pair alarm of experiment 156, with the end rule of experiments 147 and 148) forecasts the days after a transfer ends better than best guess 2 (BG2), because BG2 takes lagged power as an input and so carries the transfer into its forecast, and the mask does not. The stack costs little on the real rows outside transfers. partly supported not-for-production After a real load transfer ends, a forecast that masks the power readings of the transfer period or ignores recent power has an error score about 40% lower than best guess 2 (an XGBoost forecast that uses recent power) and about 54% lower than the same forecast with no mask (6.32 against 10.09 and 13.69 points of effective capacity). This rests on 7 logged transfers, and two long winter transfers carry most of the gain. On ordinary days the mask scores 0.03 points worse than no mask, and best guess 2 and the stack are indistinguishable over the year, with the stack better in winter and worse in other months. The next step is more logged transfers, or a forecast that drops recent power while the pair alarm or the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) is active. also relevant 00162 switching-shaped-transfers-donor-demand-and-pv-shapes A load transfer moves houses, factories, and solar sites, not a constant number of megawatts, so the power it moves follows the donor's demand and solar shapes. Part 1: on the logged real transfers, a donor residual during the transfer is fitted better by a daily shape, -(a x the donor's demand term + b x its solar term) from the convex model (GAM), than by a constant offset, and the fit separates a from b only for transfers that last several days and contain both sunny and dull days. Part 2: an injection whose moved power follows the donor's solar term vanishes at night and is small at midday in winter, so the half-size-reversal end rule and the step threshold of the detectors misfire on it, and a constant-MW injection (and, less so, today's injection, which moves a share of the donor's net power) flatters the detectors. partly supported not-for-production If a transfer removed a daytime load that follows the donor's solar output, or removed solar output itself, the refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) would find about half of them instead of 91%, and the live end rule would cover 22% of the true interval instead of 62%. The pair alarm loses far less once a step may start at first light. The 25 logged real transfers cannot say whether they move solar output, because a daily shape fits them no better than it fits quiet stretches. A realistic mix of houses and small solar sites is nearer the share-of-net-power injection of earlier experiments, which the detectors find as easily as a constant transfer. also relevant 00159 switching-d8-multi-day-drops-recurrence-and-report Descriptive, with no hypothesis test beyond the prediction below. D8 is a Primary substation whose power drops by 3 to 5 MW for days at a time while the convex demand model's forecast does not follow. The experiment lists every such drop, asks whether the drops recur on a pattern, and asks whether a connected metered neighbour steps up by a similar amount at the same time (a load transfer) or does not (a customer load change or an outage). partly supported not-for-production D8's multi-day drops are 29 episodes since 2022, nearly all since mid-2023, in which D8's power runs about 2.7 megawatts below the demand regression model's expectation for 2 to 19 days. The three connected metered neighbours step up with the drops at a rate not clearly above their rate at random times, so the drops do not clearly look like load moved onto them, and they show no detectable weekday, hour, bank-holiday, or seasonal pattern. Most of the switching detector's alarms on D8 are away from the drops (10 of 52 are within 6 hours of an edge), so the detector does not find the drops. The next step is to ask NGED which load moved or which switching took place, starting with the six drops that have no logged closure. also relevant 00156 switching-faster-onset-alarm-from-opposite-steps RO-NC (the refit-offset neighbour-count detector) learns of a load transfer about 48 hours after it starts, because its step statistic needs 24 hours of data after the step and its peak test needs 24 hours more. A transfer between two metered substations makes opposite-signed steps of similar size at the two, while weather, Economy 7, and holidays make same-signed steps.
