An alarm that fires when one node steps by k noise units and a connected metered node steps the opposite way by at least k/2, measured over a window of 2, 4, or 6 hours, therefore learns of the transfer within hours instead of days, at the same rate of real false alarms as RO-NC. A mask forecast (readings from the alarm onset set missing until the end rule fires) driven by this alarm then scores better than the same mask driven by RO-NC, because the mask starts days sooner. partly supported not-for-production An alarm built from opposite steps at a metered neighbour is known 3 to 9 hours after a load transfer starts, instead of 48, and masking readings from it closes 95% of the forecast-error gap on the transfers it finds. It finds few transfers, though: 38% of simulated transfers and 5 of 35 real ones. On all rows after a transfer begins, no mask beats a forecast that ignores recent power, so the next step is a forecast that drops recent power while a transfer is suspected, not a better mask. also relevant 00153 latent-nra-state-in-the-gam-k-filter Experiment 141's two-regime filter lets the level follow a load transfer, and 141 scored observed power, so neither tested the forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA). If the filter instead holds the NRA as its own slowly moving state and routes the transfer into a separate, fast offset state that is switched on by the causal alarm and left out of the forecast, the forecast of the NRA moves towards the true NRA series during and after a transfer, and stays where it was when no transfer happens. partly supported not-for-production Giving the transfer its own offset state in the Kalman filter forecasts the normal running arrangement as well as the filter that ignores power does, and no better than simply dropping the readings inside a detected alarm. Dropping them is a smaller change, because it needs no second filter state on the serving path, so the extra state is not worth building. The no-change test on real alarms also failed: most real alarms coincide with genuine level shifts, and on them the new filter moved the median forecast by about 4 points of capacity. primary 00151 nra-forecast-rescored-against-the-true-nra-series The detector-driven correction of experiment 141 was scored against observed power, which rewards a filter for following a load transfer. Aim 2 of the switching work is a forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA), the power the substation would have drawn had no transfer happened. Scored against that true NRA series, a forecast whose filter subtracts the megawatts (MW) of each detected transfer from its input closes a useful share of the gap between the filter that ignores transfers and the filter fed the true NRA series, once the alarm has been raised. The two-regime filter of experiment 141 closes little, because it still follows the transfer. partly supported not-for-production Once the detector has raised its alarm, taking the transfer out of the recent power closes most of the gap to a forecast fed the true normal-running-arrangement series, but ignoring recent power altogether closes nearly as much. Subtracting the detected megawatts is fragile (it rests on a few transfers at one substation), and masking the readings is steadier. Counting the 64% of transfers that the detector missed and the 2 days before the alarm, subtracting the detected MW gains nothing and masking gains 21%, so the next step is a detector that alarms sooner and a forecast that drops recent power while a transfer is suspected. primary 00141 switching-detector-fed-into-gam-k Telling GAM-K's Kalman filter when the RO-NC detector has seen a load transfer lowers the forecast's quantile score on days after a transfer begins, because the filter's level then adapts within hours instead of over days. The same signal given as plain features (event age and signed step size) does the same, more weakly. not supported not-for-production Telling the forecast's filter when a load transfer started and ended helped inside the transfer and hurt in the 72 hours after it, because the filter holds the transfer's step over the whole 7-day forecast. The switching detector's alarm arrives 48 hours after the step and did no better than a random placebo. The next test is a correction that decays over the typical transfer duration. primary 00116 differentiable-physics-nra-edge-flows-between-primaries Flows on the electricity network's interconnection edges, fitted to a frozen convex model's residuals with a sparse-step penalty, recover injected conserved transfers between MW-metered Primaries; removing them gives a normal running arrangement (NRA) model trained without hand labels that forecasts no worse outside events; and fed causally into the Kalman filter as a known input, they improve the metered forecast during and after a transfer. inconclusive not-for-production The method that looks for load moved between neighbouring substations did not work: with the settings we fixed in advance it found under a quarter of the load we added artificially, and it changed no forecast. Looser settings found more, but they also found load moving between substations that are not connected, probably the slow drifts of demand that our model does not describe. The gate failed for a structural reason: at the settings we fixed in advance, the fit cannot find any transfer shorter than 7 to 9 days, and the longest test transfer lasts under 5 days, so the failure is a limit of the method as specified, not a bug in the solver. The zero flow we first saw on the unconnected pairs was also an artefact of the order the fit visits its paths, so those pairs were never clean. Adding a drift term to the model, or accepting a flow only where the two substations are connected, is the next thing to test. also relevant 00100 drop1-random-lag-dropout-widens-intervals An XGBoost quantile model for Primary substation demand that is trained with labelled switching half-hours removed from its targets and with its lagged power inputs set to missing at random intervals, and that has those lags set to missing when they lie inside a labelled switching event, widens its 5% to 95% band on the half-hours whose lags are missing, so that the band's coverage moves from 0.784 towards the nominal 0.90, without widening the band elsewhere. inconclusive not-for-production Training the demand forecast with lags hidden at random did not make its band wider on half-hours where a lag is missing: on real rows the band covered 0.80 (hidden in 10% of training rows) to 0.84 (30%) of actuals, against a nominal 0.90. Hiding lags in 30% of rows did remove the accuracy loss that masking alone causes on injected transfers (-0.02 points, 95% interval -0.35 to +0.38 against the plain model). Hiding lags in 10% of rows left +0.26 (98.75% interval -0.15 to +0.85), not separable from zero or from the loss. An input that tells the XGBoost model a lag is missing, or a separate XGBoost model of the quantile spread, are untested routes to a wider band. also relevant 00096 sw2-23-synthetic-switches-injected-into-training A forecast of the normal running arrangement (NRA, the network as it is when no switching transfer is on) recovers the power a Primary substation would have drawn had no transfer happened better when its XGBoost model was also trained on many synthetic transfers than when it was trained on the real logged transfers only. In a synthetic transfer, known MW is added to the recorded power of a donor and its receivers, the half-hours of the transfer are dropped as training targets, the lags are corrected by the transfer's MW, and the MW is given as a column. The gain holds when the MW at forecast time comes from the causal refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC) or from the largest detector step, and not only when the MW is the injected truth. inconclusive not-for-production C1, synthetic-trained minus real-trained with the injected MW: +0.079 points of capacity (98.75% interval -0.031 to +0.153). primary 00091 sw2-26-calibrated-probability-of-abnormal-arrangement The refit-offset neighbour-count detector (RO-NC), run causally (with only the data before a forecast origin), can give for each past half-hour in the lag window a probability that the half-hour lies inside an abnormal running arrangement (ARA). The probability is calibrated, and it separates better than the detector's yes-or-no flag. inconclusive not-for-production A probability built from the causal switching detector was not shown to beat the detector's yes-or-no flag: on the planned rows its Brier score was 3.3% lower (97.5% interval -7.6% to +1.6%), against the 20% the plan required. Only in a post hoc subset of injected transfers large enough to see was the gain 11.2% (-20.3% to -2.0%). Against NGED's switching logs it has almost no skill (area under the curve 0.52 to 0.53), so a rule that widened the uncertainty bands when the probability is high would cover only about 8% of the half-hours that the logs mark as switching. primary 00090 sw2-28-lag-unusualness-inputs-all-rows-and-switching For the 16 Primary substation demand series, telling the monthly-refitted (P-roll) XGBoost model how unusual each of its three lags is (the probability integral transform, PIT, of each lag against a probabilistic climatology of the series) lowers the quantile score on all half-hours outside switching, and widens the quantiles on the half-hours whose lag lies inside a logged switching event, when both arms train on normal-arrangement targets only. refuted not-for-production C1, clim_pit minus plain on all rows outside switching: +0.355 points (97.5% interval +0.209 to +0.513). primary 00089 sw2-22-longest-history-nra-forecast-with-ara-lags-masked For the 16 Primary substations, an XGBoost demand model refitted monthly and trained on the longest history of ECMWF ensemble control-member forecasts (2021-03 onward), with every half-hour inside an abnormal running arrangement (ARA) removed from the training targets, scores below the same model on the standard 12-month window, and setting to missing every lagged power input that lies inside an ARA lowers the score on the half-hours whose lags lie inside an ARA. refuted not-for-production C1, LM minus L on rows with a lag in an ARA: +0.409 points (98.33% interval +0.281 to +0.517). primary 00088 sw2-21-nra-forecast-recovers-normal-arrangement-during-and-after-injected-switches When a Primary substation (a substation that steps down to the local distribution network) is inside a load transfer, or has just left one, an XGBoost demand model that was trained without the transfer's half-hours as targets, with the lags corrected by the transfer's signed MW and the MW as a column ("full NRA", NRA being the normal running arrangement), forecasts the power the substation would have drawn had no transfer happened better than the plain model does. This holds when the MW comes from the RO-NC detector of experiment 82 (a logistic score on the 24-hour residual step) run causally on data up to the forecast origin, but by less than when the MW comes from the injected truth. inconclusive not-for-production C1, arm 4 with RO-NC MW as built minus plain: -0.149 points of capacity (98.75% interval -1.174 to +0.148), closing 16% (-17% to +67%) of the gap to the ceiling, negative in 2 of 4 months. primary 00086 sw2-12-detector-labels-for-nra-forecast On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of experiment 48, giving the monthly-refitted (P-roll) Primary demand model the lags minus the MW that switching moved, together with that MW as three columns, lowers the quantile score on the half-hours whose lag sits inside a switching event, when the events and MW come from the RO-NC load-transfer detector of experiment 82 instead of NGED's logs, and the gain is smaller than with the oracle labels of experiment 41 by the share of events RO-NC misses. inconclusive not-for-production Lags corrected with the detector's labels did not lower the quantile score on rows with a lag inside a logged event. primary 00075 sw2-11-nra-forecast-with-labelled-switching-masks On the 292 daily ENS forecast runs of experiment 48, a weekly-refitted Primary substation demand model whose training targets leave out the labelled switching half-hours forecasts the normal running arrangement (NRA) no worse than the plain weekly model, and giving the model the signed MW that switching moved at each lagged power input, or replacing each lag by the lag minus that MW, lowers the quantile score on half-hours outside switching. inconclusive not-for-production C1, masked minus plain: +0.004 points (98.33% interval -0.026 to +0.025). primary 00044 sw2-2-switching-share-of-best-guess-score Half-hours in labelled switching events, and half-hours whose lagged power falls inside one, carry a larger share of the best guess's quantile score and tail score than their share of half-hours, and a perfect switching detector could lower the Primary quantile score or tail score by 3% or more. refuted not-for-production In the band of events the labeller finds most reliably, a perfect switching detector would lower the best guess's quantile score by 0.42% (95% interval -0.47% to 1.96%) and its tail score by nothing, against a threshold of 3%. Switching in that band touches 3 of the 16 Primary series and few half-hours, in one validation year. primary

docs.title: Load-shift labels in the forecast: research plan
docs.text:
No proposal in this theme is waiting.

Experiment 00116 (differentiable physics, NRA) also bears on this theme. It fits flows on the interconnection edges between Primary substations and scores them on injected transfers; see the Network research plan.

docs.title: Planned experiments
docs.text: Experiment Hypothesis Relevance

docs.title: Weather products and blending
docs.text:
Of the weather changes tested, only training on estimates of past weather (ERA5) clearly lowered the error in a test without power lags, for 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to 6 days ahead, and no extra weather forecast has yet been shown to help in a way a live service could use.

A weather product is a source of weather data, such as the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS), the Met Office's UKV (a 2 km forecast of the UK), the US ensemble GEFS, or ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional forecast). The experiments trained XGBoost models on one product's history, then added a second product as extra input columns or as a blend. They scored 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, and 16 Primary substations, each over one validation year. For Primary demand, even weather as accurate as ERA5 lowered the score by only 0.10 points.

Training on ERA5 lowered the mean absolute error of the ensemble-mean forecast at 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms up to day 6, and not beyond. Source: experiment 1. Lower is better.

docs.title: Does it work?
docs.text:
Training on ERA5 lowered the solar and wind farm error up to day 6. Over all leads, the ERA5-trained XGBoost model scored 15.39 against 17.09 for wind (-1.70, 95% interval -2.33 to -1.08) and 7.67 against 8.25 for solar (-0.57, -0.83 to -0.32), in points of capacity, with no calendar or lag columns (experiment 1). The contrasts were revised after two reviews, so they are not pre-registered. A later test used the quantile score and power lags at 24 to 54 hours. It found the ENS-trained model 0.218 points lower than the ERA5-trained best guess for wind (-0.472 to +0.069) and 0.107 lower for solar (-0.327 to +0.053). Both differences are unresolved (experiment 54, experiment 57).

For demand series it did not carry over. On 22 series that are not wind or solar farms, 16 of them Primaries, the ERA5-trained model scored 1.37 points worse (+0.68 to +2.17) with weather columns only. Starting the ERA5 history in 2023-09 instead of 2019-09 lowered the error by 1.32 (-1.81 to -0.90), a post hoc read that does not separate drift in the series from bad early data (experiment 3).

Weather as accurate as ERA5 gave a small gain for Primary demand, measured only for a model trained on ENS. Swapping ENS for ERA5 weather in the stack of experiment 19 (a half-life of 0.5 years) lowered the quantile score by 0.10 (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04) at 16 Primaries over 73 runs. Shortwave radiation alone gave -0.084, and inside 2 days there was no gain (experiment 22). Training on CAMS sunshine instead of ERA5 shortwave gave -0.035 (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), against a planned 0.2 (experiment 9). Mapping the ENS shortwave onto CAMS first (stage 0) gave a further -0.067 (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039). The CAMS-trained arm with stage 0 scored 0.102 below the ERA5-trained arm. The verdict stays inconclusive because the monthly mismatch to CAMS reached 18.6% (experiment 14).

A second global ensemble, GEFS, did not improve the sunshine anomaly. The anomaly is a forecast's sunshine minus its own monthly mean, scored against the CAMS anomaly at 5 Primaries on daylight rows from April to September. Cross-validated squared error was 1.109 times ENS's for GEFS (worse in all 9 held-out months) and 1.002 times for a fitted blend, against the 0.99 needed (refuted, experiment 50).

GEFS correlated worse with the CAMS anomaly than ENS did, and the blend matched ENS. Source: experiment 50.

A UKV and ENS blend lowered the squared error of the same anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours in cross-validation, and the validation year cannot confirm it. The validation correlation gain was +0.011 (-0.006 to +0.027), and the blend beat ENS in 3 of the 6 months of forecast origin that the intervals resample. The test was post hoc. Six or 7 origin months understate the uncertainty (experiment 53).

UKV wind lowered the wind-farm quantile score by about 0.2 points at 24 to 54 hours, a small gain that is an upper limit. An ENS-trained XGBoost model given UKV wind as extra columns, trained on UKV's own history, scored -0.198 (-0.316 to -0.069) at 3 wind farms. The interval's end nearest zero does not reach the pre-registered 0.15, and a shuffled-UKV placebo scored +0.013 (-0.012 to +0.040). One farm gained clearly (-0.413) and one did not (+0.018), post hoc. The UKV data come from the CEDA archive, which differs statistically from the live feed (experiment 54; UKV-CEDA study).

Giving UKV wind to an ENS-trained model lowered the wind-farm score, and the shuffled-UKV placebo did not. Source: experiment 54.

The same test with UKV shortwave, cloud, and temperature at 6 solar farms was inconclusive. The score changed by -0.035 (-0.119 to +0.037), so a gain of 0.10 can be neither shown nor ruled out (experiment 57). Averaging the wind best guess with ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast (IFS) gave -0.055 (-0.200 to +0.072) at days 1 and 2, also inconclusive, and the products' runs were half a day older than ENS (experiment 52).

docs.title: Best design so far
docs.text:
The best recipe tested here depends on the target, and none beat the reference by a resolved margin. For farms the reference is the best guess, as the generator-forecasting Summary explains.

  • Solar and wind farms, up to day 6: train the weather-to-power model on ERA5 and apply it to each of the 51 ENS members (experiment 1). This was measured without power lags, and experiments 54 and 57 found the ENS-trained model within an unresolved margin at 24 to 54 hours. For solar, CAMS sunshine as the training input scored -0.140 (99.5% interval -0.277 to -0.044), short of the planned -0.15 and inconclusive (experiment 12).
  • Wind farms, 24 to 54 hours: add UKV wind as columns to an ENS-trained model, trained on UKV's history (experiment 54). This is an upper limit, measured on the CEDA research archive.
  • Primary substations: keep the model trained on ENS. If training on estimates of past weather, start in 2023-09 (experiment 3) and map the ENS shortwave onto CAMS (experiment 14).

docs.title: Candidates for production
docs.text:
Two experiments are marked candidate, and neither is ready to port as it stands.

  • ERA5-trained weather-to-power model for solar and wind farms (experiment 1). Production would train on ERA5 and CAMS history and serve ENS members, which needs the staged design. The caveat under "Best design so far" about power lags applies.
  • Stage 0 mapping of ENS shortwave onto CAMS for Primaries (experiment 14). Production would fit the mapping on 14 or more months of ENS and CAMS pairs. The mapping left monthly mismatches, widened the member spread by 27%, and needs a CAMS-trained model.

No second weather product (GEFS, UKV, ICON-EU, IFS) is ready. Experiments 50, 52, 53, 54, and 57 are not-for-production.

docs.title: Gotchas and implementation details
docs.text:
• Train each product on its own history. The arms are ENS-trained, ENS plus the other product as columns, and the other product alone; an ERA5-trained model is only a reference. A model trained on ENS and fed ERA5 weather understates what ERA5 training would give (experiment 22). The ERA5-trained wind model fed uncorrected ICON-EU winds alone scored 2.5 points worse than the best guess, and IFS winds 1.3 points worse, at days 1 and 2 (experiment 52). Re-check when the model, the product, or the bias correction changes.
  • "Better weather adds little" was measured only for a model trained on ENS. Experiment 22 trained on the ENS control member, and ERA5 differs from ENS in bias (mean shortwave 132.6 against 139.1 W/m2). Experiment 9's CAMS-trained arm gained 0.88 daylight points at observed weather and 0.04 over all leads with ENS input (experiment 9). Look for a Primary demand model trained on ERA5 and scored on experiment 22's stack.
  • Pass a shuffled-product placebo through every step. In experiment 54 the placebo showed that extra columns alone do nothing. In experiment 52 it scored +0.343 because July's equal weights and the spread factor, not the shuffled forecasts, drove the score, so fit the spread factor on blends made under the same weights (experiment 54, experiment 52). Re-check if the blend weights or the spread factor are fitted a different way.
  • Use the live feed, and check its variables on a recent run. The CEDA UKV archive has no 100 m wind and lacks four hourly steps, UKV was upgraded on 2026-01-21, and Open-Meteo's UKV history stops at lead day 0 (experiment 54, experiment 57). Feeds gain fields over time, so an old date gives a wrong answer. Re-check when a live UKV history exists.
  • Feed the run the service would have. Experiment 52 fed runs half a day older than ENS, and experiment 53 assumed a 3-hour UKV delivery time without measuring it (experiment 53). Look for a measured delivery time before reading a blend's gain. Re-check once the live delivery time is known.
  • Give a guard arm the variant it guards. A guard arm is a control built to catch one artefact; in experiment 3 it was the ENS-trained arm with one row per valid time. The ENS training frame repeats each valid time about 15 times, so calendar columns let an ENS-trained model memorise the calendar position, and a one-row-per-valid-time guard arm with lags failed by construction (experiment 1, experiment 3). Re-check when the input columns or the training rows change.
  • Calibrate each source's anomaly, and cross-validate by whole months. GEFS's raw anomaly was about 15% too large, and the interval width follows the number of origin months (experiment 50, experiment 53). Re-check with a longer validation period, which gives more origin months.
  • Check the hour-of-day peak of every source. CAMS and ENS are means labelled at the period end and UKV is instantaneous, so a mislabelled UKV control peaked at 10 UTC instead of 12 UTC (experiment 53). Re-check for any new product whose shortwave is instantaneous.
  • Take the planned threshold from a contrast between like arms. Experiment 9 planned 0.2 and resolved 0.035 (experiment 9). Report a pooled share with and without the largest series: a fixed CAMS correction removed 46.6% of the daylight squared residual, one substation set the pooled figure, and a fixed bias alone removed 39.1% (experiment 7, inconclusive). Re-check whenever a pooled share is quoted.

docs.title: What we have not settled
docs.text: Whether a live UKV history gives the wind-farm gain, whether ICON-EU and IFS help when read at the service's own time, and whether a source of a different kind helps solar farms. Experiment 50 tested GEFS against the CAMS solar anomaly at 5 Primaries only. The open proposals are in the research plan.

docs.title: Weather products and blending: experiments
docs.text:
This page lists every experiment tried in the theme, newest first. An experiment that belongs mainly to another theme but bears on this one is marked "also relevant".

Experiment Hypothesis Verdict Production status Take-home message Relevance 00437 neural-demand-thermal-lag-solar-gain-and-tariff-feature-bundles The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 425 sees one valid time per row, so it cannot see the hours before or after that time. Adding columns that summarise those hours (bundle T, thermal lag; bundle S, solar gain; bundle F, look-ahead) or that carry the calendar, tariff, and national signals (bundle C) lowers its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at days 1 to 10, because the network trains across all 16 Primaries (and, in the pretrained form, across 6 years of ERA5 and CAMS history) and may find signal that the per-Primary XGBoost model and the GAM stack missed. not supported not-for-production Adding thermal-lag, solar-gain, look-ahead, calendar, tariff, or national-signal columns to the pooled plain mixture density network did not lower its continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) by the registered 0.03 points of capacity, in either the ensemble-only or the pretrained form. Seven of the eight arms were worse than their control at the six signed-MW Primaries, by 0.016 to 0.059 points. The thermal-lag bundle lowered the CRPS at the eight MVA-only Primaries (by 0.022 and 0.029) in only 2 of 4 folds, which is too weak a result to act on. The screen could not detect effects below 0.045 to 0.064 points, so the bundles are left out, not ruled out. also relevant 00429 unified-forecaster-wind-ablations A single pooled neural network can forecast the three metered wind farms as well as Wind farms research default 2 (experiment 347's y2: a frozen ERA5-trained power curve run on each of the 51 ensemble members, followed by a mixture-density head). Each difference between that design and the Primary-demand design (experiment 425's arm A: one pass on the ensemble mean and spread, no physics, an unbounded head) is kept only if an ablation shows it is needed. partly supported not-for-production Neural wind forecasts do not need the extra machinery. A plain pooled network fed the ensemble members ties Wind farms research default 2 (10.533 against 10.518 points), and neither passing members through the network (-0.008 against the one-pass design), a power-curve layer (+0.000), nor a censored head (+0.018, worse) changes the score by the 0.10-point margin. The weakness all arms share is the upper tail: 2.2% to 2.8% of observations exceed q99, because the forecasts under-predict windy half-hours, and censoring did not fix it. The plain network is the design that matches the default; the upper tail is the open problem, and the architecture comparison does not explain it. also relevant 00424 neural-mva-export-gated-signed-ens-serving-test Experiment 420's export-gated network (arm A) still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with its gate shut (P0) when both are trained and scored on ECMWF ensemble (ENS) mean and spread weather, which is the weather a live service would hold, instead of the recorded CAMS irradiance and ERA5 temperature of the laboratory test. The gain shrinks, because the ENS forecast of cloud is less accurate than recorded cloud, but most of the laboratory gain comes from letting the forecast go below zero, which does not depend on weather accuracy. supported candidate With ensemble weather forecasts instead of recorded weather, the neural network with the export gate still forecasts signed power on reverse-flow half-hours much better than the same network with the gate shut (a gain of 15.7 points of capacity, 95% interval 13.8 to 17.4, against 19.2 with recorded weather), and it harms the forecast by no more than 0.05 points where no solar farm exports. The gate opened at the same two of the eight apparent-power-only substations as before. An unplanned finding is that the network trained on recorded weather and applied unchanged to ensemble weather scored 5.5 points better (95% interval 4.4 to 6.6) than the network retrained on ensemble weather, so how to train on ensemble weather is the open question. also relevant 00419 pooled-mixture-density-network-solar-summary-sunny-flag-and-half-life-input-ports The XGBoost model's gain from a two-column solar summary (experiment 381: -0.051 points at the signed-MW six on the scored year) carries over to the pooled plain neural network, which has the solar geometry but no cloud-aware summary, and the 0.25-year half-life that lowered the score at D15 and D18 and on cold nights in experiment 407 does so again with new random seeds. not supported not-for-production The XGBoost model's solar-summary input did not carry over to the pooled plain neural network: it lowered the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) at the six signed-MW Primaries by only 0.012 points of capacity (-0.043 to +0.013), one sixth of the 0.0738 minimum detectable effect. Refitting the same neural network with new random seeds changed the MVA-only eight by -0.047, about six times as far as the solar summary did there (-0.008), and changed the signed-MW six by the same amount as the solar summary did (+0.011 against -0.012). Adding the sunny flag and a 1-year half-life was worse than the solar summary alone, and the 0.25-year half-life raised the signed-MW six CRPS (+0.044) while lowering it at D15 and D18. None of the input changes is adopted, and the reference stays. All five test months are interim. also relevant 00418 mdn-pretrain-on-era5-and-cams-then-fine-tune-on-ens The pooled plain mixture density network of experiment 397, pretrained on the Primaries' own power and ERA5 and CAMS weather from 2019-09 and then fine-tuned on the ENS rows, scores lower CRPS at days 1 to 10 than the same network trained on the ENS rows alone, because the ENS archive starts on 2024-04-01 and the pooled network sees at most 18 to 24 months of it. supported candidate Teaching the neural network first on six years of past weather and power, then on the forecast archive, lowers its error by about 0.06 points of capacity (2.1%) at the six signed-direction substations and 0.16 points (4.2%) at the eight apparent-power-only substations over 12 test months. Changing how much of the network is retrained, or adding forecast-like noise, changes the score by less than the interval of the estimate. With only 6 months of forecast archive on 4 test months the gain is about 1.3 points, although the ENS-only baseline degrades badly there. also relevant 00396 xgboost-recipe-screen-demand-calendar-winter-hyperparameters-ensemble-summary At least one change in each of five families (calendar columns, winter weather columns, hyperparameters, ensemble-summary inputs, a split of the model by lead band) lowers the days 1 to 10 CRPS of the weekly member of experiment 87, refitted monthly, by more than the refit noise floor at the signed-MW six or the MVA-only eight Primaries, and the families that act on a specific slice (holiday days, winter and the top demand quartile, high ensemble spread) gain more on that slice than on all rows. partly supported candidate Giving the weekly XGBoost demand model the ensemble's view of the weather, either its mean and spread or a model trained on the ensemble mean, lowered the error by 0.4% to 2.7% in both test months, and no other change we tried did so as clearly. Holiday columns help on Easter bank holidays but raised the error on all days in January and at the signed-MW six at Easter, and winter weather columns do not help, so a full-year test should start with the ensemble-input arms. also relevant 00395 xgboost-level-state-winter-spread-anchor-stored-forecasts A level state in the style of the GAM stack's Kalman filter, run on the weekly XGBoost bundle's own residuals, closes the bundle's gap to the GAM stack at D11 and D14, and a one-state filter with three numbers per Primary does so almost as well as the stack's two-state filter. partly supported not-for-production A Kalman-filter-style level state helps the weekly XGBoost model at D14 and hurts it at D11, so the filter is not the whole explanation of the gap to the GAM stack. A cheap one-state version (three numbers per Primary) recovers about half of the two-state filter's gain at D14 only, so the first production update should not carry it. Adding the winter ensemble-spread columns lowers cold-night scores but not cold-night coverage, and does not widen the band where weather is most uncertain. A short-history level anchor cuts D15's median bias but worsens the other 14 Primaries by about 0.1 points. When recent power readings lie inside a labelled load-shift event, every forecast loses q95 coverage on the signed-MW six, and only the GAM stack does on the MVA-only eight. The GAM stack's score worsens most, though its interval overlaps the others'. also relevant 00394 xgboost-ensemble-mean-and-std-columns-separately Experiment 389's gain from four ensemble columns (the mean and standard deviation across the 51 members of temperature and of shortwave) comes mostly from the two mean columns, because the gain was largest at 0 to 24 hours and at the middle quantiles and absent at q01 and q99. supported not-for-production Giving the XGBoost demand forecast, as an extra input, the mean across 51 ensemble weather members of the temperature and of the shortwave radiation lowers its error (CRPS) by 0.052 points of capacity at the 6 substations that record the direction of flow, and by 0.029 points at the other 8. That is the whole improvement of four extra columns at the 6 and 82% of it at the 8 (0.035 points). The members' spread adds almost nothing, and it does not help more on days when the members disagree most. The tails do not materially improve with either input: on cold nights the forecast's 95% quantile lies above only 0.77 to 0.78 of outcomes at the 6. also relevant 00381 simple-weekly-xgboost-demand-against-gam-stack A single XGBoost model per Primary, refitted weekly on the ENS control member with experiment 87's recipe (the BG2 weekly member), plus at most four small input or weighting changes, scores no worse than the GAM stack ("stack without S below 168 h", experiment 377) at every one of the 14 countable Primaries at days 1 to 10. partly supported candidate A single XGBoost model per Primary, refitted weekly, is as good as the GAM stack at 9 of 14 Primaries and better on average at the eight whose meters hide reverse flow (D8 by 1.6 points; clearly so at D8, D12, and D22), so the stack's extra parts do not pay at those eight. At the six Primaries with signed readings the XGBoost model is level on average (+0.08, not distinguishable from zero) but worse at D11 and D14 and has a narrower upper tail, so the stack still protects against curtailment better there: its avoidable curtailment cost at a limit of 0.9 times the maximum observed export is lower at 4 of 6. The input changes that helped in practice were a daily solar summary (-0.05) and a 1-year half-life (-0.02); an Economy 7 input did nothing, and no input tried fixed the 4.9-point under-forecast of sunny demand at D12. also relevant 00379 bg2-components-all-16-primaries-to-14-days Under the demand-v1 protocol at all 16 Primaries, no single component of BG2 carries its lead over a single weekly-refitted XGBoost model, so dropping any one of the five blend members, the solar offset, or the spread factor moves the CRPS of days 1 to 10 by less than 0.10 points of effective capacity. supported not-for-production A plain weekly-refitted XGBoost model scores within 0.05 points of BG2 (about 1.5% of its error) at the six Primaries whose meters record the sign of the flow, and within 0.02 points at the eight whose meters do not, so the five-model blend adds little to the first release candidate. Two of BG2's five models (monthly XGBoost and the pooled-by-type model) add nothing measurable, and the solar offset twins act only at the five Primaries that carry them. BG2's upper tail is too narrow at the six signed-MW Primaries: 93.2% of outcomes fall below its 95% quantile and 97.6% below its 99% quantile. also relevant 00371 d8-monthly-xgboost-input-group-ablation One input group of monthly XGBoost (the weather inputs the GAM lacks, the three origin lags, the 0.5-year recency weighting, or the 51-member mixture) accounts for most of its 0.64-point lead over the GAM stack at substation D8. supported not-for-production Monthly XGBoost beats the GAM stack at substation D8 mostly because it uses three lagged values of the power measured shortly before the forecast starts: without them its score rises from 7.70 to 8.25, within 0.1 of the GAM stack's 8.34. The five extra weather inputs (0.05) and the ensemble mean (0.01) explain little of the gap, and the recency weighting (0.23 at D8) explains a smaller part and only at D8. The lags also help at two other Primary substations (D4 +0.28, D2 +0.11), so the pre-registered expectation that only D8 would respond failed. A GAM term that uses recent power is the next candidate to test. This is one substation and one scored year. also relevant 00343 wind-research-default-1-train-on-ensemble-mean Wind farms research default 1 trains XGBoost on ERA5 and runs it on each of the 51 ensemble members, then corrects with the offset table. The ensemble's 100 m wind speed at the grid cell is lower than at the turbines (a factor of 1.13 closed 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle in experiment 307). An XGBoost model trained on the 51-member mean of the ensemble's own history (arm M, 2024-04 to 2025-06, no calendar columns) would learn that bias and need less offset-table correction. Arm MS adds the member standard deviation of the 100 m and 10 m speeds. The three metered wind farms W1 to W3 are scored at 1 to 10 days. not supported not-for-production A wind model trained on the ensemble mean needs almost no offset table (the table changes its score by 0.017 points, against 0.345 for the default), but its forecast is no better than the default's: 0.08 points worse on the headline rows, an amount the data cannot distinguish from zero, and worse at low winds and in the 0.99 quantile. The default's recipe (ERA5 training plus the table) stays; mean training is a simpler recipe that scores about the same. also relevant 00333 primary-demand-foundation-model-zero-shot A pre-trained time-series foundation model (Chronos-2, 120 million parameters, Apache-2.0) forecasts a Primary substation's half-hourly demand from the substation's own history. Without weather inputs Chronos-2 cannot match Primary demand research default 3 at leads of 1 to 10 days. With the ensemble-mean temperature, the sun's elevation, and calendar columns passed as covariates, Chronos-2 closes part of the gap, but not all of it. partly supported not-for-production A pre-trained time-series foundation model, used without any training on our data, forecasts Primary demand clearly worse than Primary demand research default 3 at every lead from 0.5 to 240 hours. Giving the foundation model the temperature forecast, the sun's elevation, and the calendar recovers about one sixth of the gap, and makes sunny-daylight half-hours worse. Chronos-2, the one foundation model we tested, is not a candidate to replace the default, and a foundation-model forecast would have to be scored alone against the default before use as a blend member. also relevant 00329 primary-demand-default-3-member-solar-distribution-at-7-to-10-days At 168 to 240 hours the 51 ensemble members have little skill for individual days, so the forecast centres on average sunshine and the half-hours that turn out sunny have realised demand below the median. The weakness of Primary demand research default 3 on sunny daylight (5.07 against the manual heuristic's 4.82 in experiment 317, for the convex chain before any blend) is therefore a fault of the predictive distribution (the lower tail on realised-sunny half-hours), not of the median. Replacing the two-number Gaussian summary of the members' solar responses with the 51 responses themselves (X1), mixing them with a climatology of the response (X2), or adding the members of the two previous daily runs (X3) fixes the distribution. not supported not-for-production The 7-to-10-day weakness on sunny half-hours no longer exists in the research demand forecast: the two-number solar summary and the daylight-only blend with the manual heuristic already took it from 5.2% worse than the heuristic to 6.6% better, so no new distribution method is needed there. What remains is one coastal Primary (D5), where the forecast is 11% worse than the heuristic, which points back at the solar term and not at the width of the bands. also relevant 00325 primary-demand-default-3-sunshine-response-refit-and-restriction Experiment 323's sunshine response (F1) harmed all daylight half-hours because the Kalman filter's level, the winter night offset, and the median correction were estimated on the errors of a fit without a response and so counted the same error twice (double counting), or because the response acts too widely, at forecast clear-sky index where the damped ensemble-mean forecast index mis-applies the response. Refitting those corrections on the response's own errors (F1r) removes the first cause, and restricting the response to clear-sky index above 0.6 and sun elevation above 15 degrees (F1s) removes the second. small gain not-for-production The sunshine response, once the rest of the forecast chain is refitted around it, no longer makes daylight forecasts worse, but the response improves the overall forecast by under 0.01 points, too little to adopt. The response improves spring daylight at two Primaries (D5 and D9) by about 0.11 points. also relevant 00323 primary-demand-default-3-flexible-sunshine-response-in-the-convex-fit Primary demand research default 3 trails the depth-1 XGBoost refit on April-to-June daylight half-hours because its solar term (the pinned capacity times the derated unit shape, with the D5 clip) is too high on clear spring middays. Experiment 322 grafted the refit's sunshine response onto the default and recovered 0.50 of the refit's advantage. A smooth correction in clear-sky index and sun elevation, fitted in the same bounded least-squares fit as the solar term, recovers a useful part of that gain with no model of other inputs. not supported not-for-production Adding a flexible sunshine curve to the solar part of the demand forecast does not recover the gap to the better-performing XGBoost model: it helps the sunniest half-hours but worsens the pooled score by about 0.4%. The advantage seen in experiment 322 is therefore not recovered by adding a smooth curve in clear-sky index and sun elevation on top of the existing level corrections, and most of the harm sits in the level shift. A boosted-tree sunshine term could use more inputs at once, and whether to test it is a decision for the research plan. also relevant 00319 primary-demand-default-1-solar-summary-and-heuristic-blend-at-7-to-10-days Primary demand research default 1 has two weak spots at 168 to 240 hours: sunny daylight half-hours, where it scores 5.2% worse than the manual heuristic, and April to October, where it beats climatology by only 4%. Default plus x1 (the two-number solar summary S, the mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses, extended from 0.5 to 168 hours out to 240 hours) lowers the sunny-daylight score at 168 to 240 hours. Default plus x2 (a blend of the convex chain's median with the manual heuristic's, with the weight fitted per 24-hour lead band and season group) lowers the pooled score at 168 to 240 hours, mostly in April to October. partly supported candidate The demand forecast for 7 to 10 days ahead improves by about 2% when its solar term also uses the spread between the 51 weather-forecast members, and the gain is largest on sunny days (6.6%), where the forecast had been worse than the manual heuristic that National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) staff use. Blending in the manual heuristic improves the forecast by 4.5%, but the blend worsens the coldest winter nights beyond the agreed tolerance, so only the solar change is adopted. also relevant 00307 wind-farm-power-as-wind-sensor The wind that the three metered wind farms' own power implies (the fitted physics core's power curve run backwards) is closer to a high-resolution analysis than to ERA5 at 9 to 14 m/s, and at least half of the ensemble's shortfall (observed power below the forecast's median on 34.1% of rows instead of 50%) is in the spread and timing of the members, not in their mean speed. not supported not-for-production The ensemble's low wind-power forecast comes mostly from wind speeds that are too slow, by about 1.1 m/s on average and more at longer leads. Multiplying every member's wind speed by a factor fitted on the 14 months before the scored year closed about 78% of the gap to the ERA5 oracle, while widening the members or shifting them in time closed almost none. The median is slightly better calibrated when the factor is fitted to the wind that the farms' power implies than when it is fitted to ERA5 on the same rows (1.7 percentage points), but the quantile score is not better. also relevant 00292 metered-farm-ens-neighbourhood A day-ahead cloud field is often right in shape and wrong in position by tens of kilometres, so summaries of the ensemble's irradiance over the hexagonal cells around a metered solar farm carry information that the farm's own cell lacks. Giving H5 (the plant plus a neural network that outputs all 11 quantile offsets) those summaries lowers its quantile score at 12 to 36 hour leads. not supported not-for-production At the six metered solar farms tested, the ensemble's irradiance on the cells around a farm adds almost nothing to the day-ahead forecast: the quantile score improves by 0.36%, against the 2% the plan needed, and the gain is not robust to dropping one farm. Adjacent cells, 15 km apart, differ from the farm's own cell by only about 3% of the irradiance, so the ensemble mean is too smooth between them to show where a cloud edge will fall. A weather source of a different kind is the next experiment to run, rather than more processing of the same ensemble. also relevant 00272 metered-farm-weather-adapter-gam-vs-neural Extra weather variables that the solar-farm power model (the plant) ignores, fed through a learned correction to the plant's irradiance and temperature, close part of the gap between the plant driven by the ensemble weather forecast (about 0.91 of output fitted on sunny half-hours) and the plant driven by observed weather (0.973), and a small neural network does this better than additive curves. not supported not-for-production The extra ensemble weather variables (longwave radiation, humidity, precipitation, pressure, wind, and 500 hPa height) showed no usable information for the solar-farm power model at these six farms, whether they enter through additive curves or a small neural network, and the real variables do no better than placebo copies. A neural network with no plant, given the lagged power and the ensemble spread, scores 2.7% better than the plant but not better than the linear fit of experiment 257, so a correction to the plant's weather is not the route to a better forecast. also relevant 00270 metered-farm-xgboost-vs-plant-diagnostic XGBoost beats the plant (the solar-farm power model of experiments 218 and 224) on the six metered farms because of inputs the plant never sees, namely the farm's own lagged power and the ensemble spread, and not because of a better map from the ensemble-mean weather to power. Calendar columns and extra weather variables add little once those two are present. partly supported candidate XGBoost beats the solar-farm power model by about 3% in the quantile score even when it sees only the power model's own weather inputs, and the gain is in the width of the forecast band (the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles), not in the median forecast. The same gain comes from giving the power model a forecast band that depends on the ensemble spread or the clear-sky index, and that band also beats XGBoost at the 0.99 quantile. Lagged power, calendar columns, and extra weather variables add little in own history. also relevant 00262 wind-aifs-members-and-climatology-by-lead For the three metered wind farms (W1 to W3), a lead-dependent mixture of the ECMWF ensemble's member forecasts, the AIFS ensemble's member forecasts (both run through experiment 230's ERA5-trained XGBoost wind model A0r), and climatology lowers the quantile score and the 0.99 pinball loss against the ECMWF members alone, after both are corrected by a table of offsets per lead day, quantile, and farm; and a small neural gate that reads the two ensembles' spread and disagreement chooses better weights than weights by lead alone. partly supported candidate Adding the AIFS ensemble's wind forecasts to the ECMWF ensemble's improves the wind forecast at 3 to 6 days ahead, by about 5% of the quantile score, but does not improve the high-power tail that matters for curtailment. Climatology and a small neural network that picks the mixing weights add nothing once the table of offsets has corrected the common low bias. The AIFS arms also need testing on a second year, because one year of Tuesday runs sets the weights. also relevant 00246 metered-farm-ens-ukv-icond2-blend The DWD ICON-D2 regional weather forecast (2 km grid, run every 3 hours, 48 hours ahead) carries information about cloud over a metered solar farm that neither the ECMWF ensemble nor the Met Office UKV carries, so adding it to the ensemble plus UKV lowers the farm's day-ahead error. The evidence against is that at day 1 every single product lost to the ensemble mean for solar in the matched-lead study, and ICON-D2's errors are likely to be correlated with UKV's. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used is the CEDA research archive. small gain not-for-production Adding the German ICON-D2 weather forecast to the ECMWF ensemble and the Met Office UKV lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1%, which is under the 1.5% we set as worth a fourth weather source. ICON-D2 is available for only 12 to 29 hours of the day ahead at an 08 UTC forecast time, and the UKV archive used is a research archive, so this is an upper limit for production. also relevant 00237 dp-two-number-solar-summary-with-clip The mean and standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses lower the daylight quantile score of the demand forecast also when each member is passed through the clipped solar term, because cloud uncertainty and the clip both act at midday only partly on the same rows. supported candidate At D5, in one year of data, summarising the ensemble weather members as a mean and a standard deviation keeps at least about 90% of its gain when the solar output is clipped at 60% of the solar capacity held for D5 (110%, interval 91% to 141%). On the sunniest third of daylight rows the point estimate of the remaining gain is about half (interval -12% to 88%). A post hoc arm using the standard deviation alone kept the gain there, which suggests testing that form. also relevant 00229 metered-farm-ens-ukv-blend The Met Office UKV weather model (2 km grid, 54 hours) carries information about cloud over a solar farm that the 51-member ECMWF ensemble lacks, so giving a metered solar farm's forecast both products lowers its day-ahead error against the ensemble alone, and closes part of the gap between the ensemble-driven fit (0.91 of output on sunny half-hours) and the fit with observed weather (0.973) of experiment 218. Every gain is an upper limit for production, because the UKV archive used here is the research archive on CEDA, which differs statistically from the live UKV. small gain not-for-production Adding the Met Office UKV forecast to the ECMWF ensemble lowers the day-ahead error of a metered solar farm by about 1% to 2%. The gain is under the 3% we set as worth a second weather source, and the farms' fit on sunny half-hours moves only about 6% of the way to the fit with observed weather. The UKV archive used here is a research archive, and the live UKV differs, so this result is an upper limit for production; a weather product of a different kind is the option we see for a larger gain. also relevant 00202 dp-ens-two-number-rolling-replay Experiment 193 found that two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the 51 ensemble members' solar responses) lower the daylight quantile score by 2.20% in the scored year. Its two fitted factors per lead band were fitted on interleaved months (the odd months of 2024-07 to 2025-06), some of them later than the replicate months they were applied to, and its numbers were held in float64. A replay of the live weather layer, which stores the two numbers as float32 columns computed from the one ensemble run published before each origin and refits the factors each month on history that has completed before that month, keeps most of the gain. supported candidate A weather layer that stores two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the 51 ensemble members' solar-generation estimates) and refits its two scaling factors every month, using only runs that had finished before the month began, lowers the daylight quantile score (the score for the forecast's uncertainty bands) by 2.3% at five substations over one year, which is as much as running all 51 members. This confirms experiment 193's result under production-style timing, so the next step is to build the two columns into the weather layer. also relevant 00193 dp-ens-two-number-solar-summary Experiment 187 found that passing each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term lowers the daylight quantile score of the full best-guess stack by 2.23%, and that a Gaussian with each row's own mean and spread of the 51 responses recovers 95% of that gain. Two numbers per half-hour (the mean and the standard deviation of the members' solar responses) therefore carry nearly all of the gain, so a serving path can store two columns instead of running 51 passes. supported candidate Summarising the 51 ensemble weather members' solar estimates by their mean and standard deviation lowers the daylight quantile score by about 2% (98% of the gain from running all 51 members, 93% in the replicate months), at the five substations scored over one year. The weather layer could store two columns per half-hour instead of 51, and the 10th and 90th percentiles add nothing measurable. A follow-up experiment could test the two numbers in the live weather layer. also relevant 00192 dp-ens-members-temperature-cold-nights Experiment 187 found that passing the 51 ECMWF ensemble members through the solar term of the demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%. The demand response to heating is also nonlinear (a hinge at 15.5 degrees C), and the ensemble mean smooths away the cold tail. Passing each member's temperature through the temperature terms therefore lowers the quantile score on cold winter nights. not supported not-for-production Running each ensemble member's temperature through the demand model gave no detectable improvement in the forecast bands on cold winter nights, because the 51 members' temperatures differ too little to signal the day's error. The cold-night bands are already too narrow. The cause of the cold-night error is still unknown; widening the bands directly, and testing wind, night cloud cover, and switching as inputs, are the candidates. also relevant 00187 dp-ens-members-in-stack Experiment 184 found that running each of the 51 ensemble members through the solar term of the convex demand model lowers the daylight quantile score by 2.2%, but its verdict was capped at inconclusive because a monotone gate failed on rows where the unit PV shape itself falls as irradiance rises. With a gate that matches that shape, the same arm passes, and its gain lies where the best-guess stack leaves the largest sunny-daylight error, at the substation D5. supported candidate Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model still improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2% on top of the full best-guess stack, and night is untouched. About two thirds of the gain needs that day's own members, and two numbers per half-hour (the mean and spread of the members' solar responses) carry nearly all of it, so a cheaper two-number version is the next thing to test. also relevant 00184 dp-ens-daylight-calibration Experiment 169 found that passing the ensemble's spread to the width of the forecast's bands adds nothing when scored over all half-hours. The benefit may be confined to daylight half-hours, especially sunny and partly cloudy ones, where the clouds that the 51 ensemble members disagree about change the output of embedded solar generation, and so the demand. Passing each member's irradiance through the convex model's solar term (arm M), or using the spread of the members' irradiance as a fraction of clear-sky to set the band width in daylight (arm S), calibrates the daylight bands better than the existing bands (arm A). inconclusive not-for-production Running each of the 51 ensemble weather members through the solar part of the demand model improves the daylight forecast bands by about 2%, mostly in the lower tail and on partly cloudy half-hours, while night is untouched. Placebos that widen the bands the same way but without the real members gain little, so most of the benefit is information about cloud. The next step is a production-cost check of the member pass and a test of its gain on top of the best-guess forecast. also relevant 00174 dp-unlabelled-worst-days-weather-shared-or-single-site Most of the excess loss on the unlabelled worst days of experiment 172 is weather error, and the unlabelled worst days are mostly shared with other Primaries. Replacing the ensemble-mean weather with the estimate of past weather (ERA5 temperature and CAMS irradiance) in arm D's forecast removes at least 50% of the unlabelled days' excess loss, and at least a third of the unlabelled days are also in the worst 5% of days of at least one other Primary. partly supported not-for-production Most of the forecast's error on its worst unlabelled days is not weather error: with past weather in place of the forecast weather, about 69% of the excess loss stays. Other Primaries share these days about as often as random shifting gives, so the data show at most a weak shared cause. The remaining loss could therefore come from events at one substation, such as undetected switching, a change in behaviour, or a metering fault. The next place to look is the substation's own recent readings and the switching records on those days. also relevant 00125 differentiable-physics-n8-ens-members-through-gam-k-and-the-spread-around-them Placing GAM-K's residual quantiles, fitted on a forecast driven by the analysis proxy (so they hold model and filter error and almost no weather error), around each of the 51 ENS members gives tails closer to nominal than today's table, which is fitted on ensemble-mean residuals, and the gain is largest at long leads and on cold winter nights, where the hinge turns a temperature error into a large demand error. The comparison is against GAM-K re-tuned on the same factor grid, so a plain scale error cannot pass for a better design. inconclusive not-for-production Putting the forecast-error table around each of the 51 weather members, and fitting it on analysis-driven forecasts so that it holds no weather error, did not improve the tails of GAM-K's demand forecast. The weather members' spread is small against the model's own error, so the weather error was counted twice in the code but is too small to matter. The next step is the cold winter nights, where demand exceeds the 95% quantile about a quarter of the time in every arm. The verdict is inconclusive, because no arm reached 14 of 16 calibration cells. also relevant 00119 differentiable-physics-enc-weather-patch-encoder-on-ens A small neural network that reads the ENS grid boxes around a Primary, and not only the one box GAM-K reads, lowers GAM-K's quantile score a little on average and more on the cold, showery, and badly forecast days NGED cares about, either as a correction to GAM-K's quantiles or as a replacement for its single-box temperature and irradiance. inconclusive not-for-production A small neural network that reads the ensemble weather around a Primary lowers GAM-K's quantile score by 0.062 points of effective capacity in one scored year and 0.035 in the other (both statistically significant, 5 of 5 substations better), and the gain is smaller in winter (0.041 and 0.027 points) but never a loss. About two-thirds of the gain survives when the network reads the wrong date's weather (0.043 and 0.022), so it is probably a recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the lead, the hour, and GAM-K's own forecast, and the surrounding boxes add nothing to the centre box (patch minus centre box: -0.002 and +0.003 points). The known-answer gate failed, so the verdict is inconclusive, and the next step is a plain recalibration of GAM-K's quantiles with the centre box's extra fields (dew point, pressure, precipitation, and member spread), not a patch encoder. also relevant 00111 differentiable-physics-6-ens-forecast-engine-against-bg2 Driven by ECMWF ENS forecasts, the convex DP demand model forecasts Primary demand up to 7 days ahead better than lagless XGBoost given the same recent-level correction, and, used as the base margin of the BG2 recipe's lagged XGBoost, makes the production recipe better like for like. partly supported candidate Driven by real ensemble weather forecasts, the physics-based demand model with a filter on its recent errors (GAM-K) scored 2.80 points against 2.78 for the production recipe (BG2) at five Primary substations. The 0.02 difference cannot be told from zero (-0.109 to +0.157), and the comparison is not like for like. GAM-K scored 0.13 points better than lagless XGBoost with the same filter (-0.305 to +0.014, 4 of 5 substations better), so the verdict is partly supported. The filter's gain is the firmly supported part: 0.15 points, 0.39 in the first day, with the sign held in the replicate months. Giving lagged XGBoost the physics model's forecast as a starting point changed nothing measurable. The known-answer gate passed 22 of 22 readings on its second run, after a sign error in the gate's own test data (both runs are kept). The departures were that the XGBoost compute estimate was 20 times too low, so the margin arms refitted monthly; lagless XGBoost for the scored year reused SIMP1's refits and had no spread factor; and the confirmation comparison was not run. GAM-K is a candidate for Flexpectation v2's roughly 1,300 substations on the measured filter gain, with four caveats: five substations over one year, a short XGBoost history, the undecided XGBoost comparison, and a margin that gave no gain. also relevant 00057 product-trained-xgboost-solar-farms For the six metered solar farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's shortwave radiation, total cloud, and temperature as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead hours 24 to 54 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. inconclusive not-for-production Giving UKV forecasts to an ENS-trained solar-farm model changed the quantile score by -0.035 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval -0.119 to +0.037), which is too small to resolve. The data cannot show a gain and cannot rule out the 0.10-point gain that would justify a new weather feed. UKV helped the six solar farms far less than it helped the three wind farms. also relevant 00054 product-trained-xgboost-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, an XGBoost quantile model trained on ENS and given UKV's wind as extra input columns scores lower on the quantile score at lead days 1 and 2 than the same model trained on ENS alone, with every arm trained on the same window, rows, and seeds. UKV is read from the CEDA archive, which is not the live product, so the contrast is a ceiling read. small gain not-for-production Giving the Met Office's UKV wind forecast to an ENS-trained wind-farm model lowered the quantile score by about 0.2 points of capacity at 1 to 2 days ahead (95% interval 0.07 to 0.32), and a shuffled-UKV placebo shows the gain is information and not extra columns. The UKV data come from a research archive and not the live feed, so the gain is an upper limit on what a service could get. also relevant 00053 ukv-vs-ens-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW that decide experiment 00046's verdict (D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), the Met Office UKV forecast of the solar anomaly (the output of a generic solar fleet minus its own month-by-half-hour mean), alone or blended with the ECMWF ensemble mean (ENS) using weights fitted on the training window, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone does within the UKV's lead range of 120 hours. small gain not-for-production At 5 Primary substations, a fitted blend of the Met Office's UKV and ENS lowered the cross-validated squared error of the sunshine anomaly by 7.6% over 0 to 54 hours (3.8% to 13.8% in each band), but the validation year cannot confirm it (correlation gain +0.011, 95% interval -0.006 to +0.027). The test was post hoc and its intervals rest on 6 or 7 origin months, so they understate the uncertainty. UKV alone was worse than ENS, and the UKV data are a research archive, so any gain is an upper limit. primary 00052 more-nwp-products-for-wind-farms For the three metered wind farms, averaging the quantiles of the experiment 33 wind best guess (the ERA5-trained mixture over the 51 ENS members, with the power-curve margin and the spread factor) with the quantiles of the same ERA5-trained model fed ICON-EU's and IFS 0.25 degree's forecast wind lowers the quantile score at 1 to 2 days ahead, with weights chosen only on earlier months. inconclusive not-for-production Averaging the wind best guess with two extra weather forecasts, ICON-EU and the ECMWF high-resolution forecast, scored 0.055 points of capacity better at lead days 1 and 2, but the 95% interval (-0.200 to +0.072) includes zero. Three wind farms cannot show whether the extra forecasts help, and the blend scored 0.122 worse at days 3 to 6. also relevant 00050 second-weather-forecast-for-solar-anomaly At the five Primary substations metered in MW in experiment 00046's verdict set (anonymised series D9, D10, D11, D14, and D16), an anomaly forecast that blends the NOAA GEFS ensemble mean with the ECMWF ENS ensemble mean, with weights fitted on the training window only, tracks the CAMS solar anomaly more closely than ENS alone. Laid into experiment 00046's solar term with its fitted lead-dependent coefficient, the blended anomaly lowers the quantile score by at least 0.1 points of capacity against the same term built from ENS alone. refuted not-for-production The stage 1 gate stopped the experiment: in cross-validation on the training window GEFS's squared error against the CAMS anomaly is 1.109 times ENS's (worse in all 9 held-out months) and the fitted blend's is 1.002 times, against the 0.99 needed. primary 00022 era5-weather-ceiling-primary-demand For the 16 Primary substation demand series, giving the winning recipe of experiment 00019 (the single-stage ENS-trained quantile model N1 with a recency half-life of 0.5 years, the 14-day error correction, and the 1.15 spread factor) ERA5 weather in place of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) weather at serving time lowers the quantile score by at least 0.3 points of capacity over all leads. refuted not-for-production ERA5 weather in place of ENS weather lowered the quantile score over all leads by 0.10 points of capacity (99.38% interval -0.16 to -0.04), so the 0.3-point gain the rule asked for is ruled out. also relevant 00014 cams-trained-stage1-with-stage0-ens-correction-demand A stage 0 that maps the ECMWF ensemble (ENS) member's shortwave irradiance onto the irradiance of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) lowers the Primary substation quantile score of the CAMS-trained stage 1a XGBoost demand model, relative to feeding that model the raw ENS shortwave, because the ENS shortwave is about 7% above CAMS and stage 1a never saw that offset in training. inconclusive candidate C2, stage 0 minus raw ENS for the CAMS-trained arm, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.067 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.094 to -0.039), better than the planned -0.03. primary 00009 cams-trained-stage1a-vs-era5-trained-demand A stage 1a XGBoost demand model trained with irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) in place of ERA5 shortwave, and applied to the shortwave of ECMWF ensemble (ENS) members, has a lower quantile score at Primary substations than the same model trained on ERA5 shortwave, because the satellite-derived irradiance is closer to the irradiance that the substations' embedded solar generation responded to. refuted not-for-production C1, CAMS-trained minus ERA5-trained, Primary quantile score over all leads: -0.035 points of capacity (97.5% interval -0.070 to +0.001), a sixth of the planned 0.2-point gain. primary 00007 cams-static-correction-stage1a-residual Most of the daytime residual of the stage 1a demand model at Primary substations is a fixed error in the ERA5 irradiance input and not a growing embedded-solar capacity, so a correction with fixed coefficients on irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), fitted on one year of out-of-fold residuals, removes most of the residual in the next year. inconclusive not-for-production The static correction removes 46.6% of the next year's daylight squared residual, just below the planned 50%, and a fixed bias alone removes 39.1%. primary 00003 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained-demand A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 (2019-09 onward) and applied to the 51 ENS members, with the member forecasts averaged, has a lower mean absolute error on electricity demand series than the same columns trained on ENS weather. not supported not-for-production D1, s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, weather only, all leads: +1.37 (+0.68 to +2.17), 22 series; with calendar +1.38 (D2, against the one-row-per-valid-time arm: +1.67); with calendar and lags +0.10 (-0.26 to +0.50). primary 00001 era5-trained-stage1a-vs-ens-trained A weather-to-power XGBoost model trained on ERA5 and CAMS (2019-09 onward) and applied to ENS weather has a lower point-forecast error than the same columns trained on ENS weather. supported candidate P1 (revised), s1_memberavg minus ens_trained, all leads: wind -1.70 (-2.33 to -1.08), solar -0.57 (-0.83 to -0.32); material up to day 6, not beyond. primary
