docs.title: Which single weather forecast should be added to ECMWF's ensemble mean first?
docs.text:
At 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms in Lincolnshire, adding one weather forecast to the mean of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast (ENS) lowered the power forecast's error in some of the 32 (blend, setting) combinations tested, and the page can name a first product only for solar at day 2. Each comparison gives an XGBoost model (a gradient-boosted tree model) the ENS mean's weather plus one product's weather, and scores the power forecast as a mean absolute error in percentage points of the generator's capacity. A negative difference means the added product helps. Differences are the blend's error minus that of an XGBoost model given the ENS mean alone, with 95% intervals from resampling whole months and a fitting seed. Every result is on the single rows (the 16 months from March 2025 in which the 00 UTC run of AIFS (Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System) Single, ECMWF's machine-learned forecast, lies inside one version era), at the primary hyperparameter setting with the sensitivity setting in brackets, and is uncorrected for multiplicity unless the text says otherwise. The exception is WeatherNext 3 (WN3, Google DeepMind's machine-learned forecast), which has 7 months and is fitted at the primary setting only.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5). Several independent Claude reviewers have checked the method, the evidence, and the prose adversarially.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• At wind day 1, adding ICON-EU (the German weather service's regional ICON model for Europe) at the optimistic lead (exploratory; an upper bound on a live service's gain) lowers the error by 0.58 points [0.48, 0.69] (0.55 at sensitivity), from the ENS mean's 8.20%. The result survives a Bonferroni correction. At the conservative lead the gain is 0.165 [0.063, 0.264] (0.158), which does not survive the Bonferroni correction (wind results).
  • At solar day 2, adding AIFS Single lowers the error by 0.33 points [0.18, 0.48] (0.27) from 10.13%, survives the Bonferroni correction, and beats the optimistic ICON-EU blend by 0.20 [0.03, 0.37]. At sensitivity that difference's upper bound is -0.000, on the line (solar results).
  • At solar, ICON-EU at the conservative lead shows no detectable gain at day 1 or day 2. A gain above 0.08 points is excluded at both days and both settings. The conservative lead is older than a live service would read, so the result does not show that ICON-EU adds nothing.
  • At wind day 1, adding AIFS Single lowers the error by 0.31 points [0.10, 0.60] (0.17 [0.07, 0.28]). At wind days 1 and 2, AIFS Single and ICON-EU are not separable, except that AIFS Single is worse than the optimistic ICON-EU blend at day 2 (+0.39 [+0.25, +0.59], +0.29 at sensitivity). The optimistic blend is an upper bound for ICON-EU, so the rule does not rank ICON-EU above AIFS Single.
  • UKV (the Met Office's UK variable-resolution weather model) at day 1, an optimistic upper bound, lowers the wind error by 0.64 points [0.41, 1.01] (0.46). The solar gain, 0.16 [0.03, 0.27], fails the Bonferroni correction.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The question is which one weather forecast to add to the ENS mean first. The matched-lead page scores each product alone against ENS and tests one blend of ENS with two products. AIFS Single is ECMWF's machine-learned forecast. ICON-EU is the German weather service's regional forecast, and UKV is the Met Office's UK forecast. The ICON-EU blend is fitted at two leads. The optimistic lead reads ICON-EU's freshest run at least N days before the valid hour, where N is the lead day. The conservative lead reads the run at least N+1 days before.

No ICON-EU blend uses the lead a live service would get. ENS and AIFS Single read the 00 UTC run, so their day-1 leads run from about 24 to 47 hours. The optimistic blend reads a run fresher than ENS's for most hours, and the conservative blend reads a run older than ENS's for every hour. The two blends therefore bracket the live value: the optimistic blend is an upper bound on ICON-EU's gain and the conservative blend a lower bound. A live 09:00 UTC issue would read roughly the 00 or 03 UTC ICON-EU run, about as old as ENS's. This page fits UKV at day 1 only, and UKV's day-1 value probably reads a run fresher than a 09:00 UTC service would, so its blend is an optimistic upper bound and is never ranked.

Product Days fitted Rows AIFS Single 1, 2, 7, 14 single: 16 months ICON-EU, optimistic and conservative lead 1, 2 single UKV 1 single WN3 1, 2, 7, 14 wn3: 7 months (February to April and June to 10 September 2026)

docs.title: Data and methods
docs.text:
Each blend is compared with an XGBoost model given the ENS mean alone, and with a control of equal column count. The control shuffles the product's columns among hours that share a generator, a year-month, and an hour of day. The rows, folds, settings, seeds, and GPU device are those of the saved AIFS Single blends in per_study/nwp_forecast_comparison/aifs_blends, which this study reuses. The fitting script fits the ICON-EU, UKV, and WN3 arms, and refits the five AIFS Single (arm, setting) pairs that folder lacked. The fitting script raises unless its build stamp and every new arm's (site, time, seed, fold) keys equal the saved ones.

Five contrasts were planned before any fit. C1 is the conservative ICON-EU blend minus ENS at days 1 and 2. C2 is the AIFS Single blend minus ENS at days 1, 2, and 7. C3 is the UKV blend minus ENS at day 1. C4 is each blend minus its control. C5 is the AIFS Single blend minus each ICON-EU blend at days 1 and 2. Every other row is exploratory, including the optimistic ICON-EU blend, WN3, and day 14.

The ranking rule was fixed before any fit. A blend lowers the error at a lead only if the blend minus ENS and the blend minus its control both have an upper bound below zero at both settings. AIFS Single ranks above ICON-EU only if C5 against the optimistic ICON-EU blend has an upper bound below zero at both settings. ICON-EU ranks above AIFS Single only if C5 against the conservative blend has a lower bound above zero at both settings.

docs.title: Solar results
docs.text:
Adding AIFS Single lowers the solar error at day 2 and day 7 (uncorrected) but not at day 1. The differences are -0.044 [-0.162, +0.073] at day 1, -0.325 [-0.479, -0.181] at day 2, and -0.396 [-0.578, -0.201] at day 7. Only the day-2 result survives the Bonferroni correction at both settings. At sensitivity day 2 is -0.265 [-0.384, -0.136].

The conservative ICON-EU blend gains nothing detectable. The differences are -0.024 [-0.075, +0.028] at day 1 and -0.005 [-0.078, +0.062] at day 2 (+0.001 [-0.048, +0.055] and -0.011 [-0.073, +0.049] at sensitivity). The optimistic blend gains 0.171 [0.063, 0.295] and 0.129 [0.046, 0.198], which fail the Bonferroni correction at sensitivity (+0.001 at both days). The UKV blend gains 0.156 [0.031, 0.272] (0.139), which fails the correction.

AIFS Single beats both ICON-EU blends at day 2, and the gap to the optimistic blend is fragile. C5 gives -0.319 [-0.465, -0.175] against the conservative blend and -0.195 [-0.373, -0.029] against the optimistic blend, with sensitivity values -0.255 and -0.136 (upper bound -0.000). At day 1 the two products are not separable.

docs.title: Wind results
docs.text:
Adding ICON-EU at the optimistic lead (exploratory; an upper bound on a live service's gain) lowers the wind error at both days. The differences are -0.576 [-0.689, -0.483] at day 1 and -0.605 [-0.779, -0.444] at day 2 (-0.547 and -0.486 at sensitivity), and both survive the Bonferroni correction. At the conservative lead they are -0.165 [-0.264, -0.063] and -0.251 [-0.440, -0.080] (-0.158 and -0.144), and neither survives it.

Adding AIFS Single lowers the wind error at day 1 and survives the Bonferroni correction. The differences are -0.305 [-0.603, -0.099] (-0.167 [-0.278, -0.073]) at day 1 and -0.211 [-0.383, -0.049] at day 2 (-0.200), which fails the correction. At day 7 the primary difference is -0.274 [-0.586, +0.064] and the sensitivity difference -0.361 [-0.529, -0.183].

AIFS Single and ICON-EU are not separable at wind day 1 or day 2, except that AIFS Single is worse than the optimistic ICON-EU blend at day 2. C5 against the optimistic blend is +0.270 [-0.050, +0.484] at day 1 and +0.394 [+0.250, +0.587] at day 2 (+0.380 and +0.286). Against the conservative blend it is -0.140 [-0.462, +0.097] and +0.040 [-0.176, +0.275]. The optimistic blend is an upper bound for ICON-EU, so the rule does not rank ICON-EU above AIFS Single.

The UKV blend lowers the wind error at day 1. The difference is -0.644 [-1.008, -0.412] (-0.457 [-0.562, -0.368]), and it survives the Bonferroni correction.

At wind day 14, the AIFS Single blend shows no detectable difference. By the ranking rule the primary difference, +0.302 [+0.015, +0.644], lies above zero, and the blend is worse than its own control by +0.379 [+0.065, +0.739]. The sensitivity interval, +0.115 [-0.075, +0.336], spans zero. AIFS Single alone is worse than its shuffled copy by +0.569 [+0.071, +1.080], so the AIFS Single input at day 14 appears to add noise rather than skill.

docs.title: WeatherNext 3 on 7 months
docs.text: The WN3 blend's differences from an ENS mean refitted on the 7 WN3 months are not differences from the 21-month ENS mean. The 21-month ENS mean is the matched-lead page's leaderboard reference. An XGBoost model given the ENS mean alone and fitted on the 7 WN3 months scores worse than the 21-month ENS mean by +0.539 [+0.085, +1.194] at solar day 1, +0.729 [+0.042, +1.654] at solar day 2, +0.377 [+0.144, +0.626] at wind day 1, and +0.841 [+0.561, +1.054] at wind day 2. Against the 21-month ENS mean, the WN3 blend differs by +0.189 [-0.241, +0.744] and +0.100 [-0.391, +0.782] at solar days 1 and 2, by -0.286 [-0.742, +0.196] and -0.012 [-0.322, +0.309] at wind days 1 and 2, and by +1.487 [+0.320, +2.897] at wind day 14. The 7 months overlap WN3's training data, so the page draws no ranking from WN3.

docs.title: Multiplicity and the controls
docs.text:
About 2 of the 40 intervals listed per setting, across both technologies, would reach the 5% level by chance. The Bonferroni correction divides the 5% level across all 40 intervals and widens only the blend-minus-ENS intervals, which is conservative. The wind day-1 conservative ICON-EU upper bound becomes +0.010, and the solar UKV, solar AIFS Single day-7 (+0.031 at sensitivity), and solar optimistic ICON-EU day-2 (+0.007) bounds also stay above zero.

The controls are a weak guard. Controls are significantly worse than the ENS mean in 14 of the 32 (blend, setting) combinations, 9 of them solar, so the blend-minus-control test passes more easily than the blend-minus-ENS test, which decides. At wind day 2 with the primary setting, both ICON-EU controls beat the ENS mean alone (-0.118 [-0.253, -0.015] and -0.158 [-0.296, -0.056]). The primary fit of the ENS mean alone looks weak there, so the primary wind day-2 blend-minus-ENS gains are probably inflated.

docs.title: Discussion: what to use
docs.text: Only solar day 2 has a first choice, AIFS Single, and it is fragile. Everywhere else the rule finds AIFS Single and ICON-EU not separable. A live service would read an ICON-EU run about as old as ENS's, so expect less than the optimistic wind gain. What would change this: ICON-EU fitted at the lead a 09:00 UTC service would read, and more months of data.

docs.title: Limitations and scope
docs.text: The results rest on one region, 16 months, and a lead that no live service reads. The sample is weather episodes, not generator-hours, and the intervals resample months. Every figure uses the effective-capacity table built for the matched-lead study. The study does not cover blends of two products, days 3 and 5, or probabilistic scores. The UKV-CEDA page tests UKV from the CEDA archive at days 1 to 4.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: The inputs and fitted losses are in the private data store, and every output carries only the anonymised site label. The code is studies/nwp_forecast_comparison/fit_product_blends.py and dot_interval_vs_ens.py --blends, with fit_aifs.py and src/studies/. XGBoost 3.4.1 fitted every model on one RTX A6000 GPU.

docs.title: No estimate of a solar plant's capacity lowered day-ahead forecast error detectably at 6 plants, and a daily Kalman filter raised it
docs.text:
Bottom line. We tested replacing the one fixed number that a solar forecast divides each plant's power by (the plant's static capacity, its 99th-percentile output) with a capacity estimate, an estimate updated every day of how much power the plant can produce. At 6 solar plants over 18 months, no capacity estimate lowered the day-ahead error detectably, and the Kalman filter that the study plan's rule selected raised it by 0.255 points of capacity (percentage points of the static capacity) [+0.004, +0.563], against a baseline error of 8.93 points, at the primary XGBoost setting, and not detectably at the second setting. For Flexpectation (this project), the plan's rule therefore says that a capacity estimator is not worth building for the day-ahead forecast, but the record cannot tell whether a better estimator would lower the error, because only 3 of 106 plant-months are the low-output kind of loss that an estimator exists to repair (one plant producing about 70% of its neighbours' output for a month). The next step this study suggests is to test a hold-at-static detector (HYST, designed after the results) on more plants.

How the study works. Stage A plants known losses (steps, ramps, and intermittent losses of 5% to 40% of power) in real power and asks each estimator to find them, which is the recovery test, with no forecast in the loop. False movement is the share of days on which an estimator's capacity moves more than 5% in plant-months in which nothing should have changed. Stage B divides the lag-features study's baseline forecast, B0, by the estimator that the plan's fixed rule selects, and compares forecast errors. The rule requires a candidate to pass a false-movement gate, and when no candidate does, it picks the best recoverer and calls the pick an ungated pick.

Is a capacity estimator worth implementing for the day-ahead forecast? Not worth building by the plan's rule, and not shown either way for a better estimator. The selected Kalman filter changed the error by +0.255 points [+0.004, +0.563] at the primary setting and +0.259 points [−0.022, +0.599] at the second, so both intervals exclude a gain of the plan's 0.179-point threshold. The Kalman filter's setting is the most agile one tried (its process standard deviation 0.08 sat at the edge of the tuning grid, and a stiffer filter never reached Stage B). The Kalman filter would beat B0 overall only above 6.5% of rows, and would reach the threshold only at about 9.7%, if the 5.180-point gain from one plant carried over (Figure 7).

Which techniques look most promising? For forecast error, HYST had the lowest point estimate of the 8 post hoc arms, −0.081 points [−0.216, +0.015] at the primary setting and −0.113 points [−0.260, +0.004] at the second, and HM (+0.004 [−0.223, +0.320]), PR (+0.093 [−0.088, +0.268]), and CX2 (+0.175 [−0.024, +0.330]) were also indistinguishable from B0 (Figure 1). For recovering a planted loss, the Kalman filter had the smallest error (1.86 points against 5.02 for doing nothing), then CX1, CX2, PR, and NR (2.04 to 2.39). DP1, the most explainable of the 11 estimators graded, recovered 4.03 points (Figure 3, Figure 10).

A possible reason that the best recoverer raised forecast error, not isolated: the Kalman filter's raw level has a seasonal shape, 0.72 to 0.88 of each plant's median in December, which the recovery test cancels (Figure 5). It raised error by +0.841 points [+0.032, +1.604] from December to February and lowered it by 5.180 points in the 3 low plant-months (Figure 6). The explanation is untested: DSKF removes the shape and still raised error by +0.290 points, and dropping the day-of-year column from B0 lowered its error by 0.117 points, more than HYST's gain.

Did any estimator stay still when nothing changed? Only HYST (2.6% of days) and the two references (S0 and EM, which cannot follow a loss). The 9 candidates moved on 31.5% to 80.5% of days against the plan's 10% gate, and none passes even a 30% gate, so the ungated pick is not fragile (Figure 4).

Can the study detect a loss at all? Yes. When a 30% step was planted in 17 plant-months, the oracle (told the true loss) lowered the error by 1.467 points [−2.084, −0.854], and the Kalman filter recovered 0.89 of that gain (Figure 8).

What can these data support? These data support the absence of a forecast gain from the daily Kalman filter at these 6 plants, and a hypothesis that holding the static capacity until a drop lasts does no harm. The data do not support a claim about wind, domestic solar, more than 18 months, hundreds of plants, or a plant that loses capacity in a way that its neighbours do not share.

Terms used on this page.

  • Points: percentage points of a plant's static capacity. A difference is an arm's error minus the baseline's, so negative means a lower error. In the recovery test, a gap of 0.02 in the share of power left is 2 points.
  • Arm: one XGBoost model configuration with its own estimator. The baseline arm, B0, divides by the static capacity (lag-features study). Every other arm trains on power divided by an estimator's capacity, multiplies its forecast back, and is scored in megawatts against the static capacity.
  • Hyperparameter setting: a choice of XGBoost depth, learning rate, and number of rounds. The primary setting and the second, shallower setting with more rounds come from the lag-features study, and a result that holds at both belongs to the inputs and not to the setting.
  • Planted loss: a synthetic loss, multiplied into real power in a month chosen at random.
  • Planned, exploratory, post hoc: a planned contrast was written into the study plan before any result existed. Every other number is exploratory. A post hoc number was designed after the first results were seen and is therefore a hypothesis.
  • Interval: the range of changes in error that the data are consistent with, allowing for month-to-month weather. A 95% interval is a t-interval over the 18 scored months unless its subtitle says that it resamples whole months.
  • Oracle: an arm told the true size of a planted loss.
  • Low-output plant-months: the 3 plant-months in which one plant produced between 0.67 and 0.71 of its neighbours' output, below a neighbour ratio of 0.8. The count of 3 rests on that threshold.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5 for the code, the analysis, the figures, the text, and the code reviews, and Claude Opus 5.5 for the plan and its two reviews). Several independent Claude reviewers have checked the method, the evidence, and the prose adversarially.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• The convex estimators did not beat the Kalman filter at recovery. CX1 recovered a planted loss 0.177 points worse than the Kalman filter [0.092, 0.262] (planned contrast E1) and raised forecast error by 3.222 points [+2.380, +4.238] (post hoc), and DP1 recovered a loss 1.992 points worse than CX1 [1.745, 2.240] (planned contrast E2) (Figure 3).
  • HYST detects most planted steps, slowly. HYST detected 37 of 53 planted steps with a mean delay of 8.4 days, and missed 7 of the 44 steps that fell where its seasonal profile exists (Figure 2).
  • The hindsight estimate did not beat the causal one. The hindsight Kalman filter's error was 0.423 points above the causal filter's [−0.048, +1.086], and 0.030 points above without two plant-months (Figure 11).
  • DP1 is the candidate to build on if version 2 of Flexpectation is a differentiable-physics model. DP1 scored highest for explainability and is the only estimator graded yes for differentiability, and it trails on recovery (Figure 10, Groundwork for version 2).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Flexpectation needs to know whether dividing a plant's power by an estimate of its available capacity improves the plant's forecast. Every solar forecast in this repository divides power by one fixed number per plant. A plant that loses a string, an inverter, or part of its output to curtailment is, for forecasting, a different plant, and the baseline cannot see the difference. The lag-features study found one plant producing two thirds to three quarters of its neighbours' output in 3 of 18 months. The baseline XGBoost model, given the day of the year, learned those months and then under-forecast a normal March by 14.6 points (lag-features study). The question came from issue #1143 (Is a time-varying effective capacity worth estimating for solar forecasts?), and the roadmap names this head-to-head as its decision.

The project's energy-forecasting review names the published methods, and most estimators here follow one of them. CX1 and CX2 are linear-programme counterparts of the quadratic optimisation of Viotti et al. (2026), who fit a capacity time series against a capacity factor simulated from weather and a power curve. DP1 follows the differentiable-physics route of Pierrot and Pinson (2024), who fit capacity as a bound with uncertainty, and of Gijón et al. (2025), who fit a physical model to metered power. KF is a sequential Bayesian update, as the honourable-mention team used in Authen et al. (2026). PR divides power by modelled output driven by satellite irradiance, as RdTools does. CSQ takes a quantile of output over clear-sky output (the output under a cloudless sky), the idea behind Meyers et al. (2020). EM is the running maximum that Dantas and Browell (2026) use and that Viotti et al. quote their figures against. The review found no published precedent for NR or HM, and DSKF and HYST were designed after the main results.

Three published methods are not tested. The Solar Data Tools pipeline and StatisticalClearSky would add dependencies to the repository's lock file. Joint estimation with the forecast (Pierrot and Pinson) needs a different forecaster from the lag-features study's. Per-park power curves (Authen et al.) are for wind.
