The two settings give the same order, with one swap. At 10 m for wind, MOGREPS-UK's and the local ECMWF ENS series swap places, and their gap is at most 0.04 points in both settings. The three seeds moved each error by less than 0.04 points, so gaps smaller than that are noise.

The local ECMWF ENS series scores worse than Open-Meteo's ECMWF ENS mean. The gap is 1.2 points for solar, 0.2 for wind at 10 m, and 0.3 for wind at 100 m. The two series come from the same ensemble on different grids and with different stitching and interpolation, so the gap may reflect the pipeline. The next section tests some of the candidate causes.

docs.title: Why the local ECMWF ENS series scores worse than Open-Meteo's
docs.text:
Holding each 3-hour irradiance value flat over its step accounts for about two-thirds of the solar gap, and the rest is consistent with the local series having older runs. The tests are descriptive: each is one 88-day summer, at the first hyperparameter setting, with no interval. The solar gap is 1.21 points of capacity between the local series (8.89%) and Open-Meteo's ECMWF ENS mean (7.68%). Interpolating the local irradiance through the clearness index (the ratio of irradiance to the irradiance at the top of the atmosphere) gave 8.08%, so the gap fell to 0.40 points. Against CAMS's irradiance, the hourly mean absolute error of the local series fell from 86 to 59 W/m², beside 54 W/m² for Open-Meteo's mean. Averaged over the local series' own 3-hour windows, where the hold cannot matter, the local series' error is 53 W/m² against 49 W/m² for Open-Meteo's mean. The hold therefore accounts for most of the hourly gap in irradiance error (27 W/m²), and 4 W/m² remains at 3-hour resolution. The interpolation does not conserve the 3-hour means: the interpolated series departs from the held one by 6 to 11 W/m² on average over the windows of each step, and by 1 to 7 W/m² on signed average. Open-Meteo's own method of spreading 3-hour steps onto hours is not documented in the sources this study read, so the interpolation is one plausible method and not a copy of Open-Meteo's.

Design Open-Meteo ECMWF ENS mean Local, held over each step Local, clearness index interpolated Local, from a run about a day older Solar 7.68 8.89 8.08 9.74 Wind 10 m 5.79 6.00 not built 6.89 Wind 100 m and 10 m 5.71 6.00 not built 6.82

A run about a day older raised the local error by 0.8 to 0.9 points in every design, which bounds what a difference in run age can explain. The local series comes from one 00:00 UTC run a day, so its leads run from 3 to 24 hours (mean 14 hours). The day-old series takes the newest run at least 27 hours ahead, so its leads run from 27 to 48 hours (mean 38 hours), and the script checks that every step inside the scored window has a run exactly 24 hours older than the stored series' run. The rise per hour of run age is therefore about 0.04 points, measured on the held series and assumed to carry over to the interpolated series. The figure also assumes that the error grows in a straight line with run age, which the study did not test. Open-Meteo's ECMWF ENS product starts a run every 6 hours (the Ensemble API page), and the Historical Forecast API page says each run's first few hours are stitched into one series. If the ensemble-mean archive follows the same rule, Open-Meteo's leads are about 0 to 6 hours, and a lead 8 to 11 hours shorter than the local series' would account for 0.3 to 0.4 points, which is the solar gap left after the interpolation. The page does not verify either assumption, because the ensemble-mean series carries no run time.

The gap between the two series changes with the hour of the day in a way that fits a lead effect for wind and an irradiance effect for solar. For wind at 10 m, the local series scored better than Open-Meteo's mean in the two steps with the shortest local leads (0.28 and 0.08 points better at steps ending 03:00 and 06:00 UTC, with mean leads of 4 and 7 hours) and worse in the six other steps, by 0.17 to 0.57 points. Hub-height wind shows the same pattern. The hourly labels of the 03:00 step lie between two runs, because linear interpolation joins the last step of the previous day's run to the first of the new run. For solar, the gap is largest at midday, where the irradiance is largest, and not at the longest lead.

Step ending (UTC) Mean local lead (hours) Solar: local minus Open-Meteo, held Solar: local minus Open-Meteo, interpolated Wind 10 m: local minus Open-Meteo 03:00 3.7 no sunlit hours no sunlit hours -0.28 06:00 6.7 -0.04 0.01 -0.08 09:00 9.7 1.19 0.23 0.30 12:00 12.7 1.94 0.64 0.17 15:00 15.7 1.70 0.71 0.39 18:00 18.7 0.84 0.32 0.57 21:00 21.7 -0.06 -0.09 0.18 00:00 24.2 no sunlit hours no sunlit hours 0.39

The study did not test the grid or the member count, so a share of the remaining gap has no tested cause. The local table averages the 0.25 degree grid points that overlap each H3 resolution-5 hexagon (weighted by overlap area), and derives wind speed from the averaged east and north components. Open-Meteo's source code and documentation, as read for this study, do not say how its 0.25 degree product picks a grid point for a location. The local mean is over 51 members, and the study did not count the members behind Open-Meteo's ECMWF ENS mean.

docs.title: Whether ICON-D2-EPS's lead comes from updating more often
docs.text:
ICON-D2's advantage over ECMWF is a short-lead advantage, but the data cannot show how much of ICON-D2-EPS's 0.3-point solar lead over ECMWF ENS comes from its more frequent runs. Open-Meteo starts an ICON-D2-EPS run every 3 hours and an ECMWF ENS run every 6 hours, so under the first-few-hours rule above, the ICON-D2-EPS mean's leads would average about 1.5 hours and the ECMWF ENS mean's about 3 hours. Both estimates use solar slopes only. At the slope of the ECMWF-based local series (about 0.04 points an hour), 1.5 hours is 0.05 points. The slope of ICON-D2's deterministic run is steeper (2.04 points over 24 hours, or 0.085 points an hour, from the table below), and at that slope 1.5 hours is 0.13 points. Both estimates are smaller than the 0.32-point difference, on assumptions the page could not check. The study did not estimate a wind slope for the ensemble means.

Deterministic model Solar, freshest run Solar, run 24 hours older Wind 10 m, freshest run Wind 10 m, run 24 hours older ICON-D2 7.85 9.89 5.97 7.39 ECMWF IFS 0.25 degree 7.93 8.89 6.01 6.77 ICON-EU 8.29 9.35 6.56 7.81 UKV 8.77 10.54 5.94 7.68

With the freshest run, ICON-D2 led ECMWF IFS by 0.08 points for solar and 0.04 points for wind at 10 m, and with the run 24 hours older, ECMWF IFS led ICON-D2 by 1.0 and 0.6 points. At hub height the same swap holds: ICON-D2 led by 0.56 points with the freshest run and trailed by 0.12 points with the older run. For solar, ICON-D2 has the largest rise: its error rose 2.0 points from the freshest to the older run, against 1.0 for ECMWF IFS, 1.1 for ICON-EU, and 1.8 for UKV. For wind at 10 m, ICON-D2 is not the most sensitive (rises of 1.42 points for ICON-D2, 0.76 for ECMWF IFS, 1.25 for ICON-EU, and 1.74 for UKV). A run-age difference between the products would therefore favour ICON-D2-EPS for solar, and the wind data do not show that it would for wind. The deterministic gap at the freshest run (0.08 points) is smaller than the ensemble-mean gap (0.32 points), which leaves a difference that the ensemble averaging of ICON-D2-EPS's 20 members could produce, and this study did not test that explanation. The four deterministic series are single runs, so their errors differ from those of the ensemble means for reasons besides run age.

The ECMWF ENS, ICON-D2-EPS, and MOGREPS-UK means sit much closer to their deterministic models' freshest runs than to the runs 24 hours older, and the ICON-EU-EPS mean sits much closer for irradiance but only slightly closer for 10 m wind. Together the distances point to short leads, and they are not a clean reading of run age. For ICON-EU-EPS, the 10 m wind speed is 2.27 km/h from the freshest run and 2.89 km/h from the older run. The mean absolute distance of ECMWF ENS's mean from the IFS freshest run was 0.87 km/h for 10 m wind speed, against 1.74 km/h from the older run. For the local series the distances were 1.91 and 1.94 km/h. For irradiance the local series is 67 W/m² from the IFS freshest run, because of the hold. The comparison mixes a mean of members with a single member and, for the local series, leads of 3 to 24 hours, which straddle the older run's 24-hour offset. Open-Meteo's leads therefore look shorter than the local series', and the distances do not put a number on them.

docs.title: What Open-Meteo's source code does for the MOGREPS-UK mean
docs.text:
In the Open-Meteo source code read for this study, the MOGREPS-UK ensemble mean is an unweighted mean over the 3 members of one hourly run, and no code combines members of different runs. The Met Office's 18-member MOGREPS-UK ensemble is six hourly runs of 3 members lagged together (Porson et al. (2020)). The evidence below is from the open-meteo/open-meteo repository at commit cc3f4e5e956b39a56ab182faeccfd3d936ae6b4c (committed on 2026-09-23), read from a shallow clone.

  • Sources/App/UKMO/UkmoDomain.swift gives uk_ensemble_2km 3 members (countEnsembleMember), an hourly update interval, and a run delay of about 4 hours.
  • Sources/App/UKMO/UkmoDownloader.swift downloads one run at a time and, for each forecast step of that run, writes each member of the run's file into a step writer that carries an ensemble-mean calculator.
  • Sources/App/Helper/OmSpatialTimestepWriter.swift creates one EnsembleMeanCalculator per run and forecast step, so a calculator never receives another run's members.
  • Sources/App/Helper/OmWriter/EnsembleMeanCalculator.swift keeps a running mean and a sample standard deviation (divisor n - 1) with equal weight for every member it receives.
  • Sources/App/Helper/OmFileSplitter.swift (updateFromTimeOrientedStreaming3D) merges each new run into the stored series by overwriting every stored value with the new run's value wherever the new value is not NaN, so each valid time keeps the newest run written for it.
  • Sources/App/Controllers/ForecastapiController.swift serves ukmo_uk_ensemble_mean_2km from the single domain uk_ensemble_mean_2km, with no mixing across domains.
  • A case-insensitive, word-bounded search of every .swift file in Sources for "lag", "lagged", "time-lag", and "timelag" found no match, so words such as "flag" did not count.

These points are not verified. The page did not call the API, so it did not check that served values equal a 3-member mean. The code was read as of 2026-09-23 and the archive covers 2026-06-25 onwards, so earlier releases of the code may have behaved differently. The page did not read the NetCDF files Open-Meteo downloads from the Met Office, so it did not check that each file holds only 3 members. The finding does not show what Open-Meteo intends. It shows that the source code has no weighting or lagging.

A 3-member mean is a smaller ensemble than the MOGREPS-UK product name suggests, and it can be noisier than a mean over 18 lagged members. The MOGREPS-UK mean scored 8.69% for solar, behind every other ensemble mean here except the local ECMWF ENS series, and 0.08 points better than UKV's freshest deterministic run (8.77%). The result is consistent with a mean of 3 members adding little to a single run, but it does not show that, because the products differ in more than member count. The roadmap records why members of lagged runs need weights and run ages.

The Met Office's calibrated IMPROVER blend of MOGREPS-UK holds no raw members, so the blend cannot stand in for MOGREPS-UK members (details).

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The window is short and holds one summer. The 88 days give 12 held-out weeks. The window does not sample autumn or winter wind, and it samples only summer cloud regimes.

The generators share weather. Among the 6 solar generators, MOGREPS-UK's and ICON-D2-EPS's means serve 5 distinct series, ICON-EU-EPS's 4, and ECMWF ENS's 2, because neighbouring generators fall in one grid cell. Among the 3 wind generators, ECMWF ENS's mean serves 2 distinct series and the other products 3. The effective sample is smaller than the number of generator-hours.

The scoring is interpolation. Training rows include the days on both sides of each scored week. A model scored on a later season would show larger errors.

The ensemble means are stitched series with unmatched leads. They carry no run time, so their leads are short, mixed, and different between products, and the page has not measured them. ICON-D2-EPS probably has the shortest leads, which probably flatters it. The page says nothing about day-ahead skill or about how the error grows with lead.

Products differ in coverage. ICON-D2 does not cover South West England or South Wales, and every generator here lies inside its domain. MOGREPS-UK's and ICON-EU-EPS's means have no 100 m wind, and the origin of ICON-D2-EPS's 100 m wind is unchecked.

The capacity denominator is the latest effective capacity per generator in data/effective_capacity when the study ran on 26 September 2026.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The study does not cover ensemble spread or probabilistic scores, leads beyond the stitched series, other seasons, generators outside Lincolnshire, wind direction, other Open-Meteo ensembles, or the beam and diffuse split of radiation. The study does not test whether any difference is statistically significant at the 5% level.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: The four Open-Meteo ensemble means, CAMS, and ERA5 are public downloads, and the metered power is private. The Open-Meteo means are in data/studies/downloads/NWP/OPEN-METEO-ENSEMBLE-MEANS/. The local ECMWF ENS series is built from data/studies/downloads/NWP/ENS_SITE_EXTRACT/, which reads this project's own ENS Delta table. NGED's power readings are private. Every output carries only the anonymised labels A to F and W1 to W3. The code is in studies/open_meteo_ensemble_means/ and src/studies/, at the commit that adds this page.

docs.title: Reproducing the figures
docs.text:
uv run python studies/open_meteo_ensemble_means/ensemble_means_mae.py
uv run python studies/open_meteo_ensemble_means/ensemble_means_chart.py
npx svgo@4 --multipass --precision=1 --final-newline docs/studies/assets/ensemble_means_mae.svg
uv run python studies/open_meteo_ensemble_means/local_ens_gap.py

The first command writes the tables and report.md under data/studies/per_study/open_meteo_ensemble_means/ and takes about 15 minutes on the CPU. The script refuses to overwrite, so move the existing files to a superseded/ subfolder first. --report-only rebuilds the tables from the saved losses. The last command writes the tables of the two new sections to data/studies/per_study/open_meteo_ens_gap/, reads the saved frames of the first command, and takes about 8 minutes on the CPU.

docs.title: Extra IFS variables and a second forecast for day-ahead to three-day-ahead solar power
docs.text:
At six solar farms in Lincolnshire, adding a second weather forecast to a single 9 km forecast cut the error of day-ahead to three-day-ahead power forecasts by about 1 percentage point of capacity on top of the minimal set (P4) and by about 0.8 points on top of all 20 IFS variables (P5), but the gain is likely to be much smaller for the production service. The single forecast comes from IFS, the Integrated Forecasting System of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF). The 9 km is the grid spacing of that weather model. The second forecast is AIFS Single, the deterministic version of ECMWF's machine-learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS). The production service is this project's live power forecast, which reads IFS ensemble data from Dynamical.org. The IFS ensemble also runs at 9 km, and Dynamical.org serves it on a 0.25-degree grid. The production service reads a smoother input, the IFS ensemble mean, which averages 51 runs of IFS (a control and 50 members with perturbed starting conditions and model physics). The ensemble mean is smoother because averaging the members smooths out the differences between them. Adding the ensemble mean to the single forecast gives about the same 1-point gain (0.96 against 1.04; the difference was not tested; post hoc). Adding AIFS Single to the ensemble mean lowers the error by only 0.13 points, which is too uncertain to call a gain (post hoc). Extra IFS variables lowered the error by about 0.45 points in total (exploratory). No planned step gave a resolved gain: adding total cloud cover, adding the cloud layers, and adding every other variable each left the gain unresolved. On top of FP, the production reference, total cloud cover lowers the error by 0.13 points (unresolved) and total cloud cover plus the three cloud layers by 0.28 points (a gain), both post hoc.

How to read the numbers. Every error is a mean absolute error as a percentage of a farm's capacity, and a difference of 0.1 is 0.1 percentage points of capacity, called "points". A row is one daylight hour at one farm. A contrast is the error of one variable set less the error of another, so a negative contrast is a gain, everywhere on this page. Where the text says an input lowers the error by 0.12 points, the bracket shows the difference as −0.12. A bracket holds a 95% interval from resampling whole months, unless the text says 99%. Five planned contrasts are tested together, so their intervals are set at 99%. A gain is resolved if the interval's upper bound is below −0.1 points, the smallest improvement worth acting on. There is no gain if the interval's lower bound is above −0.1 points. Otherwise the result is unresolved. The plan was fixed before any result existed, and reviewers then read the first results (the first scientific review). A contrast is planned if the plan named it, post hoc if it was added after that review had seen results, and exploratory otherwise. "Main setting" and "second setting" refer to the two XGBoost tuning settings defined under Data and methods. The forecasts are the 00 UTC (coordinated universal time) run of every day. Lead day L means the run was issued L days before the day the run describes. Hours are labelled by their end, so 19 UTC is 18:00 to 19:00.

Variable sets and contrasts. The variable sets are F0, the minimal set (IFS radiation and air temperature); F1, which adds total cloud cover; F2, which adds the three cloud layers; and F6, all 20 IFS variables. Each of F1 to F6 includes every group before it in the table under Introduction. FP is F0 plus four variables (dew point, surface pressure, precipitation, wind speed) that the production service's IFS feed carries; the feed also carries long-wave radiation, which no variable set here includes. FB adds AIFS Single's radiation and temperature to F0, and F6B adds the same two variables to F6. P1 is F1 minus F0, P2 is F2 minus F1, P3 is F6 minus F2, P4 is FB minus F0, and P5 is F6B minus F6.

  • Do extra IFS variables help predict solar farm output at lead days 1 to 3? Not one step at a time, by a resolved amount. Total cloud cover (P1) lowers the error by 0.12 points, the cloud layers (P2) by 0.19 points, and every other variable together (P3) by 0.14 points (pooled over lead days 1 to 3, 99% intervals [−0.19, −0.04], [−0.32, −0.06], and [−0.31, +0.03]). All three intervals straddle −0.1 points, so all three are unresolved. Twenty-five months of data cannot resolve effects this small. A preview of the interval widths, computed before any fit from the errors in the ERA5 study, predicted as much. ERA5 is a reanalysis: a weather model re-run after the event and corrected with observations. All 18 extra variables together (F6 minus F0) lower the error by 0.45 points (95% interval [−0.59, −0.32], exploratory). At the six lead days taken one at a time, the gain is 0.29 to 0.54 points.
  • Does a second forecast help? Yes, on top of the single 9 km forecast. Adding AIFS Single's radiation and temperature to the minimal set lowers the error by 1.04 points (P4, 99% interval [−1.42, −0.67]), and adding the same two variables to all 20 IFS variables lowers the error by 0.79 points (P5, [−1.25, −0.44]). P4 and P5 are gains at both XGBoost tuning settings and against a control with the same number of columns. P4 and P5 use the 14 months from March 2025, when AIFS Single became operational, to April 2026. Both gains are measured on 14-month fits whose F0 is 0.4 to 0.7 points worse than F0 from the 25-month fits on the same rows, so part of the gain may come from the short training set.
  • Does a second forecast help the production service? Probably by less, at most about 0.3 points on this evidence (the 99% interval's lower end is −0.29), and the study cannot resolve how much. The production service reads the IFS ensemble mean. On the same rows, adding the ensemble mean to the minimal set lowers the error by 0.96 points, about as much as AIFS Single does (0.96 against 1.04; the difference was not tested; post hoc). Adding AIFS Single to the ensemble mean lowers the error by 0.13 points (post hoc, 99% interval [−0.29, +0.02]). The base of that contrast is the minimal set with the 6-hourly ensemble mean in place of IFS's own radiation and temperature. By lead day, the change is +0.07 at lead day 1, a point estimate above zero that the study cannot tell from no change, −0.21 at lead day 2, and −0.25 at lead day 3. The per-lead-day values are post hoc and carry no intervals on this page. The single 9 km forecast has a higher raw radiation error against CAMS irradiance (the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service's satellite-derived estimate of past sunshine) than AIFS Single or the ensemble mean.
  • Is it worth ingesting the 12 variables that only ECMWF's MARS archive serves, or another forecast? The pre-set rule returns "second forecast", and this page does not act on that outcome. MARS, the Meteorological Archival and Retrieval System, is ECMWF's full archive. The ERA5 study found that 12 ERA5 variables, whose operational IFS counterparts only MARS serves, give a gain of 0.13 points (unresolved by this page's rule; the ERA5 study's interval is 99.5%, not this page's 99%). The pre-set rule was fixed before any result existed. It asks for the second forecast if P5 is a gain. It asks for the MARS-only variables if P5 is not a gain and the ERA5 gain for them is resolved. Otherwise the routes are not separated. P5 is a gain, so the rule returns "second forecast". Neither number is the gain the production service would see, because P5 is measured on the single 9 km forecast and the ERA5 gain on a reanalysis. The closest comparison that this study and the ERA5 study offer is AIFS Single on top of the ensemble mean (0.13 points, unresolved, post hoc) against the 12 MARS-only variables on top of the 22 other ERA5 variables (0.13 points at the main setting, 99.5% interval [−0.18, −0.08]). The two point estimates are equal, but the contrasts differ in rows, months, base set, and interval level, and the AIFS Single interval runs from −0.29 to +0.02. The ERA5 gain may be smaller at forecast lead. The ratio behind that statement, about twice as much from ERA5's cloud variables as from IFS's, was measured for the cloud variables at lead day 1 only.
  • Which variables should the production service ask Dynamical.org to add? The production service should request total cloud cover first, which here means the one group in the free open-data feed that was tested on top of FP, on post hoc evidence. Added to FP, total cloud cover lowers the error by 0.13 points at the main setting and 0.15 at the second (pooled over lead days 1 to 3, 99% intervals [−0.18, −0.07] and [−0.22, −0.09], unresolved). Adding the three cloud layers as well lowers the error by 0.28 and 0.27 points (99% intervals [−0.39, −0.18] and [−0.38, −0.16], a gain at both settings). The layers' own step, from FP plus total cloud cover, is 0.15 and 0.11 points (unresolved). The free open-data feed that Dynamical.org repackages does not carry the layers. These contrasts are post hoc, so they carry the caveats listed under Limitations (Figure 9b). All 14 variables beyond FP together lower FP's error by 0.36 points (F6 minus FP, 95% interval [−0.44, −0.27], exploratory, main setting only), and 8 of those 14 are not in the free feed.
  • Does the production service need a second IFS feed, for the cloud layers or the direct beam, which ECMWF's free open-data subset does not carry? Not on this evidence, although the rule as written before any result says yes. The production service gets IFS from Dynamical.org, which repackages ECMWF's free open-data feed. Removing the cloud layers from all 20 variables raises the error by 0.074 points at the main setting, more than the shuffled control's 0.035. The pre-set rule, applied at the one setting the rule named, therefore recommends a second feed. After the first scientific review, the same run at the second setting gave a raise of 0.057, below its control's 0.101. Both raises are below 0.1 points. Requiring both settings to agree was added after the results were seen, so the both-settings reading is post hoc. The production feed also carries long-wave radiation, a cloud signal that this study did not test.
  • What can the study support? Statements about the 9 km IFS forecast and the AIFS Single forecast at six farms in one county, at lead days 1 to 3, over 25 months (14 for the second forecast). Three limits matter most. Every planned gain is measured on top of a single deterministic 9 km forecast, the farms share weather, and 25 months give wide intervals.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5, and Claude Opus 5.5). Several independent Claude reviewers have checked the method, the evidence, and the prose adversarially.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• The forecast's error rises from about 10% of capacity at lead day 1 to about 15% at lead day 9 for the minimal set, and the full set lowers the error by 0.29 to 0.54 points. On the farm-hours that all six lead days hold, F0's error is 10.0% at lead day 1 and 15.4% at lead day 9. On the same farm-hours, F6 minus F0 is −0.41 points at lead day 1 and −0.31 at lead day 9 (Figure 3). The contrast values in the questions and answers above use each lead day's own rows.
  • At lead day 1, the cloud variables gained about half as much in the IFS forecast as in ERA5 on the same rows (exploratory): 0.33 points against 0.67. All 20 IFS variables gained 0.39 points and ERA5's 34 variables 1.20 points. The two full sets hold different variables (Figure 7).
  • P4, the gain from adding a second forecast to the minimal set, is larger at lead days 2 and 3 than at lead day 1, and the study does not establish why (post hoc). P4 is −0.79, −1.11, and −1.22 points at lead days 1 to 3. The differences between lead days have no interval. The radiation error of the single 9 km IFS forecast against CAMS irradiance rises by 26% from lead day 1 to 3, against 18% for AIFS Single and 20% for the ensemble mean, so "rises fastest" is a ranking of point estimates. Adding the ensemble mean to F0 gives a gain that does not grow with lead day (−0.96, −0.90, and −1.03 points) (Figure 10).
  • One winter fold enlarges P5's lead-day-3 gain. The only winter months of the 14 blend months are held out together, so the XGBoost model that scores those winter months trains on no winter row. Without that fold, P5 at lead day 3 is −0.73 points, not −1.02. P4 at lead day 3 is −1.04 without the winter fold and −1.22 with it.
  • As in the ERA5 study, the full set is worse than the minimal set at low sun. At 06, 07, 19, and 20 UTC, F6 is worse than F0 by 0.08 to 0.29 points (Figure 8).
  • Shuffled copies of the variables tend to make the error worse. One shuffled cloud column made F0's error 0.02 points worse, and 14 shuffled columns made F2's error 0.04 points worse. Both intervals include zero. Two shuffled copies of AIFS Single's variables made the error of F0 worse by 0.21 points [+0.11, +0.32], so the 14-month fits are noisy (Figure 5).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The question is which variables of IFS, beyond its solar radiation and temperature, help a day-ahead to three-day-ahead solar power forecast, and whether a second weather forecast would do more. The ERA5 study asked which variables of ERA5 help estimate solar output. ERA5 is a reanalysis, a weather model re-run after the event and corrected with observations. Some of ERA5's fields are corrected with observations taken after the hour the fields describe, so those fields can hold information that no forecast has. The ERA5 study found signs that part of the ERA5 study's gain came from ERA5's cloud fields having seen observations from after the hour. This study repeats the question on real past forecasts, at the lead times a forecast service would use. Three decisions depend on the answer: which variables to ask Dynamical.org to add, whether the production service needs a second IFS feed, and whether to ingest the 12 MARS-only variables (variables that only ECMWF's MARS archive serves) or another forecast.

Group Adds IFS variables (Open-Meteo names) In ECMWF's free open-data feed F0 the minimal set shortwave_radiation, temperature_2m yes F1 total cloud cloud_cover yes F2 cloud layers cloud_cover_low, cloud_cover_mid, cloud_cover_high no F3 direct radiation direct_radiation no F4 humidity, column water, boundary layer dew_point_2m, total_column_integrated_water_vapour, boundary_layer_height the first two F5 convection and visibility cape, convective_inhibition, visibility no F6 surface and weather state surface_temperature, snow_depth, snowfall, precipitation, surface_pressure, wind_speed_10m, wind_gusts_10m yes FP the production reference F0 plus dew_point_2m, surface_pressure, precipitation, wind_speed_10m yes

Each variable set F1 to F6 includes every group above its own row in the table. The free feed's availability was read from ECMWF's open-data index files for the 2026-10-09 00 UTC run. The feed carries mucape, a different convective available potential energy (CAPE) diagnostic from the cape field Open-Meteo serves.

Three contrasts add variables to FP: F6 minus FP (exploratory), (FP + total cloud) minus FP, and (FP + total cloud + layers) minus FP (both post hoc). FP is the production feed's current variables other than long-wave radiation. FP contains none of F1's or F2's cloud columns, so F1 minus FP and F2 minus FP swap variables rather than add them. A column is an input variable given to an XGBoost model, and the columns include sun position and calendar variables beside the weather variables. FP has 13 columns. FP + total cloud adds F1's column to FP, and FP + total cloud + layers adds F1's and F2's four columns. Both were fitted at both XGBoost tuning settings.

docs.title: Data and methods
docs.text:
The rows are 43,921 daylight farm-hours at 6 farms, from March 2024 to April 2026, and the forecasts are the 00 UTC IFS run of each day. The rows, the targets, and the solar geometry come from the ERA5 study, so the cleaning rules are the same: hours that hold a zero half-hour are dropped, hours the network operator constrained are scored but not trained on, and output is a fraction of each farm's capacity (a high percentile of its metered output). Lead days 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, and 9 are scored.

Each hour reads the forecast issued L days earlier, averaged to the hour as the ERA5 study averaged ERA5. Lead day L of an hour is read from the run issued L days before the hour's day, at forecast hour 24L plus the hour of day. Instantaneous variables are the mean of the values at the two ends of the hour, as the ERA5 study averaged ERA5's snapshots. Radiation is the preceding-hour mean, precipitation and snowfall are the preceding-hour sums, and gusts are the preceding-hour maximum, as Open-Meteo serves them. Open-Meteo is the archive that served the IFS forecasts. Open-Meteo interpolates values beyond forecast hour 90, which includes a few evening hours of lead day 3. Lead day 5 is read from 3-hourly output and lead days 7 and 9 from 6-hourly output, so every hour at those lead days is interpolated. That interpolation contributes to the error's rise with lead day.

IFS changed model cycle twice in the archive, so the study cuts folds inside two eras. Cycle 49r1 went live on 2024-11-12 and cycle 50r1 on 2026-05-12. The study drops 2024-11, and drops 2026-05 and everything after. The first era starts on 2024-03-15, so the first era's first month is a 17-day part-month. The two eras hold 25 months. Each farm's rows in each era are cut into five folds, blocks of whole months, with the same fold for the same hour at every lead day. Every fold is scored by XGBoost models trained on the other folds of the same farm, so every score comes from months the XGBoost model never saw.

One XGBoost model is fitted per farm, lead day, and variable set, at two tuning settings. XGBoost is a gradient-boosted tree model. Each XGBoost model is fitted three times with different random seeds. The main setting uses trees of depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 500 boosting rounds, minimum child weight 20, and L2 penalty 1. The second setting uses trees of depth 4, learning rate 0.03, 1,200 boosting rounds, minimum child weight 50, and L2 penalty 5. The plan required both settings to agree for the planned verdicts P1 to P5. Extending the both-settings requirement to the drop-one rule was done after the first scientific review, so that extension is post hoc. Intervals come from resampling whole months, paired across variable sets, with one of the three seeds drawn in each resample. The planned contrasts use 10,000 resamples and the other contrasts 2,000. The month bootstrap ignores the dependence between months scored by the same fitted models, and with 14 or 25 months a 99% percentile interval is likely to be too narrow. The 17-day part-month counts as one month in the resampling. The report prints 95% intervals for the low-sun hours, the ERA5-against-IFS ratio has no interval, and the study does not count its exploratory contrasts.

The planned contrasts (P1 to P5) are on farm output only, pooled over lead days 1 to 3 with equal weight. The planned contrasts use the 99% level. The verdict labels are the ones defined under How to read the numbers.

Each planned contrast is checked against a control with the same number of columns, in which the new variables are shuffled. The shuffling is within each farm, month, and hour of day. A planned contrast must also be a gain against its control. A positive control (a control expected to help) adds CAMS irradiance. The drop-one rule asks whether removing a group from the full set raises the error by more than a control with the same number of shuffled columns does.

The second forecast is AIFS Single, and the rows from the 14 months on which it exists are called the blend rows. AIFS Single runs on a grid of about 31 km at 6-hour steps. It became operational on 2025-02-25, so the blend rows start in March 2025. The partner is AIFS Single, the second forecast whose two columns (radiation and temperature) are added to a variable set. A blend arm is a variable set that includes the partner, such as FB and F6B. AIFS Single's radiation is a 6-hourly mean that is rebuilt hourly through a clear-sky index. A clear-sky index is measured sunlight divided by the sunlight a cloudless sky would give. The temperature of AIFS Single is interpolated to the hour. The partner's two columns come from the AIFS Single store only, with no CAMS or power value in them. F0 and F6 are refit on the blend rows, so each blend contrast compares variable sets on identical rows.

The IFS ensemble mean used here is 6-hourly, coarser than the 3-hourly mean the production service reads. The ensemble-mean contrasts are post hoc. It is the 6-hourly ensemble mean from the ensemble-mean blend study.

docs.title: IFS forecasts against CAMS irradiance on three days
docs.text: IFS and CAMS agree on the shape of a day and disagree in detail, more at longer leads. Figure 2 draws IFS's radiation at lead days 1 and 7, and its cloud covers at lead day 1, against CAMS irradiance on three days at one farm: the clearest, most variable, and dullest by CAMS's clear-sky index.

docs.title: The error rises with lead day, and the extra variables gain little
docs.text: The minimal set's error rises from 10.0% of capacity at lead day 1 to 15.4% at lead day 9, and the full set lowers the error by 0.29 to 0.54 points. The full set (F6) beats the minimal set (F0) by 0.39 points at lead day 1, 0.50 at lead day 2, 0.48 at lead day 3, 0.45 at lead day 5, 0.54 at lead day 7, and 0.29 at lead day 9. The six gains are exploratory numbers on each lead day's own rows. Figure 3 plots the farm-hours that all six lead days hold, where the gains are 0.41, 0.49, 0.47, 0.44, 0.55, and 0.31 points.

docs.title: The XGBoost models track measured output on unseen months
docs.text: Predictions follow the measured output on months the XGBoost models never saw. Figure 4 draws three days at every farm, chosen separately for each farm by CAMS's clear-sky index, with each farm's error for four variable sets: F0, F2, FP, and F6. The farms are labelled A to F.

docs.title: Controls
docs.text: The positive control lowers the error by 4.7 points at lead day 1, so the method detects a large effect, but the shuffled controls show only small penalties. Adding CAMS irradiance to F2 gives an error of 5.0% at lead day 1, against 9.7% for F2. One shuffled total-cloud column makes F0 worse by 0.02 points pooled over lead days 1 to 3, and 14 shuffled columns make F2 worse by 0.04 points. Both intervals include zero at the main setting. The controls for AIFS Single, on the 14 blend months, are clearer: two shuffled copies of AIFS Single's variables make F0 worse by 0.21 points and F6 worse by 0.09 points. The controls do not change any verdict.

docs.title: Every variable set at every lead day
docs.text:
The leaderboard gives each variable set's error at each lead day, with intervals. The leaderboard's intervals overlap more than the paired differences of Figure 1 do, because every variable set's error rises and falls with the weather.

Pooled over lead days 1 to 3, the two cloud steps lower the error most, by 0.12 points (F1) and 0.19 points (F2), and no later step lowers the error by more than 0.10 points. Figure 6b shows variable sets F0 to F6 as a chain of steps. Each orange line is the 95% interval of one step's paired difference, drawn from the dot of the row below, so the interval compares each variable set with the one before on the same months. The orange line is not the uncertainty of the step's dot, and the intervals of different steps must not be added, because the same months are resampled for every step. The F6 step raises the error by 0.04 points. The F1 and F2 steps are the planned contrasts P1 and P2, and their 99% intervals are in Figure 1. Every other step is exploratory. Every step depends on the order in which the groups were added.

docs.title: The gain at forecast lead is smaller than the ERA5 study showed
docs.text: At lead day 1 on the same rows, ERA5's full set lowers the error by 1.20 points and IFS's full set by 0.39 points. The ERA5 study's screen was its comparison of ERA5 variable sets at the same hour, which made no claim about forecasts. On the like-for-like cloud sets, ERA5's total and layered cloud cover give 0.67 points against IFS's 0.33 points, about twice as much. The two full sets hold different variables, 34 ERA5 variables against 20 IFS variables. The gap is consistent with ERA5's cloud fields having seen later observations than its solar radiation, with the difference between a same-hour estimate and a forecast, and with ERA5's older model cycle and coarser grid. The page leaves all three explanations open. The ratio of the two gains has no interval.

docs.title: The gain by season, cloud regime, and hour
docs.text: The full set is worse than the minimal set at low sun. F6 is worse than F0 by 0.08 points at 06 UTC, 0.16 at 07, 0.29 at 19, and 0.13 at 20 UTC. The ERA5 study found the same pattern. The pattern is consistent with the penalty coming from the farms' low-sun output. The pattern is equally consistent with a wide variable set overfitting where the signal is weakest. The report prints 95% intervals for these hours, and this page does not. Figure 8 shows the gain by ERA5 cloud regime, season, and hour of day, with the hour-of-day panel in percent of F0's error.

docs.title: Removing one variable group from the full set
docs.text: Removing one group from all 20 variables raises the error by less than 0.1 points when pooled over lead days 1 to 3. The rule asks that removing a group raises the error by more than a control with the same number of shuffled columns does. Removing the cloud layers raises the error by 0.074 points at the main setting and 0.057 at the second, against controls of 0.035 and 0.101. The rule as written before any result applied the test at the main setting only, where the cloud layers pass. The both-settings version is post hoc, as is the comparison with 0.1 points. The both-settings version also changes the answer for humidity, column water, and boundary-layer height. The humidity, column-water, and boundary-layer group raises the error by 0.036 points at the main setting, which passes its control by 0.002 points, and by 0.016 points at the second setting, which fails its control. The group's raise is 0.118 points at lead day 3 and about zero at lead days 1 and 2 (post hoc). The raises and their margins over the controls have no intervals. The cloud-layer control moves from 0.035 to 0.101 between the settings, so neither a pass nor a fail is resolved.

docs.title: Which cloud variables to add to the production reference
docs.text: Request total cloud cover from Dynamical.org first, as the one free-feed group tested on FP and on unresolved evidence of 0.13 to 0.15 points. Added to FP, total cloud cover lowers the error by 0.13 points at the main setting and 0.15 at the second (99% intervals [−0.18, −0.07] and [−0.22, −0.09], unresolved). Adding the three cloud layers as well lowers the error by 0.28 and 0.27 points (99% upper bounds −0.18 and −0.16, a gain at both settings). The layers' own step is 0.15 and 0.11 points (unresolved), and the free open-data feed does not carry the layers. The drop-one result under "Removing one variable group from the full set" still governs the second-feed decision, because that rule asks whether the full set relies on the layers and the layers' own step is unresolved here. These contrasts are post hoc and exploratory, and have no negative control (a fit padded with shuffled copies of the same inputs) to show how much of a gain extra columns produce alone. Figure 9b draws 95% step intervals at the main setting, and the 99% intervals that set the verdicts are in the text.

docs.title: A second forecast and the ensemble mean
docs.text:
Adding AIFS Single to the single 9 km forecast lowers the error by about 1 point, and adding the IFS ensemble mean does the same. Panel 1 of Figure 10 shows the three gains that the decision between the MARS-only variables and a second forecast compares: P4, P5, and the ERA5 study's gain for the MARS-only variables. Panel 2 shows the post hoc contrasts: AIFS Single added to the ensemble mean (−0.13 points, unresolved) and the ensemble mean added to F0 (−0.96 points, a gain; 0.96 against AIFS Single's 1.04, a difference the study did not test).

The single 9 km forecast has the highest raw radiation error of the three forecasts at every lead day, and its error rises fastest. Against CAMS irradiance, the radiation of Open-Meteo's 9 km IFS forecast has a raw error of 65.7, 73.3, and 82.7 W m⁻² at lead days 1 to 3, a rise of 26%. "Rises fastest" is a ranking of point estimates, because the differences between lead days have no interval. AIFS Single's raw error is 62.0, 66.9, and 73.1 (a rise of 18%), and the ensemble mean's is 61.4, 67.6, and 74.0 (20%). One possible explanation, which the study did not test, is that a sharp forecast is wrong twice when it puts a cloud in the wrong hour, and a smoother forecast hedges. The explanation does not fit the ensemble mean's gain, which does not grow with lead day.

The XGBoost models on the blend rows train on fewer months than the main fits, so P4 and P5 are measured against a reference that had less training data. Each XGBoost model on the blend rows trains on 11 or 12 of the 14 months. In 10 calendar months, the scored month has no training row of the same calendar month. F0 refit on the blend rows is 0.4 to 0.7 points worse than F0 from the main fits on the same rows.

One winter fold holds the only winter months, so its XGBoost models train on no winter row. The fold-level differences are printed in the report: P4 and P5 are negative in each of the five folds at every lead day. The direction holds for both. Pooled over lead days 1 to 3, P4 is −1.04 points with the winter fold and −1.01 without it, so its size holds. P5 is −0.79 points with the winter fold and −0.67 without it, so its size shrinks.

docs.title: Discussion: what to use
docs.text:
• Request total cloud cover from Dynamical.org first, and treat the evidence as post hoc. Added to FP, total cloud cover lowers the error by 0.13 points (unresolved), and total cloud cover with the three cloud layers by 0.28 points (a gain at both settings). The layers are not in the free open-data feed that Dynamical.org repackages, so the 0.28-point gain needs a source other than the free feed. All 14 variables beyond FP together lower FP's error by 0.36 points (exploratory, main setting only), and 8 of those 14 are not carried by the free feed. The gains are measured on top of a single 9 km forecast and may be smaller on the ensemble mean. No fit measured the other groups of the free feed added to FP one at a time.
  • Do not take a second IFS feed for the cloud layers on this evidence. The cloud layers pass the pre-set drop-one rule at the main setting only, and their raise is below 0.1 points at both settings. Their gain on top of FP is unresolved at 99% (the layers' own step is 0.15 and 0.11 points), so the page does not treat it as established. The production feed's long-wave radiation, a cloud signal, was not tested.
  • Do not choose between the MARS-only variables and a second forecast from P5. The pre-set rule returns "second forecast". On the ensemble mean the production service reads, a second forecast adds about 0.13 points, which is unresolved. That point estimate equals the 0.13 points the ERA5 study found for the MARS-only variables, but the two contrasts differ in rows, months, base set, and interval level. A reanalysis gains about twice what a forecast does at lead day 1 on the cloud sets, so the MARS-only variables' gain at forecast lead may be below 0.13 points, although the ratio was measured for the cloud variables at lead day 1 only. The 3-hourly ensemble mean the production service reads may do better than the 6-hourly mean used here, which would leave a second forecast even less to add.
  • Do not read the 1-point gain as the value of AIFS Single. The ensemble mean gives a gain of similar size over the 9 km forecast (0.96 against 1.04; the difference was not tested), so the gain does not appear specific to AIFS Single.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• Every planned gain is measured on top of a single deterministic 9 km point forecast. A smoother reference, such as the ensemble mean, leaves less for any added input to fix, so every planned gain here is likely to be smaller in production.
  • The production service's 3-hourly ensemble mean is not tested. The ensemble mean used here is on 6-hourly steps.
  • Twenty-five months are few. The intervals resample whole months and are approximate. The resampling ignores the dependence between months scored by the same fitted models, so 99% intervals are likely to be too narrow. The contrasts on the blend rows use 14 months.
  • The first era includes a 17-day part-month, and November is scored with no November in training. The blend rows have 10 calendar months with no training row of the same calendar month.
  • The newest IFS cycle is not scored. Cycle 50r1 is in use from 2026-05-12. The months since 2026-05-12 are too few to cut into folds.
  • The planned contrasts were checked against controls with the same number of columns, but the exploratory ones were not. The page does not correct exploratory intervals for multiple comparisons, and does not count its exploratory contrasts. Of the exploratory contrasts, 32 lie near the 0.1-point line and have no second-setting run.
  • The contrasts that add cloud variables to FP compare variable sets with different column counts. FP + total cloud has 14 columns and FP + total cloud + layers 17, against FP's 13, and no negative control pads FP with shuffled copies of the same columns. The controls of P1 and P2 show the penalty for the ladder variable sets only.
  • Some analyses are post hoc. Several analyses were added after the first scientific review: the contrasts that add cloud variables to FP, the ensemble-mean contrasts, the winter-fold reading, the raw-error table, the second-setting drop-one runs, and the rule that both settings must agree for the drop-one test (the plan required agreement for P1 to P5 only). The both-settings rule reversed the pre-set outcome of the second-feed decision. The report labels each post hoc analysis. Only P1 to P5, their controls, their five verdicts, and the three decision rules as written were fixed in the plan before any result existed.
  • ICON-EU was not tested as a second forecast.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The page says nothing about wind, other regions, or leads beyond 9 days. The study tests Open-Meteo's 9 km IFS forecast and AIFS Single only. The IFS ensemble also runs at 9 km and the production service reads it on a 0.25-degree grid, as the ensemble mean, which is smoother than the single 9 km forecast because it averages members.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: IFS forecasts come from Open-Meteo's Single Runs archive, AIFS Single and the ensemble mean from the Dynamical.org store, and CAMS irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Data Store. The page contains modified Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service information. The farms' output is private to National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED) and appears only as fractions of each farm's capacity under labels A to F. The code is in studies/ifs_solar_variables/ and src/studies/. XGBoost runs on a graphics processing unit with colsample_bytree=1.

docs.title: Reproducing the figures
docs.text:
uv run python studies/weather_downloads/fetch_open_meteo_ifs_solar_variables.py
uv run python studies/ifs_solar_variables/ifs_ladder_build_dataset.py
uv run python studies/ifs_solar_variables/ifs_ladder_build_dataset.py --ens-only
uv run python studies/ifs_solar_variables/ifs_ladder_fit.py --view ladder --target both

uv run python studies/ifs_solar_variables/ifs_ladder_fit.py --view ens --lead-days 1 2 3

docs.title: A same-hour power lag did not improve day-ahead solar forecasts at 6 plants in Lincolnshire
docs.text:
At 6 solar plants over 18 months, giving an XGBoost model each plant's own power from the same hour 2 days earlier did not change its day-ahead error by a statistically significant amount in any of the five planned comparisons. For this lag, the 99% interval of the change in mean absolute error runs from −0.075 to +0.073 percentage points of the plant's capacity, against a baseline error of 8.93 points. A post hoc reading of the planned intervals rules out a gain as large as the 0.18 points the study plan treated as worth acting on, for a lag against no lag and for a two-step forecast against a lag with its weather. For Flexpectation (this project), that lag is therefore not worth building into the day-ahead service for these 6 utility-scale plants on this evidence. Inputs that track a plant's recent output did better in post hoc analyses. Most of their gain, however, came from one plant whose months of low output were in the training data, so those results are hypotheses to test on more plants and not a recommendation. Eighteen months at 6 plants in one box 25 km across cannot show whether a longer history, more plants, or a faster data feed would change the result.

Terms used on this page.

  • Points: percentage points of a plant's capacity, where capacity is the plant's 99th percentile of metered output and not its nameplate rating. Differences are an input's error minus the baseline's, so a negative difference means a lower error.
  • Lag: the plant's power at the same clock hour on the latest whole day before the forecast is issued, which is 2 days (48 hours) before the target hour for a day-ahead forecast.
  • Arm: one XGBoost model configuration with its own inputs. The baseline arm, B0, has no lagged power. Two tables in "Data and methods" name the arms.
  • Lead-day: days between the weather forecast run and the target day. Day-ahead is lead-day 1.
  • Fold: a block of whole months held out from training, so that every month is forecast by an XGBoost model that never trained on that month.
  • Screen: the first 10 of the 18 scored months, on which the arm with the lowest error was chosen before any planned comparison was run.
  • Planned, exploratory, post hoc: a planned contrast was fixed before any result existed. Every other number is exploratory. A post hoc number was added after the first results were seen and is therefore a hypothesis.
  • Interval: the range of changes in error that the data are consistent with, allowing for month-to-month weather and the random fitting seed. An interval that includes zero means no detectable change. The forecast's own 10%–90% range is called the forecast band.
  • Oracle: an arm told the true size of a planted power loss. It shows what knowing the loss exactly gains an XGBoost model.
  • CRPS: the continuous ranked probability score, an error score for a whole forecast distribution, in the same points as mean absolute error. Lower is better.

Can a same-hour lag improve a day-ahead point forecast? No change was detectable. The lag changed the error by −0.001 points [−0.075, +0.073] at the primary hyperparameter setting and by +0.012 points [−0.043, +0.058] at a second, more regularised setting (planned comparison P1, 99% intervals).

Can the lag improve the probabilistic forecast? No change was detectable: the CRPS changed by +0.009 points [−0.020, +0.036] (P4). The 10%–90% forecast band held 68.9% of hours without the lag and 68.5% with it, against a nominal 80%.

Does the lag help one XGBoost model shared by all plants? No change was detectable: −0.059 points [−0.151, +0.029] (P5).

Do the other lagged inputs help? None of the planned comparisons found a gain. The analogue ensemble, chosen by the screen, was no better than the lag on the other 8 months (+0.012 points [−0.243, +0.278], P2), and a two-step forecast was no better than the lag with its weather forecast (+0.039 points [−0.059, +0.143], P3).

How large a gain can the study rule out? The 2% threshold (0.18 points) is about half of what an oracle gains from knowing a 10% power loss in half the months (0.39 points), so the study can rule out only a large gain, at these 6 plants pooled. The plan's own verdict for all five comparisons is "unresolved" (Results).

Did the study detect a planted power loss, and which inputs could? The lag did not detectably recover a planted power loss. In a post hoc test that cuts every plant's power by 10% in the same 9 months, the lag recovered 0.09 [−0.04, 0.27] of what the oracle recovers, weekly statistics 0.39 [0.21, 0.73], and the ratio of power to satellite irradiance 0.74 [0.57, 1.21] (95% intervals, Figure 8).

Do the level-tracking inputs help in the real data? Mostly not. The satellite ratio and weekly statistics gained 0.23 and 0.17 points over the baseline on the 8 months they were picked on (post hoc, so biased upward). Removing one plant's 3 low-output months from its training cut the two gains to 0.04 and 0.05 points, with intervals that include zero (Figure 11).

Do lags help at the longest leads? Weekly statistics lowered the error by 0.45 points [−0.74, −0.16] at day 14 (exploratory). A 50/50 blend of the baseline with a climatology built only from earlier years lowered it by 1.16 points [−1.50, −0.80] (post hoc), so no lag arm beat that simpler fix (Figure 14).

Can lagged inputs describe each plant to an XGBoost model shared by many plants? Partly (post hoc, intervals over months and not over plants). The plant's ratio of power to forecast irradiance and its daily shape lowered a shared model's error by 0.31 points [−0.49, −0.14], and by 0.32 points [−0.51, −0.14] for a plant left out of training (Figure 16).

What can these data support? These data support the absence of a large gain from the same-hour lag at these 6 plants, and a hypothesis that inputs tracking a plant's recent output mostly repair training months in which the plant's output was low. The data do not support a claim about domestic solar, other regions, more than 18 months, a plant that is partly offline in the scored month, or hundreds of plants.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5). Several independent Claude reviewers have checked the method, the evidence, and the prose adversarially.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
• The screen's winner lost most of its gain outside the months it was chosen on. The analogue ensemble beat the baseline by 0.231 points [−0.392, −0.102] in the screen and by 0.046 points [−0.243, +0.169] on the other 8 months. Part of that fall is the winner's curse, and part may be the different months (Figure 9, Figure 10).
  • The baseline, given the day of the year, learned one plant's low March 2025 and under-forecast a normal March 2026, and the inputs that see recent output corrected that error. In March 2026 the plant produced as much as the other 5 relative to their output, but in March 2025, December 2024, and April 2026 it produced two thirds to three quarters as much (post hoc, Figure 11).
  • At day 14 the baseline XGBoost model, trained on 18 months, scores worse than a climatology built from up to 6 earlier years, and a random-day lag gains too. The baseline scored 15.35 points against 14.18, and a random-day lag lowered the error by 0.07 to 0.12 points depending on the draw (post hoc, Figure 13).
  • Too many hours fall outside both ends of the forecast band: 14.0% below the 10% quantile and 17.0% above the 90% quantile, for the baseline and the lag alike (post hoc, Figure 18).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Flexpectation needs to know whether a plant's own recent power helps its forecast. A lag could correct for soiling, panel degradation, a failed string, part of a plant offline, and changes in the weather forecast product. In an XGBoost model shared by many plants, a lag could also tell the shared model about each plant, such as the plant's ratio of direct-current to alternating-current capacity, without a physical model of the plant. The question came from issue #1138 (Lag features for solar power forecasting).

Short-term photovoltaic forecasting often uses recently observed power as an input. Bacher et al. (2009) forecast up to 36 hours ahead from 15-minute power observations, and the review by Antonanzas et al. (2016) covers forecast horizons from seconds to weeks. This study asks the narrower question of whether a lag of recently observed power helps an XGBoost model that already has a numerical weather forecast, at one lead (a day ahead) and at utility-scale plants.

The study compares an XGBoost model with no lag (B0) against 17 other arms, each an XGBoost model given a different input or set of inputs, at 6 solar plants of National Grid Electricity Distribution (NGED). The forecast is for the day after the day it is issued (lead-day 1), driven by the mean of the 51-member ensemble forecast from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), called the ENS mean. The reference forecasts that read no weather forecast score far worse on the same 29,445 rows, one per plant per daylight hour: diurnal persistence (the lag used directly as the forecast) 16.56 points and climatology 14.54, against the baseline's 8.93.

Input Source and grid Lead read Plant data read Delay assumed ENS mean of ECMWF's 51 members ECMWF open data at 0.25° (the forecast system runs at about 9 km), averaged over each plant's H3 cell; 3-hourly steps to 144 hours and 6-hourly beyond, interpolated to hourly as in the matched-lead study the 00 UTC run, lead-days 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, and 14, treated as available at 09:00 UTC NGED power up to the issue time (09:00 UTC on the run's day; 00 UTC at lead-day 0) none for power: the live service reads NGED power from an S3 bucket updated every 6 hours, and a delay of up to 9 hours changes only one arm All-sky global horizontal irradiance from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) Radiation Service, retrieved from Meteosat Second Generation imagery (one input, PC) point time series at each plant: hourly irradiation, stamped at the end of the hour whole days before the issue day not applicable 1 day: at 09:00 UTC the whole previous day is available (the service's latency since February 2026; 2 days before then)

docs.title: Data and methods
docs.text:
The rows. The study uses the rows of this project's matched-lead study, which are limited to the months for which that study holds archived ENS-mean forecasts: 35,263 hourly solar rows at 6 plants, all daylight hours, from December 2024 (the first whole month after ECMWF's Cycle 49r1) to September 2026. January 2026 is absent because the matched-lead study drops the month in which the Met Office upgraded its UK variable-resolution weather model (UKV). No ENS data are missing. The power record the lags are read from ends on 2026-07-01, the start of a final test period that this study does not open, and that end drops 5,144 rows. Of the remaining 30,119 rows, the 29,445 that have a lag at lead-day 1 cover 18 calendar months. Every error is divided by its own plant's capacity before any mean or difference. Errors are divided by the effective-capacity table built for the matched-lead study.

The models. Each XGBoost model uses the absolute-error objective, column subsampling off, three fitting seeds, and five folds of whole months. The primary hyperparameter setting is depth 6, learning rate 0.05, 500 rounds, and row subsampling 0.8. The baseline B0 has seven columns: hour of day, day of year, an era code (which of three periods, split at 2025-10 and 2026-02, the row falls in), the sun's elevation and azimuth, and the ENS mean's irradiance and temperature at the same lead. The era code and the folds follow the matched-lead study's cuts. The 2025-10 cut comes from that study's shared fold helper and marks no change in any weather product. The 2026-02 cut follows the UKV upgrade, which does not affect the ENS mean. The study does not cut at the one ENS change inside the record, ECMWF's Cycle 50r1 on 2026-05-12. Reading a test month's power as a lag does not leak the test month's answer into the XGBoost model, because the model is trained to predict the training row's own power, so the study keeps rows near fold boundaries. B0's error is 8.93 points over all 18 months and 9.20 over the screen, and the matched-lead study published 8.771% for the same XGBoost model, which the reproduction check matched exactly.

The arms. Every arm other than B0 adds columns to those seven. Arms with more columns can score slightly differently purely because the XGBoost model has more columns to split on, and the study does not pad narrower arms with copies, because an XGBoost model never uses a copied column. The study measures that effect with random-day lag columns instead (see Figure 7).

Code Name What it adds to B0 L1 the lag the plant's power at the same hour 2 days before the target hour IM issue morning the plant's power on the issue day's morning, up to 09:00 UTC L2 lag with weather L1 plus that hour's weather forecast CTX7 seven daily lags seven separate daily lags and their weather forecasts W7 weekly statistics the minimum, maximum, and mean of the same hour over the last 7 whole days Q30 30-day percentiles the 30-day 90th percentile and median of the same hour CK clipping ceiling the plant's running 99.5th percentile and 60-day maximum of power, and the share of clear hours near that ceiling TF transfer ratio the 30-day ratio of power to forecast irradiance, and that ratio times the target hour's forecast irradiance AN analogue ensemble on the 5 of the last 30 days whose forecast clear-sky index was closest to the target's: the mean and spread of their power, each rescaled by the Haurwitz clear-sky model's irradiance, and their mean forecast clear-sky index PC satellite ratio the 7-day ratio of power to CAMS satellite irradiance, and the 30-day ratio of CAMS to forecast irradiance S2, S3 two-step forecasts S2: L1 plus first-stage XGBoost forecasts for the target hour and the lag hour, and the first-stage residual at the lag hour. S3: the first-stage mean residual over the last 1, 7, and 30 days RP relative output the plant's recent energy relative to the other plants T1 days since start days since the record began, which lets trees interpolate a test month's level from the months on both sides KS combination L1, IM, W7, Q30, TF, S3, and RP together N1, N2 random-day controls one random day 8 to 28 days earlier (N1), or one from months not being scored (N2), in place of the lag

The first run also fitted the daily shape (DT, two 30-day columns: how far the plant's power curve sits earlier or later in the day than clear-sky irradiance, and the share of energy produced in hours when clear-sky irradiance is low), a plant code (a column identifying the plant), the fingerprint (TF, DT, and CK together). The follow-up runs added PC2 (PC with a 2-day wait for CAMS), CL (B0 plus the climatology as a column), two- and three-column random-day controls (N2-2 and N2-3), B0 and other arms without the day of the year, and blends of B0 or W7 with a climatology. Post-model corrections need no fit: rescalings of B0's forecast by recent error, quantiles of recent residuals added to B0's forecast, and a clamp at the clipping ceiling. Every window except N2's random day is anchored at the issue day, and the build asserts and probes that no window reads data after the issue time. PC's 30-day ratio of CAMS to forecast irradiance contains no power, so part of PC's and TF's gain may correct the weather forecast's bias and not track the plant. The live service does not ingest CAMS, so PC would need a new data feed.

The screen chose the analogue ensemble before any planned comparison was run. The screen scores each arm on the first 10 months and chooses the arm with the lowest error among 11 arms eligible for the choice. Those are the 17 arms other than B0, without L1, L2, S2, N1, and N2 (which the planned comparisons use anyway) and without T1 (which interpolates between months and could not run live).

The five planned comparisons are:

  • P1: the lag minus B0, one XGBoost model per plant.
  • P2: the screen's chosen arm minus the lag, on the 8 months the screen did not use.
  • P3: S2 minus L2.
  • P4: the CRPS of the lag minus the CRPS of B0.
  • P5: the lag minus B0 in one XGBoost model shared by all plants.

The plan's rule counts a lag as helping if both hyperparameter settings give a 99% interval wholly below zero and a point estimate of at least 2% of the reference arm's own error. The plan treated 2% of the reference arm's error as the smallest gain worth acting on. The rule labels a contrast "unresolved" when the interval includes zero, and has no outcome for "any gain is smaller than the threshold". The statement that a contrast rules out a gain that large is therefore a post hoc reading. The plan is the file plans/study-lag-features-1138.md in the repository's git history (on the study branch, pull request #1139).

What the significance test covers. Each interval comes from 2,000 resamples, each of which draws whole calendar months, the same months for every arm, and one of the three fitting seeds. The test covers month-to-month weather and the fitting seed, not differences between plants. These 6 plants pooled are therefore the unit, and no interval shows how a seventh plant would fare. With only 8 or 18 months to resample, a percentile bootstrap tends to give intervals that are too narrow, so the follow-up runs also give t-intervals over months. The planned comparisons use 99% intervals (a Bonferroni correction over five) and need both settings to agree. The intervals on the oracle's and the lag's gains over B0 in the planted-loss control are 99% too, and all other intervals on this page, the recovery shares included, are 95%.

Exploratory intervals are not corrected for multiple comparisons, and shared months make them cluster. An exploratory interval for an input with no real effect has a nominal 5% chance of excluding zero. The number of exploratory inputs with no real effect is unknown, and shared months make the false exclusions cluster. Of 83 exploratory intervals in the first run, 14 lay wholly below zero and 20 wholly above. Of 87 exploratory intervals in the first follow-up runs, 27 lay wholly below zero and 7 wholly above. With no real effects, about 2 in 83 would lie wholly on each side, but the arms share columns and months, so the intervals are not independent tests.

Controls. N2, a random day from months not being scored, shows what an extra column does. N1, a random day 8 to 28 days earlier, carries the plant's recent level but little of the recent weather, so N1 shows what a level-only lag does. A positive control plants a power loss, at 5% and at 10% (and at 2% in the first run), by multiplying power by 1 minus the loss in 9 of the 18 scored months and in a random half of the months used only for training. The loss is applied before the lags are built. An oracle arm given the true loss factor shows what knowing the loss exactly gains an XGBoost model. A second control, the plant-steps control, gives each plant its own persistent steps in power, each lasting 4 to 12 weeks. An arm's recovery share is its gain over B0 on the data with the planted loss, minus its gain on the original data, divided by the oracle's gain. The oracle's gain is itself uncertain, so a share's interval is wide and unstable where the oracle's gain is small. The months with the planted loss are also one random draw. The study has not established why the plant-steps control's oracle gains about a quarter as much as the month-level control's oracle at a 10% loss.

Cleaning. Outage, commissioning-ramp, and export-cap hours are dropped from targets and lags. The cleaning rule that drops every hour of a run of 24 or more zero hours looks at later hours. A live service cannot yet know whether a run of zeros will last 24 hours, so a backtest lag inside such a run is cleaner than a live service's lag. The cleaning kept whole months in which one plant produced a fraction of its usual output (see Figure 11). The study therefore cannot say whether a lag helps when a plant is partly offline in the scored month.
