Early stopping roughly doubles the CRPS of the single biofuel generator (+1.16 [0.80, 1.54]), so exclude that series or check its score 3 Train with quantile loss at 9 levels instead of squared error, and score every member times every level post hoc −2.39 [−2.52, −2.27], 12 of 12 −2.60 [−2.74, −2.46], 15 of 15 Training takes about 8 times longer; the forecast becomes 51 × 9 values. Against spread rescaling on the same 45 later runs the gain is 0.4 points for the plain arm and 0.8 to 1.0 for the best arm (see the quantile section) 4 Show wind farms fewer columns (drop weekday, radiation, dew point, precipitation type, time of year) post hoc −0.32 [−0.38, −0.26], 12 of 12 (wind alone −3.3) −0.35 [−0.45, −0.25], 15 of 15 One column list 5 Add the forecast lead time in hours as a column planned −0.05 [−0.08, −0.03], 10 of 12 −0.08 [−0.11, −0.05], 15 of 15 Small change. The arm beats a control arm padded with one shuffled column by 0.05 points [0.02, 0.07], so the gain is not an artefact of column count. The gain sits at 48 to 72 hours and in wind farms 6 Rescale each series' ensemble spread by a factor fitted on past outcomes, for the point-forecast arms planned idea, post hoc form −1.9 for production with cleaning, −1.3 to −1.4 for the best point arm (CRPS only) −1.95 and −1.3 (seed 0) A post-processing step and a state file 7 One XGBoost model per series type, with a site identifier post hoc −0.82 [−0.96, −0.69], 12 of 12 −0.51 [−0.81, −0.28], 15 of 15; adds nothing to the best point arm A new training layout (see the cautions below) 8 Drop from training every half-hour before a meter has been live for 6 weeks post hoc −0.31 [−0.62, −0.06], 9 of 12 months, at 2 series; the t-interval [−0.61, +0.02] includes zero No effect by construction A rule in the cleaning step

Row 7 carries two cautions. The site identifier is the raw series number used as an ordered value. That has not been tested at 2,500 series, so use a categorical identifier or per-site target encoding. On fold B, pooling cut the demand gain from −0.65 to −0.35 (t-interval [−0.87, +0.13]).

The four changes together score a CRPS of 7.85% on fold A, 3.50 points [−3.71, −3.28] below production with cleaning and 3.7 points below the study's refit of the stored production configuration. The combination is quantile training (3), the lead-time column (5), the wind-farm columns (4), and the pooled layout with a site identifier (7), with the cleaning rule (8) already in the control arm. The study did not combine rows 1, 2, or 6 with quantile training (which replaces the row 1 objective), and did not rescale the quantile arm's spread. The best point-forecast arm combines rows 1, 2, 4, 5, and 7 and scores 9.95% [9.41, 10.42], 1.40 points below production with cleaning. Fold B shows no gain from pooling on top of the other point-forecast changes (−1.16 against −1.23), so the pooled layout is the least certain row.

Production's colsample_bytree of 0.8 scored 0.10 points better than 1.0 on fold A and 0.07 points better on fold B. Every contrast on this page uses 1.0, so that arms with different numbers of columns are compared fairly. A production change should be tested at 0.8 before it ships, because the combinations here were never fitted at 0.8.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The production forecast is a first version, and the cheap ideas for improving it had not been tried together. The XGBoost improvements page lists them. The maintainer's starting hunches were that solar farms, wind farms, and substations need different columns, that the probabilistic forecast needs calibrating, and that a handful of other ideas would help. The study also tried several ways of cleaning the training data, and the XGBoost settings of earlier studies on this site (such as min_child_weight 20).

The question came from issue #1150 (Study: quick wins for the production XGBoost forecast). The study changes no production code and uses only the production system's data, which are ECMWF ENS weather forecasts and NGED power. It scores CRPS and MAE and benchmarks every arm against production. During the study, the aim widened from finding quick wins to diagnosing why the XGBoost forecast scores worse than the heuristic, so the page answers that too.

This is a looser study than this repository's study standard. The arms were tried in rounds. Round 0 compared ways of cleaning the training data. Round 1 tried ideas one at a time. Round 2 combined the ideas that won. Round 3 repeated the key arms with two more seeds and on a backwards-in-time fold. After each round, the next round's arms were chosen by judgement, and a later diagnostic round added quantile training, a learning curve, the heuristic's inputs, and a blend with the heuristic's members. The plan named four contrasts: the chosen cleaning against no cleaning (P0), the round 2 combination against production on fold B (P1), per-type physics columns for solar farms only (P2), and spread calibration against the same forecast unrescaled (P3). The results of the four contrasts are in Round 1 (P2), Round 2 (P1), Round 0 (P0), and Calibration (P3). Every other number is exploratory.

docs.title: Data and methods
docs.text:
Fold A is the leaderboard fold, and every arm is scored on 53 ECMWF ENS runs started every 7 days from 1 July 2025. Each run forecasts out to about 15 days. Scores labelled all leads use every lead to 351 hours. The lead bands are days 0 to 2 (under 72 hours), days 3 to 10 (72 to 263 hours), and days 11 and later. The 31 series are 6 solar farms, 3 wind farms, 16 disaggregated-demand substations, 4 raw-flow substations, 1 battery, and 1 biofuel generator. The study did not submit to the leaderboard scorer, so every score is the study's own.

The study's refit of production on the graphics processing unit (GPU) scores 6.27 MW, against 6.33 MW for the stored production forecast. The stored production forecast scores a CRPS of 6.33 MW on these runs. The refit on the GPU scores 6.27 MW, which is 0.2% below the refit on the central processing unit (CPU), 6.29 MW, and 0.15% below the lowest stored retrain, slightly outside the stored runs' range. The CPU refit is inside that range. Every arm here was fitted on a GPU.

Every arm is the production recipe with one named difference. Production fits one XGBoost model per series, with 24 columns, 500 trees, learning rate 0.05, depth 6, row subsampling 0.8, and squared error, on the control member's rows. The report prints every arm's columns, objective, and cleaning rule. The CRPS of a quantile arm is computed on the sample made of every member crossed with every quantile level, 459 values per half-hour.

Round 0 chose one cleaning rule, and every later arm applies it. The rule drops from the training rows every half-hour before a meter has been live for 6 weeks. "Production with cleaning" is production plus this rule, and it is the control arm for every later contrast. The round 0 section below gives the evidence.

Intervals resample whole validation months, with the same draw for every arm. The 31 series share their weather, so months are the independent units. The page quotes the 95% interval from 2,000 resamples and the number of months in which the arm beat its reference. A percentile interval from 12 months is too narrow, so the months-better count matters. The report also gives a t-interval over the monthly differences.

Three fitting seeds measure the noise of the fit, and it is small. Across seeds the CRPS of any arm varies by at most 0.05 points, against differences of 0.05 to 3.5 points. The seed changes row subsampling only. Fold B was fitted with one seed for most arms and two for four of them.

Fold B is a robustness check. It trains on the validation year and scores the 15 months before the training window, with the same 31 series. Some demand meters did not exist in the early months, so those months average over fewer series. The new-meter rule changes nothing on fold B, so P0 cannot be decided there. Fold B shares series and weather regimes with fold A, so agreement between them does not show that a result holds at other series. Neither fold is cut at ECMWF's ensemble upgrade of 12 November 2024.

docs.title: Production scores worse than a manual heuristic, and four changes close most of the gap
docs.text: Figure 1 ranks every arm on fold A, with the stored production forecast, manual_heuristic, and climatology as reference lines. The best arm scores a CRPS of 7.85% of capacity [7.43, 8.24], against 11.34% for production with cleaning. Its MAE of 10.74% sits below the heuristic's 11.00%. Intervals for absolute scores overlap because every arm swings with the weather from month to month. The paired contrasts are sharper.

docs.title: Round 1: ideas on their own
docs.text:
Two planned ideas help clearly, one helps a little, and several did not help. The absolute-error objective and early stopping each lowered CRPS by about 0.4 points. The lead-time column lowered it by 0.05 points. A post hoc cut of 8 columns for wind farms lowered wind CRPS by 3.3 points (row 4 of the recommendations). Recency weights (half-life 120 days) and the holiday and ordinal-day columns for demand series changed CRPS by +0.05 and +0.06 points with intervals that include zero.

Removing the power lags and weekday columns from solar and wind farms raised the error, and adding physics columns did not undo the rise. The removal raised the error by 0.19 points [0.14, 0.23], and per-type physics columns added to the removal left it 0.15 points above production with cleaning. The planned contrast P2, the per-type physics columns for solar farms, raised solar CRPS by 0.30 points [0.05, 0.56]. An XGBoost model with min_child_weight 20, as in the earlier studies, changed CRPS by +0.01 points.

The error falls most in wind farms, raw-flow substations, and solar farms, and the 16 demand substations change least. The objective and early stopping help wind and raw flow most. The pooled model with a site identifier lowers demand error most (−1.18 points) and does little for solar and wind. The absolute-error objective also lowers demand error, by 0.15 points. Three wind farms and four raw-flow series carry many of the gains, so a wind result rests on three farms.

Removing the four power lags raised the CRPS of solar, wind, and demand series, including at day-ahead, which the lag-features study did not find for solar. A post hoc arm removed only the four lag columns (24, 48, 168, and 336 hours) and kept every other column, on all series types (fold A, three seeds). CRPS rose by 0.19 points [0.08, 0.31] for solar farms, 1.33 points [0.95, 1.74] for wind farms, and 0.27 points [0.19, 0.34] for demand. For solar farms the rise is +0.55 points below 24 hours, +0.68 at 24 to 48 hours, +0.09 at 48 to 72 hours, and +0.12 beyond. The lag-features study found that a same-hour lag did not change day-ahead MAE at 6 solar plants. The two studies differ in four ways:

  • Lags: four lags here, one there.
  • Forecast: 51 members and CRPS here, the ensemble mean and MAE there.
  • Rows: half-hourly rows including night here, hourly daylight rows there.
  • Model: one XGBoost model per series with 24 columns here, and one XGBoost model per plant there.

Two candidate explanations remain untested, and one caveat limits both studies. First, production's 24-hour lag is blanked at leads of 24 hours or more, so at day-ahead only the 48-hour, 168-hour, and 336-hour lags are available, and the 168-hour and 336-hour lags may carry weekly regime information that the lag-features study's single 2-day lag does not. Second, the lag-features study scored the ensemble mean by MAE, while this study scored CRPS over 51 members, where a lag may mainly sharpen the members' spread. The caveat is that the solar result here rests on 6 farms in one weather region, as the lag-features result does, so neither is a statement about a seventh plant. A follow-up should run both setups on identical rows and score both by MAE and CRPS. This study cannot say which difference explains the gap.

The weekday columns do not explain the lag result, and the lags should stay in production. The earlier arm that also removed the weekday columns gave almost the same losses (solar +0.27, wind +1.38). Do not remove the lags in production on the strength of the lag-features study.

docs.title: Round 2: combining the winners
docs.text:
The combination arms add one change at a time, in an order chosen by judgement from the round 1 table. The absolute-error objective with early stopping lowers CRPS by 0.63 points. Adding the lead-time column brings the total to 0.65 points, and adding the wind-farm column cut brings it to 0.73 points. Adding the pooled layout brings it to 1.40 points on fold A.

On fold B, the round 2 combination lowers CRPS by 1.16 to 1.23 points (P1). The point-forecast arms without pooling reach 1.23 points, and pooling gives 1.16, which is no gain. The lowering holds in both lead bands: on fold B the best arm lowers CRPS by 1.75 points at days 0 to 2 and 1.19 at days 3 to 10. P1, the round 2 combination against production on fold B, is −1.16 points [−1.67, −0.72] for the pooled combination and −1.23 [−1.50, −0.97] for the combination without pooling.

docs.title: Round 0: data cleaning, chosen before every later round
docs.text:
Seven rules were tried, four named in the plan and three written after an exploratory read of the training window. The plan named the first-N-months, isolated-zero, spike, and commissioning-ramp rules. A read of the training months (April 2024 to June 2025) only, with no validation data, led to three more: new-meter settling, solar and wind dropouts, and switching days. The read flagged late-starting meters, multi-day steps in some demand series, a staged solar commissioning, and solar dropouts while the other farms produced. The notes of that read are not part of the report, so the page quotes only what each rule drops.

Only the new-meter rule lowered CRPS by more than 0.1 points on its own, and it changed only 2 demand series. The rule drops every half-hour up to 6 weeks after a series first has 48 consecutive half-hours above 5% of its capacity. It removes 4,747 training half-hours from 2 demand series, and lowers the mean CRPS by 0.31 points [−0.62, −0.06] (9 of 12 months) against production (P0, fold A). The t-interval over the monthly differences, [−0.61, +0.02], includes zero. The other 29 series are unchanged.

Every other rule that could be scored changed CRPS by 0.07 points or less. The first-1, first-2, and first-3-months rules scored −0.07, +0.03, and −0.07 points with intervals that include zero, and the first-6-months rule, which removes 19,838 half-hours from 4 series, could not be scored because it leaves one demand series with no training rows. The isolated-zero and spike rules changed CRPS by 0.00 and +0.01 points. The commissioning-ramp rule removed 8,866 half-hours of one solar farm and raised the error by 0.02 points [0.01, 0.04]; the study did not test why. The solar-dropout and switching-day rules scored −0.01 and −0.07 points, and the combination of the new-meter, ramp, dropout, and switching rules scored −0.25 points [−0.52, −0.02]. We chose the new-meter rule as the cleaning for every later arm. Its value is for series the system will meet in future, because the two series it helps began in early 2025. It was written after reading the training months (post hoc), and fold B cannot test it.

docs.title: Quantile training: the spread and the point forecast improve together
docs.text:
Training each series' XGBoost model with quantile loss at 9 levels (0.1 to 0.9) gave the largest single gain. To score it, every ensemble member is crossed with every level, so each half-hour has 459 values. On fold A the quantile arm scores a CRPS of 8.95% [8.37, 9.48] against 11.34%, which is −2.39 points [−2.52, −2.27] (12 of 12 months), and a CRPS 2.60 points lower on fold B [−2.74, −2.46]. Every series type gains: −1.69 for demand, −2.30 for solar, −4.38 for wind, and −4.52 for raw flow.

Adding the lead-time column, the wind-farm columns, and pooling with a site identifier gives the best arm, a CRPS of 7.85% and an MAE of 10.74%. On fold B the difference from production is −3.44 points [−3.98, −3.00].

Adding the heuristic's weekly inputs to the best arm lowered CRPS by a further 0.2 points on seed 0 (7.63%) and on fold B. On seed 0 the paired contrast between the two arms is −0.22 points [−0.38, −0.06] on fold A (8 of 12 months better) and −0.22 [−0.61, +0.54] on fold B (11 of 15), with solar and wind farms worse and demand better. The arm is post hoc.

Quantile training has two drawbacks. Training takes about 8 times longer (see the training-time section), and the 9 levels and the equal weighting of the 459 values are untuned.

The gain over spread rescaling is smaller than the gain over raw production. On the 45 later runs that the rescaling can be scored on (seed 0, fold A), the quantile arm scores a CRPS 0.44 points lower [−0.53, −0.37] than rescaled production with cleaning (11 of 11 months). On those 45 runs, the best quantile arm scores 7.81% against 8.89% for the best rescaled point-forecast arm, which is 1.05 points lower [−1.27, −0.84] (11 of 11 months). The quantile arms were not rescaled, so these gains are conservative.

Crossing the quantiles with the 51 members is not clearly the right way to issue the forecast. The 459-value sample holds the outcome in 57% of half-hours for a 10% to 90% band (nominal 80%): 80% for solar farms, 59% for wind farms, 50% for demand substations, and 39% for the biofuel generator. The 9 quantiles of the control member alone score a CRPS 0.33 points lower [−0.35, −0.30] than the 459-value sample (12 of 12 months), on every series type. The fair CRPS may account for part of that gap. It divides its spread term by m(m − 1), where m is the number of values, instead of by m². That multiplies the spread term by m/(m − 1), which is 9/8 for 9 values and 459/458 for 459, and a larger spread term lowers the score, so the smaller set gains an advantage. The 9 levels (0.1 to 0.9) are also not the midpoints of 9 equal-probability bins, which would run from 0.056 to 0.944. Score both sets with the same CRPS estimator before reading the gap as a real difference.

The study did not test why the crossed sample is too narrow. One candidate cause, that crossing the quantiles with the members counts the weather uncertainty twice, would make the sample too wide, not too narrow. A likelier cause is in-sample fitting: the XGBoost quantile models learn smaller residuals on the rows they were fitted on than they produce on later runs. After the like-for-like re-score, and before quantile training is re-implemented in production, test issuing the control member's quantiles, with or without the members' spread.

docs.title: Calibration: the ensemble spread is far too narrow
docs.text:
The production ensemble's 10% to 90% band holds the outcome in about one half-hour in ten. The members differ only by the weather inputs, so their spread reflects the weather forecast's uncertainty and not the XGBoost model's own error. We rescaled each series' members about their mean by a factor from a fixed grid (0.6 to 12). Each run's factor is the one with the lowest CRPS for that series on earlier runs, using only outcomes whose valid time precedes the run's initialisation time. The first 8 weekly runs are dropped from both sides of the contrast. The mean, and so the MAE, does not change.

The rescaled forecast scores a CRPS 1.9 points lower for production with cleaning and 1.3 to 1.4 points lower for the best point-forecast arm, with the same sign in all three seeds and on fold B (P3). On fold A, CRPS falls from 11.60% to 9.71% for production with cleaning, and from 10.24% to 8.89% for the best point arm, on the 45 later runs. On fold B it falls from 11.95% to 10.00% and from 10.76% to 9.50%. The band holds 60% of outcomes for production and 49% for the best point arm, still under 80%.

The grid's largest factor (12) was chosen for about a third of the series and runs of production, so a wider grid might lower the CRPS further.

The rescaled forecast still scores worse than the heuristic. On the same 45 later runs the heuristic scores 7.4%, against 8.9%.

docs.title: Example forecasts
docs.text: Figures 7 to 10 show the forecasts themselves for four series, Figure 11 shows the 10% to 90% band, and Figure 12 shows error by lead day, for runs chosen by the actual power and not by the forecast error. Each series is the one ranked in the lower middle of its type by the CRPS of production with cleaning. Each panel shows the ensemble mean of several arms against the measured power, as a share of the series' capacity, for one run of the weekly sample. The solar and wind farms are anonymous. The axes count days from the run's start and show no dates.

docs.title: Comparing with the heuristic, and the length of the training window
docs.text:
The best arms beat the heuristic's MAE at days 0 to 2, fall level with it at days 3 to 10, and fall behind it from day 11. For all 31 series, the best point arm's MAE is 9.5% at days 0 to 2 against 11.3% for the heuristic and 12.9% for climatology. At days 3 to 10 the best arms score 10.7% to 10.8% against 10.9%, and at days 11 and later 11.7% to 11.8% against 11.1%. For wind farms the gap at days 0 to 2 is 10.0% against 19.2%, since the heuristic uses no weather. For demand substations the heuristic leads at every lead: its CRPS is 5.7% to 5.8% against 6.4% to 7.4% for the best quantile arm.

Mixing the heuristic's members into the XGBoost ensemble did not beat the heuristic alone. On the runs where the heuristic has a forecast, production with cleaning scores 11.33%, the heuristic 7.21%, and a blend of the 51 XGBoost members with the heuristic's 13 members 9.97%. With each heuristic member repeated 4 times, the blend scores 8.52%. For the best point arm, the plain blend scores 8.93% and the blend with each heuristic member repeated 4 times scores 7.92%. Each blend is better than XGBoost alone, and worse than the heuristic alone except for wind farms, where the equal-weight blend with the best point arm scores 12.5% against 13.0% for the heuristic. The study did not test why the blend beats XGBoost alone, and blended only seed 0 of production with cleaning and of the best point arm.

Showing XGBoost the heuristic's weekly inputs helped demand substations a little. Adding the 6 weekly analogue observations and their mean, median, minimum, and maximum lowered CRPS by 0.24 points [−0.39, −0.07] (9 of 12 months), and by 0.45 points [−0.69, −0.21] for demand, with the same sign on fold B (−0.60 overall, −0.94 for demand). The weekly inputs raised solar CRPS by 0.12 points on fold A.

A longer training window helps, with diminishing returns. Training on the last 12 months of the 15 raises CRPS by 0.07 points [−0.01, 0.14], on the last 9 months by 0.31 [0.21, 0.41], and on the last 6 months by 0.48 [0.24, 0.71]. On fold B (12 training months), the last 9 and 6 months raise CRPS by 0.40 and 0.68. Wind and raw-flow series are noisier than the all-types curve. The shorter windows drop whole seasons, so the curve mixes the effect of fewer months with the effect of fewer seasons.

docs.title: Input features: a visual check of the feature engineering
docs.text:
The input columns look right apart from four faults, found by plotting every column for one forecast run of four example series and by checking null shares and ranges for all 31 series (Figure 18). The lag alignment is correct: for the demand series in the drawn run, each lag column equals the cleaned power at the valid time minus the lag, with a maximum difference of 0. The four faults are worth fixing in production, and the study tested none of them. No column is constant apart from the UTC offset.

Precipitation type is missing from 50% of the training rows and from none of the scored rows. The column is null for every ECMWF run initialised before 13 November 2024, which is 7 of the 15 training months. The model therefore trains with half the column missing and is scored with none missing. The first run with the column is one day after ECMWF's ensemble upgrade of 12 November 2024. The study did not test whether the upgrade is the cause, or whether dropping the column or the early months changes the score.

Windchill is computed outside the range where its formula is valid. The formula applies at 10 °C or below with wind of at least 4.8 km/h, and production applies it everywhere. Windchill exceeds the air temperature in 18% of the rows at 10 °C or above.

Short-wave radiation is positive after sunset. In December training rows its median is 14.2 W/m² at 20:00 UTC and 2.6 W/m² at 23:00 UTC. In all training rows, 82% exceed 1 W/m². The study did not verify the likely cause, interpolation of the 3-hourly and 6-hourly accumulated fields.

Wind direction and the weekday are fed as numbers that wrap around. Wind direction is in raw degrees, so the control member jumps between 0 and 360, and the sine and cosine of the direction are the usual replacement. The weekday column is an ordinal from 0 to 6 that jumps from Sunday back to Monday.

The 336-hour power lag is null for about 6% of the rows at days 0 to 2 because of gaps in the power history. The nulls are not join failures.

docs.title: Training time at 2,500 series
docs.text:
Training time grows linearly with the number of series for one XGBoost model per series, and memory becomes the limit for one XGBoost model per series type. The table gives the median training time of each arm at the study's 31 series on one GPU, and a straight multiple of 80.6 for 2,500 series. The estimate assumes each series keeps the same length of history, so it is a rough guide, not a measurement. The peak memory of training one arm was about 8 GB.

Layout Arm 31 series, GPU 2,500 series, GPU (estimate) One model per series squared error (production) 37 s 50 min One model per series absolute error 41 s 55 min One model per series early stopping 22 s 30 min One model per series 9 quantile levels 5 min 6.9 h One model per series type squared error, site identifier 18 s 24 min One model per series type absolute error and early stopping 24 s 33 min One model per series type 9 quantile levels 2 min 3.0 h

The per-type estimates are lower bounds, because 2,500 series of rows do not fit in GPU memory. On 8 CPU cores the production recipe trained in 141 s at 31 series, so about 3.2 hours at 2,500 series. The 31 series hold 9.76 million training rows, so 2,500 series of the same length would hold about 790 million rows, which does not fit in 30 GB of GPU memory as one table per type. The per-type estimates therefore need row subsampling, chunking, or external memory, and the per-type time is a lower bound.

One model per series type also changes the serving cost. The 2,500 saved XGBoost models become about 6, but each prediction run feeds every series through a larger XGBoost model.

Building the feature frame for 2,500 series needs chunking by series. The study's frame for 31 series took 5 minutes 19 seconds and 5.3 GB, which extrapolates to about 7 hours and 430 GB in one process.

docs.title: What did not help
docs.text:
These ideas were tried and are not recommended. Numbers are fold A, three seeds where stated, as CRPS differences against production with cleaning.

  • Removing the power lags and weekday columns from solar and wind (planned): +0.19 points [+0.14, +0.23], with the loss largest at days 0 to 2.
  • Adding solar, wind, and heating physics columns to the lag and weekday removal (planned): +0.15 points, which is 0.04 points better than removing the lags alone.
  • Lean columns for solar farms (post hoc): +0.26 points for solar [+0.10, +0.45].
  • Recency weights, half-life 120 days (planned): +0.05 points [−0.06, +0.15].
  • Holiday and ordinal-day columns for demand (planned): +0.06 points [−0.01, +0.14].
  • min_child_weight 20 (post hoc): +0.01 points.
  • One model per type without a site identifier (post hoc): −0.28 points [−0.46, −0.07], a small gain that raises raw-flow error by 1.04 points.
  • The first-N-months, isolated-zero, spike, commissioning-ramp, solar-dropout, and switching-day cleaning rules (round 0): each scored rule changed CRPS by 0.07 points or less.

docs.title: Ideas left for future research
docs.text:
Issue #1156 plans experiments on several of the ideas below: the two-stage forecaster, the climatology column, the feature faults, the transfer ratio and daily shape, issuing the control member's quantiles directly, training on CRPS, and features from the ensemble itself.

  • A two-stage forecaster: train a first stage on ERA5 for many years, then a second stage on the ECMWF forecasts' errors, as described on the switching-events roadmap page. The study's learning curve cannot say whether extra years help.
  • A climatology column, built so that a training row's own value never enters its own climatological mean.
  • Fix and test the feature faults listed under "Input features": precipitation type missing for half the training rows, windchill outside its valid range, wind direction as raw degrees, and radiation positive at night. See the follow-up feature audit for diagnosis and forecast effects.
  • The transfer ratio and daily shape of each plant, for pooled models: the transfer ratio (power over forecast irradiance) and daily shape from the lag-features study, in place of a raw site number. In that study, the clipping ceiling (the plant's running 99.5th percentile and 60-day maximum of power) raised the error for plants left out of training.
  • Issuing the control member's quantiles directly, with or without the members' spread, because the 9 control quantiles scored better than the 459-value crossed sample.
  • Training on CRPS itself, with a custom objective or a neural network.
  • A residual-based predictive distribution: draw each member's value as the point forecast plus a sample of past residuals for the series, season, and lead.
  • Training on every member, or on the ensemble mean, so the model sees the spread. The study did not fit an ensemble-mean arm.
  • Features from the ensemble itself: member spread and quantiles.
  • Monotone constraints on the weather inputs for solar and wind, which force the forecast not to fall as, for example, radiation rises.
  • A blend with climatology at long leads, which the lag-features study found lowered error by 1.2 points at day 14 for 6 solar plants (a post hoc result of that study).
  • Tuning depth, learning rate, and the number of trees, which the study left at production's values.
  • The auto-research agent, a large language model agent for automated experiments described in issue #1038 could take the cheap, repeatable arms here, since each changes a configuration and is scored the same way.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
• The scope is 31 NGED series in the trial area, scored for one year and a backwards fold of 15 months. The 6 solar farms are close together and share their weather, and so do the 3 wind farms. A wind result rests on 3 farms.
  • The two folds are not independent. Fold B uses the same series, and weather regimes recur.
  • Several ideas and every combination arm were chosen after the first results. The gain of the winning arm on fold A is biased upward. Fold B repeats the direction at a similar size.
  • The scores are not leaderboard scores. The study did not submit to the scorer. Its 53-run sample is a subset of the leaderboard's runs. Its quantile arms also number ensemble_member from 0 to 458, a range that the leaderboard's power_forecasts table cannot hold in its Int8 ensemble_member column.
  • Nothing was fitted at colsample_bytree 0.8 except the production arm.
  • The quantile arms use 9 untuned levels and weight every member and level equally, and the resulting 459-value distribution is too narrow (57% coverage of a nominal 80% band). The control member's 9 quantiles and the 459-value crossed sample were scored with the same fair CRPS, which gives the smaller set a larger spread term, so the comparison of those two sets may not be like for like.
  • Calibration by rescaling is evaluated for CRPS only, on the later 45 of 53 runs, and rescaling the weather ensemble's spread does not make the forecast a proper predictive distribution.
  • One demand series reads negative throughout and has a large error, so the mean over series is sensitive to it.
  • Neither fold is cut at ECMWF's 12 November 2024 ensemble upgrade.
  • The study checked the input columns visually but did not audit the feature pipeline, and did not check the stored production run's MLflow configuration, because none was registered.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text: The scripts are in studies/quick_wins/, and the tests are in tests/studies/quick_wins/. report_summary.py prints the tables this page quotes into summary.md, and report_compute.py prints the training-time table. The input data are private. The commands that reproduce the study are in the folder's README.

docs.title: At three Lincolnshire wind farms, adding archived UKV forecasts to ECMWF's ensemble mean lowered the wind power error at lead days 1 and 2, and the solar gain of about 0.1 points met the planned rule at day 3 only
docs.text:
At three wind farms in Lincolnshire, the power-forecast error at lead days 1 and 2 was lower for an XGBoost model (a gradient-boosted tree model) given the Met Office's UK variable-resolution (UKV) weather forecast from the archive of the Centre for Environmental Data Analysis (CEDA) as well as the mean of the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble forecast (ENS) than for an XGBoost model given the ENS mean alone. The result holds at both hyperparameter settings, against both shuffled controls, after the Bonferroni correction, and with any one calendar month dropped. The gain is 0.24 to 0.27 points of capacity at day 1 and 0.19 to 0.21 points at day 2, across the two settings. At wind day 3 the gain rests heavily on February 2026. At six solar farms the gain is about 0.1 points of capacity at days 1 to 3, and the planned rule is met at day 3 only. At day 4 the study is inconclusive for both technologies. UKV's run starts 3 hours after ENS's run. Two post hoc tests that move UKV's run earlier cannot say how much of any gain comes from UKV's weather and how much from the later start. This page calls the UKV data from the CEDA archive UKV-CEDA.

The error is a mean absolute error in percentage points of the generator's capacity, and every difference is the first XGBoost model's error minus the second XGBoost model's error. A negative difference means the XGBoost model given UKV-CEDA forecasts better. Each bracketed pair is a 95% interval from resampling whole calendar months and a fitting seed (the random-number seed of XGBoost's training). Every number comes from one of the study's five reports: report.md, and the post hoc report_2.md, report_3.md, report_4.md, and report_5.md. The page names the report wherever the number is not in report.md or report_2.md. The two hyperparameter settings, the XGBoost training options fixed before any fit, are the primary setting and a sensitivity setting (the primary setting first, then the sensitivity setting in brackets or in a second row). Data and methods defines the shuffled controls, the planned rule, and the Bonferroni correction.

How this page was made. The research question came from a human. Everything else — the code behind every result, the analysis, the figures, and the text — was written by Claude, Anthropic's AI model (for this page, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5, with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 also reusing shared code that earlier Claude sessions wrote). Several independent Claude reviewers have checked the method, the evidence, and the prose adversarially.

docs.title: Key findings
docs.text:
For a day-ahead wind forecast, adding UKV-CEDA's winds to the ENS mean lowers the error at lead days 1 and 2 by about 0.2 to 0.3 points of capacity at the three wind farms. A UKV-CEDA run that is 12 hours older than the run tested keeps about half the day-1 gain.

For solar, adding UKV-CEDA lowers the error by about 0.1 points at days 1 to 3 at the six solar farms, and the planned rule is met at day 3 only. A post hoc permutation test ranks the gain first of 18 at days 1 to 3, and licenses no claim of statistical significance at the 5% level.

At wind day 3 the gain rests on February 2026, and at day 4 the study cannot say whether UKV-CEDA helps.

  • At wind days 1 and 2, adding UKV-CEDA's winds lowers the error at both settings, against both controls, after the Bonferroni correction, and with any one month dropped (wind results). The differences are -0.239 [-0.314, -0.170] (-0.269 at sensitivity) at day 1 and -0.210 [-0.313, -0.105] (-0.190) at day 2, from errors of 8.236% and 9.470% for the ENS mean alone. The planned rule is met, and both results survive the Bonferroni correction at both settings.
  • At wind day 3, the gain rests on February 2026 (wind day 3). The difference is -0.277 [-0.533, -0.081], and the planned rule is met. Without February 2026 and at the sensitivity setting, the interval reaches +0.022, and the correction fails at that setting even with every month.
  • At solar days 1 to 3, adding UKV-CEDA lowers the error by about 0.1 points, as one pattern (solar results). The differences run from -0.082 to -0.163 across days and settings. The planned rule is met at day 3 only. A post hoc permutation test, added after the two planned controls had been seen, ranks the planned blend's gain first of 18 at days 1 to 3 (p = 0.056, the smallest p-value that 17 shuffled controls allow), and the planned readings at days 1 and 2 stay "unresolved".
  • At day 4, the study is inconclusive (day 4). The intervals do not exclude a gain of 0.172 points for solar or 0.295 points for wind, as large as the gains at days 1 to 3.
  • Older UKV-CEDA runs keep part of the gain, and the study cannot say whether lead or run timing causes the loss (older runs). The post hoc stale blend, which reads a UKV-CEDA run one day older, keeps 65% and 49% of the planned wind gain at days 2 and 3, and 30% at day 1. The post hoc older-run blend, which reads a UKV-CEDA run 12 hours older, keeps 40% to 70% of the planned gain at the primary setting (report_5.md).

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The question is whether the Met Office's UKV, read at lead days 1 to 4, lowers the power-forecast error of ECMWF's ensemble mean. UKV is the Met Office's 2 km weather model for the United Kingdom. The blends page tests UKV at day 1 only, from Open-Meteo's archive of live UKV. CEDA's archive holds whole UKV runs out to 120 hours, so this page tests days 2 to 4 as well. The page covers solar and wind power separately, at the 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms used by the matched-lead page. The weather products survey describes both products.

The ENS mean and UKV-CEDA read different runs, and UKV-CEDA's run starts later. For a valid hour on day D at lead day N, ENS reads the 00 UTC run of day D−N (UTC is Coordinated Universal Time), at a lead of 24N plus the hour of the day. UKV-CEDA reads the 03 UTC run of the same day, which a service running at 09:00 UTC could read. UKV-CEDA's lead is therefore 3 hours shorter at every hour.

Product Grid Coverage History Assumed availability ECMWF ENS mean (51 members) About 9 km native, served on 0.25° cells; the study averages the cells overlapping each generator's H3 hexagon (a cell of the H3 hexagonal grid) Global From 2024-04-01 Not measured; the 00 UTC run is assumed readable at 09:00 UTC UKV-CEDA 2 km; the study reads the cell nearest each generator United Kingdom CEDA's archive holds runs from 2016-03-16, and the study reads December 2024 to September 2026 Not measured for CEDA; the 03 UTC run is assumed readable at 09:00 UTC Product Run read for lead day N Lead of the hour of day h Resolution in time ECMWF ENS mean (51 members) 00 UTC run of day D−N 24N + h hours 3-hourly, upsampled UKV-CEDA 03 UTC run of day D−N 24N + h − 3 hours hourly to lead 48 hours, then 3-hourly to 120

Day 5 is not tested. At day 5 the lead is 24 × 5 + h − 3 hours, which exceeds UKV-CEDA's 120-hour reach for every hour after 03:00 UTC.

docs.title: Data and methods
docs.text:
A blend is an XGBoost model given ENS's mean weather and UKV-CEDA's weather, and the page compares the blend with two other XGBoost models. The padded ENS model is given ENS's mean weather and exact copies of the same columns, so that it has the blend's column count (9 for solar, 11 for wind). The shuffled-control model has the blend's columns, but its UKV-CEDA columns are shuffled among hours that share a generator, a year-month, and an hour of day. The shuffle keeps each generator's monthly distribution of UKV-CEDA at each hour of day, so a shuffled control carries no hour-by-hour information from UKV-CEDA. The study fits two shuffled controls, with shuffle seeds 0 and 1000.

Equal column counts matter because an XGBoost model with more columns can win without carrying more information. A check at wind day 1 and solar day 1 found the padded ENS model's per-row losses identical to the unpadded ENS model's (padding_check.json, which fit_ukv_ceda_blends.py --check writes once and report_2.md prints). The padded ENS model carries no extra information, so the blend minus the padded ENS model measures what UKV-CEDA adds to the ENS columns given, and not what it adds beyond every field ENS publishes.

The solar models are given ENS's mean global irradiance and temperature, and UKV-CEDA's global irradiance and temperature. The wind models are given ENS's 100 m wind speed, the sine and cosine of its 100 m direction, and its 10 m wind speed. UKV-CEDA's wind columns are its native 10 m wind speed, the sine and cosine of its 10 m direction, and its wind speed at the 925 hPa pressure level, roughly 750 m above sea level. None of UKV-CEDA's wind columns is a 100 m wind. Every XGBoost model also has the hour of day, the day of the year, and an era code (the three eras are set out in the next paragraph), and the solar models have the sun's elevation and azimuth. Each model named above is fitted separately at each generator, as one XGBoost model per generator.

The rows, folds, and intervals follow the matched-lead page. The study scores 21 months of valid hours, from December 2024 to September 2026, with January 2026 dropped because the Met Office upgraded UKV on 21 January 2026. The eras are: era 0 before October 2025 (10 months), era 1 from October to December 2025 (3 months, too few for an interval), and era 2 from February 2026 (8 months). Folds are blocks of whole months within each era, and every forecast is made out of fold, by an XGBoost model not trained on that forecast's fold. Each row, one generator at one valid hour, is scored only if ENS and UKV-CEDA both have values for the row, so every XGBoost model of a lead day is trained and scored on the same rows: 38,253 to 38,287 solar rows and 41,526 to 41,541 wind rows per lead day. Each row's error is divided by its own generator's capacity before any mean or difference. The intervals resample whole calendar months and one of three fitting seeds, paired across XGBoost models. The intervals cover month-to-month weather and fitting-seed variation, and not differences between generators.

Two contrasts are planned. A planned contrast was written into the study plan before any result existed. P1 is the blend minus the padded ENS model. P2 is the blend minus each shuffled control, with one contrast per shuffle seed. The reading rule is: the blend "lowers the error" at a technology and lead day only if the upper 95% bound of P1 and of both P2 contrasts is below zero at both settings. The study reports P1's Bonferroni-adjusted 99.375% interval, a wider interval that allows for reading the 8 P1 intervals per setting at once. The study does not adjust P2. Where P1 is below zero at both settings and a P2 bound is not, the reading is "unresolved: lower than padded ENS, control test not passed".

Every other number is exploratory, and the page does not correct the exploratory rows for multiple comparisons. The page labels the analyses made after the first scientific-validity review as post hoc. Each exploratory row has a nominal 5% chance of reaching statistical significance at the 5% level with no real effect behind it. The number of spurious rows is unknown, and the rows' shared months make spurious results cluster. Where the reports flag a contrast as near the 5% line, the page says so.

Every fit is on one graphics processing unit (GPU). The page reports a refit of one XGBoost model on a central processing unit (CPU) as a noise floor (Limitations).

docs.title: The XGBoost models make sane forecasts
docs.text:
Out of fold, the wind and solar models follow the measured output across the weeks chosen by rule. Figures 3 and 4 plot the day-1 blend's out-of-fold forecast against measured output, with each generator's output as a percentage of its own capacity, over one week per era chosen from measured output alone. A week is left out for an era in which no week has every generator covered on all 7 days. Solar has no fully covered week in era 1 (October to December 2025), so Figures 3a and 3b show the weeks of February 2025 and March 2026. Figures 4a, 4b, and 4c show the wind weeks of September 2025, December 2025, and February 2026.

The mean absolute error of every XGBoost model rises with the lead day, and the padded ENS model's error is the reference level. For solar, the padded ENS model's error is 8.820% of capacity at day 1 and 11.692% at day 4. For wind, the padded ENS model's error is 8.236% at day 1 and 12.328% at day 4. The tables give every XGBoost model's own error, at both settings, from report_2.md. The errors carry no intervals, because every XGBoost model's error rises and falls together from month to month, and pairing cancels that shared swing. Figures 5 and 6 draw the primary-setting errors, and Figures 7 and 8 draw the errors at each generator.

docs.title: Wind days 1 and 2 meet the planned rule and survive four robustness checks
docs.text:
At wind days 1 and 2, the planned rule is met, and the gain survives both settings, both controls, the Bonferroni correction, and the loss of any one month. At day 1, P1 is -0.239 [-0.314, -0.170] at the primary setting and -0.269 [-0.357, -0.192] at the sensitivity setting. P2 against the seed-0 control is -0.226 [-0.307, -0.145] (-0.270) and against the seed-1000 control -0.243 [-0.321, -0.162] (-0.286). At day 2, P1 is -0.210 [-0.313, -0.105] (-0.190 [-0.272, -0.103]), P2 is -0.181 [-0.296, -0.069] (-0.236) against seed 0 and -0.190 [-0.285, -0.097] (-0.218) against seed 1000.

The Bonferroni intervals stay below zero at both settings. At day 1 the Bonferroni intervals are [-0.342, -0.144] and [-0.379, -0.173], and at day 2 [-0.338, -0.071] and [-0.298, -0.061].

Dropping any one month leaves the wind upper bounds at days 1 and 2 below zero. In the exploratory, post hoc leave-one-month-out check (nothing refitted), the highest upper bound over the 21 single-month drops is -0.151 at day 1 (dropping January 2025) and -0.083 at day 2. The sensitivity setting gives -0.178 and -0.088.

The gain is similar in era 0 and era 2, and clear at two of the three generators. In the exploratory era rows, day 1 gives -0.260 [-0.367, -0.131] in era 0 and -0.228 [-0.348, -0.149] in era 2, and day 2 gives -0.215 [-0.386, -0.025] and -0.185 [-0.293, -0.057]. Era 1 has 3 months and no interval, with -0.198 at day 1 and -0.249 at day 2. By generator, the day-1 differences are -0.273 [-0.394, -0.178] at W1, -0.294 [-0.408, -0.191] at W2, and -0.146 [-0.329, +0.035] at W3. The day-2 differences are -0.147 [-0.257, -0.037], -0.231 [-0.361, -0.105], and -0.251 [-0.488, -0.049]. Figure 9 draws the generators.

The shuffled controls differ from each other by no more than 0.058 points at any wind lead day. The largest gap is at day 4 and the sensitivity setting (-0.058 [-0.201, +0.056]). No wind gap is statistically significant at the 5% level. At wind days 1 and 2 the gap between the controls is therefore far smaller than P1.

docs.title: Wind day 3 rests on February 2026
docs.text:
At wind day 3 the planned rule is met, and the gain depends on one month. P1 is -0.277 [-0.533, -0.081] at the primary setting and -0.180 [-0.384, -0.010] at the sensitivity setting, and both P2 contrasts are below zero at both settings. The Bonferroni interval at the primary setting is [-0.625, -0.025], but at the sensitivity setting it is [-0.463, +0.035], so the gain does not survive the correction at both settings. Dropping February 2026 gives -0.186 [-0.348, -0.046] at the primary setting and -0.111 [-0.242, +0.022] at the sensitivity setting, so the sensitivity interval reaches zero. February 2026 is the first month of era 2. In the exploratory era rows, era 2 gives -0.437 [-0.989, -0.085] and era 0 gives -0.227 [-0.518, -0.002]. P1 and both P2 contrasts at wind day 3 are near the 5% line at both settings (report_5.md).

By generator, wind day 3 is clear at W2 only. The differences are -0.101 [-0.315, +0.076] at W1, -0.452 [-0.765, -0.213] at W2, and -0.271 [-0.613, +0.052] at W3. The page therefore reports wind day 3 as met by the planned rule and as dependent on one month, and does not place wind day 3 beside days 1 and 2.

docs.title: Solar: about 0.1 points of capacity at days 1 to 3
docs.text:
For solar, adding UKV-CEDA lowers the error by about 0.1 points of capacity at days 1 to 3, and the study cannot say that day 3 differs from days 1 and 2. P1 is -0.105 [-0.177, -0.017] (-0.091 [-0.155, -0.017]) at day 1, -0.086 [-0.155, -0.018] (-0.082 [-0.158, -0.006]) at day 2, and -0.163 [-0.250, -0.079] (-0.116 [-0.188, -0.044]) at day 3, so P1 is statistically significant at the 5% level at both settings on each day. The planned rule is met at day 3 only. Two of day 3's P2 upper bounds, -0.006 and -0.001, lie within 0.01 points of zero.

At solar days 1 and 2 the reading is "unresolved: lower than padded ENS, control test not passed". The blend's error is lower than the padded ENS model's by 0.08 to 0.11 points at both settings. At day 1 the rule fails because the seed-1000 control's interval reaches zero at the primary setting: P2 is -0.064 [-0.142, +0.029]. At day 2 the rule fails because both controls' intervals reach zero at the primary setting, with upper bounds of +0.002 (seed 0, P2 -0.134 [-0.269, +0.002]) and +0.013 (seed 1000, P2 -0.092 [-0.194, +0.013]). After the Bonferroni correction the P1 interval reaches zero at the primary setting at both days ([-0.200, +0.020] at day 1 and [-0.187, +0.001] at day 2), and at the sensitivity setting too ([-0.175, +0.006] and [-0.187, +0.020]). Solar day 3 survives the correction at both settings ([-0.284, -0.052] and [-0.215, -0.016]).

Several solar contrasts are near the 5% line. The reports flag these contrasts (report_5.md): at day 1, P1 at both settings, the seed-0 P2 at the primary setting, and the seed-1000 P2 at both settings; at day 2, P1 and both P2 contrasts at both settings; at day 3, the seed-0 P2 at both settings; and at day 4, the seed-1000 P2 at the sensitivity setting.

Two shuffled controls that carry no hour-by-hour information differ from each other by about as much as the solar gain, and two draws are too few to say how far a shuffled control's error moves by chance. At day 1 the seed-0 control minus the seed-1000 control is +0.079 [+0.025, +0.133] at the primary setting and +0.062 [+0.018, +0.103] at the sensitivity setting, and at day 4 the sensitivity gap is -0.067 [-0.131, -0.006]. The intervals resample months and fitting seeds, not shuffle seeds, so the intervals understate how far a solar XGBoost model's error moves for reasons unrelated to its inputs. The wind gaps are at most 0.058 points. The page therefore describes solar as one pattern, not as four separate verdicts. The next subsection adds 15 further shuffled controls.

Solar is also fragile to the loss of one month. In the post hoc leave-one-month-out check, the highest upper bound over the drops is -0.001 at day 1 (dropping May 2026, primary setting), -0.004 at day 2 (June 2026), and +0.008 at day 2 at the sensitivity setting. At day 3 the highest upper bound is -0.063 at the primary setting (May 2026) and -0.033 at the sensitivity setting.

By generator, every solar generator's point estimate is below zero at days 1 to 3. At day 1 the differences run from -0.045 [-0.197, +0.084] at A to -0.196 [-0.356, -0.030] at E. Figure 10 draws every solar generator's difference. By era, solar day 3 gives -0.154 [-0.254, -0.059] in era 0 and -0.159 [-0.312, +0.009] in era 2, and days 1 and 2 give similar point estimates with intervals that include zero.

docs.title: At solar days 1 to 3, the gain beats all 17 shuffled controls in a post hoc permutation test
docs.text:
At solar days 1 to 3, the planned blend's gain over padded ENS is larger than the gain of every one of 17 shuffled controls. The test was added after the two planned controls had been seen, so the test is exploratory. The test fits 15 further shuffled controls per solar lead day at the primary setting, with shuffle seeds 2010 to 2150 in steps of 10, and places the planned blend's P1 among the 17 values of (shuffled control minus padded ENS) that the planned two controls and the 15 further controls give. The numbers are in report_3.md and again in report_5.md. At days 1 to 3, P1 (-0.105, -0.086, and -0.163) is lower than every control: the lowest control is -0.041, -0.025, and -0.067. P1 ranks 1 of 18, and the one-sided permutation p-value is 0.056, the smallest that 17 controls allow. At day 4, P1 (-0.054) ranks 6 of 18 (p = 0.333).

One shuffled control can move far by chance. At day 4 the lowest of the 17 controls is -0.141, larger in size than the planned blend's P1 at days 1 and 2.

The test licenses a ranking and no more. The permutation test licenses no claim of statistical significance at the 5% level, because the smallest p-value it can give is 0.056. The test changes none of the planned readings, which stay "unresolved" at days 1 and 2. The test gives no combined p-value across days 1 to 3, because the days share months and shuffle seeds. The test makes no claim about other months, because the test does not resample months. The test therefore answers a different question from the month-resampled intervals.

docs.title: Day 4 is inconclusive
docs.text: At day 4 the intervals do not exclude gains as large as the gains at days 1 to 3, so the study cannot say whether the gain fades. For solar, P1 is -0.054 [-0.172, +0.053] (-0.036 [-0.108, +0.034]), and a gain of 0.172 points is not excluded at the primary setting and 0.108 at the sensitivity setting. For wind, P1 is -0.105 [-0.268, +0.058] (-0.133 [-0.295, +0.031]), and a gain of 0.268 points is not excluded at the primary setting and 0.295 at the sensitivity setting. A gain larger than those bounds is excluded. The wind day-4 P2 contrasts are below zero at the sensitivity setting for both seeds (-0.160 [-0.315, -0.025] and -0.218 [-0.396, -0.056]). Wind day 4 is near the 5% line for P1 and both P2 contrasts at both settings (report_5.md).

docs.title: How the gain changes when UKV-CEDA's run is older
docs.text:
Two post hoc blends move UKV-CEDA's run earlier, and each changes the run's lead and its start time together. The stale blend (report_2.md) is ENS day N plus UKV-CEDA day N + 1, for N of 1 to 3, which is the 03 UTC run one day earlier. That run is 21 hours older than ENS's run, where the planned blend's run is 3 hours newer, so the start moves by 24 hours and the lead grows by 24 hours. The older-run blend (report_4.md) reads UKV-CEDA's 15 UTC run of the day before ENS's run. That run starts 9 hours before ENS's 00 UTC run and leads 12 hours longer than the planned run. Both blends were run after a scientific-validity review had seen the planned results, so both are post hoc and exploratory. Neither can separate the effect of a longer lead from the effect of an earlier start. The study did not fit a UKV-CEDA run that starts at the same moment as ENS's 00 UTC run. That run would sit between the planned blend's run (3 hours after) and the older-run blend's run (9 hours before).

Both blends also change the time resolution of UKV-CEDA's columns, a third confound. The store holds UKV-CEDA hourly only to lead 48 hours, and every hour after lead 48 hours is rebuilt from 3-hourly steps. The planned run at day 1 is read at a lead of 21 to 44 hours, so every hour is hourly. The older run at day 1 is read at a lead of 33 to 56 hours, and 25.5% of the solar rows and 33.4% of the wind rows lie beyond lead 48 hours (report_5.md). The stale blend and the older-run blend therefore have more rebuilt hours than the planned blend at days 1 and 2.

The stale blend loses most of the wind day-1 gain, and keeps about half of the wind gain at days 2 and 3. The stale blend is compared with a padded ENS model trained on the same rows, because the stale blend loses 0.3% to 0.4% of rows that have no UKV-CEDA day N + 1. The padded ENS model trained on all rows differs from the padded ENS model trained on the stale rows by at most 0.022 points (wind day 1, primary setting), so the difference in training rows does not drive the contrasts. The table gives the stale blend minus its padded ENS model (P1, stale) and the stale blend minus the planned blend, at the primary setting and the sensitivity setting (report_2.md).

Technology and lead day P1, stale (primary) P1, stale (sensitivity) Stale minus planned blend (primary) Stale minus planned blend (sensitivity) solar 1 -0.018 [-0.071, +0.036] -0.013 [-0.060, +0.026] +0.085 [-0.023, +0.184] +0.077 [-0.010, +0.157] solar 2 -0.035 [-0.135, +0.070] -0.027 [-0.098, +0.052] +0.038 [-0.064, +0.135] +0.047 [-0.036, +0.130] solar 3 +0.042 [-0.057, +0.135] +0.030 [-0.035, +0.092] +0.215 [+0.095, +0.329] +0.157 [+0.064, +0.252] wind 1 -0.072 [-0.167, +0.016] -0.065 [-0.142, +0.009] +0.188 [+0.120, +0.249] +0.224 [+0.166, +0.275] wind 2 -0.137 [-0.294, -0.015] -0.073 [-0.168, +0.010] +0.064 [-0.054, +0.175] +0.114 [+0.012, +0.208] wind 3 -0.135 [-0.267, -0.022] -0.096 [-0.241, +0.012] +0.137 [-0.015, +0.315] +0.085 [-0.033, +0.215]

At wind day 1 and solar day 3 the stale blend is clearly worse than the planned blend, and the other rows are mostly not separable. At wind day 1 the stale blend loses 0.188 [0.120, 0.249] of the planned blend's 0.239 points. Most of the day-1 gain therefore needs UKV-CEDA's lead to be 21 to 44 hours rather than 45 to 68 hours. The stale blend cannot say how much of the gain the 3-hour timing advantage carries. The stale blend's gain at wind day 1 is not statistically significant. A stale-blend gain of 0.167 points at the primary setting is not excluded. At wind days 2 and 3 the stale blend keeps 65% and 49% of the planned gain at the primary setting (38% and 53% at the sensitivity setting, report_5.md), and its gain is below zero at the primary setting (-0.137 and -0.135). The stale-minus-planned contrast at wind days 2 and 3 is not statistically significant at the primary setting. At the sensitivity setting the contrast is significant at wind day 2 (+0.114 [+0.012, +0.208]). The post hoc reading at wind days 2 and 3 stays "no detectable difference". For solar, a stale-blend gain of 0.071, 0.135, and 0.057 points at days 1, 2, and 3 is not excluded at the primary setting.

At wind day 1, a stale UKV-CEDA run still carries some information that the shuffled copy lacks. The stale blend is lower than its shuffled controls at wind day 1 at both settings and both seeds.

The older-run blend keeps 40% to 70% of the planned gain at the primary setting, and its loss at wind day 1 is statistically significant at both settings. The older-run blend's P1 is -0.138 [-0.208, -0.061] at wind day 1 against the planned blend's -0.239 on the same rows, and -0.147 [-0.234, -0.077] against -0.210 at wind day 2 (report_4.md). The older-run blend minus the planned blend at wind day 1 is +0.102 [+0.034, +0.168] at the primary setting and +0.156 [+0.090, +0.219] at the sensitivity setting. At solar, the older-run P1 interval includes zero at the primary setting at all three days. The older-run minus planned contrast at solar is statistically significant only at day 2 at the sensitivity setting (+0.062 [+0.008, +0.114]). The older-run readings in report_4.md rest on one control seed and no Bonferroni correction, so an older-run reading is weaker than a planned reading.

Technology and lead day Planned P1 (primary) Older-run P1 (primary) Older-run minus planned blend (primary) Older-run minus planned blend (sensitivity) solar 1 -0.105 [-0.177, -0.017] -0.042 [-0.102, +0.024] +0.063 [-0.015, +0.128] +0.051 [-0.017, +0.109] solar 2 -0.086 [-0.155, -0.018] -0.036 [-0.134, +0.068] +0.050 [-0.018, +0.111] +0.062 [+0.008, +0.114] solar 3 -0.163 [-0.250, -0.079] -0.076 [-0.161, +0.009] +0.087 [-0.003, +0.183] +0.030 [-0.045, +0.110] wind 1 -0.239 [-0.314, -0.170] -0.138 [-0.208, -0.061] +0.102 [+0.034, +0.168] +0.156 [+0.090, +0.219] wind 2 -0.210 [-0.313, -0.105] -0.147 [-0.234, -0.077] +0.063 [-0.040, +0.162] +0.089 [-0.016, +0.198] wind 3 -0.277 [-0.533, -0.081] -0.141 [-0.301, +0.017] +0.135 [-0.057, +0.358] +0.085 [-0.058, +0.248]

At day 1, the wind loss holds on hourly rows, and the solar loss sits in the late hours of the day. Splitting the day-1 rows at lead 48 hours keeps both runs hourly on the rows at or before the limit (report_5.md). At wind day 1 the older-run minus planned contrast on those rows (66.6% of the rows) is +0.115 [+0.048, +0.186] at the primary setting and +0.166 [+0.109, +0.226] at the sensitivity setting, so the time resolution does not explain the wind loss. At solar day 1 the contrast is +0.034 [-0.047, +0.108] on the rows at or before the limit (74.5% of the rows), and +0.148 [+0.041, +0.241] beyond the limit. The rows beyond the limit are the late hours of the day, so the split cannot separate time resolution from hour of day. The solar loss is not attributable to either cause.

The two blends support one reading: a UKV-CEDA run that starts earlier and leads longer gives less of the gain, and the study cannot say how much of the loss each change causes. The stale blend keeps 65% and 49% of the wind gain at days 2 and 3 at the primary setting (38% and 53% at the sensitivity setting, where the stale-minus-planned contrast at day 2 is statistically significant: +0.114 [+0.012, +0.208]). At the primary setting the stale-minus-planned intervals are +0.064 [-0.054, +0.175] at day 2 and +0.137 [-0.015, +0.315] at day 3. Neither interval excludes losing most of the gain (0.210 and 0.276 points), and the day-3 interval does not exclude losing all of it. The study therefore cannot say how much of the wind gain at days 2 and 3 the 3-hour timing advantage carries. The older-run blend keeps about half of the planned gain, which measures a 12-hour longer lead and a 12-hour earlier start together. The older-run blend's wind day-1 loss holds on hourly rows. The study did not fit the run that would separate the two causes.

docs.title: What the gain could come from
docs.text:
Four explanations other than UKV's skill remain, and the study does not test any of them.

  • Time resolution at day 1. UKV-CEDA is hourly to lead 48 hours, while ENS is 3-hourly and upsampled, so some of the day-1 gain may come from the finer time steps. At days 3 and 4 both products are 3-hourly, so the time resolution cannot explain the day-3 gains. The older-run split above shows that the wind day-1 loss from an older run holds on hourly rows.
  • Wind heights. The wind blend adds UKV-CEDA's 10 m wind and its 925 hPa wind, a level that no ENS column in this study carries. Part of the gain may come from the 925 hPa level, rather than from a better forecast of the wind near hub height. The page's finding is about an XGBoost model given UKV-CEDA's 10 m and 925 hPa winds.
  • Spatial support. The study reads UKV-CEDA at each generator's nearest 2 km cell, and ENS as the mean over the hexagon that contains the generator. Part of the gain may come from how well a nearest cell represents a site. A hexagon-mean read of UKV-CEDA was not tried.
  • Delivery time. The 09:00 UTC availability of the 03 UTC run is an assumption that was not measured for CEDA.

docs.title: Discussion: what to use
docs.text:
For wind at days 1 and 2, the result supports testing live UKV as an addition to the ENS mean. This page cannot say how a blend with live UKV would do, and the licence of the UKV-CEDA data does not settle whether the data may be used in production. If a service's UKV run is 12 hours older than the run tested here, the post hoc older-run blend suggests the service would keep about half of the day-1 wind gain (the older-run blend keeps 57% at the primary setting and 42% at the sensitivity setting). The post hoc stale blend suggests a run 24 hours older would keep less (30% and 24%, report_5.md). What would change this recommendation: a blend that reads a hexagon mean of UKV-CEDA, the same blend fitted on live UKV, and more months of data.

For solar and for wind at day 3, the page does not recommend adding UKV-CEDA. The solar gain of about 0.1 points meets the planned rule at day 3 only, and is unresolved under the planned rule at days 1 and 2. Two shuffled controls differ from each other by about as much as the solar gain. A post hoc permutation test ranks the solar gain first of 18 at days 1 to 3, which licenses no claim of statistical significance at the 5% level. The wind day-3 gain rests on one month. At day 4 the study is inconclusive, and the page does not say that UKV-CEDA does not help there.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
The results rest on one region, 21 months, and an archive that differs from the live service. The 6 solar farms and 3 wind farms are in Lincolnshire, the sample is weather episodes and not generator-hours, and the intervals resample months. Every figure uses the effective_capacity table at version 1, committed on 2026-09-22, as the matched-lead page records. A rebuilt table would move every number.

  • UKV-CEDA differs statistically from the live UKV. An XGBoost model trained on UKV-CEDA must not be run on live UKV, and the page cannot say how a blend with live UKV would do.
  • The upgrade era is short. The Met Office upgraded UKV on 21 January 2026. Era 1 has 3 months and no interval of its own, and the study drops January 2026.
  • The fitting noise floor is small. A CPU refit of the day-1 blend at wind generator W1 differs from the GPU fit by 0.7513 points of capacity per row on average (7.8589 at most), and the two fits' mean errors are 6.6993 (CPU) and 6.6893 (GPU), which differ by 0.0100 points. Two GPU fitting seeds of the same blend differ by 0.7013 points per row on average (7.6923 at most), and the three seeds' mean errors span 0.0140 points (report_5.md). The CPU fit's mean error therefore differs from the GPU fit's by less than the span of the three GPU fitting seeds, and per row the CPU-GPU gap is about the size of the gap between two GPU seeds.
  • The scored months are shared across generators. Neighbouring generators share their weather, so the effective sample is the 21 months and the intervals do not cover differences between generators.
  • The radiation timestamp may handicap the blend. UKV-CEDA's hourly radiation is a mean of two snapshots and is centred slightly later than the power hour. The study does not measure how the later centring changes the error.
  • The licence of the UKV-CEDA data is not settled on this page. The fetch script records the licence as Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-ShareAlike 4.0 (non-commercial use only). The weather products survey lists it only as the "Met Office licence via CEDA", and the CEDA catalogue record that the survey cites does not state the terms. The page can say that the study is research use and cannot say that production use is permitted.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The study does not cover day 5, live UKV, a UKV run that starts at the same moment as ENS's run, a hexagon-mean read of UKV-CEDA, probabilistic scores, other regions, or any product other than UKV-CEDA. The study tests the blend of the ENS mean and UKV-CEDA only, and not UKV-CEDA alone. The study tests two UKV-CEDA runs: the 03 UTC run of ENS's own day, and, post hoc and at days 1 to 3 only, the 15 UTC run of the day before.

docs.title: Data and code availability
docs.text:
The inputs and fitted losses are in the private data store, and every output carries only the anonymised site label. The generators are labelled A to F for solar and W1 to W3 for wind. The code is in studies/nwp_forecast_comparison/ and src/studies/. The reports were written by the code at commit 4d12892c.

XGBoost 3.4.1 fitted every XGBoost model on one RTX A6000 GPU, at two hyperparameter settings. The primary setting is a learning rate of 0.05, a maximum tree depth of 6, a minimum child weight of 20, 500 boosting rounds, an L2 penalty of 1.0, and a row subsample of 0.8. The sensitivity setting is a learning rate of 0.03, a maximum depth of 4, a minimum child weight of 50, 1,200 rounds, an L2 penalty of 5.0, and a subsample of 0.8.

docs.title: Reproducing the figures
docs.text:
Run each step only after the step before it exits 0.

uv run python studies/nwp_forecast_comparison/build_ukv_ceda_inputs.py

docs.title: How should we interpolate wind components?
docs.text:
Keep linear interpolation of u/v for now. In this focused test on the three wind farms in National Grid Electricity Distribution's (NGED) dataset, PCHIP and modified Akima produced slightly higher power-forecast error in both lead bands and both XGBoost settings. The small, mostly uncertain differences support retaining linear interpolation for this comparison; the results do not establish that linear interpolation always wins.

Positive differences mean higher mean absolute error (MAE) than linear interpolation. Points pool matched farm/forecast rows. Each setting is fitted with three random seeds. Bars are nominal 95% intervals from resampling whole validation months and selecting one paired random-seed fit. Each farm's error is divided by its maximum cleaned training power. The primary setting uses 500 depth-6 trees; the sensitivity setting uses 1,200 depth-4 trees.

How this page was made. The human maintainer defined the question and four inputs. OpenAI Codex wrote the experiment, figures, and explanation. Independent Codex reviewers checked the code and numerical evidence. The private metered generators are anonymised.

docs.title: Smoother curves require extra assumptions
docs.text:
Interpolate eastward u and northward v, then derive speed and meteorological bearing. All three methods use exactly the same native forecast samples. Linear interpolation joins each component's samples with straight lines. PCHIP and Makima use neighbouring slopes to form smooth curves. The synthetic illustration has no assumed truth between samples.

PCHIP is a shape-preserving piecewise cubic Hermite interpolating polynomial. Makima is modified Akima interpolation. Smoother component curves alone do not establish more accurate wind or power predictions.

docs.title: Reconstructing wind and predicting power are different checks
docs.text:
The smooth methods reconstructed hidden native samples slightly better. Removing the 3-hour samples between 6-hour anchors gave average reconstruction errors of 1.174 m/s for linear, 1.158 m/s for PCHIP, and 1.153 m/s for Makima. Each sample's error is the root mean square of the 10 m and 100 m vector-error magnitudes, averaged over samples. The withheld samples are forecast values, not measured wind or half-hourly truth; the exploratory reconstruction check does not establish power skill.

The small reconstruction gain did not translate into lower pooled power error here. With the primary XGBoost setting, linear interpolation's MAE was 8.858 and 17.598 percentage points of training maximum at day 1 and day 7. PCHIP increased linear interpolation's errors by 0.057 and 0.054 points; Makima increased linear interpolation's errors by 0.031 and 0.072 points. The second setting also favoured linear in its pooled point estimates. Individual farms can differ; the result is specific to this comparison.

docs.title: The direct station check also favours retaining linear interpolation
docs.text:
Measured station winds from the Met Office MIDAS Open archive gave no improvement from smoothing. The post-hoc check used 15 stations' measured nominal 10 m wind speed from April 2024 through December 2025. Linear interpolation's pooled MAE was 1.198 m/s at day 1 and 2.001 m/s at day 7. Smooth methods increased MAE by about 0.002 m/s at day 1, with uncertain differences.

At day 7, PCHIP increased MAE by 0.0059 m/s (95% interval 0.0013–0.0105); Makima increased it by 0.0073 m/s (0.0019–0.0126). The tiny day-seven increases remain statistically significant at the 5% level under the four-comparison correction. The station comparison supports retaining linear interpolation here.

The Met Office guide specifies surface synoptic (SYNOP) wind reports as means from 20 to 10 minutes before each report's timestamp. Forecasts came from each station's containing H3 grid cell. Forecast speed was averaged over the same window with converged numerical integration, then compared on identical station/forecast rows. Whole-month intervals preserve weather shared across stations; stations contribute according to available observations. This exploratory extension fits no models. Nominal measurement height, exposure, and point-to-cell differences remain limitations. The station result does not establish performance for other regions or power-forecast configurations.

docs.title: What was held fixed
docs.text:
The inputs were wind speed and direction at 10 m and 100 m only, derived after interpolation. Bearings remained in degrees. Each method had a separate XGBoost fit on the graphics processing unit (GPU) for each farm and lead band, with seeds 0, 1, and 2 and both fixed settings. There were no power lags, calendar inputs, solar models, or demand models.

Native samples came from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) ensemble (ENS) control member 0, component-table snapshot 924. Each complete 00:00 UTC run was interpolated over its full native horizon, without extrapolation. Day 1 covered leads 24–47.5 h at half-hour intervals; day 7 covered 168–191.5 h. There were 51,851 matched validation rows per band, covering July 2025–June 2026. Training began in April 2024 and stopped before 24 June 2025, ahead of the earliest validation initialisation. Cleaned power snapshot 76 provided the targets; zeros were retained. No incomplete site-runs were excluded.

The four planned comparisons were PCHIP and Makima against linear at each lead band, chosen before results existed. Other summaries are exploratory. Intervals cover these farms' weather months and fitting seeds, not variation across a population of farms. The numerical evidence includes all absolute errors, per-farm errors, 95% intervals, and 98.75% intervals correcting the four comparisons within each setting. No smooth-method benefit was supported consistently across settings. This is not a leaderboard submission or a full ensemble test.

docs.title: Reproduce
docs.text:
The private numerical weather prediction (NWP) and cleaned-power tables are required. The scripts preserve anonymised inputs, forecasts, losses, gains, and provenance under data/studies/per_study/wind_interpolation/. Use a fresh output directory for a new run; existing fits can be resumed only with matching inputs and fitting code/settings. Versions: XGBoost 3.4.1 and SciPy 1.18.1; fits used the RTX A6000.

uv run python studies/wind_interpolation/wind_interpolation_experiment.py
uv run python studies/wind_interpolation/midas_interpolation_check.py
uv run python studies/wind_interpolation/plot_wind_interpolation_results.py

docs.title: Wind component storage measurement
docs.text:
Storing u/v uses 8.90 % more Parquet bytes than speed/bearing in this 24-run sample. Here, u is eastward velocity and v is northward velocity; polar storage holds speed and meteorological bearing. Adding scalar-mean speeds increases the u/v total by another 17.90 %. The maintainer chose u/v alone. The measurement compares storage and spatial cancellation; no forecasting model was trained or scored.

The contrasts (planned) compare u/v against polar storage, then scalar means against u/v. Planned means specified before measurement, rather than proposed future work. The sample contains the 15th and last day of every month in 2025, all at 00Z, with no unavailable dates or substitutions. Each forecast contains 85 native steps, 51 members, and 1,671 H3 cells: 7,243,785 rows per forecast and 173,850,840 rows per representation. Seasons group forecasts by initialization month; forecasts may cross season boundaries. The comparison uses the same downloaded bytes and H3 weights for all representations and the actual production write_nwp, including 13-bit significand rounding, sort order, and writer properties. Non-wind compressed-column bytes match exactly in every pair.

Scalar-gap statistics precede writer rounding and measure spatial cancellation. Native rows receive equal weight, rather than weighting 6-hour intervals twice as much as 3-hour intervals. These descriptive sample statistics have no sampling confidence interval and should not be read as turbine-power losses or forecast-skill changes. The scalar means use grid-point magnitudes before H3 aggregation; vector magnitudes use aggregated u/v.

Parquet totals include file metadata; Delta-log bytes are separate. MB means 10⁶ bytes.
